LAW302 Conflict of Laws

Each lesson takes one of your exam pre-writes (J1–J7 for Question 1, C1–C3 for Question 2), prints it word for word, then teaches it from zero: plain-English boxes, 83 flowcharts, 30 "facts in one picture" illustrations, worked examples, exam-ready sentences and 187 multiple-choice questions with every option explained.

▶START HERE
How conflict of laws works, and how to use the router
Every conflict question asks one of three things: can a Singapore court hear this case, which country's law decides it, and will Singapore give effect to a foreign judgment. Question 1 tests the first and third, contract by contract; Question 2 tests the second, issue by issue.
19 min · 4 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 11 questions

Question 1 · Jurisdiction, injunctions and foreign judgments

J1Q1 · J1
Clause triage: what the jurisdiction clause promises, and the CCAA
Read the jurisdiction clause first and ask what it promises. That tells you who, if anyone, is in breach, and breach decides the test later (strong cause or Spiliada). If the Hague Convention applies through the CCAA, it overrides everything: the chosen court must hear the case and other courts must step aside.
42 min · 7 flowcharts · 3 illustrations · 26 questions
J2Q1 · J2
Existence when the defendant is in Singapore: service in and submission
The court has jurisdiction as of right over a defendant served in Singapore or who submits. For every route, name two things together: the founding provision (which part of s 16 SCJA) and the mode of service (which rule). Only a never-registered foreign company needs the Adams v Cape presence test.
26 min · 7 flowcharts · 3 illustrations · 18 questions
J3Q1 · J3
Existence when the defendant is abroad: service out
A defendant outside Singapore can be brought in only through O 8: without approval if the contract allows service out, otherwise with approval on the "appropriate court" ground, where the claimant must show (a) a good arguable case of nexus through a para 63(3) factor, (b) Singapore is forum conveniens, and (c) a serious question to be tried.
30 min · 9 flowcharts · 3 illustrations · 18 questions
J4Q1 · J4
Exercise: Spiliada, forum conveniens and strong cause
Once the court has jurisdiction, ask whether it should use it. If someone broke a jurisdiction clause, the party in breach must show strong cause. If no one did, run Spiliada: is another forum clearly more appropriate (stage 1), and would the claimant be denied substantial justice there (stage 2)? Who bears the burden depends on service in or out, and stay or set-aside.
27 min · 8 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 18 questions
J5Q1 · J5
The SICC: written agreements, transfer and joinder
The SICC is a division of the High Court for international commercial cases. A case gets there in three ways: a written jurisdiction agreement (primary jurisdiction), transfer from the General Division ("more appropriate"), or joinder. Once there under a written agreement, Spiliada and strong cause disappear: the SICC declines only if hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of process.
21 min · 7 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 11 questions
J6Q1 · J6
Anti-suit injunctions: stopping a party suing abroad
An ASI is an order against a person, not a foreign court, telling it to stop suing abroad. Name your basis first, because the elements differ. Contractual: amenability, breach of the clause, no strong reasons. Vexation: amenability, sufficient interest (usually natural forum), vexation, no undue injustice. Abuse of process: amenability and Singapore's self-evident interest in protecting its own process.
25 min · 7 flowcharts · 3 illustrations · 16 questions
J7Q1 · J7
Foreign judgments: enforcement, recognition and AEIs
First ask whether the party wants to enforce the foreign judgment (a sword, to recover money) or have it recognised (a shield, or an estoppel). Then pick the regime: CCAA if the foreign court was the chosen court in a Hague case; REFJA is not examinable; otherwise the common law, where the judgment must be on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction (presence or submission), final and conclusive, and for a definite sum, with no defence such as fraud, natural justice or public policy.
27 min · 11 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 16 questions

Question 2 · Choice of law

C1Q2 · C1
Choice of law methodology: characterise, connect, apply
Choice of law is a three-step machine: characterise the issue (contract? tort? property? procedure?), pick the connecting factor for that category, and apply the law it points to. Procedure always stays with Singapore law. Foreign law must be pleaded and proved like a fact; if no one pleads it, Singapore law applies. Two overlays can override the chosen law: Singapore's mandatory rules and its fundamental public policy.
25 min · 6 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 18 questions
C2Q2 · C2
Contract choice of law: the proper law and illegality
A contract is governed by its proper law, found in three stages: an express choice (virtually conclusive if bona fide, legal and not against public policy), else an implied choice, else the law of closest and most real connection. Formation, form and capacity have their own rules. Illegality can enter by seven routes: the proper law, forum public policy, Foster v Driscoll, Lemenda, Ralli Brothers, tainting, and reliance as a defence.
29 min · 9 flowcharts · 3 illustrations · 20 questions
C3Q2 · C3
Tort choice of law: double actionability and the flexible exception
A tort claim must be actionable under BOTH Singapore law (as if everything happened here) AND the law of the place where the tort was in substance committed. The claimant proves the first limb; the defendant must plead and prove that the foreign law gives no liability. A strictly applied flexible exception can displace either law, or both, where it is purely fortuitous.
27 min · 8 flowcharts · 5 illustrations · 15 questions

  • In each lesson, glance at the full pre-write once, then work down the sections. Every section shows its own slice of the pre-write in a fold-out box, so you always see the words you will use in the exam.

LAW301 Legal Theory and Philosophy

Your 10-page exam sheet is built around eleven archetypes: the recurring kinds of exam statement (sections 2–12). Each lesson below takes one archetype, prints it in full from the sheet, then teaches it from scratch, block by block, with plain-English boxes, 104 flowcharts, 45 "facts in one picture" illustrations, worked examples and 546 multiple-choice questions in all.

1START HERE
How the sheet works, and how an answer uses it
The exam hands you a statement to attack or defend. Each archetype is a ready-made route through one family of statements. Your job is to spot the family, then fill the route with the question's own words.
56 min · 6 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 39 questions
2ARCHETYPE 2
LP v NLT, and why theory matters
Saying what counts as "law" is already an evaluation, so the choice between legal positivism and natural law is live, and hard cases such as Riggs v Palmer turn on a theory of what law's grounds are.
72 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 46 questions
3ARCHETYPE 3
Rule of law and Fuller
The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee that the laws it governs are just.
67 min · 8 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 47 questions
4ARCHETYPE 4
Moral objectivity and scepticism
The sceptic's case is inconclusive, and the sceptic's own demands (tolerate! don't judge!) presuppose moral truth. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma or silence.
63 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 40 questions
5ARCHETYPE 5
Finnis for law-makers
Finnis gives legislators real limits (never intend to destroy a basic good) and a framework common good, then leaves much to prudence. He guides law-makers without dictating to them.
66 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 44 questions
6ARCHETYPE 6
Pluralist legislation: Rawls v Finnis
No law on a contested issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen (Rawls's discipline), sound on the merits (Finnis and TSH) and prudently fitted to circumstances.
82 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 52 questions
7ARCHETYPE 7
Enforcement of morals
Every answer to "should law enforce morality?", repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.
66 min · 9 flowcharts · 2 illustrations · 44 questions
8ARCHETYPE 8
Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity
An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and whether something is law never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it (Hart).
74 min · 9 flowcharts · 5 illustrations · 48 questions
9ARCHETYPE 9
Adjudication: Dworkin, ALR, CLS
Judges justify by fit and political morality. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and in the open cases political morality, not personal preference, closes them.
80 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 47 questions
10ARCHETYPE 10
Lawyering: Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy
The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, moral dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it. Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.
74 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 50 questions
11ARCHETYPE 11
Constitution and judicial role
A supreme written Constitution relocates the natural law v positivism debate rather than settling it. Courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.
83 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 51 questions
12ARCHETYPE 12
Roles: who decides
Roles have limits, so "stay in your lane" is right as a presumption. But where a role ends is contested, drawing the line is a moral judgment, and refusing your own role's work (abdication) is as much a vice as taking another's (usurpation).
59 min · 9 flowcharts · 4 illustrations · 38 questions
ℹ HOW TO USE THIS SITE
  • Do Lesson 1 first: it explains how a sheet block is built and how an answer uses it.
  • In each lesson, read the archetype in full once, then work down the blocks. Answer every quick check before moving on.
  • Wrong answers are remembered (the amber “missed before” tag) and gathered on the Review page.
  • After a lesson, open its hypo lesson: every block applied to made-up facts, with the application hidden until you have tried it. Each block in a lesson links to its hypos.
  • The Sheet page holds the rest of the sheet (engine, comparisons, theorist bank, frameworks, Singapore bank) with links between blocks.

How conflict of laws works, and how to use the router

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every conflict question asks one of three things: can a Singapore court hear this case, which country's law decides it, and will Singapore give effect to a foreign judgment. Question 1 tests the first and third, contract by contract; Question 2 tests the second, issue by issue.

THE ROUTER IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
00 Start Here: Exam Router
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

(Open this first. Q1 files are J1-J7 (jurisdiction to judgments); Q2 files are C1-C3 (choice of law). Every cross-reference names its file: "J4.2" is file J4, section 2. The order below follows Prof Chong's suggested answer framework for the sample final (AY19-20 T2 paper, updated March 2026): Q1 runs contract by contract, then judgments last; Q2 runs issue by issue in the order the facts raise them.)

00.1 BEFORE WRITING
  • List the contracts for each, note [date]; jurisdiction clause [EJC / NEJC / asymmetric / floating] for [court]; express proper law [X]; [claimant]'s and [defendant]'s claims as given. Chong spells out the parties and the claims, so stay inside them.
  • Dates are traps HCCCA entry into force for [State] vs the contract date (J1.2.2); the date fixing whether "Singapore High Court" includes the SICC (J5.2.3); a ban before or after contracting (Foster vs Ralli: C2.10.3, C2.10.5).
  • Format and scope (Chong, seminars) two compulsory hypos; follow [the hypo structure] from the seminars. Off-syllabus: [renvoi's operation] and subject-matter jurisdiction, except the SICC's (J5.1).
  • Technique (Chong, seminars) plan in bullets or [a table of connecting factors] before typing, then allocate time; cite [provisions] without copying them out; for each route state [founding provision] + [mode of service] (J2.0.2); if a threshold is unclear, assume it is met and continue; justification earns the marks.
  • Every "Assume ..." line is an issue "valid under [X] law but not [Y] law" means the answer turns on which law applies, so run both routes and pick one.
00.2 Q1 TEMPLATE: RUN ONCE PER CONTRACT
  1. Clause triage (J1): [Contract], dated [date], contains cl [X], [an EJC / a NEJC / an asymmetric clause] for [Singapore / X], with [law X] as its express proper law. Characterise it under its proper law (J1.1).
    • Foreign ruling first: if [foreign court] has already held that the HCCCA applies, ask whether that ruling binds as an issue estoppel (J7.3.2.3); if not, Singapore decides for itself.
    • HCCCA case? Contracting State; timing; international; civil or commercial; exclusive or deemed exclusive (J1.2). Asymmetric clauses fall outside (Hartley–Dogauchi Report; Credit Suisse) (J1.2.1).
  2. If an HCCCA case: Singapore chosen → must hear unless null and void (J1.3); serve out on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (J3.0, Route 1). Singapore not chosen → must stay or dismiss unless an s 12(1) exception applies (J1.4). If Singapore is chosen, go on to the SICC (step 4).
  3. Jurisdiction over [defendant] in the General Division:
    • Existence: service in (J2) or out (J3). Out: O 8 r 1(1) "appropriate court" with a para 63(3) gateway (J3.1; J3.1.2), or O 8 r 1(3) where the contract allows service (J3.1.5). With a Singapore clause, in practice [claimant] need only show it is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J3.2; J1.5; J1.6).
    • Exercise: breach of the clause → strong cause on the party in breach (J4.3); no promise or no breach → Spiliada or forum conveniens (J4.1; J4.2). Burden map: J4.0.2. Stage 2 "injustice" facts, e.g. [foreign court delay / damages cap / limitation gap] (J4.1.3); a second bite if stage 1 fails on service out (J4.2.3).
  4. SICC, side by side (J5): international and commercial (J5.1). Primary jurisdiction via a written jurisdiction agreement, served as of right under O 5 r 6(2)(a) (J5.2; J5.2.4), exercise only under O 2 r 3 (J5.3). Otherwise only by transfer from the General Division, the "more appropriate" test in O 2 r 4(1)(c) (J5.4). Does "Singapore High Court" include the SICC? (J5.2.3).
  5. ASI (J6), as ancillary relief to the Singapore action (J6.0.1):
    • (a) amenability: "as above" (J6.1);
    • (b) sufficient interest, not needed where the ASI rests on breach of agreement (Cooperative Muratori) (J6.2; J6.2.1);
    • (c) basis: breach of a Singapore clause, then strong reasons (J6.3.1); otherwise vexation or oppression (J6.3.2);
    • (d) vexation cases only: no undue injustice to [respondent] (J6.4).
    • Twist: seeking the ASI may itself breach a foreign clause, so ask who bears the strong-cause burden (J6.3.1). HCCCA cases: J6.5.3.
    • Judgment already given abroad: [applicant] needs an AEI, which adds exceptional circumstances to (a)–(d) (Sun Travels) (J7.6).
00.3 Q1 AFTER ALL CONTRACTS: EFFECT OF THE FOREIGN JUDGMENTS
  • Regime CCAA Part 3 if [foreign court] was the chosen court in an HCCCA case, recognised to the extent it has effect there (s 13(2)) (J7.5); it ousts REFJA (s 2A REFJA) but leaves [the common law] open (s 21 CCAA). REFJA is not examinable (Chong, seminar): if [X] is gazetted, one line (J7.4), then the common law (J7.0.2).
  • Common law requirements on the merits; international jurisdiction by presence ([carrying on business in X]) or submission ([the clause]) (J7.1.2); final and conclusive (J7.1.3); a fresh money judgment for a definite sum (J7.1.4). A non-money ruling, e.g. [a declaration of no breach], may still bind as an estoppel (J7.3).
  • Defences public policy, e.g. where Singapore has granted an ASI (J7.2.4); proceedings in breach of a dispute-resolution agreement, only if [the clause] is promissory (J7.2.6); fraud (J7.2.2); natural justice (J7.2.3).
  • Restraint Abroad if [debtor] wants [creditor] stopped from enforcing in [X / Y], an AEI needs exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability, e.g. [fraud / no knowledge until judgment] (Sun Travels) (J7.6).
00.4 Q2 TEMPLATE: ISSUE BY ISSUE

("Assume the Singapore court will assume jurisdiction" means no J files. Characterise first (C1.1), then follow the facts.)

  • Choice of law clause floating / unilateral / conflicting → validity by the lex fori (Shanghai Turbo) or by the OPL: argue both (C2.2.5); invalid → straight to the OPL (C2.2.8). Evasion → bona fide (Vita Foods; Peh Teck Quee) (C2.2.2). Vitiating factor infecting the clause (C2.2.3). Choice vs incorporation (C2.2.9).
  • No effective choice implied choice (C2.3); objective proper law (C2.4).
  • Formation disputed putative proper law; "double bootstraps" (C2.6).
  • Formality lex causae or lex loci contractus (C2.7); the provision may be procedural (C1.2; Goh Suan Hee).
  • Capacity C2.8.
  • Statute that may override the chosen law UCTA, licensing, gambling, the Misrepresentation Act (C1.7).
  • Illegality routing (C2.10.1); forum public policy (C2.10.2); Foster v Driscoll, an intention to break a friendly state's law (C2.10.3); Lemenda (C2.10.4); Ralli, a supervening ban at the place of performance (C2.10.5); tainting, by the lex fori or the proper law: argue both (C2.10.6); reliance as a defence (C2.10.7).
  • Tort double actionability (C3.1; C3.2); locate the tort, misrepresentation being made / received / relied on (C3.3; C3.3.2); flexible exception (C3.6), including party autonomy via the contract's law (C3.6.5); IP and territorial torts (C3.7.2).
  • Contract clause raised against the tort claim the contract negates an element (C3.8.1); an exemption, limitation or non-reliance clause as a defence (C3.8.2).
  • Foreign law not proved presumption of similarity (C1.6.3; C3.5).
  • Remedy, quantum, limitation substance vs procedure (C1.2); remedies (C1.3); damages (C1.4); limitation and the FLPA (C1.5; C3.9).
  • Overlays public policy (C1.8); renvoi only if the reference to foreign law is challenged (C1.9).

1Start here: the whole subject in one page

Conflict of laws (also called private international law) is what happens when a dispute touches more than one country. A Singapore seller, a German buyer, goods shipped from China, a contract that says "English law applies" and "the courts of Hong Kong have jurisdiction". Which court? Which law? And if a court somewhere else has already ruled, does that ruling count here?

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of an international football match. Before anyone kicks a ball you need to settle three things. Which stadium and referee? (jurisdiction: can this court hear the case?) Which rulebook? (choice of law: whose law decides who wins?) Does a result from another league count here? (foreign judgments: will Singapore enforce a ruling made abroad?) Conflict of laws is just those three questions, asked carefully, with rules for each.

Walk the three questions through that one story:

  1. Jurisdiction (Question 1). BuyCo is in Germany, so SellCo must serve it abroad, which needs the court's approval and a link to Singapore (J3). The clause also points to Hong Kong. Does it forbid suing anywhere else (exclusive) or merely allow Hong Kong (non-exclusive)? That one reading decides almost everything that follows (J1.1).
  2. Choice of law (Question 2). Suppose Singapore does hear the case. Whether the goods were defective and what BuyCo owes are contract questions, and the contract chose English law (C2.2). So a Singapore judge decides the case by applying English contract law, which the parties must prove as a fact (C1.6).
  3. Foreign judgments (end of Question 1). Suppose instead BuyCo won a ruling in Hong Kong first, saying it owes nothing. Does that ruling bind SellCo in Singapore? That depends on whether Hong Kong had jurisdiction over SellCo in Singapore's eyes (SellCo agreed to Hong Kong courts in the clause, which can count as submission) and whether the ruling was final (J7).

Keep the three questions apart. Singapore can have jurisdiction and still apply English law. A Hong Kong court can be the "right" court and still apply English law too. The most common beginner's mistake is to blur "which court" with "which law".

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
JurisdictionThe court's power to hear a case against this defendant.
Existence v exerciseExistence: does the court have the power at all? (Was the defendant validly served, or did they submit?) Exercise: even with the power, should it hear the case, or send the parties elsewhere? Two separate questions, always in that order.
Service in / service outHanding the court papers to a defendant in Singapore (power exists automatically) or out of Singapore abroad (needs the court's approval and a link to Singapore).
EJC / NEJCExclusive jurisdiction clause ("only the courts of X") / non-exclusive jurisdiction clause ("the courts of X may hear disputes").
SpiliadaThe test for sending a case elsewhere when no clause is broken: is another court clearly more appropriate?
Strong causeThe test when someone breaks a jurisdiction clause: the court holds them to their bargain unless they show a strong reason not to.
HCCCA / CCAAThe Hague Choice of Court Convention and the Singapore Act that brings it in. Where it applies, it overrides the ordinary rules.
SICCSingapore International Commercial Court: a division of the High Court for international commercial cases, with its own rules.
ASI / AEIAnti-suit injunction: an order stopping a party from suing abroad. Anti-enforcement injunction: an order stopping a party from enforcing a foreign judgment.
Proper lawThe law that governs a contract.
Lex foriThe law of the court hearing the case (for us, Singapore law).
Lex causaeThe law that governs the issue, once choice of law has picked it.
Lex loci delictiThe law of the place where a tort happened.
CharacterisationSorting the issue into a legal category (contract? tort? procedure?) so you know which choice of law rule to use.
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Existence and exercise, with a doctor's clinic

Think of a clinic. Existence is whether the patient is registered there at all: if not, the doctor cannot see them, however good the reason. Exercise is whether, even though the patient is registered, the doctor should refer them to a specialist hospital that is better placed to treat them. A defendant served in Singapore (or one who submits) is "registered": the court has power (J2, J3). Spiliada and strong cause decide whether to "refer" the case to a better-placed foreign court (J4). You never ask about referral until you know the patient is registered.

2How the exam is built

🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Two compulsory hypothetical questions. Follow the hypo structure from the seminars. Plan in bullets or a table of connecting factors before typing, cite provisions without copying them out, and remember that justification earns the marks. If a threshold is unclear, assume it is met and carry on. Off-syllabus: how renvoi operates, and subject-matter jurisdiction (except the SICC's).

The router splits the paper into two questions that run in different orders:

Question 1Question 2
TopicJurisdiction, injunctions, foreign judgmentsChoice of law
FilesJ1–J7C1–C3
OrderContract by contract (clause → existence → exercise → SICC → ASI), then judgments lastIssue by issue, in the order the facts raise them
Start withClause triage, J1Characterisation, C1.1
? WHY IT MATTERS

Prof Chong's March 2026 answer framework runs Q1 one contract at a time, because each contract usually has its own clause, its own parties and its own claims. If you mix contracts together you lose track of who breached what. Q2 has no "contracts" to loop over: it is a list of separate issues (Is the choice of law clause valid? Is the contract illegal? Where was the tort committed?), so you take them one by one.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
What "contract by contract" looks like on a hypo

Facts (shortened): Alpha (Singapore) signs two contracts with Beta (Indonesia). The supply contract says "the courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction". The guarantee, signed a year later, says "the courts of Jakarta may hear disputes". Beta sues Alpha in Jakarta on both. Alpha sues Beta in Singapore on both. (Assume the Hague Convention does not apply.)

Do not write one blended answer. Write two passes:

Supply contract (Singapore EJC)Guarantee (Jakarta NEJC)
TriageExclusive, Singapore chosenNon-exclusive, foreign court named
Who is in breach?Beta, by suing in Jakarta, and again if it objects to SingaporeNobody: a foreign NEJC forbids nothing
Exercise testStrong cause, burden on BetaSpiliada; the burden depends on service and the application
ASI?Contractual basis availableOnly on the vexation or oppression basis

The same two parties end up under different tests, because their two contracts say different things. That is why the router insists on one contract at a time.

300.1 Before you write a word

▤ On your pre-write: 00.1 BEFORE WRITING (word for word)
00.1 BEFORE WRITING
  • List the contracts for each, note [date]; jurisdiction clause [EJC / NEJC / asymmetric / floating] for [court]; express proper law [X]; [claimant]'s and [defendant]'s claims as given. Chong spells out the parties and the claims, so stay inside them.
  • Dates are traps HCCCA entry into force for [State] vs the contract date (J1.2.2); the date fixing whether "Singapore High Court" includes the SICC (J5.2.3); a ban before or after contracting (Foster vs Ralli: C2.10.3, C2.10.5).
  • Format and scope (Chong, seminars) two compulsory hypos; follow [the hypo structure] from the seminars. Off-syllabus: [renvoi's operation] and subject-matter jurisdiction, except the SICC's (J5.1).
  • Technique (Chong, seminars) plan in bullets or [a table of connecting factors] before typing, then allocate time; cite [provisions] without copying them out; for each route state [founding provision] + [mode of service] (J2.0.2); if a threshold is unclear, assume it is met and continue; justification earns the marks.
  • Every "Assume ..." line is an issue "valid under [X] law but not [Y] law" means the answer turns on which law applies, so run both routes and pick one.
🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. List the contracts. For each: its date, its jurisdiction clause (exclusive, non-exclusive, asymmetric or floating, and for which court), its express proper law, and exactly what each party is claiming. Prof Chong spells out the parties and claims, so answer only those.
  2. Watch the dates. Three dates decide outcomes: (a) did the Hague Convention enter into force for that State before the contract was made? (b) when was the clause made, which decides whether "Singapore High Court" includes the SICC? (c) did a ban on performance come before the contract (Foster v Driscoll territory) or after it (Ralli)?
  3. Technique. Plan first. For each route to jurisdiction, name the founding provision and the mode of service together.
  4. Every "Assume…" line is an issue. If the facts say "assume the clause is valid under X law but not under Y law", the answer turns on which law applies. Run both routes, then pick one.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Spotting the date trap

A contract dated 1 March 2015 picks "the exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts". The Hague Convention entered into force for Singapore on 1 October 2016. So the CCAA cannot apply to this clause: it was concluded before entry into force (J1.2.2). You go straight to the common law rules.

⚠ TRAP
"Assume" is not decoration

Students skim "Assume that under Ruritanian law the clause is void". That sentence is the examiner telling you which issue carries marks. Ask: when would Ruritanian law be the relevant law? Then argue both outcomes.

400.2 Question 1: the template for each contract

▤ On your pre-write: 00.2 Q1 TEMPLATE: RUN ONCE PER CONTRACT (word for word)
00.2 Q1 TEMPLATE: RUN ONCE PER CONTRACT
  1. Clause triage (J1): [Contract], dated [date], contains cl [X], [an EJC / a NEJC / an asymmetric clause] for [Singapore / X], with [law X] as its express proper law. Characterise it under its proper law (J1.1).
    • Foreign ruling first: if [foreign court] has already held that the HCCCA applies, ask whether that ruling binds as an issue estoppel (J7.3.2.3); if not, Singapore decides for itself.
    • HCCCA case? Contracting State; timing; international; civil or commercial; exclusive or deemed exclusive (J1.2). Asymmetric clauses fall outside (Hartley–Dogauchi Report; Credit Suisse) (J1.2.1).
  2. If an HCCCA case: Singapore chosen → must hear unless null and void (J1.3); serve out on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (J3.0, Route 1). Singapore not chosen → must stay or dismiss unless an s 12(1) exception applies (J1.4). If Singapore is chosen, go on to the SICC (step 4).
  3. Jurisdiction over [defendant] in the General Division:
    • Existence: service in (J2) or out (J3). Out: O 8 r 1(1) "appropriate court" with a para 63(3) gateway (J3.1; J3.1.2), or O 8 r 1(3) where the contract allows service (J3.1.5). With a Singapore clause, in practice [claimant] need only show it is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J3.2; J1.5; J1.6).
    • Exercise: breach of the clause → strong cause on the party in breach (J4.3); no promise or no breach → Spiliada or forum conveniens (J4.1; J4.2). Burden map: J4.0.2. Stage 2 "injustice" facts, e.g. [foreign court delay / damages cap / limitation gap] (J4.1.3); a second bite if stage 1 fails on service out (J4.2.3).
  4. SICC, side by side (J5): international and commercial (J5.1). Primary jurisdiction via a written jurisdiction agreement, served as of right under O 5 r 6(2)(a) (J5.2; J5.2.4), exercise only under O 2 r 3 (J5.3). Otherwise only by transfer from the General Division, the "more appropriate" test in O 2 r 4(1)(c) (J5.4). Does "Singapore High Court" include the SICC? (J5.2.3).
  5. ASI (J6), as ancillary relief to the Singapore action (J6.0.1):
    • (a) amenability: "as above" (J6.1);
    • (b) sufficient interest, not needed where the ASI rests on breach of agreement (Cooperative Muratori) (J6.2; J6.2.1);
    • (c) basis: breach of a Singapore clause, then strong reasons (J6.3.1); otherwise vexation or oppression (J6.3.2);
    • (d) vexation cases only: no undue injustice to [respondent] (J6.4).
    • Twist: seeking the ASI may itself breach a foreign clause, so ask who bears the strong-cause burden (J6.3.1). HCCCA cases: J6.5.3.
    • Judgment already given abroad: [applicant] needs an AEI, which adds exceptional circumstances to (a)–(d) (Sun Travels) (J7.6).

This is the spine of Question 1. You run it once per contract. Each step has its own lesson; the flowchart shows how they connect.

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Clause triage (J1). Read the clause. Is it exclusive or not, for Singapore or for a foreign court? Characterise it under its own proper law. If a foreign court has already ruled the Convention applies, ask whether that ruling binds you as an issue estoppel (J7.3).
  2. Hague Convention case? If yes and Singapore is chosen, Singapore must hear it. If yes and a foreign court is chosen, Singapore must stay unless an exception applies.
  3. Otherwise, the common law. Does the court have jurisdiction (existence: J2 if the defendant was served here, J3 if served abroad)? Should it use it (exercise: J4)? Exercise turns on one question: did anyone break the clause? Break it → strong cause. No break → Spiliada.
  4. SICC (J5). Is there a written agreement to the SICC? If not, can the case be transferred there?
  5. ASI (J6). Does the claimant want an order stopping the other side's foreign lawsuit? Four steps: amenability, sufficient interest, a basis (breach of a clause, or vexation/oppression), and no undue injustice.
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
Clause → Court → Convince → SICC → Stop

Clause (triage), Court has power? (existence), Convince it to use it? (exercise), SICC, Stop the foreign suit (ASI). Then judgments at the very end.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
One contract, start to finish (outline)

Facts: a 2020 supply contract between a Singapore seller (S) and a Japanese buyer (B) says "the courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction". B sues S in Tokyo. S sues B in Singapore and serves B in Japan.

  1. Clause triage: an EJC for Singapore (J1.1).
  2. HCCCA? Only if Japan and Singapore's dates, internationality and subject matter all fit (J1.2); if it applies, Singapore must hear the case (J1.3).
  3. Common law (if not HCCCA): existence by service out with the court's approval (J3). B objecting to Singapore breaks its promise not to object, so B must show strong cause (J4.3).
  4. SICC: does the clause name the SICC, or can the case be transferred there (J5)?
  5. ASI: B's Tokyo suit breaks the EJC, so S can seek an ASI on the contractual basis, and B must show strong reasons why it should not issue (J6.3.1).

Notice how the clause does most of the work. Because it is a Singapore EJC, B is in breach twice over: once by suing in Tokyo, and again if it objects to Singapore. Every later step builds on that finding.

Flip one fact. Make the clause "the courts of Japan shall have exclusive jurisdiction". Now the picture inverts: S is the party in breach by suing in Singapore, so S must show strong cause to keep its action alive (J4.3), and S has no contractual basis for an ASI against B's Tokyo suit, because B is suing exactly where it promised.

500.3 After every contract: the foreign judgments

▤ On your pre-write: 00.3 Q1 AFTER ALL CONTRACTS: EFFECT OF THE FOREIGN JUDGMENTS (word for word)
00.3 Q1 AFTER ALL CONTRACTS: EFFECT OF THE FOREIGN JUDGMENTS
  • Regime CCAA Part 3 if [foreign court] was the chosen court in an HCCCA case, recognised to the extent it has effect there (s 13(2)) (J7.5); it ousts REFJA (s 2A REFJA) but leaves [the common law] open (s 21 CCAA). REFJA is not examinable (Chong, seminar): if [X] is gazetted, one line (J7.4), then the common law (J7.0.2).
  • Common law requirements on the merits; international jurisdiction by presence ([carrying on business in X]) or submission ([the clause]) (J7.1.2); final and conclusive (J7.1.3); a fresh money judgment for a definite sum (J7.1.4). A non-money ruling, e.g. [a declaration of no breach], may still bind as an estoppel (J7.3).
  • Defences public policy, e.g. where Singapore has granted an ASI (J7.2.4); proceedings in breach of a dispute-resolution agreement, only if [the clause] is promissory (J7.2.6); fraud (J7.2.2); natural justice (J7.2.3).
  • Restraint Abroad if [debtor] wants [creditor] stopped from enforcing in [X / Y], an AEI needs exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability, e.g. [fraud / no knowledge until judgment] (Sun Travels) (J7.6).

When a court abroad has already given judgment, Question 1 finishes by asking what effect that judgment has in Singapore. This is J7.

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • Which regime? If the foreign court was the chosen court in a Convention case, use the CCAA's recognition rules (J7.5). The CCAA also ousts REFJA but leaves the common law open (s 21 CCAA). REFJA itself is not examinable (Prof Chong said so in the seminar), so give it one line at most.
  • Common law requirements. The foreign court must have had international jurisdiction over the debtor, by the debtor's presence there (for a company, carrying on business there) or by submission (for example, through a jurisdiction clause). The judgment must be final and conclusive and for a definite sum of money.
  • Defences. Public policy (for example where Singapore had granted an ASI), proceedings brought in breach of a dispute-resolution agreement (only if the clause is promissory), fraud, and breach of natural justice.
  • Stopping enforcement abroad. If the debtor wants the creditor stopped from enforcing in other countries, it needs an AEI, which requires exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability (Sun Travels) (J7.6).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A foreign judgment, start to finish

Facts: A Hong Kong court orders Delta, a Singapore company, to pay HK$2 million to Echo. Delta filed a defence in Hong Kong and fought the case on the merits. Delta has no assets in Hong Kong, so Echo comes to Singapore to collect.

  1. Which regime? No exclusive clause chose Hong Kong in a Convention case, so the CCAA's recognition rules are out. REFJA gets one line at most. Go to the common law (J7.4).
  2. International jurisdiction: Delta fought the case on the merits in Hong Kong. That is submission (J7.1).
  3. Final and conclusive, for a fixed sum: a final money judgment for a definite amount.
  4. Defences: fraud, breach of natural justice, public policy, breach of a jurisdiction clause. Nothing in the facts raises any of them (J7.2).
  5. Result: Echo sues Delta in Singapore on the judgment debt. It does not have to prove the original claim again, and Singapore does not re-check whether Hong Kong got the merits right.

Change one fact. Delta never appeared in Hong Kong, never agreed to Hong Kong courts and does no business there. Now there is no presence and no submission, so the judgment cannot be enforced at common law, however correct it was on the merits.

600.4 Question 2: issue by issue

▤ On your pre-write: 00.4 Q2 TEMPLATE: ISSUE BY ISSUE (word for word)
00.4 Q2 TEMPLATE: ISSUE BY ISSUE

("Assume the Singapore court will assume jurisdiction" means no J files. Characterise first (C1.1), then follow the facts.)

  • Choice of law clause floating / unilateral / conflicting → validity by the lex fori (Shanghai Turbo) or by the OPL: argue both (C2.2.5); invalid → straight to the OPL (C2.2.8). Evasion → bona fide (Vita Foods; Peh Teck Quee) (C2.2.2). Vitiating factor infecting the clause (C2.2.3). Choice vs incorporation (C2.2.9).
  • No effective choice implied choice (C2.3); objective proper law (C2.4).
  • Formation disputed putative proper law; "double bootstraps" (C2.6).
  • Formality lex causae or lex loci contractus (C2.7); the provision may be procedural (C1.2; Goh Suan Hee).
  • Capacity C2.8.
  • Statute that may override the chosen law UCTA, licensing, gambling, the Misrepresentation Act (C1.7).
  • Illegality routing (C2.10.1); forum public policy (C2.10.2); Foster v Driscoll, an intention to break a friendly state's law (C2.10.3); Lemenda (C2.10.4); Ralli, a supervening ban at the place of performance (C2.10.5); tainting, by the lex fori or the proper law: argue both (C2.10.6); reliance as a defence (C2.10.7).
  • Tort double actionability (C3.1; C3.2); locate the tort, misrepresentation being made / received / relied on (C3.3; C3.3.2); flexible exception (C3.6), including party autonomy via the contract's law (C3.6.5); IP and territorial torts (C3.7.2).
  • Contract clause raised against the tort claim the contract negates an element (C3.8.1); an exemption, limitation or non-reliance clause as a defence (C3.8.2).
  • Foreign law not proved presumption of similarity (C1.6.3; C3.5).
  • Remedy, quantum, limitation substance vs procedure (C1.2); remedies (C1.3); damages (C1.4); limitation and the FLPA (C1.5; C3.9).
  • Overlays public policy (C1.8); renvoi only if the reference to foreign law is challenged (C1.9).

Question 2 usually starts with the words "Assume the Singapore court will assume jurisdiction". That means: no J files at all. Go straight to choice of law.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Splitting a Question 2 fact pattern into issues

Facts: "Assume the Singapore court will assume jurisdiction." Fox (Singapore) hires Gull (Malaysia) to carry machinery under a contract that says "governed by English law" and caps Gull's liability at $10,000. The machinery is dropped and damaged in a Malaysian port. Fox sues for breach of contract and in negligence. Gull says the claim is out of time under Malaysian law.

Turn that into a list of issues before writing anything:

IssueCharacterise asGo to
Is the "English law" choice effective?ContractC2.2
Did Gull breach the contract?Contract, so the proper law decidesC2
Was Gull negligent?Tort, so double actionabilityC3.1
Does the $10,000 cap also limit the negligence claim?A contract clause raised against a tort claimC3.8
Is the claim out of time?Limitation: substance or procedure?C1.5

Each row then becomes a mini-answer: rule, apply, conclude. The checklist card below is the same idea, in the order fact patterns usually raise the issues.

The Question 2 checklist
▤ Router 00.4, in the order facts usually raise them
  1. 1Choice of law clause problems: floating, unilateral or conflicting clauses (C2.2.5); evasion and bona fides (C2.2.2); a vitiating factor infecting the clause (C2.2.3); choice v incorporation (C2.2.9).
  2. 2No effective choice: implied choice (C2.3), then objective proper law (C2.4).
  3. 3Formation disputed: putative proper law and "double bootstraps" (C2.6).
  4. 4Formality (C2.7) and capacity (C2.8).
  5. 5A Singapore statute that may override the chosen law (C1.7).
  6. 6Illegality: routing, forum public policy, Foster v Driscoll, Lemenda, Ralli, tainting, reliance (C2.10).
  7. 7Tort: double actionability, locating the tort, the flexible exception, IP torts (C3).
  8. 8A contract clause raised against the tort claim (C3.8).
  9. 9Foreign law not proved: presumption of similarity (C1.6).
  10. 10Remedy, quantum, limitation: substance v procedure (C1.2–C1.5).
  11. 11Overlays: public policy (C1.8); renvoi only if the reference to foreign law is challenged (C1.9).
⚠ TRAP
Do not do jurisdiction in Question 2

If Question 2 says "assume the Singapore court will assume jurisdiction", spending time on service out or Spiliada earns nothing. Characterise and go.

7How to read a pre-write

Every lesson prints your pre-write file in full at the top (folded) and then shows each slice of it in a fold-out box labelled "On your pre-write". The files share a few conventions:

You seeIt means
[claimant], [clause X]A blank to fill with the facts. Replace it with the party's name, the clause number, the country.
Rule A label naming what the point does: rule, application, counter-argument, trap.
(+) (−) (±)Who the point helps: the party relying on the rule, the other side, or argue both ways.
"Per Vinmar", "per C&Y"The source: a case, the Chong & Yip textbook, a statute, or "Per Chong (seminar)".
J4.3A cross-reference to another part of the pre-writes. Click it here to jump.
Similar to 6DM, where…An analogy sentence: you compare your facts to the case's facts.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Turning a pre-write line into an exam sentence

Pre-write: "Per Vinmar, [the party relying on clause X] must show a good arguable case that it exists and applies to [the dispute]."

Exam: "Per Vinmar, Alpha must show a good arguable case that cl 20 exists and covers its claim for unpaid freight."

What changed: the blank "[the party relying on clause X]" became a name (Alpha), "clause X" became the real clause number, and "[the dispute]" became the actual claim. The rule and the source stayed exactly as written. That is the whole technique: keep the law, swap in the facts.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Reading the symbols on one line

Suppose a line reads: "(±) Witnesses: [non-party witnesses] in [country] point to [country] if their evidence is arguably relevant (JIO); less weight if they will give evidence by video."

  • (±) says this factor can be argued both ways, so write both sides, then decide.
  • Witnesses: is the label. Start your paragraph with it so the marker sees the point at once.
  • The square brackets are blanks: "The port inspectors in Jakarta point to Indonesia…"
  • JIO is the source, cited without a paragraph pinpoint.
J1: Clause triage and the CCAA →
LESSON J1 · Q1 · JURISDICTION AND JUDGMENTS · ABOUT 42 MIN · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 3 ILLUSTRATIONS · 26 QUESTIONS

Clause triage: what the jurisdiction clause promises, and the CCAA

⚡ BIG IDEA

Read the jurisdiction clause first and ask what it promises. That tells you who, if anyone, is in breach, and breach decides the test later (strong cause or Spiliada). If the Hague Convention applies through the CCAA, it overrides everything: the chosen court must hear the case and other courts must step aside.

PRE-WRITE J1 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
J1 Choice Of Court Agreements: Clause Triage And The Ccaa
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

(Run first for every contract: its date, clause type, express proper law, and whether it is an HCCCA case (Chong's sample-final framework). Existence → J2 / J3; exercise → J4; SICC → J5; ASI → J6; judgments → J7. Legend: (+) helps [party relying on the clause]; (−) helps [party resisting it]; (±) argue both ways.)

J1.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Three regimes: the General Division at common law (J2–J4), the CCAA (J1.2–J1.4) and the SICC (J5). The CCAA displaces both others within its scope; the SICC displaces Spiliada for cases heard there. "Not every Convention case will be an SICC case, and not every SICC case will be a Convention case" (Yeo). At common law, ask two questions: is anyone in breach, and who bears the burden?)

  1. Regime router (J1.0.2): CCAA first, then the SICC, else the common law, for [clause X] in [contract].
  2. Characterise [clause X] (J1.1): [exclusive / non-exclusive], [Singapore / foreign], [asymmetric / floating], construed under [its proper law].
  3. CCAA scope (J1.2): [actual / deemed] exclusive (s 3), not asymmetric, for [one Contracting State], concluded after [entry into force], international (s 4), civil or commercial (s 9).
  4. Singapore chosen (J1.3): [Singapore] must hear [the case] unless null and void (s 11).
  5. Singapore not chosen (J1.4): [Singapore] must stay unless [an s 12(1) exception] applies.
  6. Scope (J1.5): does [clause X] cover [the claim] and [these parties]?
  7. Existence and validity (J1.6): a good arguable case; does [the vitiating factor] reach [clause X] itself?
  8. Found jurisdiction (J3.2): [service in], where a foreign clause goes only to exercise, or [service out] under O 8 r 1(3) or r 1(1).
  9. Breach? By [claimant], in suing here, or by [defendant], in objecting to [the named Singapore court].
  10. Breach → strong cause on [the party in breach], whether [stay or set-aside], [served in or out] (J4.3).
  11. No breach → Spiliada, burden set by [service in / out] and [set-aside / stay] (J4.1; J4.2).
  12. Other effects (J1.7): [damages], [ASI], [recognition defence].
  • Links Back a Singapore [jurisdiction clause] is a gateway under para 63(3)(d)(iv) and (r) (J3.1.2), may dispense with approval under O 8 r 1(3) (J3.1.5), and is an agreement to submit, not [submission by conduct] (J2.2.3).
J1.0.1 Quick Application Template
  • CCAA: Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant] in [Singapore] on [contract], whose [clause X] gives [the courts of State] exclusive jurisdiction. The CCAA [applies, [clause X] being concluded on [date] after the HCCCA entered into force there, in an international, commercial case (J1.2) / does not apply, as [clause X] is [asymmetric / non-exclusive / within s 9]].
  • CCAA result: So [Singapore must hear the case (J1.3) / Singapore must stay unless [s 12(1) exception] applies (J1.4) / the SICC may decline only under O 2 r 3(2) (J5.3)].
  • Common law, characterise: Presently, [clause X] provides that disputes ["shall be submitted to the [exclusive / non-exclusive] jurisdiction of the courts of [Singapore / X]"]. Construed under [the proper law / Singapore law by the presumption of similarity], it is [an EJC / a NEJC] for [Singapore / X] (J1.1).
  • Scope and validity: [The claim] falls [within / outside] [clause X] because [it arises from the same incident as the contract claims], and [defendant]'s plea of [misrepresentation as to price] does not reach the clause itself (CIMB; PT Selecta) (J1.5–J1.6).
  • Breach and result: [Claimant / defendant] breaches by [suing here / objecting to Singapore], so it must show strong cause (J4.3), which it [cannot, the factors being foreseeable at contracting / can, because [unforeseeable event]]. So [stay granted / service set aside / jurisdiction exercised].
J1.0.2 Regime Router

(one line per contract, then go to the relevant part)

  • CCAA First If [clause X] is an exclusive agreement for the courts of [Contracting State] in an international, civil or commercial case, the CCAA applies (s 8) and overrides [Spiliada] and [strong cause] (per C&Y).
  • SICC Second If not, or if [Singapore] is the chosen court, ask whether [the case] is in the SICC by [a written jurisdiction agreement (J5.2) / transfer (J5.4) / joinder (J5.6)].
  • Common Law Residual Otherwise, existence is by [service in (J2) / service out (J3)], and exercise by [strong cause for an EJC or a Singapore NEJC / Spiliada for a foreign NEJC] (J4).
  • Overlap A post-2016 exclusive ["Singapore High Court"] clause includes the SICC (s 2(2)–(3) CCAA; O 2 r 2(1) SICC Rules). The CCAA decides whether [Singapore] must hear [the case]; the SICC Rules allocate it internally, subject to s 11(5) and O 2 r 4(4) (J5.4).
J1.1 CHARACTERISING THE CLAUSE (write first: what [clause X] promises decides who, if anyone, is in breach)
  • Three Promises (must write) A choice of court agreement may contain (1A) a promise to submit to [the chosen court]; (1B) a promise not to object to its exercise of jurisdiction, e.g., on [FNC grounds]; and (2) a promise not to sue [anywhere else]. (1A) and (1B) are prorogation; (2) is derogation.
  • EJC v NEJC An EJC contains all three, so [claimant] suing in [a non-chosen court] breaches (2), and [defendant] objecting to [the chosen court] breaches (1B). Per Bambang Sutrisno (in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), a NEJC contains (1A) but not (2); whether it contains (1B) is construction under [its proper law].
  • How Exclusivity Is Decided Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] is construed under [its governing law], but its effect on Singapore's jurisdiction is for [the lex fori]. Per C&Y, "exclusive" is the conclusion, not the starting point: labels get their ordinary meaning, but many clauses are [unlabelled / paired with an FNC waiver / asymmetric].
  • Wording Indicators In [clause X], ["exclusively"] → EJC; ["shall be heard by"] → mandatory, so likely exclusive under [the proper law]; ["may be referred to" / "submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of"] → NEJC.
  • SICC Clause If [clause X] names [the SICC], s 18F SCJA presumes it exclusive absent express contrary words, though whether s 18F applies where [foreign law] governs a non-CCAA clause is debated (J5.2.2).
J1.1.1 Singapore NEJC: the Contractual Approach (must write)
  • Rule Presently, [defendant] "submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Courts of Singapore" but now [seeks a stay / applies to set aside service] on [FNC grounds]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), adopting Noble Power, Singapore takes the contractual approach (left open in Orchard Capital), not the general approach under which [a NEJC] is merely a Spiliada factor.
  • Construction Under Singapore law, "submit" means consenting to [the named court]'s jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise (Yeo's "narrow waiver of objection"). Otherwise [clause X] would be "devoid of purpose" (Briggs, adopted in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), and this holds even if [Singapore] had no jurisdiction without [clause X].
  • Consequence Any challenge by [defendant], whether [setting aside service] or [a stay], even in favour of [another named court], is an attempt to escape [clause X], so [defendant] must show strong cause (J4.3).
  • Old Cases Overruled Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), High Court cases treating [a Singapore NEJC] as a mere Spiliada factor were wrongly decided. The CA went "one step further" than Bambang Sutrisno, whose clause had [an express FNC waiver].
  • Open Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), whether the same applies to [a NEJC] in [a standard form / non-negotiated contract] was left open; by analogy with Vinmar, probably yes (J4.3).
J1.1.2 Proper Law and Foreign NEJCs
  • Proper Law of the NEJC (±) Whether [clause X] contains (1B) is for [the proper law]. If [law X] is unproved, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver. If [Ruritanian law] is proved and implies no waiver, [clause X] contains only (1A), so [defendant]'s FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J4.1; J4.2).
  • Foreign NEJC: No Breach Either Way [Claimant] sues here though [clause X] names [the courts of X] non-exclusively. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the "wide waiver of objection" is rejected, so suing here is no breach, and [defendant]'s objection is none either, as [Singapore] is not named. Plain Spiliada applies (J4.1).
  • Weight of a Foreign NEJC Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] shows only that [X] is an appropriate forum, not clearly more appropriate, so it carries little weight; how much depends on whether it was [closely negotiated / chosen for neutrality].
  • Drafting Around the Defaults (practice) For [a Singapore NEJC] without the waiver, add ["without prejudice to each party's right to object on FNC grounds"]; to make [a foreign NEJC] bind, add [a promise not to sue elsewhere].
  • FNC Waiver Per Bunge, where [the Singapore EJC] carries [an FNC waiver, e.g., "no Party will argue to the contrary"], grounds founded on convenience cannot amount to strong cause, so [defendant]'s reliance on [witnesses / documents abroad] fails.
J1.1.3 Floating and Multi-Forum Clauses
  • Floating Jurisdiction Clause Valid Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike [a floating choice of law clause], which is void (C2). It needs an election mechanism, e.g., [one party's option / a prescribed event].
  • Severance Presently, [clause X] couples [a floating choice of law] with [a jurisdiction choice]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the void law part is severable where the two are joined only by ["and"] and [the contract has a severance clause]; contrast The Iran Vojdan, where [the forum choice] was parasitic on [the law choice].
  • No Mechanism → Both Courts Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), ["Singapore/or PRC"] with no election mechanism is a NEJC to both [Singapore] and [PRC], each party submitting to whichever is seised. Letting [the claimant] elect at suit was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.
  • Several Named Fora Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the waiver applies to each named forum, so [defendant]'s objection in either [Singapore] or [X] is a breach.
J1.1.4 Clause Bank (handout exercise)
  • Foreign EJC → Strong Cause on Claimant ["exclusively to the courts of [X]"], ["exclusively to the courts of [X] or [Y]"] (two fora, all others excluded) and ["shall be heard by the courts of [X]"] (mandatory, so likely exclusive). [Claimant] suing here breaches, so [claimant] bears strong cause, whether [served in, defendant seeking a stay] or [served out] (J3.2).
  • Foreign NEJC → Spiliada ["may be heard by the courts of [X]"] or ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of [X]"]: no one breaches by suing here, so Spiliada, with the burden set by [service in / out] and [set-aside / stay] (J3.2; J4).
  • Singapore NEJC → Strong Cause on Defendant ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore"] or ["of the courts of [X] or Singapore"] (the Shanghai Turbo pattern): [defendant] objecting to [Singapore] breaches, so [defendant] bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, With Submission ["[A] may sue [B] in any court, [B] submitting to it; [B] may sue [A] only in [Y]"]. If [A] sues here, [B] agreed to submit, so [B] bears strong cause to stay; if [B] sues here, [B] breaches its [Y]-only promise and bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, Without Submission (±) If [clause X] merely lets [A] sue [B] [anywhere], without [B] submitting to that court, [A] suing here is permitted but [B] never agreed to submit, so [B]'s stay goes to Spiliada (Week 10 handout). [B] suing here still breaches [the EJC for Y] → strong cause on [B].
  • Protective Promise ["all submit to [X]; under no circumstances shall [B] be subjected to any other court"]. [A] suing [B] here breaches the second limb → strong cause on [A]; [B] suing [A] here breaches nothing → Spiliada.
J1.2 DOES THE CCAA APPLY? (s 8)

(Three principles: [the chosen court] must hear; [a non-chosen court] must decline; [its judgment] must be recognised (J7.5). Gateways: exclusive; one Contracting State; concluded after entry into force; international; civil or commercial. Write only those in issue.)

J1.2.1 Exclusive Choice of Court Agreement (s 3)
  • Express EJC (+) Per s 3(1), [clause X] is exclusive: concluded [in writing / by accessible electronic means], it designates [the courts of State] for disputes in connection with [contract], to the exclusion of any other court.
  • Deemed Exclusive (+) Per s 3(2), [clause X] (["the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts"]) is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. At common law the same unlabelled clause could go either way under [its proper law] (J1.1).
    • Rebuttal (−): [clause X] [says "non-exclusive" / allows suit "in any other competent court"], so s 3(2) is displaced and [the CCAA] does not apply.
    • Trap: per Chong (seminar), where the facts call [clause X] [non-exclusive], do not invoke s 3(2): [the CCAA] does not apply, a recurring exam error.
  • Asymmetric Clause (−) Presently, [clause X] gives [State B] exclusive jurisdiction but lets [the lender] sue [the borrower] [anywhere]. Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), such a clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged even on [the court's own motion], and even though [defendant] conceded the point.
    • Support: Per Etihad (EWCA) (obiter), the Convention probably excludes [asymmetric clauses] like [clause X], the Diplomatic Session having rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties".
    • Counter (+): Earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the Convention's wording as wide enough for [clause X], but [the lender]'s reliance on them is weak after CHLOE V.
    • Consequence: At common law [clause X] stays exclusive against [the restricted party] (per C&Y), so J1.1 applies.
  • Floating Clause (±) Presently, [clause X] lets [party] choose between [Court A] and [Court B]; per C&Y, CCAA coverage is unclear. (−) Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement. (+) Once [notice of election] was served on [date], [clause X] crystallised into a mutually exclusive choice of [Court A], probably within the CCAA.
    • Unilateral election (±): s 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably [party]'s election suffices where [all parties agreed it could elect / [other party] received written notice and did not object].
  • More Than One State (−) [Clause X] designates [Singapore or England], not the courts "of one Contracting State" (s 3(1)), so it is outside the CCAA, though [possibly exclusive at common law].
  • Separability (+) Per s 5, [clause X] is independent of [contract], so its validity cannot be challenged solely because [contract] is said to be [void for misrepresentation / terminated].
J1.2.2 Contracting State and Date
  • Temporal Scope [State of chosen court] is a Contracting State, and [clause X] was concluded on [date], after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). [Check the HCCH status table.]
    • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
J1.2.3 International Case (s 4)
  • International (+) Per s 4(1), [the case] is international unless the parties reside in the same Contracting State and everything else, apart from the chosen court's location, is connected only with that State. [Defendant] resides in [State], so the exception fails.
  • Company Residence Per s 6, [a company party] resides at its [statutory seat / place of incorporation / central administration / principal place of business], so [defendant] resides in [State].
  • Wholly Domestic (−) Both parties reside in [Singapore], and [contract] was negotiated and performed wholly here; only [the chosen court in State B] is foreign. So [the case] is not international and the CCAA does not apply (per C&Y).
J1.2.4 Civil or Commercial Matter (ss 9–10)
  • Civil or Commercial (+) Per C&Y, "civil or commercial" is autonomous, mainly excluding public and criminal law. [A claim for price] under [supply contract] is commercial, and insurance is not excluded merely by its subject matter (s 9(6)).
  • Excluded (−) Per s 9(1), the CCAA excludes [consumer] and [employment / collective] agreements; per s 9(2), matters such as [insolvency / carriage of goods / competition / personal injury / non-contractual property damage / rights in rem in land / IP validity]; per s 9(3), arbitration.
    • IP (±): non-contractual infringement of [patent / trade mark] (not copyright) is excluded unless it could have been brought as a breach of [contract] between the parties (s 9(2)).
    • Preliminary question (+): per s 9(5), [IP validity] raised only as a preliminary question or [defence] does not exclude the case; per s 9(7), [a State] being a party does not either.
  • Interim Measures (+) Per s 10, interim measures are outside the CCAA, so Singapore may still grant [a Mareva / an interim ASI] whatever [the chosen court] (J6.5.3).
J1.2.5 Validity, Existence and Capacity
  • Validity Presently, [party] says [clause X] is invalid for [misrepresentation / duress]. Per ss 11(1) and 12(1)(a) and the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, validity is for the law of [the chosen court's State], including its choice of law rules, a single reference point that deters forum shopping.
    • Example: if [Singapore] is chosen and [contract] is governed by [French law], Singapore's choice of law rules point to French law; even then, per s 5, [clause X] survives unless attacked directly.
  • Existence (Consent) The CCAA is silent, but per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), whether [party] consented to [clause X] is also for the law of [the chosen court], avoiding a validity and existence split.
  • Capacity If [the chosen court's law] treats capacity as validity or existence, it governs. As a non-chosen court, [Singapore] may also refuse a stay if [party] lacked capacity under Singapore law (s 12(1)(b)), also a ground to refuse recognition (s 15(1)(b); J7.5).
J1.3 SINGAPORE IS THE CHOSEN COURT (s 11)
  • Must Hear (must write) [Clause X] designates [the Singapore High Court / the SICC] and the CCAA applies (J1.2). Per s 11(1), [Singapore] must not decline unless [clause X] is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules.
  • No FNC, No Lis Pendens Per s 11(2), [Singapore] cannot decline in favour of [State B], so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and per C&Y no other s 11(3) ground has been prescribed. [Defendant]'s points that [witnesses / governing law] point to [State B], or that proceedings are pending there, are irrelevant.
  • Null and Void (−) [Defendant] argues [clause X] is null and void because [it was procured by fraud / [defendant]'s agent lacked authority]. That is for Singapore law including its choice of law rules (s 11(1)), and per s 5 the alleged invalidity of [contract] does not by itself affect [clause X].
  • Internal Allocation (±) Per s 11(4), Singapore's [subject-matter / value / internal allocation] rules are unaffected. But per s 11(5), on a discretionary transfer of [the case] to [another Singapore court], the court must take the parties' choice into account; otherwise, per art 8(5) HCCCA, [a foreign court] may refuse recognition against [a party] that objected in time (J5.4.2).
  • Serving Abroad: General Division (+) [Claimant] seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, so [no nexus] and [no forum conveniens] inquiry arises (per C&Y; J3.1.1). If [contract] permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5).
    • Open (±): whether [defendant] may still argue [the claim] is outside the CCAA, and so resist "has the jurisdiction", should be raised inter partes (J3.1.1).
  • Serving Abroad: SICC (+) No permission is needed to serve [defendant], [a party to the written jurisdiction agreement] (O 5 r 6(2)(a) SICC Rules; J5.2.4).
J1.4 SINGAPORE IS NOT THE CHOSEN COURT (s 12)
  • Must Stay or Dismiss (must write) [Claimant] sued here, and [defendant] seeks a stay because [clause X] designates [the courts of State B]. Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", [Singapore] must stay or dismiss unless exception (a)–(e) applies; per s 12(2), a stay on other grounds remains possible.
  • Two Stages Per 6DM, the court asks (1) whether there is an exclusive agreement not designating [a Singapore court] for these proceedings, then (2) whether [an s 12(1) exception] applies.
  • Standard Per 6DM, [defendant] must show a good arguable case at stage 1, not the arbitration prima facie standard, because the CCAA has [no kompetenz-kompetenz equivalent] and [no supervisory appeal structure], and a good arguable case matches the robust common law stay analysis.
J1.4.1 Stage 1: An EJC That Does Not Designate Singapore
  • Ambiguous Clause (+) [Clause X] refers to ["the local courts" / "the courts of the Seller's country"]. Similar to 6DM, where "the local courts" in an English-law distribution agreement meant England because it renewed an earlier English-clause agreement on a related party's template, [clause X] means [State B] given [prior dealings / the template / the governing law].
  • Clause Covers Singapore or Is Outside the CCAA (−) [Claimant] answers that [clause X] [designates Singapore / is asymmetric / is non-exclusive]. Then s 12 is not engaged (CHLOE V), and [the stay] is decided at common law: [strong cause for an EJC / Spiliada for a foreign NEJC] (J4).
J1.4.2 Stage 2: The Exceptions (s 12(1)(a)–(e))
  • Starter Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), exceptions (c) and (d) apply "only in the most exceptional circumstances" and are read narrowly. If [an exception] applies, [Singapore] may exercise jurisdiction under its own law, and [defendant]'s stay falls to the common law (J4).
  • (a) Null and Void (±) [Claimant] argues [clause X] is null and void for [ground] under [State B]'s law, including its choice of law rules, not Singapore law. [Claimant] must prove [State B law] as fact, or the presumption of similarity applies (C1.6.3); by analogy, [the s 12(1)(c) argument] in 6DM failed for want of evidence of English law.
  • (b) Incapacity (+) [Claimant] lacked capacity to conclude [clause X] under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, because of [e.g., minority, or a statutory bar under its foreign law of incorporation (C2.8)] (s 12(1)(b)). Per ss 23, 25 and 25B CA, [a Singapore company] rarely lacks capacity (C2.8.2).
  • (c) Manifest Injustice: Rule (−) Per 6DM, adopting the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, manifest injustice covers, e.g., [no fair trial for bias or corruption in State B], [party-specific reasons precluding suit there] or [an agreement procured by fraud]. Per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM), it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative.
  • (c) Public Policy: Rule (−) Per 6DM, public policy means [basic norms], not [the chosen court's technical departure from a forum mandatory rule], and [clause X] is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under [Singapore domestic law].
  • (c) Fragmentation (−) Similar to 6DM, where the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed s 12(1)(c), [claimant]'s argument that [third party] cannot be joined in [State B] fails. The test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and [claimant] led no evidence of [State B law].
  • (c) Domestic Policy (−) Similar to Motacus (in 6DM), where England's policy of fast construction adjudication did not justify ignoring a Paris EJC, absent any evidence that enforcement could not proceed in Paris, [claimant]'s reliance on [Singapore policy on X] fails. Parliament could have made [an art 21 declaration].
  • (c) Exceptional Case (+) [Claimant] leads cogent evidence that [State B's courts are not independent / [claimant] faces arrest there / [clause X] was procured by fraud], the kind of case the Hartley–Dogauchi Report contemplates.
  • (d) Cannot Reasonably Be Performed (±) Per s 12(1)(d), this needs exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control, arguably akin to frustration. (+) [War in State B / its courts ceasing to function] means [the case] cannot be heard there. (−) Mere [delay / expense] is not enough.
  • (e) Chosen Court Declined (+) [The State B court] has [declined jurisdiction / dismissed [claimant]'s claim on jurisdictional grounds], so [Singapore] may hear [the case] under its own rules without breaching the Convention.
  • Case Management (−) Per 6DM, any risk of [inconsistent outcomes with related proceedings] can be met by a limited case-management stay of [those proceedings], especially at an early stage (J4.5).
  • Conclusion [No exception applies, so [the action] is [stayed / dismissed] under s 12(1) / exception [(x)] applies, so [defendant]'s stay is decided at common law (J4.1)].
J1.5 SCOPE OF THE AGREEMENT (write before strong cause: if [the claim] or [the party] is outside [clause X], ordinary Spiliada applies instead (J4.1 / J4.2))
  • Governing Law Per C&Y, subject-matter and party scope are for [the proper law of clause X], not the lex fori. If [law X] is unproved, Singapore construction applies by the presumption of similarity, with [contra proferentem] as a fallback where [the governing law] recognises it.
J1.5.1 Subject-Matter Scope
  • Broad Construction (+) [Claimant] argues [the tort / statutory claim] is outside [clause X]. Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes arising out of [their relationship] decided in one forum unless [the words] clearly exclude them.
  • Reframing Rarely Escapes (+) Per The Jian He (and Rickshaw), [claimant] may frame its claim in [tort / equity], but reframing [a contractual dispute] rarely escapes a widely drafted [clause X].
  • Separate Agreement Within Scope (+) Similar to Trisuryo, where a trust claim resting on a separate oral agreement fell within the Indonesian EJC because it contradicted the deeds' warranty that the shares were free of others' rights, [claimant]'s claim under [side agreement] falls within [clause X] since it [contradicts / turns on] [a term of contract].
  • No Presumption at the Outset (−) Per COSCO (CA), the inquiry does not start from a presumption that all competing claims go to one forum; it depends on [the nature of the claims] and [clause X's express words], "forum fragmentation [being] a fact of life". Where [the claim] falls outside, fragmentation is accepted (Asiana).
  • Tests Are Tools (±) Per COSCO (CA), the causative-connection, closely-knitted and parallel-claims tests are tools, not formulae. A [tort claim] that can be recast in contract plainly falls within, and so may one met by [contractual cross-claims] from the same incident (The Angelic Grace), e.g., [an allision during cargo loading].
  • Jurisdiction Clauses Too Though COSCO (CA) concerned [an arbitration clause], scope is construed the same way for [an EJC] (Fiona Trust; per C&Y), so [defendant] may rely on it for [the tort claim].
  • Global Partners (+, persuasive) Per Global Partners (NSWCA), "in connection with" in [clause X] cannot be read down, and an EJC is construed as liberally as [an arbitration clause], securing one coherent forum for [all disputes from the relationship]. A globally operating [contract] invites multiplicity, so there is no basis for a narrow reading.
J1.5.2 Multiple Contracts and Competing Clauses
  • Extended Fiona Trust (±) [Clause X] sits in [Contract A], and [the dispute] arises under [Contract B], which has no clause. Per Allianz v Goh Andress, adopting Terre Neuve:
    • (a) Words: [clause X]'s words must be fairly capable of covering [Contract B] disputes.
    • (b) Presumption: [clause X] normally applies where [the parties] are the same and the contracts are interdependent, concluded together as one package, and/or cover [the same subject matter].
  • Nature and Ultimate Question Per Allianz, this is construction of [clause X], not incorporation into or variation of [Contract B], and the factors are guides. The question is whether [the outcome] is one the parties, as rational businesspeople, sensibly envisaged; Trisuryo is an earlier multi-contract example.
  • Competing Clauses (±) Where [Contract A] and [Contract B] contain competing clauses, there is no extended Fiona Trust presumption (Allianz). Per Bunge, adopting Oei Hong Leong, apply the clause the parties objectively intended, i.e. the one with which [the dispute] has the closest connection in its "pith and substance", presuming commercial parties do not intend [similar claims] to fall under inconsistent clauses.
    • Application: Similar to Bunge, where the Singapore EJCs in the only contracts between the two disputants governed their negative declaration claim, [clause X] governs because it is in the only contract between [claimant] and [defendant].
  • Court Clause Plus Arbitration Clause (±) Where [contract] contains both [an arbitration clause] and [a Singapore court clause], per the slides they may be reconciled as arbitration for [disputes], with the court clause conferring supervisory jurisdiction over [the arbitration].
J1.5.3 Party Scope

(argue privity first)

  • Privity First (−) [The non-party] invokes, or is sued in the teeth of, [clause X] in [the A–B contract]. Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether [clause X] avails claims against [third parties] is construction, and, in keeping with privity, it usually will not absent "a quite clear indication otherwise".
  • Third Party Relying: Proper Law Per C&Y, [the third party] may rely on [clause X] if [its governing law] permits. Per VKC v VJZ, CRTPA s 2(1)(b) ("purports to confer a benefit") does not apply to an EJC, as it confers [a procedural, not substantive, right] and the Act deals expressly only with [arbitration clauses] (s 9).
    • Critique (+): per Chong (seminar), the "procedural" label is wrong: if [an EJC] were merely procedural, its breach could not found [an ASI] or [damages] (J1.7).
  • Third Party Relying: Routes Left Per VKC v VJZ, [the third party] might "arguably" rely on s 2(1)(a) ([clause X] expressly provides it may enforce) or s 2(3) (identified by [name / class / description]); the equitable route (Hai Jiang 1401) was left open. So draft [an express third-party right] if protection is wanted.
  • Third Party Bound (−) Generally no, by privity, unless [the third party] takes by [assignment / subrogation / agency] or otherwise claims under [contract], taking the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401; J6.5.2).
  • Closely Connected Non-Parties (+, persuasive) Similar to Global Partners, where group companies named as "Indemnified Persons" who took part in the very decisions complained of were "not strangers" ("there are non parties and non parties"), so the EJC bound the claimant in its claims against them, [clause X] binds [claimant] in its claims against [the affiliates], who [implemented the contract / hold contractual indemnities].
  • Counter (−) Per Hive Marketing (NSWCA), a stay of related claims against [non-parties] is not automatic or presumptive merely because of [a risk of multiplicity]. After Asiana and COSCO (CA), Global Partners is an example of the "quite clear indication", not the default, so it fails where [the affiliates] are [strangers linked only by common ownership].
  • Bypass Manoeuvre Where [claimant] sues only [the non-party] abroad to sidestep [clause X], though [the contracting party] is the obvious defendant, the suit may be restrained as vexatious even if [clause X] does not bind [the non-party] (Clearlake, in Asiana; J6.5.2).
J1.6 EXISTENCE, VALIDITY AND GOVERNING LAW OF THE CLAUSE (write where [a party] denies the clause, or attacks the contract containing it)
  • Threshold and Burden Per Vinmar, [the party relying on clause X] must show a good arguable case that it exists and applies to [the dispute], i.e. "the better of the argument": more than prima facie, less than a balance of probabilities, and not a "much better argument". The court may decide [questions of law] but will not resolve [contested facts].
  • Incorporation and Service Out Per C&Y, whether [clause X] was incorporated, e.g., by [a course of dealing], is for [the proper law]. Where [clause X] founds service out, [claimant] keeps that burden inter partes (J3.2).
  • Governing Law of the Clause Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] may in principle have its own law, but absent [contrary provision] it follows [the main contract's proper law], an express choice for the contract implying the same for the clause. Only one party can have the better of the argument on [the governing law], and the court applies that view throughout.
  • Separability Per C&Y, separability is a matter of substantive contract law, so ask whether [the clause's governing law] recognises it. If [contract] is [voidable but unrescinded], [clause X] operates.
  • Attacking the Contract, Relying on the Clause (±) [Defendant] alleges [contract] is [voidable for misrepresentation / void for fraud] yet invokes [clause X] to stay [claimant]'s action. Per CIMB, where the parties dispute existence or validity (rather than agreeing there was no contract), [the dispute] is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid.
    • Why: otherwise a mere allegation of [fraud] would neutralise [clause X] (CIMB, adopting The Parouth and Ash v Lloyd's).
  • Infection Test Per PT Selecta and CIMB, the question is whether [the vitiating factor] also infects [clause X]. It does only where there was clearly [no concluded contract at all] or [non est factum]; [fraud / duress] in procuring the contract, or [a common mistake as to subject matter] (CIMB), does not touch consent to [clause X].
  • Application Similar to PT Selecta, where the parties expressly brought disputes as to [the contract's] "validity" within the clause (per C&Y), [defendant]'s plea of [misrepresentation as to X] does not reach [clause X].
