J6.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP
  1. Preliminary points (J6.0.2): is it an ASI (Oro Negro); power [s 4(10) CLA / s 18(2) SCJA / s 12A IAA / s 4(10A) CLA]; [interim / permanent] (Grover v SetClear); [General Division / SICC] (BCS v Baker); a foreign refusal to stay is no bar (Lakshmi); apply promptly (Sun Travels).
  2. Pick the basis (J6.0.1): the Kirkham factors are no box-ticking statute, and [applicant] must name its [contractual / vexation / abuse of process] basis, as the elements differ (Cooperative Muratori; slide 20):
    • [Contractual]: amenability + breach of [clause X] + no strong reasons; natural forum and injustice drop out (Cooperative Muratori).
    • [Vexation]: amenability + sufficient interest, usually [Singapore as natural forum] + vexation + no undue injustice to [respondent] (Kirkham).
    • [Abuse of process]: amenability + self-evident interest; [respondent]'s [foreign advantage] is no answer (BCS v Baker).
  3. Amenability (J6.1): [respondent] [submitted / was validly served]; always required (Cooperative Muratori; C&Y); cf Akai.
  4. Sufficient interest (J6.2): [Singapore EJC / NEJC / SICC clause] (J6.2.1); [Singapore's process] (J6.2.2); alternative fora (J6.2.3); single forum (J6.2.4); dual fora (J6.2.5); [foreign EJC] (J6.2.6); [foreign-seated arbitration] (J6.2.7).
  5. Legitimate interest, any one suffices (J6.3; Sun Travels; BCS v Baker): breach of [clause X], then strong reasons, then delay (J6.3.1); vexation, clearest cases only (J6.3.2); abuse of [Singapore's process] (J6.3.3); [Singapore public policy] (J6.3.4).
  6. No undue injustice to [respondent] (J6.4): vexation only; [undertakings] neutralise; a cynically created advantage counts for little; conclusion (J6.4.1).
  7. Special situations (J6.5): anti-anti-suit (J6.5.1); [third parties], slide 19's four scenarios (J6.5.2); [HCCCA] (J6.5.3); anti-enforcement injunctions (pointer J6.5.4; full in J7.6).
J6.0.1 Quick Application Template
  • Starter: Presently, [applicant] seeks an [interim / permanent] ASI from the [General Division / SICC] restraining [respondent] from [continuing [claim] in [foreign court]]. Per SNIA and Lakshmi, as it indirectly interferes with [foreign court], it issues only where the ends of justice require, with caution. [Applicant] bears the burden (Kirkham; C&Y) and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori).
  • One ASI per foreign proceeding: Per Chong (seminar), analyse [foreign claim] and [foreign ASI application] separately: under [a Singapore NEJC], suing abroad is no breach (vexation, J6.3.2), but seeking [a foreign ASI against Suit X] is (contractual, J6.3.1.2).
  • [Contractual ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); suing in [foreign court] breaches [clause X], construed under [proper law] (J6.3.1); and [respondent] shows no strong reasons, its [delay / third-party / fragmentation] point failing (J6.3.1.4) (Cooperative Muratori). Natural forum does not arise.
  • [Vexation ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); Singapore has interest as [the clearly more appropriate forum / protector of [insolvency / Singapore-centred dealings]] (J6.2.3–J6.2.4); [foreign proceedings] are vexatious for [bad faith / relitigation / a lost contribution claim] (J6.3.2); and [respondent] loses [no legitimate advantage / one neutralised by [undertaking]] (J6.4).
  • [Abuse of Process ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); Singapore's interest in protecting [Suit X judgment] is self-evident (J6.2.2); and [foreign claim] [relitigates / collaterally attacks] [Suit X] (J6.3.3). [Respondent]'s [foreign advantage] is no answer (BCS v Baker).
  • Result: The ASI [is / is not] granted [on [applicant]'s undertaking to [X] / only until [preconditions in clause X] are met] [, though delay let [foreign proceedings] reach [stage]] (J6.3.1.5; J6.4.1).
J6.0.2 Preliminary Points

(Use only the points the facts raise.)

  • Is It an ASI? Per Oro Negro, an ASI restrains [respondent] from commencing or continuing [proceedings in [foreign court]]. Presently, the order only stops [respondent] [purporting to act for [applicant]]. Similar to Oro Negro, it is not an ASI though it practically ends [foreign proceedings], so this framework does not apply (C&Y).
    • [Statutory Moratorium]: Per C&Y, ss 64–65 IRDA let the court restrain [local / foreign] proceedings against [company] proposing [a scheme / compromise]: in effect a statutory ASI, outside this general framework.
  • Source of Power Per C&Y, the [General Division] may grant injunctions "just or convenient" under s 4(10) CLA, and has the s 18(2) SCJA First Schedule powers (para 14; the handout also lists para 5). Presently, [applicant] seeks a [permanent] ASI, whose source is unsettled:
    • (−) Per Swift-Fortune (CA, arguably obiter as a Mareva case) and Hilton (HC, Ang J, bound by it), s 4(10) is [interlocutory] only, and [permanent] power lies in s 18(2) with para 14 SCJA.
    • (+) Per R1 International (HC), and Chan, Tan and Poon on a plain reading (per C&Y), s 4(10) also gives [permanent] power. The CA in Sun Travels merely noted Ang J's view, so it turns on whether "by an interlocutory order" governs [injunctions] or only [receivers] (C&Y).
  • Arbitration Per R1 International and C&Y, an [interim] ASI in aid of [Singapore / foreign]-seated arbitration issues under s 12A(2) with s 12 IAA, whatever [the seat] (s 12A(1)). A [permanent] ASI for [a foreign seat] is not found in s 12A (J6.2.7).
    • Limits (−): The court may refuse where [the foreign seat] makes it inappropriate (s 12A(3)), and acts only if [tribunal] cannot act effectively (s 12A(6)). Non-urgent orders need [tribunal]'s permission or written agreement (s 12A(5)); urgent ones preserve [evidence / assets] (s 12A(4)).
  • Proceedings Abroad Per C&Y, s 4(10A) CLA (in force 2022) gives power to grant interim relief, if just or convenient, in aid of [civil or commercial] proceedings [commenced / to be commenced] in [Court B], subject to ss 4(10B)–(10D). Power is not discretion (J6.2.5).
  • Governing Law Per C&Y, interim remedies raising comity, such as ASIs, are governed solely by the lex fori, so [Singapore law] decides whether to restrain [foreign proceedings], whatever [the lex causae] (C1.3).
  • Interim vs Permanent Presently, [applicant] seeks an [interim / permanent] ASI. The same Kirkham framework applies, but per Grover v SetClear, an interim ASI issues "sparingly and with great caution", and [respondent] gets the benefit of the doubt where [the facts] are unclear (−). A permanent ASI after [a merits judgment declaring breach of clause X] needs less caution (+) (C&Y).
    • Practicality: Per C&Y, an interim ASI is often a practical necessity against [anticipated foreign proceedings], its effect often "virtually that of a permanent" one, and it may be sought before [respondent] sues in [foreign court].
  • SICC Per BCS v Baker and C&Y, the same framework governs [the SICC]. If seised by [transfer from the General Division], it applies unmodified and natural forum stays relevant; if seised under [a written SICC agreement], sufficient interest and strong reasons are modified (J6.2.1; J6.3.1.3).
  • If [Respondent] Ignores the ASI Breach is contempt, so the ASI bites only if [respondent] has [assets / a presence] here (SNIA; C&Y). A [foreign judgment] obtained in breach is refused recognition as contrary to public policy (Nimbus; C&Y; J7.2.4), and [damages for breach of clause X] may be claimed (J1.7).
  • Foreign Court Refused a Stay (+) Presently, [foreign court] refused to stay [foreign proceedings]. Per Lakshmi, comity does not generally bar an ASI if Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum and [respondent] sued vexatiously. Similar to SNIA, granted though Texas had refused a stay, [foreign court]'s refusal is not decisive.
    • No estoppel (+): Per Lakshmi, [foreign court]'s natural forum ruling raises no issue estoppel against [the ASI application]: the ASI test also needs vexation, and the outcome should not turn on [scheduling] (J7.3.2.3).
    • Comity (−): [Respondent] says [foreign court] is best placed to decide its own natural forum (Amchem; Barclays v Homan; Deutsche Bank v Highland, per Lakshmi). Per Lakshmi, most cases sit between Airbus's "stricter" approach (ASIs only to protect [jurisdiction / public policy]) and the "laxer" one (any vexation suffices).
    • Middle ground (+): Per Lakshmi, a sufficient connection plus [unconscionable conduct] breaches no comity, absent exceptional circumstances. Deference is weaker where [respondent] carved [issue] out of pending [Suit X] to sue abroad, and a refusal given while [the Singapore appeal] was pending should not decide the outcome by scheduling.
    • Timing (must write if [applicant] waited): Per C&Y, [applicant] should object in [foreign court] and seek the ASI here simultaneously. Delay is not excused by [pending objections abroad] (Sun Travels), and comity weighs more the later [the application] (Lakshmi) (J6.3.1.5).
J6.1 AMENABILITY

(Always required, whatever the basis: the court enjoins only [a respondent] within its in personam jurisdiction, against whom the ASI is effective (Cooperative Muratori; Koh Kay Yew; C&Y). Find jurisdiction in J2 / J3 and state the result here.)

  • Submission or Valid Service (+) Presently, [respondent] is amenable, having [submitted by [appearing / defending / counterclaiming] in [Suit X]] or been validly served [in / out of] Singapore (Koh Kay Yew; Westbridge v Mittal; C&Y). Per Cooperative Muratori, being within the court's in personam jurisdiction is what amenability requires.
  • Claimant Here (+) Per Glencore, [respondent], having sued [applicant] in [Suit X], submitted to all its incidents, including [counterclaims] and related relief such as [an ASI] (J2.2.2).
  • No Challenge (+) Similar to BCS v Baker, where the appellants, BCS being a Singapore company, appeared without objecting to jurisdiction, [respondent] [defended / took part in] [Suit X] without contesting jurisdiction, and is amenable.
  • Service Out Alone May Not Suffice (−) Similar to Akai, where the respondent, though served out on ostensible evidence, was not amenable as it had no presence or assets here and only opposed the ASI, [respondent] has [no [office / assets] in Singapore] and [only resists the ASI].
    • Reply (+): The slides contrast Kirkham, and the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service or submission suffices. [Respondent]'s lack of [assets] goes only to [effectiveness] (J6.0.2).
  • Not Amenable (−) If [respondent] is [abroad and has not submitted], [applicant] must first obtain permission to serve [the ASI claim] out under O 8 r 1 ROC 2021 (J3.1). Without it, no ASI issues, however vexatious [foreign proceedings] are.
J6.2 SUFFICIENT INTEREST

(Classify first; use only the matching subsection. Natural forum is only a proxy: it proves interest, but Singapore may have interest without it, and there must be a good reason for Singapore, not [foreign court], to stop [foreign proceedings] (BCS v Baker, citing Barclays v Homan). Contractual ASI: natural forum does not arise (Cooperative Muratori); a Singapore clause supplies the connection (J6.2.1), but if Singapore is not chosen the point stays live (J6.2.6–J6.2.7), hence slide 20's "(b)(?)".)

J6.2.1 Jurisdiction Agreement for Singapore
  • Singapore EJC (+) Presently, [clause X] gives the [General Division] exclusive jurisdiction. Per Westbridge v Mittal and C&Y, [clause X] itself supplies the connection, even if [the parties / the events] have no other link with Singapore; no natural forum inquiry is needed.
  • Why (+) Per Cooperative Muratori (citing Turner v Grovit and UniCredit), [applicant] need not show [Singapore] is more appropriate; the agreement does that. It should take more to sanction a breach of [clause X] than to deny [respondent] its natural forum (Yeo, endorsed in Vinmar).
  • Singapore NEJC (+) Presently, [clause X] is a Singapore NEJC governed by [Singapore law]. Arguably, per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, a defendant sued here must show strong cause not to be held to its submission, so [clause X] works like an EJC and supplies the connection.
    • Contrast: [The NEJC] supplies interest only; suing in [foreign court] is not itself a breach (J6.3.1.2).
  • SICC Clause, Exclusive or Not (+) Presently, [clause X] is a written [exclusive / non-exclusive] SICC agreement and [the claim] is international and commercial. Per C&Y, Spiliada is irrelevant: O 2 r 3 SICC Rules 2021 supplies the connection test (J5.3).
    • Test: The SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its [international and commercial character] or [an abuse of its process] (O 2 r 3(2)), and not solely because [the action] is connected to [foreign state] (O 2 r 3(3)).
    • Exception (−): Not so if [the claim is not international and commercial] or [suing in the SICC is abusive, e.g., tactical delay] (J6.3.1.3).
J6.2.2 Protecting Singapore's Own Process
  • Self-Evident Interest (+) Presently, [respondent]'s [foreign claim] abuses Singapore's process by [relitigating [Suit X]]. Per BCS v Baker, natural forum is then irrelevant: Singapore's interest in protecting its processes, jurisdiction and judgments is "generally self-evident", and only it can judge [the need for protection].
  • Concurrent Proceedings (−) (Non-contract cases.) Presently, [Singapore action] and [foreign action] are both pending, so per Baker v BCS (SICC) and C&Y, [applicant] must show Singapore is the natural forum (J6.2.3).
  • Consecutive Proceedings (+) Presently, Singapore has given judgment in [Suit X], so it has interest to protect [the judgment] from collateral attack by [respondent] relitigating res judicata issues abroad (Baker v BCS; C&Y). Per BCS v Baker, the need extends to [anticipated judgments] but is underscored once judgment exists.
  • Which Is It? Per BCS v Baker, ask when [the specific claim] to be enjoined was raised in [foreign court], not when the actions began. Presently, [respondent] raised [claim] on [date], after [judgment / dismissal of the appeal], so it is consecutive. (C&Y's footnote states this the other way; follow the judgment.)
  • Resisting Enforcement (−) Per Baker v BCS (SICC) and C&Y, it is a "fine line": if [respondent] merely resists [applicant]'s enforcement of [Singapore judgment] in [foreign court], Singapore generally leaves [foreign court] to decide that judgment's effect there.
  • Foreign Judgment Already Given (−) Per BCS v Baker (citing ED & F Man v Haryanto), an ASI stopping [respondent] relying abroad on [foreign court]'s [judgment] is ordinarily inappropriate, and [applicant] needs exceptional circumstances (Sun Travels; J7.6).
  • Interest Without Natural Forum (+) Similar to Shell v Coral Oil (per BCS v Baker), where England had a "very strong interest" in shielding a party already protected by its ASI from further vexatious Lebanese claims, Singapore may protect [applicant] from [further claims] after [earlier ASI / Suit X], though [foreign court] is also a natural forum.
J6.2.3 Alternative Fora: Singapore Is One Forum
  • Natural Forum (+) Presently, [the dispute] can be heard in Singapore or [foreign court]. Per BCS v Baker and Airbus, an ASI is normally granted where Singapore is the natural forum and the other requirements are met. Per Lakshmi, [applicant] must show Singapore is "clearly the more appropriate forum", weighing the quality, not quantity, of [the JIO factors] (J4.1.2).
  • Lakshmi: Real Substance (+) Similar to Lakshmi, where a BVI share mattered only because its subsidiaries held 22 Singapore condominium units, [respondent]'s claim to [asset in [foreign state]] is in truth about [Singapore property], so [foreign state]'s link is only [place of incorporation].
  • Lakshmi: Witnesses (+) Per Lakshmi, video links reduce the weight of witness location, but [third-party witnesses, e.g., [bank officers]] compellable here and not shown compellable in [foreign court] matter where [the dispute] is factual.
  • Lakshmi: Overlap (+) Per Lakshmi, different reliefs in [foreign court] do not show different issues: as [respondent]'s [foreign claim] and [Suit X] are binary, proof of one disproves the other.
  • Lakshmi: Little Weight (−) Per Lakshmi, [governing law] matters little where [both systems] are common law and the issues factual. Little weight goes to [a place of performance assuming [respondent]'s claim succeeds], [a place of enforcement offset by [applicant]'s undertaking] or [the place of an oral telephone contract]; [residence in third states] is neutral.
  • Natural Forum Alone Is Not Enough (−) Per SNIA and C&Y, natural forum alone never justifies an ASI, or Singapore could arrogate to itself [a mere difference of view] with [foreign court] on the natural forum. In SNIA, the ASI turned on the lost contribution claim (J6.3.2). Presently, [applicant] must also show [prejudice in [foreign court]].
  • Advantages Are Not Connecting Factors (+) Similar to SNIA, where Texas lawyers' evidence-gathering, the contingency fee system and an early trial were advantages to the plaintiffs, not connecting factors making Texas the natural forum, [respondent]'s [pre-trial steps / lawyers' expertise] in [foreign court] do not shift the natural forum (J6.4).
J6.2.4 Single Forum: Only [Foreign Court] Can Hear the Claim
  • Framing (must write) Presently, [respondent]'s [claim, e.g., [foreign antitrust claim]] lies only in [foreign court], so Singapore can never be the natural forum. Per Airbus and BCS v Baker, the questions are whether Singapore still has sufficient interest and whether pursuing [claim] is unconscionable. Per C&Y, the ASI is especially harsh, denying [respondent] its only redress.
    • Not Spiliada availability: Per C&Y, "single forum" means [Singapore law] gives no cause of action, so the question is [unconscionability], not [appropriateness]; Spiliada availability asks only whether [a court] can hear the claim.
  • Insolvency (+) Per BCS v Baker (citing Stichting Shell), [Singapore] has interest where the ASI protects its jurisdiction in administering [the insolvency of [company]] against [a creditor suing abroad] (J6.3.3).
  • Predominantly Singaporean Dealings (+) Similar to Midland Bank v Laker, where an English bank's dealings with Laker were English banking business under English law, "overwhelmingly English" in character (Airbus), [applicant]'s dealings with [respondent] were [conducted in Singapore / under Singapore law], so the ASI is consistent with comity.
    • Contrast (−): If [applicant]'s dealings were [in [third state] under its law], an ASI merely because [respondent] is amenable here would be "surprising" (Airbus, on a hypothetical Indian bank).
  • Singapore Public Policy (+) Per BCS v Baker and Airbus (citing Laker v Sabena), Singapore has interest where the ASI protects [Singapore public policy on [X]]; in very exceptional cases this may override even [a foreign EJC] (C&Y) (J6.3.4).
  • Not Unconscionable (−) Similar to British Airways v Laker, where BA and BCal, by taking licences to fly UK–US routes, voluntarily submitted to US antitrust law, [applicant] voluntarily [submitted to [foreign regime]], so [respondent]'s suit is not unconscionable and no ASI issues.
J6.2.5 Dual Fora: Singapore Is Neither
  • General Rule (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [Court A] while the natural forum is [Court B]. Per Airbus, comity generally requires Singapore to have sufficient interest before indirectly interfering. Per Akai, [Court A] and [Court B] may legitimately differ, and Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (C&Y; heeded in R1 International).
  • Natural Forum Powerless (−) Similar to Airbus, where India, the natural forum, could not reach the claimants, [Court B]'s inability to [restrain [respondent]] does not justify Singapore acting: "only the courts of an interested jurisdiction can act". That [Court A] does not apply [forum non conveniens] is also not enough (Airbus).
  • Extreme Cases (+) Per Airbus and C&Y, an ASI may issue without sufficient connection in "extreme cases", e.g., where [foreign state]'s conduct forfeits the respect comity normally requires. Presently, [describe [state interference / sham proceedings] in [Court A]].
  • Strong Reasons by Analogy (+) Per R1 International (HC, obiter; C&Y), a permanent ASI supporting [a foreign arbitration] may issue on strong reasons, e.g., [the seat lacks effective interim measures]. Arguably, by analogy, strong reasons exist where [Court B] [cannot grant ASIs].
  • s 4(10A) CLA (±) Arguably, s 4(10A) now gives power to grant interim relief, possibly [an interim ASI], in aid of [Court B]'s proceedings (slide 18). But it confers power only: Singapore must still justify interfering with [Court A] (Airbus; Akai).
J6.2.6 EJC for a Foreign Court
  • Go to the Chosen Court (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [Court A] in breach of an EJC for [Court B]. Per C&Y, [applicant] should ordinarily seek the ASI from [Court B]. Similar to Akai, where the insurer had not applied to the English court though Akai, having sued there, was amenable to it, [applicant] has not applied to [Court B].
    • Reply (+): per Chong (seminar), Akai is old and its "busybody" point may carry less force today, especially where [Court B] is in [an HCCCA Contracting State] (J6.5.3).
  • Reasons to Come Here (+) [Applicant] argues [Court B] [does not grant ASIs / lacks the remedy], or that it must shield its [Singapore assets] from [Court A]'s judgment (C&Y). For HCCCA states, see J6.5.3.
    • Rebuttal (−): Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then. As in Akai, where the insurer sued here only to protect its Singapore assets, any later enforcement against [applicant]'s [assets] is "an entirely different matter", met by resisting [recognition] then (J7).
J6.2.7 Arbitration Seated in [Foreign Seat]
  • Busybody Risk (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [foreign court] in breach of [arbitration agreement] seated in [foreign seat]. Per C&Y, Singapore generally refrains from ASIs supporting foreign arbitration. Per R1 International (obiter), a permanent ASI needs strong reasons, e.g., [the seat lacks effective interim measures]; interim ASIs come from s 12A IAA (J6.0.2).
  • Contract Supplies the Connection (+) Per UniCredit (UKSC, persuasive), Spiliada is not the test: parties should be held to their bargain by any court before which they "can properly be brought" (Enka), and Airbus's sufficient-interest rule was tied to non-contractual cases. An ASI enforcing [an arbitration agreement] always comes from a court that is neither [the natural] nor [the agreed forum].
  • Comity and Connection (+) Per UniCredit, comity has little role where [foreign court's state] and [seat state] are New York Convention states. Presently, [arbitration agreement] is governed by [Singapore law], a substantial connection like the English-law rights in UniCredit; whether [personal jurisdiction alone] suffices was left open (IPOC, noted in UniCredit).
  • Applying Here Is Not a Breach (+) Per UniCredit (cf Model Law art 9), [arbitration agreement] does not impliedly bar applying to [a court] for relief holding the other party to it, though choosing [foreign seat] implies no agreement to sue in [Singapore].
J6.3 LEGITIMATE INTEREST (ANY ONE SUFFICES)
  • Choosing the Basis Presently, [applicant] relies on [breach of [clause X] (J6.3.1) / vexation (J6.3.2) / abuse of process (J6.3.3) / public policy (J6.3.4)]. Per C&Y, the categories are not closed. Per BCS v Baker, abuse invokes the inherent power (disruption to [Singapore's processes]); vexation invokes equity (the personal equities); the overriding test is the interests of justice.
  • Keep Them Apart (must write if run together) Per Cooperative Muratori, a contractual ASI is a distinct species (citing VKC), and though several strands may operate on [the facts], they are conceptually distinct: [applicant] should not argue that breaching [clause X] is itself vexatious. Breach needs no vexation (Sun Travels; C&Y).
J6.3.1 Breach of Agreement
J6.3.1.1 Step 1: Breach
  • Exclusive Clause Breached (+) Per C&Y, breach is a question of interpretation under [proper law]. Presently, [respondent] breached [clause X], an exclusive [Singapore / SICC / arbitration] clause, by suing in [foreign court]. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no unconscionability is needed, and the ASI ordinarily issues absent strong reasons (J6.3.1.4).
  • Rationale Per Finaport, the basis is equity's jurisdiction to ensure [contractual bargains] are honoured, on the "clear and simple ground" that [respondent] promised not to sue in [foreign court] (The Angelic Grace, per Sun Travels). Comity matters less, as Singapore enforces [the bargain] rather than claiming [the dispute] (Sun Travels; C&Y).
  • Other Agreements (+) Per C&Y, the same applies to suits in breach of [an arbitration agreement] or [an agreement not to sue], e.g., the settlement in Grover v SetClear (permanent ASI upheld), and in principle [a mediation agreement] valid under its proper law whose enforcement is not contrary to Singapore public policy.
    • Caution (−): Per C&Y (BTN v BTP), suing is not always a breach of [an arbitration agreement]: [a conditional clause] may let parties sue in [court X] until [arbitration is invoked].
  • Multi-Tiered Clause (+) Similar to Finaport, where "shall first attempt" negotiation, then SMC mediation, then litigation was mandatory, [clause X]'s ["shall first"] wording makes [negotiation / mediation] a precondition, so suing in [foreign court] first breaches it. Per Finaport, there is no principled distinction between [tiered clauses] and EJCs or arbitration agreements.
    • Scope: Per Finaport, suing is not a per se breach, so the ASI restrains [respondent] only until [the preconditions in [clause X]] are met, with liberty to apply. A non-contractual ASI was refused there.
    • Impracticality no answer: Per Finaport (citing Don King), [a beneficiary] suing on [the trustee]'s rights cannot complain the tiers are impractical; it takes [the bargain] as it is (J6.5.2).
  • Choice of Law Clause (−) Presently, [applicant] says [respondent] breached [clause Y], choosing [law X], by suing in [foreign court] to apply [foreign law]. Per Ace Insurance, such a clause is ordinarily declaratory, not promissory, so it founds no implied promise not to sue where [law X] will not apply; "very clear language" is needed (C2.5).
    • No breach anyway (−): Similar to Ace, where the Californian court would in fact have applied the chosen Australian law, [foreign court] would apply [law X], so [the premise] fails.
    • Counter (+): Briggs argues that suing to defeat the chosen law "looks like" a breach (considered in Ace). Argue this only if [clause Y] expressly promises [not to sue where [law X] will not apply].
J6.3.1.2 Singapore NEJC: Generally No Breach
  • No Breach (−) Presently, [clause X] is a Singapore NEJC. Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, suing in [foreign court] is not ordinarily a breach, the parties having accepted parallel proceedings; only a challenge to [Singapore]'s jurisdiction, e.g., [a stay application in [Suit X]], needs strong cause. So [applicant] relies on vexation (J6.3.2) or abuse (J6.3.3).
  • Breach Arguable (+) Per the handout, Shanghai Turbo's narrow-waiver reading implies a promise not to object to [Singapore]'s jurisdiction. Presently, [respondent] did not merely sue in [foreign court] but sought [an ASI / a declaration] there [to stop [Suit X]], in substance such an objection and so a breach.
    • Construction: Per C&Y, breach turns on construing [clause X] under [proper law], e.g., whether it makes [the court first seised] exclusive.
  • Suing to Stop Enforcement of Rights (±) Similar to Sabah Shipyard v Pakistan, where Pakistan's local injunction against calling on a guarantee stopped Sabah suing in England under an English NEJC, [respondent]'s [foreign application] aims to stop [applicant] [enforcing [right] in Singapore]. (+) The English CA called this "clearly a breach of contract".
    • But (−): Per UBS v Telesto and C&Y, Sabah is a vexation case: the breach lay in suing to stop Sabah enforcing its contractual rights, not in breaching the NEJC. So plead [vexation] (J6.3.2) in the alternative to [breach].
J6.3.1.3 SICC Written Jurisdiction Agreement

(Only where [the SICC] was seised under a written agreement; after [transfer from the General Division], apply J6.3.1.4 unmodified (C&Y).)

  • Starter Per C&Y, the SICC may decline only where exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its [international and commercial character] or [an abuse of its process] (O 2 r 3(2)), so upholding [clause X] is even stronger than in the General Division. But an ASI, unlike a stay, affects [foreign court], so comity still matters (Donohue).
  • Exclusive SICC Clause (+) Presently, [clause X] is an exclusive SICC clause. Per C&Y, arguably the strong reasons test does not apply at all, so [respondent]'s [foreign proceedings] in breach should always be restrained.
  • Modified Test (−) Alternatively, per C&Y, strong reasons are modified to fold in O 2 r 3(2). Presently, [applicant] waited [period] without good reason, taking a tactical "wait and see" approach while [foreign proceedings] reached [stage]. An SICC taking its international character seriously should respect comity and refuse; [such tactics] may instead go to discretion (J6.3.1.5).
  • Non-Exclusive SICC Clause (−) Presently, [clause X] is non-exclusive, so the parties implicitly accepted suits elsewhere. Per C&Y, the SICC should refrain where [foreign proceedings] began before [the SICC proceedings] on [date]; [applicant] will likely rely on vexation (J6.3.2).
J6.3.1.4 Step 2: Strong Reasons (Burden on [Respondent])
  • Starter (must write) As [respondent] sued in [foreign court] in breach of [clause X], the ASI ordinarily issues unless [respondent] shows strong reasons (Sun Travels; Cooperative Muratori; Donohue). Per C&Y, this is in practice the strong cause test for stays (J4.3), consistency between the two mattering (Vinmar). [Respondent]'s [lost juridical advantage] may count here (Cooperative Muratori).
  • Applicant Itself in Breach (−) Presently, [clause X] lets [respondent] sue in [foreign court], so its suit breaches nothing, but [applicant] promised to submit there. Per Chong (answer scheme), seeking the ASI is then [applicant]'s own breach, so ask who bears strong cause: arguably [applicant], as the party in breach.
  • Third Parties or Claims Outside the Clause (−) Similar to Donohue, where New York proceedings in breach of an English EJC continued because they involved non-parties and RICO claims outside the clause, [foreign proceedings] involve [third party C], not bound by [clause X], and [claim] outside its scope. Per C&Y, an ASI would fragment the litigation, risking inconsistent outcomes.
    • Reply (+): Per Asiana, fragmentation "should not be overstated", especially for [arbitration agreements]; per UniCredit, for arbitration, parallel proceedings carry no weight in themselves. Where [respondent] deliberately split [contract and tort claims], the fragmentation is its own (Clearlake, in Hai Jiang).
  • Foreign Property (−) Per Impala v Wanxiang and C&Y, enforceability abroad may be a strong reason where [claim] concerns [property / shares] in [foreign state], especially to recover it, as the situs courts control it. Presently, a Singapore judgment on [recovery of [property]] would be ineffective in [foreign state].
    • Reply (+): [Respondent] refused [applicant]'s reasonable offer to [arbitrate], which would have avoided that prejudice (Impala). A bare "unenforceable in some places" argument fails, as that risk was foreseeable when [clause X] was agreed (Impala; Westbridge v Mittal; C&Y).
  • Applicant's Submission Abroad (−) Per UniCredit, the court's discretion, like delay, may weigh [applicant] having submitted to [foreign court], e.g., by [defending on the merits / counterclaiming] (J6.3.1.5). Presently, [applicant] [took [step] in [foreign proceedings]], arguably waiving [clause X].
    • Contrast (+): Per IGCF v Al Jomaih (PC), applying abroad for [a stay in favour of arbitration] or to [recall an injunction] is protest, not submission; the same test applies for ASIs as for enforcement (J7.1.2.4). But contesting jurisdiction does not excuse delay (J6.3.1.5).
  • Foreign Court Bound to Decline (+) Per UniCredit, comity has little role where [foreign state] is bound by treaty to decline jurisdiction, e.g., by art II(3) New York Convention for [an arbitration agreement] (arguably also art 6 HCCCA for [an exclusive COCA]: J6.5.3). Presently, [foreign court] [ignored / was barred by [local law] from] that duty.
  • No Strong Reasons (+) On balance, [respondent]'s [reason] is [a foreseeable commercial risk / an advantage it bargained away], so per C&Y the general rule applies and [clause X] is enforced by ASI.
J6.3.1.5 Delay and Comity
  • Comity Re-Enters With Delay (−) Presently, [applicant] waited [period] after [foreign proceedings] began on [date]. Per Sun Travels (following Ecobank and Sea Powerful), comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far [foreign proceedings] have progressed matters more than the delay's length, as an ASI then wastes more of [foreign court]'s resources (C&Y).
    • Application: Similar to Hilton (HC), where the Maldivian proceedings were already "too far advanced" for an ASI (C&Y), [foreign proceedings] have reached [trial / judgment], so the ASI should be refused.
  • Early Stage (+) Presently, [foreign proceedings] are at an early stage, with only [the claim filed / a jurisdiction challenge pending], which points to the ASI (Baker v BCS (SICC); C&Y). Per ZHD v SQO (C&Y), where [no merits hearing] is imminent or held, the length of delay alone does not point against it.
  • Contesting Jurisdiction Is No Excuse (−) [Applicant] says it first objected to [foreign court]'s jurisdiction. Per Sun Travels (citing The Angelic Grace, Toepfer and Ecobank), that does not excuse delay: no "two bites at the cherry". Similar to ADM v PT Budi, refused on "general discretionary considerations and the needs of comity", [applicant] should have [objected abroad and applied here] together.
  • Foreign Judgment Already Given (−) Per Sun Travels, once [foreign court] has given [judgment], [applicant] must show exceptional circumstances on top of the usual requirements; the relief is then really an anti-enforcement injunction (J7.6).
  • Where Delay Sits (±) Per C&Y, English law treats strong reasons (justifications for suing abroad) as distinct from discretion ([applicant]'s delay or unconscionable conduct) (Donohue; ADM). Sun Travels cited ADM approvingly, but the point is open and makes little practical difference. Must write one line: either way, [applicant]'s delay [does / does not] defeat the ASI.
  • Applicant's Unconscionable Conduct (−) Per Donohue and C&Y, an ASI is equitable, so [applicant] may lose it by [dilatoriness] or [unconscionable conduct, e.g., [misleading [foreign court]]].
J6.3.2 Vexation or Oppression

(Non-contractual ASIs: amenability (J6.1) + sufficient interest, usually natural forum (J6.2.3) + vexation (J6.3.2) + no undue injustice (J6.4) (Kirkham; slide 20). J6.3.2 and J6.4 are "two sides of the same coin" (Kirkham), so write them together if short of time.)

  • Starter (must write) Even without [a breach of agreement], [applicant] argues [respondent]'s [foreign proceedings] are vexatious or oppressive. Per Kirkham and UBS v Telesto (C&Y), an ASI issues only in "the clearest of circumstances"; it depends on [the facts], the overarching question being whether the ends of justice require it (SNIA).
  • Unconscionability Per C&Y, "unconscionable" is used interchangeably with "vexatious or oppressive" (the latter preferred) but is technically wider. Per Asiana, unconscionability is the underlying principle and [the list] is not closed. Presently, [respondent]'s [conduct] is unconscionable because [reason].
  • Bad Faith or No Good Reason (+) Similar to Lakshmi, where the BVI suit began years after accrual and a day after Mr J learned the estate would take over the Singapore suit, and should have been a counterclaim, [respondent] sued in [foreign court] [long after [claim] accrued / just after [trigger in Suit X]] instead of counterclaiming in [Suit X].
  • Bound to Fail (±) (+) Per Kirkham, suing on [a hopeless claim] is vexatious. (−) But per VKC (C&Y), the court should be prudent: weakness is only "a factor ... together with more weighty factors". [Applicant] should stress [respondent]'s conduct, e.g., a claim "cynically created and pursued" after it [agreed [new arrangement] inconsistent with it] (VKC).
  • Oppressive Procedures or Extreme Inconvenience (+) Per Kirkham and C&Y, [foreign proceedings] subject [applicant] to [oppressive procedures, e.g., [ex parte seizures]] or [extreme inconvenience, e.g., [a remote venue / foreign language]].
  • Key Witness Not Compellable (+) Per UBS v Telesto and C&Y, it is vexatious where [a key witness] cannot be compelled to attend [foreign court]'s trial. Presently, [witness] is [a non-party resident here] whose evidence on [disputed fact] is central.
  • Rights Unlawfully Challenged (+) Per Evergreen v Volkswagen and C&Y, it is vexatious where [respondent] uses [foreign proceedings] to challenge [applicant]'s legal rights unlawfully, e.g., [to undo [right] established under Singapore law].
  • Lost Remedy Available Only Here (+) Similar to SNIA, where suing in Texas cost SNIA its contribution claim against the Malaysian operator, which would submit to Brunei but not Texas, [foreign proceedings] deprive [applicant] of [a claim against [third party]] available only in [Singapore]. That is oppressive if [applicant]'s undertakings protect [respondent]'s legitimate advantages (J6.4).
  • Relitigation (+) Similar to BCS v Baker, where a Californian judicial estoppel claim after the SICC judgment repackaged the decided trust issue, [respondent]'s [foreign claim] reopens [issue] decided in [Suit X] under a new label: both vexatious and an abuse (J6.3.3).
  • Parallel Proceedings Alone Not Enough (−) Per UBS v Telesto and C&Y, parallel proceedings and the risk of conflicting judgments do not alone justify an ASI, especially where the parties agreed [an NEJC]. Presently, [respondent] merely [sued in [foreign court] on the same dispute].
    • Something more (+): Per PT Sandipala (C&Y), the case is stronger where [parties and claims] significantly overlap and [respondent] voluntarily took part in [Suit X], now far advanced. Per Asiana (citing VEW v VEV), duplication plus [something more] may be vexatious.
  • Deliberate Fragmentation (+) Similar to Clearlake, where the respondent sued in contract in one forum and tort in another on the same issues, [respondent] deliberately split [claims] between [Singapore] and [foreign court]. Per Hai Jiang (C&Y), this is undecided here but "justified in some circumstances", consistent with Tomolugen's "bold approach".
  • Claim Unknown Here Is Not Vexation (−) Presently, [foreign claim, e.g., [treble damages]] cannot be brought in [Singapore]. Per British Airways v Laker, respect for foreign substantive law is part of comity, so that alone is not vexatious, unless [the claim] is used oppressively or targets [a transaction overwhelmingly centred here] (Midland Bank v Laker) (J6.2.4).
  • Suing a Non-Party to Bypass the Clause (+) Where [A] sues [non-party C] to bypass [clause X], see J6.5.2, scenario 4 (Asiana).
J6.3.3 Abuse of Singapore's Process

(Amenability (J6.1) + self-evident interest (J6.2.2) only: slide 20, Kirkham (a) and (b).)

  • Starter (must write) Per BCS v Baker, this ASI rests on the inherent power to protect the integrity of [Singapore's processes, jurisdiction and judgments], the focus being the disruption [foreign proceedings] cause them. [Singapore's interest] is self-evident and natural forum irrelevant (J6.2.2).
  • Relitigating Decided Matters (+) Similar to Masri (No 3) (per BCS v Baker; C&Y), where after an English judgment that a 1992 agreement had not been terminated the defendants sued in Yemen for the opposite declaration without any enforcement there, [respondent] seeks a declaration in [foreign court] contradicting [Singapore judgment]: a collateral attack, not resistance to enforcement.
  • Duplicate Suit Pending Appeal (+) Similar to Beckkett v Deutsche Bank (per BCS v Baker), where Beckkett sued in South Jakarta for the same declarations on the same grounds while its Singapore appeal was pending, [respondent] seeks in [foreign court] [the reliefs refused in [Suit X]] while [the appeal] is pending.
  • Could and Should Have Been Raised (+) Per BCS v Baker (citing Elektrim), abuse also covers litigating abroad [issues] that could and should have been raised in [Suit X] (a Henderson-type abuse). Presently, [respondent] kept [issue] in reserve.
  • Insolvency (+) Per BCS v Baker (citing SNIA), abuse also covers [respondent] suing abroad to gain an advantage over [other creditors] in [Singapore insolvency proceedings of [company]].
  • A New Label Does Not Matter (+) Similar to BCS v Baker, where the judicial estoppel claim was the decided trust issue under a new label ("different sides of the same coin"), added as an afterthought, [respondent]'s [foreign cause of action] is in substance [issue decided in [Suit X]]; that it could not be brought here is irrelevant.
  • Foreign Policy Does Not Outweigh the Affront (+) [Respondent] relies on [foreign court]'s [public policy / interest in its own law]. Per BCS v Baker (citing Beckkett), neither foreign policy nor comity outweighs the affront to [Singapore's processes] where [foreign claim] duplicates [Singapore judgment].
  • Genuinely New Facts (−) Similar to BCS v Baker, where the Wrongful Settlement Claims rested on later-discovered facts and were not restrained, [respondent]'s [claim on [later events]] raises matters not decided in [Suit X], so the ASI should not extend to it.
  • Resisting Enforcement Is Not Abuse (−) If [respondent] only resists [applicant]'s enforcement of [Singapore judgment] in [foreign court], see J6.2.2.
J6.3.4 Singapore Public Policy
  • Basis (+) Per C&Y, an ASI may give effect to [Singapore public policy], in very exceptional cases overriding even [a foreign EJC]. Similar to Petter v EMC, where an English ASI protected an employee in employment litigation despite a foreign EJC, [applicant] relies on [policy protecting [employees / consumers]] (see also Evergreen).
  • High Threshold (−) Per Stichting Shell (citing Barclays v Homan) and C&Y, not every policy suffices: an ASI is appropriate only where [Singapore]'s and [foreign state]'s policies are "so at variance" that comity is overridden. Presently, [foreign law] merely [differs on [point]].
J6.4 NO UNDUE INJUSTICE TO [RESPONDENT]

(Vexation ASIs only. Abuse of process: the advantage is irrelevant (BCS v Baker). Contractual ASIs: no separate limb; [respondent]'s points go to strong reasons (J6.3.1.4) (Cooperative Muratori).)

  • Balancing (must write) Per Kirkham, vexation and injustice to [respondent] are "two sides of the same coin"; the injustice "feeds into" vexation (Cooperative Muratori). Per SNIA and C&Y, the court weighs [respondent]'s loss of [legitimate juridical advantage] against the injustice to [applicant] if the ASI is refused.
  • Factors Per C&Y, weigh (i) the [advantage] lost, e.g., [higher damages / discovery / jury trial], which counts less where [foreign court] is not the natural forum (UBS v Telesto); (ii) [the remedy] sought abroad; and (iii) how far [foreign proceedings] have advanced (J6.3.1.5).
  • Undertakings Neutralise (+) Similar to SNIA, where SNIA's undertakings preserved the plaintiffs' Texas advantages in Brunei, and Lakshmi, where the appellant undertook to consent to a mirror BVI judgment, [applicant] undertakes to [waive [limitation point] / consent to [discovery] / submit to a mirror judgment in [foreign state]].
  • Cynically Created Advantage (+) Similar to BCS v Baker (citing VKC), where the US-only judicial estoppel claim, raised after the trust issue was fully argued, was "cynically" pursued to attack the Suit 3 judgment, [respondent]'s advantage in [foreign court] was [created by its own timing] to [relitigate [issue]], so it counts for little.
  • Abuse: Advantage Is No Answer (+) Per BCS v Baker, "it is the very existence of an advantage outside the forum which may justify injunctive relief" where [foreign laws] are used to interfere with [Singapore's processes]. Presently, [respondent]'s [foreign remedy] is exactly what makes [foreign proceedings] abusive.
  • Genuine Advantage Outweighs (−) Presently, [respondent] would lose [a genuine advantage, e.g., [a claim against [party] suable only in [foreign court]]] with no [undertaking] from [applicant]. Weighing both sides' injustice (SNIA), and [foreign court] being a natural forum, the ASI should be refused.
J6.4.1 Conclusion
  • Granted Presently, [respondent] is amenable (J6.1); Singapore has interest as [the natural / chosen forum / court whose judgment is attacked] (J6.2); [foreign proceedings] [breach [clause X], with no strong reasons / are vexatious / abuse [Suit X]] (J6.3); and [respondent] suffers no undue injustice [given [undertaking]] (J6.4). An [interim / permanent] ASI issues [until [preconditions] are met].
  • Refused Despite [strength], the ASI is refused because [Singapore lacks interest (J6.2.5–J6.2.6) / delay let [foreign proceedings] reach [stage] (J6.3.1.5) / [respondent] shows strong reasons (J6.3.1.4)].
  • Fallbacks Foreign courts can take offence (the Düsseldorf CA refused to serve an English ASI), so [applicant] may prefer [a stay application in [foreign court]], damages for breach of [clause X] (J1.7), a declaration, resisting recognition of [the foreign judgment] (J7.2.6), or an anti-enforcement injunction (J7.6).
J6.5 SPECIAL SITUATIONS
J6.5.1 Anti-Anti-Suit Injunctions
  • Protecting Singapore Proceedings (+) Presently, [respondent] [has applied / threatens to apply] to [foreign court] for an ASI against [Suit X]. Per Airbus and C&Y, Singapore may restrain [respondent] from seeking it, to protect its own proceedings, on the usual requirements (J6.1–J6.4).
  • Contractual Anti-Anti-Suit (+) Per C&Y, it may also issue where [a foreign ASI] [has breached / would breach] [the contract]. Similar to Sabah Shipyard, where Pakistan's injunction against calling on the guarantee stopped Sabah suing in England under an English NEJC, and the English CA upheld an ASI against the Pakistani proceedings, [respondent]'s [foreign application] would stop [applicant] [enforcing [right] here].
    • Caution (−): After UBS v Telesto, plead [vexation] as well as [breach], as Singapore reads Sabah as a vexation case (J6.3.1.2).
J6.5.2 Third Parties: Quasi-Contractual ASIs

(Set-up: A and B agreed [a Singapore EJC]; C is a non-party connected to [the contract / the dispute]. Identify the scenario first (slide 19).)

  • Scenario 1: A Sues B and C; B Seeks the ASI (±) (+) Against A's claim on B, the ASI rests on breach of [clause X] (J6.3.1). (−) But C's presence and [claims outside clause X] may be strong reasons (Donohue) (J6.3.1.4). (+) Fragmentation "should not be overstated" (Asiana).
  • Scenario 2: C Sues A; A Seeks the ASI (+) The ASI rests on [clause X] only if C is bound. Per Hai Jiang and C&Y, C is bound if it derives rights from a party by [subrogation / assignment / a statutory or equitable right], taking the benefit subject to the burden. Presently, C is [B's subrogated insurer / assignee].
    • Vandepitte beneficiary: Similar to Finaport, where Techteryx, suing in Hong Kong under the Vandepitte procedure, was bound by the trustee's tiered clause as the cause of action stayed the trustee's, [C] sues on [trustee B]'s cause and is bound as [B] would be (not a derived-rights case: no transfer).
  • Scenario 2 Variant: Applicant Denies Being a Party (+) Per Hai Jiang and C&Y, where [respondent] sues [applicant] abroad on [contract] which [applicant] denies being party to, the claim is "inherently subject" to [clause X]. [Applicant] must show (a) breach, (b) its right to enforce [clause X], (c) validity, and (d) [foreign claim] within scope.
  • Scenario 3: A Sues C; C Seeks the ASI (−) Per VKC v VJZ and C&Y, C cannot use CRTPA s 2(1)(b): Parliament deliberately extended the Act to [arbitration agreements] (s 9) but not [jurisdiction clauses], and an EJC confers no substantive benefit.
    • Critique (+): per Chong (seminar), the "procedural" label is wrong: if [an EJC] were merely procedural, its breach could not found [an ASI] or [damages].
    • Routes left open (+): C may "arguably" rely on s 2(1)(a) if [contract] expressly confers the right, or on s 2(3), or on equity as in Hai Jiang (VKC). Presently, [clause X] [expressly names [C / a class including C]].
    • Comparison (±): Contrast Global Partners v Babcock & Brown (NSWCA), where [group companies] that took part in the decisions complained of and were "Indemnified Persons" could rely on [the English clause] (J1.5.3).
    • Fallback: Otherwise C must show [vexation] to [C] in its own right (J6.3.2) (Asiana).
  • Scenario 4: A Sues C; B Seeks the ASI (±) Per Asiana, B, a party to [clause X], may restrain A's suit against non-party C in [foreign court] only on (a) or (b):
    • (a) Construction (−): [clause X] on its true construction covers claims against C, i.e., A promised B to sue C only in [Singapore]. That needs a "quite clear indication" (Asiana, adopting Team Y&R). Presently, [clause X] covers only disputes ["between the parties"].
    • (b) Bypass (+): The real purpose of suing C is to bypass [clause X], making the suit vexatious as between A and B (Asiana, citing Clearlake and Giorgio Armani). Presently, C is [B's [director / subsidiary]] and A's claim [mirrors its claim against B].
    • Rejected (−): Per Asiana, B's "sufficient interest", e.g., [its liability to indemnify C], is not enough (Lord Scott in Donohue): it is over-inclusive. C may still seek its own ASI if [A's suit] is vexatious to [C].
J6.5.3 HCCCA / CCAA Cases
  • Starter Per C&Y, the HCCCA reduces but does not remove [parallel proceedings], as a non-chosen [Contracting State court] must generally decline save under art 6. Singapore may grant [interim measures] whatever [the chosen court] (s 10 CCAA; J1.2.4).
    • Art 7: Per C&Y, art 7 neither requires nor precludes [interim measures]; they are not "judgments" (art 4), but per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report they support [the agreement], so [an interim or permanent ASI] arguably falls within art 7.
  • Singapore EJC; Non-Contracting State Suit (+) Presently, [clause X] chooses [Singapore] and [respondent] sued in [foreign court], outside the HCCCA. Apply an ordinary contractual ASI (J6.3.1); per C&Y, the chosen court's ASI upholds [the agreement].
  • Singapore EJC; Other Contracting State Suit (+) Per C&Y, as the chosen court, Singapore may be given more leeway, consistent with the HCCCA's primacy for [the chosen court]. [Foreign court] should itself have declined under art 6, so the ASI supports [the Convention scheme].
  • Deemed-Exclusive Singapore Clause (±) Presently, [clause X] is exclusive only by s 3(2) CCAA and, under [law X], arguably has no promissory content. Per Chong (answer scheme), [clause X] still supplies sufficient interest and the ASI is run on vexation or oppression (J6.3.2); as the chosen court, Singapore "will likely grant the ASI".
    • Breach arguable (+): per C&Y, s 3(2) deems [clause X] "exclusive in effect", and the chosen court's ASI against a suit in [a non-chosen court] in breach of the agreement upholds it, so a contractual ASI is arguable (J6.3.1).
    • Reply (−): per C&Y, breach is contract interpretation under [the proper law]; if [law X] gives [clause X] no promise, s 3(2) arguably settles only [jurisdiction] (analysis). Chong's scheme leaves breach open: "no promissory content?" (J7.2.6).
  • Foreign Contracting-State EJC; Non-Contracting State Suit (−) Presently, [clause X] chooses [Court B] and [respondent] sued in [Court A], outside the HCCCA. Per C&Y, no HCCCA concern arises, but Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (Akai) (J6.2.6).
  • Foreign Contracting-State EJC; Other Contracting State Suit (±) (+) Per C&Y, a Singapore ASI against [Court A] arguably makes [clause X] more effective, especially if [Court B] cannot grant ASIs. (−) But if [Court A] took jurisdiction under an art 6 exception, an ASI would undermine [the HCCCA's uniform rules] and fragment responses, so Singapore should generally refrain.
  • ASI Against the Chosen Court (−) Per C&Y, an ASI by [a non-chosen court] against proceedings in [the chosen court] never supports the agreement and should not issue.
  • s 4(10A) CLA (±) Power to aid [Court B]'s proceedings is not discretion: the Akai objection to interfering with [Court A] remains (J6.2.5).
J6.5.4 Anti-Enforcement Injunctions (AEIs)
  • Pointer Where [foreign court] has already given [judgment], [applicant] needs an AEI: run J6.1–J6.4 as the floor, then the Sun Travels "exceptional circumstances" overlay in J7.6 (fraud; no knowledge until [judgment]).

1Start here: J6 in plain English

An anti-suit injunction (ASI) is a Singapore court order telling a party (the respondent) to stop, or not start, a lawsuit in a foreign court. It is addressed to the person, not the foreign court, and breaching it is contempt. But it still interferes indirectly with the foreign court, so comity (respect between legal systems) runs through every step (SNIA; C&Y).

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine two neighbours with a written agreement that any quarrel goes to the village elder. One neighbour runs off to the next village's elder instead. You cannot order the other village's elder to stop listening. But you can order your neighbour to stop going there, and punish him if he disobeys. That is an ASI: aimed at the person, effective only if he is within your reach, and used carefully because the other village will feel slighted.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three stories, three bases

In each story, Beta has started a lawsuit against Alpha in Ruritania, and Alpha asks the Singapore court to stop it.

StoryBasisAlpha's key point
Their contract says "the Singapore courts shall have exclusive jurisdiction".Contractual (J6.3.1)"Beta promised not to sue anywhere else." No need to prove unfairness.
No clause at all. Beta sued in Ruritania the day after learning the Singapore case was going badly for it, and Singapore is clearly the natural forum.Vexation or oppression (J6.3.2)"Beta's foreign suit is unconscionable, and Singapore is the right place."
The Singapore court already gave judgment for Alpha last year. Beta now sues in Ruritania on the same issue under a new label.Abuse of Singapore's process (J6.3.3)"Beta is attacking a Singapore judgment through the back door."

Each basis has a different list of elements. The first job in any ASI answer is to name the basis, then run only its elements.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Applicant / respondentThe party asking for the ASI / the party to be restrained from suing abroad.
AmenabilityThe respondent is within Singapore's in personam jurisdiction (submitted, or validly served). Always required.
Sufficient interestA good reason for Singapore, rather than the foreign court, to act. Usually Singapore is the natural forum, or the parties chose Singapore.
Contractual ASIBased on breach of a jurisdiction, arbitration or non-suit agreement.
Vexation or oppressionUnconscionable foreign proceedings: bad faith, relitigation, a lost remedy, oppressive procedure.
Abuse of process ASIProtects Singapore's own processes and judgments from collateral attack abroad.
Strong reasonsWhat the respondent must show to avoid a contractual ASI. In practice, the strong cause test (J4.3).
ComityMutual respect between courts of different countries.
AASI / AEIAnti-anti-suit injunction (stopping someone getting a foreign ASI) / anti-enforcement injunction (stopping enforcement of a foreign judgment, J7.6).

2J6.0 Preliminary points

🧩 Practise J6.0 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: J6.0.2 Preliminary Points (word for word)
J6.0.2 Preliminary Points

(Use only the points the facts raise.)

  • Is It an ASI? Per Oro Negro, an ASI restrains [respondent] from commencing or continuing [proceedings in [foreign court]]. Presently, the order only stops [respondent] [purporting to act for [applicant]]. Similar to Oro Negro, it is not an ASI though it practically ends [foreign proceedings], so this framework does not apply (C&Y).
    • [Statutory Moratorium]: Per C&Y, ss 64–65 IRDA let the court restrain [local / foreign] proceedings against [company] proposing [a scheme / compromise]: in effect a statutory ASI, outside this general framework.
  • Source of Power Per C&Y, the [General Division] may grant injunctions "just or convenient" under s 4(10) CLA, and has the s 18(2) SCJA First Schedule powers (para 14; the handout also lists para 5). Presently, [applicant] seeks a [permanent] ASI, whose source is unsettled:
    • (−) Per Swift-Fortune (CA, arguably obiter as a Mareva case) and Hilton (HC, Ang J, bound by it), s 4(10) is [interlocutory] only, and [permanent] power lies in s 18(2) with para 14 SCJA.
    • (+) Per R1 International (HC), and Chan, Tan and Poon on a plain reading (per C&Y), s 4(10) also gives [permanent] power. The CA in Sun Travels merely noted Ang J's view, so it turns on whether "by an interlocutory order" governs [injunctions] or only [receivers] (C&Y).
  • Arbitration Per R1 International and C&Y, an [interim] ASI in aid of [Singapore / foreign]-seated arbitration issues under s 12A(2) with s 12 IAA, whatever [the seat] (s 12A(1)). A [permanent] ASI for [a foreign seat] is not found in s 12A (J6.2.7).
    • Limits (−): The court may refuse where [the foreign seat] makes it inappropriate (s 12A(3)), and acts only if [tribunal] cannot act effectively (s 12A(6)). Non-urgent orders need [tribunal]'s permission or written agreement (s 12A(5)); urgent ones preserve [evidence / assets] (s 12A(4)).
  • Proceedings Abroad Per C&Y, s 4(10A) CLA (in force 2022) gives power to grant interim relief, if just or convenient, in aid of [civil or commercial] proceedings [commenced / to be commenced] in [Court B], subject to ss 4(10B)–(10D). Power is not discretion (J6.2.5).
  • Governing Law Per C&Y, interim remedies raising comity, such as ASIs, are governed solely by the lex fori, so [Singapore law] decides whether to restrain [foreign proceedings], whatever [the lex causae] (C1.3).
  • Interim vs Permanent Presently, [applicant] seeks an [interim / permanent] ASI. The same Kirkham framework applies, but per Grover v SetClear, an interim ASI issues "sparingly and with great caution", and [respondent] gets the benefit of the doubt where [the facts] are unclear (−). A permanent ASI after [a merits judgment declaring breach of clause X] needs less caution (+) (C&Y).
    • Practicality: Per C&Y, an interim ASI is often a practical necessity against [anticipated foreign proceedings], its effect often "virtually that of a permanent" one, and it may be sought before [respondent] sues in [foreign court].
  • SICC Per BCS v Baker and C&Y, the same framework governs [the SICC]. If seised by [transfer from the General Division], it applies unmodified and natural forum stays relevant; if seised under [a written SICC agreement], sufficient interest and strong reasons are modified (J6.2.1; J6.3.1.3).
  • If [Respondent] Ignores the ASI Breach is contempt, so the ASI bites only if [respondent] has [assets / a presence] here (SNIA; C&Y). A [foreign judgment] obtained in breach is refused recognition as contrary to public policy (Nimbus; C&Y; J7.2.4), and [damages for breach of clause X] may be claimed (J1.7).
  • Foreign Court Refused a Stay (+) Presently, [foreign court] refused to stay [foreign proceedings]. Per Lakshmi, comity does not generally bar an ASI if Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum and [respondent] sued vexatiously. Similar to SNIA, granted though Texas had refused a stay, [foreign court]'s refusal is not decisive.
    • No estoppel (+): Per Lakshmi, [foreign court]'s natural forum ruling raises no issue estoppel against [the ASI application]: the ASI test also needs vexation, and the outcome should not turn on [scheduling] (J7.3.2.3).
    • Comity (−): [Respondent] says [foreign court] is best placed to decide its own natural forum (Amchem; Barclays v Homan; Deutsche Bank v Highland, per Lakshmi). Per Lakshmi, most cases sit between Airbus's "stricter" approach (ASIs only to protect [jurisdiction / public policy]) and the "laxer" one (any vexation suffices).
    • Middle ground (+): Per Lakshmi, a sufficient connection plus [unconscionable conduct] breaches no comity, absent exceptional circumstances. Deference is weaker where [respondent] carved [issue] out of pending [Suit X] to sue abroad, and a refusal given while [the Singapore appeal] was pending should not decide the outcome by scheduling.
    • Timing (must write if [applicant] waited): Per C&Y, [applicant] should object in [foreign court] and seek the ASI here simultaneously. Delay is not excused by [pending objections abroad] (Sun Travels), and comity weighs more the later [the application] (Lakshmi) (J6.3.1.5).
Preliminary points (use only those the facts raise)
▤ J6.0.2
  1. 1Is it an ASI? It must restrain commencing or continuing foreign proceedings. An order only stopping someone acting for the applicant is not one, even if it practically ends the foreign case (Oro Negro).
  2. 2Source of power. s 4(10) CLA ("just or convenient") and s 18(2) SCJA First Schedule. For a permanent ASI it is unsettled: Swift-Fortune (CA, arguably obiter) and Hilton (Ang J) say s 4(10) is interlocutory only; R1 International and a plain reading say it covers permanent ASIs too.
  3. 3Arbitration. Interim ASIs in aid of any arbitration under s 12A IAA (with its limits); a permanent ASI for a foreign seat is not in s 12A.
  4. 4Governing law. The lex fori alone decides whether to restrain foreign proceedings (C1.3).
  5. 5Interim v permanent. Same framework, but an interim ASI issues "sparingly and with great caution" (Grover v SetClear); a permanent ASI after a merits judgment needs less caution.
  6. 6SICC. Same framework (BCS v Baker): unmodified if seised by transfer; modified if seised under a written SICC agreement.
  7. 7If ignored. Contempt bites only if the respondent has assets or presence here; a foreign judgment obtained in breach may be refused recognition (Nimbus; J7.2.4).
  8. 8Foreign court refused a stay. No bar (Lakshmi; SNIA); no issue estoppel from its natural-forum ruling. Object abroad and apply here at the same time.

3J6.1 Amenability

🧩 Practise J6.1 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: J6.1 AMENABILITY (word for word)
J6.1 AMENABILITY

(Always required, whatever the basis: the court enjoins only [a respondent] within its in personam jurisdiction, against whom the ASI is effective (Cooperative Muratori; Koh Kay Yew; C&Y). Find jurisdiction in J2 / J3 and state the result here.)

  • Submission or Valid Service (+) Presently, [respondent] is amenable, having [submitted by [appearing / defending / counterclaiming] in [Suit X]] or been validly served [in / out of] Singapore (Koh Kay Yew; Westbridge v Mittal; C&Y). Per Cooperative Muratori, being within the court's in personam jurisdiction is what amenability requires.
  • Claimant Here (+) Per Glencore, [respondent], having sued [applicant] in [Suit X], submitted to all its incidents, including [counterclaims] and related relief such as [an ASI] (J2.2.2).
  • No Challenge (+) Similar to BCS v Baker, where the appellants, BCS being a Singapore company, appeared without objecting to jurisdiction, [respondent] [defended / took part in] [Suit X] without contesting jurisdiction, and is amenable.
  • Service Out Alone May Not Suffice (−) Similar to Akai, where the respondent, though served out on ostensible evidence, was not amenable as it had no presence or assets here and only opposed the ASI, [respondent] has [no [office / assets] in Singapore] and [only resists the ASI].
    • Reply (+): The slides contrast Kirkham, and the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service or submission suffices. [Respondent]'s lack of [assets] goes only to [effectiveness] (J6.0.2).
  • Not Amenable (−) If [respondent] is [abroad and has not submitted], [applicant] must first obtain permission to serve [the ASI claim] out under O 8 r 1 ROC 2021 (J3.1). Without it, no ASI issues, however vexatious [foreign proceedings] are.

Amenability is always required, whatever the basis: the court enjoins only a respondent within its in personam jurisdiction (Cooperative Muratori; Koh Kay Yew).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is Beta within reach?
FactsAmenable?
Beta sued Alpha in Singapore first, then also sued in Ruritania.Yes. A claimant here submits to all the incidents of the litigation, including an ASI (Glencore).
Beta was served in Singapore while its director visited, through its registered branch.Yes, validly served in (J2).
Beta has never been here, never been served, never appeared.No, however vexatious the Ruritanian suit. Alpha must first get approval to serve its ASI claim out under O 8 (J3).
Beta was validly served out, has no assets in Singapore, and turns up only to oppose the ASI.Yes on the settled view. The lack of assets goes to whether the ASI will work (contempt has little bite), not whether Beta is amenable.

4J6.2 Sufficient interest

🧩 Practise J6.2 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: J6.2 SUFFICIENT INTEREST (word for word)
J6.2 SUFFICIENT INTEREST

(Classify first; use only the matching subsection. Natural forum is only a proxy: it proves interest, but Singapore may have interest without it, and there must be a good reason for Singapore, not [foreign court], to stop [foreign proceedings] (BCS v Baker, citing Barclays v Homan). Contractual ASI: natural forum does not arise (Cooperative Muratori); a Singapore clause supplies the connection (J6.2.1), but if Singapore is not chosen the point stays live (J6.2.6–J6.2.7), hence slide 20's "(b)(?)".)

J6.2.1 Jurisdiction Agreement for Singapore
  • Singapore EJC (+) Presently, [clause X] gives the [General Division] exclusive jurisdiction. Per Westbridge v Mittal and C&Y, [clause X] itself supplies the connection, even if [the parties / the events] have no other link with Singapore; no natural forum inquiry is needed.
  • Why (+) Per Cooperative Muratori (citing Turner v Grovit and UniCredit), [applicant] need not show [Singapore] is more appropriate; the agreement does that. It should take more to sanction a breach of [clause X] than to deny [respondent] its natural forum (Yeo, endorsed in Vinmar).
  • Singapore NEJC (+) Presently, [clause X] is a Singapore NEJC governed by [Singapore law]. Arguably, per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, a defendant sued here must show strong cause not to be held to its submission, so [clause X] works like an EJC and supplies the connection.
    • Contrast: [The NEJC] supplies interest only; suing in [foreign court] is not itself a breach (J6.3.1.2).
  • SICC Clause, Exclusive or Not (+) Presently, [clause X] is a written [exclusive / non-exclusive] SICC agreement and [the claim] is international and commercial. Per C&Y, Spiliada is irrelevant: O 2 r 3 SICC Rules 2021 supplies the connection test (J5.3).
    • Test: The SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its [international and commercial character] or [an abuse of its process] (O 2 r 3(2)), and not solely because [the action] is connected to [foreign state] (O 2 r 3(3)).
    • Exception (−): Not so if [the claim is not international and commercial] or [suing in the SICC is abusive, e.g., tactical delay] (J6.3.1.3).
J6.2.2 Protecting Singapore's Own Process
  • Self-Evident Interest (+) Presently, [respondent]'s [foreign claim] abuses Singapore's process by [relitigating [Suit X]]. Per BCS v Baker, natural forum is then irrelevant: Singapore's interest in protecting its processes, jurisdiction and judgments is "generally self-evident", and only it can judge [the need for protection].
  • Concurrent Proceedings (−) (Non-contract cases.) Presently, [Singapore action] and [foreign action] are both pending, so per Baker v BCS (SICC) and C&Y, [applicant] must show Singapore is the natural forum (J6.2.3).
  • Consecutive Proceedings (+) Presently, Singapore has given judgment in [Suit X], so it has interest to protect [the judgment] from collateral attack by [respondent] relitigating res judicata issues abroad (Baker v BCS; C&Y). Per BCS v Baker, the need extends to [anticipated judgments] but is underscored once judgment exists.
  • Which Is It? Per BCS v Baker, ask when [the specific claim] to be enjoined was raised in [foreign court], not when the actions began. Presently, [respondent] raised [claim] on [date], after [judgment / dismissal of the appeal], so it is consecutive. (C&Y's footnote states this the other way; follow the judgment.)
  • Resisting Enforcement (−) Per Baker v BCS (SICC) and C&Y, it is a "fine line": if [respondent] merely resists [applicant]'s enforcement of [Singapore judgment] in [foreign court], Singapore generally leaves [foreign court] to decide that judgment's effect there.
  • Foreign Judgment Already Given (−) Per BCS v Baker (citing ED & F Man v Haryanto), an ASI stopping [respondent] relying abroad on [foreign court]'s [judgment] is ordinarily inappropriate, and [applicant] needs exceptional circumstances (Sun Travels; J7.6).
  • Interest Without Natural Forum (+) Similar to Shell v Coral Oil (per BCS v Baker), where England had a "very strong interest" in shielding a party already protected by its ASI from further vexatious Lebanese claims, Singapore may protect [applicant] from [further claims] after [earlier ASI / Suit X], though [foreign court] is also a natural forum.
J6.2.3 Alternative Fora: Singapore Is One Forum
  • Natural Forum (+) Presently, [the dispute] can be heard in Singapore or [foreign court]. Per BCS v Baker and Airbus, an ASI is normally granted where Singapore is the natural forum and the other requirements are met. Per Lakshmi, [applicant] must show Singapore is "clearly the more appropriate forum", weighing the quality, not quantity, of [the JIO factors] (J4.1.2).
  • Lakshmi: Real Substance (+) Similar to Lakshmi, where a BVI share mattered only because its subsidiaries held 22 Singapore condominium units, [respondent]'s claim to [asset in [foreign state]] is in truth about [Singapore property], so [foreign state]'s link is only [place of incorporation].
  • Lakshmi: Witnesses (+) Per Lakshmi, video links reduce the weight of witness location, but [third-party witnesses, e.g., [bank officers]] compellable here and not shown compellable in [foreign court] matter where [the dispute] is factual.
  • Lakshmi: Overlap (+) Per Lakshmi, different reliefs in [foreign court] do not show different issues: as [respondent]'s [foreign claim] and [Suit X] are binary, proof of one disproves the other.
  • Lakshmi: Little Weight (−) Per Lakshmi, [governing law] matters little where [both systems] are common law and the issues factual. Little weight goes to [a place of performance assuming [respondent]'s claim succeeds], [a place of enforcement offset by [applicant]'s undertaking] or [the place of an oral telephone contract]; [residence in third states] is neutral.
  • Natural Forum Alone Is Not Enough (−) Per SNIA and C&Y, natural forum alone never justifies an ASI, or Singapore could arrogate to itself [a mere difference of view] with [foreign court] on the natural forum. In SNIA, the ASI turned on the lost contribution claim (J6.3.2). Presently, [applicant] must also show [prejudice in [foreign court]].
  • Advantages Are Not Connecting Factors (+) Similar to SNIA, where Texas lawyers' evidence-gathering, the contingency fee system and an early trial were advantages to the plaintiffs, not connecting factors making Texas the natural forum, [respondent]'s [pre-trial steps / lawyers' expertise] in [foreign court] do not shift the natural forum (J6.4).
J6.2.4 Single Forum: Only [Foreign Court] Can Hear the Claim
  • Framing (must write) Presently, [respondent]'s [claim, e.g., [foreign antitrust claim]] lies only in [foreign court], so Singapore can never be the natural forum. Per Airbus and BCS v Baker, the questions are whether Singapore still has sufficient interest and whether pursuing [claim] is unconscionable. Per C&Y, the ASI is especially harsh, denying [respondent] its only redress.
    • Not Spiliada availability: Per C&Y, "single forum" means [Singapore law] gives no cause of action, so the question is [unconscionability], not [appropriateness]; Spiliada availability asks only whether [a court] can hear the claim.
  • Insolvency (+) Per BCS v Baker (citing Stichting Shell), [Singapore] has interest where the ASI protects its jurisdiction in administering [the insolvency of [company]] against [a creditor suing abroad] (J6.3.3).
  • Predominantly Singaporean Dealings (+) Similar to Midland Bank v Laker, where an English bank's dealings with Laker were English banking business under English law, "overwhelmingly English" in character (Airbus), [applicant]'s dealings with [respondent] were [conducted in Singapore / under Singapore law], so the ASI is consistent with comity.
    • Contrast (−): If [applicant]'s dealings were [in [third state] under its law], an ASI merely because [respondent] is amenable here would be "surprising" (Airbus, on a hypothetical Indian bank).
  • Singapore Public Policy (+) Per BCS v Baker and Airbus (citing Laker v Sabena), Singapore has interest where the ASI protects [Singapore public policy on [X]]; in very exceptional cases this may override even [a foreign EJC] (C&Y) (J6.3.4).
  • Not Unconscionable (−) Similar to British Airways v Laker, where BA and BCal, by taking licences to fly UK–US routes, voluntarily submitted to US antitrust law, [applicant] voluntarily [submitted to [foreign regime]], so [respondent]'s suit is not unconscionable and no ASI issues.
J6.2.5 Dual Fora: Singapore Is Neither
  • General Rule (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [Court A] while the natural forum is [Court B]. Per Airbus, comity generally requires Singapore to have sufficient interest before indirectly interfering. Per Akai, [Court A] and [Court B] may legitimately differ, and Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (C&Y; heeded in R1 International).
  • Natural Forum Powerless (−) Similar to Airbus, where India, the natural forum, could not reach the claimants, [Court B]'s inability to [restrain [respondent]] does not justify Singapore acting: "only the courts of an interested jurisdiction can act". That [Court A] does not apply [forum non conveniens] is also not enough (Airbus).
  • Extreme Cases (+) Per Airbus and C&Y, an ASI may issue without sufficient connection in "extreme cases", e.g., where [foreign state]'s conduct forfeits the respect comity normally requires. Presently, [describe [state interference / sham proceedings] in [Court A]].
  • Strong Reasons by Analogy (+) Per R1 International (HC, obiter; C&Y), a permanent ASI supporting [a foreign arbitration] may issue on strong reasons, e.g., [the seat lacks effective interim measures]. Arguably, by analogy, strong reasons exist where [Court B] [cannot grant ASIs].
  • s 4(10A) CLA (±) Arguably, s 4(10A) now gives power to grant interim relief, possibly [an interim ASI], in aid of [Court B]'s proceedings (slide 18). But it confers power only: Singapore must still justify interfering with [Court A] (Airbus; Akai).
J6.2.6 EJC for a Foreign Court
  • Go to the Chosen Court (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [Court A] in breach of an EJC for [Court B]. Per C&Y, [applicant] should ordinarily seek the ASI from [Court B]. Similar to Akai, where the insurer had not applied to the English court though Akai, having sued there, was amenable to it, [applicant] has not applied to [Court B].
    • Reply (+): per Chong (seminar), Akai is old and its "busybody" point may carry less force today, especially where [Court B] is in [an HCCCA Contracting State] (J6.5.3).
  • Reasons to Come Here (+) [Applicant] argues [Court B] [does not grant ASIs / lacks the remedy], or that it must shield its [Singapore assets] from [Court A]'s judgment (C&Y). For HCCCA states, see J6.5.3.
    • Rebuttal (−): Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then. As in Akai, where the insurer sued here only to protect its Singapore assets, any later enforcement against [applicant]'s [assets] is "an entirely different matter", met by resisting [recognition] then (J7).
J6.2.7 Arbitration Seated in [Foreign Seat]
  • Busybody Risk (−) Presently, [respondent] sued in [foreign court] in breach of [arbitration agreement] seated in [foreign seat]. Per C&Y, Singapore generally refrains from ASIs supporting foreign arbitration. Per R1 International (obiter), a permanent ASI needs strong reasons, e.g., [the seat lacks effective interim measures]; interim ASIs come from s 12A IAA (J6.0.2).
  • Contract Supplies the Connection (+) Per UniCredit (UKSC, persuasive), Spiliada is not the test: parties should be held to their bargain by any court before which they "can properly be brought" (Enka), and Airbus's sufficient-interest rule was tied to non-contractual cases. An ASI enforcing [an arbitration agreement] always comes from a court that is neither [the natural] nor [the agreed forum].
  • Comity and Connection (+) Per UniCredit, comity has little role where [foreign court's state] and [seat state] are New York Convention states. Presently, [arbitration agreement] is governed by [Singapore law], a substantial connection like the English-law rights in UniCredit; whether [personal jurisdiction alone] suffices was left open (IPOC, noted in UniCredit).
  • Applying Here Is Not a Breach (+) Per UniCredit (cf Model Law art 9), [arbitration agreement] does not impliedly bar applying to [a court] for relief holding the other party to it, though choosing [foreign seat] implies no agreement to sue in [Singapore].

Classify first and use only the matching subsection. Natural forum is only a proxy for interest: Singapore can have interest without being the natural forum, and there must be a good reason for Singapore, not the foreign court, to stop the foreign case (BCS v Baker, citing Barclays v Homan).

SituationRule and key case
Singapore EJC (+)The clause supplies the connection even if nothing else links the case to Singapore (Westbridge v Mittal). It should take more to sanction a breach than to deny a natural forum (Yeo, endorsed in Vinmar).
Singapore NEJC (+)Arguably works like an EJC to supply interest (Shanghai Turbo), but suing abroad is not itself a breach (J6.3.1.2).
SICC clause (+)Spiliada irrelevant; O 2 r 3 supplies the test, unless the claim is not international and commercial or suing in the SICC is abusive.
Protecting Singapore's process (+)Self-evident (BCS v Baker). Concurrent proceedings: must show natural forum. Consecutive (after a Singapore judgment): interest to protect it. Merely resisting enforcement abroad: leave it to the foreign court.
Alternative fora (+/−)Singapore must be "clearly the more appropriate forum" (Lakshmi), quality not quantity. Natural forum alone never justifies an ASI (SNIA): show prejudice too. Advantages abroad (contingency fees, early trial) are not connecting factors (SNIA).
Single forumSingapore can never be the natural forum, so ask interest plus unconscionability (Airbus).
