LESSON J7 · Q1 · JURISDICTION AND JUDGMENTS · ABOUT 27 MIN · 11 FLOWCHARTS · 2 ILLUSTRATIONS · 16 QUESTIONS

Foreign judgments: enforcement, recognition and AEIs

⚡ BIG IDEA

First ask whether the party wants to enforce the foreign judgment (a sword, to recover money) or have it recognised (a shield, or an estoppel). Then pick the regime: CCAA if the foreign court was the chosen court in a Hague case; REFJA is not examinable; otherwise the common law, where the judgment must be on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction (presence or submission), final and conclusive, and for a definite sum, with no defence such as fraud, natural justice or public policy.

PRE-WRITE J7 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
J7 Recognition And Enforcement Of Foreign Judgments
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

Oct 27, 2026 · @elly

J7.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Scan first. Ask in order: (1) does [party] want to ENFORCE [the X judgment] (sword: recover money) or have it RECOGNISED (shield / estoppel)? (2) which regime: CCAA, then REFJA, then common law? (3) are the requirements met? (4) does a defence apply? (5) does [debtor] want an AEI instead? Legend: [creditor] = judgment creditor; [debtor] = judgment debtor; [X] = country of origin; [Y] = a third country; (+) helps [creditor]; (−) helps [debtor]; (±) argue both ways.)

  1. Regime router (J7.0.2): CCAA where [the X court] is the chosen court under an exclusive COCA in a Hague Contracting State (ousts REFJA; common law fallback); REFJA where [X] is gazetted (bars the common law action); otherwise a common law action on the judgment debt.
  2. Common law procedure (J7.0.3): serve [debtor] in Singapore as of right (J2.1) or out with permission (s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA; O 8 r 1 ROC 2021; para 63(2), (3)(m) SCPD 2021); assets here not needed but a legitimate benefit may be (Demirel); forum conveniens arguably irrelevant (Licea v Curacao).
  3. Common law requirements (J7.1), per C&Y: on the merits, incl default, interlocutory and limitation rulings, not a judgment on a judgment (The Sennar (No 2); FLPA s 5; Sang Cheol Woo) (J7.1.1); international jurisdiction by presence (Adams v Cape; Lucasfilm; Dunlop v Cudell; Littauer Glove; Vogel) or submission (Nimbus; IGCF; Henry v Geoprosco; Giant Light Metal; Vizcaya Partners) (J7.1.2); final and conclusive under [X] law (Sang Cheol Woo; Humpuss) (J7.1.3); fresh money judgment for a definite sum (Poh Soon Kiat; Giant Light Metal) (J7.1.4); reciprocity left open (Merck) (J7.1.5).
  4. Common law defences (J7.2), burden on [debtor] (Eleven v Boxsentry): no review for mistake (J7.2.1); fraud (Hong Pian Tee; Ong Han Nam) (J7.2.2); natural justice (Paulus Tannos; Sang Cheol Woo) (J7.2.3); public policy (Poh Soon Kiat; Venetian Macau) (J7.2.4); penal, revenue and public laws (Maler Foundation; Licea) (J7.2.5); breach of a dispute-resolution agreement (J7.2.6); conflicting judgments (Merck) (J7.2.7); satisfaction and limitation (J7.2.8).
  5. Recognition as res judicata (J7.3): cause of action estoppel (Arnold; Ocean Tankers) (J7.3.1); issue estoppel and its outer limits (Merck; Gonzalo Gil White; Lakshmi; Desert Sun; First Laser) (J7.3.2); Henderson v Henderson (Humpuss) (J7.3.3); the Arnold exception (J7.3.4).
  6. REFJA (J7.4): not examinable; outline only, as analogues for [the common law]: what is enforced (J7.4.1); jurisdiction and defences (J7.4.3).
  7. CCAA (J7.5): scope (J7.5.1); procedure and effect (J7.5.2); mandatory refusal, s 14 (J7.5.3); discretionary refusal, ss 15–16, and severance, s 19 (J7.5.4); judgment of a non-chosen court (J7.5.5).
  8. Anti-enforcement injunction (J7.6): exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability (Sun Travels).
J7.0.1 Quick Application Template

Presently, [creditor] seeks to [enforce / rely on as res judicata] [the X judgment], a [money / non-money] [judgment after trial / default judgment / consent judgment] of [the X court] ordering [debtor] to [pay [sum] / perform [obligation]]. Regime: [the CCAA applies as [X] is a Contracting State and [the X court] is the court chosen in [clause] (J7.5) / [X] is gazetted, but REFJA is not examinable, so note it in one line (J7.4) / neither applies, so [creditor] sues on the judgment debt at common law (J7.1)]. Procedure (common law): [debtor] is [in Singapore, so [creditor] serves as of right (J2.1) / in [Y], so [creditor] obtains permission to serve out under O 8 r 1 ROC 2021 via para 63(3)(m) SCPD 2021, forum conveniens being arguably irrelevant (Licea v Curacao)] (J7.0.3). Requirements (C&Y): [the X judgment] is (a) on the merits as it decided [liability and quantum] (J7.1.1); (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction, [debtor] having been [present in [X] at service through [a fixed place of business at [address]]] or [having submitted by [defending on the merits / prior agreement in [clause]]] (J7.1.2); (c) final and conclusive under [X] law (J7.1.3); and (d) for a definite sum of [amount], not [a tax / fine / penalty] (J7.1.4). Defences: [debtor] resists on the ground of [fraud (J7.2.2) / lack of notice (J7.2.3) / public policy (J7.2.4) / penal law or punitive damages (J7.2.5) / breach of [clause] (J7.2.6) / an inconsistent judgment (J7.2.7) / limitation (J7.2.8)], which [succeeds / fails] because [reason]. Result: [the X judgment] [is / is not] enforced [in full / save for the severed [punitive] portion].

J7.0.2 Regime Router

(write one sentence, then go to the relevant part)

  • CCAA First (Ousts REFJA) If [X] is an HCCCA Contracting State and [the X court] is the court chosen in the exclusive COCA in [clause], or its transferee, [creditor] proceeds under the CCAA (J7.5). Per REFJA s 2A, if [X] is also gazetted, [creditor] cannot fall back on REFJA should [the X judgment] fail under the CCAA.
  • Common Law Fallback (±) Per s 21 CCAA, the common law remains open, but per C&Y the CCAA is almost always better for [creditor] ([non-money relief / no limitation period / simpler procedure]); after a CCAA refusal, suing at common law may be abusive if it re-ventilates [the same issues].
  • REFJA (Not Examinable) Per Chong (seminar), REFJA will not be examined. If [X] is gazetted (per the handout: [HK / Brunei / Australia / India / Malaysia / NZ / Pakistan / PNG / Sri Lanka / UK]), note in one line that [creditor] could register (J7.4), then run the common law.
  • Common Law Residual Otherwise [creditor] sues [debtor] on the debt [the X judgment] creates, usually by [summary judgment]. Per C&Y, [debtor] gets leave to defend only by showing a fair or reasonable probability of [a real defence] under J7.2, never [the merits] (J7.2.1).
  • Non-Money Judgments [An injunction / order for specific performance] from [X] is enforceable only under REFJA (s 4(4)) or the CCAA; at common law [creditor] sues afresh on [the original cause] and pleads [the X judgment] as res judicata (J7.3.1).
  • Recognition Only Where [party] pleads [the X judgment] as a shield, or to bind [other party] on [an issue], J7.1.1–J7.1.3 must be met and no J7.2 defence apply, but there is no money requirement (J7.3).
  • In Rem: Test Per Pattni v Ali (adopted by the SGCA), [the X judgment] is in rem if [the X court], where [the property] was situated, adjudicated title against the world. Per C&Y, Singapore characterises it by [the X proceedings]' nature and intended effect.
  • In Rem: Effect Per C&Y, [the property] must have been in [X] when proceedings began (also s 5(3)(b) REFJA). It is usually recognised, e.g., [as proof of title in a conversion claim], free of the six-year bar, and [a good-faith purchaser] is protected against fraud.
  • Memorandum of Guidance (−) [Creditor] relies on the MoG between Singapore and [the X court, e.g., DIFC / China SPC]. Per C&Y, MoGs are non-binding statements of each side's existing law, so [the X judgment] must still satisfy [the common law / REFJA].
J7.0.3 Common Law Procedure: Serving the Originating Claim

(common law route only; for CCAA orders see J7.5.2)

Presently, [creditor] enforces [the X judgment] by a fresh action in the General Division, so [debtor] must be served with [the originating claim]; service founds in personam jurisdiction.

  • Service In [Debtor] is in Singapore, so [creditor] serves as of right under [s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA with O 7 r 2(1)(a) (individual) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA with s 387 or s 376 CA (company) / s 16(1)(a)(i) with Adams v Cape presence (unregistered foreign company)] (J2.1).
  • Service Out: Framework [Debtor] is in [Y], so per s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA and O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021, [creditor] must show Singapore "is the appropriate court". Per para 63(2) SCPD 2021, that needs (a) a good arguable case of nexus; (b) forum conveniens; and (c) a serious question on [the merits].
  • Nexus (+) Per para 63(3)(m) SCPD 2021, [the action] enforces [the X judgment], one enforceable at common law in executable form (C&Y). [Creditor] needs a good arguable case, more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas; J3.1).
  • Merits Subsumed (±) Per Li Shengwu (J3.1.4), a serious question need not be shown separately where the factor engages the merits. Arguably (m) does, the merits being whether [the X judgment] is enforceable; otherwise [creditor] shows a serious question on [the J7.1 requirements].
  • Assets in Singapore? (±) (−) [Debtor] has no [assets] here. (+) Per Demirel (Eng), assets are not required, but [creditor] must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit, e.g., [future assets / examining [debtor] / a judgment about to go stale].
  • Forum Conveniens: Required? (±) (+) Per Licea v Curacao, FNC does not arise as enforcement is not a fresh suit on [the merits], consistent with Art 13(2) Hague Judgments Convention. (−) [Debtor]: England (Demirel) and Canada (Chevron v Yaiguaje) keep an FC or FNC filter, so per C&Y Licea may be revisited.
  • Why FC Is Ill-Fitting (+) Per C&Y, (i) FC picks one forum for [the merits], whereas enforcement may be pursued in [Singapore and Y]; (ii) the court facilitates an obligation [the X court] already fixed rather than adjudicating; (iii) requiring both FC and a legitimate benefit is overkill for [creditor], who already holds a judgment.
  • Filter Against Abuse (±) (−) Per C&Y, some filter is sensible, as [creditor] may sue not to reach assets but to [harass [debtor] / launder [the X judgment] through a Singapore judgment]. (+) That concern is absent: [creditor] targets [debtor]'s [assets / bank accounts] in Singapore.
  • Alternatively, FC Satisfied (+) (if time) Even if FC is required, [creditor] satisfies it under Spiliada (J4.1), [debtor]'s [assets in Singapore] pointing to Singapore as [the place of enforcement].
J7.1 COMMON LAW: REQUIREMENTS FOR ENFORCEMENT

(Use where neither the CCAA nor REFJA applies, and for recognition (J7.3). Burden on [creditor]. Presence first; if it fails, submission.)

J7.1.0 Starter

Per C&Y (cf Ong Han Nam), [creditor] must show that [the X judgment] is (a) on the merits; (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction over [debtor]; (c) final and conclusive; and (d) a fresh money judgment for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. The same apply to recognition, save (d).

J7.1.1 Judgment on the Merits

Per The Sennar (No 2), [the X judgment] is on the merits as [the X court] [found the facts / stated the law / applied it to [liability / quantum]], not merely [a point of procedure].

  • Default Judgment (+) Per C&Y, [the default judgment] is on the merits although [debtor] did not appear and [the X court] may not have considered [the evidence]; non-participation goes only to fraud (J7.2.2) or natural justice (J7.2.3).
  • Interlocutory Judgment (±) Per C&Y, [the X ruling on [issue]] counts if it finally decides that issue and is not on a "procedural" issue. Per The Sennar (No 2), a ruling that [the claim is barred by [a Y jurisdiction clause]] is substantive, but one on [service / security for costs] is not.
  • Limitation Ruling (+) Per s 5 FLPA, [the X court]'s dismissal of [the claim] as time-barred under [X / Y / Singapore] law is deemed on the merits, so it can be [enforced / pleaded as res judicata against [party]].
  • Judgment on a Judgment (−) [The X judgment] merely declares [the Y judgment] enforceable in [X]. Per Sang Cheol Woo (not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead (HK)), it is unenforceable at common law, and per REFJA s 3(4)(c) not registrable. [Creditor] must enforce [the Y judgment] directly.
  • Why Not (−) Per C&Y, [the X judgment] (i) never examined [the issues], so is not on the merits; (ii) decides only its territorial effect in [X] (Merck: no estoppel, J7.3.2.4); and (iii) would launder [the Y judgment], Singapore testing [the X court] instead of [the Y court].
  • Contrary View (+) [Creditor] relies on Desert Palace (HC), which saw no difficulty in enforcing [a judgment on a judgment]; per C&Y it did not grapple with the theory, so [the X judgment] remains [unenforceable].
J7.1.2 International Jurisdiction of [the X court]

[Creditor] must prove that [debtor] was present in [X] (J7.1.2.1–J7.1.2.3) or submitted to [the X court] (J7.1.2.4–J7.1.2.5).

  • Singapore's Rules (−) Per C&Y, the test is Singapore's conflict rules, narrower than Singapore's own bases, with no mirror image. So [the X court]'s [service-out jurisdiction] does not count, and its own finding on [jurisdiction] creates no estoppel (J7.3.2.3).
  • Four Grounds Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom (SGCA), [debtor] must have been [present in [X]] or have [claimed or counterclaimed / voluntarily appeared / agreed in advance to submit]. Residence is not listed (J7.1.2.2).
  • Closed Categories (−) Per Schibsby v Westenholz, the grounds are closed. [Creditor] cannot rely on [X]'s real and substantial connection with [the claim], a Canadian ground (Beals v Saldanha) Singapore has not adopted.
J7.1.2.1 Presence: Timing and Federal States
  • Time of Presence Per Adams v Cape, [debtor] must be present in [X] at the time of suit, meaning when [the X process] was served ([date]), not issued ([date]).
  • Federal Systems (±) Per Adams v Cape (obiter, "with varying degrees of doubt"), presence anywhere in [the federation] may suffice for [a federal court], but [a state court of [state]] needs presence in [that state]. (−) Per C&Y, this is questioned, federal judgments being "foreign" in other [US states].
J7.1.2.2 Presence: Natural Persons
  • Temporary Presence (+) Per Adams v Cape (obiter), voluntary presence suffices even if temporary, so [debtor] served during [a two-day conference / a transit stop] in [X] was present.
  • Involuntary Presence (−) Per C&Y, presence must be voluntary; [debtor] [lured to [X] by [creditor]'s fraud / brought there under duress] was not present.
  • Virtual Presence (−) Per Lucasfilm, presence must be physical; [debtor]'s [website targeting [X] consumers / adverts in [X] magazines] did not make it present.
  • Residence Without Presence (±) (+) Per United Malayan Banking (obiter) and C&Y, [debtor]'s residence in [X] suffices a fortiori, being a stronger tie than [fleeting presence]. (−) English law stresses presence (Rubin), and India v Deutsche Telekom omits residence, so [debtor], absent from [X] at service, was not subject to [the X court].
  • Contrast REFJA (−) Per s 5(3)(a)(iv) REFJA, residence is required and mere presence is not enough, so [debtor]'s [business trip] to [X] would not suffice if [X] were gazetted (J7.4.3).
J7.1.2.3 Presence: Companies
  • Test Per Adams v Cape, [debtor company] is present in [X] if, for more than a minimal period, its own business was carried on at or from a fixed place of business [of its own, at its own expense / of [representative]], through [its servants / [representative]]. Per Littauer Glove, a reasonably permanent place suffices.
  • Short but Fixed (+) Per Dunlop v Cudell, a nine-day trade-fair stand was a fixed place of business, so [debtor]'s [booth / showroom] at [event] for [duration] qualifies.
  • No Fixed Place (−) Per Littauer Glove, [debtor]'s [representative] merely staying at [a hotel] for [a few days] taking orders did not carry on business at a fixed place.
  • Whose Business? Factors (±) Per Adams v Cape, [representative] must carry on [debtor]'s business, not its own. Ask whether [debtor] [acquired the premises for [representative] / paid a fixed salary, not commission / controlled the business]. Most weight goes to whether [representative] could bind [debtor] without specific prior authority.
  • Own Business (−) As in Adams v Cape (Cape's Illinois marketing companies, NAAC, AMC and CPC, carried on their own business, so Cape was not present in the US), [representative] [owned its premises / earned commission / needed approval before binding [debtor]].
  • Go-Between (−) Per Vogel, [representative] who merely [introduced customers / passed on orders] without authority to bind [debtor] carried on its own business.
  • Non-Trading Debtor Per Adams v Cape, if [debtor] is [a non-trading body, e.g., [charity / State entity]], the same test applies, substituting its [corporate activities] for "business".
J7.1.2.4 Submission by Conduct

(use if presence fails)

  • Test Per Nimbus, [debtor] submitted only by a step that necessarily waived its objection to [the X court]'s jurisdiction, judged practically, as [business people] would, not theoretically. Per IGCF (PC), adopting Rubin, a step "only necessary or only useful" if [the objection] was waived is submission.
  • Claimant or Merits Defence (+) Per C&Y and Malaysia Marine, [debtor] submitted by [suing in [X] (including related counterclaims or set-off against it) / filing a defence on the merits].
  • Merits Plea With Jurisdiction Challenge (±) Per C&Y, (+) pleading [the merits] where [X] procedure permits but does not require it is submission. (−) If [X] procedure requires both and [debtor] maintained its objection throughout, there is none, (+) unless [debtor] could withdraw [the merits plea] after losing on jurisdiction and did not.
  • Jurisdictional Objection (−) As in Nimbus (objecting in Colombo under the Sri Lankan Arbitration Act, losing and then taking no part, was not submission), [debtor]'s [objection under [clause] / challenge to [service / nexus]] in [the X court] was not submission.
  • Setting Aside on FNC Grounds (+) Per Henry v Geoprosco, [debtor]'s application to set aside [service out] because [X] was forum non conveniens asked [the X court] to decline a jurisdiction it had, so was submission. Nimbus assumed Henry is law without deciding.
  • Henry Should Not Be Followed (−) Per IGCF (PC), Henry's existence/exercise line is "unrealistic and irrational", no common law jurisdiction follows it, and REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i)(C) reverses it. Per C&Y, a failed set-aside on any ground is a protest (Re Dulles), so [debtor]'s [FNC challenge] in [X] was not submission.
  • Stay Application (±) (+) On Henry's logic, [debtor]'s stay application accepted [the X court]'s jurisdiction. (−) Per IGCF, a stay [for arbitration / on FNC grounds] is a protest, unless [debtor] sought more, e.g., [consequential relief on the merits].
  • ROC Analogy (±) (−) [Debtor] cites O 6 r 7(6) and O 6 r 12(5) ROC 2021: challenging the exercise of Singapore's jurisdiction is not submission. (+) Per C&Y, this may not carry over: there is no mirror image, and international jurisdiction uses narrower criteria than [Singapore's own].
  • Whose Law (±) Per Giant Light Metal (approving Akai), Singapore law decides, with [X] procedure as context. Per C&Y it would be strange to find submission where [X] law would not treat [debtor]'s [step] as such, though Rubin left this open.
  • Inchoate Submission (±) [Debtor] submitted to [original claim], and [creditor] says consent should be imputed for [related claim]. Per Giant Light Metal, weigh (a) the connection between the claims, a matter of degree that may span separate later proceedings between [the same parties]; and (b) fairness to both, disregarding [technical procedural impediments].
  • Inchoate: Application (+) As in Giant Light Metal (same parties and claims refiled after settlement talks failed, separate case numbers being a technicality) and Murthy v Sivajothi (submission to a Florida foreclosure action extended to related fraud cross-claims), [related claim] is [the same claim refiled / a related cross-claim].
  • Composition Plan (−) Per Humpuss, [debtor]'s unilateral inclusion as a creditor in [the X composition plan] is not, by itself, submission to [the X court].
J7.1.2.5 Submission by Agreement
  • Express Agreement (+) Per United Malayan Banking, [debtor] submitted in advance by agreeing in [clause] to the jurisdiction of [the X court / the courts of [X]].
  • Implied Agreement (±) (−) Per Malaysia Marine and other RECJA cases, it must be express. (+) Per Vizcaya Partners (PC), it may be implied if [debtor] actually consented in advance to [the X court]; it need not be contractual, and whether it exists is for [the proper law of [contract]]. Per C&Y, whether Singapore follows is open.
  • Insufficient Indicia (−) Per Vizcaya Partners, [debtor] did not impliedly submit merely because it [chose [X] law and did business in [X], even if these founded jurisdiction under [X] procedural law / held shares in an [X] company / made or was to perform [the contract] in [X]].
J7.1.3 Final and Conclusive

Per Sang Cheol Woo, [the X judgment] is final and conclusive if (a) [the X court] cannot vary, reopen or set it aside, though [the X appellate court] may hear an appeal; and (b) [the X court] regards it as res judicata. Per Humpuss and Carl Zeiss, this is tested by [X] law, proved by [expert evidence].

  • Default Judgment (+) Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, [the default judgment] is final if given final effect until set aside, although [debtor] may still apply to [the X court] to set it aside.
  • Interlocutory Judgment (±) Per Lakshmi, [the X interlocutory ruling on [issue]] is final if it finally decides [the parties]' rights on that issue, but not if [provisional / decided on a good arguable case and reopenable at trial] (First Laser).
  • Appeal Pending (±) (+) Per C&Y, a pending appeal to [the X appellate court] does not as such defeat finality, though Singapore may [stay enforcement]. (−) But as in Sang Cheol Woo (a provisionally enforceable Seoul High Court judgment was not res judicata under Korean law until the Supreme Court ruled), check [X] law.
  • Limitation Knock-On (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo, the six-year period then runs from when [the X judgment] became final under [X] law, i.e., [the final appellate decision on [date]], consistent with REFJA s 4(1)(b) (J7.2.8).
J7.1.4 Fresh Money Judgment for a Definite Sum
  • Definite Sum (+) Per C&Y, [the sum] must be fixed or arithmetically ascertainable, and [a costs order] is enforceable if final and definite, even where [the merits judgment] has no money order.
  • Fresh Obligation (±) Per Poh Soon Kiat, whether [the X judgment] imposes a fresh obligation to pay [sum] depends on [X] law. As in Poh Soon Kiat ("shall remain liable" in a later Californian fraudulent-transfer judgment was surplusage), where [the later X order] restates liability under [the earlier judgment], [creditor] must sue on [the earlier judgment].
  • Non-Money Judgment (−) Per C&Y, [an order for specific performance / an injunction] is not enforceable at common law, a relic of indebitatus assumpsit. [Creditor] must register under REFJA or the CCAA (J7.4.1; J7.5.1), or sue afresh and plead [the X judgment] as res judicata (J7.3.1).
  • Reform (±) Per C&Y, following Merck's call for convergence, the common law should enforce [non-money relief] as REFJA, the CCAA and Canada (Pro-Swing v Elta) do; the indirect route via [res judicata] already reaches [the same result], less efficiently.
  • Money Order Among Other Orders (+) Per Giant Light Metal, a definite-sum order made among [other orders] founds an action in debt. As in Giant Light Metal (refund due once the buyer made the generator sets available for collection), [creditor] has [made [the goods] available], so [the refund] is payable.
  • Severance of Mixed Orders (±) (−) Per Giant Light Metal (obiter), severance is confined to [penal or revenue] elements. (+) Per C&Y, [the money order] should be severable whenever it is not interdependent with [the non-money order].
  • Tax, Fine or Penalty (−) [The X judgment] for [tax / a fine / a penalty] payable to [the X State] is not enforceable (J7.2.5).
J7.1.5 Reciprocity (Left Open)

[Debtor] argues that [X] does not enforce Singapore judgments, so [the X judgment] should not be enforced.

  • Exam Weight Per Chong (seminar), one line suffices: Merck left [reciprocity] open and later cases have not discussed it, so [the X judgment] is not barred on that ground.
  • For Reciprocity (−) Per Merck, the point is open, and reciprocity is "entirely consonant" with comity, the CA's preferred basis for recognition, and with [the CCAA, REFJA and MORA]. So [debtor] says [X]'s [refusal to enforce Singapore judgments] should bar [the X judgment].
  • Against Reciprocity (+) Per C&Y, the common law enforces [private rights], not sovereignty; reciprocity is waning globally, rarely induces [X] to reciprocate, and penalises [creditor] for policy it cannot control. The statutes are [negotiated schemes] layered on the common law floor, so the comparison is inapt.
  • Liberal If Adopted (+) Per Merck, absence of reciprocity would rarely obstruct recognition in practice, and any requirement would be liberal, e.g., [de jure / presumed reciprocity], which [X] likely satisfies.
J7.1.6 Conclusion on Requirements

[The X judgment] [meets / fails] requirement [(a) / (b) / (c) / (d)] because [reason], so [creditor] [may enforce subject to the defences in J7.2 / must instead [register under REFJA / plead it as res judicata (J7.3)]].

J7.2 COMMON LAW: DEFENCES

(Raised by [debtor] once J7.1 is met; burden on [debtor] (Eleven v Boxsentry). Per Merck, common law defences should broadly converge with REFJA and the CCAA, so cite the statutory analogue (J7.4.3; J7.5.3–J7.5.4) where it helps.)

J7.2.0 Starter

Presently, although [the X judgment] satisfies J7.1, [debtor] resists enforcement on the ground of [fraud / natural justice / public policy / penal law / breach of [clause] / an inconsistent judgment / limitation].

J7.2.1 Mistake: No Review of the Merits
  • General Rule (+) Per Godard v Gray and Ralli v Angullia, [debtor]'s claim that [the X court] erred in [fact / law] on [issue], even on Singapore law, is irrelevant; Singapore does not sit on appeal from [the X court].
  • Error of Singapore Law (±) [Debtor] says [the X court] misapplied Singapore law on [issue]. Per Merck, it is open whether this breaches substantive public policy, the court being guardian of Singapore law. Merck contrasted existent errors (settled law misapplied) with retrospective ones (a considered view on [an unsettled point] later proved wrong).
  • Patent Errors Only (±) Per C&Y, if the ground is accepted, only patent errors count, keeping the threshold high. Presently [the X court]'s ruling on [issue] is [an obvious error / a reasonable view of unsettled law].
J7.2.2 Fraud

Per Hong Pian Tee, the test depends on the type of fraud. Per Ee Hoong Liang, extrinsic fraud is fraud [debtor] had no opportunity to examine and challenge, going to [the X court]'s jurisdiction; intrinsic fraud is fraud it could challenge, going to the merits, e.g., [false statements at trial] (Ong Han Nam).

  • Extrinsic Fraud (−) Presently, [witnesses were bribed / [debtor] was never served / [creditor] induced [debtor] to let judgment go by default]. Per Hong Pian Tee, Abouloff applies: no new evidence is needed, and [debtor] may raise the fraud though [it was rejected in [X] / it is raised here for the first time].
  • Intrinsic Fraud (+) Presently, [perjury / forged documents] at [the X trial] go to the merits. Per Hong Pian Tee, [debtor] needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have uncovered and that would likely have changed the result; presently [new evidence] [was / was not] discoverable.
  • Materiality (+) Per Ong Han Nam, for either type the fraud must have produced [the X judgment]; a catalogue of [creditor]'s [non-disclosures] is not enough unless it was the effective cause of [the X findings].
  • Characterisation (+) As in Ee Hoong Liang (non-disclosure of settlement payouts going to quantum was intrinsic), [creditor]'s [concealment of [fact]] goes to [the merits / quantum], so [debtor] must meet the diligence test.
  • Default and Summary Judgments (+) Per Eleven v Boxsentry, the intrinsic test applies to [a default judgment] though [debtor] took no part. Per Ee Hoong Liang, [a summary judgment] that [debtor] knew of is not akin to a default judgment.
  • Domestic Cases Irrelevant (+) Per Ee Hoong Liang, [debtor] cannot invoke Takhar or Façade v Mero (no diligence requirement), which concern [domestic judgments]; comity applies, and Singapore is not an appellate tribunal over [the X court].
  • Critique (±) (−) Per C&Y, Hong Pian Tee takes the side of the fraudster against his negligent opponent (Briggs), and [the extrinsic/intrinsic line] is hard to draw (Beals). (+) But the SGCA has reaffirmed it (Ong Han Nam), so [debtor]'s [lack of diligence] is fatal.
  • Exam Focus Per Chong (seminar), classify [the fraud] as extrinsic or intrinsic; [the elements of deceit] need not be proved.
  • Fraud by the Court (±) (−) Per C&Y, extrinsic fraud includes fraud by [the X court], e.g., [a bribed judge], overlapping with natural justice, so Abouloff applies. (+) Per the slides, whether Abouloff or Hong Pian Tee governs is open; arguably, if [an appeal] was available in [X], [debtor] could challenge it (Ee Hoong Liang).
    • Chong's view (−): per Chong (seminar), treat it as extrinsic for policy reasons, as [debtor] can hardly raise [the corruption] before [that court].
  • Threshold and Bars (+) Per Owens Bank v Bracco, [debtor] needs plausible evidence of a prima facie case. Per C&Y, fraud cannot be raised where [pleading it is abusive] or [a second X judgment] has rejected it (House of Spring Gardens v Waite), which in Singapore matters mainly for [extrinsic fraud].
J7.2.3 Natural Justice

Per Jacobson v Frachon (C&Y), [the X court] must have given [debtor] notice and then an opportunity to present its case. Presently, [debtor] [was never served / received [the claim] only [after judgment]], so [the X judgment] [is / is not] recognised.

  • Default After Proper Service (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo and C&Y, [debtor], [personally served], chose not to appear in [X]; letting [the default judgment] go by is no breach.
  • Later Participation No Cure (−) As in Paulus Tannos (PKPU summons not served in time; later participation under protest irrelevant), [debtor]'s later participation in [the X process] does not cure lack of notice of [the proceedings] before [the order].
  • Whose View (±) (−) Per Paulus Tannos, Singapore alone decides, unbound by [the X court]'s view that [service] was proper. (+) But where [debtor]'s [appeal on notice] is pending in [X], ruling is premature, as [the X appellate court] may correct it.
  • Substantial Justice (±) (−) Per Adams v Cape, natural justice extends to substantial justice, e.g., [damages set at counsel's average award without assessing each claim]. (+) Per Paulus Tannos and Sang Cheol Woo, it is unclear Singapore adopts this, and [debtor] should first seek correction in [X].
  • Mere Irregularity or Merits (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo, breach of [debtor]'s reasonable expectation that [X procedural rule] would apply is no defence; complaints about [Korea's deemed confession rule / the damages assessment] were merits challenges [already reviewed by the X appellate court].
J7.2.4 Public Policy

Per Burswood, a higher standard than domestic public policy applies. Per Poh Soon Kiat (applied in Sang Cheol Woo), enforcement must (a) offend a fundamental principle of justice or deep-rooted tradition of Singapore; (b) offend the general community; (c) offend fundamental morality, decency or liberty; or (d) go against a rule protecting the public interest. Presently, enforcing [the X judgment] [does / does not] offend [limb] because [reason].

  • Hierarchy (±) Per Poh Soon Kiat, statutory policy outranks common law "higher" international policy, which outranks domestic policy. Per C&Y and Chong (seminar), a statute is not automatically international policy; only one of an equally high, extraterritorial kind counts, a matter of interpretation (JIO Minerals); presently [statute] [is / is not] of that kind.
  • Judgment, Not Cause of Action (+) Per Merck and C&Y, at common law the effect of enforcing [the X judgment] must offend, not [the cause of action], unlike RECJA s 3(2)(f). So [the X judgment] on [a claim unknown to Singapore law] is not refused for that alone.
  • Egregious Cause (−) Per C&Y, [a cause of action] as egregious as [a contract under extreme physical duress / a drug-trafficking contract (ED&F Man v Haryanto)] infects [the X judgment]. Per Israel Discount Bank, a judgment on [a guarantee procured by undue influence] may be refused.
  • Critique of Israel Discount (+) Per C&Y, Israel Discount Bank wrongly looks to [the cause of action] absent egregiousness, and [undue influence] is arguably only domestic policy, so [the X judgment] should be enforced.
  • Breach of a Singapore ASI (−) Per Nimbus and C&Y, [the X judgment] obtained in breach of [a Singapore ASI against [creditor]] is contrary to public policy (J6). Breach of [a foreign ASI] is arguably not, by itself (analysis).
  • Gambling: Statutory Policy (−) Per Venetian Macau (HC 2026, REFJA), adopting Poh Soon Kiat, gambling save as regulated is contrary to Singapore policy. As s 5(2) CLA is statutory, it prevails over [higher international policy], so enforcing [the X judgment] on [a casino debt] is contrary to public policy.
  • Gambling: Common Law Route (−) Per Poh Soon Kiat (obiter), a judgment not registrable under RECJA for its gambling cause is likewise unenforceable at common law, implying s 5(2) CLA infects [the X judgment]. Per Venetian Macau, s 5(2) draws no distinction between [direct claims] and [actions on foreign judgments]; convergence (Merck) points the same way.
  • Gambling: Creditor's Reply (±) (+) [Creditor] relies on Burswood (s 5(2) only domestic policy), which the HC followed in Star v Yong Khong Yoong. (−) Per Venetian Macau, Burswood turned on the repealed RECJA's cause-of-action test and binds only there, so [the X judgment] is unenforceable.
  • Recharacterisation (±) (−) Per Poh Soon Kiat (left open), [the action on the X judgment] may be recharacterised as a direct claim for [the gambling debt], caught by s 5(2) CLA. (+) [Creditor]: it sues on [the judgment debt], and common law policy targets the judgment, not [the wager] (Merck).
  • Statutory Interest (+) As in Sang Cheol Woo (Korea's statutory 20% judgment interest, payable to the private creditor to deter delay, offended no public policy), [the X award of [interest / costs]] is enforceable.
  • Different Foreign Policy (+) Per Yap Chai Ling, that [X]'s public policy on [issue] differs from Singapore's does not mean Singapore's is breached.
  • No Estoppel; No New Facts (±) (−) Per Yukos and India v Deutsche Telekom, [the X court]'s ruling on [X]'s public policy creates no estoppel on Singapore's (J7.3.2.3). (+) But per Wu Shun Foods, [debtor] cannot raise [a fact] going to Singapore policy that it should have raised in [X].
J7.2.5 Foreign Penal, Revenue and Other Public Laws; Punitive Damages

Per Maler Foundation, [the X judgment] is not recognised if it directly or indirectly enforces [X]'s penal, revenue or other public law. Characterisation is for the lex fori; per Huntington v Attrill, "penal" means a suit in favour of the State for penalties. Presently, [the X proceedings] were [brought by [State agency] / for forfeiture to the State / for unpaid [tax]].

  • Label Not Conclusive (−) Per Maler Foundation, a place in [X]'s criminal code, or a civil form, is not conclusive. As in Maler Foundation (State-pursued civil forfeiture of officials' presumptively ill-gotten property, in the State's favour, was penal), [the forfeiture / disgorgement order] is penal.
  • Non-Money and In Rem (−) Per Maler Foundation and C&Y, the exclusion applies equally to [a judgment in rem / a forfeiture order over [property]].
  • Private Creditor (+) Per Raulin v Fischer (Eng), a sum recoverable by [creditor], a private litigant, in its own interest is enforceable. As in Sang Cheol Woo (statutory interest to a private creditor was not penal, penal meaning payable to the State), [the X award] is not penal.
  • Punitive Damages to a Private Party (±) (+) Per C&Y, refusing [the X punitive award] would be anomalous when Singapore awards punitive damages in tort (ACB v Thomson Medical). (−) But the point is uncertain, Licea leaving open [US RICO treble damages]; s 4(5) REFJA and s 16 CCAA limit [non-compensatory damages], and courts may take their cue from them.
  • Public Component (−) Per Schnabel v Lui (NSW), punitive damages punishing [non-compliance with the X court's orders] are penal though paid to [creditor]. (+) Contrast Benefit Strategies (SA): punitive damages for [brazen fraud] have no public element.
  • Severance (+) Per Licea, where [the X judgment] awards [compensatory sum] and [punitive sum], [creditor] enforces the unobjectionable part if clearly identifiable and separable; compare s 4(5) REFJA (J7.4.1) and ss 16, 19 CCAA (J7.5.4).
J7.2.6 Proceedings in Breach of a Dispute-Resolution Agreement

Presently, [debtor] argues that [the X judgment] was obtained in breach of [an arbitration agreement / an EJC for [Y / Singapore]] in [clause].

  • Breach First (±) Per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), the defence needs a breach, so [clause] must have promissory content, e.g., [an EJC], not [a non-promissory clause]. Per C&Y, [debtor] loses the objection if it [submitted to [the X court]].
  • For the Defence (−) Per C&Y, no case decides it, but (i) [debtor] could recover damages for [the breach] here anyway (Union Discount; cf Tradewaves), possibly cancelling [the judgment sum]; (ii) REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue, favouring convergence (Merck); (iii) it fits [the HCCCA]'s party autonomy. Compare UK CJJA s 32.
  • Against the Defence (+) [Creditor]: no Singapore authority recognises it, and per C&Y the HCCCA does not itself prohibit recognising [a non-chosen court's judgment] (J7.5.5), so [the X judgment] is enforced.
  • Chosen Court; Strong Cause (±) Submitted that the breach matters, not whether [Singapore / Y] was chosen; and [the X court]'s finding of [strong cause] goes to its own exercise of jurisdiction, so should not estop Singapore on [breach] (cf Merck: issues the forum decides for itself).
  • REFJA Analogue (−) Per s 5(4)(b) REFJA, [the X court] is not deemed to have jurisdiction where [the X proceedings] breached [the agreement], unless [debtor] submitted (J7.4.3).
J7.2.7 Conflicting Judgments
  • Inconsistent Singapore Judgment (−) Per Merck and C&Y, [the X judgment] is not recognised if inconsistent with [a Singapore judgment] between [the same parties], earlier or later. A later one prevails as [creditor] should have raised [the X judgment] there, and for internal coherence (compare s 15(1)(d) CCAA).
  • Competing Foreign Judgments (±) Per Merck (endorsing Prof Yeo; First Global Funds; Showlag), where [the X judgment] and [the Y judgment] are both recognisable, the earlier prevails; compare s 15(1)(e) CCAA and s 5(1)(b) REFJA.
  • Singapore Proceedings Pending (±) Per Merck, it is open whether [the X judgment], given while [Singapore proceedings on the same subject matter] were pending, is recognised. (+) Prof Yeo would recognise it. (−) Art 7(2) Hague Judgments Convention allows refusal where Singapore was seised first and [the dispute] is closely connected with Singapore.
J7.2.8 Satisfaction and Limitation
  • Satisfaction (−) Per C&Y, [debtor] has paid [amount] of [total], so [creditor] may enforce only [the balance]; a satisfied judgment cannot be enforced again (cf REFJA s 4(3), (9)).
  • Six Years, Not Twelve (−) Per Poh Soon Kiat, an action on [the X judgment] is on an implied debt, so the six-year period in s 6(1)(a) Limitation Act applies, not s 6(3)'s twelve years, which covers only [Singapore judgments]; [creditor] sued on [date], [within / out of] time.
  • When Time Runs (+) Per C&Y, time runs from [the date of the X judgment]; per Sang Cheol Woo, that means when it became final and conclusive under [X] law, e.g., [the X Supreme Court's decision on [date]] (J7.1.3).
  • Recognition or In Rem (+) Per Murakami (HC), [a judgment in rem declaring rights in [property]] is not subject to the six-year bar; nor is [recognition] generally, as no implied debt is sued on.
J7.2.9 Conclusion on Defences

On balance, [debtor]'s [defence] [succeeds / fails] because [reason], so [the X judgment] [is enforced in full / is enforced save for [the severed portion] / is not enforced].

J7.3 RECOGNITION: FOREIGN JUDGMENT AS RES JUDICATA

(Use where [party] relies on [the X judgment] as a shield, or to bind [other party] on an issue. It must be capable of recognition: J7.1.1–J7.1.3 satisfied and no defence under J7.2, but no money requirement. Here (+) helps the party relying on [the X judgment] and (−) the party resisting it.)

J7.3.0 Starter

Presently, [the X judgment] may be res judicata in [the Singapore action] because it raises [cause of action estoppel (J7.3.1) / issue estoppel (J7.3.2) / abuse under Henderson v Henderson (J7.3.3)].

  • Representation Not to Rely (−) Per Showlag v Mansour (C&Y), [party] who represented that it would not rely on [the X judgment] may be met by an estoppel by representation (a cross-estoppel), barring its plea of [res judicata].
J7.3.1 Cause of Action Estoppel

Per Arnold, it arises where the cause of action in [the Singapore action] is identical to that in [the X proceedings], between the same parties or privies, on the same subject matter; per C&Y it is an absolute bar absent [fraud / collusion].

  • No Merger (+) Per Ocean Tankers (SGCA, preliminary view), [the original claim] does not merge into [the X judgment], unlike a Singapore judgment, so [the X loser] could re-sue on it here; whether [registration under REFJA or the CCAA] merges it is "arguable".
  • Shield (+) [The unsuccessful X claimant] re-sues [defendant] in Singapore on [the same cause], so [defendant] pleads [the X judgment] as res judicata, e.g., [a German declaration of non-liability under [contract]] against [a Singapore breach claim] (slides).
  • Sword for Non-Money Judgments (+) Per C&Y, [the X winner], holding [an X order for specific performance / an injunction] outside REFJA and the CCAA, sues afresh on [the same cause] and pleads [the X judgment]; if recognisable, it binds without [the merits] being reopened.
J7.3.2 Issue Estoppel
J7.3.2.1 Requirements

Per Merck (adopting The Sennar (No 2)), [party] must show (a) a foreign judgment capable of recognition; (b) identical parties or privies; and (c) the same issue. Presently, [the X judgment] meets J7.1.1–J7.1.3 and no defence applies; [A] and [B] were parties to both; and [the issue: governing law / breach / validity of [clause]] arises in both.

  • Necessary, Not Collateral (±) Per Merck (citing Carl Zeiss), [the X finding on [issue]] must have been necessary to [the X court]'s decision, not collateral; presently it [was / was not] essential to [the result].
  • Finality Per Issue (±) Per Merck, the decision on [the specific issue] must be final under [X] law; for [a civil law judgment], only [the dispositif] may bind, not [the reasoning].
  • Identity of Issue (−) Per Gonzalo Gil White (SGCA), [the party relying] bears the burden, with special caution for foreign rulings. Ask (1) were [the issues] framed the same way; and (2) if so, did they arise under different laws? If so, no identity.
  • Identity: Application (−) As in Gonzalo Gil White (Mexican concurso rulings under Mexican law shared no identity with a Singapore-law claim), [the X ruling under [X law]] does not decide [the Singapore-law issue]; look at identity of [issues], not [consequences].
  • Outer Limits (−) Per Merck, no estoppel where (i) [the issue] is one Singapore decides for itself (J7.3.2.3); (ii) [the X judgment] is territorially limited to [X]; (iii) [party], a foreign defendant, had bona fide reasons, e.g., [cost / triviality / unfamiliar procedure] (Carl Zeiss), not to contest [the issue] fully; or (iv) Singapore's substantive public policy forestalls it.
  • Why Caution for Defendants (−) Per C&Y, [the X claimant] chose [X], whereas [defendant] was brought there, may rationally have limited its defence, and may not have expected [the issue] to bind it worldwide.
  • Pure Law (−) Per Merck, no estoppel arises on [a pure question of law] that does not directly affect [the parties]' rights.
J7.3.2.2 Procedural and Interlocutory Rulings
  • The Debate (±) (−) Per Merck, a decision on [a procedural issue], e.g., [a Y court's ruling that an X judgment raises an estoppel under Y law], is not on the merits and founds no estoppel. (+) But per Lakshmi, estoppel may arise from [interlocutory decisions], where procedural issues are usually decided.
  • Better Test (±) Per C&Y, the procedural/merits label is unhelpful, the two overlapping (The Sennar (No 2)). Ask whether [the issue] is one Singapore retains the prerogative to decide, e.g., [administration of justice / sovereignty] (J7.3.2.3).
  • Narrow Approach (±) Per Desert Sun (cited in Lakshmi), [the X interlocutory ruling on [service / jurisdiction]] estops only if (a) [the issue] was expressly submitted to [the X court]; (b) the specific issue of fact was raised and decided; and (c) Carl Zeiss caution is borne in mind.
  • Narrow: Application (−) As in Desert Sun (an Arizona ruling on jurisdiction did not decide the narrower issue of the attorneys' authority), [the X ruling] [did / did not] decide [the specific issue now raised].
  • Broad Approach (+) In English law, estoppel covers procedural and substantive issues. As in The Sennar (No 2) (the Dutch ruling that a Sudanese EJC barred the claim was substantive), [the X ruling on [the jurisdiction clause]] binds [party].
J7.3.2.3 Issues Singapore Decides for Itself (−)
  • International Jurisdiction Per C&Y, whether [debtor] submitted to [the X court] is for Singapore's conflict rules. Per Roch LJ in Desert Sun, an estoppel from [the X court]'s finding of [voluntary submission] would "sub-contract" that question.
  • Forum Non Conveniens Per Lakshmi, [the X court]'s refusal to stay because [X] is the natural forum raises no estoppel against [a Singapore ASI application]: no identity of subject matter (an ASI needs [vexation or oppression]), and estoppel would turn on [court scheduling].
  • FNC Critique Per C&Y, estoppel always depends on scheduling; Lakshmi is better explained as each court deciding its own appropriateness, so [the X court]'s view that [X] is forum conveniens never binds [the Singapore court]. Per Lakshmi, [the X ruling] may still bear on comity.
  • Public Policy Per India v Deutsche Telekom (via Gonzalo Gil White), [the X court]'s ruling on [X]'s public policy does not estop [debtor] on Singapore public policy (J7.2.4).
  • HCCCA Applicability Per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), [debtor] may argue that [the X court]'s ruling that [clause] falls within the HCCCA raises no estoppel, each Contracting State court deciding for itself whether [the HCCCA] applies (J1).
J7.3.2.4 Specific Issues
  • Governing Law (+) Per Merck (HC, not appealed) and Chong (seminar: governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself), [the X ruling on the governing law of [contract]] can found an estoppel, but per First Laser only if decided at [the final trial], not on [a stay application] decided on a good arguable case.
  • Different Choice of Law Rules (±) (+) Per First Laser, it is immaterial that [X]'s choice of law rules differ from Singapore's; estoppel never required [the Singapore court] to reach the same result. (−) But per Gonzalo Gil White, if [the issue] arose under different laws in each court, there is no identity.
    • Narrow reading (+): per Chong (seminar), identity fails only where Singapore's rules would select [Singapore law], the court being custodian of Singapore law (as there: [Mexican insolvency law] v Singapore law of incorporation). Otherwise, as Singapore never looks behind [a foreign judgment], [X]'s different rules should not matter.
  • Forum Mandatory Rule (−) Per the slides, where [the X court] held [an exemption clause] valid but it is void under UCTA applying as an overriding rule (s 27(2)), Merck's public policy limit blocks [the estoppel].
  • Judgment on a Judgment (−) Per Merck, [the X judgment] declaring [the Y judgment] enforceable in [X] raises no estoppel on [liability]; look to [the Y judgment] itself.
J7.3.3 Rule in Henderson v Henderson

Presently, [party] raises [issue / claim] in Singapore that could and should have been raised in [the X proceedings], so [other party] pleads abuse. Per Humpuss, the court weighs all the circumstances, including whether [the Singapore action] collaterally attacks [the X judgment], [fresh evidence], and bona fide reasons, e.g., [reason], for not raising it in [X].

  • No Need for Same Parties (±) Per Humpuss, identical parties are not required: [claimant] may be barred from suing [new defendant] who should have been sued in [X].
  • Not Every Point (+) Per Humpuss, [the X litigation] need not have covered every point for [party]'s raising of [point] here to be abusive.
J7.3.4 The Arnold Exception

Presently, [party] estopped on [issue] invokes the Arnold exception. Per TT International, for local judgments it must show that [the X decision on [issue]] directly affects [the parties]' future rights; is clearly wrong because [reason]; erred on [a point] not reasonably arguable before [the X court]; involves no claw-back of [accrued rights]; and that great injustice would follow, namely [consequence].

  • Foreign Judgments (±) Per Merck, it is open whether the exception applies, the CA weighing (i) not at all; (ii) issue estoppel only; (iii) a wider "working justice" test; (iv) testing [the issue]'s conclusiveness by [X] law. Per C&Y, (iv) is best, consistent with finality under [X] law (J7.1.3).
J7.4 STATUTE: REFJA (OUTLINE ONLY, FOR COMPARISON)

(Not examinable as a regime: per Chong (seminar), REFJA will not be examined, and per the Week 12 handout it is covered "in outline, mainly in comparison with the common law position". If [X] is gazetted, say one line, then run the common law (J7.1–J7.3), citing REFJA only as an analogue under Merck's convergence aim.)

  • One-Line Router Per ss 3, 4(7)(a), [a judgment of a gazetted X court] may be registered and then has local force; per s 7(1), [creditor] cannot then sue on it at common law (J7.0.2).
J7.4.1 Analogues: What Is Enforced
  • Non-Money Relief (±) Per s 4(4), [an injunction / specific performance order] is registrable if "just and convenient", unlike at [common law] (J7.1.4).
  • Excess Damages (±) Per s 4(5), only [the compensatory part] of [treble / punitive damages] is registered; compare Licea at [common law] (J7.2.5).
  • Excluded (−) Per ss 2(1), 3(4), [taxes, fines and penalties] and [a judgment on a judgment] fall outside REFJA, as at common law (J7.1.1; J7.2.5).
J7.4.3 Analogues: Jurisdiction and Defences
  • Residence, Not Presence (−) Per s 5(3)(a)(iv), [debtor] must have been [resident / a company with its principal place of business] in [X]; mere presence does not suffice, unlike at common law (J7.1.2).
  • Protest Is Not Submission (+) Per s 5(3)(a)(i), appearing only to [contest jurisdiction / invite the X court not to exercise it / protect seized property] is not submission, matching IGCF against Henry v Geoprosco (J7.1.2.4).
  • Breach of Agreement (−) Per s 5(4)(b), [the X court] is not deemed to have jurisdiction where [the X proceedings] breached [the clause] and [debtor] did not submit: the analogue for the common law defence (J7.2.6).
  • Fraud and Public Policy (±) Per s 5(1)(a)(iv)–(v), registration is set aside for [fraud] or where enforcing [the X judgment] offends public policy. Per Chong (seminar), as REFJA words public policy like the common law, Venetian Macau is authoritative for [the common law] too (J7.2.2; J7.2.4).
J7.5 STATUTE: CCAA (HAGUE CHOICE OF COURT AGREEMENTS)

(Use where [the X court], in an HCCCA Contracting State, is the court chosen in an exclusive COCA. Per REFJA s 2A, the CCAA then ousts REFJA; per s 21 CCAA, the common law remains open (J7.0.2).)

J7.5.0 Starter

Presently, [the X judgment] comes from [the chosen court] in [X], a Contracting State, so [creditor] applies under the CCAA rather than suing afresh. Per s 13(4), the court must recognise or enforce it unless a ground in ss 14–16 applies, the list being exhaustive.

J7.5.1 Scope
  • Chosen Court (±) Per s 2(1), only judgments of [the chosen court] of a Contracting State, or of a court to which it transferred the case under internal allocation rules, qualify. Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, the basis on which [the X court] took jurisdiction is irrelevant.
  • Scope Conditions (±) [The COCA] must be exclusive, in [a civil or commercial matter], international, and concluded after the HCCCA entered into force for [X] and Singapore (Singapore: 1 Oct 2016). Whether [an asymmetric clause] qualifies is for J1.
  • Judgment (+) Per s 2(1), [the X judgment] is a "judgment" as it is [a final decision on the merits / a consent order or judgment / a default judgment], or [a costs determination] relating to one, including [non-money judgments]. Per s 10, [interim relief] is excluded (Motacus), though Singapore may grant [interim relief in support] (s 10(2)).
  • Judicial Settlement (+) Per ss 2(1) and 20, [the settlement] approved by or concluded before [the chosen court], ending [the proceedings] and officially recorded, is enforced (not "recognised") like a judgment if enforceable in [X]; a [consent order] is a "judgment" instead.
  • Remedy Unknown in Singapore (±) Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, if [the X non-money remedy] is unknown here, the court gives it as much effect as possible, e.g., [the nearest equivalent order].
J7.5.2 Procedure and Effect
  • Application and Service (+) Per s 13(1) and O 37 ROC 2021, [creditor] applies to the General Division without a fresh action; per O 37 r 6(4), it may serve the order on [debtor] in [Y] without permission.
  • Time Bar (±) (+) Per C&Y, no limitation period applies, as no implied debt is sued on. (−) But per s 13(2), if [the X judgment] is no longer enforceable in [X], e.g., [time-barred under [X] law], Singapore cannot enforce it.
  • Effect in the State of Origin (±) Per s 13(2), [the X judgment] is recognised only if it has effect in [X], and enforced only if enforceable there; e.g., [an expired time-limited injunction] cannot be enforced.
  • No Review of the Merits (+) Per s 13(3)(a), the court may not review [the X judgment]'s merits save to apply Part 3; per s 13(1), it recognises it as it would [a General Division judgment].
  • Jurisdictional Findings Bind (+) Per s 13(3)(b), the court is bound by [the X court]'s findings of fact on which it assumed jurisdiction, e.g., [that the COCA was concluded / exclusive / international], unless [the X judgment] was by default. Per C&Y, only facts bind, not [their legal evaluation, e.g., "accessibility"].
J7.5.3 Mandatory Refusal (s 14)

[Debtor] argues that the General Division must refuse to recognise or enforce [the X judgment] on the ground of [ground].

  • No Timely Notice (±) (−) Per s 14(a), refusal is mandatory if [debtor] was not notified of [the originating document] in time to arrange its defence. (+) Not where [X] law allowed notification to be contested and [debtor] appeared and argued [the case] without contesting it.
  • Procedural Fraud (−) Per s 14(b), refusal is mandatory if [the X judgment] was obtained by fraud in connection with procedure, e.g., [creditor] [deliberately serving a wrong address / misleading [debtor] about the hearing / bribing [a judge or witness] / concealing key evidence]; per C&Y, this ≈ extrinsic fraud (J7.2.2).
  • Public Policy (−) Per s 14(c), refusal is mandatory if recognition would be manifestly incompatible with Singapore public policy, including where [the X proceedings] breached fundamental procedural fairness; "manifestly" sets a high bar. Per C&Y, intrinsic fraud, e.g., [perjury at trial], may fall here.
J7.5.4 Discretionary Refusal (ss 15–16) and Severance (s 19)

[Debtor] asks the court to exercise its discretion to refuse [the X judgment] on the ground of [ground].

  • COCA Null and Void (±) (−) Per s 15(1)(a), [the COCA in [clause]] is null and void under [X] law, including its choice of law rules. (+) Not if [the X court] held it valid; per C&Y, that ruling binds even in [a default judgment], on law and fact.
  • Incapacity (−) Per s 15(1)(b), [party] lacked capacity under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, to conclude [the COCA]; per C&Y, capacity is thus tested under both [X] law (via (a)) and Singapore law.
  • Service Contrary to Singapore Fundamentals (±) (−) Per s 15(1)(c), [debtor] was notified in a manner incompatible with Singapore's fundamental principles of service. (+) Per C&Y, it caters for States treating [foreign service] as a sovereign act, which Singapore does not, so it rarely applies to [the service here].
  • Inconsistent Singapore Judgment (−) Per s 15(1)(d), [the X judgment] conflicts with [a Singapore judgment] between [the same parties], earlier or later, not necessarily on the same cause of action; per C&Y, e.g., Singapore took jurisdiction under s 12 because [the clause] was void.
  • Inconsistent Earlier Foreign Judgment (±) (−) Per s 15(1)(e), [the X judgment] conflicts with [an earlier Y judgment]. (+) But [the Y judgment] must be earlier, between [the same parties], on the same cause of action, and recognisable here.
  • Pending Review or Appeal (±) Per s 15(2)–(3), if [the X judgment] is under [appeal] in [X], or time to appeal has not expired, the court may refuse, set aside or postpone, but [creditor] may apply again once [the appeal] is decided.
  • Objected Transfer (−) Per s 15(4), where [the chosen court] in [X] exercised a discretion to transfer to [X court 2] over [debtor]'s timely objection, the court may refuse [the X court 2 judgment] against [debtor]; not if [the transfer was mandated] (J5.4.2).
  • Transfer: Who Objected (±) Per C&Y (Hartley–Dogauchi), s 15(4) protects only a timely objector against whom judgment went, so [the X court 2 judgment] is enforceable against [the party who requested or did not oppose the transfer]. If [clause] names "the courts of [X]", [X court 2] is itself chosen.
  • Excess Damages (±) (−) Per s 16, the court may refuse [the X judgment] insofar as it awards damages, such as [punitive damages], exceeding compensation for actual loss. (+) It considers whether [the award] covers [costs and expenses of the X proceedings].
  • Severance (+) Per s 19, the court must enforce [a severable part] of [the X judgment] if applied for, so [creditor] enforces [the compensatory part] despite [the refused punitive portion].
  • Narrower Than Common Law (±) Per C&Y, the CCAA grounds are generally narrower (exhaustive; "manifestly"; procedural fraud only; binding findings), but add [COCA-specific grounds] (s 15(1)(a)–(b), (4), s 16), so [debtor]'s [intrinsic fraud plea] fares worse than at common law.
J7.5.5 Judgment of a Non-Chosen Court in Breach of an Exclusive COCA
  • The Gap (±) Presently, [the COCA] chose [X court 1], but [creditor] sued in [Y court] in breach. (+) Per C&Y, [the Y judgment] is outside the CCAA, which does not bar its enforcement under [REFJA / common law]. (−) Submitted that the common law should recognise a defence (J7.2.6); if [Y] is gazetted, s 5(4)(b) REFJA already applies (J7.4.3).
J7.6 ANTI-ENFORCEMENT INJUNCTIONS (AEI)

(The single home for AEIs; J6.5.4 points here. Use where [debtor] wants Singapore to restrain [creditor] from relying on or enforcing [the X judgment] in [X / Y / worldwide]. Run the J6 ASI requirements first, then this overlay. Per C&Y, breach of an AEI is contempt.)

J7.6.0 Starter

Presently, [debtor] seeks an AEI restraining [creditor] from [relying on / enforcing] [the X judgment] in [X / Y / worldwide]. Per Sun Travels and C&Y, beyond the usual ASI requirements (J6), [debtor] must show exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability.

  • Why Caution (−) Per Sun Travels, an AEI implies [debtor] delayed in not seeking an ASI earlier, wastes [the X court]'s time and costs, stops [other courts] deciding recognition themselves, and interferes with execution in [X]; it is akin to nullifying [the X judgment].
  • Breach or Vexation Not Enough (−) Per Sun Travels, neither [creditor]'s breach of [the EJC / arbitration clause] nor [vexatious conduct] suffices alone, and party autonomy is no separate basis (Arkhangelsky creates no "agreement" category).
  • Fraud (+) Per Sun Travels, [creditor]'s fraud in obtaining [the X judgment], e.g., [perjury / forged evidence], is an exceptional circumstance, as in Ellerman Lines v Read (reliance on a Turkish judgment procured by [the salvor]'s perjury was restrained).
  • No Knowledge (+) Per Sun Travels (citing Ecobank), [debtor] did not know [the X judgment] was being sought until [it was delivered], e.g., [obtained secretly or too quickly], so its delay is not unconscionable.
  • Delay (±) Per Sun Travels, mere passage of time is not enough; delay counts against [debtor] only when coupled with [knowledge] and/or [prejudice to [creditor] or third parties such as the X court]. Simply limiting [the relief] to reflect the delay, as the judge did, is not the answer.
  • Applicant's Silence (−) Per Sun Travels, both sides' conduct matters: if [debtor] knew of [the fraud] before [the X judgment] but stayed silent, the equities may tilt against it.
  • No Closed List (±) Per Sun Travels, a new category needs the equities to favour relief: either a response to [creditor]'s [unconscionable conduct], or [debtor] has not lost equity through [unconscionable delay]. As in Sun Travels (Hilton delayed until after the Maldivian judgment), [debtor]'s [delay] [defeats / does not defeat] the AEI.
  • Alternatives (+) Per Sun Travels, AEIs "should generally be refused", so [debtor] should instead [resist recognition in Singapore (J7.2) / claim damages for breach of [clause] (J1.7) / resist enforcement in [Y]].

1Start here: J7 in plain English

Sometimes a court abroad has already decided the dispute. Question 1 ends by asking what that foreign judgment is worth in Singapore. A Singapore court does not automatically obey a foreign judgment: it gives effect to it only if the foreign court had the right kind of jurisdiction and nothing unfair happened.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A foreign judgment is like a match result from another league. Singapore will count that result if the other referee had authority over the player (the player was in that league's country, or agreed to play there), the result is final (not a half-time score), and it is a clear score (a sum of money). It will not re-referee the match. But it will refuse to count the result if the match was fixed (fraud), a player was never told the match was on (natural justice), or counting it would be outrageous here (public policy).

Use 1 is enforcement: Beta wants money, so all four common law requirements apply, including a definite sum (J7.1). Use 2 is recognition: Beta only wants the Hong Kong judgment treated as deciding the matter, so there is no money requirement (J7.3). The same judgment can be both, depending on who is using it and for what. Always open your answer by saying which one the facts raise.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Creditor / debtorThe party who won money abroad / the party ordered to pay.
EnforcementGetting the money: at common law, by suing in Singapore on the debt the foreign judgment creates.
RecognitionTreating the judgment as deciding the matter: used as a shield (res judicata) or to bind on an issue. No money requirement.
International jurisdictionWhether the foreign court had jurisdiction by Singapore's conflict rules: presence or submission.
Final and conclusiveThe foreign court cannot itself reopen it, and treats it as res judicata (appeal may still be possible).
Res judicataThe matter has been decided: cause of action estoppel, issue estoppel, Henderson v Henderson abuse.
Extrinsic / intrinsic fraudFraud the debtor had no chance to challenge abroad / fraud it could have challenged at trial.
REFJAThe registration statute for gazetted countries. Not examinable: one line at most.
AEIAnti-enforcement injunction: stopping the creditor enforcing the foreign judgment anywhere.

J7.0.2 Regime Router

(write one sentence, then go to the relevant part)

  • CCAA First (Ousts REFJA) If [X] is an HCCCA Contracting State and [the X court] is the court chosen in the exclusive COCA in [clause], or its transferee, [creditor] proceeds under the CCAA (J7.5). Per REFJA s 2A, if [X] is also gazetted, [creditor] cannot fall back on REFJA should [the X judgment] fail under the CCAA.
  • Common Law Fallback (±) Per s 21 CCAA, the common law remains open, but per C&Y the CCAA is almost always better for [creditor] ([non-money relief / no limitation period / simpler procedure]); after a CCAA refusal, suing at common law may be abusive if it re-ventilates [the same issues].
  • REFJA (Not Examinable) Per Chong (seminar), REFJA will not be examined. If [X] is gazetted (per the handout: [HK / Brunei / Australia / India / Malaysia / NZ / Pakistan / PNG / Sri Lanka / UK]), note in one line that [creditor] could register (J7.4), then run the common law.
  • Common Law Residual Otherwise [creditor] sues [debtor] on the debt [the X judgment] creates, usually by [summary judgment]. Per C&Y, [debtor] gets leave to defend only by showing a fair or reasonable probability of [a real defence] under J7.2, never [the merits] (J7.2.1).
  • Non-Money Judgments [An injunction / order for specific performance] from [X] is enforceable only under REFJA (s 4(4)) or the CCAA; at common law [creditor] sues afresh on [the original cause] and pleads [the X judgment] as res judicata (J7.3.1).
  • Recognition Only Where [party] pleads [the X judgment] as a shield, or to bind [other party] on [an issue], J7.1.1–J7.1.3 must be met and no J7.2 defence apply, but there is no money requirement (J7.3).
  • In Rem: Test Per Pattni v Ali (adopted by the SGCA), [the X judgment] is in rem if [the X court], where [the property] was situated, adjudicated title against the world. Per C&Y, Singapore characterises it by [the X proceedings]' nature and intended effect.
  • In Rem: Effect Per C&Y, [the property] must have been in [X] when proceedings began (also s 5(3)(b) REFJA). It is usually recognised, e.g., [as proof of title in a conversion claim], free of the six-year bar, and [a good-faith purchaser] is protected against fraud.
  • Memorandum of Guidance (−) [Creditor] relies on the MoG between Singapore and [the X court, e.g., DIFC / China SPC]. Per C&Y, MoGs are non-binding statements of each side's existing law, so [the X judgment] must still satisfy [the common law / REFJA].
PointRule
CCAA usually better for the creditorNon-money relief, no limitation period, simpler procedure (C&Y). After a CCAA refusal, suing at common law on the same issues may be abusive.
Common law routeSue on the debt, usually by summary judgment; the debtor gets leave to defend only with a real J7.2 defence, never the merits.
Non-money judgmentsEnforceable only under REFJA (s 4(4)) or the CCAA. At common law, sue afresh and plead the judgment as res judicata (J7.3.1).
In rem judgmentsIn rem if the court where the property was adjudicated title against the world (Pattni v Ali); usually recognised.
Memoranda of GuidanceNon-binding: the judgment must still satisfy the common law (C&Y).
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

REFJA will not be examined. If the country is gazetted, note in one line that the creditor could register, then run the common law.

Routing three judgments

From the Ruritanian court chosen in a 2019 exclusive clause; Ruritania is a Contracting StateCCAA (J7.5). The creditor may still sue at common law (s 21), but the CCAA is usually better: non-money relief, no limitation period.
