LESSON C3 · Q2 · CHOICE OF LAW · ABOUT 27 MIN · 8 FLOWCHARTS · 5 ILLUSTRATIONS · 15 QUESTIONS

Tort choice of law: double actionability and the flexible exception

⚡ BIG IDEA

A tort claim must be actionable under BOTH Singapore law (as if everything happened here) AND the law of the place where the tort was in substance committed. The claimant proves the first limb; the defendant must plead and prove that the foreign law gives no liability. A strictly applied flexible exception can displace either law, or both, where it is purely fortuitous.

PRE-WRITE C3 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
C3 Tort Choice Of Law
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.
C3.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Scan first; route to the matching section.)

  1. Characterise [the claim] as tortious, [claimant] framing freely absent bad faith (Rickshaw) (C3.1).
  2. General rule: double actionability, [claimant] proving the lex fori limb and [defendant] the lex loci delicti limb (Boys v Chaplin; Rickshaw; EFT Holdings) (C3.1, C3.2).
  3. Locate the tort in [country X] by substance (Distillers; JIO Minerals; Vibrant Group) (C3.3), checking [s 101 OSRAA / s 6(4) THPA] (C3.3.4) and local torts (C3.4).
  4. Foreign law unpleaded or unproved: [Singapore law by default / the presumption] for [law X] (EFT Holdings; OMG Holdings) (C3.5).
  5. Flexible exception: strict and fortuity-based (Rickshaw), displacing [the lex fori / the lex loci delicti / both] for [the issue] (C3.6), including party autonomy (C3.6.5).
  6. Particular torts [defamation / IP / misrepresentation] (C3.7) and contract as a tort defence [Sayers / Galaxias] (C3.8).
  7. Overlays: [damages / limitation / renvoi] under [law X] (C3.9); evaluation (C3.10); other obligations (C3.11); pathways (C3.12).
C3.0.1 Quick Application Template

Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant] for [tort] arising from [acts] in [country X].

  • Limb 1: had [the acts] all occurred in Singapore, they would be [the tort] as [the elements are made out] (C3.2).
  • Limb 2: the tort was in substance committed in [country X], where [the act / receipt and reliance / publication] occurred (C3.3), and [defendant] [pleads no liability under law X / does not plead law X, so Singapore law applies] (C3.5).
  • Exception: [Singapore law / law X] [is / is not] purely fortuitous given [the connecting factors], so it [is / is not] displaced (C3.6).
  • Result: [the law] governs and [claimant] [succeeds / fails], subject to [law X]'s limitation period (C3.9.2) and [Singapore] quantum (C3.9.1).
C3.1 STARTER: THE GOVERNING RULE
C3.1.1 Global Starter

The issue is which law governs [claimant]'s claim for [negligence / misrepresentation / conspiracy / defamation / conversion] arising from [acts] in [country X]. Per Rickshaw, it is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea).

  • The Two Limbs Per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin (adopted in Rickshaw), [the wrong] must be (a) a tort under Singapore law (C3.2) and (b) give civil liability between the actual parties under [law X] (C3.3).
    • Not necessarily tortious: per Ong Ghee Soon, any civil liability under [law X] suffices, e.g. [a civil-law delict / statutory liability].
    • Defences: per C&Y, [a defence] under either law defeats [the claim].
  • Common Denominator absent displacement, [claimant] recovers only what both laws allow (Yeo), as in McElroy v McAllister where [the widow] got only funeral expenses, so [claimant] argues displacement (C3.6).
  • How Many Leges Causae? per C&Y, the rule names no single law: two generally, one if the exception displaces [the lex fori] (Red Sea) or [the lex loci delicti] (Boys v Chaplin), and [a third law] if both go (C3.6.4).
  • Burden of Proof Per EFT Holdings, [claimant] proves limb (a), while [defendant] must plead and prove non-actionability under [law X], limb (b) existing for [defendant]'s benefit.
    • Dominance: per C&Y, this burden model and the default rule (C3.5) make [the lex fori] the dominant limb over [law X].
    • Reversal: where [claimant] invokes the exception to apply [law X] (Red Sea), [claimant] must plead and prove [law X].
  • Characterisation Per C&Y, "tort" is not bound by [domestic categories], though [a domestic tort] normally qualifies, and some equitable wrongs may count (Rickshaw), e.g. [dishonest assistance] (Grupo Torras; C3.11).
    • Foreign law may inform it: where [claimant] relies solely on [law X] for [a liability unknown here], [law X]'s characterisation matters (Red Sea).
  • Framing / Concurrent Liability Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith [claimant] may frame in tort despite [the law Y clause], the claim being characterised as tort though it arises from [the contract].
    • Contrast: [equitable claims] rooted in [the contract] follow contract COL (C1.1.5), and [a "parasitic" tort] may follow [the contract's law] (C3.6.5).
  • Rationale (evaluative) limb (b) spares [defendant] not liable where it acted (EFT) and serves comity, though per Metall comity weakens where [the damage] is caused to [persons here]. Limb (a), from The Halley, is "parochial" (C&Y).
  • Development (evaluative) Phillips v Eyre's "not justifiable" limb, abused in Machado v Fontes ([criminal liability] sufficing), became civil liability in Boys v Chaplin, the proper law of the tort being rejected (Red Sea), so [claimant] cannot plead [the most connected law] directly.
C3.2 LIMB 1: ACTIONABLE AS A TORT UNDER THE LEX FORI
  • Counterfactual Test Per IM Skaugen, ask whether [the acts], if all done in Singapore, would be [a tort, e.g., Spandeck duty, breach, causation, damage], so limb 1 [is satisfied / fails].
  • Domestic Bar (−) if Singapore law [denies the head / supplies a complete defence] or does not allow [the direct claim] (Red Sea), [claimant] must displace the lex fori (C3.6.2).
  • Statutory Torts [OSRAA Parts 10 to 12 / s 6 THPA] supply limb 1 by statute (C3.3.4), but per JIO Minerals the Misrepresentation Act reaches [a misrepresentation abroad] only under [a Singapore-law contract] (C3.7.3).
C3.3 LIMB 2: CIVIL LIABILITY UNDER THE LEX LOCI DELICTI (LOCATING THE TORT)
C3.3.1 Starter: The Substance Test

[Defendant] pleads that [law X] imposes no liability because of [no duty for pure economic loss / a damages cap / a statutory defence / a shorter limitation period], so the tort must first be located.

  • The Test Per Distillers and Metall, look back over [the events] and ask where in substance the cause of action arose, finding one single place on [the elements as recognised by the lex fori] (C&Y).
  • As Pleaded per Vibrant Group, the weight of [act / reliance / damage] depends on [the tort pleaded], so [the place of reliance] counts more for [misrepresentation] than for [negligence] (C3.3.2).
  • Single Locality (+) all elements occurred in [country X], e.g. [the place of the motor accident] (C&Y), so ask only whether [law X] imposes liability.
  • Multiple Locality (−) [the act] and [the damage] span [X] and [Y], so apply the tort-specific rules (C3.3.2).
  • Damage Not Determinative per Distillers, the place of damage "may be quite fortuitous", so [claimant]'s loss at [its home base] does not by itself locate [the tort].
  • Policy Favouring the Forum (+) per Metall, the court need not "turn a blind eye" to [damage] caused to [persons here] by acts abroad, so [receipt / loss] in Singapore may be the substance.
  • Civil, Not Necessarily Tortious, Liability per Ong Ghee Soon, [negligent misstatement] was actionable under Art 41 SCO though Swiss law has no "law of negligence" category, so [law X]'s [delictual / statutory] liability suffices.
  • Same Test for Jurisdiction per Metall (citing Armagas), the same locus test serves [the tort gateway]. Whether double actionability applies at [service out] is open: yes per IM Skaugen (HC), no per Nippon Catalyst, left open in Shen Sophie (J3).
    • Divergence: the gateway needs only [an act partly / damage] here (Yeo), so [the gateway] may be met though [the tort] is located in [country X].
    • FNC: per JIO, the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum unless fortuitous, so locating it in [country X] favours [a stay] (J4).
C3.3.2 Tort-Specific Rules for Multi-Locality Torts

(select the tort pleaded)

  • Negligence: Focus on the Act Per Vibrant Group, the place of [the negligent act] prevails, so [the audit / advice] performed in [country X] locates the tort there despite [reliance and loss] in Singapore.
    • Negligent services / advice: where [the services] were or ought to have been [rendered] (Voth).
    • Trading decisions: where [the decision to speculate] was made, e.g. [Moscow] (Base Metal Trading).
    • Product liability: where [the product] was [marketed without the warning], not where [it was made] or [the damage] occurred (Distillers; Castree v Squibb).
    • Reliance weighs less: in [negligence], reliance is only one route to [a duty] (NTUC Foodfare; Vibrant).
  • Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant: Receipt + Reliance Per JIO Minerals (tentatively, citing Yeo) and Ong Ghee Soon, [a representation] directed at [claimant] and received and acted on in [Singapore] is a tort there, unless [that place] is fortuitous.
    • Where reliance crystallises: where [claimant] gave [instructions via the Singapore branch], not [administrative execution in Geneva] (Ong Ghee Soon).
    • Fortuitous receipt: receipt in [India] merely because [claimant] is based there is fortuitous (JIO).
    • Receipt and reliance split: the specific rule fails, so use [the substance test], as in JIO where [negotiations and drilling] made [Indonesia] the place.
    • Several countries of making, receipt and reliance: where [the core representations] were made, e.g. [Germany], may prevail, receipt being fortuitous for [global operators] (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel).
    • Receipt unclear on the pleadings: unevidenced receipt in [Germany] is "speculative", so [Singapore law] applies (Rickshaw).
  • Representation Made at Large per Cordova Land (and JIO), a statement to [the world at large] is a tort where made, unlike [one directed at the claimant] (The Albaforth).
  • Inducing Breach of Contract per Metall, the tort is where [the contract] was broken and [claimant] injured, e.g. [London], not where [the inducement] occurred ([New York]).
  • Conspiracy Per EFT Holdings, weigh [the conspirators' identity and location], where [they combined], [the concerted acts], [claimant]'s location and [where losses arose], as in EFT where [Taiwan] prevailed.
    • Parasitic conspiracy: one "so intimately connected" to [a contract] may follow [its law] without being located (Chen v BHNV; C3.6.5).
  • Defamation / Online / IP / Passing Off see C3.7 for [publication / download / the territorial right] in [the tort pleaded].
C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2

Limb 2 is satisfied if [law X] gives [some civil remedy] for [the conduct].

  • Limb 2 Fails Where [law X] [bars the head / provides a defence] or imposes no liability between [these parties] (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin), so [defendant] escapes unless [law X] is displaced (C3.6.3).
  • Time Bar [law X]'s [shorter period] bars [the claim] via s 3(2) FLPA, as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili (C3.9.2).
C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze

(claims under OSRAA or THPA)

  • OSRAA s 101: Tort Deemed in Singapore Per s 101 OSRAA 2025, a [Part 10 / 11 / 12] tort is treated as in Singapore if any element was (a) initiated in or from Singapore, (b) perceived here, or (c) caused [damage] here, so [the post viewed here] makes it a local tort.
    • Effect (Yeo): s 101 replaces the substance test with a statutory connecting factor, so both limbs point to [Singapore law], giving [the OSRAA torts] the character of overriding mandatory rules.
    • Jurisdiction (Yeo): it secures [nexus] and a factual presumption that Singapore is [forum conveniens], leaving FNC to sieve out [opportunistic foreign claims].
    • Exception: [defendant] may argue for [law X] where Singapore is so fortuitous that [serious injustice] results, but only exceptionally, given Parliament's intent to protect [Singapore residents] (Yeo).
    • No s 101 connection (rare): the substance test applies, [the tort] is likely abroad, and [claimant] recovers only the common denominator of [the OSRAA] and [law X] (Yeo).
    • Unilateral reading: s 101 may be a unilateral rule with no exception, but Yeo prefers [the multilateral reading] as [the wording] only redefines the connecting factor.
    • Critique (Yeo): if [law X] protects [the victim] better, s 101 still imposes [the lower OSRAA standard].
  • OSRAA s 102: No Contracting Out Per s 102, [exclusion / jurisdiction / arbitration terms] inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 ([Administrators / Platforms]) are void unless fair and reasonable, Part 10 ([Communicators]) not being covered (C3.8.2).
    • Choice of law clause: [a foreign COL clause] cannot exclude [OSRAA liability], party autonomy being unrecognised in tort (Yeo; C3.6.5).
  • THPA s 6(4): Limb 2 Abrogated Per s 6(4) THPA 2014, [conduct in or outside Singapore] causing haze is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad, so [defendant] cannot rely on [law X] for [burning in X].
    • Standing: per s 6(3), [a person] suffering [personal injury / property damage / economic loss] in Singapore sues, still proving [the statutory tort] under Singapore law.
    • Nature: an express statutory displacement of limb 2 for [haze claims], not a use of [the flexible exception]; per Chong (seminar), an overriding forum mandatory rule, so [the THPA claim] lies though [Indonesian law] imposes no liability.
    • Common law claim: per Chong (seminar), the substance test likely locates [the tort] in [Indonesia], where [the burning] occurred, so if [Indonesian law permits smallholder burning], limb 2 fails for [the negligence / nuisance claim] unless displaced (C3.6.3).
C3.4 LOCAL TORTS (TORT COMMITTED IN SINGAPORE)
  • Double Actionability Applies to Local Torts Per Rickshaw, rejecting Metall's English-law-only rule as "unduly parochial" and contrary to comity, [conversion / negligence] in Singapore still runs both limbs, both pointing to [Singapore law].
    • Point of difference: the exception may apply [foreign law] where [the Singapore locus] is purely fortuitous, no stricter test applying, though "a liberal approach must be eschewed" (Rickshaw).
    • Why England differs: per Yeo (cited in Rickshaw), before Red Sea [the lex fori] could not be displaced, so [a lex fori rule for local torts] made sense.
  • Displacing Singapore Law (−) [Defendant] argues Singapore is fortuitous as [both parties reside in X], as in Briggs' Changi transit-lounge brawl between [Australians flying home], so [Australian law] applies.
  • Rickshaw Facts (+) the CA kept [Singapore law] as most [connecting factors] were here and the German-contract defence was "vague and unclear", so [claimant] argues [the defence is unparticularised].
    • Further reasons: no evidence was adduced on [deceit], and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive (C3.6.5), so [the clause] did not reach [the torts].
  • Briggs' Critique the torts arose from [an employment relationship] under [a German-law clause] and were pleaded in tort to avoid [German law], so the exception should have applied [the contract's proper law] (C3.6.5).
    • C&Y: fortuity should be one ground only, a test on the significance of [connections, including the contract] giving more room, as English courts applying [the contract's law] show (Trafigura).
C3.5 PROOF OF FOREIGN LAW AND THE PRESUMPTION OF SIMILARITY (cross-refer C1.6)
  • Foreign Law Not Pleaded Per EFT Holdings (applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong), pleading [law X] is voluntary, so if [defendant] does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises and [Singapore law] applies without [the presumption].
    • C&Y framing: the same result is put as a presumption that [law X] equals [Singapore law].
  • Pleaded but Not Proved unproved [law X] is presumed similar where fair (Brownlie; C1.6.3), though [the party bearing the burden] may simply fail (EFT).
  • Limits of the Presumption [the party resisting it] argues it fails for [law X] because:
    • FNC: the court may accept that [civil law X] probably differs without [proof] (Rickshaw, citing PT Jaya Putra; JIO).
    • Intrusive relief abroad: no [injunction] against [conduct in X] on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings), explained by [the relief sought] (EFT).
    • Damages: for [damages / an account], the presumption presumably applies (C&Y), so [claimant] limits [the relief].
  • Cf Brownlie (UK) the default rule governs [unpleaded law] and the presumption [pleaded but unproved law], supporting the EFT split (C1.6.3).
C3.6 THE FLEXIBLE EXCEPTION
C3.6.1 Starter

Per Rickshaw, the exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea) may displace [the lex fori], [the lex loci delicti] or both for the law with the most significant relationship to [the issue] and the parties, so [party] argues [country X] is fortuitous because [factors].

  • Threshold Per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to apply it unless [the displaced law] is purely fortuitous and applying it causes [injustice], on "clear and satisfying grounds" (Lord Wilberforce), lest it become [a proper law of the tort].
  • Strictly Applied per Rickshaw, it is "imperative" that [the exception] be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility, so [party] needs [clear fortuity], not [a more favourable law].
  • Fortuity and Injustice: Conjunctive? unclear, but per C&Y applying [a fortuitous law] is itself [the injustice], so fortuity is the real test.
    • Stricter: than Red Sea and Ang Ming Chuang (weighing contacts) and Lord Wilberforce's interest analysis, so [claimant] leads with [fortuity].
    • Critique (C&Y): fortuity is too restrictive and should be one way of showing [an insignificant connection], so [party] argues [the weak connection] suffices.
  • Two Techniques in Boys Lord Hodson weighed [contacts] ("centre of gravity") while Lord Wilberforce ran an issue-specific [interest analysis] (C&Y), and Rickshaw adds fortuity.
  • Factors to Weigh per Restatement §145 (quoted in Red Sea), [the place of injury], [the place of conduct], [the parties' residence / incorporation] and [where the relationship is centred] point to [country Y].
  • Burden on the Invoking Party [the invoking party] must prove [the connecting factors] and [the foreign law] (Red Sea), a "vague and unclear" defence failing (Rickshaw).
C3.6.2 Displacing the Lex Fori (Red Sea)
  • Exclusive Lex Loci Delicti Per Red Sea, [claimant] may rely solely on [law X] though [the claim] is unknown to the lex fori, as [the insurer's direct claim] was under Saudi law, Hong Kong requiring [payment first].
  • Whole Claim per Red Sea, [one law] may govern the whole claim where "all or virtually all" factors point to it, as [the Saudi contracts, works, damage and head office] were "overwhelming", avoiding [fragmentation] (C&Y).
  • Rickshaw Test Applied (+) per C&Y, Red Sea would likely survive Rickshaw, [Hong Kong]'s only link being [incorporation], so [a bare Singapore incorporation] may be fortuitous.
  • Counter-Factor that [the forum] applies [foreign law] where its own gives no remedy is a factor, not a bar (Red Sea), [fortuity] deciding under Rickshaw.
  • Not Only for Deprived Claimants per Ang Ming Chuang (obiter), the law "must be just to defendants as well as plaintiffs", so [Taiwanese law] would have governed [SIA's claim against the CAA], and [defendant] may likewise invoke [law X].
  • Fortuity Required (−) [law X] cannot apply merely because it is [more favourable] where [the relationship] is Singapore-centred (Rickshaw).
C3.6.3 Displacing the Lex Loci Delicti (Boys v Chaplin)
  • Issue-Specific Interest Analysis In Boys v Chaplin, [British servicemen] collided in [Malta], and per Lord Wilberforce Malta had no interest in applying its [special-damages-only rule] to non-residents, so [law X]'s [damages restriction] yields for [Singapore-connected parties].
  • Rickshaw Caveat (−) per C&Y, a road accident's place is rarely fortuitous, and [soldiers stationed in Malta] are less transient than [transit passengers], so [defendant] argues [X] is the natural locus.
  • Issue-by-Issue displacement may cover [heads of damage] only (Boys), or [the whole claim] where virtually all factors align (Red Sea; C3.6.2).
C3.6.4 Applying the Law of a Third Country
  • Third Law Per Rickshaw (Red Sea "paves the way") and IM Skaugen, where [the forum] and [the place of the tort] are both purely fortuitous, [law Z] governs, e.g. [two Z residents fighting in a Y transit lounge] (C&Y).
    • Rare: per C&Y, it will rarely succeed, and [law Z]'s [limitation period] then applies (C3.9.2).
C3.6.5 Party Autonomy: Can the Contract's Law Govern the Tort?
  • The Argument [Party] argues cl [X] ("all relations" / "any dispute arising out of or in connection with") applies [law Y] to [the tort], an open question (Ong Ghee Soon), though "just a small step away" (C&Y).
  • Support per The Rainbow Joy, [the employment contract's law] "should prevail" over [the law of the flag] for [a tort on the high seas], and Rickshaw recognises an "exclusive" clause.
    • Ong Ghee Soon (obiter): cited Yeo's [hub] argument, [reforms abroad], Art 14 Rome II and Art 9(1)(g) Hague Principles (non-binding; [pre-contractual obligations]).
    • Rainbow Joy limit: it may be confined to [its facts] (Ong Ghee Soon), so [the opponent] distinguishes [the shipboard tort].
  • Why Allow It per C&Y, modern tort law allocates risk ([insurance / exemption clauses]), narrowing [the gap with contract], and autonomy brings certainty and supports [Singapore's hub policy] (Yeo).
  • Exclusive vs Non-Exclusive per Rickshaw, whether cl [X] covers [non-contractual claims] is construction under [its proper law], and [the clause] there was conceded non-exclusive.
  • Ong Ghee Soon Decided Nothing cl 7.29 was wide enough for [torts] under [Swiss law], but [the bank officer], a non-party, could not take its benefit absent a stipulation pour autrui (Art 112 SCO).
  • Foreign Restrictions Art 132 Swiss PILA (post-event choice only) bites only if [law X] includes [its PIL], a renvoi question (C3.9.3), and Art 120 PILA [consumer] status was left aside, [claimant] not being a consumer (Ong Ghee Soon).
  • Rome II Art 14 Model a choice is valid (a) after [the event], or (b) before it if all are pursuing [a commercial activity] and it is freely negotiated, with [reasonable certainty], no prejudice to [third parties], and no ouster of [the mandatory rules] of a wholly connected country.
  • Qualifications if Recognised per C&Y, [the choice] must be bona fide, legal and consistent with [public policy], and yields to forum mandatory rules (e.g. s 102 OSRAA; C3.3.4) for [the tort].
    • Pre- vs post-tort: pre-tort choices risk [weak parties] contracting unwittingly, but per C&Y there should be no blanket ban, [employees / consumers] being protected by targeted [mandatory rules].
    • Freely negotiated?: per C&Y, [businesspeople] routinely accept [boilerplate COL terms], so query whether [a standard form] should disqualify, or PIL police [bargaining power] at all.
  • Route Through the Exception (C&Y) [the chosen / proper law] applies via the flexible exception as the law of [the centred relationship], as in Chen v BHNV ([a conspiracy] "so intimately connected" to [the Belize-law contract]), Oro Negro and Trafigura.
    • Caution: Chen was an FNC ruling not running [Rickshaw's fortuity test], and Trafigura applied [s 12 PIL(MP)A], so they are analogies only.
    • Obstacle: Rickshaw's [fortuity threshold] and [non-exclusive concession] blocked it (C3.4), so [the opponent] argues [the separate tort] stays.
    • Application (+): [the platform / mandate] was the conduit, so [the proper law] displaces [both limbs].
  • Also an FNC Factor [a COL clause covering torts] points to [law Y] at Spiliada stage 1 (Rainbow Joy; Rickshaw; J4).
  • Statutory Override cl [X] cannot oust [Part 11 / 12 OSRAA] liability, s 102 voiding it unless [fair and reasonable] (C3.3.4).
C3.6.6 Public Policy Is Not a Ground for the Exception
  • Kuwait Airways the majority excised [the Iraqi confiscatory resolution] from [the lex loci delicti] via the exception, but Lord Scott (dissenting) said it is for applying [the most connected law], not disapplying [parts of it].
  • Better Route Lord Steyn refused [the resolution] on public policy within the rule itself (C&Y), so [the offending rule] is excised under [C1.8].
  • Singapore Position after Rickshaw, the exception cannot do this, [Iraq] not being fortuitous, so [law X] without [the offending rule] then [does / does not] impose liability (C1.8).
C3.7 PARTICULAR TORTS
C3.7.1 Defamation
  • Place of Publication Per Low Tuck Kwong, double actionability applies and the tort is where [the statement] is published, each publication a separate tort, so [Singapore publications] are local (C3.4) and [defendant] must plead [law X] for [X publications] (C3.5).
  • FNC Filter a claim for [foreign publication] may be stayed, the place of publication being prima facie the natural forum (C&Y), so [defendant] seeks [a stay to country X] (J4).
  • Internet Publication Per Dow Jones v Gutnick and Singapore cases (Qingdao Bohai), publication is where [the material] is downloaded and accessed, so [claimant] must show [access in Singapore].
    • Gutnick: [the publisher]'s server-law rule ([New Jersey]) was rejected; the majority relied on [practical limits], and Kirby J's global publication rule was left to [legislatures].
    • Contrast UK: s 8 Defamation Act 2013 adopts a single publication rule, unlike [the multiple-publication rule] applied to [the post].
    • Policy choice (Mills): the law of upload favours [free speech] ("race to the top") and download [reputation] ("race to the bottom"), so the choice is policy, not rationality.
    • Chan's tiered rule: combining [habitual residence], [place of reputational damage] and [publication], it is complex and unlikely to be adopted (C&Y).
    • Practice: few such claims reach Singapore, given [the O 8 r 1 / PD para 63 nexus] and [little reputational damage here] (C&Y).
    • OSRAA: s 101 reaches only [Part 10 to 12 harms, e.g., harassment or doxxing] (Yeo), so [common law defamation] stays under double actionability (C3.3.4).
  • Reform Carve-Out the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation, the lex fori limb filtering [foreign law] incompatible with [Singapore's free speech values], and move [business defamation] to [the lex loci delicti] (C3.10).
C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off
  • Territoriality per C&Y, statutory [copyright / patent / trade mark] rights are territorial: conduct abroad cannot infringe [a Singapore right], nor conduct here [a Utopian right].
  • Validity Separate [validity] follows the law of [the place of creation], and [the Singapore court] may lack jurisdiction where infringement turns on [foreign validity] (C&Y).
  • Scenarios (forum Singapore; no conventions) run [the right's origin] against [the place of infringement]:
    • (i) Singapore right infringed abroad: fails both limbs, and [the lex fori] is not fortuitous for [a Singapore right].
    • (ii) Utopian right infringed here: fails both limbs, [Singapore as locus] not being fortuitous for [the infringing acts].
    • (iii) Foreign right infringed there: [a Malaysian copyright infringed in Malaysia] may succeed via the exception displacing [a fortuitous lex fori], if [Singapore has jurisdiction] (cf Pearce v Ove Arup).
  • Passing Off a common law tort, so [territoriality] is no bar, but per OMG Holdings [an injunction] against passing off in [Malaysia] needs [Malaysian law] proved (C3.5).
C3.7.3 Misrepresentation and Conspiracy

See C3.3.2 for [the locus] of [misrepresentation / conspiracy].

  • Statutory Misrepresentation Per JIO Minerals, the Misrepresentation Act applies only if [Singapore law] governs [the issue], and to [a misrepresentation abroad] only if [the contract] is Singapore-law (C1.7; C2.9).
C3.8 INTERACTION BETWEEN CONTRACT AND TORT
C3.8.1 Contract Relied on to Negate the Tort

(the contract answers an element, e.g., [a licence / a right to remain])

  • Two Questions Per C&Y (North), (i) the effect of [the contract] on tort liability is a tort question for double actionability, and (ii) its validity a contract question for [its proper law, law Y].
  • Galaxias [the trespass] was an English tort, so English law held [a contractual right to remain] negates trespass, but Greek law (the proper law) showed [the crew] were lawfully discharged, so [the claim] succeeded.
  • In Singapore [a local tort] itself runs double actionability, and for a tort in [X] with [a law Y contract], (i) follows the lex fori and [law X] and (ii) [law Y] (North).
C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort
  • The Problem cl [X], valid under [law Y], excludes [negligence] liability that Singapore law [bars / subjects to reasonableness] ([s 2(1) / s 2(2) UCTA]).
    • Sayers: [an English worker] injured on [a Nigerian rig] was limited by [his Dutch employer]'s cl 8 compensation scheme, void under s 1(3) Law Reform (Personal Injuries) Act 1948 but valid in Dutch law.
  • Majority (Salmon and Stamp LJJ): Contractual Characterisation only the proper law of the contract mattered, and it being Dutch, "this action is dead" (Salmon LJ), so if [law Y] validates cl [X], [the claim] fails.
    • Critique (C&Y): treating [the issue] as wholly contractual is simplistic, ignoring [question (i)], so [claimant] argues [Singapore's policy] on admissibility.
  • Lord Denning: Proper Law of the Issue "we cannot apply two systems of law", so he applied the law closest to [the issues], Dutch ("Nigeria is out"), cl 8 "turn[ing] the scale" against [English law].
    • Critique (C&Y): he never asked what effect [the clause] has on [tort liability] (North).
    • Do not mix up the judgments: Salmon LJ found [the contract] Dutch, whereas Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch via [the tort].
    • Application: [law Y] is closest to [the issue] as [the relationship is centred there].
  • Preferred Approach (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan) (1) admissibility is a tort question for double actionability, and (2) validity a contract question for [its proper law], so cl [X], valid under [law Y], succeeds only if admissible under both [Singapore law] and [the lex loci delicti].
    • Incidental question: [the forum's] COL rules (simple, but [forum shopping]) or [the tort law's] (Harris: coherent, avoiding "the law of no one state") pick [the contract's law].
    • Which to choose: per C&Y, it may track Singapore's views on [renvoi] and [party autonomy] in tort.
    • Pre-existing contract: the exception may apply [law Y] to both questions (C3.6.5), though Rickshaw declined for [the employment contract].
    • OSRAA overlay: s 102 voids [the clause] as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as [procedural / mandatory] even on [the Sayers view] (C3.3.4).
  • Non-Party Reliance [a co-employee] cannot invoke cl [X] unless [the proper law] allows it (Ong Ghee Soon).
C3.9 MISCELLANEOUS OVERLAYS
C3.9.1 Damages

(cross-refer C1.4)

  • Traditional Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads ([pain and suffering]) are substantive, so [the head] must exist under both laws, but quantum is procedural, so [Singapore law] assesses it.
  • Remoteness and Mitigation substantive (C&Y), so double actionability governs whether [the loss] is too remote or [the failure to mitigate] bars it.
  • Goh Suan Hee Critique Per Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is "wholly artificial" (cf Pfeiffer v Rogerson; Art 15(c) Rome II), so if quantum is substantive [claimant] recovers only [the lower figure, e.g., the cap under law X].
    • Status: open; [the lex loci delicti]'s rules of law on assessment would apply but [pure fact questions] stay with [the forum], and [the award gap] was a neutral FNC factor (C1.4; J4).
C3.9.2 Limitation

(cross-refer C1.5.3)

  • Lex Loci Delicti's Period Per s 3(1) and s 3(2) FLPA 2012, [law X]'s domestic limitation period alone applies, renvoi being excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), so [the claim] [is / is not] barred, subject to s 4(2) undue hardship (C1.5.4).
    • No double hurdle: unlike s 1(2) UK FLPA 1984 (Metall), and where both limbs are [Singapore law] or [law X] is unpleaded, the Limitation Act applies.
  • Tactical Consequence per s 3(2) FLPA, locating the tort in [Singapore] avoids [law X]'s [shorter period] (C3.3).
  • After the Exception per C&Y, [the single lex causae]'s period applies: [law X]'s if the lex fori goes (Red Sea), the Limitation Act if [the lex loci delicti] goes (Boys), and [law Z]'s for a third law.
C3.9.3 Renvoi

(operation non-examinable; one sentence suffices)

  • No Renvoi in Tort Per Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili (PC), renvoi has never applied in obligations, so [law X] means its domestic law, applying [its limitation period] and excluding [Art 132 Swiss PILA] (raised in Ong Ghee Soon).
    • Statutory parallels: s 9(5) PIL(MP)A and Art 24 Rome II exclude it, as ss 3(5), 6(2) FLPA do for [limitation] in [Singapore].
    • Singapore status: formally open in tort (C&Y; Ong Ghee Soon said nothing of tort), so treat [Ivanishvili] as persuasive for [rejecting renvoi].
    • Reasons: [complexity / circularity], subordination of [forum policy], and forum non conveniens already controls [forum shopping] (Ivanishvili).
    • Contrast Australia: Neilson applied [Chinese COL rules] to avoid [forum-dependent outcomes], a workaround for [the missing exception], and was not persuasive to the Board.
    • For renvoi (C&Y): [uniformity] and getting "there in one bound", but courts should be cautious before [following Neilson].
C3.10 EVALUATION AND ALTERNATIVES (deploy where the question invites a view on retention or reform)
  • Critique of Double Actionability the lex fori limb is "parochial" (Red Sea, quoting the Law Commission; C&Y), born of [tort's criminal-law roots] with no [forum-connection requirement], so [claimant] fails only because [Singapore law] bars [the head].
  • SAL LRC's Five Reasons the lex fori limb is (1) out of step with [globalisation], (2) inconsistent with [other common law systems], (3) obsolete as [a default avoiding proof], (4) unnecessary given FNC and public policy, and (5) a blunt instrument for [forum interests].
  • Judicial Signals IM Skaugen ("an anachronism"); Ang Ming Chuang (would have departed [but for precedent]); Xiamen Xinjingdi ("may one day need to be reconsidered"); Lew v Nargolwala ([the lex fori] inappropriate even as [a contract fallback]).
  • Defence of the Rule limb (a) shields [Singapore defendants] from [foreign liability unknown here], limb (b) protects [defendants] and comity (EFT; Metall), and the exception gives [flexibility] (Rickshaw).
  • Reform for Parliament per Rickshaw, reform is for Parliament, with a "wise and judicious" use of the exception meanwhile, though C&Y note [the LRC proposal]'s inaction and Lew's logic for [judicial reform].
  • Departures from English Common Law Singapore applies the rule to local torts (C3.4), tests fortuity (C3.6), applies only [the lex loci delicti's period] (C3.9.2), and keeps [the common law], England having legislated (PIL(MP)A 1995; Rome II).
  • Australia Zhang v Renault (and Pfeiffer interstate) apply [the lex loci delicti] with no exception, renvoi filling [the gap] (Neilson), so [law X] alone would govern.
  • Canada Tolofson v Jensen applies [the lex loci delicti], with some flexibility for [international, not interprovincial, torts] (C&Y), so [law X] governs unless [displaced].
  • England and New Zealand statute (PIL(MP)A 1995; NZ 2017) applies [the lex loci delicti] with a flexible exception (s 12, Trafigura), the UK keeping double actionability for [defamation] and Rome II governing [most later torts].
  • Rome II Art 4(1) applies the law where [the damage] occurs (lex loci damni), whatever [the place of the event], sparing [the substance test], with party autonomy (Art 14) and no renvoi (Art 24).
    • Locus critique: the substance test depends on [the elements as alleged] under [the lex fori] (handout question), favouring lex loci damni.
  • US Interest Analysis Babcock v Jackson weighs [the states' interests], but per C&Y it is politically sensitive and queries whether PIL should serve [foreign state interests] at all.
  • Proper Law of the Tort (Morris) the law of [the most significant relationship], weighing [place of conduct and injury, residence, pre-existing relationship], was rejected in Boys and Red Sea for [uncertainty], the exception already importing it.
    • Online critique (Yeo): a physical locus is increasingly out of touch, though s 101 OSRAA may entrench [the place-of-tort factor] against [judicial development].
  • Singapore Reform Proposal the SAL LRC (2003) proposed [the lex loci delicti] with a "significantly more substantially connected" exception, excluding [personal defamation], never enacted.
  • C&Y Reform Package (1) abolish [the lex fori limb], and (2) give effect to [tort COL clauses] via the exception, so submit [retain / reform].
C3.11 OTHER OBLIGATIONS (OUTLINE ONLY)
  • Equitable Obligations Per Rickshaw, [the fiduciary / confidence claim] founded on [the contract] follows [its proper law] (C1.1.5; Rappo), a separate equitable category being left open.
    • Directors' duties: the law of [the place of incorporation] (Focus Energy), which [party autonomy] cannot vary (Base Metal Trading).
    • Breach of confidence without a relationship: unclear: [tort] (Yeo), [unjust enrichment] or [the proper law of the obligation] (Innovia Films).
    • Knowing receipt: the place of [enrichment / receipt] (Thahir v Pertamina; El Ajou), though [its fault element] leans to tort.
    • Dishonest assistance: a tort, so double actionability (Grupo Torras), problematic if [law X] alone governs and has [no accessory liability].
  • Unjust Enrichment per Dicey Rule 230 (adopted), the proper law of [the obligation]: (a) [the contract]'s (putative) proper law, (b) [the lex situs] for land (doubted), else (c) [the place of enrichment].
    • CIMB v Dresdner: [an intended but void contract] goes to (a) unless [the vitiating factor] infects [the COL clause]; [no meeting of minds] goes to (c).
    • Place of enrichment: prefer [immediate over ultimate] enrichment if balanced (HSBC v UOB), and [bribes in Singapore accounts] made [Singapore law] apply (Thahir v Pertamina).
    • Illegality: per Esben Finance (provisional), the [Foster / Ralli] comity principle extends to [unjust enrichment claims], subject to [stultification].
  • Trusts [express trusts] follow [the settlor's chosen law] or closest connection (Trisuryo: [a Singapore SPV] implied Singapore law); for [resulting / constructive trusts], C&Y prefer [the lex situs] to [the event's law] (Rappo).
  • Slide Questions [promissory estoppel] on [contractual non-performance] follows the contract's proper law, and [undue influence] is material validity for [the proper law], unless it infects [the COL clause] (CIMB).
C3.12 WORKED PATHWAYS AND EXAM NOTE
  • Pathway A: Cross-Border Misrepresentation [D in X] emails [C in Singapore], who acts here: limb 1 is met (C3.2), receipt and reliance locate the tort here unless fortuitous (JIO; C3.3.2), [D] must plead [law X] (C3.5), and the Misrepresentation Act may apply (C3.7.3).
  • Pathway B: Defamation Online [the post] read in [Singapore, X and Y] is three torts (Gutnick; C3.7.1), the Singapore one local (C3.4), and s 101 reaches only [a parallel OSRAA tort] (C3.3.4).
  • Pathway C: Contract Clause as Defence run the Sayers majority, then Lord Denning, then admissibility under [Singapore law and law X] and validity under [law Y] (C3.8.2).
  • Exam Note state [the leges causae], locate [the tort], check the burden (EFT), prove [fortuity] (Rickshaw) and keep renvoi to one sentence (Ivanishvili).

1Start here: C3 in plain English

Singapore's tort choice of law rule is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Rickshaw, adopting Boys v Chaplin and Red Sea). It is an old, unusual rule: the claim must pass two tests, one under Singapore law and one under the law of the place of the tort.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a referee who will only award a foul if it is a foul under both the home rulebook (Singapore law) and the rulebook of the stadium where it happened (the place of the tort). If either rulebook says "no foul", there is no foul. That makes the claimant win only what both rulebooks allow. But if one rulebook's involvement is pure accident (the players just happened to be in that stadium in transit), the referee can ignore it. That escape hatch is the flexible exception, and it is used sparingly.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The common denominator, in a table

Alpha is injured in a road accident in Ruritania and sues the other driver in Singapore. Which heads of damage can Alpha recover?

Head of damageSingapore law?Ruritanian law?Recoverable?
Medical billsYesYesYes
Lost earningsYesYesYes
Pain and sufferingYesNoNo: one rulebook says no
A special Ruritanian "grief payment"NoYesNo: the other rulebook says no

Only the heads both laws allow survive. In McElroy v McAllister, that logic left a widow with funeral expenses only. That harsh result is why the flexible exception exists (C3.6).

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Double actionabilityThe tort must be actionable under the lex fori and give civil liability under the lex loci delicti.
Lex loci delictiThe law of the place where the tort was committed.
Substance testWhere, in substance, did the cause of action arise? (Distillers) Used to locate the tort.
Single / multiple localityAll elements in one country / elements spread across countries.
Flexible exceptionLets the court displace a law that is purely fortuitous, for the law with the most significant relationship.
FortuitousBy chance: the connection is accidental, not meaningful.
Common denominatorWithout displacement, the claimant recovers only what both laws allow.
Local tortA tort committed in Singapore. Still runs both limbs in Singapore (Rickshaw).
OSRAA / THPAOnline Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025 / Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014: statutes changing the rules for their torts.

2C3.1 The governing rule

🧩 Practise C3.1 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: C3.1.1 Global Starter (word for word)
C3.1.1 Global Starter

The issue is which law governs [claimant]'s claim for [negligence / misrepresentation / conspiracy / defamation / conversion] arising from [acts] in [country X]. Per Rickshaw, it is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea).

  • The Two Limbs Per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin (adopted in Rickshaw), [the wrong] must be (a) a tort under Singapore law (C3.2) and (b) give civil liability between the actual parties under [law X] (C3.3).
    • Not necessarily tortious: per Ong Ghee Soon, any civil liability under [law X] suffices, e.g. [a civil-law delict / statutory liability].
    • Defences: per C&Y, [a defence] under either law defeats [the claim].
  • Common Denominator absent displacement, [claimant] recovers only what both laws allow (Yeo), as in McElroy v McAllister where [the widow] got only funeral expenses, so [claimant] argues displacement (C3.6).
  • How Many Leges Causae? per C&Y, the rule names no single law: two generally, one if the exception displaces [the lex fori] (Red Sea) or [the lex loci delicti] (Boys v Chaplin), and [a third law] if both go (C3.6.4).
  • Burden of Proof Per EFT Holdings, [claimant] proves limb (a), while [defendant] must plead and prove non-actionability under [law X], limb (b) existing for [defendant]'s benefit.
    • Dominance: per C&Y, this burden model and the default rule (C3.5) make [the lex fori] the dominant limb over [law X].
    • Reversal: where [claimant] invokes the exception to apply [law X] (Red Sea), [claimant] must plead and prove [law X].
  • Characterisation Per C&Y, "tort" is not bound by [domestic categories], though [a domestic tort] normally qualifies, and some equitable wrongs may count (Rickshaw), e.g. [dishonest assistance] (Grupo Torras; C3.11).
    • Foreign law may inform it: where [claimant] relies solely on [law X] for [a liability unknown here], [law X]'s characterisation matters (Red Sea).
  • Framing / Concurrent Liability Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith [claimant] may frame in tort despite [the law Y clause], the claim being characterised as tort though it arises from [the contract].
    • Contrast: [equitable claims] rooted in [the contract] follow contract COL (C1.1.5), and [a "parasitic" tort] may follow [the contract's law] (C3.6.5).
  • Rationale (evaluative) limb (b) spares [defendant] not liable where it acted (EFT) and serves comity, though per Metall comity weakens where [the damage] is caused to [persons here]. Limb (a), from The Halley, is "parochial" (C&Y).
  • Development (evaluative) Phillips v Eyre's "not justifiable" limb, abused in Machado v Fontes ([criminal liability] sufficing), became civil liability in Boys v Chaplin, the proper law of the tort being rejected (Red Sea), so [claimant] cannot plead [the most connected law] directly.
Double actionability: the essentials
▤ C3.1.1
  1. 1The two limbs (Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin, adopted in Rickshaw): (a) a tort under Singapore law; (b) civil liability between the actual parties under the lex loci delicti. Limb (b) need not be "tortious": any civil liability counts (Ong Ghee Soon). A defence under either law defeats the claim.
  2. 2Common denominator: absent displacement, the claimant recovers only what both laws allow. In McElroy v McAllister, the widow got only funeral expenses.
  3. 3How many laws? Generally two; one if the exception displaces the lex fori (Red Sea) or the lex loci delicti (Boys); a third law if both go.
  4. 4Burden (EFT Holdings): the claimant proves limb (a); the defendant must plead and prove non-actionability under the foreign law, since limb (b) exists for its benefit. So the lex fori is the dominant limb. Reversed where the claimant invokes the exception to apply foreign law.
  5. 5Characterisation: "tort" is not bound by domestic categories; some equitable wrongs count, e.g. dishonest assistance (Grupo Torras).
  6. 6Framing: absent bad faith, a claimant may sue in tort despite a contract's choice of law clause (Rickshaw).
? WHY IT MATTERS

Limb (b) spares a defendant who was not liable where it acted and serves comity (EFT), though per Metall comity weakens where the damage is caused to people here. Limb (a), from The Halley, is "parochial" (C&Y). History: Phillips v Eyre's "not justifiable" limb (abused in Machado v Fontes, where criminal liability sufficed) became civil liability in Boys v Chaplin; the proper law of the tort was rejected (Red Sea), so a claimant cannot plead the most connected law directly.

3C3.2 Limb 1: actionable under Singapore law

🧩 Practise C3.2 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: C3.2 LIMB 1: ACTIONABLE AS A TORT UNDER THE LEX FORI (word for word)
C3.2 LIMB 1: ACTIONABLE AS A TORT UNDER THE LEX FORI
  • Counterfactual Test Per IM Skaugen, ask whether [the acts], if all done in Singapore, would be [a tort, e.g., Spandeck duty, breach, causation, damage], so limb 1 [is satisfied / fails].
  • Domestic Bar (−) if Singapore law [denies the head / supplies a complete defence] or does not allow [the direct claim] (Red Sea), [claimant] must displace the lex fori (C3.6.2).
  • Statutory Torts [OSRAA Parts 10 to 12 / s 6 THPA] supply limb 1 by statute (C3.3.4), but per JIO Minerals the Misrepresentation Act reaches [a misrepresentation abroad] only under [a Singapore-law contract] (C3.7.3).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Limb 1 is a thought experiment: pick up the whole story and drop it in Singapore. The Ruritanian road becomes a Singapore road, the Ruritanian driver a Singapore driver. Would a Singapore court say this is a tort? If yes, limb 1 is met, even though nothing actually happened here. If no (for example, Singapore law has no such duty), the claim fails at limb 1 unless Singapore law is displaced as fortuitous.

The counterfactual test (IM Skaugen): if all the acts had been done in Singapore, would they be a tort (duty under Spandeck, breach, causation, damage)? If Singapore law denies the head, supplies a complete defence, or does not allow the direct claim (Red Sea), the claimant must displace the lex fori (C3.6.2). Statutory torts (OSRAA, THPA) can supply limb 1; but the Misrepresentation Act reaches a misrepresentation abroad only under a Singapore-law contract (JIO Minerals).

4C3.3 Limb 2: locating the tort

🧩 Practise C3.3 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.1 Starter: The Substance Test (word for word)
C3.3.1 Starter: The Substance Test

[Defendant] pleads that [law X] imposes no liability because of [no duty for pure economic loss / a damages cap / a statutory defence / a shorter limitation period], so the tort must first be located.

  • The Test Per Distillers and Metall, look back over [the events] and ask where in substance the cause of action arose, finding one single place on [the elements as recognised by the lex fori] (C&Y).
  • As Pleaded per Vibrant Group, the weight of [act / reliance / damage] depends on [the tort pleaded], so [the place of reliance] counts more for [misrepresentation] than for [negligence] (C3.3.2).
  • Single Locality (+) all elements occurred in [country X], e.g. [the place of the motor accident] (C&Y), so ask only whether [law X] imposes liability.
  • Multiple Locality (−) [the act] and [the damage] span [X] and [Y], so apply the tort-specific rules (C3.3.2).
  • Damage Not Determinative per Distillers, the place of damage "may be quite fortuitous", so [claimant]'s loss at [its home base] does not by itself locate [the tort].
  • Policy Favouring the Forum (+) per Metall, the court need not "turn a blind eye" to [damage] caused to [persons here] by acts abroad, so [receipt / loss] in Singapore may be the substance.
  • Civil, Not Necessarily Tortious, Liability per Ong Ghee Soon, [negligent misstatement] was actionable under Art 41 SCO though Swiss law has no "law of negligence" category, so [law X]'s [delictual / statutory] liability suffices.
  • Same Test for Jurisdiction per Metall (citing Armagas), the same locus test serves [the tort gateway]. Whether double actionability applies at [service out] is open: yes per IM Skaugen (HC), no per Nippon Catalyst, left open in Shen Sophie (J3).
    • Divergence: the gateway needs only [an act partly / damage] here (Yeo), so [the gateway] may be met though [the tort] is located in [country X].
    • FNC: per JIO, the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum unless fortuitous, so locating it in [country X] favours [a stay] (J4).

Per Distillers and Metall, look back over the events and ask where in substance the cause of action arose: one single place, judged on the elements as recognised by the lex fori (C&Y). The weight of act, reliance and damage depends on the tort pleaded (Vibrant Group).

C3.3.2 Tort-specific rules

▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.2 Tort-Specific Rules for Multi-Locality Torts (word for word)
C3.3.2 Tort-Specific Rules for Multi-Locality Torts

(select the tort pleaded)

  • Negligence: Focus on the Act Per Vibrant Group, the place of [the negligent act] prevails, so [the audit / advice] performed in [country X] locates the tort there despite [reliance and loss] in Singapore.
    • Negligent services / advice: where [the services] were or ought to have been [rendered] (Voth).
    • Trading decisions: where [the decision to speculate] was made, e.g. [Moscow] (Base Metal Trading).
    • Product liability: where [the product] was [marketed without the warning], not where [it was made] or [the damage] occurred (Distillers; Castree v Squibb).
    • Reliance weighs less: in [negligence], reliance is only one route to [a duty] (NTUC Foodfare; Vibrant).
  • Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant: Receipt + Reliance Per JIO Minerals (tentatively, citing Yeo) and Ong Ghee Soon, [a representation] directed at [claimant] and received and acted on in [Singapore] is a tort there, unless [that place] is fortuitous.
    • Where reliance crystallises: where [claimant] gave [instructions via the Singapore branch], not [administrative execution in Geneva] (Ong Ghee Soon).
    • Fortuitous receipt: receipt in [India] merely because [claimant] is based there is fortuitous (JIO).
    • Receipt and reliance split: the specific rule fails, so use [the substance test], as in JIO where [negotiations and drilling] made [Indonesia] the place.
    • Several countries of making, receipt and reliance: where [the core representations] were made, e.g. [Germany], may prevail, receipt being fortuitous for [global operators] (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel).
    • Receipt unclear on the pleadings: unevidenced receipt in [Germany] is "speculative", so [Singapore law] applies (Rickshaw).
  • Representation Made at Large per Cordova Land (and JIO), a statement to [the world at large] is a tort where made, unlike [one directed at the claimant] (The Albaforth).
  • Inducing Breach of Contract per Metall, the tort is where [the contract] was broken and [claimant] injured, e.g. [London], not where [the inducement] occurred ([New York]).
  • Conspiracy Per EFT Holdings, weigh [the conspirators' identity and location], where [they combined], [the concerted acts], [claimant]'s location and [where losses arose], as in EFT where [Taiwan] prevailed.
    • Parasitic conspiracy: one "so intimately connected" to [a contract] may follow [its law] without being located (Chen v BHNV; C3.6.5).
  • Defamation / Online / IP / Passing Off see C3.7 for [publication / download / the territorial right] in [the tort pleaded].
TortLocusKey cases
NegligenceWhere the negligent act was done; reliance weighs lessAudit done abroad: tort abroad despite reliance and loss here (Vibrant Group). Advice: where rendered (Voth). Trading decisions: where made (Base Metal Trading). Products: where marketed without warning, not where made (Distillers; Castree v Squibb).
Misrepresentation directed at the claimantWhere received and relied on, unless fortuitousJIO (tentatively); Ong Ghee Soon (reliance crystallised where instructions were given via the Singapore branch).
Representation at largeWhere madeCordova Land; contrast one directed at the claimant (The Albaforth).
Inducing breach of contractWhere the contract was broken and claimant injuredLondon, not New York where the inducement occurred (Metall).
ConspiracyWeigh conspirators' identity and location, where they combined, the acts, the claimant, lossesTaiwan prevailed in EFT. A "parasitic" conspiracy may follow the contract's law (Chen v BHNV).
Defamation, online, IPSee C3.7
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Why the answer is Australia

For negligence, the key element is the careless act. Reliance is only one route to a duty of care, and loss can be felt anywhere the claimant happens to be. So the tort is located where the audit was done, Australia, even though the claimant relied and suffered loss in Singapore (Vibrant Group).

Now change the tort pleaded. If the claimant sued for a misrepresentation directed at it, the key elements are receipt and reliance, so the tort would be located where it received and relied on the statement, Singapore, unless that place was fortuitous (JIO). Same facts, different tort, different place. That is why the pleaded tort decides the location.

C3.3.3 to C3.3.4 Applying limb 2, and the statutory rules

▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2 (word for word)
C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2

Limb 2 is satisfied if [law X] gives [some civil remedy] for [the conduct].

  • Limb 2 Fails Where [law X] [bars the head / provides a defence] or imposes no liability between [these parties] (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin), so [defendant] escapes unless [law X] is displaced (C3.6.3).
  • Time Bar [law X]'s [shorter period] bars [the claim] via s 3(2) FLPA, as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili (C3.9.2).

Limb 2 is met if the foreign law gives some civil remedy. It fails if the foreign law bars the head, provides a defence, or imposes no liability between these parties. A shorter foreign time bar applies via FLPA s 3(2) (as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili).

▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze (word for word)
C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze

(claims under OSRAA or THPA)

  • OSRAA s 101: Tort Deemed in Singapore Per s 101 OSRAA 2025, a [Part 10 / 11 / 12] tort is treated as in Singapore if any element was (a) initiated in or from Singapore, (b) perceived here, or (c) caused [damage] here, so [the post viewed here] makes it a local tort.
    • Effect (Yeo): s 101 replaces the substance test with a statutory connecting factor, so both limbs point to [Singapore law], giving [the OSRAA torts] the character of overriding mandatory rules.
    • Jurisdiction (Yeo): it secures [nexus] and a factual presumption that Singapore is [forum conveniens], leaving FNC to sieve out [opportunistic foreign claims].
    • Exception: [defendant] may argue for [law X] where Singapore is so fortuitous that [serious injustice] results, but only exceptionally, given Parliament's intent to protect [Singapore residents] (Yeo).
    • No s 101 connection (rare): the substance test applies, [the tort] is likely abroad, and [claimant] recovers only the common denominator of [the OSRAA] and [law X] (Yeo).
    • Unilateral reading: s 101 may be a unilateral rule with no exception, but Yeo prefers [the multilateral reading] as [the wording] only redefines the connecting factor.
    • Critique (Yeo): if [law X] protects [the victim] better, s 101 still imposes [the lower OSRAA standard].
  • OSRAA s 102: No Contracting Out Per s 102, [exclusion / jurisdiction / arbitration terms] inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 ([Administrators / Platforms]) are void unless fair and reasonable, Part 10 ([Communicators]) not being covered (C3.8.2).
    • Choice of law clause: [a foreign COL clause] cannot exclude [OSRAA liability], party autonomy being unrecognised in tort (Yeo; C3.6.5).
  • THPA s 6(4): Limb 2 Abrogated Per s 6(4) THPA 2014, [conduct in or outside Singapore] causing haze is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad, so [defendant] cannot rely on [law X] for [burning in X].
    • Standing: per s 6(3), [a person] suffering [personal injury / property damage / economic loss] in Singapore sues, still proving [the statutory tort] under Singapore law.
    • Nature: an express statutory displacement of limb 2 for [haze claims], not a use of [the flexible exception]; per Chong (seminar), an overriding forum mandatory rule, so [the THPA claim] lies though [Indonesian law] imposes no liability.
    • Common law claim: per Chong (seminar), the substance test likely locates [the tort] in [Indonesia], where [the burning] occurred, so if [Indonesian law permits smallholder burning], limb 2 fails for [the negligence / nuisance claim] unless displaced (C3.6.3).
StatuteEffect
OSRAA s 101A Part 10–12 tort is treated as committed in Singapore if any element was initiated in or from Singapore, perceived here, or caused damage here. Per Yeo: a statutory connecting factor replacing the substance test, giving these torts the character of overriding mandatory rules; FNC sieves out opportunistic foreign claims. Exception only where Singapore is so fortuitous that serious injustice results.
OSRAA s 102Exclusion, jurisdiction or arbitration terms inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 are void unless fair and reasonable (not Part 10). A foreign choice of law clause cannot exclude OSRAA liability.
THPA s 6(4)Haze-causing conduct in or outside Singapore is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad: an express statutory displacement of limb 2. Claimant must suffer injury, damage or loss in Singapore (s 6(3)).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
How the statutes cut the analysis short
  • Doxxing from abroad. A user in Malaysia posts a Singapore resident's home address and phone number, and the post is seen in Singapore. If this is a Part 10–12 OSRAA harm, s 101 treats the tort as committed in Singapore (it was perceived and caused damage here). No substance test is needed, and a foreign choice of law or exclusion clause cannot remove the liability where s 102 applies.
  • Haze. Fires on a plantation abroad send haze over Singapore, and a Singapore business loses income. Under THPA s 6(4) the conduct is actionable "whether or not" it is actionable where the fires were lit. Limb 2 simply drops out, provided the loss was suffered in Singapore (s 6(3)).
  • Ordinary defamation is not an OSRAA Part 10–12 harm, so it stays under double actionability (C3.7).

5C3.4 Local torts

🧩 Practise C3.4 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: C3.4 LOCAL TORTS (TORT COMMITTED IN SINGAPORE) (word for word)
C3.4 LOCAL TORTS (TORT COMMITTED IN SINGAPORE)
  • Double Actionability Applies to Local Torts Per Rickshaw, rejecting Metall's English-law-only rule as "unduly parochial" and contrary to comity, [conversion / negligence] in Singapore still runs both limbs, both pointing to [Singapore law].
    • Point of difference: the exception may apply [foreign law] where [the Singapore locus] is purely fortuitous, no stricter test applying, though "a liberal approach must be eschewed" (Rickshaw).
    • Why England differs: per Yeo (cited in Rickshaw), before Red Sea [the lex fori] could not be displaced, so [a lex fori rule for local torts] made sense.
  • Displacing Singapore Law (−) [Defendant] argues Singapore is fortuitous as [both parties reside in X], as in Briggs' Changi transit-lounge brawl between [Australians flying home], so [Australian law] applies.
  • Rickshaw Facts (+) the CA kept [Singapore law] as most [connecting factors] were here and the German-contract defence was "vague and unclear", so [claimant] argues [the defence is unparticularised].
    • Further reasons: no evidence was adduced on [deceit], and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive (C3.6.5), so [the clause] did not reach [the torts].
  • Briggs' Critique the torts arose from [an employment relationship] under [a German-law clause] and were pleaded in tort to avoid [German law], so the exception should have applied [the contract's proper law] (C3.6.5).
    • C&Y: fortuity should be one ground only, a test on the significance of [connections, including the contract] giving more room, as English courts applying [the contract's law] show (Trafigura).

The fight happened in Singapore, so on double actionability both limbs point to Singapore law. But the two Australians had no connection to Singapore beyond a few hours in a transit lounge. This is the textbook case for saying the Singapore locus is purely fortuitous, so the exception may apply Australian law instead. Contrast an ordinary local tort, where the parties live or do business here: Singapore law simply applies.

In Rickshaw, the CA kept Singapore law: most connecting factors were here, no evidence was adduced on deceit under German law, and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive. Briggs's critique: the torts arose from an employment relationship under a German-law clause and were pleaded in tort to avoid German law, so the exception should have applied the contract's law. C&Y: fortuity should be one ground only; a test on the significance of connections, including the contract, gives more room (Trafigura).

6C3.5 Foreign law not pleaded or not proved

🧩 Practise C3.5 on hypotheticals →
▤ On your pre-write: C3.5 PROOF OF FOREIGN LAW AND THE PRESUMPTION OF SIMILARITY (word for word)
C3.5 PROOF OF FOREIGN LAW AND THE PRESUMPTION OF SIMILARITY (cross-refer C1.6)
  • Foreign Law Not Pleaded Per EFT Holdings (applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong), pleading [law X] is voluntary, so if [defendant] does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises and [Singapore law] applies without [the presumption].
    • C&Y framing: the same result is put as a presumption that [law X] equals [Singapore law].
  • Pleaded but Not Proved unproved [law X] is presumed similar where fair (Brownlie; C1.6.3), though [the party bearing the burden] may simply fail (EFT).
  • Limits of the Presumption [the party resisting it] argues it fails for [law X] because:
    • FNC: the court may accept that [civil law X] probably differs without [proof] (Rickshaw, citing PT Jaya Putra; JIO).
    • Intrusive relief abroad: no [injunction] against [conduct in X] on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings), explained by [the relief sought] (EFT).
    • Damages: for [damages / an account], the presumption presumably applies (C&Y), so [claimant] limits [the relief].
  • Cf Brownlie (UK) the default rule governs [unpleaded law] and the presumption [pleaded but unproved law], supporting the EFT split (C1.6.3).
SituationResult
Defendant does not plead foreign lawPleading is voluntary, so no conflicts issue arises and Singapore law applies (EFT Holdings, applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong). C&Y frame the same result as a presumption.
Pleaded but not provedPresumed similar where fair (Brownlie); otherwise the party bearing the burden may simply fail (EFT).
LimitsAt the FNC stage, the court may accept that a civil law system probably differs without proof (Rickshaw; JIO). No injunction against conduct abroad on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings); damages presumably fine.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Who has to bring up the foreign law?

Alpha sues Beta in Singapore for negligence in an accident in Ruritania.

  • Beta says nothing about Ruritanian law. Limb 2 exists for the defendant's benefit, so if Beta does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises: the court applies Singapore law, and Alpha only has to make out the Singapore tort (EFT Holdings).
  • Beta pleads that Ruritanian law gives no liability, but proves nothing. The court may presume Ruritanian law is similar to Singapore law where that is fair. If it is not fair, Beta, who carries the burden on limb 2, may simply fail to make out its defence.
  • Beta pleads and proves Ruritanian law with an expert. Now limb 2 is live, and the claim succeeds only for what Ruritanian law also allows.

So in practice the defendant decides whether limb 2 is ever tested.

  • Threshold Per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to apply it unless [the displaced law] is purely fortuitous and applying it causes [injustice], on "clear and satisfying grounds" (Lord Wilberforce), lest it become [a proper law of the tort].
  • Strictly Applied per Rickshaw, it is "imperative" that [the exception] be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility, so [party] needs [clear fortuity], not [a more favourable law].

  • Burden on the Invoking Party [the invoking party] must prove [the connecting factors] and [the foreign law] (Red Sea), a "vague and unclear" defence failing (Rickshaw).

The exception may displace the lex fori, the lex loci delicti, or both, for the law with the most significant relationship. But per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to use it: only where the displaced law is purely fortuitous, on "clear and satisfying grounds", and it must be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility.

PointRule
Fortuity and injusticeConjunctive? Unclear; per C&Y, applying a fortuitous law is itself the injustice, so fortuity is the real test. Stricter than Red Sea and Ang Ming Chuang (weighing contacts).
Critique (C&Y)Fortuity is too restrictive: it should be one way of showing an insignificant connection.

FactorsRestatement §145 (quoted in Red Sea): place of injury, place of conduct, residence or incorporation, where the relationship is centred.
Works for defendants tooThe law "must be just to defendants as well as plaintiffs" (Ang Ming Chuang, obiter).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The two classic cases, side by side
Boys v ChaplinRed Sea
FactsTwo British servicemen stationed in Malta; a road accident in Malta. English law allowed general damages for pain and suffering; Maltese law allowed only special damages.A building in Saudi Arabia was defective. The insurer, sued in Hong Kong, counterclaimed directly against the supplier of the faulty materials. Hong Kong law required the insurer to pay first (subrogation); Saudi law allowed a direct claim.
Which law was displaced?The lex loci delicti (Malta), for one issue: heads of damageThe lex fori (Hong Kong), for the whole claim
Why?Malta had no real interest in applying its damages rule to two British servicemenHong Kong's only link was incorporation; all or virtually all factors pointed to Saudi Arabia
ResultEnglish law alone decided heads of damageSaudi law alone, so the direct claim could proceed

In Singapore, Rickshaw adds a strict filter: the displaced law must be purely fortuitous. C&Y doubt whether Malta was truly fortuitous in Boys, since the soldiers were stationed there, not passing through.

  • Why Allow It per C&Y, modern tort law allocates risk ([insurance / exemption clauses]), narrowing [the gap with contract], and autonomy brings certainty and supports [Singapore's hub policy] (Yeo).
  • Exclusive vs Non-Exclusive per Rickshaw, whether cl [X] covers [non-contractual claims] is construction under [its proper law], and [the clause] there was conceded non-exclusive.
  • Ong Ghee Soon Decided Nothing cl 7.29 was wide enough for [torts] under [Swiss law], but [the bank officer], a non-party, could not take its benefit absent a stipulation pour autrui (Art 112 SCO).
  • Foreign Restrictions Art 132 Swiss PILA (post-event choice only) bites only if [law X] includes [its PIL], a renvoi question (C3.9.3), and Art 120 PILA [consumer] status was left aside, [claimant] not being a consumer (Ong Ghee Soon).

    • Pre- vs post-tort: pre-tort choices risk [weak parties] contracting unwittingly, but per C&Y there should be no blanket ban, [employees / consumers] being protected by targeted [mandatory rules].

  • Route Through the Exception (C&Y) [the chosen / proper law] applies via the flexible exception as the law of [the centred relationship], as in Chen v BHNV ([a conspiracy] "so intimately connected" to [the Belize-law contract]), Oro Negro and Trafigura.
    • Caution: Chen was an FNC ruling not running [Rickshaw's fortuity test], and Trafigura applied [s 12 PIL(MP)A], so they are analogies only.
    • Obstacle: Rickshaw's [fortuity threshold] and [non-exclusive concession] blocked it (C3.4), so [the opponent] argues [the separate tort] stays.

  • Support: The Rainbow Joy (employment contract's law "should prevail" over the law of the flag for a tort on the high seas, though possibly confined to its facts); Rickshaw recognises an "exclusive" clause; Art 14 Rome II; Art 9(1)(g) Hague Principles; Yeo's hub argument.
  • Why allow it: tort law now allocates risk (insurance, exemption clauses), and autonomy brings certainty (C&Y).

  • Rome II Art 14 model: a choice after the event, or before it if all pursue a commercial activity and it is freely negotiated. Per C&Y, no blanket ban on pre-tort choices; protect employees and consumers with targeted mandatory rules.
  • Also an FNC factor: a choice of law clause covering torts points to that law at Spiliada stage 1 (J4).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In contract, the parties can pick the law. In tort, Singapore has never clearly said they can. So when a contract says "all disputes between us are governed by English law" and one party sues in tort, there are two ways to try to get English law: (1) say parties may choose the law for torts too (open, but "just a small step away" per C&Y), or (2) squeeze it through the flexible exception, which Rickshaw makes hard because the other laws must be purely fortuitous. Write both routes and say the point is undecided (Ong Ghee Soon).

ℹ NOTE
C3.6.6 Public policy is not a ground for the exception

In Kuwait Airways, the majority excised an Iraqi confiscatory resolution via the exception, but Lord Scott said the exception is for applying the most connected law, not disapplying parts of it; Lord Steyn used public policy instead. After Rickshaw, Iraq was not fortuitous, so use public policy (C1.8).

Defamation

▤ On your pre-write: C3.7.1 Defamation (word for word)
C3.7.1 Defamation
  • Place of Publication Per Low Tuck Kwong, double actionability applies and the tort is where [the statement] is published, each publication a separate tort, so [Singapore publications] are local (C3.4) and [defendant] must plead [law X] for [X publications] (C3.5).
  • FNC Filter a claim for [foreign publication] may be stayed, the place of publication being prima facie the natural forum (C&Y), so [defendant] seeks [a stay to country X] (J4).
  • Internet Publication Per Dow Jones v Gutnick and Singapore cases (Qingdao Bohai), publication is where [the material] is downloaded and accessed, so [claimant] must show [access in Singapore].
    • Gutnick: [the publisher]'s server-law rule ([New Jersey]) was rejected; the majority relied on [practical limits], and Kirby J's global publication rule was left to [legislatures].
    • Contrast UK: s 8 Defamation Act 2013 adopts a single publication rule, unlike [the multiple-publication rule] applied to [the post].
    • Policy choice (Mills): the law of upload favours [free speech] ("race to the top") and download [reputation] ("race to the bottom"), so the choice is policy, not rationality.
    • Chan's tiered rule: combining [habitual residence], [place of reputational damage] and [publication], it is complex and unlikely to be adopted (C&Y).
    • Practice: few such claims reach Singapore, given [the O 8 r 1 / PD para 63 nexus] and [little reputational damage here] (C&Y).
    • OSRAA: s 101 reaches only [Part 10 to 12 harms, e.g., harassment or doxxing] (Yeo), so [common law defamation] stays under double actionability (C3.3.4).
  • Reform Carve-Out the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation, the lex fori limb filtering [foreign law] incompatible with [Singapore's free speech values], and move [business defamation] to [the lex loci delicti] (C3.10).
  • Gutnick: the publisher's server-law rule (New Jersey) was rejected; Kirby J's global publication rule was left to legislatures. The UK now has a single publication rule (Defamation Act 2013 s 8).
  • Policy choice (Mills): the law of upload favours free speech ("race to the top"), download favours reputation ("race to the bottom").
  • Reform: the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation.

Each place where the post is downloaded and read is a separate publication, so a separate tort (Gutnick). The Singapore publication is a local tort: both limbs point to Singapore law. The Malaysian and Indonesian publications each need double actionability with that country's law, and since the place of publication is prima facie the natural forum for each, a stay of those parts is likely. A claimant who wants a simple case here usually sues only on the Singapore publication.

IP and passing off

▤ On your pre-write: C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off (word for word)
C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off

  • Validity Separate [validity] follows the law of [the place of creation], and [the Singapore court] may lack jurisdiction where infringement turns on [foreign validity] (C&Y).
  • Scenarios (forum Singapore; no conventions) run [the right's origin] against [the place of infringement]:
    • (i) Singapore right infringed abroad: fails both limbs, and [the lex fori] is not fortuitous for [a Singapore right].
    • (ii) Utopian right infringed here: fails both limbs, [Singapore as locus] not being fortuitous for [the infringing acts].
    • (iii) Foreign right infringed there: [a Malaysian copyright infringed in Malaysia] may succeed via the exception displacing [a fortuitous lex fori], if [Singapore has jurisdiction] (cf Pearce v Ove Arup).

Statutory IP rights are territorial (C&Y). Forum Singapore, no conventions:

ScenarioResult
(i) Singapore right infringed abroadFails both limbs; the lex fori is not fortuitous for a Singapore right
(ii) Utopian right infringed in SingaporeFails both limbs; Singapore as locus is not fortuitous for the infringing acts
(iii) Malaysian copyright infringed in MalaysiaMay succeed via the exception displacing a fortuitous lex fori, if Singapore has jurisdiction (cf Pearce v Ove Arup)
Passing offA common law tort, so territoriality is no bar; but an injunction against passing off in Malaysia needs Malaysian law proved (OMG Holdings)
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A Singapore trade mark is like a Singapore driving licence: it gives rights in Singapore only. Copying the mark in Malaysia does not infringe it, just as driving in Malaysia is not governed by your Singapore licence. That is why scenario (i) fails: under Singapore law, there is no Singapore-right infringement when the acts happen abroad. Passing off is different because it protects goodwill, a common law right not tied to a registration, so territoriality does not block it in the same way.

9C3.8 When contract meets tort

C3.8.1 Contract Relied on to Negate the Tort

(the contract answers an element, e.g., [a licence / a right to remain])

  • Two Questions Per C&Y (North), (i) the effect of [the contract] on tort liability is a tort question for double actionability, and (ii) its validity a contract question for [its proper law, law Y].
  • Galaxias [the trespass] was an English tort, so English law held [a contractual right to remain] negates trespass, but Greek law (the proper law) showed [the crew] were lawfully discharged, so [the claim] succeeded.

Two questions whenever a contract is raised against a tort claim
▤ C3.8, per C&Y (North)
  1. 1Effect of the contract on tort liability (does it negate an element, or is the clause admissible as a defence?): a tort question, for double actionability.
