✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Galaxias

The crew's trespass claim was an English tort, so English law held that a contractual right to remain would negate trespass. But Greek law, the contract's proper law, showed the crew had been lawfully discharged: no right to remain. So the claim succeeded.

Notice the two questions working together. The tort law asked: "would a contractual right to stay on board be a defence to trespass?" (yes). The contract's law answered: "did the crew still have that right?" (no). Neither law alone gave the answer.

▤ On your pre-write: C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort (word for word)
C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort
  • The Problem cl [X], valid under [law Y], excludes [negligence] liability that Singapore law [bars / subjects to reasonableness] ([s 2(1) / s 2(2) UCTA]).
    • Sayers: [an English worker] injured on [a Nigerian rig] was limited by [his Dutch employer]'s cl 8 compensation scheme, void under s 1(3) Law Reform (Personal Injuries) Act 1948 but valid in Dutch law.
  • Majority (Salmon and Stamp LJJ): Contractual Characterisation only the proper law of the contract mattered, and it being Dutch, "this action is dead" (Salmon LJ), so if [law Y] validates cl [X], [the claim] fails.
    • Critique (C&Y): treating [the issue] as wholly contractual is simplistic, ignoring [question (i)], so [claimant] argues [Singapore's policy] on admissibility.
  • Lord Denning: Proper Law of the Issue "we cannot apply two systems of law", so he applied the law closest to [the issues], Dutch ("Nigeria is out"), cl 8 "turn[ing] the scale" against [English law].
    • Critique (C&Y): he never asked what effect [the clause] has on [tort liability] (North).
    • Do not mix up the judgments: Salmon LJ found [the contract] Dutch, whereas Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch via [the tort].
    • Application: [law Y] is closest to [the issue] as [the relationship is centred there].
  • Preferred Approach (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan) (1) admissibility is a tort question for double actionability, and (2) validity a contract question for [its proper law], so cl [X], valid under [law Y], succeeds only if admissible under both [Singapore law] and [the lex loci delicti].
    • Incidental question: [the forum's] COL rules (simple, but [forum shopping]) or [the tort law's] (Harris: coherent, avoiding "the law of no one state") pick [the contract's law].
    • Which to choose: per C&Y, it may track Singapore's views on [renvoi] and [party autonomy] in tort.
    • Pre-existing contract: the exception may apply [law Y] to both questions (C3.6.5), though Rickshaw declined for [the employment contract].
    • OSRAA overlay: s 102 voids [the clause] as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as [procedural / mandatory] even on [the Sayers view] (C3.3.4).
  • Non-Party Reliance [a co-employee] cannot invoke cl [X] unless [the proper law] allows it (Ong Ghee Soon).
⚠ TRAP
Do not mix up the Sayers judgments

Salmon LJ found the contract Dutch. Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch law through the tort. C&Y criticise the majority as simplistic (it ignores the effect question) and Lord Denning for never asking what effect the clause has on tort liability.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The preferred approach on the Sayers facts, if sued in Singapore
  1. Validity (a contract question): is the clause valid under its proper law? Dutch law says yes.
  2. Admissibility (a tort question, double actionability): may a contract clause be raised as a defence to this negligence claim under Singapore law (limb 1) and under the law of the place of the tort (limb 2)? Both must allow it.
  3. Result: the clause defeats the claim only if it passes both steps. If either tort law refuses to let a clause of this kind exclude negligence liability for personal injury, the claim survives, even though the clause is valid in Dutch law.

The two-question split keeps contract questions with the contract's law and tort questions with the tort rule. That is why C&Y (following North) prefer it.

Evaluation: should double actionability survive?
▤ C3.10
  1. 1Against: the lex fori limb is "parochial" (Red Sea); the SAL LRC's five reasons (globalisation, inconsistency, obsolete, unnecessary given FNC and public policy, blunt); judicial signals (IM Skaugen: "an anachronism"; Ang Ming Chuang; Xiamen Xinjingdi).
  2. 2For: limb (a) shields Singapore defendants from liability unknown here; limb (b) protects defendants and comity; the exception gives flexibility.
  3. 3Reform is for Parliament (Rickshaw). The SAL LRC (2003) proposed the lex loci delicti with a "significantly more substantially connected" exception; never enacted. C&Y: abolish the lex fori limb and give effect to tort choice of law clauses.
  4. 4Elsewhere: Australia and Canada apply the lex loci delicti (Zhang v Renault; Tolofson); England and NZ by statute with an exception; Rome II Art 4(1) the place of damage; US interest analysis (Babcock v Jackson).
▤ On your pre-write: C3.11 OTHER OBLIGATIONS (OUTLINE ONLY) (word for word)
C3.11 OTHER OBLIGATIONS (OUTLINE ONLY)
  • Equitable Obligations Per Rickshaw, [the fiduciary / confidence claim] founded on [the contract] follows [its proper law] (C1.1.5; Rappo), a separate equitable category being left open.
    • Directors' duties: the law of [the place of incorporation] (Focus Energy), which [party autonomy] cannot vary (Base Metal Trading).
    • Breach of confidence without a relationship: unclear: [tort] (Yeo), [unjust enrichment] or [the proper law of the obligation] (Innovia Films).
    • Knowing receipt: the place of [enrichment / receipt] (Thahir v Pertamina; El Ajou), though [its fault element] leans to tort.
    • Dishonest assistance: a tort, so double actionability (Grupo Torras), problematic if [law X] alone governs and has [no accessory liability].
  • Unjust Enrichment per Dicey Rule 230 (adopted), the proper law of [the obligation]: (a) [the contract]'s (putative) proper law, (b) [the lex situs] for land (doubted), else (c) [the place of enrichment].
    • CIMB v Dresdner: [an intended but void contract] goes to (a) unless [the vitiating factor] infects [the COL clause]; [no meeting of minds] goes to (c).
    • Place of enrichment: prefer [immediate over ultimate] enrichment if balanced (HSBC v UOB), and [bribes in Singapore accounts] made [Singapore law] apply (Thahir v Pertamina).
    • Illegality: per Esben Finance (provisional), the [Foster / Ralli] comity principle extends to [unjust enrichment claims], subject to [stultification].
  • Trusts [express trusts] follow [the settlor's chosen law] or closest connection (Trisuryo: [a Singapore SPV] implied Singapore law); for [resulting / constructive trusts], C&Y prefer [the lex situs] to [the event's law] (Rappo).
  • Slide Questions [promissory estoppel] on [contractual non-performance] follows the contract's proper law, and [undue influence] is material validity for [the proper law], unless it infects [the COL clause] (CIMB).

11Put it together: three worked pathways

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway A: cross-border misrepresentation (C3.12)

D in Hong Kong emails C in Singapore a false statement; C relies on it here and invests. (1) Limb 1: deceit or negligent misstatement if all done here (C3.2). (2) Locus: received and relied on in Singapore, not fortuitous, so a local tort (C3.3.2): both limbs point to Singapore law. (3) D must plead Hong Kong law if it wants to argue otherwise (C3.5). (4) The Misrepresentation Act applies only if a related contract is Singapore-law (C3.7).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway B: online defamation

A post is read in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia: three torts (Gutnick). The Singapore one is local. The other two need double actionability with Malaysian and Indonesian law, and a stay is likely. OSRAA s 101 only reaches a parallel OSRAA tort (harassment, doxxing).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway C: contract clause as a defence

An employer's Dutch-law contract caps injury compensation; the employee is hurt on a rig in Nigeria. Run the Sayers majority (proper law only), then Lord Denning (law closest to the issue), then the preferred approach: admissibility under Singapore law and the lex loci delicti, validity under Dutch law (C3.8.2).

How the sheet works, and how an answer uses it

⚡ BIG IDEA

The exam hands you a statement to attack or defend. Each archetype is a ready-made route through one family of statements. Your job is to spot the family, then fill the route with the question's own words.

1What the exam asks of you

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a friend says something bold, like "everyone's opinion about right and wrong is equally good". Your job is not to shout yes or no. It is to find the part that is true, show exactly where it goes too far, and say why, using the thinkers from class as your witnesses. The sheet is a box of pre-built arguments for the kinds of bold statements the examiner likes to make.

LAW301 essay questions almost always look the same. You get a short, confident statement in quotation marks, then a task line telling you what to do with it. Liu's own sample, Sample Question 1, is worth half of the final exam:

"Legislators governing a pluralist society should treat all moral opinions as equally valid. This can be achieved by refraining from passing any law restricting liberty unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct. Only then can legislators avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life."
Critically evaluate and comment on this statement by reference to the theories of Rawls, Finnis, Hart, and Devlin covered in this course, and any relevant illustrations.

Liu explained in class how these statements are built†. The examiners write them themselves. They make them deliberately complicated, and often inconsistent with themselves, so that a good student can spot the flaw and critique it. "Critically evaluate" asks for pros and cons: what you agree with, what you disagree with, and why. There is no fixed ratio between the two. The skill that earns marks is working out what each theory implies for the statement, not reciting what the philosophers said.

Three things are true of nearly every statement like this:

  1. It has a kernel of truth. Here, a pluralist state should not force one way of life on everyone.
  2. It overreaches through one or two loaded words. Here, "equally valid", "objectively", "wrongdoer" and "only then".
  3. It belongs to a family. This one belongs to the pluralism family (archetype 6, block 6.10), with help from the scepticism family (archetype 4) and the enforcement-of-morals family (archetype 7). It is also a question about law-makers, so the Core card for law-making (13.3) has a ready verdict on each of its claims.

A strong answer does three matching things. It grants the kernel, pins the overreach on the loaded word, and explains the difference with a principle from the course. The sheet is organised so that each of these steps is already half-written for you.

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Read the task line first, then read the sentences together†. The task line tells you which theorists to use, and if it names them, you should stick to them. Then treat the statement as one argument, not three separate claims. Liu said the common mistake last year was to read the second sentence of Sample Question 1 on its own, as if it simply stated the harm principle. But that sentence is offered as the means to the first sentence, and "only then" claims it is the only means to the aim in the third. The nuance in your answer comes from that chain. Liu also stressed that good answers differ from one another, so do not try to guess what the examiner wants to hear†.

? WHY IT MATTERS
Why "archetype"?

An archetype is a recurring kind of exam statement. The questions change their facts and wording, but they keep returning to the same eleven arguments, which the sheet sets out in course order: what law is, legal positivism (LP) v natural law theory (NLT), and why theory matters (2), the rule of law and Fuller (3), whether morality is objective (4), Finnis for law-makers (5), pluralist legislation (6), enforcing morals (7), unjust laws (8), judges (9), lawyers (10), the Constitution (11), and who decides (12). Learn the eleven routes and almost any statement becomes familiar.

2The sheet at a glance

The exam is semi-open book. You may bring five sheets printed on both sides, which is ten pages†. Your ten pages are the Core version of the exam sheet. It has sixteen sections, and you do not read it front to back in the exam. You jump to the part you need.

SectionWhat it holdsWhen you use it
1 EngineThe map (1.1), menus of hooks, theses, steelmen and closes (1.2), organising distinctions (1.3), the self-critique bank (1.4) and the signature ledger (1.5)Planning every answer
2–12 ArchetypesOne family of statement each, in course order. Each has a Position, an Intro, one or two Steelman lines, its blocks and a ConclusionThe body of your answer
13 Across topics and Core cardsComparisons (13.1), current controversies (13.2), and the four Core cards (13.3–13.6), which give ready verdicts on the commonest statementsComparison questions, a fresh example, your verdict and your close
14 Theorist bankA card per thinker: purpose, claim, test, strength, critique and reply, verdict. Card 14.27 lines the thinkers up on the same questionsA question that names a theorist
15 FrameworksStep-by-step tests, such as Fuller's checklist, Finnis's two tests, Rawls's legitimacy test, Devlin's interrogatories and Hart's testProblem questions, and showing a theory applied
16 Singapore bankArticles, cases, who said what in Parliament (Hansard), statutes, and the lecture's application promptsIllustrations

The answer is page 1 first, to plan, and then the block that the question's trigger words point to. The prep page (section 0) is not printed. It holds the five-minute routine, the trigger table that maps question words to blocks, the 1,500-word frame and the rules that cost marks, so you learn it before the exam rather than reading it in the room. This site prints the matching trigger-table rows at the top of each archetype lesson.

How the numbering works
▤ The sheet's decimal numbering
  1. 1A whole number is a section: 7 is the enforcement-of-morals archetype.
  2. 2A decimal is a block inside it: 7.3 is the block on Devlin's jury box.
  3. 3A number in brackets is one of the organising distinctions in the engine: 1.3(4) is aim v mechanism.
  4. 4The four Core cards are 13.3 to 13.6 (Core A to D). Their lines carry letters: P1–P6 on Core A, Q1–Q6 on Core B and L1–L6 on Core C.
  5. 5Theorist cards are 14.n (14.13 is Hart's Law, Liberty and Morality), frameworks are 15.n, and Singapore material is 16.n.
  6. 6Some numbers are missing on purpose. Several cards and frameworks were cut to make room for the Core cards, so the bank jumps from 14.8 to 14.10 and the frameworks from 15.1 to 15.3. Every other number stayed the same.

The removed text is kept in a separate Theorist version of the sheet, but the Core version is the one you print and the one these lessons follow. If older notes cite a number that is missing from your sheet, do not rely on it in the exam.

Blocks cross-refer constantly. A number in brackets inside a line, such as the "(8.5)" in Tan Seow Hon's (TSH's) catch in 1.4, tells you to see that block for the detail. A few lines point to a section's steelman instead, as in "(5, Steelman: against Finnis)". On this site every such number is a blue link.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means on the sheet
ArchetypeA section from 2 to 12: one family of exam statement and the route through it.
BlockOne numbered part of an archetype, such as 7.11, built for one kind of statement.
Trigger wordsThe grey italic words after a block's title. If a question uses words like these, the block is a candidate.
SlotWords in square brackets, such as [the statement]. You replace them with the question's own words.
PositionYour stance for a whole archetype, in one sentence. Use it once per answer.
Intro and ConclusionThe model opening and closing paragraphs of an archetype, with slots.
SteelmanThe best case for the statement, then what it shows and what it does not show.
TagA label on a note, such as FOR, CONCEDE or TRAP, saying how to use it.
Core cardOne of four summary cards (13.3–13.6) with ready verdicts for a big kind of question.
SpineThe two- or three-sentence argument at the top of a Core card.
VERDICTA ready one-line judgement, on a Core card or a theorist card.
Repaired lineA corrected version of a statement, from a Core card. Use one per script, in your close.
FrameworkA step-by-step test that applies one theory to facts (section 15).
Actor lockEnding each body paragraph on the actor the question names, such as the MP or the judge.

3How to read an archetype block

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Each archetype is like a recipe book for one kind of statement. The first page gives your general approach (the Position), a ready opening (the Intro) and a fair account of the other cook's best dish (the Steelman). Then come the recipe cards, the blocks. The small grey words on each card are the "smells" that tell you this recipe is needed. The three numbered lines are the recipe itself: first admit what is right, then bring in a thinker, then say "so…". The tags underneath are optional extras, such as a warning, an extra ingredient, or a weakness you should own up to.

Every archetype section (2–12) is built the same way, from top to bottom.

A few sections add one more ready line. Section 12 opens with a Frame line for the standard roles question, and 4.7 is an anchor paragraph on moral objectivity that several other blocks send you to.

The steelmen

Since 10 November every archetype has one or two Steelman lines after the Intro. A steelman is the opposite of a straw man. It is the strongest version of the view you are about to criticise. Each line has the same three parts, so you can see them side by side in section 7:

Steelman: libertySteelman: shared morality
The best caseCoercion is costly. Hart calls it prima facie objectionable, and for Mill the individual is sovereign over body and mind†.Majority rule treats citizens as equals. Indranee Rajah (2007) would usually follow the majority, Lim Meng Suang left Hart v Devlin to Parliament, and Devlin says no society can do without intolerance, indignation and disgust.
What it showsThe state needs a reason before it punishes.The legislature may decide moral questions.
What it does not showThat harm to others is the only reason, or a neutral one.That majority feeling makes the decision legitimate, let alone right.

The last row is the hinge of your essay. It sits in square brackets on the sheet, because you fill it with the statement's own overreach. A good steelman therefore grants the kernel and points at the flaw in the same breath, and your body sections then prove the flaw. The 1,500-word frame gives the steelman 60–85 words, and each Steelman line is already about that long. One line, with its slots filled, is the whole paragraph. Where a section has two, use the one that makes the best case for the statement in front of you, as the worked example below does. A few blocks also carry a STEELMAN tag, the best case on one particular point, and many of these end with a reply.

The anatomy of a block

Open block 7.11 below and compare it with the labels that follow.

▤ On your sheet: 7.11 Polls are not a mandate (word for word)
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns.
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • CONCEDE I concede the 2007 debate's reply that majority opinion may indicate objective morality†. Yet consensus gauges but does not ground: majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch".
Anatomy of a block
▤ Using block 7.11, on polls
  1. 1Number and title. The number and title name the move: 7.11, Polls are not a mandate. The title prints in black.
  2. 2Trigger words, the grey italic after the dot: poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide. If a question uses words like these, this block is a candidate. They print in grey, because they are for finding the block, not for copying.
  3. 3Line 1, the kernel or first step. A poll showing disapproval is no mandate to make something a crime. Hri Kumar pointed out in 2007 that the 70% in a survey who frowned on homosexuality were never asked whether it should be a crime.
  4. 4Line 2, the theorist or authority. TSH's dilemma. If there is a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression. If there is not, it is ordinary democracy. Either way, the moral question comes back.
  5. 5Line 3, the "So" line. The verdict, written so that it can become a topic sentence. Majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  6. 6The tag. A CONCEDE line, already written in the first person. You concede the 2007 reply that majority opinion may be a sign of objective morality, and then answer it: consensus can measure morality, but it cannot be what makes something right.

Blue lines and black lines

The printed Core sheet uses colour to tell you what to do with each line. The key at the top of every page says that blue marks lines to copy.

  • Blue lines are lines you can copy into your script. These are the boxed lines (Position, Intro, Steelman, Conclusion and the menus in 1.2), the numbered lines 1–3, and nearly every note under a block: FOR, AGAINST, QUALIFY, CONCEDE, TRAP, the actor tags, and CLAIM and VERDICT on the cards. They are full sentences, so once you fill the slots they read as your own prose.
  • Black lines are for you, not the marker. Block headings with their grey trigger words are black. So is the PURPOSE line on each theorist card, and so is any line that starts with "~ ". A "~ " line is either navigation, such as "~ See 5." under block 6.6 or the line on Fuller's card that sends you to framework 15.1, or an instruction to yourself, such as the signature ledger in 1.5.

On this site, the word-for-word panels drop the "~ " and show those lines smaller and in grey.

Lines written to be copied

Two smaller changes make the tagged lines ready to use as they stand. First, CONCEDE lines are written in the first person, often with the words "I concede". In 7.9, for example, you concede that promoting a moral view coerces people too, and the line is already your own sentence. Second, objections carry their answer after the word "Reply". In 7.4 the STEELMAN tag gives Devlin's claim that immorality, like subversion, can threaten a society's existence, and the reply says that this gives the law a right to concern itself with morals, not a reason to punish any particular conduct. The CRITIQUE lines on the theorist cards work the same way.

The square brackets

Words in square brackets, such as "[majority support]" or "[the statement]", are slots. You replace them with the question's own words. This is what stops an answer reading like a pasted template. The move is pre-built, but every sentence speaks the question's language.

The tags

TagWhat it meansHow to use it
Steelman (box)The best case for the statement, what it shows and what it does notOne paragraph of 60–85 words, straight after your opening
STEELMAN (tag)The best case on one particular point, often followed by a ReplyThe strongest objection and your reply, inside the body paragraph that uses the block
FORMaterial supporting your lineEvidence for your thesis
AGAINSTMaterial against the statement, or against a rival viewYour attack
QUALIFYA nuance that narrows a claimStops you overclaiming
CONCEDEA weakness in your own side, written in the first personOne or two sentences of self-critique, inside the last body section
TRAPA common mistakeRead it before you write, and never make it
JUDGE, LAWYER, LEGISLATOR, OFFICIAL, CITIZENWhat the point means for that actorUse it when the question names that actor
A note with no tagExtra detail: a case, a reading, an exampleYour illustration

The symbols

  • † marks a point from Liu's lectures or slides, or from the public record, rather than from a set reading. It carries no week or slide number. Since 10 November the sheet gives no lecture references and no longer names Liu.
  • Page pins are gone. Page references were removed from the sheet. Where a short quotation would otherwise have no author, the sheet names one in brackets, such as "(TSH)" or "(Hart)".
  • Quotations are short. Every quotation longer than three words was paraphrased. The few words still in quotation marks, such as Hart's prima facie objectionable or TSH's warning that consensus can go dreadfully wrong, are safe to quote if you credit the author. Everything else is already in plain words, so write it as your own sentence and credit the idea. The prep page adds two rules: credit a summary to whoever summarised it, and never put the question's words into a theorist's mouth.
  • ☐ boxes in the signature ledger (1.5) are there to tick.
ℹ NOTE
Where the example statements come from

In every lesson, a statement tagged with a question number (such as Q61) is quoted from your practice bank, "LTP Practice Exam Questions (Merged)". A statement without a number is a short paraphrase built from the block's trigger words, so you can see the kind of wording that calls for the block.

⚠ TRAP
Don't paste the block

The prep page's rules say to use the Position line once, in the question's terms, and never to paste a default paragraph. The numbered lines are a skeleton. In the exam, each one becomes two or three sentences fitted to the facts in front of you.

4Theorist cards and frameworks

Three other kinds of block sit outside the archetypes: theorist cards, frameworks, and the four Core cards that the Core version added.

Theorist cards (section 14)

Each card answers the same questions about one thinker, so that you can compare thinkers quickly. The heading gives the card's number, the thinker, and after the word "use" the blocks the card supports. Here is Fuller's card, which uses nearly every label:

▤ On your sheet: 14.6 Fuller (word for word)
14.6 Fuller use: 3, 8.7, 2.4, 13.1
  • PURPOSE What separates law from naked power, and why do failures of form wrong citizens?
  • CLAIM Law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight desiderata.
  • TEST → 15.1.
  • STRENGTH It binds lawmakers first: being at the top of the chain of command "intensifies" their duty of legality.
  • CRITIQUE Is it about morality at all, or efficacy†? Reply: legality respects responsible agents† and grounds the duty by reciprocity (3.3).
  • CONCEDE Legality is thin: a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. I concede it and let the Radbruch formula test content (13.1).
  • SAY A secret statute is the greatest legal monstrosity; balancing the eight requirements takes a lawgiver's skill.
  • TRAP Fuller's remark that not all cases are hard concerns legality, not adjudication. Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula; he asks how much of a legal system survived.
  • VERDICT Fuller shows legality is a genuine but modest morality binding rulers, not that it makes their laws just.

Four cards were rewritten for the Core version. Finnis (14.8), Rawls (14.10), Hart's Law, Liberty and Morality (14.13) and Devlin (14.15) now carry the versions tested in Core D, and each points to its framework. The bank ends with 14.27, the same-question grid. It gives one line per thinker on the same questions: whether law is necessarily moral, what law may enforce, who decides, and what to do about an unjust law. Use it when you need several thinkers lined up on the same axes.

Frameworks (section 15)

A framework is a step-by-step test. Its heading gives a key question in grey (Hart's asks what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such) and a pointer to its home block. Then come numbered steps and a rule for the verdict. Use one when the question gives facts and asks what a theorist would say, as problem questions do, or when you want to show a theory applied rather than described.

▤ On your sheet: 15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) (word for word)
15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? · use: 7.9
  • Coercion is "prima facie objectionable". (1) Harm to others? Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count. (2) Paternalism, if consent is defective: punishing drug supply save on prescription.
  • (3) Public decency: offence serious and likely, weighed against the freedom lost. (4) Moralism alone: never. My rule (all law rests on force, criminal law most directly†): the more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed; Hart's own question is punishment only.

Core cards (13.3–13.6)

The Core version added four Core cards. Each condenses a model answer for one big kind of question, so that the verdict you need is already written.

CardThe kind of questionIts lines
Core A, 13.3Law-making and morality: questions about legislatorsP1–P6: the neutral state, equally valid opinions, only harm, intimate choices, majority morality, enforcing morality
Core B, 13.4Judges, lawyers and moralityQ1–Q6: judges only apply the law, adjudication is politics, theory is irrelevant, lawyers serve clients, stay within your role, law and justice
Core C, 13.5What law is, and what citizens owe itL1–L6: law is a social fact, no necessary link with morality, facts about opinion settle it, law is will or power, valid law must be obeyed, private disobedience
Core D, 13.6Testing a theory on a new issueThree tasks: assess a theory, apply it, compare it with a rival

Cores A to C have the same four parts. Core D has the spine, pivots and Repaired lines, with three Tasks in place of lettered lines:

  • Spine: the card's whole argument in two or three sentences. Core A's says that no law on a moral question is neutral, so pluralism cannot mean neutrality. It means discipline on three things: the reasons used, the amount of coercion, and the forum that decides.
  • Lettered lines (P, Q or L): each has grey trigger words, a blue VERDICT to copy, and a line placing each theorist. On P1, for example, Hart partly agrees, Devlin rejects it, and Rawls, the natural ally, accepts only a weak form.
  • Pivots: short turns of argument, each pointing to its home block.
  • Repaired: a corrected version of the statement for each topic. Use one per script, in your conclusion.

Core A also has a black Flaws line, which pairs four common flaws in exam statements with a hook and a thesis from 1.2. It is taught with the menus below. Core D's spine is worth learning on its own: a theory is not refuted because it needs moral judgement, or because it fails to dictate an answer. You test a theory three ways. Does it hold together, does it give a defensible answer on the hard case, and does it beat its rivals?

▤ On your sheet: 13.3 Core A: law-making and morality (word for word)
13.3 Core A: law-making and morality legislator questions
Spine No law on a moral question is neutral: permitting, punishing and promoting all take a stand. So pluralism cannot mean neutrality. It means discipline on three things: reasons (accessible to every citizen and sound on the merits), coercion (graded to the strength of those reasons) and forum (the legislature decides, as a trustee, not a stenographer).

P1 The state should be neutral · not endorse moral values; take no side; fixed conception; moral truth

  • Flaws F1 gap (therefore, however, only then, lest): hook word, thesis distinction · F2 absolute (only, all, simply, must): word, conditional · F3 self-refutation: self-application once, numbered · F4 equivocation: concession, conditional.

P2 Moral opinions are equally valid · equally valid; denial of moral truth; suspension of judgment; skeptical

  • VERDICT Neutrality of outcome is impossible, and even Rawls's neutrality of justification rests on moral values. The defensible kernel is narrower: the state should not make one comprehensive doctrine official, or coerce on reasons only its adherents can accept.
  • Hart partly agrees; Devlin rejects it; Rawls, the natural ally, accepts only the weak form; Finnis rejects the strong form but accepts a limit (6.2, 7.5, 6.10).

P3 Only harm to others justifies coercion · only; protect others; wrongdoer; objectively necessary

  • VERDICT Equal validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, which counsels deliberation, provisional judgment and caution in coercion, not silence.
  • Hart rejects it; Devlin partly accepts it, a dangerous ally; Rawls partly does†; Finnis rejects it, but not always for one right answer (4.2, 4.7, 6.10).

P4 A right to decide intimate matters · fundamental decisions; own destinies; intimate relationships; child rearing; private behaviour

  • VERDICT Harm to others is the right presumption for punishment, but it is not the only ground, and it is not a neutral fact: what counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions.
  • Hart partly agrees; Devlin rejects it; for Rawls it is the wrong test; Finnis partly agrees: a ground, not the only one, and he requires no ban on all that fails to pursue a good (7.1, 7.2, 6.10).

P5 Majority or societal morality · majority; majoritarian will; certain groups; minority rights; poll

  • VERDICT The right is real, but it is itself a moral claim with moral limits. It rules out punishing private consensual conduct for its immorality alone. It does not rule out regulation or promotion, and it cannot settle cases where a third party, the child or the unborn, is at stake.
  • Hart largely agrees; Devlin rejects it in principle but often agrees in practice; Rawls and Finnis partly agree (4.5, 7.9).

P6 Enforcing morality is (il)legitimate · legislating morals; unjust; illegitimate; intractable moral conflicts

  • VERDICT The majority settles who decides, not what is right. Majority feeling is evidence to weigh, never the reason that settles the law; and protecting minorities is itself a moral judgment, not an escape from one.
  • Hart rejects it as a reason; Devlin, the natural ally, refuses to count heads; Rawls rejects it; Finnis rejects it from the other side (7.3, 7.11, 12.3).
  • VERDICT Enforcing morality is not illegitimate as such, since every law enforces some morality. What can make it unjust is the reasons used, the coercion chosen and who bears it. So the limits are moral and prudential, not sceptical.
  • Devlin and Finnis hold enforcement legitimate; Hart and Rawls only in part (7.5, 7.9).
  • Pivots Neutrality is impossible (6.5, 7.5). · The coercion gradient applies (7.9). · Majority is not legitimacy (7.11, 12.3). · Scepticism is answered (4.7). · "Fixed" is a matter of degree: no theorist here imposes one complete life-plan, and each fixes some limits.
  • Repaired (one per script) Neutrality: Legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine. · Harm: Legislators should presume against punishing conduct that harms no one else, and need stronger reasons the more coercive the law. · Autonomy: Choices about one's intimate life deserve strong protection from punishment, but not immunity from all regulation, or from the state's promotion of other goods. · Majority: The majority decides, but must decide on reasons it can defend to the minority. · Enforcement: Enforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate; scepticism is no objection, but fallibility is a reason for restraint.

Comparisons and controversies (13.1, 13.2)

13.1 compares pairs of thinkers on the same axes. For example, Fuller and the Radbruch formula both deny that enactment alone settles legality, but Fuller tests a law's form while the formula tests its content. 13.2 holds current controversies, chiefly the 2022 repeal of s 377A together with Art 156. The trigger table sends questions that ask for contemporary issues here, with the advice to use two or three, one line each.

  • CONCEDE TSH's catch: where, for realists, consensus has gone "dreadfully wrong" while a local legislature tries to do right, the formula is a real problem, not merely ineffective (8.5). I concede that consensus gauges morality but does not ground it.
  • CONCEDE Alexy grants that candour is the strongest argument against non-positivism, though not fatal to it; his replies answer it (8.3).
  • CONCEDE Finnis's list of goods is contested, and incommensurable goods leave much open. His weak points are at 5.3 and 5.7. Disagreement is not falsity, but it limits coercion.
  • CONCEDE Dworkin's fit is often not unique, so whose political morality decides? (9.5)
  • CONCEDE Thunder admits that virtue under-determines cases, with inevitable disagreement on particular ones (10.5).
  • CONCEDE Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote. Hart's stopping point for paternalism is itself "based on morals", though he never punishes immorality as such (7.1). Pepper never defines "extreme", so his lawyer weighs morality throughout (10.1).

1.1 The map

A table from course topic to lead archetype, cards and tests. The first column gives each topic with its slide week and lecture. If a question is about the rule of law, the map sends you to archetype 3, card 14.6 (Fuller) and framework 15.1. The last row sends you to the Core cards: A for law-making, B for judges and lawyers, C for what law is, and D for testing a theory.

1.2 The menus

The menus hold ready-made hooks (first sentences), theses, a general steelman frame and closes, plus an optional one-sentence roadmap, a few memorable lines and a reformulation. Pick one of each, and never use the same one twice in a script. The default thesis is numbered (you make two or three claims) and the default close is verdict and principle. Some items are rationed. The self-application hook, a memorable line and the reformulation are each once per script, and the actor close is only for a question that names an actor.

HookUse it when…
SourceThe statement nearly repeats a theorist, such as George as TSH reports him, Thunder's summary of the amoral view, or Devlin's case for enforcement. You then ask whether the author's own qualification survives.
WordOne word carries the overreach: without exception, necessarily, simply, always, rightfully.
Ally turnsThe statement's natural ally, such as Hart, Devlin, Pepper or Rawls, rejects its conclusion.
CaseA case tests the statement at once: Riggs, the 2007 compromise on s 377A, Ordinance 11 or the Jaffa Cakes case†.
ConcessionThe statement is right about a kernel, but its overreach does not follow, because of a principle you name.
Self-applicationThe statement is itself a philosophy or a moral verdict, so it cannot be true in the sense it claims. Once per script.

Core A's Flaws line gives a short cut. It names four flaws that exam statements often contain and pairs each with the hook and thesis that expose it best.

Flaw in the statementSignal wordsHookThesis
F1 A gap in the reasoningtherefore, however, only then, lestWordDistinction
F2 An absolute claimonly, all, simply, mustWordConditional
F3 It refutes itselfNo fixed wordsSelf-application, onceNumbered
F4 Equivocation, one word in two sensesNo fixed wordsConcessionConditional

Sample Question 1 has three of the four. "Only then" leaves a gap, "all" and "only" are absolutes, and "equally valid" refutes itself.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A hook from the menu, filled in

The menu's Hook: word gives you a sentence with a slot for the loaded word (without exception, necessarily, simply, always, rightfully), saying that everything turns on that word and that it commits the statement to more than it can defend.

Filled for Sample Question 1: Everything turns on "equally valid", which commits the statement to more than it can defend: a legislator who treats every moral opinion as equally valid has already taken a moral side.

The menu's steelman line is the general pattern behind every archetype's Steelman: the best case for the statement, a Singapore example that supports it, then what it shows and what it does not. The closes are verdict and principle (the default), back to the hook, and the actor close, which ends on one concrete consequence for the judge, the MP or the lawyer.

1.3 Organising distinctions

This is the most powerful tool on the sheet. Each distinction splits a statement into a part that is right and a part that is wrong. The table gives twelve, each with its home block and the kinds of statement it fits, and a black "Also" line adds six more, numbered (13) to (18). Choose one per answer and let it shape the body.

It fits…DistinctionWhat it splitsHome
"the majority wants it", "let the people decide"(1) who decides v what is rightA vote or a role settles who may make the law, not what it should say.section 12, 11.5
"necessarily"(2) presupposed v operativeMorality is always presupposed in judging, but operative only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.9.8
"always", "sufficient", "rules only"(3) floor v ceilingThe law sets the minimum, not everything a judge or lawyer should do.11.7, 10.5

Distinction (1) answers almost any majority-will statement. The section ends with a reminder worth using whenever you weigh one theory against another: rival models are judged by how persuasive and useful they are, not by proof†.

1.4 Self-critique bank

These are honest weaknesses of the positions you are likely to defend, each already written as a CONCEDE line:

  • TSH's catch. Her test lets judges strike down only laws that a broad historical consensus condemns as intolerably unjust. She admits the test becomes a real problem where that consensus has gone dreadfully wrong while a local legislature tries to do right (8.5).
  • Alexy's admission that candour is the strongest argument against his view, though not a fatal one (8.3).
  • Finnis's list of goods is contested, and goods that cannot be measured on one scale leave much open. His weak points are taught at 5.3 and 5.7. Disagreement does not make him wrong, but it limits what the state may coerce.
  • Dworkin's admission that fit is often not unique (9.5).
  • Thunder's admission that virtue leaves many cases open (10.5).
  • A last line on three allies. Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote. Hart's stopping point for paternalism is itself a moral judgement, though he never punishes immorality as such (7.1). Pepper never defines the extreme cases in which a lawyer may object, so his lawyer weighs morality throughout (10.1).

The first line shows the pattern. You concede that consensus measures morality, but deny that it is what makes something right. Put one or two such sentences inside your last body section.

1.5 Signature ledger

The ledger lists memorable examples, grouped by archetype, each with a home block, an alternate and a tick box. It includes the grudge informer (alternate: Ordinance 11), the effluent case (10.2) and Jaffa Cakes† (2.6, alternate: the "vehicle" example). Every line starts with "~ ", so the whole ledger prints black. It is a checklist for you, not text to copy. Use each example once per script, in its home block. Tick it after your first answer, and use the alternate after that.

6From question to answer in five minutes

The prep page gives a five-minute routine. Here it is as a chart, with Liu's advice to read the task line first added at the start.

Two details matter in the scan. Every word you circle must reach your thesis or a topic sentence, because the examiner planted it for a reason. And the actor lock is strict: end each body paragraph on the actor the question names, and give any other actor one sentence at most.

The trigger table

The trigger table (prep 0.2) is the bridge from the question to the sheet. Each row gives some question words, the move they call for, and the blocks to go to. Here are a few rows:

Question wordsMoveGo to

The 1,500-word frame

The 1,500-word frame
▤ Prep page 0.3
  1. 1Opening, 120–150 words: hook and thesis from 1.2, then the section's Intro.
  2. 2Steelman, 60–85 words: copy one of the section's Steelman lines, the one that fits the statement, with its slots filled.
  3. 3Body: three sections of 300–340 words, or four of 235–255, with the self-critique inside the last.
  4. 4Conclusion, 100–130 words: the section's Conclusion, then a Repaired line from a Core card (13.3–13.6), then the actor close if the question names an actor.

Each body paragraph, of about 300 words, follows the same pattern. Start with the claim in the quote's own words. Develop one theorist in two or three sentences. Give the strongest objection, and your reply to it (in two of your sections only). Add one illustration, and finish with a "so" line. Keep within three caps: develop at most two authorities in a paragraph, use one Singapore case per proposition, and give numbers only when the number is the argument.

When the task line says "critically evaluate … by reference to" named theorists, the frame adds two rules. Give your verdict in the first two sentences. Then write one developed paragraph per named theorist, including a test of the theorist you endorse. With four named theorists, that points to four body sections of 235–255 words.

Rules that cost marks

The prep page (0.4) lists the rules that lose marks when broken:

  • Actor lock. End each body paragraph on the named actor. In a legislator or lawyer question, give the Radbruch formula, Rajeevan, Lim Meng Suang or TSH's broad-historical-consensus test one sentence at most.
  • Position once. Use the archetype's Position line once, in the question's terms, and never paste a default paragraph. Raise TSH's broad-historical-consensus test and the Radbruch formula's threshold only in questions about judges, and test them once, with the self-critique in 1.4.
  • Quotes. Quote only what the sheet itself gives as a quotation, paraphrase everything else, and spell out each abbreviation the first time you use it.
  • Scope. Liu's slides are course material. Use facts from outside the course only if you know them cold, one line each.
  • Stock moves. Moves such as "hidden premise" or "a better formulation" are each allowed once per script. It is better to name the word that carries the premise.

Two-hats problems, problem questions, memos and comparisons have their own shapes on the prep page (0.5). The two-hats format is taught in Lesson 12.

7Worked example: Sample Question 1

Let us run the routine on Liu's sample statement. The task line names Rawls, Finnis, Hart and Devlin, so those four are your cast, and Liu's advice is to stay with them†.

The aim survives. The principle defeats itself, and the mechanism is neither necessary nor neutral. The steps below show how the sheet gets you there.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 1: scan the words
WordWhat it commits the statement toGo to
"equally valid"That every moral opinion is as good as every other, which is itself a moral claim4.7, 6.10; Core A, P2
"objectively"That there are moral facts, which sits uneasily with treating every opinion as equally valid6.10
"wrongdoer"That some conduct is wrong, again a moral judgement. Liu noted in class that a wrongdoer's conduct might be immoral without being harmful†6.10, 7.1
"others"A decision about who counts as another person, which in the abortion debate raises whether the unborn count6.5, 7.1
"only then"That the harm mechanism is the only route to the aim6.10: read the sentences as a chain†
"fixed conception"That anything short of the mechanism imposes one way of lifeCore A, P1, and its pivot that "fixed" is a matter of degree
"legislators"The actor lock: end each body paragraph on the MPPrep 0.4
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 2: route

Lead section 6, block 6.10, with 4.7 for "equally valid" and 7.1, 7.2, 7.3 and 7.9 for the harm mechanism. Distinction 1.3(4), aim v mechanism. The aim (do not impose a fixed conception of the good life) is defensible. The principle (treat every opinion as equally valid) defeats itself, and the mechanism (legislate only against harm to others) is neither neutral nor necessary.

Because this is a legislator question, Core A (13.3) gives a ready map of where each named theorist stands on the statement's three claims:

TheoristP1: the state should be neutralP2: opinions are equally validP3: only harm to others
RawlsAccepts only the weak formPartly accepts it†The wrong test
FinnisRejects the strong form, but accepts a limitRejects it, though not because there is one right answerPartly agrees: a ground, not the only one
HartPartly agreesRejects itPartly agrees
DevlinRejects itPartly accepts it, a dangerous allyRejects it

Self-critique from 1.4: Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Step 3: opening and thesis (about 145 words)

Everything turns on "equally valid", which commits the statement to more than it can defend. The statement is right about its aim but wrong about its means. Legislators should not impose a fixed conception of the good life, and Rawls and Finnis both share that aim. But I make three claims. First, treating all moral opinions as equally valid is itself a moral position, so it defeats itself. Second, legislating only against harm to others is not the only route to the aim, since Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective. Third, that mechanism is not neutral either, since Rawls counts Mill's liberalism as one comprehensive doctrine among others. The statement can keep its aim only by dropping its mechanism. Rawls rightly requires reasons each citizen could accept, but his neutrality is of justification, not outcome, so a law on a moral question still takes a side.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Step 4: steelman (about 75 words)

The best case for the statement starts from reasonable pluralism. Political power is the power of free and equal citizens acting together, so imposing one faction's good life treats dissenters as subjects, not partners. In 2007 both camps in the s 377A debate were sure they were absolutely right. This shows that the state must not make one comprehensive doctrine official. It does not show that legislators can treat every opinion as equally valid, or take no side.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 5: body plan (four named theorists, so four sections of 235–255 words)
  1. Rawls (6.1, 6.2, 6.11). The aim echoes Rawls, and Rawls partly accepts equal validity†. No doctrine is privileged in advance, yet unreasonable doctrines, meaning those that refuse fair terms rather than those that are false, are set aside†. His neutrality is of justification, not outcome. Objection: the label "reasonable" does the overriding (TSH). Reply: his standard is moral, though political. So Rawls supports the aim, but equal validity only among reasonable doctrines.
  2. Finnis (5.5, 6.2). Finnis rejects equal validity, but not because there is one right answer: a range of opinions is reasonable†. Protecting others is a ground for law, not the only one†. His common good is a framework in which citizens pursue their own plans, so the aim survives on his terms. Test: Finnis is not neutral either. Concede it, since no law is.
  3. Hart (7.1, 7.2, 7.9). The mechanism is not necessary. Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective, as with restricting drug supply, and harm itself is not a neutral fact. Building on Hart's point that coercion is prima facie objectionable, the coercion gradient matches the strength of the reason to the amount of force, though Hart's own question was punishment only.
  4. Devlin, with the self-critique (7.3, 1.4). Devlin is a dangerous ally. As a cultural relativist he partly accepts equal validity between societies, yet he lets each society enforce its shared morality, and he refuses to count heads. So the alternative to equal validity is not majority feeling. Self-critique: Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote.

Because of the actor lock, each section ends on what its point means for the MP.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Step 6: close (about 100 words)

The statement is therefore partly right. Its aim, that a pluralist state should not impose one way of life, is one Rawls and Finnis share. But neutrality cannot deliver it, since any law on a moral question takes a side, and treating all opinions as equally valid defeats itself. A defensible version would read: legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine. For the MP, this means voting only for laws whose reasons can be defended to those who disagree, and demanding stronger reasons the more coercive the bill.

The close follows the frame. It starts from section 6's Conclusion, adds Core A's Repaired line for neutrality, and ends with the actor close because the question names legislators. You will meet this question again in Lesson 6, where block 6.10 is taught in full and the essay is planned with the whole archetype in place.

Picture the sheet as a satnav. The trigger words are the address you type in. The archetype block is the route. The steelman is the warning about the strongest traffic against you.
