Lesson 2: What law is →
LESSON 2 · ARCHETYPE 2 · ABOUT 72 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 46 QUESTIONS

LP v NLT, and why theory matters

⚡ BIG IDEA

Saying what counts as "law" is already an evaluation, so the choice between legal positivism and natural law is live, and hard cases such as Riggs v Palmer turn on a theory of what law's grounds are.

ARCHETYPE 2 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
2 LP v NLT, and why theory matters
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Naming [law] is an evaluation, so LP v NLT is a live choice, and hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.
Intro [The statement] treats identifying law as neutral and theory as optional. LP's two theses, law as social fact and no necessary link with morality†, are coherent. But LP must still choose whose recognition counts, and the Riggs judges, agreeing that the law bound them, split over what it required. So [the statement] is [wrong / partly right]: theory decides hard cases.
Steelman: for LP The best case for [the statement] is clarity: law lies in legislation, cases and custom, which anyone can check; lawyers look it up and must know it before reforming it; and LP arose in states with no shared moral base†. This shows that sources usually identify law. It does not show [that identifying it is value-free].
Steelman: for NLT The best case for [the statement] is that naming law is never neutral: LP finds law in what courts uphold, so its premise becomes its conclusion†, and to equate law with what people regard as law is to evaluate, not merely describe†. This shows that LP is a choice. It does not show [that ordinary injustice unmakes law]: only intolerable injustice can.
2.1 Descriptive? neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes
  1. LP and NLT are not at [cross-purposes]: both ask what law is (TSH).
  2. Treating [official recognition] as conclusive is a choice: once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, its injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH).
  3. So LP is not simply [neutral and objective]: preferring it for a pluralist state is itself a value choice.
  • TRAP "No necessary connection" allows contingent links, incorporation and critique†: the Riggs maxim, a legal rule with moral content, troubles no positivist†.
  • AGAINST Finnis doubts law can be described from a "rubbish heap" of facts without evaluative criteria.
2.2 Internal "ought" mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation
  1. Law is more than [commands obeyed from habit]: Hart's rules carry an internal "ought", a critical reflective attitude.
  2. But that "ought" need not be moral: Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit.
  3. So Hart escapes [mere habit] without conceding moral evaluation.
2.3 Elitist? only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down
  1. NLT does not rest on [moral truths only the devout can see]: natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH).
  2. Nor does it [license any judge to strike down]: the RF voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3), and for Finnis an unjust law is no nullity to disregard.
  3. So [the statement] hits only strong NLT, where every rule must embody morality; weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme divergence, such as a law to execute all redheads†.
  • QUALIFY Strong NLT would have judges second-guess tax law†. Grotius made natural law secular; Aquinas has four kinds of law: eternal, divine, natural, human†.
  • CONCEDE TSH admits "no easy answer" on who pronounces natural law, so I concede judges' doubtful authority below the threshold (12.1).
2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? all but name
  1. Fuller and Dworkin are NLT's allies, not [natural lawyers in all but name]: neither lets injustice as such defeat validity.
  2. Fuller's is a thin "procedural natural law"†: legality demands rules, whether fair or unfair.
  3. Dworkin's judge must interpret the legal history found, even a wicked one, leaving intolerable injustice open, so [all but name] overstates.
2.5 Judges disagree? only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
  1. [Judges only disagree about obeying] mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance: in Riggs all accepted the law's authority but split over what it required.
  2. In McLoughlin, too, the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether policy may limit liability (2.8; 9.2).
  3. So [no law to apply] assumes the plain-fact view, when which arguments count as law is the point in dispute.
  • Empirical disagreement asks whether agreed grounds of law are met; theoretical disagreement disputes the grounds themselves, which the plain-fact view and semantic theories hide.
  • For Dworkin, LP paints judges as "well-meaning liars" (pretence) or "simpletons" (borderline cases), yet these were "pivotal" cases.
  • QUALIFY Dworkin is arguably unfair to LP†: it need not make every disagreement empirical, and soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests.
  • LAWYER Counsel should run both policy arguments (9.2).
2.6 Theory useless? luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes
  1. Fish grants [the statement] a kernel: Rawls cited in court will likely seem "window dressing" at best, showing off at worst.
  2. Yet marshalling rules is purposive: without a strong sense of the general project, rehearsing them is "an empty gesture" (Fish).
  3. So [theory is a luxury] confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9), hard cases on rival ones.
  • Jaffa Cakes† (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2), LON/91/160): the VAT tribunal used core attributes, class commonalities, thought experiments and social context, a philosophy of cakeness, and held them cakes (stale cakes harden, biscuits soften). Reasonable people agree on the factors but weigh them differently, the shape of most jurisprudential disputes†.
  • TSH: purpose may settle "vehicles", but contested words like "law" engage LP v NLT.
  • Leff†: judging whether a thing is done well requires knowing what is being done, so excellence presupposes theory.
  • AGAINST [Theory cannot help anyone decide] fails: disagreement is not absence of fact (4.7; Constitution: 11.7).
2.7 Singapore pragmatism prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
  1. [Singapore's prevailing philosophy] is often called pragmatism: keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach pragmatic, preserving social cohesion.
  2. Yet pragmatism is itself a theory: in any postmodern pragmatic society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" guiding principles (TSH).
  3. So [philosophy is unnecessary here] fails: theory exists to guide practice, and in law as in life the question of right and wrong cannot be shunned (TSH).
2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin
  1. Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions; McLoughlin, on whether policy may distinguish precedent.
  2. Each answer presupposes a theory of [law].
  • Riggs v Palmer: Elmer, 16, poisoned his grandfather lest he revoke the will; read literally, the statute of wills let him inherit. Held 5–2 that he took nothing. Earl relied on intention and on maxims founded in "universal law", and said this took no property from Elmer; Gray, dissenting, put the question outside conscience's domain and said courts cannot add to the respondent's penalties.
  • McLoughlin v O'Brian: not at the scene, she saw her injured family, begrimed, in hospital hours later, and a daughter died. Held 5–0, reversing the CA, that her shock was recoverable. Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell let policy limit liability, but not here; Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable"; Bridge called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication".
  • LP reads Riggs as Gray's posited text†, or Earl's maxim as posited common law with moral content†, or as a gap for discretion. In McLoughlin the CA, as Dworkin reads it, found no law once precedent ran out and filled the gap by policy.
  • Dworkin reads Riggs as two morally grounded theories: Gray's guards a principle of justice (fixed penalties); Earl's guards coherence. In McLoughlin precedent's force was disputed: Scarman thought himself bound by principles embedded in the precedents.
  • ALR: rules are fitted to results reached on other grounds (Riggs) and reasons follow results; yet reasons split a unanimous House (McLoughlin).
  • Riggs bears two readings†, and neither need be chosen: (a) both sides argued about law, the majority's including common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates; (b) the dispute was whether law is always subject to universal moral principles, as Earl's "universal law" suggests. Neither side kept to the statute's four corners†.
Conclusion [The statement] is [wrong / partly right]. LP rightly ties law to sources, and Dworkin is unfair to call it blind to theoretical disagreement. But naming law is an evaluation, and rival theories split Riggs and the Lords' reasons in McLoughlin, so theory is not optional. Weak NLT earns its keep only at extreme injustice (8); Riggs needed only a choice of theory about law's grounds.

1Start here: archetype 2 in plain English

Archetype 2 asks the oldest question in the course: what makes something count as law? Two families of theory answer it. Legal positivism (LP) says law is whatever the recognised sources lay down, such as statutes, cases and custom, and that whether it is any good is a separate question. Natural law theory (NLT) says human law answers to a higher standard that reason can work out, so a rule that is monstrously unjust fails as law.

Exam statements in this family usually make one of two moves. Some say that identifying law is easy and neutral: look it up, and leave morality to the preachers. Others say that legal theory is a luxury, because a practical lawyer needs only the statute, the cases and a good dictionary.

Your answer is the same every time. Choosing a test for what counts as law is already a judgement about what matters. Positivism is a coherent choice, and sources usually do identify the law. But it is still a choice, and in hard cases the choice decides the result. In Riggs v Palmer every judge accepted that the law bound them. They split over what the law required, because they held different theories of what makes something law.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Legal positivism (LP)The view that law is identified by its source (who made it, and how), not by its merit. It has the two theses below.
Social fact thesisLP's first thesis. Whether something is law depends on social facts, such as what was enacted and what officials recognise†.
Separation thesisLP's second thesis. There is no necessary connection between law and morality†. The two often overlap, but they do not have to.
Natural law theory (NLT)The view that human law must conform to a higher law, which reason can discover, in order to count fully as law.
Strong v weak NLTStrong NLT says every rule must embody morality to be law. Weak NLT says a rule loses its legal status only when it departs from morality to an extreme degree†. You only ever defend weak NLT.
Internal point of viewHart's term for treating a rule as a standard that you and others ought to follow, rather than as a habit or a threat.
Rule of recognitionHart's master rule: the test officials actually use to identify valid law. In Singapore officials treat the Constitution as supreme, so it sits at the top.
Soft positivismA version of LP in which the rule of recognition may, as a matter of fact, include moral tests.
Grounds of lawDworkin's term for whatever makes a statement of law true. "The speed limit is 55" is true because the legislature passed a text saying so.
Plain-fact viewDworkin's name for the idea that law is simply what institutions have laid down in the past, so every legal question has a historical answer you can look up.
Empirical v theoretical disagreementEmpirical: judges agree on the grounds of law but dispute whether they are met. Theoretical: judges dispute what the grounds are.
Principle v policyA principle concerns rights and fairness between the parties. A policy concerns the community's collective goals, such as avoiding a flood of claims. This is distinction 1.3(8).

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: naming law is an evaluation, so LP v NLT is a live choice, and hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.

Put simply, when you decide what counts as law, you decide what matters. A positivist who says "law is whatever officials recognise" has chosen official recognition as the test, and has thereby decided that a rule's injustice does not affect its status as law. That may be a good choice. But it is a choice, not an observation. So the quarrel between positivism and natural law is a real one, and in a hard case like Riggs the result depends on which view of law's grounds the judge holds.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement treats identifying law as neutral and theory as optional. You grant that LP's two theses, law as a social fact and no necessary link with morality†, are coherent. But LP must still choose whose recognition counts. And the Riggs judges, who all agreed that the law bound them, split over what it required. So the statement is wrong, or at best partly right, because theory decides hard cases.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. LP is right to tie law to its sources, and Dworkin is unfair when he calls LP blind to theoretical disagreement. But naming law is an evaluation, and rival theories split both the judges in Riggs and the Lords' reasons in McLoughlin. So theory is not optional. Weak natural law earns its keep only at extreme injustice, which is the subject of section 8. Riggs did not need it. Riggs needed only a choice of theory about law's grounds.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before replying to it. Section 2 gives you one steelman for each camp. Use whichever one the statement needs.

  • Steelman: for LP. The best case for positivism is clarity. Law lies in legislation, cases and custom, which anyone can check. Lawyers advising clients look the law up, and you must know what the law is before you can argue for reforming it. LP also grew up in states with no shared moral or religious base, where people needed a test of law that everyone could apply†. This shows that sources usually identify the law. It does not show that identifying it is value-free, because the reasons for preferring LP, such as certainty and peace among people who disagree, are themselves values.
  • Steelman: for NLT. The best case for natural law is that naming law is never neutral. LP finds law in what courts uphold, so it assumes the very answer it claims to discover, and its premise becomes its conclusion†. And to treat what people regard as law as simply being law is to evaluate, not merely to describe†. This shows that LP is a choice. It does not show that ordinary injustice unmakes law. Only intolerable injustice can.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
2.1"Positivism just describes; natural law preaches."Both answer the same question, what law is. Making official recognition the test is already a choice.
2.2"Law is just commands obeyed out of habit." Or: "Hart's 'ought' admits that law needs morality."Law is more than habit, because Hart's rules carry an internal "ought". That "ought" marks a standard, which officials may accept out of fear or self-interest. It is not a moral verdict.
2.3"Natural law is for believers and lets any judge strike down laws."Natural law is worked out by reason, and weak NLT reaches only extreme injustice.
2.4"Fuller and Dworkin are natural lawyers in all but name."They are allies, but neither lets injustice as such unmake law.
2.5"Judges only ever disagree about whether to obey."In Riggs and McLoughlin they disagreed about what the law was. That is theoretical disagreement.
2.6"Theory is a luxury; a dictionary will do."Lawyers rarely cite theory but always use it. Even the Jaffa Cakes tribunal needed a theory of what a cake is.
2.7"Singapore is pragmatic, so it needs no theory."Pragmatism is itself a theory. It hides its principles rather than removing them.
2.8(Case cards)Riggs and McLoughlin are your evidence for every block above.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Choosing a test for law is already a judgement, and in hard cases that judgement decides the result.

2The big picture: what is law?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two referees argue about a football match. One says, "A goal is whatever the rulebook says is a goal." The other says, "A goal is what the rulebook says, but the rulebook exists to make a fair game, so if a rule would reward cheating, it isn't really doing its job." Both care about rules. They disagree about what makes something count. Legal positivism is the first referee, and natural law theory is the second.

Archetype 2 is the foundation of the course. Its statements ask what law is, and whether it matters which answer we give. The rest of the lesson shows that it does.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
AustinLaw is the command of a sovereign, backed by the threat of a sanction. The sovereign is whoever is habitually obeyed and obeys no one else. Austin is candid that a law's existence is one thing and its merit another. But Hart showed that habit and fear cannot explain why officials treat law as binding (14.3).
HartLaw is a union of primary rules, which impose duties ("do not steal"), and secondary rules, which tell officials how to recognise, change and apply the primary rules. Officials accept these rules from the internal point of view (14.4).
AquinasHuman law binds because it derives from natural law, the part of a higher moral order that human reason can grasp. A law contrary to natural law is a corruption of law (14.2).
FinnisA modern natural lawyer. An unjust law is not a nullity you may simply ignore. It lacks its usual moral power to bind in conscience.
RadbruchUnjust statutes remain law unless their injustice is intolerable. This test, the Radbruch formula (RF), is taught in section 8.
FullerLaw has an inner morality of form. Rules must be general, public, prospective, clear and so on. But a rule can meet every one of these requirements and still be wicked (14.6).
DworkinLaw is interpretive. Judges read the legal record for fit and for value, so they often disagree about what the law is, not just about whether to obey it (14.5).
FishPractising law happens inside an enterprise with a purpose, shaped by a view of how the state may use force. Rules recited without that view mean little (14.1).
TSH (Tan Seow Hon)LP and NLT answer the same question, what law is. Treating official recognition as decisive is itself a choice, and pragmatism is itself a theory.

Key distinctions

  • Necessary v contingent connection. LP denies only that law must be moral. It accepts that morality often shapes what Parliament enacts, gets written into law (many statutes use words like "reasonable"), and is used to criticise law. Those links are contingent: they happen to exist, but they could be removed.
  • Strong v weak NLT. Strong NLT says a rule must fully embody morality to be law, which would let judges second-guess even tax law. Weak NLT says only extreme injustice, such as a law to execute all redheads, strips a rule of legal status. Every natural lawyer worth defending is weak.
  • Empirical v theoretical disagreement. Judges who agree on what makes law law, and dispute whether those conditions are met, disagree empirically. Judges who dispute what makes law law disagree theoretically. Dworkin's whole attack on positivism starts here (2.5).
  • Habit v standard v moral approval. A habit is a pattern of behaviour. A standard is a rule people use to judge conduct. Moral approval is a belief that the rule is right. Hart needs the second, not the third (2.2).
  • Citing theory v using it. Lawyers rarely name a philosopher, but every lawyer acts on some view of what law is and what it is for (2.6).
  • Principle v policy (distinction 1.3(8)). In McLoughlin the Lords split over whether policy arguments, such as fear of a flood of claims, are a proper ground for judges at all (9.2).

Notice what the chart shows. On an ordinary statute, a positivist and a weak natural lawyer give the same answer: it is law. They disagree about what makes it law, and that difference only bites at the extreme. So when you defend natural law in this archetype, you are defending a narrow claim, not a licence for judges.

The case at the heart of it

Nobody in Riggs disputed the words of the statute, and nobody thought murder was acceptable. The question was what law those words made. Dworkin compares the judges to critics who agree on every word of a poem but disagree about what the poem means. To get from the text to the "real statute", a judge needs a theory of legislation. Gray's theory gave the words their plain meaning with no unstated exceptions. Earl's theory read the statute in the light of what its makers would have intended and of the common law's principles. That is why this archetype says hard cases turn on a theory of law's grounds.

⚠ TRAP
Don't turn the debate into "describe v preach"

Students often write that LP says what law is and NLT says what it ought to be. That is the very claim block 2.1 attacks. Weak NLT also says what law is: at the extreme, an intolerably unjust rule is not law at all. The two schools give rival answers to one question.

Words in a question that send you here
▤ Trigger table, prep page 0.2
Question wordsMoveGo to
"precedent runs out"; "floodgates"principle v policy9.2, 2.8
"theory is a luxury"Fish on both sides2.6
"prevailing philosophy"pragmatism is a philosophy2.7

32.1 Descriptive?

🧩 Practise 2.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.1 Descriptive? (word for word)
2.1 Descriptive? neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes
  1. LP and NLT are not at [cross-purposes]: both ask what law is (TSH).
  2. Treating [official recognition] as conclusive is a choice: once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, its injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH).
  3. So LP is not simply [neutral and objective]: preferring it for a pluralist state is itself a value choice.
  • TRAP "No necessary connection" allows contingent links, incorporation and critique†: the Riggs maxim, a legal rule with moral content, troubles no positivist†.
  • AGAINST Finnis doubts law can be described from a "rubbish heap" of facts without evaluative criteria.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A positivist says, "I'm just describing law, like a map-maker describes a coastline." But a map-maker has to decide where the coast is: at high tide or at low tide. Deciding whose recognition makes something "law" is that kind of choice. So the "neutral description" already contains a judgement.

What the statement claims

"The endless argument over whether an unjust law is really law is a misunderstanding: one side describes what the law is, the other preaches what it ought to be, and the two never meet. Even so, a modern pluralist state should plainly prefer the first view, which simply records what officials recognise as law, neutrally and objectively, without taking sides." (Q4)

The statement makes two claims. First, positivism and natural law are at cross-purposes, because one describes and the other prescribes. Second, positivism is neutral and objective, so a state whose citizens disagree about morality should prefer it. The statement is tempting because positivism really does look like description. A positivist reports what officials do, much as a geographer reports where a river runs. The block shows that the "description" contains a choice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Positivism and natural law answer the same question. TSH argues that the two schools are not at cross-purposes, because both ask what law is. Natural law is not a sermon about what law ought to be. It is a rival account of what law is, at least at the extremes. So when a positivist says "valid but wicked" and a natural lawyer says "not law", they are giving opposite answers to one question.
  2. Making official recognition decisive is a choice. LP identifies law by what officials, and finally the highest court, recognise. TSH points out what follows. Once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, LP treats its injustice as irrelevant to whether it is law. Deciding that injustice does not count is a decision about what matters, not something you can see by looking.
  3. So positivism is not simply neutral and objective. You may still prefer it, for example because a pluralist state needs a test of law that people of every faith can apply. But that preference rests on values such as certainty and peace among people who disagree. Preferring LP is therefore itself a value choice.

The extra lines, explained

  • TRAP · "no necessary connection" is not "no connection". The separation thesis allows contingent links between law and morality. Morality can influence what is enacted, it can be incorporated into law, and it can be used to criticise law†. The maxim applied in Riggs, that no one may profit from his own wrong, is a legal rule with moral content. It troubles no positivist†, because it is law by virtue of being laid down in the common law, not by virtue of being moral. Never write that positivists think law has nothing to do with morality.
  • AGAINST · Finnis's rubbish heap. Finnis doubts that anyone can describe law from a mere rubbish heap of facts. To decide which facts belong in a description of law, and which are just the rules of a chess club or the threats of a gang, you need criteria of what is important. Those criteria are evaluative. So even the most careful description of law presupposes an evaluation, which supports line 2.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A wicked statute reaches the top court

A made-up case. Ruritania's Parliament, following every proper procedure, passes a law confiscating, without compensation, every farm owned by one minority group. Ruritania's highest court upholds it. A farmer asks: is it law, so the bailiff may lawfully take my farm?

SpeakerAnswerWhat the answer assumes
A positivistYes. It came from a recognised source and the top court upheld it. It is law, though wicked.That official recognition is the test. That choice, not anything observed, makes the injustice irrelevant.
A weak natural lawyerNo, if the injustice is intolerable.That extreme injustice can defeat legal status. Also a choice, made openly.
A commentator"They are talking past each other. One describes, the other preaches."Wrong. The farmer asked one question and got two opposite answers to it.

Both main answers rest on a view about what makes law law. That is lines 1 and 2 of the block working together.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement says LP and NLT are at cross-purposes, but TSH shows that both ask the same question, what law is. Natural law is a rival answer to that question, not a sermon about what law ought to be. Positivism's answer, that law is what officials recognise, is coherent but not neutral. Once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, LP treats its injustice as irrelevant to its legal status, and that is a decision about what matters. One may still prefer LP for a pluralist state, but that preference rests on values such as certainty, so it is a value choice, not a neutral description.

42.2 Internal "ought"

🧩 Practise 2.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.2 Internal "ought" (word for word)
2.2 Internal "ought" mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation
  1. Law is more than [commands obeyed from habit]: Hart's rules carry an internal "ought", a critical reflective attitude.
  2. But that "ought" need not be moral: Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit.
  3. So Hart escapes [mere habit] without conceding moral evaluation.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two drivers stop at a red light at 3 a.m. with no one around. One stops only because a camera might fine her. The other stops because "that's the rule and I should follow it". Hart says law only makes sense if some people, especially officials, take the second attitude. But that "should" need not be a moral should. You can accept a rule because it is convenient, or habitual, or good for your career.

What the statement claims

"In explaining law through the internal point of view and the language of 'ought', Hart concedes that law cannot be understood without moral evaluation." (Q6)

The statement notices that Hart, a positivist, describes law using the word "ought". Since "ought" is the language of morality, it concludes that Hart has quietly admitted that law depends on morality. It is tempting because Hart did reject the idea that law is only habit and threats, and the word he used to explain what was missing sounds moral.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Hart's rules carry an "ought" that habits lack. Austin thought law was commands obeyed out of habit. Hart replied that a habit is only a pattern of behaviour. A rule also has an internal side. People treat it as a standard, criticise those who break it, demand that others follow it, and accept that such criticism is justified. Hart calls this the critical reflective attitude, and its natural language is "ought", "must" and "should".
  2. That "ought" need not be moral. Hart allows officials to accept a rule for many reasons: fear, self-interest, habit, or genuine moral approval. What matters is that they use the rule as a standard, not why they do. A judge who applies the rule of recognition because it secures her career still takes the internal point of view.
  3. So Hart escapes Austin's problem without conceding moral evaluation. He explains why law is more than habit by pointing to acceptance, and acceptance is a social fact that need not involve a moral judgement. The statement mistakes the grammar of "ought" for a moral verdict.

Support from the cards, explained

Block 2.2 has no tagged lines of its own. Its support comes from the cards on Austin and Hart.

  • Austin, the target (14.3). Austin defined law as the command of a sovereign who is habitually obeyed and obeys no one, backed by a sanction. Hart made two criticisms. Habit misses the internal "ought". And rules that confer powers, such as the rules for making a valid will, enable people rather than order them about, so they are not commands at all. Dworkin still grants that Austin's main idea, as Hart restated it, has never wholly lost its grip on lawyers.
  • CRITIQUE · Dworkin's Nazi dilemma (14.4). Dworkin presses Hart with a dilemma. Many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler only out of fear. If that counts as acceptance, Hart's difference from Austin seems to vanish. If it does not count, then Nazi Germany apparently had no law. The reply is that acceptance, even out of fear, self-interest or habit, still treats the rules as standards to apply and enforce, which a mere habit of obedience does not. So Hart can say Nazi Germany had law without saying its officials approved of it.
  • CRITIQUE · TSH: only officials need accept (14.4). TSH notes that, for Hart, only officials need take the internal point of view, while ordinary citizens need only obey. So Hart's picture may be little different from a power view, and LP is not necessarily democratic. Hart himself admits that where only officials accept the rules, the sheep may end in the slaughter-house. The reply is that describing law is not praising it. Hart tells us when a legal system exists, not that it is a good one.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Spot the difference
AttitudeWhat it sounds likeDoes Hart need it?
Habit"People here usually stop at red lights."No. This is Austin's level, a pattern with no rule in it.
Internal point of view"Drivers ought to stop at red lights, and a driver who doesn't deserves criticism."Yes. This is what turns a pattern into a rule.
Moral approval"Stopping at red lights is morally right."No. It is one possible reason for accepting a rule, not a condition of having one.

The statement treats the second row as if it were the third.

⚠ TRAP
Hart's "minimum content of natural law" is not a natural-law test

Hart did say every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit, because people are vulnerable, roughly equal and of limited goodwill, and people do not belong to suicide clubs. He called this the minimum content of natural law. But it is a practical necessity for survival, not a test of legal validity†, so it does not make Hart a natural lawyer. Harris calls it a sociological conception, since it is consistent with slavery or racial oppression.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Hart does show that law is more than commands obeyed from habit. His rules carry an internal "ought": officials take a critical reflective attitude, criticising deviation and demanding conformity. But that "ought" need not be moral, since Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit as well as approval. So Hart escapes Austin's problem without conceding that law needs moral evaluation. Dworkin's dilemma about Nazi officials fails for the same reason: even officials who obeyed from fear treated the rules as standards, and that is all Hart's account requires.

52.3 Elitist?

🧩 Practise 2.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.3 Elitist? (word for word)
2.3 Elitist? only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down
  1. NLT does not rest on [moral truths only the devout can see]: natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH).
  2. Nor does it [license any judge to strike down]: the RF voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3), and for Finnis an unjust law is no nullity to disregard.
  3. So [the statement] hits only strong NLT, where every rule must embody morality; weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme divergence, such as a law to execute all redheads†.
  • QUALIFY Strong NLT would have judges second-guess tax law†. Grotius made natural law secular; Aquinas has four kinds of law: eternal, divine, natural, human†.
  • CONCEDE TSH admits "no easy answer" on who pronounces natural law, so I concede judges' doubtful authority below the threshold (12.1).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some people think natural law means "the priests decide what's right and the judges must obey them". But natural law, as this course teaches it, is about what reason can work out, which anyone can do. And modern natural lawyers don't let any judge tear up any law he dislikes. Only truly monstrous laws are in question.

What the statement claims

"The second rests on moral truths that only the devout can see, and it licenses any judge to strike down whatever law he personally considers unjust." (Q4)

This sentence comes from the same question as block 2.1, and "the second" is natural law. It makes two charges. Natural law is elitist, since only believers can know its content. And it is dangerous, since any judge can strike down any law he dislikes. The charges are tempting because natural law grew up in religious thought, and because the slogan "an unjust law is no law" sounds like a licence for judges.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Natural law is worked out by reason, not revealed to the faithful. TSH stresses that natural law, unlike divine law, can be grasped by reason. Aquinas kept the two apart: divine law is revealed in scripture, while natural law is what every human being can reach by practical reasoning. So natural law does not rest on truths only the devout can see.
  2. Natural law does not let any judge strike down any law. The Radbruch formula, taught in section 8, denies legal status only to statutes whose injustice is intolerable (8.2, 8.3). And Finnis says even an unjust law is not a nullity to be disregarded. It only loses its usual moral power to bind in conscience.
  3. So the statement hits only strong natural law. Strong NLT says every rule must embody morality to be law, and nobody defends it. Weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme departure from morality, such as a law to execute all redheads†. A judge who finds a statute merely unfair must still apply it.

The extra lines, explained

  • QUALIFY · strong v weak, and the kinds of law. Strong NLT would have judges second-guessing even tax law†, which is why you never defend it. Two background points help you show that natural law is not a creed. Grotius made natural law secular, arguing that it would have the same content even if God did not exist. And Aquinas distinguished four kinds of law†, set out in the table below. Only one of them, divine law, depends on revelation.
  • CONCEDE · who decides? TSH admits there is no easy answer to who may pronounce on what natural law requires. So concede that a judge's authority to override law below the threshold of extreme injustice is doubtful. That question belongs to archetype 12 (12.1).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Aquinas's four kinds of law
KindWhat it is
Eternal lawGod's plan, governing all of creation.
Divine lawGod's law as revealed in scripture. Known through revelation.
Natural lawHumans' share in eternal law, grasped through practical reason. Open to everyone.
Human lawRules laid down by rulers in line with natural law. Some are deduced from its principles, like conclusions in a science. Others are a determination, like an architect designing one particular house from the general idea of a house.

The statement confuses the second row with the third. Once you separate them, the charge of elitism falls away.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement attacks a version of natural law that nobody defends. Natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason, as TSH stresses, and Grotius made it secular. Nor does it license any judge to strike down any law. The Radbruch formula voids only intolerably unjust statutes, and for Finnis even an unjust law is no nullity to disregard. The statement therefore hits only strong natural law, under which every rule must embody morality. Weak natural law strips legal status only at extreme divergence, such as a law to execute all redheads, though I concede, with TSH, that there is no easy answer to who may pronounce on natural law.

62.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers?

🧩 Practise 2.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? (word for word)
2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? all but name
  1. Fuller and Dworkin are NLT's allies, not [natural lawyers in all but name]: neither lets injustice as such defeat validity.
  2. Fuller's is a thin "procedural natural law"†: legality demands rules, whether fair or unfair.
  3. Dworkin's judge must interpret the legal history found, even a wicked one, leaving intolerable injustice open, so [all but name] overstates.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Fuller and Dworkin both say law isn't just "whatever's written down". That makes them sound like natural lawyers. But neither says "a very unjust law stops being law". They are cousins of natural law, not members of the family.

What the statement claims

"Fuller and Dworkin are natural lawyers in all but name." (Q7)

Both theorists reject the positivist picture of law as simply whatever was laid down. Fuller says law has an inner morality. Dworkin says moral principles are part of the law judges apply. So the statement concludes that both belong in the natural law family. It is tempting because both are on natural law's side in many arguments with positivism.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The test for a natural lawyer is whether injustice, on its own, can stop a rule being law. Fuller and Dworkin are allies of natural law, since both deny that enactment alone settles what law is. But neither says that a rule's injustice as such defeats its validity. So neither is a natural lawyer in all but name.
  2. Fuller's natural law is thin and procedural. Liu calls it a procedural natural law†. Fuller's eight requirements of legality ask whether rules are general, public, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to obey, reasonably stable, and applied as written. They concern the form of law, and they demand rules whether those rules are fair or unfair. So a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked (Lesson 3).
  3. Dworkin's judge is bound to the legal history he finds. For Dworkin, a judge interprets the legal record by asking which reading fits it and shows it in its best light. But the judge must work with the history that is actually there, even a wicked one. So Dworkin leaves intolerable injustice unanswered, and "all but name" overstates.

Support from the cards, explained

Block 2.4 has no tagged lines of its own. Its support comes from the cards on Fuller and Dworkin and the comparison in 13.1.

  • Fuller: legality is thin (14.6). Fuller's card concedes that legality is a modest morality: a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked, so you need the Radbruch formula to test content. The card's TRAP adds that Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula. Facing the Nazi regime, he asked how much of a legal system had survived, and he judged statutes by their form, not by whether their injustice was intolerable.
  • Dworkin: no exit from a wicked history (14.5). Dworkin's card concedes two things. A judge's best reading rests on beliefs others can contest. And integrity gives no exit from a wicked legal history. The outer limit is guarded by Radbruch, not by Dworkin.
  • Fuller v the Radbruch formula (13.1). Both deny that enactment alone settles legality, but they test different things. Fuller tests form and grades it by degree, so an unclear statute is less a law. The Radbruch formula tests content and voids only intolerable injustice. Only the second is natural law in the sense the statement needs.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Who tests what?

Take one statute: clear, public, prospective and properly passed, but wicked in content.

TheoristWhat can make a rule fail as law?The wicked but well-made statute
Austin, HartNothing about its merit as such. For Hart's soft positivism, merit matters only if the rule of recognition happens to include a moral test.Law, unless the rule of recognition includes a moral test it fails.
FullerFailures of form, such as secrecy, retroactivity or unclarity.Law, because its form is fine.
DworkinNothing outside the legal record. The judge reads that record in its best light.The judge must still work with it. Integrity offers no exit.
Radbruch (weak NLT)Intolerable injustice.Not law, if the injustice is intolerable.

Only the last row says injustice as such can unmake law. That is why Fuller and Dworkin are allies, not members.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Fuller and Dworkin are natural law's allies, not natural lawyers in all but name, because neither lets injustice as such defeat a rule's validity. Fuller's is a thin, procedural natural law: his requirements of legality concern form and demand rules whether fair or unfair, so a clear, public and prospective law can still be wicked. Dworkin makes law interpretive, but his judge must interpret the legal history he finds, and integrity offers no exit from a wicked one. Both therefore leave intolerable injustice open, and it takes the Radbruch formula to guard that limit. "All but name" overstates.

72.5 Judges disagree?

🧩 Practise 2.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.5 Judges disagree? (word for word)
2.5 Judges disagree? only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
  1. [Judges only disagree about obeying] mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance: in Riggs all accepted the law's authority but split over what it required.
  2. In McLoughlin, too, the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether policy may limit liability (2.8; 9.2).
  3. So [no law to apply] assumes the plain-fact view, when which arguments count as law is the point in dispute.
  • Empirical disagreement asks whether agreed grounds of law are met; theoretical disagreement disputes the grounds themselves, which the plain-fact view and semantic theories hide.
  • For Dworkin, LP paints judges as "well-meaning liars" (pretence) or "simpletons" (borderline cases), yet these were "pivotal" cases.
  • QUALIFY Dworkin is arguably unfair to LP†: it need not make every disagreement empirical, and soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests.
  • LAWYER Counsel should run both policy arguments (9.2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two judges disagree about a will. A cynic says, "They both know what the law says. One just doesn't want to obey it." Dworkin says no. They both want to obey the law, but they disagree about what the law is, because they disagree about what makes something law in the first place.

What the statement claims

"When judges divide, they are never disagreeing about what the law is, only about whether to obey it. In Riggs v Palmer, the majority simply ignored the plain words of the statute of wills to deny a murderer his inheritance … once the precedents run out, the judge has no law to apply." (Q2)

The statement assumes that what the law is can always be looked up. So a judge who departs from the plain words must be defying the law, and a judge facing a novel case must be making law up. That is what Dworkin calls the plain-fact view. It is tempting because many legal disagreements really are about facts, or about whether to follow a rule everyone can see.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Splits between judges are often theoretical, not defiance. Dworkin separates two kinds of disagreement. Empirical disagreement accepts the grounds of law and asks whether they are met: was the statute passed, was it amended? Theoretical disagreement disputes the grounds themselves: does a statute carry exceptions it does not state? In Riggs every judge accepted that the law bound them. They split over what it required, which is a theoretical disagreement, not a quarrel about obedience.
  2. McLoughlin shows the same thing in the common law. All five Lords agreed that the mother should recover. But they split over whether courts may let policy, such as the fear of a flood of claims, limit liability (2.8; 9.2). A unanimous result hid a deep disagreement about what counts as a legal argument.
  3. So "no law to apply" assumes the very thing in dispute. The claim that law runs out when the precedents do follows only if law is just the written rules, which is the plain-fact view. Which arguments count as law, principles as well as rules, is exactly what the judges were arguing about.

The extra lines, explained

  • Two kinds of disagreement. Empirical disagreement asks whether agreed grounds of law are met. Theoretical disagreement disputes the grounds themselves. Dworkin argues that the plain-fact view and what he calls semantic theories hide the second kind. A semantic theory assumes lawyers share hidden criteria for using the word "law", so any apparent theoretical disagreement must be fake. Dworkin replies that if Earl and Gray really used different criteria, they would be talking past each other, like two people arguing about "banks" when one means riverbanks and the other means savings banks. Nobody thinks the judges in Riggs were doing that.
  • Well-meaning liars and simpletons. Dworkin says LP has two ways to explain away a case like Riggs, and both make judges look bad. The pretence defence says judges are really making new law while pretending to find it, which paints them as well-meaning liars. The borderline defence says they are only arguing over the edge of a word, like whether Buckingham Palace counts as a house, which paints them as simpletons. Yet these were pivotal cases, decided by serious judges who believed they were stating the law.
  • QUALIFY · Dworkin is arguably unfair to LP†. A positivist need not turn every disagreement into an empirical one. Soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests, so a positivist can explain a genuine dispute that turns on moral argument. Liu reads LP as a sociological account of which practice we label law, and Hart himself called his book descriptive sociology†. Use this to keep your answer honest. Dworkin beats the plain-fact view, but not necessarily every positivist.
  • LAWYER · run both policy arguments. Because judges split on whether policy may limit liability, counsel in a novel case should argue on both footings (9.2). Argue that drawing policy lines is for Parliament, not the court. Then argue, in the alternative, that even if the court does weigh policy, it does not defeat this claim.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Empirical or theoretical?
The disputeKindWhy
Was the statute of wills validly passed?EmpiricalEveryone agrees statutes are law. The question is whether this one exists.
Was it amended last year?EmpiricalSame grounds. It is a fact about the record.
Does the statute of wills let a murderer inherit, when it says nothing about murderers? (Riggs)TheoreticalIt disputes whether law is the bare text, or the text read with the common law's principles.
May a court deny a claim for reasons of policy, such as fear of a flood of claims? (McLoughlin)TheoreticalIt disputes whether policy is a legal ground for judges at all.
⚠ TRAP
Unanimous is not the same as plain

A 5–0 result can hide a theoretical split. In McLoughlin the Lords agreed on the outcome and divided on the reasons. Never cite a unanimous decision as proof that the law was plain.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance. In Riggs every judge accepted the law's authority, yet they split over what it required, because they disputed law's grounds, not whether to obey. McLoughlin shows the same in the common law: the Lords agreed on the result but divided over whether policy may limit liability. "No law to apply" therefore assumes the plain-fact view, when which arguments count as law is the very point in dispute. Dworkin is arguably unfair to positivism, since soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests. But he is right that these were disagreements about what the law is.

82.6 Theory useless?

🧩 Practise 2.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.6 Theory useless? (word for word)
2.6 Theory useless? luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes
  1. Fish grants [the statement] a kernel: Rawls cited in court will likely seem "window dressing" at best, showing off at worst.
  2. Yet marshalling rules is purposive: without a strong sense of the general project, rehearsing them is "an empty gesture" (Fish).
  3. So [theory is a luxury] confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9), hard cases on rival ones.
  • Jaffa Cakes† (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2), LON/91/160): the VAT tribunal used core attributes, class commonalities, thought experiments and social context, a philosophy of cakeness, and held them cakes (stale cakes harden, biscuits soften). Reasonable people agree on the factors but weigh them differently, the shape of most jurisprudential disputes†.
  • TSH: purpose may settle "vehicles", but contested words like "law" engage LP v NLT.
  • Leff†: judging whether a thing is done well requires knowing what is being done, so excellence presupposes theory.
  • AGAINST [Theory cannot help anyone decide] fails: disagreement is not absence of fact (4.7; Constitution: 11.7).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says, "You don't need to know what a cake is to decide whether a Jaffa Cake is a cake. Just look it up." But the tribunal that actually decided it had to work out what makes something a cake: what it is made of, how it goes stale, how people eat it. That is theory, done quietly.

What the statement claims

"Jurisprudence is an academic luxury … To decide whether Jaffa Cakes were cakes or biscuits for VAT purposes, the tribunal needed only the legislation, the case law and a good dictionary." (Q1)

The statement says theory is optional. Real disputes turn on what the statute and the cases say, and hard words are settled by a dictionary. It is tempting because practitioners almost never cite legal philosophers, and because most legal work feels like looking things up.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Fish grants the statement a kernel. Stanley Fish agrees that explicit theory rarely appears in practice. A barrister who cited Rawls in court would probably be seen as offering window dressing at best, and as showing off at worst.
  2. But practice has a purpose, so it uses theory all the time. Fish argues that marshalling rules takes place inside an enterprise with a point: a view of how the state may and may not use the force it monopolises. Without a strong sense of that general project, reciting rules is an empty gesture. Searle's football example makes the same point. Describe a game purely physically, as men running about and a chain on two sticks, and you miss the game entirely.
  3. So "theory is a luxury" confuses citing theory with using it. Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory (9.9). Hard cases are hard because they hold rival ones. Either way theory is at work, whether or not anyone names it.

The statement uses this case as its proof, and the case proves the opposite. The tribunal did not open a dictionary. It asked what makes a cake a cake and what makes a biscuit a biscuit, and it weighed several factors against each other. Liu's lesson from the case is that reasonable people agree on the relevant factors but weigh them differently†. That is the shape of most disputes in legal theory, including the dispute over what law is.

The extra lines, explained

  • The Jaffa Cakes case†. In United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2) the tribunal used the four standard philosophical moves (set out in the table below), in effect built a philosophy of cakeness, and held Jaffa Cakes to be cakes. Use it whenever a statement says a dictionary or the statute alone will do.
  • TSH · "vehicles" v "law". TSH accepts that a rule's purpose may settle an everyday word. A ban on vehicles in a park exists to keep the park safe and quiet, and that purpose can decide whether a child's slow toy car counts. But a contested word like "law" cannot be settled that way, because what law is for is the very question LP and NLT dispute.
  • Leff† · excellence needs a theory. Leff argues that you cannot judge whether a thing is done well until you know what is being done. So a claim that a lawyer's excellence is purely technical already assumes a view of what lawyering is for. Use this against any statement that praises "pure skill".
  • AGAINST · "theory cannot help anyone decide". Some statements say philosophers disagree endlessly, so theory is useless. But disagreement is not the absence of a fact (4.7). People once disputed how many planets there are, and there was still a right answer. Rival theories decided Riggs and McLoughlin. And a written Constitution does not end the need for theory either (11.7).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The four moves, applied to Jaffa Cakes
MoveWhat the tribunal looked at
Core attributesWhat the item is made of, its texture and its size.
Commonalities within a settled classHow it compares with things everyone already calls cakes, or biscuits.
Thought experimentWhat happens when it is left out and goes stale? Cakes go hard and biscuits go soft. This test weighed heavily.
Social contextIts name, packaging and marketing, and the usual way people eat it.

Practice Q11 asks you to run the same four moves on "vehicle" (an electric scooter, a tricycle, a war-memorial tank). Running them on "law" is what this archetype is about.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is right that practitioners rarely cite theory: as Fish grants, Rawls cited in court would likely seem window dressing at best and showing off at worst. But marshalling rules is purposive, and without a strong sense of the general project, rehearsing them is an empty gesture. The statement's own example backfires. The Jaffa Cakes tribunal did not use a dictionary. It weighed core attributes, comparisons, thought experiments and social context, an indirect philosophy of cakeness. "Theory is a luxury" therefore confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory, and hard cases on rival ones.

92.7 Singapore pragmatism

🧩 Practise 2.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.7 Singapore pragmatism (word for word)
2.7 Singapore pragmatism prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
  1. [Singapore's prevailing philosophy] is often called pragmatism: keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach pragmatic, preserving social cohesion.
  2. Yet pragmatism is itself a theory: in any postmodern pragmatic society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" guiding principles (TSH).
  3. So [philosophy is unnecessary here] fails: theory exists to guide practice, and in law as in life the question of right and wrong cannot be shunned (TSH).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Calling yourself "practical, not philosophical" is like saying "I don't have an accent". Everyone speaks with some accent. You just don't notice your own. Pragmatism is a philosophy too.

What the statement claims

"Singapore's prevailing philosophy is pragmatism: we have no use for legal theory here."

The statement takes a common description of Singapore, a country that prides itself on doing what works, and draws a conclusion from it: theory is unnecessary. It is tempting because Singapore's leaders really do describe their approach as pragmatic, and because "what works" sounds free of philosophy.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The label fits, and the Government used it. When Parliament kept s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach pragmatic, one that preserved social cohesion. So the premise of the statement is fair. Pragmatism is often called Singapore's prevailing philosophy.
  2. But pragmatism is itself a theory. TSH argues that in any postmodern pragmatic society, the view that law is whatever a court says glosses over the principles that actually guide decisions. Calling a choice pragmatic does not remove the principles behind it. It only hides them.
  3. So "philosophy is unnecessary here" fails. TSH holds that theory exists to guide practice, and that in law, as in life, the question of right and wrong cannot be avoided. A pragmatic decision still has to choose what counts as working, and that choice is a moral one.

The 2007 debate, explained

The 2007 debate is the best illustration of line 2. The Government presented keeping s 377A, without proactively enforcing it, as a pragmatic balance. PM Lee added that Singapore was not starting from a blank slate, so the question was whether to change an existing law, not whether to enact it afresh. That is a reason for caution about change, which is itself a principle about how law should develop.

TSH then shows that "social cohesion" did no real work. Those who wanted to keep the law used it to mean the legitimacy of acting on majority norms. Those who wanted repeal used it to mean respect for minority rights. The same practical word carried two opposed moral views. In TSH's reading, both arguments really turned on one moral question: whether the conduct was wrong, or whether there was a right to it. That is why she concludes that the question of right and wrong cannot be shunned. Archetype 7 takes this debate further (Lesson 7).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Singapore's prevailing philosophy is often called pragmatism: in keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government described its approach as pragmatic, preserving social cohesion. Yet pragmatism is itself a theory. As TSH argues, in any postmodern pragmatic society the view that law is whatever a court says glosses over the principles that guide decisions. The 2007 debate shows it: both sides invoked social cohesion, but one side meant majority norms and the other minority rights, so the real question was moral. The statement therefore fails. Theory exists to guide practice, and in law, as in life, the question of right and wrong cannot be shunned.

102.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin

🧩 Practise 2.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin (word for word)
2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin
  1. Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions; McLoughlin, on whether policy may distinguish precedent.
  2. Each answer presupposes a theory of [law].
  • Riggs v Palmer: Elmer, 16, poisoned his grandfather lest he revoke the will; read literally, the statute of wills let him inherit. Held 5–2 that he took nothing. Earl relied on intention and on maxims founded in "universal law", and said this took no property from Elmer; Gray, dissenting, put the question outside conscience's domain and said courts cannot add to the respondent's penalties.
  • McLoughlin v O'Brian: not at the scene, she saw her injured family, begrimed, in hospital hours later, and a daughter died. Held 5–0, reversing the CA, that her shock was recoverable. Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell let policy limit liability, but not here; Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable"; Bridge called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication".
  • LP reads Riggs as Gray's posited text†, or Earl's maxim as posited common law with moral content†, or as a gap for discretion. In McLoughlin the CA, as Dworkin reads it, found no law once precedent ran out and filled the gap by policy.
  • Dworkin reads Riggs as two morally grounded theories: Gray's guards a principle of justice (fixed penalties); Earl's guards coherence. In McLoughlin precedent's force was disputed: Scarman thought himself bound by principles embedded in the precedents.
  • ALR: rules are fitted to results reached on other grounds (Riggs) and reasons follow results; yet reasons split a unanimous House (McLoughlin).
  • Riggs bears two readings†, and neither need be chosen: (a) both sides argued about law, the majority's including common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates; (b) the dispute was whether law is always subject to universal moral principles, as Earl's "universal law" suggests. Neither side kept to the statute's four corners†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Riggs: a teenager poisons his grandfather to get the inheritance sooner. The law about wills, read literally, says he inherits. Should a court read in an unwritten exception? McLoughlin: a mother rushes to hospital and sees her family horribly injured. Earlier cases only covered people at the scene of the accident. Can she sue for the shock? Both cases ask what counts as the law when the written rules don't clearly answer.

What the question asks

"A testator leaves his estate to his nephew. The nephew, impatient for his inheritance, kills the testator and is convicted of the killing. The relevant succession statute says only that a validly executed will 'shall take effect according to its terms'. Write two short judgments … one allowing the nephew to inherit and one denying him the inheritance, each faithful to a different conception of what law is." (Q10)

These cards are the evidence for every block above. Q10 is Riggs in disguise. It asks you to do what the judges in Riggs did: build the law from the same words using two different theories of what law is.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The two cases raise different questions. Riggs asks whether a clear statute has exceptions it does not state. McLoughlin asks whether policy may be used to distinguish precedent, that is, to refuse to extend earlier cases to new facts.
  2. Each answer presupposes a theory of law. If law is the bare text, Elmer inherits. If law is the text read with the common law's principles, he does not. If law is only the rules of past cases, the mother in McLoughlin falls outside them and the court must fill a gap. If the principles embedded in those cases are law too, there was law to apply.

Riggs v Palmer

The facts are in the picture near the start of this lesson. Elmer, aged 16, poisoned his grandfather to stop him revoking the will. Read literally, New York's statute of wills let Elmer inherit.

  • Held. By 5 to 2, Elmer took nothing.
  • Majority (Earl J). Statutes are read by what their makers intended, and in the light of the common law's maxims, which Earl said were founded in universal law. The legislature could not have meant a murderer to benefit, and no one may profit from his own wrong. Earl added that denying the inheritance took no property from Elmer. It only stopped him acquiring property by his crime.
  • Dissent (Gray J). Gray held that the question lay outside the domain of conscience. The statute set out exactly how a will may be altered or revoked, and murder was not among them. Stripping Elmer of the inheritance would add to the penalties the criminal law had already fixed, which a court may not do.

McLoughlin v O'Brian

  • Held. The House of Lords was unanimous, reversing the Court of Appeal: her shock was recoverable.
  • The reasons split. Lords Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell held that policy may limit liability, but not on these facts. Lord Scarman held that where to draw a policy line is not justiciable. It is for Parliament, and judges should stick to principle. Lord Bridge said that refusing to go beyond the decided cases would be an unwarranted abdication.
  • Why the Court of Appeal used policy. It feared a flood of claims, fraudulent claims, higher insurance costs and harder proof. These are the community's collective goals, which is what "policy" means in distinction 1.3(8).

Three ways to read the cases

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
One case, three theories
TheoryRiggsMcLoughlin
LPGray's reading follows the posited text†. Or Earl's maxim is itself posited common law with moral content†. Or the statute was silent, leaving a gap for the judge's discretion.As Dworkin reads it, the Court of Appeal found no law once precedent ran out, and filled the gap with policy.
DworkinTwo morally grounded theories of the statute. Gray's protects a principle of justice: penalties are fixed in advance. Earl's protects the coherence of the law as a whole.The force of precedent was itself disputed. Scarman thought himself bound by principles embedded in the precedents, so there was law to apply.
ALR (American legal realism)Rules are fitted to results reached on other grounds. The judges chose the outcome, then found a rule to fit it.Reasons follow results. Yet here the reasons split a unanimous House, which is awkward for the realist.

You rarely need all three rows. Pick the row that answers the statement in front of you, and use the others as rivals.

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID
Two readings of Riggs, and neither need be chosen

Liu offers two readings of Riggs and does not pick one†. On reading (a), both sides argued about law, and the majority's law included common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates how deep the disagreement went. On reading (b), the real dispute was whether law is always subject to universal moral principles, as Earl's appeal to universal law suggests. On either reading, neither side kept to the four corners of the statute†. Gray's dissent, too, rested on a moral principle about fixed penalties.

⚠ TRAP
Two different Grays

Gray J, who dissented in Riggs, is not J C Gray, the American legal realist who said law is the rules laid down by courts. Keep them apart in your answer.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Riggs and McLoughlin show that hard cases turn on a theory of law. In Riggs all agreed that the statute of wills, read literally, let Elmer inherit, yet the court held by 5 to 2 that he took nothing. Earl relied on legislative intention and on maxims founded in universal law, while Gray held the question lay outside conscience and that courts cannot add to a wrongdoer's penalties. Dworkin reads these as two morally grounded theories of the statute, one protecting coherence and the other fixed penalties. In McLoughlin the Lords were unanimous in result but split over whether policy may limit liability, Scarman holding line-drawing policy not justiciable and Bridge calling a halt at the decided cases an unwarranted abdication. Each answer presupposed a view of what law is.

11Putting it together: Practice Q2

"When judges divide, they are never disagreeing about what the law is, only about whether to obey it. In Riggs v Palmer, the majority simply ignored the plain words of the statute of wills to deny a murderer his inheritance, and in doing so usurped the legislature. Novel cases such as McLoughlin v O'Brien are different: once the precedents run out, the judge has no law to apply and should openly weigh the community's social and economic goals, including the risk of opening the floodgates."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Dworkin, legal positivism and natural law theory.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

Everything turns on "simply". The statement assumes that the plain words of a statute simply are the law, so that a court reading in an exception defies it. That is the plain-fact view, and it is the very point the judges in Riggs disputed. I make three claims. First, judicial splits are often theoretical disagreements about law's grounds, not quarrels about obedience. Second, the Riggs majority did not usurp the legislature but read the statute by its makers' intention and the common law's maxims. Third, when precedent runs out, the judge still has law to apply, namely principle, and, as I argue with Scarman, open policy-weighing is the real threat to the legislature's role.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Dworkin's theoretical disagreement (2.5). The Riggs judges all accepted the law's authority and split on what it required. Steelman for LP: soft positivism can absorb moral tests, so Dworkin is arguably unfair to positivism†.
  2. Riggs (2.8). Earl's intention and maxims against Gray's fixed penalties, two morally grounded theories on Dworkin's reading. Earl's maxim is itself posited common law†, so "simply ignored" overstates.
  3. McLoughlin and floodgates (9.2). All five Lords allowed recovery, but Scarman held line-drawing policy not justiciable while Bridge called stopping at decided cases an unwarranted abdication. The statement's own advice, to weigh social goals openly, is exactly Scarman's target, so it hands the legislature's work to judges more than the Riggs majority did. Flag that this is Scarman's view, which Edmund-Davies called novel and startling, and defend it as a choice, not as the case's lesson (9.2). Self-critique: Dworkin's fit is often not unique (1.4).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore wrong in its premise and in its advice. Judges divide over what the law is, not only over whether to obey it, and the Riggs majority read the law rather than defied it. When precedent runs out, a court still argues from principle. On Scarman's view, which I defend as a choice, it is open weighing of social goals, not reading in a maxim, that would hand the legislature's work to judges.

12Recap

Archetype 2 on one card
▤ Sections 2.1–2.8
  1. 1Naming law is an evaluation. LP is coherent, but making official recognition decisive is a choice (2.1).
  2. 2Hart's internal "ought" marks a standard, accepted even from fear or self-interest. It is not a moral verdict (2.2).
  3. 3Natural law is reasoned, not revealed, and weak NLT bites only at extreme injustice (2.3).
  4. 4Fuller and Dworkin are natural law's allies, not members: neither lets injustice as such unmake law (2.4).
  5. 5Judges disagree theoretically, about law's grounds, not only about whether to obey (2.5).
  6. 6Theory is used even when it is not cited: Fish, Leff and the Jaffa Cakes tribunal (2.6).
  7. 7Pragmatism is itself a theory, and it hides its principles (2.7).
  8. 8Riggs and McLoughlin are the evidence: same words or same result, rival theories (2.8).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture the Riggs courtroom. Earl and Gray sit at one table, reading the same page of the statute of wills, and neither of them wants to defy it. The only thing they argue about is what else belongs on the table: the statute alone, or the statute together with the common law's maxims. Choosing what goes on the table is the theory. Every statement in this archetype pretends the table sets itself.
