LESSON 3 · ARCHETYPE 3 · ABOUT 67 MIN · 8 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 47 QUESTIONS

Rule of law and Fuller

⚡ BIG IDEA

The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee that the laws it governs are just.

ARCHETYPE 3 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
3 Rule of law and Fuller
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The rule of law] is a real but thin morality: it binds rulers and comes in degrees, but cannot guarantee [just laws].
Intro [The statement] treats legality as [mere efficiency / a guarantee of justice]. For Fuller, total failure of one requirement leaves no legal system at all; otherwise legality is a matter of degree. I [agree only in part]: legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims to criticism, but cannot make bad laws just.
Steelman: legality is not moral The best case for [the statement] is that a tyrant could meet every requirement, so the label "morality" seems misapplied, the real concern being efficacy†. This shows that legality is thin. It does not show [that it is morally empty]: it binds the ruler too and treats subjects as responsible agents.
Steelman: legality is enough The best case for [the statement] is that law drags the monster into the light†: a regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern. This shows that even thin legality protects. It does not show [that it guarantees justice]: rules also legitimise and spread evil ("it's the law")†.
3.1 Ranking rank them; not all equally important
  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule, so I rank [prospectivity in crime] first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned"; non-enforcement of [s 377A] strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches compound, as unclarity may force retroactive laws, so low rank never licenses neglect.
  • Requirements can conflict, as curative retroactivity shows†.
3.2 Unenforced law sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost
  1. [A sham] overstates: open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. For TSH the 2007 "overt announcement" breached Fuller's requirement but showcased a competing value, the symbolic message.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95† does for slight harm.
  • STEELMAN Perera: non-enforcement gives the Government and the AGC too much power (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022).
  • Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)†: the AG's 2018 assurance bound the AG until clear notice (7.7). Before the decision, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule (pure divergence), and as discretion it hit generality; after it, officials' statements can silently change the law†.
  • CONCEDE TSH is harsher (breach, not strain): I concede the breach and defend only the trade-off.
3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails
  1. [A tyrant could follow it] is half right: legality is moral but thin; at minimum it demands rules, whether fair or unfair.
  2. It is moral because reciprocity grounds the duty, it treats people as responsible agents†, and it binds even a self-seeking monarch.
  3. So [legality guarantees justice] fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules†; intolerable injustice needs the RF (8.3).
  • AGAINST Inner and outer morality decay together almost inevitably (Fuller).
  • A single secret or retroactive rule grounds no moral duty; an unclear one is "less a law"; validity is for the RF (8).
3.4 Discretion rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics
  1. [Every grant of discretion is a small surrender] overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute as undermined by uncontrolled administrative discretion; [enforcement only against critics] approaches it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if bounded by law and reviewable.
  • JUDGE The court reviews legality, not merits: Art 35(8)† discretion is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†).
  • Discretion erodes generality by degree†: principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not.
3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
  1. Mandatory sentences look like [the purest expression of the rule of law], but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Hart's justice in administering the law treats like cases alike by any standard of "like", however elevated or perverted (Fuller).
  3. So [leaving nothing to judges] is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.
3.6 Rules v standards same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules
  1. Holding [a learner driver] to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma; by analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity can justify it, never in crime.
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is at times harsh, intimate justice cannot be even-handed, so law tempers the reasonable man.
  3. So [clear rules are always better] overstates: "good faith" standards can clarify; specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness.
  • Nettleship v Weston†: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard; Cook v Cook† lowered it where the passenger knew (overruled: Imbree v McNeilly, 2008†).
3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will
  1. [The duty springs from authority] is the command view, which confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority.
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty: once government ruptures it finally and completely, the citizen's duty has no ground left.
  3. So [goodwill] cannot suffice: no single centre of intelligence and goodwill can secure law's enterprise.
  • Where officials disregard rules, obedience at some point becomes futile, like casting a vote that will never be counted.
  • AGAINST [Majority will, accurately expressed]: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments.
  • QUALIFY In a crisis "grim necessity" may justify a secret weapons appropriation, but no emergency justifies a secret law creating a new crime (Fuller).
3.8 Judge-made law never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so [can never fully satisfy] holds in form, though a new rule may only confirm views already widely held.
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is [a price worth paying]: prospective rulings remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent.
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave people "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation.
  • Abdul Nasir† (CA 1997): life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only (8.6); it engages constancy, not branding as criminals.
3.9 Thin v thick; Marx ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials
  1. [A slogan] for class power overstates: legal form binds rulers too, since law cannot be "built on law".
  2. Against the Marxist†, law has its own character: it applies legal criteria by standards of universality and equity (crits: 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats [the whims of its officials]: published rules give notice and invite criticism.
Conclusion [The statement] is [right only in part]. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents, exposes aims to criticism and comes in degrees, so [not a legal system at all] needs total failure. But it is thin and cannot guarantee just laws: intolerable injustice is the Radbruch formula's work.

1Start here: archetype 3 in plain English

Archetype 3 is about the rule of law: governing through proper rules, not through the whims of whoever holds power. The course's guide is Lon Fuller. Fuller says law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, and that it only works if the rules are general, published, forward-looking, clear, consistent, possible to obey, reasonably stable, and actually applied by officials. He calls these eight requirements law's inner morality.

Exam statements in this family push one of two extremes. Some say legality is mere efficiency, a set of drafting tips a tyrant could follow, or a slogan the powerful use to look respectable. Others say legality is a guarantee of justice. Many take one practical issue, such as an unenforced law, discretion, mandatory sentences, judge-made law or the duty to obey, and treat it as wholly good or wholly bad.

Your answer is the same every time. The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It is real because it binds the rulers who make the rules and lets citizens plan their lives. It is thin because it concerns the form of law, not its content, so a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. And it comes in degrees: only a total failure of one requirement means there is no legal system at all.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Legality / the rule of lawGoverning through rules that people can know and follow, and that officials actually keep to.
DesiderataFuller's word for his eight requirements. A desideratum is something wanted.
Inner v external moralityInner morality is the eight requirements of form. External morality is the justice of a law's content.
Thin v thickA thin rule of law asks only for good form. A thick one also demands just content. Your Position treats it as thin.
Matter of degreeA system can be more or less legal. Only the total failure of one requirement means no legal system at all.
ReciprocityA two-way deal: here are the rules, and we will judge you by them. The duty to obey rests on the government keeping its side.
CongruenceFuller's eighth requirement: officials act on the rules as announced. Openly not enforcing a law is a congruence problem.
Prospective v retrospectiveA prospective rule governs the future. A retrospective (retroactive) rule changes the legal effect of acts already done.
Command viewLaw is whatever those in power order, so we obey their authority. Fuller says it confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority.
Radbruch formula (RF)The test in Lesson 8. It denies legal character only to intolerably unjust statutes. It tests content, which Fuller does not.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee just laws.

Put simply, following Fuller's eight requirements really does matter morally. A government that rules through clear, public, forward-looking rules has to keep to them itself, and its citizens know where they stand. But the requirements say nothing about what a law commands, so a published, general statute can still strip a minority of its homes. Never let a statement call legality empty, and never let it call legality a guarantee of justice.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement treats legality either as mere efficiency or as a guarantee of justice. For Fuller, the total failure of one requirement leaves no legal system at all, and anything less is a matter of degree. You agree only in part: legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims to criticism, but it cannot make bad laws just.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. The statement is right only in part. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents, exposes aims to criticism and comes in degrees, so "not a legal system at all" needs a total failure. But legality is thin and cannot guarantee just laws. Intolerable injustice is the Radbruch formula's work (8.3), not Fuller's.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before answering it. Section 3 gives you two, one for each extreme.

  • Steelman: legality is not moral. A tyrant could meet every one of Fuller's requirements, publishing clear, general, prospective rules for wicked ends. If so, the label "morality" seems misapplied, and the real concern is efficacy, as sharpness is a virtue of a knife whatever it cuts†. This shows that legality is thin. It does not show that legality is morally empty, because it binds the ruler too and treats subjects as responsible agents. Use it when the statement says Fuller's morality is neither inner nor moral.
  • Steelman: legality is enough. Law drags the monster into the light†. A regime that writes its aims into published rules nails its colours to the mast, so citizens can criticise it, organise against it, or flee. Arbitrary power shows no pattern. This shows that even thin legality protects people. It does not show that legality guarantees justice, because rules also legitimise and spread evil: people carry out a wicked rule because "it's the law"†. Use it when the statement says being ruled by law is enough. The same point answers statements that call published persecution no better than whims (3.9).

The nine blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
3.1"Rank Fuller's eight requirements."Priority depends on the branch of law. In crime, prospectivity comes first and congruence for one rule comes last. But breaches compound.
3.2"An unenforced law is a sham: enforce it or repeal it."It strains congruence, but one rule survives. The law can openly exempt trivial cases instead.
3.3"Fuller's morality isn't moral. A tyrant could follow it."Half right. Legality is thin, but it is moral: reciprocity, respect for agents, and it binds the ruler. It still cannot guarantee justice.
3.4"Every grant of discretion surrenders the rule of law."Only uncontrolled discretion does. Discretion bounded by law and reviewable by courts fits legality.
3.5"Mandatory sentences are the purest rule of law."They buy certainty, not justice. Treating like cases alike is fair only if the line tracks real differences.
3.6"Hold everyone to the same standard. Clear rules always win."Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma: a civil surcharge, never in crime. Honest vagueness can beat false clarity.
3.7"We obey because the state has authority."That is the command view. The duty rests on reciprocity, and only a complete rupture ends it.
3.8"Judge-made law is never prospective."True in form. A fair price in civil cases. Crime differs.
3.9"The rule of law is a class slogan."Legal form binds rulers too. Published rules give notice and invite criticism, which beats whims.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Legality is real but thin: it binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it is not justice.

2The big picture: Fuller's inner morality of law

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a king who wants to rule by law but gets everything wrong. He decides each case on a whim. He keeps his rulebook secret. He punishes people for things that were allowed yesterday. He writes rules nobody can understand, rules that contradict each other, and rules nobody could obey, and he changes them every day. And when he sits as judge, he ignores his own rules anyway. His subjects can't follow anything. Fuller says that is not a bad legal system. It is not a legal system at all.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
FullerLaw is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight requirements. Failing them is a matter of degree. Fuller's strongest point is that legality binds law-makers first: the higher you sit in the chain of command, the heavier your duty to make clear, workable law.
King RexFuller's imaginary king. Rex means well, but he fails to make law in eight ways, one for each requirement, and never makes a single law.
HartThe positivist. A rule is valid if it passes the test officials accept, however poorly it meets Fuller's requirements (13.1). The objection that Fuller's "morality" is really efficacy is usually linked to Hart.
TSH (Tan Seow Hon)Says the 2007 announcement that s 377A would not be proactively enforced breached Fuller's congruence requirement, but showcased a competing value, the law's symbolic message (3.2).
Liu (lectures)Adds four things: three clarifications to Fuller's list (see the trap below), the monster into the light argument, a reading of Tan Seng Kee, and the point that discretion erodes generality by degree†.
The MarxistLaw is the ruling class's instrument, dressed in the language of universality and equity. The reply: law has a character of its own (3.9).
Radbruch formulaTests a statute's content, and denies legal character only to intolerable injustice (8.3). Fuller tests form.

Fuller's eight requirements

Fuller's eight requirements
▤ Framework 15.1: can people follow this rule as made and applied?
  1. 1General: there must be rules at all, not case-by-case rulings.
  2. 2Promulgated: the rules must be published, so people can get at them.
  3. 3Prospective: rules govern the future, not acts already done.
  4. 4Clear: people can understand them.
  5. 5Consistent: they do not contradict each other.
  6. 6Possible: they do not demand the impossible.
  7. 7Constant: they do not change too often.
  8. 8Congruent: officials act on the rules as announced.

Key distinctions

  • Total failure v matter of degree. If one requirement fails completely, as with Rex, the result is no legal system at all. Anything less is a question of degree. This defeats any statement that calls a flawed system "not a legal system at all".
  • The system v a single rule. The degree point is about whole systems. A single secret or retroactive rule grounds no moral duty to obey, and an unclear rule is less a law than a clear one. Whether such a rule is still valid is a separate question, for the Radbruch formula (Lesson 8).
  • Form v content (distinction 1.3(13)). Fuller tests form: can people follow this rule as made and applied? The Radbruch formula tests content, and for courts TSH adds her strike-down test (15.13). As 13.1 puts it, both deny that enactment alone settles legality, but they test different things.
  • Fidelity to law v deference to authority. Fidelity is respect for a working system of rules. Deference is loyalty to whoever holds power. Rex's subjects stayed loyal to Rex as king, but could not be faithful to his law, because he never made any (3.7).

King Rex's eight ways to fail

Rex's story shows that good aims cannot replace rules people can follow, and that the total failure of any one requirement is enough. Rex did not need to fail all eight.

⚠ TRAP
Three easy mistakes about the list

These come from the TRAP line in framework 15.1†.

  • Generality means having rules at all, not broad rules. Palm-tree justice (a wise elder deciding each case on its merits), bills of attainder (laws aimed at named people) and unfettered discretion fail it.
  • Promulgation needs access, not universal knowledge. Nobody reads every statute.
  • Prospectivity bars only the abuse of retroactive laws. A law that cures an earlier failure of form can be fine (3.1).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is Singapore "not a legal system at all"? The checklist on Q13

Q13 lists four flaws and concludes that Singapore "is not a legal system at all".

The chargeRequirementTotal failure, or degree?
Ministers' "unfettered" discretionGeneralityDegree. Bounded, reviewable discretion fits legality (3.4).
"Life imprisonment" redefinedConstancyDegree. Abdul Nasir applied the new reading only to future cases (3.8).
Judges announce rules after the eventsProspectivityIn form only, and a fair price in civil cases (3.8).
A learner driver held to the ordinary standardPossibilityDegree. A civil surcharge, though never in crime (3.6).

Each charge is at most a partial failure, so the conclusion does not follow. Breaches do compound (3.1), but "not a legal system at all" needs a Rex.

33.1 Ranking

🧩 Practise 3.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.1 Ranking (word for word)
3.1 Ranking rank them; not all equally important
  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule, so I rank [prospectivity in crime] first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned"; non-enforcement of [s 377A] strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches compound, as unclarity may force retroactive laws, so low rank never licenses neglect.
  • Requirements can conflict, as curative retroactivity shows†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If you had to give up one of Fuller's eight requirements, which would hurt least? Fuller says it depends on the area of law. In criminal law, punishing someone for an act that was lawful when they did it is the worst failure of all. One rule that the police quietly stop enforcing is bad but survivable. But beware: one failure tends to cause another, so "least important" never means "safe to ignore".

What the statement claims

"Fuller says his eight requirements are not all equally important. Rank them in order of importance and justify your ranking. Use at least one Singapore illustration to support your placement of the requirement you rank first and the one you rank last." (Q27)

This short-answer question seems to invite a fixed league table. That is the trap. Fuller refuses to rank the eight once and for all, so a good answer says which branch of law its ranking is for, and ends with a warning.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Fuller lets the ranking change with the area of law, so pick one. Priority varies with the branch of law and the kind of rule. In criminal law, rank prospectivity first: the state must not punish people for acts that were lawful when they did them.
  2. Put prospectivity in crime at the top and congruence for one rule at the bottom. Fuller says the retrospective criminal statute is universally condemned. At the other end, Singapore's open non-enforcement of s 377A after 2007 strained congruence, the match between a rule and what officials do, but the legal system still stood. So congruence for a single rule ranks last.
  3. But a low rank never means the requirement can be neglected. Breaches compound. An unclear law may later force the legislature to pass a retroactive law to sort out the confusion, so one weak requirement can drag a strong one down.

The extra line, explained

  • Requirements can conflict†. The standard example is the curative retroactive statute. Fuller imagines marriages made void because the printing office ran out of the state stamps the law required. A retroactive statute validating them breaks prospectivity, but repairs earlier failures of promulgation and possibility. "Curative" is no blank cheque, though: after the 1934 Röhm purge, a retroactive statute turned killings into lawful executions, which cured nothing. As card 14.6 says, balancing the eight takes a lawgiver's skill (14.6).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Fuller accepts that his requirements are not equally important and that their priority varies with the branch of law and the kind of rule, so I rank them for criminal law. Prospectivity comes first, because Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute universally condemned. Congruence for a single rule comes last: Singapore's open non-enforcement of s 377A after 2007 strained the match between rule and practice, yet the legal system still stood. But a low rank never licenses neglect, because breaches compound. Unclear law may later force a retroactive fix, so one weak requirement can pull down a strong one.

43.2 Unenforced law

🧩 Practise 3.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.2 Unenforced law (word for word)
3.2 Unenforced law sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost
  1. [A sham] overstates: open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. For TSH the 2007 "overt announcement" breached Fuller's requirement but showcased a competing value, the symbolic message.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95† does for slight harm.
  • STEELMAN Perera: non-enforcement gives the Government and the AGC too much power (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022).
  • Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)†: the AG's 2018 assurance bound the AG until clear notice (7.7). Before the decision, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule (pure divergence), and as discretion it hit generality; after it, officials' statements can silently change the law†.
  • CONCEDE TSH is harsher (breach, not strain): I concede the breach and defend only the trade-off.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sign in a park says "No ball games", but the park warden openly says he will never enforce it. Is the sign a sham? Not entirely, because it still says something about what the park wants. But the gap between what the rule says and what the officials do is a real cost. Fuller calls it a failure of congruence.

What the statement claims

"A law that the state openly declines to enforce is a sham. Keeping s 377A on the books while the Attorney-General disclaimed proactive prosecution made a mockery of the rule of law, no different from the old offence of 'imagining' the death of the President. If conduct is wrong enough to be made a crime, it must either be enforced fully or be repealed, because the criminal law is not a moral signpost." (Q14)

The statement offers only two choices: enforce the law fully, or repeal it. It assumes that a law has value only if it is enforced, so that any gap between the law on the books and what officials do turns the law into a sham. It is tempting because the gap really is a problem, and the comparison with the "imagining" offence makes the gap look worse than it is.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Calling the law a sham overstates. Openly not enforcing a law strains congruence, Fuller's requirement that officials act on the rules as announced. But congruence failing for one rule is very different from congruence failing across a system. One rule that is rarely enforced does not bring a legal system down.
  2. TSH sees a trade-off, not a sham. Tan Seow Hon says the 2007 overt announcement that s 377A would not be proactively enforced did breach Fuller's requirement. But it also showcased a competing value, the law's symbolic message. Keeping the offence while not enforcing it was a choice between two values, not an empty gesture.
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark. There is a third path. The law itself can openly exempt trivial cases, as s 95 of the Penal Code does for slight harm†. When the exemption is written into the law, the rule and the practice match again.

The extra lines, explained

  • STEELMAN · Perera's warning. In the 2022 repeal debate, Perera argued that non-enforcement gives the Government and the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) too much power. A law that stays on the books, but is used only when officials choose, hands them a weapon. This is the best case for "enforce or repeal", and it links to discretion (3.4).
  • Tan Seng Kee and Liu's before-and-after. In Tan Seng Kee (Court of Appeal, 2022) the court held that the Attorney-General's 2018 assurance bound the AG until he gave clear notice otherwise (7.7). Liu splits the analysis at that decision†. Before it, non-enforcement was only what officials did, not a rule, so there was a pure divergence between rule and practice. Treated as prosecutorial discretion, it also hit generality, since the law in practice applied to some people and not others. After the decision a new problem appears: officials' statements can silently change the law, without any amendment that a citizen could read.
  • CONCEDE · TSH calls it a breach. TSH is harsher than line 1. She calls the announcement a breach of Fuller's requirement, not merely a strain on it. Concede the breach. Then defend only the trade-off: the symbolic message may be worth the cost, and the cost falls short of a sham.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
"No different from the old 'imagining' offence"?

Q14 compares s 377A with the old Penal Code s 121A, in force before 2019, which punished imagining the President's death, hurt or restraint with death or life imprisonment. Liu uses s 121A as an example of congruence and discretion problems†.

s 121A (imagining)s 377A after 2007
What the rule targetsA thought, which no official can observeConduct
Can it be applied evenly?No. It can only be enforced by arbitrary meansYes, but officials openly chose not to enforce it proactively
CongruenceGuaranteed to fail, whatever officials intendStrained for one rule, by an open choice

So "no different" overstates. s 121A is the clearest kind of congruence failure, a rule that could never be properly applied. s 377A's announced non-enforcement is a milder and open gap.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Calling s 377A a sham overstates. Open non-enforcement strained congruence, Fuller's requirement that officials act on the rules as announced, but one rule that is rarely enforced does not bring down a legal system. TSH accepts that the 2007 overt announcement breached Fuller's requirement, yet she shows that it served a competing value, the law's symbolic message. I concede the breach and defend only the trade-off. The strongest objection is Perera's: an unenforced law leaves too much power with the Government and the prosecutors. But the answer is not the stark choice between full enforcement and repeal, since the law can openly exempt what it does not mean to punish, as s 95 does for slight harm.

53.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral)

🧩 Practise 3.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) (word for word)
3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails
  1. [A tyrant could follow it] is half right: legality is moral but thin; at minimum it demands rules, whether fair or unfair.
  2. It is moral because reciprocity grounds the duty, it treats people as responsible agents†, and it binds even a self-seeking monarch.
  3. So [legality guarantees justice] fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules†; intolerable injustice needs the RF (8.3).
  • AGAINST Inner and outer morality decay together almost inevitably (Fuller).
  • A single secret or retroactive rule grounds no moral duty; an unclear one is "less a law"; validity is for the RF (8).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Could a cruel dictator follow all eight of Fuller's rules? Probably yes. He could publish clear, general, forward-looking laws that are evil. So legality is not the same as justice. But following the eight rules still does something good. It lets people know where they stand and plan their lives, it treats them as adults who can choose whether to obey, and it ties the dictator to his own published rules.

What the statement claims

"Fuller's 'inner morality of law' is neither inner nor moral. It is a recipe for efficient governance that a tyrant could follow as faithfully as a democrat." (Q20)

The statement makes two charges. The first is that the eight requirements are about efficiency, not right and wrong. That is the steelman legality is not moral. The second is that, because a tyrant could follow them, legality cannot tell good regimes from bad ones. The opposite statement, that legality guarantees justice, is answered by the same block.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "A tyrant could follow it" is half right. Legality is moral but thin. At a minimum it demands that there be rules, whether those rules are fair or unfair. So in principle a tyrant could publish clear, general, prospective rules for wicked ends, and the checklist would have nothing to say against them.
  2. But legality is still moral, for three reasons. First, reciprocity grounds the citizen's duty to obey: the government asks citizens to follow its rules and promises to judge them by those rules. Second, ruling through rules treats people as responsible agents†. They are told the consequences in advance and can decide whether to comply. Third, legality binds even a self-seeking monarch. Fuller's fable of a selfish king who never checks who obeyed, or who words his commands so vaguely that nobody knows what he wants, shows that such a ruler makes no law at all, not even bad law. Whatever his aims, a ruler who wants to govern through law must accept its inner morality and keep to the rules he announces.
  3. So "legality guarantees justice" fails as well. Wicked aims can run through clear, public rules†. When a law's content is intolerably unjust, the right tool is not Fuller's checklist but the Radbruch formula (8.3).

The extra lines, explained

  • STEELMAN (section-level) · efficacy. The best case for the statement is the first steelman above. If a tyrant could meet every requirement, the word "morality" seems misapplied, and the real concern is efficacy†. Card 14.6 gives the reply: legality respects responsible agents and grounds the duty to obey by reciprocity.
  • AGAINST · inner and outer morality decay together. Fuller argues that the two moralities are linked in practice. A decline in one almost inevitably produces a decline in the other. Wicked regimes find legality inconvenient, because they need secret directives, retroactive statutes and vague powers. So a tyrant could follow all eight in theory, but tyrants rarely do in practice.
  • A single rule. The block also covers statements about one rule rather than a whole system. A single secret or retroactive rule grounds no moral duty to obey, because nobody could have followed it. Fuller calls the secret statute the greatest legal monstrosity (14.6). An unclear rule is, in Fuller's phrase, less a law than a clear one. But whether such a rule is still valid law is the Radbruch formula's question (Lesson 8), not Fuller's.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The perfectly legal persecution

Take the regime in Q12. It strips a minority of its homes through a carefully drafted, published, general statute that applies only to the future, and it applies the statute exactly as written.

QuestionAnswer
Does it meet Fuller's eight?Assume it does.
So is it just?No. Wicked aims can run through clear, public rules.
So is legality worthless here?No. The victims had notice, outsiders can criticise a published aim, and the regime is bound by its own words (3.9).
Would such a regime stay within the eight?Fuller doubts it. Inner and outer morality tend to decay together.
Is it law?Fuller's checklist does not answer questions of content. That is the Radbruch formula's job (8.3).
⚠ TRAP
Concede the right thing

Concede that a regime can meet all eight requirements and still be wicked. Card 14.6 makes exactly this concession and hands the content question to the Radbruch formula. Don't concede that legality is morally empty. That gives the statement its whole case.

⚠ TRAP
Fuller is not Radbruch

Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula. When he looked at Nazi Germany, he asked how much of a legal system survived, which is a question of degree about form (14.6). The Radbruch formula asks a different question, whether a statute's content is intolerably unjust. Keep them apart.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is half right. Legality is thin: at a minimum it demands rules, whether fair or unfair, so a tyrant could in principle publish clear and general rules for wicked ends. But it is not morally empty. It grounds the citizen's duty to obey in reciprocity, it treats subjects as responsible agents who can plan and choose, and it binds even a self-seeking ruler to the rules he announces. Fuller adds that inner and outer morality tend to decay together, since wicked regimes need secrecy and retroactivity. Legality cannot guarantee just laws, though, and intolerable injustice is the Radbruch formula's work, not Fuller's.

63.4 Discretion

🧩 Practise 3.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.4 Discretion (word for word)
3.4 Discretion rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics
  1. [Every grant of discretion is a small surrender] overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute as undermined by uncontrolled administrative discretion; [enforcement only against critics] approaches it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if bounded by law and reviewable.
  • JUDGE The court reviews legality, not merits: Art 35(8)† discretion is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†).
  • Discretion erodes generality by degree†: principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A referee who can award a penalty "whenever she likes" is not refereeing by the rules. A referee who must award penalties for fouls, but can judge what counts as a foul, is still refereeing by rules. Discretion inside rules is fine. Discretion with no limits is rule by people, not by law.

What the statement claims

"Every grant of discretion is a small surrender of the rule of law to the rule of men. Singapore's wide grants of executive and prosecutorial discretion therefore sit uneasily with its professed commitment to legality." (Q18)

The statement treats all discretion as the same thing. On its view, any room for an official's judgement is a step away from law and towards arbitrary power. It is tempting because discretion really can be abused, and because Fuller's first requirement, generality, is about having rules instead of case-by-case decisions.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men. "Every grant" overstates. Officials need judgement to apply rules to real cases. The danger is discretion with no limits, where an official's will simply replaces the rule.
  2. Fuller's example is a Nazi statute of 1934. Fuller condemns it as undermined by uncontrolled administrative discretion. Under that statute a prosecution needed the order of the Minister of Justice, and the Minister decided whom it protected. A law that is enforced only against the government's critics comes close to the same thing.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if it is bounded by law and reviewable. The question is not whether officials have discretion. It is whether the law limits that discretion, and whether the courts can check that it was used lawfully.

The extra lines, explained

  • JUDGE · review legality, not merits. A court checking discretion asks whether it was used lawfully, not whether it was used wisely. Singapore's Attorney-General has constitutional discretion to prosecute under Art 35(8)†. But that discretion is subject to Art 12, the guarantee of equality before the law, as the Court of Appeal held in Ramalingam†. This is what "bounded and reviewable" looks like in practice.
  • Discretion erodes generality by degree†. Prosecutorial discretion exists almost everywhere. Used with principled restraint, it is compatible with legality. Used to protect allies and punish foes, it creates one law for the favoured and another for everyone else, which eats away at Fuller's first requirement.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Veritas, run through the checklist
FeatureRequirementHow bad?
"Contrary to public morality", filled in by a ministerClarityVery unclear. Nobody can tell what is banned.
The guidelines are unpublishedPromulgationSecret rules: they ground no moral duty to obey (3.3).
Revised every few weeksConstancyStrained. Nobody can keep up.
Deemed to apply from the start of the yearProspectivityA retroactive criminal rule, the worst breach in criminal law (3.1).
Enforced only against criticsGenerality and congruenceUncontrolled discretion, close to Fuller's 1934 statute.

The Act shows breaches compounding: vagueness and secrecy go hand in hand with retroactivity and selective enforcement. On Fuller's view, how much of a legal system survives is a matter of degree, and Veritas sits near the bad end. Whether the judge should refuse to apply the Act is a further question, about content and about her role, which belongs to the Radbruch formula (8.3) and to obedience (8.7).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"Every grant of discretion" overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men. Fuller condemned a 1934 Nazi statute as undermined by uncontrolled administrative discretion, and a law enforced only against the government's critics comes close to it. Discretion erodes generality by degree. Principled restraint is compatible with legality, while protecting allies and punishing foes is not. Singapore's discretion therefore fits the rule of law so long as it is bounded by law and reviewable. That is how the courts treat it: the Attorney-General's discretion under Art 35(8) is subject to Art 12, as Ramalingam holds, and the court reviews legality, not merits.

73.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions

🧩 Practise 3.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions (word for word)
3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
  1. Mandatory sentences look like [the purest expression of the rule of law], but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Hart's justice in administering the law treats like cases alike by any standard of "like", however elevated or perverted (Fuller).
  3. So [leaving nothing to judges] is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A rule says: "Anyone caught with more than a set amount of a drug gets one fixed sentence." It is predictable, and it applies to everyone equally. But treating people "equally" is only fair if the rule draws its line in the right place. If two very different offenders fall on the same side of the line, treating them alike is not justice.

What the statement claims

"Mandatory sentences and statutory presumptions are the purest expression of the rule of law: they treat like cases alike and leave nothing to the personal views of judges." (Q19)

A statutory presumption tells the court to assume one fact once another is proved, for example that a person caught with more than a set weight of a drug was trafficking, unless the accused proves otherwise. The statement assumes that the rule of law means predictability and equal treatment, so the less room judges have, the more legal the system. It is tempting because certainty and treating like cases alike really are part of legality. The block shows that they are not the whole of justice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Mandatory sentences look like the rule of law at its purest, but they buy certainty, not justice. A fixed sentence tells everyone in advance what will happen, which is a real good. It does not tell you whether the sentence is deserved.
  2. Treating like cases alike works with any standard. Hart describes justice in administering the law as treating like cases alike. Fuller points out that this can be done by any standard of what counts as "like", however elevated or perverted. A rule that treats everyone with red hair alike is perfectly consistent, and perfectly arbitrary.
  3. So leaving nothing to judges is just only if the rule's line tracks real differences in harm or fault. If two offenders with very different blame fall on the same side of the line, the rule treats them alike when they are not alike.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Like cases, by what standard?

A statute fixes one sentence for anyone caught carrying more than a set weight of a drug.

OffenderFactsSide of the lineAlike in fault?
ARuns a supply network, caught with well over the set weightOverSerious fault
BA first-time courier, misled about the bag's contents, caught just over the weightOverFar less fault than A, same sentence
CRuns a network like A, caught just under the weightUnderSame fault as A, different sentence

The rule is perfectly consistent. It treats A and B alike and A and C differently. But it is just only if weight tracks fault, and here it does not. That is line 3 of the block.

ℹ NOTE
Pair it with 7.8

Hart says that whether to punish and how severely to punish are separate questions (7.8). So even where some punishment is justified, a harsh fixed penalty needs its own justification.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Mandatory sentences look like the purest expression of the rule of law, but what they buy is certainty, not justice. Treating like cases alike, which Hart calls justice in administering the law, can be done by any standard of what counts as "like", however elevated or perverted, as Fuller points out. Consistency alone therefore tells us nothing about whether the line is in the right place. Leaving nothing to judges is just only if the rule's line tracks real differences in harm or fault. And since whether to punish and how severely are separate questions, a harsh fixed penalty needs a justification of its own.

83.6 Rules v standards

🧩 Practise 3.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.6 Rules v standards (word for word)
3.6 Rules v standards same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules
  1. Holding [a learner driver] to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma; by analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity can justify it, never in crime.
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is at times harsh, intimate justice cannot be even-handed, so law tempers the reasonable man.
  3. So [clear rules are always better] overstates: "good faith" standards can clarify; specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness.
  • Nettleship v Weston†: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard; Cook v Cook† lowered it where the passenger knew (overruled: Imbree v McNeilly, 2008†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Should a learner driver be judged by the standard of an ordinary competent driver, even though a learner cannot yet meet it? A clear rule ("everyone drives to the same standard") is easy to apply, but it can be harsh. A flexible standard ("what is reasonable for you") is kinder, but less even. Fuller says the law has to live with that tension.

What the statement claims

"A fair legal system holds everyone to the same standard, even those who cannot meet it." (Q23)
"Clear rules are always better than flexible standards." (Q24)

Both statements prize evenness. The first says fairness means one standard for all, whatever a person's abilities. The second says a precise rule always beats an open standard such as "reasonable". They are tempting because one standard for all looks impartial, and clear rules are easy to follow. The block shows that evenness has costs of its own.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Holding a learner driver to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma. An objective standard may demand what a particular person cannot achieve, which comes close to requiring the impossible. In civil law it can be justified by analogy with strict liability. It works like a surcharge on taking up a risky activity such as driving. In criminal law, Fuller says, it is never justified, because the surcharge idea does not carry over to punishment.
  2. Fuller's antinomy: evenness and individual fairness pull apart. An aloof justice, which applies one standard to everyone, is bound at times to be harsh. An intimate justice, which looks closely at each person's abilities, cannot be even-handed. So the law takes a middle course and tempers the reasonable-man standard at the edges.
  3. So "clear rules are always better" overstates. A standard such as "good faith" can be the clearest way to say what the law wants. And a rule that only looks precise, which Fuller calls specious clarity, can do more harm than an honest, open-ended standard.

The extra line, explained

  • The learner-driver cases†. Nettleship v Weston, Cook v Cook and Imbree v McNeilly (2008) show the antinomy in action: the courts swung from one standard for all, to a standard fitted to the person, and back. The table below sets them out.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The courts' swing on the learner driver
CaseWhereThe learner's standardWhich side of the antinomy
Nettleship v WestonEnglandThe ordinary competent driverAloof: one standard for all
Cook v CookAustraliaLowered where the passenger knew the driver was a learnerIntimate: fitted to the person
Imbree v McNeilly (2008)AustraliaOverruled Cook: back to the ordinary standardAloof again

Courts moving back and forth is exactly what Fuller's antinomy predicts. Neither side is simply right, so the law keeps adjusting.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Holding a learner driver to the ordinary driver's standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma. In civil law it can be justified by analogy with strict liability, as a surcharge on taking up a risky activity, but in criminal law never. Fuller's antinomy explains why the law cannot simply choose one side. An aloof justice is at times harsh, and an intimate justice cannot be even-handed, so the law tempers the reasonable man at the edges. The courts' swing from Nettleship to Cook v Cook and back in Imbree shows the tension at work. Nor are clear rules always better: a "good faith" standard can be the clearest guide, and specious clarity can do more harm than honest vagueness.

93.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis

🧩 Practise 3.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis (word for word)
3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will
  1. [The duty springs from authority] is the command view, which confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority.
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty: once government ruptures it finally and completely, the citizen's duty has no ground left.
  3. So [goodwill] cannot suffice: no single centre of intelligence and goodwill can secure law's enterprise.
  • Where officials disregard rules, obedience at some point becomes futile, like casting a vote that will never be counted.
  • AGAINST [Majority will, accurately expressed]: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments.
  • QUALIFY In a crisis "grim necessity" may justify a secret weapons appropriation, but no emergency justifies a secret law creating a new crime (Fuller).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Why obey the law? "Because the government says so" is the command view. Fuller says obedience is more like a deal. The government gives you clear, stable rules and promises to judge you by them, and you follow them. If the government tears up its side completely, nothing is left to support your duty.

What the statement claims

"During COVID-19, the rules on masks, gatherings and even company board meetings changed constantly and were often announced at short notice, yet citizens were right to obey them. The duty to obey springs from the authority of the government that issues the rules, not from how well it drafts or publicises them. Clarity, consistency and constancy are matters of administrative efficiency, not morality: a government that announces its rules late wrongs no one." (Q15)
"Any government ultimately follows the law because it wants to." (Q21)

The first statement gets the result right (citizens were right to obey) but gives the wrong reason (authority). It also repeats the steelman that the requirements are mere efficiency. The second says legality rests on nothing but the rulers' goodwill. Both treat the law as a one-way order from the top.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "The duty springs from authority" is the command view. It treats law as whatever those at the top order. Fuller says this confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority. Rex's subjects deferred to Rex as king throughout his reign, yet there was no law for them to be faithful to.
  2. The duty to obey rests on reciprocity. The government in effect says: these are the rules we expect you to follow, and if you follow them, they are the rules we will apply to you. The citizen's duty depends on the government keeping that promise. Once the government ruptures the bond finally and completely, the citizen's duty has no ground left. Anything short of that, such as rules that change fast but are published, strains the deal without ending it.
  3. So goodwill cannot be enough. Q21 says governments follow the law only because they want to. Fuller's answer is that legality is a shared enterprise. No single centre of intelligence and goodwill, however wise, can secure it alone. Law-makers, officials, judges and citizens all depend on each other.

The extra lines, explained

  • The voter. Fuller compares a citizen whose officials disregard the rules to a voter casting a ballot that will never be counted. Obeying is still possible, but at some point it becomes futile. Use this image to explain what a partial rupture does to the duty to obey.
  • AGAINST · majority will. Some statements say law is simply majority will, accurately expressed. Fuller's reply is that a law which tracked a shifting majority from day to day would break constancy, just like Rex's daily amendments. A majority may decide who makes the law, but the law must stay stable enough to follow.
  • QUALIFY · crisis. Emergencies can justify some departures from the requirements. Fuller accepts that grim necessity may justify a secret appropriation for weapons. But no emergency justifies a secret law creating a new crime. COVID rules changed fast, which strained constancy, but they were published and forward-looking, so they stayed on the right side of that line.
ℹ NOTE
Where the Core cards use this block

Core C (13.5) uses 3.7 twice. Against "law is simply will or power", Hart and Fuller both reject the claim, because the will makes law only through rules that also bind it. Against "valid law must be obeyed", Fuller grounds obedience in reciprocity, not in validity alone.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Q15, claim by claim
What Q15 saysYour reply
The rules changed constantly, often at short noticeConstancy and promulgation were strained. That is a matter of degree.
Citizens were right to obeyAgree with the result.
The duty springs from the government's authorityWrong ground. That is the command view. The duty rests on reciprocity, which the strain did not rupture.
Clarity, consistency and constancy are mere efficiencyThat is the steelman legality is not moral. Legality is thin, not empty: it treats people as agents.
A government that announces its rules late wrongs no oneIt does wrong citizens. Rules announced too late leave them unable to plan, so they are not treated as responsible agents. Card 14.6 names this as one of Fuller's questions: why do failures of form wrong citizens?
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is right that citizens were bound to obey, but wrong about why. Grounding the duty in authority is the command view, which confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority. Fuller grounds the duty in reciprocity: the government asks citizens to follow its rules and promises to judge them by those rules, and only a final and complete rupture of that bond leaves the duty with no ground. Rules that changed fast during COVID strained constancy, but they were published and prospective, so the bond held. Nor is legality a matter of goodwill alone, since no single centre of intelligence and goodwill can secure law's enterprise.

103.8 Judge-made law

🧩 Practise 3.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.8 Judge-made law (word for word)
3.8 Judge-made law never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so [can never fully satisfy] holds in form, though a new rule may only confirm views already widely held.
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is [a price worth paying]: prospective rulings remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent.
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave people "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation.
  • Abdul Nasir† (CA 1997): life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only (8.6); it engages constancy, not branding as criminals.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When a judge decides a new point, the rule is announced after the events happened, so it reaches back a little. Usually that is fine, because the judge is often confirming what people already expected. But in criminal law, punishing someone for relying on what the courts had said was lawful would be unfair.

What the statement claims

"The common law can never fully satisfy Fuller's requirements of promulgation and prospectivity, because judges announce the law only after a dispute has arisen." (Q22)

The statement is partly right, and that is what makes it tempting. A court does decide disputes about the past. The block accepts the point in form, then shows that how much it matters depends on whether the case is civil or criminal.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. True in form. Adjudication is partly retrospective. A court decides a dispute about events that have already happened, and its ruling applies to them. So the statement holds in form. But a new judge-made rule often only confirms views already widely held, so nobody is really taken by surprise.
  2. In civil cases, retrospective overruling is a price worth paying. Suppose a court's new ruling applied only to future cases. The litigant who persuaded the court to overrule a bad precedent would then gain nothing from winning. Nobody would bother to challenge bad precedents, and the law would not improve.
  3. Criminal cases are different. If a court overruled an earlier reading of the law and applied a harsher new reading backwards, people who had relied on the earlier judicial interpretation would be branded as criminals. That is the retrospective criminal law Fuller condemns.

The extra line, explained

  • Abdul Nasir · constancy, not branding. Keep two ideas apart. Being branded as criminals concerns a court overruling a reading under which conduct was lawful, so that people who relied on it become criminals. Abdul Nasir is different. Nobody became a criminal: the conduct was a crime before and after. What changed was the meaning of an existing sentence. Applying the longer meaning to those already sentenced would have unsettled a law people had planned around, so the court applied it only to the future. That engages constancy. Block 8.6 adds that a longer term is less objectionable than a new crime (8.6).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement holds in form. Adjudication is partly retrospective, since a court rules on events that have already happened, though a new rule often only confirms views already widely held. In civil cases, retrospective overruling is a price worth paying. A purely prospective ruling would leave the litigant who overturned a bad precedent with nothing, and so remove the incentive to challenge it. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave people branded as criminals for relying on a judicial interpretation. Singapore's courts have shown the care this needs. In Abdul Nasir the Court of Appeal held that life imprisonment means natural life, but applied that reading only to future cases, protecting the constancy of the law.

113.9 Thin v thick; Marx

🧩 Practise 3.9 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 3.9 Thin v thick; Marx (word for word)
3.9 Thin v thick; Marx ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials
  1. [A slogan] for class power overstates: legal form binds rulers too, since law cannot be "built on law".
  2. Against the Marxist†, law has its own character: it applies legal criteria by standards of universality and equity (crits: 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats [the whims of its officials]: published rules give notice and invite criticism.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A Marxist says "the rule of law" is just a fancy costume worn by the powerful. Fuller replies that once the powerful dress in law, the costume constrains them too. They have to follow their own published rules, which tells everyone what they are doing and lets people criticise, resist or leave.

What the statement claims

"Law is the instrument of the ruling class, dressed in the language of universality and equity. Judges who claim to apply neutral rules, legislators who claim to serve the common good, and lawyers who claim to serve justice all take part in the same disguise." (Q17)
"A regime that strips a minority of its homes and livelihoods through carefully drafted, published and general statutes is no better than one that does so through the whims of its officials; the victims suffer exactly the same." (Q12)

Both statements say legal form adds nothing. The first says it is a disguise for class power. The second says persecution by published statute is no better than persecution by whim. They are tempting because the victims of a wicked statute do suffer, and because rulers do use law to look respectable.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "A slogan for class power" overstates, because legal form binds the rulers too. Fuller says law cannot be built on law. A legal system cannot rest on rules alone: the power to make law has to be accepted, and the law-maker has to commit to governing through the rules he announces. Once rulers make that commitment, legal form binds them as well.
  2. Against the Marxist, law has a character of its own†. The Marxist says law is only the ruling class's tool. The reply is that law applies its own criteria, judged by standards of universality and equity. Those standards can be turned against the powerful who invoke them. (The critical legal scholars, or crits, such as Unger, make a related attack on legal doctrine in 9.3, though they generally distance themselves from the Marxist view that law is only a tool of the ruling class.)
  3. So thin legality beats the whims of officials. Published rules give notice, so victims can see what is coming. They also invite criticism, because the regime's aims are on the record.

How the steelman fits here

Block 3.9 has no tagged extra lines of its own. Its main support is the second steelman, legality is enough. In Q12 that steelman becomes your reply, because the statement goes to the other extreme and says legality is worthless.

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu's image is that law drags the monster into the light†. A regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern that anyone can plan around. Liu also gives the other side. Rules can legitimise and spread evil, because people carry out a wicked rule when told "it's the law"†. Use both sides: the first defeats "no better than whims", the second stops you claiming that legality guarantees justice.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Persecution by statute v persecution by whim
By published statuteBy officials' whims
Can the victims see it coming?Yes. The rules give notice.No. There is no pattern.
Can others criticise and organise?Yes. The aims are on the record.Hardly. There is nothing to point to.
Are the rulers bound?Yes, by the rules they announced.No.
Is it just?No.No.
The special danger"It's the law" can legitimise and spread the evil.Terror without any pattern.

The victims may suffer the same, but they are not equally placed. That is the answer to Q12's first sentence. Neither column is just, which is why legality alone cannot be your whole answer.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The victims may suffer the same, but they are not equally placed. Published, general, prospective rules tell them what is coming, invite criticism and bind the rulers who made them, since law cannot be built on law: legal form binds those who use it. Against the Marxist, law has a character of its own, applying its criteria by standards of universality and equity that can be turned against the powerful. Law drags the monster into the light, though I concede that rules can also legitimise and spread evil. What legality cannot do is make the statutes just. That requires a test of content, such as the Radbruch formula.

12Putting it together: Practice Q12

"A regime that strips a minority of its homes and livelihoods through carefully drafted, published and general statutes is no better than one that does so through the whims of its officials; the victims suffer exactly the same. Law has only ever been the instrument of whichever class holds power, and 'the rule of law' is a slogan that dresses that power up as something respectable. A society is truly ruled by law rather than by men only when its laws are substantively just."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Fuller, Hart and Marxism.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement runs together two claims: that legality is worthless, and that only just laws make a society ruled by law. The first is wrong, and the second confuses form with content. I make three claims. First, published, general rules leave victims better placed than whims, because they give notice and bind the rulers. Second, the rule of law is no mere class slogan, since its form constrains those who use it. Third, the statement is right that legality cannot guarantee just laws, so a regime may be ruled by law and still be wicked.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Fuller's thin morality (3.3, 3.9). Reciprocity, respect for responsible agents, and law cannot be built on law. Then the second steelman: law drags the monster into the light.
  2. The efficacy objection and the Marxist (3.3, 3.9). State the first steelman: perhaps the eight requirements are about efficacy, not morality†. Add the Marxist charge of legitimation. Reply with Fuller's point that inner and outer morality decay together, and with law's own character (universality and equity). Concede that rules can also spread evil.
  3. "Only when substantively just" (3.3, Lesson 8). Hart would say a persecuting statute can be valid but wicked. Saying intolerable injustice is "not law" is the Radbruch formula's move, not Fuller's: Fuller asks how much of a legal system survived. Concede that a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore right only in part. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents and exposes their aims to criticism, so carefully drafted statutes are not the same as whims. But legality is thin. It cannot make bad laws just, and naming intolerable injustice "not law" is the Radbruch formula's task, not Fuller's.

13Recap

Archetype 3 on one card
▤ Sections 3.1–3.9
  1. 1Rank by branch of law: prospectivity in crime first, congruence for one rule last. Breaches compound (3.1).
  2. 2Open non-enforcement strains congruence, but one rule survives. The law can exempt the trivial openly (3.2).
  3. 3Legality is moral but thin: reciprocity, respect for agents, and it binds rulers. It does not guarantee justice (3.3).
  4. 4Only uncontrolled discretion is rule by men. Bounded and reviewable discretion fits (3.4).
  5. 5Treating like cases alike gives certainty, not justice (3.5).
  6. 6The reasonable-man dilemma: a civil surcharge, never in crime. Honest vagueness can beat specious clarity (3.6).
  7. 7The duty to obey rests on reciprocity, not authority or goodwill. Only a complete rupture ends it (3.7).
  8. 8Judge-made law is retrospective in form: a fair price in civil cases, not in crime. Abdul Nasir is about constancy (3.8).
  9. 9Legal form binds rulers. Published rules give notice and invite criticism, so they beat whims (3.9).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture the rule of law as a glass box around power. The glass holds the rulers in, because they must keep to their own rules. Everyone can see what is inside, which is the monster dragged into the light. But glass does not change what is in the box: a wicked law behind glass is still wicked, and that is the Radbruch formula's problem. The glass can be smudged a little or a lot (a matter of degree). Only when one pane is missing entirely, as with King Rex, is there no box at all.
