LESSON 4 · ARCHETYPE 4 · ABOUT 63 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 40 QUESTIONS

Moral objectivity and scepticism

⚡ BIG IDEA

The sceptic's case is inconclusive, and the sceptic's own demands (tolerate! don't judge!) presuppose moral truth. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma or silence.

ARCHETYPE 4 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
4 Moral objectivity and scepticism
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position The sceptic's case is inconclusive and its demands presuppose moral truth, so [the sceptic's conclusion] fails: fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not [tolerance as dogma / silence].
Intro That morality is [just opinion / a social construct] is offered as a reason for [tolerance / neutrality / keeping it out of law], yet that conclusion is itself a moral demand the sceptic cannot ground. So [the statement] [fails / is overstated]: disagreement and unprovability do not show there is no moral truth, and realism demands deliberation, not imposition.
Steelman: for the sceptic The best case for [the statement] is humility: cultures differ, we have been wrong before, and no moral claim is proved deductively, so coercion should rest only on what is widely shared. This shows that moral judgement is fallible. It does not show [that there is no moral truth]: humility is a realist's case, since genuine realism commits one to deliberation.
4.1 Map just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture
  1. [The statement] runs together relativism (cultures differ), scepticism (no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (mere sentiment).
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism a moral claim is like [disliking durian], neither true nor false; realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So [nobody has proved it], the sceptic's point, bites only if proof means deduction, a test natural science fails too.
  • "Shades of grey" is no argument, and "merely opinions" assumes the point in dispute†.
  • TRAP Subjective does not mean controversial (heliocentrism was controversial, not subjective), and moral realism is unrelated to legal realism†.
4.2 Self-refutation all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct
  1. The sceptic's [we must tolerate / no one may judge] is itself an objective moral demand of the kind the statement denies.
  2. A [social construct] that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism; if that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So [the statement] defeats itself; true subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force.
  • CONCEDE Self-refutation binds only the sceptic who makes demands, and it settles no content: further debate is a squabble among moral realists, so realism must still argue for each norm.
  • TRAP TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist†; the sceptic who says none are bound is consistent but argues for nothing ("True skepticism"†).
4.3 Appeals nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values
  1. That [nobody can agree] shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. TSH explains disagreement: the mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience.
  3. So [we have been wrong before] counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.
  • Imposition is no monopoly of realists: others too can be bigoted and intolerant.
4.4 Is–ought Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should
  1. Hume's gap holds: [the biological facts] alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts: the basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as [embryology] show only how they apply.
  3. So [it tells us nothing] overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, facts fix the stakes.
  • Hume's two arguments†: (1) wrongness lies in our sentiments, not the act, since reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X"); (2) no "ought" follows from an "is".
  • AGAINST (1)† Statement X is itself neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact, so by its own test it is neither true nor false. (2) The gap is only logical: agreed ought-premises (eg the dignity of man) plus facts yield oughts.
4.5 Hidden judgment consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral
  1. Calling [X] not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is autonomy's primacy, which rests on equal worth; unlimited, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So [the law should stay neutral] fails: where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices; there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).
  • Finnis charges that appealing only to subjective preference, then grounding that in the intrinsic value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction".
4.6 Whatever is enacted? law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer
  1. If [law is whatever is enacted], nothing stands above the lawgiver, and man arguably becomes "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying [citizens are safer] if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising [what is enacted], without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.
  • Alexy: only the "strong" connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one (RF) keeps law open to critique. Hart's case for separation: 8.2.
Conclusion [The statement] therefore [fails / is overstated]. Scepticism cannot deliver the [tolerance / safety / neutrality] it promises, since that promise is itself a moral norm; its reasons are "inconclusive", though that proves no moral fact. The realist's weak point is access, not existence: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps arguably claimed moral truth. So I hold moral judgements provisionally, demanding more of them the more coercive the law.
4.7 Objectivity anchor
Paragraph Demanding [tolerance / deference] because [morality is just opinion / personal / a social construct] defeats itself: the demand binds others, which abandons subjectivism, and if it rests on equal moral worth the sceptic is a moral realist. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets; the unproven is not the false. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out is itself a moral choice. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH).
  • Use: 4.1–4.3, 4.5 (just opinion; nobody can agree; it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality; private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); 10.4 (no one can say objectively).

1Start here: archetype 4 in plain English

Archetype 4 asks one question: is there such a thing as moral truth, or is morality just opinion? A moral truth would be a claim such as "torturing people for fun is wrong" that is true whatever anyone happens to think or feel about it. The sceptic says there is no such thing, or none we could ever know.

Exam statements in this family nearly always make two moves in a row. First they say morality is opinion, taste or culture. Then they draw a conclusion for law: "so the law must stay neutral", "so no judge may impose values", "so we must tolerate everything". The second move is where they fail. "You must tolerate" and "nobody may judge" are themselves moral rules that bind other people, which is exactly what the sceptic said moral rules cannot do.

Your answer has the same shape every time. Show that the sceptic's reasons (disagreement, past mistakes, lack of proof) do not prove there is no moral truth. Show that the sceptic's demand assumes moral truth. Then concede honestly what the sceptic gets right. We can be wrong about morality, and that is a real problem. But it calls for careful deliberation and provisional judgement, not for silence, and not for tolerance as an unquestionable dogma.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Moral realismSome moral claims are true or false whatever anyone believes or feels. If two people disagree about one, at least one of them is wrong.
SubjectivismThe umbrella label for every view that denies realism. Morality depends on the person, the culture or the feeling. The next three rows all fall under it.
RelativismRight and wrong vary with the culture (or the person), and no culture's view is truer than another's.
ScepticismEither there is no moral standard at all, or there is one but we cannot know it.
Non-cognitivismHume's view that a moral claim expresses a feeling, like "yuck" or "yum", and so is neither true nor false.
Self-refutationA claim that defeats itself when it is applied to itself, like a sign that reads "Ignore all signs".
DeductionProof in which the conclusion follows with logical certainty from the premises, as in maths.
Is–ought gapHume's point that facts on their own (what is) never tell you what you ought to do. You also need a moral premise.
Existence v accessTwo different questions. Is there a moral truth (existence)? Can we know it (access)? The realist is weak on access, not on existence.
Provisional judgementA moral view held firmly enough to act on, but open to correction if better reasons appear.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the sceptic's case is inconclusive and its demands presuppose moral truth, so the sceptic's conclusion fails, and fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not tolerance as dogma or silence.

Put simply, the sceptic has two problems. The first is that the arguments are inconclusive. Disagreement, past mistakes and lack of proof are all consistent with there being a moral truth that some people have missed. The second problem is worse. The moment the sceptic says "so you must tolerate" or "so nobody may judge", the sceptic is relying on a moral truth that binds everyone. What survives is a sound point about humility. We can be wrong, so we should think hard, give reasons and hold our views provisionally. It does not follow that nobody may ever judge.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement offers "morality is just opinion" (or "a social construct") as a reason for tolerance, neutrality or keeping morality out of law. But that conclusion is itself a moral demand, and the sceptic has no ground for it. So the statement fails, or is overstated. Disagreement and unprovability do not show that there is no moral truth, and believing in moral truth commits you to deliberation, not to imposing your views.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. Scepticism cannot deliver the tolerance, safety or neutrality it promises, because that promise is itself a moral norm. Its reasons are inconclusive, though that does not prove any moral fact either. Then comes the honest concession. The realist's weak point is access, not existence. Consensus can be wrong, and in the 2007 s 377A debate both camps arguably claimed moral truth. So you hold moral judgements provisionally, and you demand stronger reasons the more coercive the law.

The steelman

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before answering it. Section 4 gives you one.

  • Steelman: for the sceptic. The best case is humility. Cultures differ, we have been wrong before (slavery is the obvious example), and no moral claim can be proved by deduction. So, the sceptic says, the state should coerce people only on what is widely shared. This shows that moral judgement is fallible, and you should grant it. It does not show that there is no moral truth. In fact humility is a realist's argument. You can only worry about getting something wrong if there is something to get right, and genuine realism commits you to deliberation, which is exactly what humility asks for.

The seven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
4.1"Morality is just opinion, and nobody has proved anything."Split the three kinds of sceptic. "Unproved" bites only if proof means deduction, which science fails too.
4.2"All views are equally valid, so you must tolerate.""You must tolerate" is a moral rule. The sceptic either drops it or becomes a realist.
4.3"Nobody agrees, and we have been wrong before."Disagreement shows that someone is wrong, not that nobody is right. Past error calls for slowness, not silence.
4.4"You cannot get an ought from an is, so the facts tell us nothing."Facts alone do need a moral premise. Add an agreed one and the facts matter a great deal.
4.5"It is consensual and harms no one, so it is not wrong. Stay neutral."That is a moral verdict, resting on the primacy of autonomy. There is no neutral ground.
4.6"Law is whatever Parliament enacts, and that is safer.""Safer" is a moral claim. Natural law stays a touchstone for criticising what is enacted.
4.7(A ready-made paragraph)Four moves for any "just opinion" argument, in any archetype.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

"You must tolerate" is a moral rule, so a sceptic who demands it has already stopped being a sceptic.

2The big picture: is morality just opinion?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some people say right and wrong are just opinions, like loving or hating durian. If that were true, then "you must respect other people's opinions" would also be just an opinion, and nobody else would have to accept it. The sceptic wants everyone to be tolerant, but tolerance is a moral rule. That is the trap the sceptic falls into. The sceptic does have one real insight, though. We can get morality wrong, so we should argue carefully and hold our views with some humility.

Your job in every answer has three parts. First, separate the different sceptical claims, because each needs a different reply. Second, show that the sceptic's conclusion defeats itself. Third, concede what the realist cannot prove, and turn that concession into a working principle: the more coercive the law, the stronger the reasons it needs.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
HumeThe sceptic's best ally, with two arguments. The first says wrongness lies in our feelings, not in the act. Reason can only know relations of ideas (truths of logic and maths) and matters of fact (what we observe), and a moral claim is neither. Liu calls this claim "Statement X"†. The second argument is the is–ought gap: no "ought" follows from an "is" alone.
TSH (Tan Seow Hon), The Problems with Moral SubjectivismA subjectivist cannot hold anyone else to a moral standard without ceasing to be a subjectivist. So subjectivists can barely argue about morality at all. Their moral dialogue is gravely limited. Her topic is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist†.
FinnisThe basic goods (life, knowledge, friendship and so on) are self-evident. We grasp them by practical reason, and do not infer them from facts. So Finnis never tries to derive an "ought" from an "is", and Hume's gap does not touch him (Lesson 5).
AlexyPositivists fear that linking law to morality makes people treat whatever is law as right. Alexy replies that only the strong version of the link has that risk. The weak version, Radbruch's formula, keeps law open to criticism (Lesson 8).
Thio Li-annIn the 2007 s 377A debate she said there is no Switzerland of ambivalence, meaning no neutral place to stand on a moral question.

Key distinctions

  • Realism v subjectivism, and the three subjectivisms. Realism says moral claims can be true or false. Subjectivism is the umbrella for everything else. Under it sit relativism (it varies by culture), scepticism (there is no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (moral claims only express feelings). Statements often blur all three together, and 4.1 pulls them apart.
  • Existence v access. Whether there is a moral truth is one question. Whether and how we can know it is another. On existence, the sceptic's case is inconclusive, and self-refutation catches any sceptic who makes demands. Neither proves that moral facts exist. The realist's honest weak point is access. Consensus can be wrong, and people on both sides of a debate can be sure they are right.
  • The demanding sceptic v the true sceptic. A sceptic who says "nobody is bound by anything" is consistent, but argues for nothing. A sceptic who says "so you must tolerate" is making a moral demand. Self-refutation catches only the second (4.2).
  • Subjective v controversial. A question can be fiercely disputed and still have a true answer. Whether the Earth goes round the Sun was once controversial, but it was never subjective.

The chart is the whole archetype in miniature. The sceptic and the realist agree on the starting point, that people get morality wrong. They part company over what follows. Only the third branch is consistent with the starting point, because the first two either act on a moral view while denying it or demand something scepticism cannot support.

Ali has not been caught out by a debating trick. He has run into the central problem of the archetype. If he really believes all opinions are equally valid, he must give up demanding tolerance from Beth, because his demand is only one more opinion. If he keeps the demand, he believes at least one moral claim is true for everyone, namely that people deserve respect. TSH's verdict on such a sceptic is that he is just another moral realist. Every block in this lesson is a version of this scene.

⚠ TRAP
Realism is not a party line

Liu stressed two points about what realism does not mean†. First, realism tells you nothing about content. A pacifist and a genocidal Nazi could both be realists, since each thinks his view is true for everyone. So proving realism never wins a particular moral argument. Second, realism is not intolerance. A realist can hold views provisionally and listen hard, because a realist thinks there is something to be found out.
