34.1 Map

🧩 Practise 4.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.1 Map (word for word)
4.1 Map just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture
  1. [The statement] runs together relativism (cultures differ), scepticism (no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (mere sentiment).
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism a moral claim is like [disliking durian], neither true nor false; realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So [nobody has proved it], the sceptic's point, bites only if proof means deduction, a test natural science fails too.
  • "Shades of grey" is no argument, and "merely opinions" assumes the point in dispute†.
  • TRAP Subjective does not mean controversial (heliocentrism was controversial, not subjective), and moral realism is unrelated to legal realism†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Nobody has proved it" sounds strong. But we cannot prove most things the way we prove a sum in maths, not even in science. If "proof" means a watertight deduction, then science fails the test too. So the sceptic must mean something weaker, and then the argument loses its punch.

What the statement claims

"Morality is just opinion. Every culture draws the line between right and wrong in a different place, and after thousands of years nobody has proved which side is correct … a moral view can no more be true or false than a taste for durian." (Q28)

The statement sounds like one argument, but it is three. Each sentence takes a different sceptical route. It is tempting because each route sounds modest on its own. Cultures do differ, nobody has produced a moral proof, and moral views can feel like tastes. The block's job is to separate the three so you can answer each one.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The statement blends three different claims. Relativism says moral views vary between cultures. Scepticism says there is no moral standard, or none we can know. Non-cognitivism says moral claims merely express feelings. Each needs a different reply, so split them before you answer. Q28 manages all three in two sentences, which is why a reader who does not split them ends up fighting a blur.
  2. The durian comparison is Hume's non-cognitivism. If "cheating is wrong" works like "I dislike durian", it only reports a feeling, and so it cannot be true or false. Moral realists reply that a moral claim is about the act, not about the speaker. TSH's example is Lucy hitting Linus whenever she feels crabby. To call that wrong is to say something about what Lucy does, not about how anyone feels.
  3. So "nobody has proved it" bites only if proof means deduction. Deduction means the conclusion follows with logical certainty from the premises. By that standard natural science proves nothing either, since no fact about the past entails that the sun will rise tomorrow. So the sceptic must mean a weaker kind of proof, and on a weaker standard morality is not obviously worse off than science.

On Hume's view the two disagreements are the same kind of thing, two people reporting different feelings. Most people sense a difference. In the first, it would be odd to say Beth is mistaken about durian. In the second, it is natural to say that Beth is mistaken about the overcharging. The realist explains why. "Durian is disgusting" is about Beth's palate, while "cheating a tourist is wrong" is about the act. The durian is this block's signature example, so use it here and nowhere else in a script.

The extra lines, explained

  • Liu's two quick replies†. Two stock lines turn up in almost every sceptical statement. "It's all shades of grey" is no argument at all, since saying a question is hard is not saying it has no answer. And "they're merely opinions" assumes the very point in dispute, that moral views are not statements of fact. That is begging the question: using your conclusion as a premise.
  • TRAP · two confusions. First, subjective does not mean controversial. Heliocentrism, the view that the Earth goes round the Sun, was once fiercely controversial, yet there was a fact of the matter all along. Second, moral realism has nothing to do with legal realism†. Moral realism says moral claims can be true or false. Legal realism is the American school that says judges decide first and justify afterwards (9.1). The shared word is a coincidence, and mixing them up costs marks.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Sorting Q28, phrase by phrase
Phrase in Q28Which sceptic?Your reply
"Every culture draws the line … in a different place"RelativismBeliefs vary. That does not show no belief is wrong, any more than old disputes about the planets showed there were no planets.
"nobody has proved which side is correct"ScepticismProof by deduction is a test natural science fails too. Unproved is not false.
"nothing in ethics is black and white"A stock lineShades of grey is no argument†. A hard question can still have an answer.
"no more be true or false than a taste for durian"Non-cognitivism (Hume)A moral claim is about the act, not the speaker's taste.
"condemn as intolerant any legislator or judge"None. This is a moral demandHere the statement refutes itself (4.2).

The last row matters most. Q28 spends three sentences denying moral truth and then, in its fourth and final sentence, issues a moral command.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement runs together three different claims. Relativism says moral views vary between cultures, scepticism says there is no moral standard or none we can know, and Hume's non-cognitivism says a moral claim merely expresses a sentiment, like disliking durian. Realists hold that a moral claim is about the act and so can be true or false. The sceptic's strongest phrase, that nobody has proved which side is correct, bites only if proof means deduction, and natural science fails that test too. Saying that ethics is all shades of grey is no argument, and calling moral views merely opinions assumes the very point in dispute.

44.2 Self-refutation

🧩 Practise 4.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.2 Self-refutation (word for word)
4.2 Self-refutation all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct
  1. The sceptic's [we must tolerate / no one may judge] is itself an objective moral demand of the kind the statement denies.
  2. A [social construct] that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism; if that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So [the statement] defeats itself; true subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force.
  • CONCEDE Self-refutation binds only the sceptic who makes demands, and it settles no content: further debate is a squabble among moral realists, so realism must still argue for each norm.
  • TRAP TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist†; the sceptic who says none are bound is consistent but argues for nothing ("True skepticism"†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sceptic says, "There are no moral rules, so you MUST tolerate everyone." But "you must tolerate" is a moral rule. Either the sceptic drops the demand, and then has nothing to say to a bully, or keeps it, and is no longer a sceptic.

What the statement claims

"A multicultural society should therefore accept that no conduct is objectively wrong, and condemn as intolerant any legislator or judge who uses the law to insist otherwise." (Q28)
"All moral opinions are equally valid. Who are you to judge?" "Morality is a social construct."

The statement presents tolerance as the natural partner of scepticism. If nobody's morality is better than anybody else's, surely nobody should impose theirs? It is tempting because it sounds humble and kind. The block shows that the statement's last step, the demand, contradicts its first step, the denial of moral truth.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "You must tolerate" and "nobody may judge" are moral rules. They tell other people what they ought to do, whether they agree or not. That is exactly the kind of objective moral demand the statement says does not exist. Q28 shows it plainly. Having said that no conduct is objectively wrong, it tells society to condemn the intolerant.
  2. A "social construct" that binds outsiders is no longer subjectivism. Suppose a relativist says outsiders must respect his culture's norms. That demand reaches beyond his culture, so it appeals to what TSH calls a meta-cultural standard, a rule that sits above all cultures. Ask why outsiders are bound, and the usual answer is that every person has equal moral worth. At that point, TSH argues, the sceptic has become a moral realist.
  3. So the statement defeats itself, and pure subjectivism leaves only force. A subjectivist who stays consistent cannot tell anyone that they are really wrong. TSH's genocide hypothetical, below, shows the result. When one culture commits genocide, a consistent subjectivist has no argument left, only the option of force.

The chart has three exits, and none of them is a comfortable home for the statement. The sceptic who demands nothing is consistent but cannot tell society to condemn anyone. The sceptic whose demand binds only himself has stated a preference. And the sceptic who grounds the demand properly, in equal worth or fairness, has adopted a moral truth. Liu's slide makes the same point about "social construct". If it means "so we are not bound", that is true scepticism. If it means "so we are bound by the consensus", the reason why the consensus binds (dignity, fairness, reciprocity) is a realist premise†.

TSH's point is not about international law, which she sets aside. It is about argument. If Country B is a consistent relativist, all it can say is that A's norms do not bind B, and Country A says exactly the same back. Dialogue breaks down, and only brute force can settle the matter. Country B can escape only by appealing to something above both cultures, such as the equal worth of every person, and that is realism. The same holds for an individual who says "no moral law binds anyone, so you cannot judge me". That relies on a moral principle, the primacy of autonomy, which 4.5 examines.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · what self-refutation does not do. Self-refutation catches only the sceptic who makes demands, and it settles no content. Once everyone admits there is moral truth, the argument about which norms are true goes on, as what TSH calls a squabble among moral realists. So concede that realism must still argue for each norm it wants the law to enforce. Proving that there is a right answer never tells you what the answer is.
  • TRAP · TSH proves less than students think. Liu stresses that TSH's topic is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist†. Her argument shows that a subjectivist cannot argue morally without turning realist. It does not show that moral facts exist. And a sceptic who says nobody is bound by anything is perfectly consistent. Liu's slide calls this true skepticism†. It is consistent, but it can argue for nothing, tolerance included.
Card 14.7: TSH on moral subjectivism, in plain words
▤ The card behind 4.2
  1. 1Question. Is morality personal or cultural opinion, and can subjectivists argue with anyone?
  2. 2Claim. Subjectivists cannot hold others to any standard independent of their beliefs without ceasing to be subjectivists, so their moral dialogue is gravely limited.
  3. 3Test. Does the sceptic's premise bind someone who rejects it? A relativist who binds outsiders needs a standard above cultures, and if that standard honours equal worth, the relativist is a realist.
  4. 4Strength. The genocide hypothetical. And if everyone may do as they please, everyone becomes equally worthless. Add limits, and the subjectivist is just another moral realist.
  5. 5Critique and reply. The epistemic sceptic, TSH's second kind, asks who knows the moral facts. That is a fair question but a dead end for law-making. Finnis's basic goods offer a way forward†, and realism means deliberating, with judgements held more provisionally.
  6. 6Verdict. TSH shows that a subjectivist who argues or demands must turn realist, and that the case for subjectivism is inconclusive. She does not show that moral facts exist. How we know what is right is left to deliberation.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement's demand that we condemn the intolerant is itself an objective moral claim, the very kind of claim the statement says does not exist. A relativist who insists that outsiders respect his culture's norms appeals to a standard above all cultures, and if that standard rests on the equal worth of persons, he is, in TSH's terms, just another moral realist. Taken to its end, consistent subjectivism leaves its adherents no reply to genocide except force. This shows only that a sceptic who argues or demands must turn realist. It does not settle which norms are true, so realism must still argue for each one.

54.3 Appeals

🧩 Practise 4.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.3 Appeals (word for word)
4.3 Appeals nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values
  1. That [nobody can agree] shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. TSH explains disagreement: the mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience.
  3. So [we have been wrong before] counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.
  • Imposition is no monopoly of realists: others too can be bigoted and intolerant.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"People have always disagreed, so there is no right answer." But people disagreed about whether the Earth goes round the Sun. Disagreement shows that someone is wrong, not that nobody can be right. And "we were wrong before about slavery" only makes sense if there is a right answer that we were wrong about.

What the statement claims

"Since nobody can agree on what objective morality requires, lawmakers should stop searching for it." (Q30)
"We have been wrong about morality before, so we should not use law to enforce it now." (Q34)
"Our forefathers thought slavery acceptable and were wrong, which proves that today's convictions are just as arbitrary." (Q29)

These statements appeal to three facts about our moral life. We disagree, we have made mistakes, and we cannot be sure. From those facts they draw a practical conclusion, which is to stop judging, or at least to stop legislating. They are tempting because the facts are true. The block accepts the facts and rejects the conclusion.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Disagreement shows that someone is wrong, not that nobody is right. Astronomers have disagreed about how many planets there are, and nobody concludes that there was no fact about the planets. Disagreement would disprove moral truth only if morality were whatever people agree on, and that is the very point in dispute. The anchor in 4.7 uses the planets for this point.
  2. TSH explains why people disagree, without denying the truth. She gives three reasons. The mores of the times, the attitudes a society takes for granted, can pervert reasoning, as when a whole society grows up accepting slavery. Weakness of will lets passion win over conscience. And self-interest, hardened by habit, dulls the sense of guilt. Each explains how decent people can be wrong about a moral truth.
  3. So past error counsels slowness, not abstention. To call slavery an error you must believe there was a right answer that slave-owning societies missed. So "we were wrong before" relies on moral truth. Its real lesson is to go slowly and give reasons before using law to coerce, which is also Devlin's caution and Hart's demand for reasons in 7.8. It is not a lesson to stop judging.

The extra line, explained

  • Imposition is no monopoly of realists. The statement often says realists are dangerous, because people who think they know the truth will impose it. TSH answers that people who deny moral truth can be just as bigoted and intolerant. Calling a view "merely subjective" can also end a debate, since it dismisses the other person's reasons without answering them†. And a genuine realist has a reason to keep listening, because she thinks there is something to find out and that she might have got it wrong.
? WHY IT MATTERS
Why this block is where the steelman lives

The section's steelman, humility, draws on the same facts as this block. So when you meet a statement here, write the steelman first and grant its kernel, that moral judgement is fallible. Then answer it with line 3. Humility is itself a realist's virtue, because only someone who thinks there is a right answer can worry about missing it. The concession you owe in return goes in your last body section. The realist's weak point is access, not existence, since consensus can err and in 2007 both camps over s 377A arguably claimed moral truth. The self-critique bank puts it in one clause: consensus gauges morality but does not ground it (1.4).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Four appeals, four replies
The appealWhat is true in itWhy the conclusion fails
"Nobody can agree."People do disagree, deeply.Disagreement shows that someone is wrong. TSH explains it by social pressure, weakness and self-interest.
"We have been wrong before."Slavery was once widely accepted.Calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer. Go slowly, but do not abstain.
"It is safer not to judge."Coercing people on a mistaken view does real harm.Refusing to act on a judgement can amount to acting on its opposite (4.7). Refusing to judge slavery would have meant leaving it in place.
"Imposing values is intolerant."Some realists have been bigots.So have some sceptics. Realism, properly held, commits you to deliberation.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

That nobody can agree shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about, just as old disputes over the number of planets never showed there were no planets. TSH explains moral disagreement without denying moral truth. The mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience. The claim that we have been wrong before therefore counsels slowness, not abstention, because calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer. Nor is imposition a realist monopoly, since sceptics too can be bigoted, and genuine realism commits one to deliberation.

64.4 Is–ought

🧩 Practise 4.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.4 Is–ought (word for word)
4.4 Is–ought Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should
  1. Hume's gap holds: [the biological facts] alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts: the basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as [embryology] show only how they apply.
  3. So [it tells us nothing] overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, facts fix the stakes.
  • Hume's two arguments†: (1) wrongness lies in our sentiments, not the act, since reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X"); (2) no "ought" follows from an "is".
  • AGAINST (1)† Statement X is itself neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact, so by its own test it is neither true nor false. (2) The gap is only logical: agreed ought-premises (eg the dignity of man) plus facts yield oughts.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"The embryo has human DNA, so abortion is wrong." Hume says you are missing a step. Facts alone cannot tell you what you should do. You also need a moral premise, such as "it is wrong to kill an innocent human being". Add that, and the facts suddenly matter a lot.

What the statement claims

"Hume showed that one cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is'. Robert George's account of the human embryo is a statement of biological fact. Therefore, it tells us nothing about whether abortion should be legal." (Q59)
"Studies show X, so legislators should do Y."

The two statements make opposite mistakes. The first uses Hume to say that facts are useless in moral argument. The second jumps straight from facts to a law, as if Hume had never written. Both misread what Hume's gap actually shows.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Hume's gap holds. A fact about embryos, however well established, cannot on its own settle whether abortion should be legal. An argument of the form "the embryo is a living human organism, so abortion should be banned" is invalid as it stands, because the "should" appears from nowhere. Something must be added.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts. Finnis accepts that you cannot infer values from facts. His basic goods, such as life and knowledge, are self-evident. We grasp them directly by practical reason, and do not deduce them from biology. Facts such as embryology then show only how those goods apply, for instance whether a particular being is alive and human.
  3. So "it tells us nothing" overstates. Hume's gap is only a logical point. It removes the shortcut from fact to ought, but not the facts. Once the parties agree on a moral premise (the sheet's example is the dignity of man), the facts fix the stakes and can decide a great deal.

Liu's lesson from this exercise was that big moral disputes break down into smaller ones†. Keep asking "why?" of each moral premise and you reach a bedrock premise, such as "equality matters", that is hard to reason past. Finnis tries to supply bedrock goods that everyone can recognise (Lesson 5).

The extra lines, explained

  • Hume's two arguments†. Hume has two arguments, and students often know only the second. The first is "Statement X": wrongness lies in our feelings, not in the act, because reason only knows relations of ideas (logic and maths) and matters of fact (what we observe), and moral claims are neither. The second is the is–ought gap: no "ought" follows from an "is". The first denies that moral claims can be true. The second only says they cannot be proved from facts alone.
  • AGAINST · Statement X fails its own test†. Apply Statement X to itself. It is not a truth of logic or maths, and it is not something we observe either. So by its own test it is neither true nor false. Liu's slide puts this as a question: is Statement X self-refuting? Use it as a short, sharp reply whenever a statement leans on Hume's first argument.
  • AGAINST · the gap is only logical. Harris notes that, on the standard reading, Hume makes a point about logic and nothing more. It takes away natural law's deductive shortcut from nature to duty. But, Harris adds, if the parties share an ought-premise, such as the dignity of man, ought-conclusions do follow from facts. So Hume's gap sinks a moral argument only where no premise is shared.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Repairing the embryo argument (Q59)
StepThe embryo argument
Fact (is)Robert George: the embryo is a living human organism.
Missing premise (ought)It is wrong intentionally to kill an innocent human being.
ConclusionAbortion should be restricted.

Q59 says George's fact "tells us nothing". That overstates. Hume's gap shows only that the middle row must be argued for. If someone accepts that premise, George's biology decides a great deal. If someone rejects it, the argument has moved to the right place, the premise, and away from the biology. Finnis would add that the good at stake, life, is self-evident, and that embryology shows only how it applies here. Either way the dispute shrinks to one bedrock premise.

ℹ NOTE
Where this block comes back

Core card C uses this block against statements that treat facts about opinion as decisive (13.5, L3). Facts about what people think are evidence to weigh, and they fix the stakes. But they cannot settle what the law should be, because no ought follows from an is alone. The card's pivot puts it in one line: what people made is not what they should make. The same move answers polls in 7.11.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Hume's gap holds, since the biological facts about the embryo cannot alone settle whether abortion should be legal. But the gap is only logical. Finnis draws no ought from facts at all, because the basic goods are self-evident and facts such as embryology show only how they apply. Once an ought-premise is agreed, for example that it is wrong intentionally to kill an innocent human being, the facts fix the stakes. So the claim that George's biology tells us nothing overstates Hume, and the real dispute is about the premise, not the inference. Hume's other argument fares worse, since Statement X is neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact, and so fails its own test.

74.5 Hidden judgment

🧩 Practise 4.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.5 Hidden judgment (word for word)
4.5 Hidden judgment consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral
  1. Calling [X] not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is autonomy's primacy, which rests on equal worth; unlimited, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So [the law should stay neutral] fails: where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices; there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).
  • Finnis charges that appealing only to subjective preference, then grounding that in the intrinsic value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"It's not wrong because it's between consenting adults and hurts no one." That sounds neutral, but it assumes something big: that what consenting adults choose matters most. That is a moral view, and maybe a good one, but it is not "no view at all".

What the statement claims

"Act X is not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else." (Q75)
"The state should stay neutral."

The statement presents itself as the absence of a moral view. It does not say X is good, only that X is not wrong, and it asks the state simply to stay out. It is tempting because consent and harm sound like plain facts that anyone can check. The block shows that a moral judgement is hiding inside the word "because".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Not wrong because consensual and harmless" is a moral verdict. It is not a neutral fact. It states a theory of what makes conduct wrong, namely that only harm to others, or harm without consent, does. That is a substantive moral position, held by many people and denied by others.
  2. The hidden premise is that autonomy comes first, and it rests on equal worth. Why should a person's consent settle the matter? Because, the answer runs, each person has equal moral worth and so deserves to run their own life. TSH then sets a dilemma. If autonomy is unlimited, anyone may do anything to anyone, and everyone ends up equally worthless. If autonomy has limits, such as bodily integrity and property, those limits form a moral law, which is realism.
  3. So "the law should stay neutral" fails. Deciding where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices. A child's consent, a desperate seller's consent and a third party's interests all need a moral ruling before the "consensual and harmless" test can even be applied. In the 2007 s 377A debate Thio Li-ann put it in one image: there is no Switzerland of ambivalence.

Neither side spoke as a sceptic. Siew Kum Hong argued that only recognisable, tangible harm should count. Thio Li-ann argued that intangible harm counts too. That is a disagreement about where harm stops, which line 3 says is a moral choice. The scene also supports the Conclusion's concession. In 2007 both camps arguably claimed moral truth, which shows how hard access is, even for people who agree that there is a truth to find. The phrase Switzerland of ambivalence is this block's signature, so use it here.

The extra line, explained

  • Finnis's charge of self-contradiction. Finnis attacks liberals who say the law should respect only what people subjectively prefer, and who then defend that by appeal to the intrinsic value of self-governance. The second step treats self-governance as a real good that binds everyone, which the first step said there was no such thing as. Finnis calls this outright self-contradiction. Use it to show that the "neutral" liberal is quietly relying on an objective good.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Applying the hidden judgment: Q75's three cases

Q75 asks you to apply the analysis to three cases. In each, the "consensual and harmless" test cannot be applied until a moral question is answered.

CaseWhose consent counts?Where does harm stop?
An adult sells one of her kidneysIs a poor seller's consent free, or pressured by need?Is the risk to her own health a harm the law may weigh?
A commercial surrogacy arrangementThe adults consent. The child, a third party, cannot.Does the arrangement touch the child's interests?
An adult gambles away his life savings at a casinoIs his consent clouded, as Hart asks of cravings (7.2)?Do his dependants count as "others" who are harmed?

None of these questions can be read off the facts. That is line 3 in action, and it is why a liberal legislator who relies on the hidden principle still has to make moral choices at every step.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Calling conduct not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact. Its hidden premise is the primacy of autonomy, which rests on the equal worth of persons. As TSH shows, unlimited autonomy leaves everyone "equally worthless", while limited autonomy is a moral law. So the claim that the law should stay neutral fails, since where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices. As Thio Li-ann told Parliament in 2007, there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence". Finnis adds that grounding respect for mere preference in the intrinsic value of self-governance is "outright self-contradiction".

84.6 Whatever is enacted?

🧩 Practise 4.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.6 Whatever is enacted? (word for word)
4.6 Whatever is enacted? law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer
  1. If [law is whatever is enacted], nothing stands above the lawgiver, and man arguably becomes "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying [citizens are safer] if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising [what is enacted], without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.
  • Alexy: only the "strong" connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one (RF) keeps law open to critique. Hart's case for separation: 8.2.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If "law is whatever Parliament says", then nothing stands above Parliament. Some people say that is safer for citizens. But "it's safer" is a moral claim about what is good for people. You cannot escape morality by saying the law has no moral limits.

What the statement claims

"Failing that, law should simply be whatever the people's elected representatives enact. Either way, citizens are safer, because no leader will ever again be able to dress up his laws as moral truth." (Q30)
"Law is whatever people say is law." "Separating law from morality is safer for citizens."

This is the sceptic's view carried over to law. Liu's slide asks what is left if morals are set aside, and one answer is that law is simply whatever people say it is, with any content at all†. The statement adds a reason. If law makes no claim to moral truth, no leader can hide behind it. It is tempting because it sounds like a protection against tyranny.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. If law is whatever is enacted, nothing stands above the lawgiver. If morality is also mere opinion, as the sceptic says, there is then no standard by which to call an enactment bad, only a different preference. Liu asks whether that makes man the ultimate lawgiver† over his fellow men, with whoever holds power answering to nobody.
  2. "Citizens are safer" is itself a moral claim. It is a claim about the value of safety, liberty and the proper limits of power. So the statement cannot avoid morality. It uses a moral argument to tell us to keep morality out of law.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising what is enacted. A touchstone is a standard you test something against. Natural law lets citizens say an enactment is unjust. It does not have to say that every merely unjust enactment is not law. That stronger claim is a different thesis, explained below.

The extra line, explained

  • Alexy · strong v weak connection. Positivists worry that linking law and morality makes people uncritical. If law is necessarily moral, then whatever is law must be right, so nobody questions it. This is the objection of uncritical legitimation. Alexy accepts that it fits the strong connection thesis, on which a norm is law only if it is morally right. But Radbruch's formula (RF) uses the weak thesis. A law loses its legal character only when its injustice becomes intolerable. On the weak thesis plenty of ordinary law is unjust and still law, so citizens can and should criticise it. Hart's own case for keeping law and morality apart, which rests on candour, is in 8.2.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

If law is whatever is enacted, nothing stands above the lawgiver, and man arguably becomes the ultimate lawgiver over his fellows. The claim that citizens are safer when law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power, so the statement cannot keep morality out. Natural law therefore stays a touchstone for criticising what is enacted, without denying that merely unjust enactments are law. As Alexy shows, only the strong connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation. The weak thesis of Radbruch's formula keeps ordinary law open to critique, which is the very safety the statement wants.

94.7 Objectivity anchor

🧩 Practise 4.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 4.7 Objectivity anchor (word for word)
4.7 Objectivity anchor
Paragraph Demanding [tolerance / deference] because [morality is just opinion / personal / a social construct] defeats itself: the demand binds others, which abandons subjectivism, and if it rests on equal moral worth the sceptic is a moral realist. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets; the unproven is not the false. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out is itself a moral choice. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH).
  • Use: 4.1–4.3, 4.5 (just opinion; nobody can agree; it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality; private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); 10.4 (no one can say objectively).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some arguments come up in every topic, so it pays to have one ready. This block is a ready-made paragraph for any statement that leans on "morality is just opinion", whether the statement is about judges, lawyers, Parliament or the Constitution. It packs the whole archetype into four moves. The demand defeats itself, disagreement is not proof, refusing to judge is a choice, and realism means careful deliberation.

What the statement claims

"The moral sceptic makes the safest judge, the most tolerant legislator and the most dependable lawyer." (Q31)

The anchor is for statements like this one, where scepticism is offered as a virtue in some legal actor. It also works whenever a statement in another archetype slips in "equally valid", "personal morality" or "no one can say objectively".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The demand defeats itself. Demanding tolerance, or deference, because morality is just opinion, personal or a social construct binds other people, which subjectivism cannot do. If the demand rests on the equal moral worth of persons, the sceptic is a moral realist (4.2).
  2. Disagreement is not disproof. Disputes no more disprove moral facts than past disputes over the number of planets disproved facts about the planets. What has not been proved has not thereby been shown false (4.3).
  3. Refusing to judge is a choice. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite. A legislator who declines to protect someone, because "who am I to judge?", has in effect judged that the protection was not owed. So keeping morality out of law is itself a moral choice.
  4. Realism means deliberation. Believing in moral truth demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition. A realist argues, listens and stays open to correction, because she might be the one who is wrong (TSH).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The planets, the stick and slavery: three pictures of "unproven is not false"
PictureWhat it showsUse it to answer…
The planets (the signature)Astronomers have disagreed about how many planets there are. The planets were there all along, whatever anyone believed."Nobody can agree, so there is no truth."
A stick bent in water (the alternate)A straight stick looks bent when half in water. How a thing appears and how it is can come apart."Things look different from where each culture stands, so there is no fact."
Slavery (4.3)Whole societies once accepted it. We now call that an error."We were wrong before, so nothing is really right."

Use only one of the first two in a script. The signature ledger gives the planets to 4.7 and keeps the stick as the alternate (1.5).

Core card P2: "Moral opinions are equally valid"
▤ 13.3, Core A
  1. 1Verdict. Equal validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, which counsels deliberation, provisional judgement and caution in coercion, not silence.
  2. 2Hart rejects it. A society's shared views can be wicked, so they must be tested by critical morality (7.3).
  3. 3Devlin partly accepts it, which makes him a dangerous ally. He enforces a society's actual morality, honestly held, right or wrong, so he never asks whether it is true. But he uses that to justify enforcement, the opposite of the tolerance the sceptic wants.
  4. 4Rawls partly accepts it†. He treats reasonable doctrines as equally valid from the start, unreasonable ones excepted (6.10).
  5. 5Finnis rejects it, but not for one right answer. He accepts that a range of opinions can be valid, not just one (6.10).
  6. 6Pivot and repair. Scepticism is answered by the anchor. Enforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate. Scepticism is no objection, but fallibility is a reason for restraint.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph (the anchor, filled in)

Demanding tolerance because morality is just opinion defeats itself. The demand binds others, which abandons subjectivism, and if it rests on the equal moral worth of persons, the sceptic is a moral realist. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets disproved facts about the planets, and the unproven is not the false. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out of law is itself a moral choice. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where else the anchor works
ArchetypeTrigger wordsWhat the anchor answers
4 (4.1–4.3, 4.5)just opinion; nobody can agree; it is saferThe home use.
11 (11.7)personal morality; private conscienceA judge who says "my morals are private" still meets the reply that subjectivism defeats itself.
6 (6.10)equally valid"Equally valid" defeats itself.
7 (7.5)neutralRepeal is not neutral either.
10 (10.4)no one can say objectivelyRoles are not wholly idiosyncratic, and prudence applies the virtues.

10Putting it together: Practice Q28

"Morality is just opinion. Every culture draws the line between right and wrong in a different place, and after thousands of years nobody has proved which side is correct; even so-called universal human rights are merely one tradition's preferences. Since nothing in ethics is black and white, a moral view can no more be true or false than a taste for durian. A multicultural society should therefore accept that no conduct is objectively wrong, and condemn as intolerant any legislator or judge who uses the law to insist otherwise."

Instruction: evaluate the statement by reference to Hume, Finnis and Alexy, and say what the analysis suggests about the use of moral scepticism in arguments for law reform.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement asks a multicultural society to condemn as intolerant anyone who insists that some conduct is objectively wrong. That demand is itself an objective moral claim, so the statement defeats itself. I make three claims. First, the statement runs together relativism, scepticism and Hume's non-cognitivism, and none of them shows there is no moral truth. Second, its conclusion, tolerance as a duty binding legislators and judges, presupposes the very objectivity it denies. Third, the sceptic is right that our access to moral truth is fallible, but that calls for deliberation and provisional judgement in law reform, not for silence.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Hume and the map (4.1, 4.4). The durian, and Hume's non-cognitivism behind it. "Nobody has proved" assumes that proof means deduction, which science fails too. Statement X fails its own test.
  2. Self-refutation and Finnis (4.2, 4.4). "Condemn as intolerant" binds others. TSH shows that a relativist who binds outsiders appeals to a standard above cultures, and that grounding it in equal worth makes him a realist. Finnis's goods are self-evident, not inferred from culture or fact, so they answer "nobody has proved" without needing a deduction.
  3. Alexy, judges and law reform (4.6, 8.3). The weak connection thesis keeps law open to critique. Against the argument from relativism, Alexy says that in rights-steeped states a consensus on rights answers the relativist judge. Self-critique: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps over s 377A arguably claimed moral truth.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close (answering the extra question)

Moral scepticism is therefore a poor tool for law reform. It cannot deliver the tolerance it promises, since that promise is itself a moral norm, and its reasons are inconclusive, though that proves no moral fact either. The realist's weak point is access, not existence. Reformers do better to argue openly for the moral premise their proposal needs, holding it provisionally and demanding more of it the more coercive the law.

ℹ NOTE
Engine tools that fit archetype 4
  • The self-application hook (1.2) is made for this archetype. The statement is itself a moral verdict, so it cannot be true in the sense it claims. Use it once per script.
  • Core card A lists self-refutation as flaw F3, answered with that hook and a numbered thesis (13.3).
  • If you need a one-sentence repair, use Core A's: enforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate, and fallibility, not scepticism, is the reason for restraint.

11Recap

Archetype 4 on one card
▤ Sections 4.1–4.7
  1. 1Split relativism, scepticism and non-cognitivism. Proof is not only deduction (4.1).
  2. 2The demanding sceptic refutes himself, but content stays open (4.2, 14.7).
  3. 3Disagreement shows someone is wrong. Past error counsels slowness, not silence (4.3).
  4. 4Hume's gap is only logical. Supply and argue the ought-premise (4.4).
  5. 5"Consensual and harms no one" hides a moral verdict (4.5).
  6. 6"Whatever is enacted" and "safer" are moral claims. Only the strong thesis risks uncritical legitimation (4.6).
  7. 7The anchor: self-refutation, the planets, refusing is a choice, deliberation (4.7).
  8. 8Steelman: humility shows fallibility, not that there is no truth. Concede access, not existence.
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a sign on a classroom wall. It reads THERE ARE NO MORAL RULES, and underneath, in smaller letters, AND YOU MUST RESPECT THAT. The second line breaks the first, which is self-refutation. Through the window is the night sky. People have argued about how many planets there are, and the planets never changed, so disagreement is not disproof. On the board, write your own moral view in pencil, not pen. It is firm enough to act on and open to correction, which is the provisional judgement and deliberation that fallibility really calls for.

← Lesson 3: Rule of lawLesson 5: Finnis →
LESSON 5 · ARCHETYPE 5 · ABOUT 66 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 44 QUESTIONS

Finnis for law-makers

⚡ BIG IDEA

Finnis gives legislators real limits (never intend to destroy a basic good) and a framework common good, then leaves much to prudence. He guides law-makers without dictating to them.

ARCHETYPE 5 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
5 Finnis for law-makers
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Finnis gives legislators real limits on [the issue] and leaves much to prudence.
Intro [The statement] assumes that a theory of the good must either [dictate how citizens live / offer no guidance]. Finnis shows a third path. Seven basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield a few absolute limits, such as never intending to kill the innocent, and a common good that is a framework, not a life-plan. Within those limits legislators choose prudently, and reasonable people may differ.
Steelman: for Finnis The best case for [Finnis] is that he guides without dictating: the common good is a framework of conditions, not a life-plan; no value is inferred from fact; and he can say why a law is wrong even if most people approve. This shows that a theory of the good need not be a state life-plan. It does not show [that his goods bind those who reject them]: accessible is not accepted.
Steelman: against Finnis The best case against [Finnis] is method: self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing†, and the means/side-effect line is "honestly pretty artificial" and, since consent cannot cure intended harm, a heavy limit on autonomy†. He is also less liberal than he looks (5.5). This shows that his goods cannot alone justify coercion. It does not show [that he gives no guidance]: the absolutes and the common good remain.
5.1 Goods and priorities basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident, not inferred: anyone reflecting on why they act can grasp [knowledge] as good in itself.
  2. The goods are equally fundamental, though one may prioritise†: there is no objective hierarchy among them.
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and [the state must do the ranking] does not follow.
  • The seven†: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and "religion" (agnostic or negative answers count). They are pre-moral: morality comes with the nine requirements.
  • Test†: strip out every use to the other goods and ask whether something is left.
  • The golfer passing a drowning stranger is indifferent to others easily helped.
5.2 The nine requirements as structure plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure the pursuit of goods, and most transpose to [a legislature], though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each fundamental and irreducible, though they can read as prudent advice†: neglecting (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral.
  3. So I test [the law] chiefly by three: no arbitrary preference among persons (3), respect for every basic good (7) and the common good (8).
  • (1) Coherent plan of life; (2) no arbitrary preference among values, (3) or persons (Golden Rule); (4) detachment: no fanatical policy; (5) commitment: keep faith; (6) efficiency within reason (5.4); (7) respect every basic value in every act (5.3); (8) common good (5.5); (9) conscience.
5.3 Absolutes and double effect shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life directly as a means, so [shooting one hostage to free ten] is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention: damaging a good as means or end differs from damaging it as a side effect, though plans cannot be characterised "ad lib".
  3. So [a foreseen death is just as dead] misses the point: side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.
  • The scientist† who, intending only knowledge, takes a living person's heart acts impermissibly: even as a side effect, the death is unfair.
  • Pregnancy cases† (applied): chemotherapy or removing a cancerous womb treats the mother, death a side effect; direct termination intends it; pre-eclampsia is hard (my reading).
  • TRAP Double effect is Aquinas's; for Finnis the casuists' doctrines are not themselves principles of practical reasonableness. The test is intention, not foresight: a certain death can be a side effect†.
5.4 Against utilitarianism greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings
  1. Finnis calls [the greatest happiness] incoherent outside limited technical contexts: goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are not so much false as senseless.
  2. Nozick's experience machine counts against pleasure as the point of it all: a sensible person would not plug in, wanting to do certain things, not merely feel them.
  3. So maximising [satisfied preferences] is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right.
  • Maximising is reasonable over a wide range of wants, but sadists' preferences are discounted and certain intentional killings and frauds excluded.
  • STEELMAN Efficiency is a real requirement, so [healthcare savings] matter; but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.
5.5 From person to state transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism
  1. Finnis's common good is a set of conditions enabling members to attain reasonable objectives for themselves.
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: committing to a life-plan is nothing like setting out to bake a cake.
  3. Yet it is definite enough to exclude many political arrangements and laws, so [almost no guidance] understates Finnis.
  • LEGISLATOR Working summary†: law is a framework that facilitates the goods, never intends to damage them and may prohibit acts that do; the rest is prudence (hate speech, fake news), weighing chilling effects in particular places† (15.4).
  • CONCEDE Finnis is less liberal than he looks: we must favour the basic goods and discourage their contraries. I concede non-neutrality; the state still keeps only peace and justice.
5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment
  1. Following nature can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends; the Stoics saw man as having natural ends known by the reflective intellect.
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges: many, like "gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and no value is inferred from fact.
  3. So [law should give people what they want] mistakes urges for goods: living from moment to moment on immediate cravings is unreasonable.
5.7 Finnis tested critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
  1. Finnis's weak points are method and the seventh requirement: self-evidence rests on contested intuitions†, the means/side-effect line is "artificial"†, and accessible is not accepted (is [casino gambling] play?).
  2. He replies that there is no magic in the number seven, and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable".
  3. So I concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what [the state] may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
Conclusion Finnis therefore gives legislators real limits: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure conditions in which each citizen pursues a plan of their own. Beyond that, [the issue] calls for prudence, and since his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions and his means/side-effect line is arguably artificial†, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in coercion. [The statement] is [overstated]: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

1Start here: archetype 5 in plain English

Archetype 5 asks one question: what can John Finnis's natural law tell a law-maker? Finnis argues that some things are good for every human being, such as life, knowledge and friendship. He calls them basic goods. He then sets out nine requirements for pursuing those goods reasonably, and from the goods and the requirements he builds an account of what a state may and may not do.

Exam statements in this family push one of two extremes. Some say Finnis's theory is a blueprint, so a state that followed it would dictate how everyone must live. Others say it is so vague, or so personal, that it gives a legislator no real guidance. A third group attacks his method. They say the goods are just his taste, or that his line between intending a harm and foreseeing it is a word game.

Your answer is the same every time. Finnis sets a few firm limits and leaves the rest to prudence. The firm limits come from his seventh requirement, which says never choose directly against a basic good. So a law may never intend to kill the innocent. The rest comes from his common good, which is a framework of conditions in which each citizen pursues a plan of their own. It is not one plan for everybody. Inside that framework legislators use practical judgement, and reasonable people may differ. And because Finnis's starting points are contested, disagreement about them is a reason for caution before the state uses force.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Basic goodsThe seven things Finnis says are worth having for their own sake: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and "religion".
Self-evidentYou see that a good is good by reflecting on why you act. It is not proved from facts about human nature.
Pre-moralThe goods give you reasons to act, but on their own they do not yet say what is morally right. Morality arrives with the nine requirements.
IncommensurableThe goods cannot be measured on one scale. There is no exchange rate between friendship and knowledge.
Practical reasonablenessBringing your own intelligence and judgement to your choices. It is one of the seven goods, and it is also the name for the nine requirements that tell you how to choose well.
The nine requirementsFinnis's tests for a reasonable choice: have a coherent plan, don't play favourites among goods or among people, don't be fanatical, keep your commitments, be efficient within reason, never choose directly against a good, serve the common good, and follow your conscience.
Double effectAquinas's doctrine that aiming at a harm, as your end or your means, differs from accepting it as a foreseen side effect of aiming at something else.
Golden RuleTreat others as you would want to be treated. Finnis uses it to test whether a side effect is fair.
Common goodFor Finnis, a set of conditions that lets each member of a community pursue reasonable goals of their own. It is not a single shared life-plan.
PrudencePractical judgement about the best way to act in particular circumstances, where no rule settles the answer.
Accessible v acceptedDistinction 1.3(12). A reason can be open to everyone in principle (accessible) and still be rejected by many people (not accepted).

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: Finnis gives legislators real limits on the issue and leaves much to prudence.

Put simply, Finnis rules some laws out completely, and for everything else he tells legislators to use good judgement. He accepts that sensible people will reach different answers in that second zone. So a statement that calls Finnis a dictator overstates his theory, and a statement that calls him useless understates it.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement assumes that a theory of the good must either dictate how citizens live or offer no guidance. Finnis shows a third path. Seven basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield a few absolute limits, such as never intending to kill the innocent, and a common good that is a framework, not a life-plan. Within those limits legislators choose prudently, and reasonable people may differ.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. Finnis gives legislators real limits. They must never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and must secure the conditions in which each citizen pursues a plan of their own. Beyond that, the issue calls for prudence. And since Finnis's self-evident goods rest on contested intuitions, and his line between means and side effects is arguably artificial†, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in coercion. The statement is overstated, because Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

The two steelmen

Section 5 gives you two steelmen, because a Finnis question may ask you to defend him or to attack him. Each one tells you what it proves and where it stops.

  • Steelman: for Finnis. Finnis guides without dictating. His common good is a framework of conditions, not a life-plan for the nation. He infers no value from facts about nature. And he can explain why a law is wrong even when most people approve of it, which a theory built on majority feeling cannot do. This shows that a theory of the good need not become a state life-plan. It does not show that his goods bind people who reject them, because accessible is not accepted.
  • Steelman: against Finnis. The best attack is on his method. Liu argues that what feels self-evident depends on intuitions shaped by upbringing†. He also calls the line between means and side effects "honestly pretty artificial", and because consent cannot cure an intended harm, that line puts a heavy limit on personal autonomy†. Finnis is also less liberal than he looks (5.5). This shows that his goods cannot, on their own, justify coercion. It does not show that he gives no guidance, since the absolutes and the common good remain.

The seven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
5.1"Finnis's goods are just his taste, and someone must rank them."They are self-evident on reflection, and none ranks above another. Each person's plan ranks them, not the state.
5.2"The nine requirements are for individuals, not legislatures."Most carry over, except the single life-plan. Test a law chiefly by requirements (3), (7) and (8).
5.3"Count the lives: shoot one hostage to save ten. A foreseen death is just as dead."Never choose directly against a basic good. Intending a death differs from foreseeing it, and side effects are judged by fairness.
5.4"Aim at the greatest happiness of the greatest number."The goods have no common unit, so maximising the total is senseless. Efficiency counts only within reason.
5.5"Finnis's common good is a plan for everyone, or no guidance at all."It is a framework of conditions, not a destination. But it still rules out many laws.
5.6"Follow nature: give people what they want."Urges are not goods. A craving for cruelty answers to no good at all.
5.7"Critically evaluate Finnis. Is casino gambling play?"His weak spots are self-evidence and the side-effect line. Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Finnis gives a few hard limits and a framework, and inside the framework he leaves room for prudence and reasonable disagreement.

2The big picture: Finnis's new natural law

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a good life as a garden with seven kinds of plant: health, learning, play, beauty, friendship, wise choosing and a sense of meaning. You cannot grow them all equally, so you choose. Nine gardening rules tell you how to choose well. Have a plan, don't sneer at any plant, don't favour one gardener over another without reason, don't obsess over one bed, keep tending what you started, don't waste water, never deliberately trample a plant, help the neighbourhood garden, and trust your own judgement. A government is like the council that keeps the shared paths and the water running so that everyone can garden. It does not tell you what to plant.

John Finnis's book Natural Law and Natural Rights rebuilds natural law without deriving "ought" from facts about nature. Fuller (Lesson 3) told us what makes law good as law. Finnis asks the further question that legislators actually argue about: what law should be for. His answer has three layers, and every block in this archetype draws on one of them.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
FinnisThe modern natural lawyer. Seven basic goods are self-evidently worth pursuing, nine requirements tell us how to pursue them reasonably, and the common good is a framework in which each person pursues their own plan. In his article on abortion he adds that the state's job is only to keep peace and justice, using reasons that are open to everyone whatever their religion.
AquinasThe medieval natural lawyer whose tradition Finnis develops. The doctrine of double effect is his, not Finnis's.
The StoicsAncient philosophers who, as Harris describes them, took "follow nature" to mean pursuing the ends human beings are capable of, known by the reflective intellect rather than by urges.
NozickInvented the experience machine, which Finnis uses to show that pleasure is not the point of life.
The utilitariansSay law should aim at the greatest happiness of the greatest number. Finnis's main target in 5.4.
RawlsFinnis's rival on pluralism (Lesson 6). The state should coerce only on reasons every reasonable citizen could accept. Your answer concedes part of this in 5.7.

Layer 1: the seven basic goods

A basic good is something worth having for its own sake, for anyone. Here are Finnis's seven, in the sheet's order†.

#GoodWhat it coversAn example
1LifeBodily and mental health, survival and freedom from pain. Finnis also includes procreation, though he admits that is debatable.Road safety laws and medical schools are ways of pursuing life.
2KnowledgeKnowing the truth for its own sake, not only because it is useful.Chasing down a footnote nobody will ever check, simply because you want to know†.
3PlayActivities enjoyed for their own sake, with no point beyond the activity itself.Chess, football, banter.
4Aesthetic experienceExperiencing beauty, in art or in nature. Unlike play, it need not involve any action of your own.Stopping on the way to work to take in a sunrise†.
5Sociability (friendship)A range, from basic peace and harmony between people up to full friendship, where you act for a friend's sake.Helping a friend with something that matters to them, at a cost to yourself.
6Practical reasonablenessBringing your own intelligence and judgement to your choices, so that your life is shaped by you, not by luck or impulse.Deciding what kind of life to live, and living it.
7"Religion"Thinking about life's ultimate meaning and your place in the order of things. Agnostic or negative answers count. It does not mean organised religion.Someone who concludes that this life is all there is, and so resolves to treat others kindly†.

Three features of the goods matter in every answer.

  • Self-evident, not inferred. Finnis gives almost no argument for each good. He invites you to recognise it in your own life. Because nothing is deduced from facts about nature, he avoids the charge of deriving an "ought" from an "is" (4.4).
  • Pre-moral. The goods supply reasons to act, but on their own they say nothing about what is morally right. Morality arrives only when the nine requirements bear on an actual choice. So "knowledge is good, therefore the state must make you study" skips a whole layer.
  • Equally fundamental and incommensurable. There is no objective ranking of the goods and no common unit to measure them in. Each person may still prioritise. Finnis's scholar ranks knowledge above everything, yet may one day risk his life to save a drowning man. The change is in the scholar's plan, not in the value of the goods.

Layer 2: the nine requirements of practical reasonableness

Knowing that there are seven goods does not tell you what to do. There are many goods, each can be pursued in countless ways, and life is short. So the goods raise the question of what to do, rather than answering it. Finnis's nine requirements answer it. All nine bind together, and he says each is fundamental and cannot be derived from the others. The checklist below runs one choice through all nine. 5.2 shows what each one asks of a legislature.

Layer 3: the common good and the state

The eighth requirement is the bridge from the person to the community. Finnis's common good is a set of conditions that enables each member of a community to pursue reasonable goals for themselves. It is not one shared goal. In his article on abortion Finnis adds two limits from the natural law tradition. The state's role is not to make people integrally good, that is, good in every part of their lives, but only to keep peace and justice. And rulers may impose only principles that are accessible to all, whatever their religion.

The theory judges law in two ways†. It judges a law directly, so a law that authorises an act against a basic good is wrong (for Finnis, the death penalty and abortion). And it judges how well the state helps people pursue the goods, where even coordination counts: one rule about which side of the road to drive on lets everyone travel safely. Finnis thus supplies substance where Fuller supplies procedure (13.1).

Key distinctions

  • Goods v requirements. The goods are pre-moral reasons, and the nine requirements turn them into moral "oughts". Life is a good, and requirement (7) applies, so we ought not to kill.
  • Intending v foreseeing. Damaging a good as your end or your means is barred. Damaging it as a side effect is judged by fairness (5.3).
  • Weigh v veto. Requirement (6) lets you weigh consequences. Requirement (7) can veto an act however good its consequences.
  • Urges v ends (distinction 1.3(14)). "Human nature" can mean what we crave or what we are capable of. Finnis takes nothing from urges (5.6).
  • Accessible v accepted (distinction 1.3(12)). A reason open to everyone may still be rejected by many. This is where Finnis is most exposed (5.7).
⚠ TRAP
Finnis is not a crude perfectionist

Do not write that Finnis wants the state to make citizens pursue all seven goods. The goods are pre-moral, people may reasonably prioritise them differently, and the state's job is only peace and justice. What Finnis forbids is acting against a good. He is far less concerned that everyone pursues every good. He is not neutral either, as 5.5 shows, but he is liberal in means, not in ends.

Question wordsMoveGo to
"greatest happiness"no common unit5.4
"human nature"; "urges"ends, not urges5.6
