35.1 Goods and priorities

🧩 Practise 5.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.1 Goods and priorities (word for word)
5.1 Goods and priorities basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident, not inferred: anyone reflecting on why they act can grasp [knowledge] as good in itself.
  2. The goods are equally fundamental, though one may prioritise†: there is no objective hierarchy among them.
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and [the state must do the ranking] does not follow.
  • The seven†: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and "religion" (agnostic or negative answers count). They are pre-moral: morality comes with the nine requirements.
  • Test†: strip out every use to the other goods and ask whether something is left.
  • The golfer passing a drowning stranger is indifferent to others easily helped.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Is knowledge more important than friendship? Finnis says there is no fixed ranking, because each good is basic. A scholar may put knowledge first and a parent may put family first, and both can be reasonable. The ranking happens inside each person's plan of life. It is not something the state has to do for everyone.

What the statement claims

"Talk of knowledge, friendship or play being 'obviously' good for everyone is just one person's taste dressed up as truth." (Q37)
"Since the goods of life cannot be ranked against one another, no theory can tell a golfer whether to finish his round or save a stranger drowning nearby, so the state must do the ranking for him." (Q45)

The first statement says the basic goods are Finnis's personal preferences. The second accepts that the goods are unranked but draws a dramatic conclusion: if no theory can rank them, the state must. Both are tempting. Finnis really does give almost no argument for his list, and "no ranking" can sound like "no guidance".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The goods are seen by reflection, not taken from Finnis's taste. Ask yourself why you are doing something, and keep asking. Sooner or later you reach something like knowledge, which you see is worth having in itself. Finnis calls this self-evident. Nothing is inferred from facts, and his method is an invitation to recognise the good in your own life rather than a proof.
  2. The goods are equally fundamental, though each person may prioritise†. There is no objective hierarchy among them. Each one, when you focus on it, can reasonably look like the most important, which is why a drowning person thinks only of life and a scholar mostly of knowledge. You may rank them for yourself, but no single ranking binds everybody.
  3. So life-plans rank the goods, and it does not follow that the state must. The statement jumps from "no objective ranking" to "the state must rank". Finnis draws the opposite conclusion. Because no ranking is objectively right, the ranking belongs to each person's reasonable plan of life, and the state's job is to secure the conditions in which those plans can be pursued.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is it a basic good? Liu's strip test†

Strip out everything the candidate does to help you get the other goods. If something worth having is still left, it may be basic. If nothing is left, it is only a means.

CandidateStrip out its uses, and…Verdict
KnowledgeA fact that will never help you, such as an obscure footnote, still feels worth knowingBasic
GossipIt is low-grade knowledge, but still a way of knowingWeak participation in knowledge, not a counter-example
MoneyRemove what it buys and nothing is leftOnly a means. Finnis calls overvaluing wealth unreasonable
PleasureIt comes with the goods, but a dry, joyless search for truth is still good as far as it goesAn aspect of the goods, not the point of them
FriendshipRemove the help a friend gives you, and caring for them for their own sake remainsBasic

Liu adds that someone who lacks a good does not show it is not a good†. A person driven to suicide by suffering is already deprived of life's goods. That does not show life is not one.

The extra lines, explained

  • The seven†, and why they are pre-moral. The sheet lists the seven goods so that you can name them in one sentence, and adds that they are pre-moral. They tell you what is worth pursuing, but morality only arrives with the nine requirements (5.2).
  • Liu's test†. Strip out every use a candidate has for the other goods and ask whether something is left. This is how you defend the list against "it is just his taste", because it turns a bare intuition into a test the reader can run.
  • The golfer. A golfer walks past a stranger drowning nearby to keep his tee time. Finnis treats this as indifference to others whom one could easily help, which breaches requirement (3). Use it directly against Q45. The goods may be unranked, but that does not leave the golfer without guidance, so the state need not step in to rank the goods for him.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement mistakes self-evidence for taste. Finnis's seven basic goods are not inferred from facts but grasped by anyone who reflects on why they act, as when knowledge is seen to be good in itself. The goods are equally fundamental, and while each person may prioritise them, there is no objective hierarchy among them. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and "the state must do the ranking" does not follow. Nor does the lack of a ranking leave us without guidance. The golfer who walks past a drowning stranger shows indifference to others he could easily help, which Finnis's third requirement condemns.

45.2 The nine requirements as structure

🧩 Practise 5.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.2 The nine requirements as structure (word for word)
5.2 The nine requirements as structure plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure the pursuit of goods, and most transpose to [a legislature], though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each fundamental and irreducible, though they can read as prudent advice†: neglecting (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral.
  3. So I test [the law] chiefly by three: no arbitrary preference among persons (3), respect for every basic good (7) and the common good (8).
  • (1) Coherent plan of life; (2) no arbitrary preference among values, (3) or persons (Golden Rule); (4) detachment: no fanatical policy; (5) commitment: keep faith; (6) efficiency within reason (5.4); (7) respect every basic value in every act (5.3); (8) common good (5.5); (9) conscience.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The nine requirements are like the rules of a good kitchen. Plan your menu, don't waste ingredients, never ruin one on purpose, and cook fairly for everyone at the table. A government kitchen can follow most of the same rules. The one difference is that it does not cook a single meal that everyone must eat.

What the statement claims

"Most of Finnis's requirements of practical reasonableness, such as a coherent plan of life, detachment, commitment and efficiency within reason, are framed as guidance for an individual living a good life. Can they be transposed into guidance for a state making laws?" (Q52)
"A flourishing life is devoted single-mindedly to one great project and pursued with maximum efficiency; spreading oneself across friendship, play, learning and faith is mere dabbling." (Q45)

The first is a question, but it hides an assumption: rules for living a good life may not work for a parliament. The second statement turns two requirements upside down. It praises the single-minded devotion to one project that detachment warns against, and the unlimited efficiency that requirement (6) keeps "within reason".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Most of the nine carry over to a legislature, except the single life-plan. The requirements structure how anyone pursues the goods, and most of them make sense for a law-maker. Make coherent policy, don't treat citizens unequally without reason, don't pursue one goal at any cost, be efficient, never authorise acts aimed at destroying a basic good, and serve the common good. The one that does not fit is the plan of life, because a state governs millions of people with different plans (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, but some read like prudent advice†. Finnis says each requirement is fundamental and irreducible, and a choice must satisfy all nine to be fully reasonable. Liu doubts that they are all moral in the same way. Someone who neglects detachment (4) or commitment (5) seems unwise rather than wicked†.
  3. So test a law chiefly by three of them. The sharpest tests for a law are no arbitrary preference among persons (3), respect for every basic good (7) and the common good (8). Requirement (3) catches laws that discriminate without a reason. Requirement (7) catches laws that authorise choosing against a good. Requirement (8) asks whether the law helps people pursue the goods at all.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Transposing the nine to a legislature

Practice Q52 asks you to take at least three requirements and say what each would demand of a legislature. Here are all nine.

RequirementFor a personFor a legislature
(1) Coherent plan of lifeGeneral policies, such as "greens at every meal", not a deathbed test for every lunch†Coherent programmes, not knee-jerk laws. No single plan for every citizen
(2) No arbitrary preference among valuesNever treat a good as worthlessNever treat a basic good as of no account
(3) No arbitrary preference among personsThe Golden RuleNo arbitrary distinctions between citizens (15.4)
(4) DetachmentDon't stake everything on one projectNo fanatical policy, pursued at any cost
(5) CommitmentKeep faith with your commitmentsKeep faith with programmes once adopted, and do not drop them lightly. Liu reads (4) and (5) alike as prudent advice†
(6) Efficiency within reasonUse limited time and means wellCost–benefit reasoning, within limits (5.4)
(7) Respect every basic valueNever choose directly against a goodNever authorise acts that intend to destroy a good (5.3)
(8) Common goodFavour the good of your communitiesSecure the conditions in which all can flourish (5.5)
(9) ConscienceFollow your own reasoned judgementEach law-maker stays responsible for their own judgement

What is gained is a structure with real limits. What is lost is the single plan of life, and with it any idea that the state should choose one way of living for everyone.

The extra line, explained

  • The list of nine, with its cross-links. The sheet ties efficiency (6) to 5.4, respect for every basic value (7) to 5.3 and the common good (8) to 5.5. In an answer, name the nine quickly, then spend your words on the three that bite. Against Q45, use detachment (4) and requirement (2): a life given single-mindedly to one project stakes everything on it and treats the other goods as worthless.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Finnis's nine requirements structure the pursuit of the basic goods, and most of them transpose to a legislature, although a state has no single life-plan. A legislature can make coherent policy, avoid fanatical goals, weigh costs and benefits within reason, never authorise acts that intend to destroy a basic good, and serve the common good. All nine bind together, each fundamental and irreducible, though some read as prudent advice: neglecting detachment or commitment looks unwise rather than immoral. I therefore test the law chiefly by three: no arbitrary preference among persons, respect for every basic good, and the common good.

55.3 Absolutes and double effect

🧩 Practise 5.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.3 Absolutes and double effect (word for word)
5.3 Absolutes and double effect shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life directly as a means, so [shooting one hostage to free ten] is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention: damaging a good as means or end differs from damaging it as a side effect, though plans cannot be characterised "ad lib".
  3. So [a foreseen death is just as dead] misses the point: side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.
  • The scientist† who, intending only knowledge, takes a living person's heart acts impermissibly: even as a side effect, the death is unfair.
  • Pregnancy cases† (applied): chemotherapy or removing a cancerous womb treats the mother, death a side effect; direct termination intends it; pre-eclampsia is hard (my reading).
  • TRAP Double effect is Aquinas's; for Finnis the casuists' doctrines are not themselves principles of practical reasonableness. The test is intention, not foresight: a certain death can be a side effect†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two doctors. One gives a patient a strong painkiller to ease pain, knowing it may shorten the patient's life. The other gives an overdose in order to end the patient's life. Both patients die. Finnis says the acts are different. The first doctor aims at relieving pain and accepts the death as a side effect. The second aims at death. The seventh requirement forbids aiming at the destruction of a basic good, but it judges side effects differently.

What the statement claims

"Morality is about outcomes, and a decent person simply counts the lives at stake. If a gunman will release ten hostages once you shoot one of them, you should shoot; and a scientist who could save thousands by removing one healthy person's heart for research should be free to do so. Lawmakers who distinguish between harm a person intends and harm he merely foresees are playing with words: a foreseen death is just as dead. The only honest test of any act, private or public, is whether it leaves the world better off." (Q38)

The statement makes three moves. Count the lives, so shoot the hostage. Let the scientist do the same sum. And dismiss the line between intending and foreseeing as wordplay. It is tempting because counting lives looks like plain decency, and because the difference between intending and foreseeing a death can seem empty when the person is dead either way.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes. Requirement (7) says never choose directly against a basic good. Applied to life, it means never take a life directly as a means to something else. So shooting one hostage to free ten is barred, however many lives the shot would save. No weighing happens here, because (7) is a veto, not a factor.
  2. What you intend defines the act. Finnis identifies acts primarily by intention. Damaging a good as your end (what you want) or as your means (how your plan works) is different from damaging it as a side effect (something you foresee but do not aim at). But you cannot redescribe your plan however you like. Plans cannot be characterised "ad lib". The man pushed off a footbridge to stop a runaway trolley is still the means. To claim you hoped he would survive is fanciful, because his body must stop the trolley†.
  3. So "a foreseen death is just as dead" misses the point. Side effects are not automatically allowed. They are judged too, by fairness (the Golden Rule) and by the commitments you have made. What Finnis refuses is the sum, adding up lives saved against lives lost as if they were units on one scale.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Running the two cases through 15.3
StepThe hostageThe scientist†
(1) Which good is pursued?Life, for the tenKnowledge
(2) Is a good damaged as end or means?Yes. Killing the one is the means to the gunman's bargain. The release would come later, by the gunman's own free choiceNo. He does not want the death, and his research would succeed just as well if the donor somehow survived
(3) Is the side effect fair?Does not ariseNo. He would never accept losing his own heart for someone else's research
VerdictBarred, even if the hostage volunteersImpermissible, because unfair

The two cases fail at different steps. The hostage shows the absolute bar on intended harm. The scientist shows that even a true side effect must pass the fairness test, so the distinction is no loophole.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Liu's rulings on framework 15.3†
CaseRulingWhy
Shoot one hostage, even a volunteerBarredThe killing is the means. Consent does not help
Push a man off a footbridge to stop a trolleyBarredHis body is the means
Injure yourself for an insurance payoutBarredThe self-injury is the means
The death penalty, even for HitlerBarredThe death is the end, or the means of protecting society
Euthanasia, even on requestBarredKilling is the means of ending suffering
SuicideBarredIt chooses directly against life
Switch a runaway trolley onto a track with one personPermitted or arguableThe death is a side effect of diverting it
Triage: leave the dying to save the savablePermitted or arguableNot saving is not killing
A mining job that will damage your lungsPermitted or arguableA side effect of productive work
Shoot an attacker to disarm him, foreseeing deathPermitted or arguableYou aim at disarming, not killing

The sheet's rule of thumb: requirement (6) weighs, and requirement (7) vetoes.

The extra lines, explained

  • The scientist†. A scientist who wants only knowledge removes a living person's heart for research. Even if the donor's death is truly a side effect, the act is impermissible because it is unfair. Use it to show that double effect is not a loophole.
  • Pregnancy cases†, applied (my reading). Chemotherapy for a pregnant woman with cancer, or removing a cancerous womb, treats the mother, and the unborn child's death is a side effect. A direct termination intends the death. Pre-eclampsia is a hard case. Present this as your application of Finnis, not his stated view. It is the alternative signature example to the hostage and scientist (1.5).
  • TRAP · whose doctrine, and which test. Double effect is Aquinas's doctrine. Finnis treats it, like other doctrines of the casuists (moralists who worked out rules for hard cases), as a useful summary, not as a principle of practical reasonableness in its own right. And the test is intention, not foresight. A death that is certain to happen can still be a side effect†, so "he knew it would happen, so he intended it" is a mistake.
  • The critique to pair with it. Liu calls the line "honestly pretty artificial"†: it clashes with many intuitions, gives little help to someone facing an attacker, and refuses even the volunteer hostage. That is the Steelman against Finnis, developed in 5.7.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement's sum is exactly what Finnis's seventh requirement forbids. Never choosing directly against a basic good yields absolutes, such as never taking life directly as a means, so shooting one hostage to free ten is barred however many are saved. Acts are identified primarily by intention: damaging a good as an end or a means differs from damaging it as a side effect, though a plan cannot be redescribed at will. "A foreseen death is just as dead" therefore misses the point, since side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum. That is why the scientist who takes a living person's heart acts wrongly even if the death is only a side effect, because he could not accept it were he the one harmed. I concede that the line is arguably artificial, and that since consent cannot cure intended harm it is a heavy limit on autonomy†.

65.4 Against utilitarianism

🧩 Practise 5.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.4 Against utilitarianism (word for word)
5.4 Against utilitarianism greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings
  1. Finnis calls [the greatest happiness] incoherent outside limited technical contexts: goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are not so much false as senseless.
  2. Nozick's experience machine counts against pleasure as the point of it all: a sensible person would not plug in, wanting to do certain things, not merely feel them.
  3. So maximising [satisfied preferences] is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right.
  • Maximising is reasonable over a wide range of wants, but sadists' preferences are discounted and certain intentional killings and frauds excluded.
  • STEELMAN Efficiency is a real requirement, so [healthcare savings] matter; but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Utilitarianism says: add up all the happiness, and choose whatever gives the biggest total. Finnis says you cannot add apples, music and friendship into one number, because there is no common unit. So "maximise the total good" is not just wrong, it is meaningless, except for small technical problems where a common measure exists.

What the statement claims

"[Lawmakers] should aim instead at the greatest happiness of the greatest number, which can be measured and calculated as scientifically as a national budget." (Q30)
"A good legal system gives people whatever makes them happy … the law should respect that and maximise satisfied preferences across society." (Q37)
A minister argues: "Smokers impose fewer long-term costs on the healthcare system because they tend to die earlier. On a proper calculation of costs and benefits, the State has no reason to discourage smoking." (Q35)

All three treat the good as one measurable quantity: happiness, satisfied preferences or money saved. The appeal is obvious. A sum looks scientific and neutral, and it seems to spare the legislator any contested moral judgement.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Maximising the total is senseless, not merely false. Finnis calls the greatest-happiness principle incoherent outside limited technical contexts. The basic goods are incommensurable, so there is no common unit in which to add them up. Act-utilitarianism (judge each act by its results) and rule-utilitarianism (follow the rules whose general observance gives the best results) are, in his view, not so much false as senseless. Trying to sum the goods is like trying to add the size of a page, the number six and the mass of a book.
  2. The experience machine shows that pleasure is not the point. Nozick imagines a machine that gives you any experience you like for the rest of your life. Finnis says a sensible person would not plug in at all, because we want to do certain things and be certain people, not merely have the feeling of doing and being them. If pleasure were the whole point, the machine would be the perfect life.
  3. So maximising preferences is reasonable only inside the other requirements. Satisfying people's wants is a real part of requirement (6), efficiency within reason. But it works only inside the limits set by the other requirements, and it is never the measure of what is right.
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

The experience machine is a fragile proof†. If an "obvious" intuition splits a class 14 to 10, it may reflect upbringing, which feeds the Steelman against Finnis. But Finnis does not need everyone to refuse the machine. He needs only that converting the goods into units of satisfaction loses something, which is enough to defeat the sum†.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where weighing works, and where it stops

Requirement (6) is a real requirement, so Finnis is not against cost–benefit reasoning. He is against making it the whole of morality.

SituationMay you weigh?Why
Choosing between two techniques for one fixed goalYesA technical context with a common measure
Satisfying a wide range of ordinary wantsYesEfficiency within reason
Counting a sadist's pleasure in crueltyNoThe other requirements discount sadists' preferences
Netting an intentional killing or a fraud against its benefitsNoSuch acts are excluded altogether, above all by (7)
Treating smokers' early deaths as a saving to the health budgetNoLife is a basic good, not a cost to net off

The extra lines, explained

  • The limits on maximising. Finnis accepts that maximising is reasonable across a wide range of everyday wants. But the other requirements fence it in. Sadists' preferences are discounted, and certain intentional killings and frauds are excluded however much satisfaction they would produce. This is how you answer Q37 without sounding hostile to people's choices: preferences count, inside a frame.
  • STEELMAN · healthcare savings. The minister in Q35 has a point. Efficiency is a real requirement, so healthcare savings genuinely matter to a legislator. But the argument treats smokers' early deaths as a saving, and that is where it fails. Life is a basic good, not a cost to be netted off against a budget.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Finnis calls the greatest-happiness principle incoherent outside limited technical contexts. The basic goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are not so much false as senseless: there is no common unit to maximise. Nozick's experience machine counts against pleasure as the point of it all, since a sensible person would not plug in, wanting to do certain things, not merely feel them. Maximising satisfied preferences is therefore reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right. The minister is right that healthcare savings matter, but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.

75.5 From person to state

🧩 Practise 5.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.5 From person to state (word for word)
5.5 From person to state transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism
  1. Finnis's common good is a set of conditions enabling members to attain reasonable objectives for themselves.
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: committing to a life-plan is nothing like setting out to bake a cake.
  3. Yet it is definite enough to exclude many political arrangements and laws, so [almost no guidance] understates Finnis.
  • LEGISLATOR Working summary†: law is a framework that facilitates the goods, never intends to damage them and may prohibit acts that do; the rest is prudence (hate speech, fake news), weighing chilling effects in particular places† (15.4).
  • CONCEDE Finnis is less liberal than he looks: we must favour the basic goods and discourage their contraries. I concede non-neutrality; the state still keeps only peace and justice.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A family can agree on one holiday destination. A country cannot, because millions of people want different lives. So Finnis's state does not pick a destination. It builds the roads, keeps them safe and fair, and bans driving people off cliffs. That still rules out a lot of bad laws.

What the statement claims

"Finnis tells legislators clearly what they must never do but offers them almost no guidance on what they should do." (Q47)
"Finnis's common good, understood as a framework of conditions that enables each member of the community to pursue their own flourishing, is closer to liberalism than Finnis admits." (Q53)
"Online falsehoods corrupt our knowledge of the world, so Singapore's law empowering ministers to order corrections of false statements is justified here and would be justified in any country, whatever its side effects on free speech." (Q39)

These statements pull in different directions. Some readers think a theory of the good must turn the state into a planner of everyone's life. Others notice that Finnis's common good is a framework, and conclude either that it says almost nothing (Q47) or that it is really liberalism (Q53). Q39 goes the other way, treating one basic good as a licence to legislate whatever the side effects.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The common good is a set of conditions. Finnis defines it as the conditions that enable members of a community to attain reasonable goals for themselves. Think of public order, courts, fair rules and the coordination that lets people live side by side. It does not require everyone to share the same goals.
  2. A state is not a ship heading for one port. Finnis rejects the image of a ship of state with a single destination. A political community has no completable goal, and there is no single reasonable life-plan the state should get its citizens to adopt. As he puts it, committing yourself to a life-plan is nothing like setting out to bake a cake. There is no recipe to follow and no finished product.
  3. Yet the framework has teeth. The common good is still definite enough to exclude many political arrangements and laws. A law that intends to destroy a basic good, or that discriminates arbitrarily, or that blocks people from pursuing the goods without justification, fails it. So "almost no guidance" understates Finnis.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
POFMA through 15.4
StepApplied to a law against online falsehoods
(1) AimProtecting public knowledge is part of peace and justice.
(2) MeansThe law intends no damage to any good. It targets deliberate falsehood, which does.
(3) ReasonsThat truth matters to public life is a reason open to everyone, whatever their religion.
(4) PrudenceA broad law may chill true speech and so damage the very good it protects†.

So Finnis gives a limit, a direction and a method. That is guidance, not dictation. It also answers Q39: "whatever its side effects" ignores step 4, and "in any country" ignores that chilling effects depend on particular places†.

The extra lines, explained

  • LEGISLATOR · Liu's working summary†. Law is a framework that helps people pursue the goods. It must never intend to damage them, and it may prohibit acts that do. Everything else is prudence, as with hate speech and fake news, where the legislator weighs chilling effects in particular places†. This is framework 15.4 in one sentence, and your best answer to "almost no guidance".
  • CONCEDE · less liberal than he looks. Finnis says reason requires us to favour the basic goods and discourage their opposites, so his state is not neutral about the good life. Concede that. But the state's job is still only peace and justice, not making people integrally good. Against Q53, the comparison in 13.1 gives the balanced verdict: like liberalism, Finnis makes the common good a framework of conditions and limits the state to peace and justice, but he is not neutral. He is liberal in means, not in ends.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Finnis's common good is a set of conditions enabling members to attain reasonable objectives for themselves, not a destination for the state. A state is no ship bound for one port, since committing to a life-plan is nothing like setting out to bake a cake. Yet the common good is definite enough to exclude many political arrangements and laws, so "almost no guidance" understates Finnis. Law facilitates the goods, never intends to damage them and may prohibit acts that do, and the rest is prudence: a law against online falsehoods protects knowledge, but its breadth must be weighed against chilling effects in the particular place. I concede that Finnis is less liberal than he looks, since reason requires favouring the basic goods, but his state still keeps only peace and justice.

85.6 Human nature: urges or ends?

🧩 Practise 5.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? (word for word)
5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment
  1. Following nature can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends; the Stoics saw man as having natural ends known by the reflective intellect.
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges: many, like "gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and no value is inferred from fact.
  3. So [law should give people what they want] mistakes urges for goods: living from moment to moment on immediate cravings is unreasonable.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Follow your nature" could mean "do what you crave right now" or "become what you are capable of being". Finnis means the second. A craving to be cruel is natural in one sense, but it does not point to anything good.

What the statement claims

"Follow nature."
"Law should give people what their nature wants."
"We should live in the moment."

Each statement treats what people want, or what they feel like now, as the measure of what is good. It is tempting because natural law sounds as if it should mean "follow your nature", and because satisfying wants seems respectful of people's freedom.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Following nature" has two meanings. It can mean obeying your urges, or pursuing the ends that human beings are capable of. The older natural lawyers meant the second. The Stoics saw human beings as having natural ends that are known by the reflective intellect, that is, by thinking about what is worth doing, not by feeling a pull.
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges. Many urges answer to no good at all. The urge to "gratuitous cruelty" is natural in one sense, yet it points to no basic good, so it gives no reason to act. And Finnis infers no value from any fact, including facts about what people happen to want.
  3. So "give people what they want" mistakes urges for goods. For Finnis, living from moment to moment on immediate cravings is unreasonable. It breaks requirement (1), the coherent plan of life. Law should help people pursue the goods, not simply satisfy whatever they crave.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Urge or end?
The pullWhat kind of pull?Does it answer to a basic good?
Curiosity about how things workAn urge that points to an endYes: knowledge
Friendliness towards othersAn urge that points to an endYes: sociability
Gratuitous crueltyA bare urgeNo good at all
Taking more than one's shareA bare urgeNo good at all
Following each craving as it comesUrges with no planNot in itself. It breaks requirement (1)

The last row is the answer to "live in the moment". Finnis does not ask you to scrutinise every choice. He asks for a plan at the level of general commitments, so that your choices form a pattern you can stand behind.

⚠ TRAP
Finnis does not read values off human nature

The Stoic line explains what "ends" means, but it is not Finnis's method. Finnis's goods are self-evident, not deduced from biology or psychology. Facts about human nature show only how the goods apply in a particular case (4.4). So never write "Finnis argues from human nature that X is good". Write that Finnis says X is self-evidently good, and that facts show how the good applies.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"Following nature" can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends. The Stoics saw human beings as having natural ends known by the reflective intellect, and Finnis infers nothing from urges at all. Many urges, such as the urge to gratuitous cruelty, answer to no basic good, and in any case no value is inferred from fact. The statement that law should give people what they want therefore mistakes urges for goods. Living from moment to moment on immediate cravings is, for Finnis, simply unreasonable.

95.7 Finnis tested

🧩 Practise 5.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 5.7 Finnis tested (word for word)
5.7 Finnis tested critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
  1. Finnis's weak points are method and the seventh requirement: self-evidence rests on contested intuitions†, the means/side-effect line is "artificial"†, and accessible is not accepted (is [casino gambling] play?).
  2. He replies that there is no magic in the number seven, and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable".
  3. So I concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what [the state] may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Finnis says the goods are obvious. But are they obvious to everyone? Is casino gambling "play"? If reasonable people disagree, perhaps the state should be careful about forcing Finnis's answer on them, even if Finnis is right.

What the statement claims

"Finnis's basic goods may be uncontroversial in the abstract, but hard cases turn on whether a particular activity genuinely realises one of them. Is casino gambling a form of play? … Who should decide such questions, and by what method?" (Q51)

This is the open "critically evaluate Finnis" question. Its sting is in the second half. Even if everyone agrees that play is good, people disagree about whether a particular activity counts as play. If the theory cannot settle that, who decides, and what entitles the state to impose its answer?

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Finnis is weakest on method and on the seventh requirement. There are three points. Self-evidence rests on contested intuitions†, and the class split on the experience machine suggests that what feels obvious may reflect upbringing. Liu calls the means/side-effect line "artificial"†. And accessible is not accepted: even if anyone can see that play is good, people dispute whether casino gambling is play at all.
  2. Finnis has two replies. First, there is no magic in the number seven. The list could be organised differently, and what matters is the value each label captures, not the labels. Second, people who dissent on basic questions may be "inculpably erroneous", meaning mistaken without being to blame, rather than "perfectly reasonable" as Rawls would say. Disagreement does not prove that there is no right answer.
  3. So concede to Rawls on coercion. Even where Finnis is right about the good, reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force on people. This concession keeps your answer balanced. Finnis can be right about what is good and still have to respect disagreement when the question is whether to use force.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is casino gambling play?
The argumentThe good in play
ForPeople can enjoy gambling for its own sakePlay
AgainstCompulsive gambling serves no good and damages othersSociability (family life, friendship)
The gapThe good is accessible to all, but whether this activity realises it is disputedAccessible v accepted, 1.3(12)
UpshotFinnis's framework does not answer the question mechanicallyRegulate rather than ban

This is why a measured response such as a levy suits Finnis better than either horn of Q44's dilemma. The state may discourage what damages the goods, but where reasonable people dispute whether an activity realises a good, disagreement counsels the lighter measure.

Lines elsewhere on the sheet, explained

  • 1.4 CONCEDE · the self-critique. Finnis's list of goods is contested, and incommensurable goods leave much open. The key sentence is that disagreement is not falsity, but it limits coercion. Use it once, as the self-critique in a Finnis answer.
  • 14.8 CRITIQUE and reply. Besides "no magic in seven" and "inculpably erroneous", Finnis replies that these are not logical necessities. His case is not a deductive proof, so showing that intuitions, or even facts about human nature, shape it does not defeat it. Harris, who presses that point, still calls the method reasoning.
  • 14.8 VERDICT. Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good. It is the closing line of most Finnis answers.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Finnis's weak points are his method and his seventh requirement. Self-evidence rests on contested intuitions, the means/side-effect line is arguably artificial, and accessible is not accepted: even if play is plainly good, whether casino gambling is play is disputed. Finnis replies that there is no magic in the number seven, and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous" rather than "perfectly reasonable", so disagreement does not show there is no right answer. I nonetheless concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good. That is why a levy on gambling suits his framework better than an outright ban.

10Putting it together: Practice Q47

"Finnis tells legislators clearly what they must never do but offers them almost no guidance on what they should do."

Instruction: critically evaluate by reference to Finnis's theory and at least one illustration covered in the course, such as POFMA or casino gambling.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement is right that Finnis's clearest teaching is negative: never choose directly against a basic good. It does not follow that he offers almost no guidance, because his common good is a framework definite enough to exclude many political arrangements and laws. I make three claims. First, the seventh requirement gives legislators absolute limits. Second, the common good gives them positive direction: facilitate the goods, never intend to damage them, and, where prudent, prohibit acts that do. Third, prudence fills the rest, which is a strength, although contested goods limit how far the state may coerce.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. What legislators must never do (5.3, 15.3). The hostage and the scientist. Intention, not foresight, decides, and side effects are tested for fairness. Liu's critique that the line is artificial†.
  2. What legislators should do (5.5, 15.4). Conditions, not a cake. Facilitate the goods, act only on accessible reasons, and use prudence. POFMA: knowledge is a good the state may protect, and chilling effects are the prudence question.
  3. Prudence and its limit (5.7). Is casino gambling play? Accessible is not accepted. Concede to Rawls that disagreement limits coercion, which favours a levy over a ban.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

Finnis therefore gives legislators real limits: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure the conditions in which each citizen pursues a plan of their own. Beyond that, online falsehoods and casinos call for prudence, and since his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions and his means/side-effect line is arguably artificial, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in coercion. The statement is overstated: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

11Recap

Archetype 5 on one card
▤ Sections 5.1–5.7
  1. 1Seven self-evident, equally fundamental goods. Life-plans rank them, not the state (5.1).
  2. 2Nine requirements. Most transpose to a legislature. Test a law chiefly by (3), (7) and (8) (5.2).
  3. 3Requirement (7): never choose directly against a good. Intention, not foresight. Side effects are judged by fairness (5.3, 15.3).
  4. 4Utilitarianism is senseless, since the goods have no common unit. The experience machine. Efficiency only within reason (5.4).
  5. 5The common good is a framework that still excludes much. Peace and justice, accessible reasons, prudence (5.5, 15.4).
  6. 6Ends, not urges (5.6).
  7. 7Weak points: self-evidence, the artificial line, accessible is not accepted. Disagreement limits coercion (5.7).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a fence around an open field. The fence is the seventh requirement: a few things the law may never do, such as intend to kill the innocent. Inside the fence, the state lays paths and keeps the peace so that each citizen can plant their own crops (the common good). Where the crops grow is left to prudence. And when the neighbours argue about whether a plant is a weed (is gambling play?), the state reaches for a gate, not a bulldozer.

← Lesson 4: Is morality objective?Lesson 6: Pluralism →
LESSON 6 · ARCHETYPE 6 · ABOUT 82 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 52 QUESTIONS

Pluralist legislation: Rawls v Finnis

⚡ BIG IDEA

No law on a contested issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen (Rawls's discipline), sound on the merits (Finnis and TSH) and prudently fitted to circumstances.

ARCHETYPE 6 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
6 Pluralist legislation: Rawls v Finnis
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position No law on [the issue] is neutral; its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.
Intro The statement asks [Parliament] to [take no side / rest only on grounds every citizen shares]. Rawls rightly requires reasons each citizen could accept, but his neutrality is of justification, not outcome: [permitting X] still takes a moral side. I argue that [accessible is not accepted / process rests on substance]: a law's reasons must be open to all, sound and fitted to circumstances.
Steelman: for public reason The best case for [the statement] starts from reasonable pluralism. Political power is the power of free and equal citizens collectively, so imposing one faction's good life treats dissenters as subjects, not partners; in 2007 both camps were arguably sure they were absolutely right. This shows that the state must not make one comprehensive doctrine official. It does not show [that it can take no side].
Steelman: for moral truth The best case for [the statement] is that neutrality is unavailable. Every society takes a public stand (Finnis), even Rawls concedes that our actions imply a view, and process too rests on substantive values (TSH). This shows that legislators cannot avoid moral judgment. It does not show [that truth alone justifies coercion]: accessible is not accepted.
6.1 Rawls grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility
  1. Rawls asks more than [a majority], less than unanimity: power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse.
  2. Public reason binds judges more strictly, and also officials, candidates and citizens voting as if legislators, on essentials and basic justice so far as possible, never churches or media.
  3. So [civility, not justifications] inverts Rawls: civility is a moral duty to justify, though when officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law".
  • AGAINST Finnis's dilemma†: read predictively, the test gives a gross veto; read normatively, it judges merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does (14.10).
  • QUALIFY Rawls cannot equate public reason with majority views, so he must show pro-choice votes not unreasonable (TSH); Finnis sees only the "power of numbers" (14.10).
  • One of Rawls's deepest divides is between one reasonable good (Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition") and reasonable pluralism.
6.2 Not neutral takes no side; neutral fact
  1. That [the state takes no side] is a moral position: even Rawls concedes that our actions imply a view on salvation.
  2. Even its filter is moral: "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the dispute (6.11).
  3. So [neutrality] is unattainable: even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family (Masagos, 2022).
  • TRAP A doctrine of no salvation outside the church may be true; it is unreasonable because it would enforce that with the public's political power. Tolerance need not be a tenet: only hostility to reciprocity excludes a doctrine†.
  • AGAINST Liberal neutrality favours doctrines already institutionally and socially reinforced†; Rawls admits his political conception is itself moral.
6.3 OC v modus vivendi what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi
  1. [Legislating what the faiths share] is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC: a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each affirms it on its own moral grounds, so it survives shifts in political power, as a modus vivendi cannot.
  3. So OC is no [modus vivendi in philosophical dress], though "reasonable" decides who belongs.
  • OC is on principles, not reasons: the Golden Rule is held as divine teaching or as reciprocity†, and secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill). Tolerance works outside the overlap: I may be right, yet legislating my view would be unfair†.
6.4 Sorting reasons whose morality is admissible; four MPs
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than [whose morality is admissible]: Rawls sorts reasons by kind, Chua by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones, but admits Catholic common-good views expressed in political values.
  3. So the lines blur: in TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade, a test more far-reaching than Rawls's.
  • CONCEDE Rawls: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises; TSH replies that process too rests on substance. I concede that merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).
  • A bad reason is not a non-public one, nor a motive the justification†; a Kantian's absolute ban on lying is barred too†. Public reason moves with the background culture.
6.5 Abortion nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise
  1. [A permissive law is neutral] fails: Chua said learned men could not agree, then declared that an early conception is no human being.
  2. If [nobody can say when life begins], TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire.
  3. So [Parliament] cannot stand aside: permission settles the metaphysical question; I would argue for limits from accessible consequences.
  • Rawls called a doctrine denying the first-trimester "qualified right" unreasonable to that extent; later he accepted arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason, and said Catholics "need not exercise" it. For Finnis that is a slave-owner's reply, mere impudence or thoughtlessness.
  • AGAINST Macedo's "fairly close call" is no neutral midpoint: pro-choicers would reject a pro-life middle (TSH, reporting Wolfe and George).
  • AGAINST Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls: why draw the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity at birth?
  • CONCEDE TSH: consensus on human worth does not yet extend to who counts as human, so I argue for circumspection, not victory.
  • TRAP Finnis's article is no argument that abortion is wrong†: it tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, else it would be owed fair terms.
  • Is the unborn a clump of cells†? If not, must the woman "house" it (Thomson's violinist)? Either answer settles a moral question; for Finnis, Rawls cites another Thomson argument to lend pro-choice views a "reasonable" status they lack.
6.6 Finnis for law-makers never v should; rank the goods
  • See 5.
6.7 Religion religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious: the Good Samaritan may be cited if public reasons follow "in due course".
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to agnostic or negative answers, supports [religious freedom]; Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity.
  3. So [ban it because a faith condemns it] fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion little practical impact.
  • TSH: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical; whether it is political is itself contested (polygamy), so the classification arguably begs the question†.
6.8 Whip party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
  1. A whipped House may not represent majority opinion (TSH), so [one clear voice] need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip on occasion is "an option", with each member encouraged to see a role in deciphering higher law; another is judicial.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason; treating [s 377A] as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgment.
  • The abortion free votes of 1969 and 1974 arguably endorsed considering religious perspectives (TSH).
6.9 Close make people better
  1. Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but [the law's task is to make people better] overreaches.
6.10 Aim and mechanism equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life
  1. The statement's aim, not imposing [a fixed conception of the good life], and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2), nor neutral: Rawls files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines.
  3. So [the statement] keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism: Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.
  • "Objectively" presupposes realism; "wrongdoer", a wrong; "others", who counts (6.5); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).
  • Read the sentences as a chain†: (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means. Finnis: a range of opinions is valid, not one, and protecting others is a ground, not the only one. Rawls: opinions are "equally valid" a priori, unreasonable doctrines excepted; critics: toleration is itself imposed.
6.11 Freestanding yet overriding freestanding; overriding; contradictory
  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is political yet moral.
  2. On essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are "very great values", governing the basic framework of social life; reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital".
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it.
  • STEELMAN Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply secular, universal values, not individual religious beliefs (2022); even Finnis finds reciprocity broadly reasonable (14.10).
Conclusion The statement is therefore [wrong / overstated / partly right]. Rawls rightly demands coercion justifiable to every citizen, but neutrality cannot deliver it: any law on [the issue] takes a moral side, as Finnis's abortion test case shows. Pluralism asks equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions: reasons must be accessible, sound and prudently fitted to circumstances.

1Start here: archetype 6 in plain English

Archetype 6 asks one question: how should a country make laws when its citizens hold very different religious and moral views? Singapore is the standing example. Its people follow many faiths or none, yet Parliament still has to decide questions such as abortion, assisted dying and marriage, on which those faiths disagree.

Two camps answer differently. Rawls says that on basic questions the state should rely only on reasons that every reasonable citizen could accept, whatever their religion. An argument that makes sense only inside one faith or one philosophy should not, on its own, decide how the state uses force. Finnis and TSH (Tan Seow Hon) reply that some reasons are simply better than others, and that a state which claims to "take no side" has already taken one.

Exam statements in this family usually say that the state can, and should, be neutral. They ask it to "take no side", to "rest only on grounds every citizen shares" or to "treat all opinions as equally valid". Your answer is the same every time. No law on a contested issue is neutral, because permitting, punishing and promoting all take a moral stand. What you can fairly demand is discipline on the law's reasons. They should be open to every citizen to examine, good on the merits, and sensibly fitted to the circumstances.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Reasonable pluralismThe fact that free, sensible people end up with different religions and moral views. Rawls treats this as the normal result of freedom, not a mistake to be cured.
Comprehensive doctrineA full view of how to live: a religion, or a complete philosophy such as Kant's or Mill's. It can be religious or secular.
Political conception of justiceA narrower set of shared political values, such as liberty, equality and fair cooperation, that people of many faiths can all sign up to.
Public reasonArguing for laws on basic questions with those shared political values, so that other citizens could reasonably accept your reasons.
Constitutional essentials and basic justiceThe basic questions public reason covers: who holds power, what rights citizens have, and how the basic goods of social life are shared out.
Public political forumThe places where public reason binds: judges, officials, candidates, and citizens when they vote. The background culture (churches, universities, the media) stays free.
The provisoRawls's rule that a religious or other comprehensive argument may be offered, so long as public reasons follow in due course.
ReciprocityOffering reasons you honestly think others could accept as free and equal citizens, not merely understand.
Overlapping consensus (OC)Each reasonable doctrine supports the same political principles, each for its own reasons, so the agreement is stable.
Modus vivendiA truce between rivals that lasts only while neither side is strong enough to win.
Reasonable v unreasonableFor Rawls, a doctrine is unreasonable if it refuses fair terms, for example by wanting state power to enforce it. Unreasonable does not mean false.
Accessible v acceptedA reason is accessible if every citizen can examine it. It is accepted only if they agree with it. Many reasons are the first without being the second.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: no law on the issue is neutral, and its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.

Put simply, whatever Parliament does on a contested question takes a moral side, and that includes doing nothing. A law that permits abortion has decided that the unborn may be ended. A law that bans it has decided the opposite. So never let a statement pretend that one option is "neutral". Ask three things of the law's reasons instead. Can every citizen examine them, whatever their faith? Are they actually good reasons? And are they applied with sense to the situation, which is what Finnis calls prudence?

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement asks Parliament to take no side, or to rest only on grounds every citizen shares. Rawls is right that laws need reasons each citizen could accept. But his neutrality is about how a law is justified, not about what it does, and permitting something still takes a moral side. You then argue one of two things: that a reason open to everyone is not thereby accepted by everyone, or that a fair process itself rests on substantive values. Either way, a law's reasons must be open to all, sound and fitted to the circumstances.

The Conclusion gives your verdict: the statement is wrong, overstated or partly right. Rawls rightly demands that coercion be justifiable to every citizen, but neutrality cannot deliver that, because any law on the issue takes a moral side, as Finnis's abortion test case shows. Pluralism asks for equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions. The law's reasons must be accessible, sound and prudently fitted to the circumstances.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before attacking it. Section 6 gives you two. Which one you use depends on which way the statement leans.

  • Steelman: for public reason. Use it when the statement says laws must rest on shared grounds or take no side. It starts from reasonable pluralism. Political power belongs to all citizens together, as free and equal people. So if one faction uses that power to impose its own idea of the good life, it treats everyone else as subjects, not partners. Singapore's 2007 s 377A debate shows why this matters: TSH observed that both camps were sure they were right, and absolutely so. This shows that the state must not make one comprehensive doctrine official. It does not show that the state can take no side.
  • Steelman: for moral truth. Use it when the statement says law should follow what is truly right, or attacks neutrality. Its point is that neutrality is not available. Finnis argues that every society takes a public stand on questions such as abortion. Rawls himself concedes that our political actions imply a view on deep questions. TSH adds that even a fair process rests on substantive values. This shows that legislators cannot avoid moral judgement. It does not show that truth alone justifies coercion, because a reason can be accessible to everyone without being accepted by everyone.

The eleven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
6.1"Laws must rest only on grounds every citizen can share." "Legitimacy is a majority plus civility."Rawls asks for more than a majority and less than unanimity, and civility is a duty to justify. Finnis's dilemma: a veto, or a judgement on the merits.
6.2"The state should take no side."Taking no side is a side. Even Rawls's filter, the word "reasonable", is moral.
6.3"Legislate what the faiths share." "OC is a truce in disguise."Shared condemnation is Devlin, not Rawls. An OC survives shifts in power, and a truce does not.
6.4"Rawls and Finnis differ only on whose morality counts."They sort reasons differently: by kind (Rawls), by motive (Chua), by merit (Finnis and TSH).
6.5"On abortion, the state should stand aside."Permitting is deciding. If you cannot tell what moves behind the bush, do not shoot.
6.6"Finnis says what never to do, not what to do."Taught in Lesson 5.
6.7"Religious arguments have no place in law-making."No argument is barred for being religious, if public reasons follow. "My faith condemns it" alone is not enough.
6.8"Whipped MPs cannot discern justice."Partly right. But a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason.
6.9"The law's task is to make people better."Moral truth limits law, but this overreaches. The state keeps peace and justice.
6.10Sample Question 1: "treat all opinions as equally valid", restrict liberty only to protect others.Keep the aim and drop the mechanism, which is neither necessary nor neutral.
6.11"Rawls's view is freestanding yet overriding, which is contradictory."Freestanding means not built from one doctrine, not value-free. The fight is over who counts as "reasonable".
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Neutral in justification is not neutral in result. Every law on a contested issue takes a side, so its reasons must be open to all, sound and fitted to the facts.

2The big picture: making law for people who disagree

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Five flatmates of different religions share a kitchen and need house rules. One option is "the majority's religion decides". Rawls says that is unfair. Rules about the basics should rest on reasons everyone could accept as fair, even people who believe different things. Finnis replies that this is fine as far as it goes, but some reasons are simply better than others. And a house that "takes no side" on whether meat may be cooked in the shared pans has still made a rule that someone will hate.

This archetype covers statements about how a pluralist society, one with many religions and moral views, should legislate. It is also the home of Liu's Sample Question 1, which you planned in Lesson 1.

Rawls and Finnis start from the same problem and go in opposite directions. Both ask how people with different ideas of the good life can cooperate and argue with each other. Finnis thinks that beneath the disagreement there are objective goods and principles that reason can find. Rawls starts from permanent diversity. On his view we will never agree on the right answers, or even on the principles, so we need rules that everyone can accept as fair even though they match nobody's view exactly.

Note what they do not disagree about. Both think law needs moral justification. Both want reasons that are open to everyone, whatever their faith. Their quarrel is about whether a law may rest on the truth about the good, or only on what reasonable citizens could accept.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
RawlsIn Political Liberalism and a later essay on public reason, Rawls asks how a state can bind free and equal citizens who reasonably disagree about religion and the good life. His answer is that on basic questions, coercion must rest on reasons every reasonable citizen could accept.
FinnisIn an article on abortion and public reason, Finnis argues that Rawls's test is either a veto or a hidden judgement on the merits, and that some basic moral questions have right answers. Liu stresses that the article tests Rawls's method. It is not an argument that abortion is wrong†.
TSHTan Seow Hon studied Singapore's 1969 and 1974 abortion debates. She argues that arguments should be judged by whether they are accessible and sound, not by the speaker's religion, and that sidelining the question of when life begins already answers it.
Chua Sian ChinSingapore's Health Minister, who steered the abortion laws through Parliament. He brushed aside his opponents' arguments, even medical ones, as religion in disguise. TSH calls this a test of motive.
MacedoA liberal theorist who treats abortion as a close call between two reasonable sides and proposes a middle ground. TSH replies that his middle is not neutral.
Masagos and ShanmugamMinisters in the 2022 debates. Masagos said decisions apply secular, universal values, and admitted that the MOE sexuality curriculum reflects a view of the family. Shanmugam treated s 377A as a matter of policy, not conscience.

Key distinctions

  • Neutral in justification v neutral in result. Rawls asks that a law's reasons favour no comprehensive doctrine. He does not claim that its effects will be equal for every way of life. Statements in this archetype usually confuse the two.
  • Reasonable v true. For Rawls, a doctrine is unreasonable when it refuses fair terms, not when it is false. A doctrine can be true and still unreasonable, if its followers want state power to enforce it.
  • Political v comprehensive. Political values, such as liberty, equality and public health, belong to citizens as citizens. Comprehensive values belong to a whole view of life. Rawls says moral autonomy (Mill's ideal of living your own way), moral desert and monogamy as such are comprehensive, not political.
  • Acceptable to all v sound (distinction 1.3(9)) and accessible v accepted (1.3(12)). Rawls tests a reason by whether everyone could accept it. Finnis and TSH test it by whether it is sound, and by whether everyone can examine it. A sound argument open to all can still be rejected by many, which is why soundness alone does not license coercion (5.7).
  • Aim v mechanism (1.3(4)). A statement's goal can be right while its method is wrong. This is the key to Sample Question 1 (6.10).

Step (3) is where most exam answers live. Rawls does not mind where an argument starts. A Christian MP may begin with the Good Samaritan. What he minds is an argument that jumps straight from a doctrine to a law, with no political value in between. Rawls calls such an argument too immediate and fragmentary. Step (4) is reciprocity. It is not enough that the losing side can understand your reasons. Rawls's example is the heretic Servetus, who could understand perfectly well why Calvin wanted to burn him. The reasons must be ones the losers could accept as free and equal citizens.

⚠ TRAP
Public reason is not secular reason

Rawls is not anti-religious. A secular philosophy, such as a strict Kantian's ban on all lying, is limited in exactly the same way as a religious one (14.10). And a religious MP who argues from political values, such as protecting vulnerable citizens, is using public reason. Never write "Rawls excludes religion from politics".

Rawls in Singapore: the 2022 package

Liu set this as a class exercise†. On balance, a Rawlsian can approve the package. The public consultation was the background culture at work, and the consensus it reached was that sex between men should no longer be a crime, not that same-sex unions should be treated as equal. Art 156 stops the courts outrunning that consensus. Sending a divisive question to Parliament rather than to unelected judges is itself a public reason, because it is a reason about who should decide. Liu also warned that a bad reason is not the same as a non-public one, and that a motive is not the same as the justification offered†. The strongest objection points the other way. Rawls's own model of public reason is the Supreme Court, so moving a question away from judges is not obviously Rawlsian. Keep both points ready, and see 13.2 for the coercion gradient behind the package.
