36.1 Rawls

🧩 Practise 6.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.1 Rawls (word for word)
6.1 Rawls grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility
  1. Rawls asks more than [a majority], less than unanimity: power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse.
  2. Public reason binds judges more strictly, and also officials, candidates and citizens voting as if legislators, on essentials and basic justice so far as possible, never churches or media.
  3. So [civility, not justifications] inverts Rawls: civility is a moral duty to justify, though when officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law".
  • AGAINST Finnis's dilemma†: read predictively, the test gives a gross veto; read normatively, it judges merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does (14.10).
  • QUALIFY Rawls cannot equate public reason with majority views, so he must show pro-choice votes not unreasonable (TSH); Finnis sees only the "power of numbers" (14.10).
  • One of Rawls's deepest divides is between one reasonable good (Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition") and reasonable pluralism.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Rawls is not saying "do whatever the majority wants", and he is not saying "pass only laws everyone agrees with". He sits in between. On basic questions, give reasons that any reasonable citizen could accept as fair, even one who loses the vote. If you do that and the majority still passes the law, the law is legitimate. Finnis then asks the awkward question: who decides what a reasonable person "could accept"?

What the statement claims

Two exam statements land in this block:

"In a multicultural society the state must never criminalise conduct merely because some citizens believe it is 'really' wrong; laws must rest only on grounds that every citizen can share." (Q36)
"Once the debate is over, a law's legitimacy rests on one thing alone: whether it commands a majority. Officials owe citizens civility, not justifications framed in terms that everyone can accept." (Q41)

The two statements pull in opposite directions. The first sets the bar at unanimity, since only grounds that every citizen shares will do. The second sets it at a bare majority with good manners on top. Both sound like a description of fair democracy, and both misread Rawls, who sets the bar between them.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Rawls asks for more than a majority and less than unanimity. Political power is legitimate only when it is used under constitutional essentials that all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse. That does not mean everyone actually agrees, which no society achieves. It means every reasonable citizen could accept the basis of the law as fair, even if they would have voted the other way. A bare majority is not enough, because Rawls sees political power as the power of all citizens together, as free and equal people.
  2. Public reason binds certain speakers on certain questions. It binds judges most strictly. It also binds officials, candidates for office, and ordinary citizens when they vote, because Rawls asks voters to think as if they were legislators. It covers constitutional essentials and basic justice, as far as possible. It never binds churches or the media, which belong to the free background culture.
  3. So "civility, not justifications" turns Rawls upside down. For Rawls, civility is a duty to justify. It is a moral duty, not a legal one, to explain your votes and proposals in terms others could accept. And when officials and citizens keep that duty, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law", binding even on those who think it mistaken.

The extra lines, explained

  • AGAINST · Finnis's dilemma†. Finnis says Rawls's test is ambiguous. Read as a forecast of what citizens will in fact endorse, it gives what Finnis calls a gross veto to any group stubborn enough to refuse. Read as a standard of what citizens should endorse, it requires judging the merits of their views, which is exactly what Rawls promised not to do. Rawls does it anyway when he calls rationalist believers, people who say their faith can be proved by reason alone, "mistaken". This is your main attack on 6.1 (card 14.10).
  • QUALIFY · numbers are not legitimacy. TSH points out that Rawls cannot simply equate public reason with what the majority thinks. So when a majority votes for a permissive abortion law, Rawls must still show that those votes are not unreasonable. Pointing to the count is not enough. Finnis goes further, and says Rawls's scheme in the end leaves the gravest questions to the sheer "power of numbers" (14.10).
  • Rawls's deepest divide. Rawls himself says that one of the deepest divides in political thought is between theories that hold there is one reasonable good for everyone and theories that accept reasonable pluralism. The first group runs from Plato to Aquinas, and Rawls calls it "the dominant tradition". Finnis stands squarely inside it. That one sentence is the cleanest statement of Rawls v Finnis.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Does public reason bind this speaker?
SpeakerBound?Why
A Court of Appeal judge in a constitutional caseYes, most strictlyJudges make law that binds everyone and rule on the Constitution.
An MP speaking in a bill debateYesOfficials use the state's coercive power on everyone's behalf.
A candidate at a rally, or the campaign managerYesThey are seeking that power.
A citizen in the polling boothYes, as an idealRawls asks voters to think as if they were legislators.
A pastor preaching on the billNoChurches belong to the background culture, where any argument is free.
A newspaper columnistNoThe media sit outside the public political forum.

Rawls is not limiting what people may say in general. He is limiting what may justify the state's force on basic questions, and so he targets the people who wield or seek that force.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement reads Rawls as asking for unanimity, or else for a majority with good manners, but he asks for something in between. Political power is legitimate only when it is used under constitutional essentials that all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse. Public reason binds judges most strictly, and also officials, candidates and citizens voting as if they were legislators, on essentials and basic justice so far as possible, though never churches or the media. Civility is therefore a moral duty to justify, and when that duty is kept the majority's enactment is legitimate law. Finnis's dilemma still bites. Read as a forecast, the test hands any stubborn group a veto, and read as a standard, it judges the very merits Rawls claimed to set aside.

46.2 Not neutral

🧩 Practise 6.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.2 Not neutral (word for word)
6.2 Not neutral takes no side; neutral fact
  1. That [the state takes no side] is a moral position: even Rawls concedes that our actions imply a view on salvation.
  2. Even its filter is moral: "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the dispute (6.11).
  3. So [neutrality] is unattainable: even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family (Masagos, 2022).
  • TRAP A doctrine of no salvation outside the church may be true; it is unreasonable because it would enforce that with the public's political power. Tolerance need not be a tenet: only hostility to reciprocity excludes a doctrine†.
  • AGAINST Liberal neutrality favours doctrines already institutionally and socially reinforced†; Rawls admits his political conception is itself moral.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A referee who "takes no side" still has to decide whether a goal counts. Choosing to stay out is a decision with effects, and one team will feel it. The same is true of a state. Even Rawls admits that his political liberalism, which tries to stay out of religious questions, still implies a view on some of them.

What the statement claims

"The only fair basis for law in a diverse society is a state that takes no side on how anyone should live." (Q42)
"Decriminalising it takes no side at all: it simply leaves each citizen free to decide for himself." (Q36)

The statement treats neutrality as something a state can simply choose, like staying silent in an argument. It is tempting because the alternative sounds sinister: a state that "takes sides" on how people live. The block shows that silence is not available, and that even Rawls's careful version of neutrality rests on moral choices.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "The state takes no side" is itself a moral position. Choosing which questions the state stays out of is a decision about what the state is for. Rawls admits as much. Even when political liberalism refuses to assert or deny any religious truth, he concedes that what we do politically still implies a view on deep questions such as salvation.
  2. Even Rawls's filter is moral. Rawls sets aside "unreasonable" doctrines, meaning those that refuse fair terms, not those that are false. But deciding who counts as reasonable is exactly what is in dispute (6.11). A doctrine that rejects "live and let live" is shut out, and shutting it out is a moral choice in favour of tolerance.
  3. So neutrality cannot be achieved. Singapore's own government said as much. In 2022 Masagos told Parliament that MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family. A curriculum that calls itself secular still teaches a view of family life.

The extra lines, explained

  • TRAP · unreasonable is not false. Rawls's own example is a doctrine holding that outside the church there is no salvation. That doctrine may even be true, and Rawls does not say otherwise. It is unreasonable only if its followers would enforce it with the public's political power. Liu adds that tolerance need not be one of a doctrine's own teachings. A doctrine is shut out only if it is hostile to reciprocity†.
  • AGAINST · neutrality favours the established. Liberal neutrality tends to favour doctrines that are already reinforced by institutions and society†. Views that are widely held only seem neutral, because they are familiar. Rawls himself admits his political conception is a moral conception, so he never claimed to be value-free. The critique bites on any claim to be neutral in effect.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Reasonable or unreasonable?
A citizen holds…Reasonable for Rawls?Why
"Outside my church there is no salvation", kept to church lifeYesRawls does not judge whether it is true. It may even be true.
The same belief, plus "the state should enforce it"NoIt would use the public's political power to impose a comprehensive doctrine.
"Our lineage entitles us to more privileges, though we won't be harsh"NoIt offers terms others could not accept as free and equal. Reciprocity fails†.
A faith with no teaching on tolerance, but no hostility to fair termsYesTolerance need not be a tenet. Only hostility to reciprocity excludes†.
A strict Kantian's "all lying is wrong", as a personal creedYes, as a creedBut it cannot ground a law on its own (6.4).

The test is never truth. It is whether the doctrine accepts fair terms with people who disagree.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

That the state takes no side is itself a moral position, and even Rawls concedes that our political actions imply a view on questions such as salvation. His filter is moral too. A doctrine is unreasonable for refusing fair terms, not for being false, and who counts as reasonable is exactly what is in dispute. Neutrality is therefore unattainable, as Masagos admitted in 2022 when he said MOE's secular sexuality curriculum reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family. Liberal neutrality also tends to favour doctrines already reinforced by institutions and society. The honest question is not whether the state takes a side, but whether its reasons are ones every citizen can examine.

56.3 OC v modus vivendi

🧩 Practise 6.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.3 OC v modus vivendi (word for word)
6.3 OC v modus vivendi what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi
  1. [Legislating what the faiths share] is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC: a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each affirms it on its own moral grounds, so it survives shifts in political power, as a modus vivendi cannot.
  3. So OC is no [modus vivendi in philosophical dress], though "reasonable" decides who belongs.
  • OC is on principles, not reasons: the Golden Rule is held as divine teaching or as reciprocity†, and secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill). Tolerance works outside the overlap: I may be right, yet legislating my view would be unfair†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A modus vivendi is two rivals agreeing to a ceasefire because neither can win right now. If one gets stronger, the deal is off. An overlapping consensus is different. Each side, for its own deep reasons, believes the deal is right, so it lasts even when the balance of power changes. And neither is the same as "ban whatever most religions dislike".

What the statement claims

"Rawls's overlapping consensus is nothing more than a modus vivendi in philosophical dress." (Q48)
"Where the religious and moral convictions of most Singaporeans converge in condemning some conduct, Parliament should prohibit it, because that overlap of convictions is precisely what keeps a diverse nation stable." (Q40)

The first statement says Rawls's consensus is only a truce with a fancy name. The second borrows Rawls's word "overlap" but uses it for something else, the conduct that most faiths condemn. Both are tempting because Rawls himself cares about stability. The block shows that Rawls's overlap is on political principles, held for moral reasons, not on shared condemnation, and not on a balance of power.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Legislate what the faiths share" is Devlin's idea, not Rawls's. Banning what most faiths condemn is Devlin's shared morality (Lesson 7). Rawls's OC is something narrower. It is a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice, such as equal liberty and fair cooperation, not on which private conduct is wicked.
  2. Each doctrine backs the OC for its own moral reasons, so it survives shifts in power. A religious citizen may support equal liberty because faith cannot be forced. A secular liberal may support it because people should run their own lives. Because each side believes the principle is right, neither would drop it if its own view became dominant. A modus vivendi cannot pass that test.
  3. So the OC is not a truce in disguise, though "reasonable" decides who belongs. The consensus is moral, not tactical. But only reasonable doctrines are invited into it, and as 6.2 showed, who counts as reasonable is the point in dispute.

The extra line, explained

  • The overlap is on principles, not reasons. Liu's example is the Golden Rule. A believer holds it as divine teaching, and a secular humanist holds it as reciprocity. They agree on the principle for different reasons, and that is enough†. Secular doctrines join the overlap too, such as Kant's and Mill's. Liu adds where tolerance comes in. Inside the overlap no tolerance is needed. It is needed for the parts of your own view that lie outside it: you may be right, yet you recognise that forcing your view on others by law would be unfair†.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Truce or consensus?
ArrangementWhy the parties accept itWhat happens if one side gains power?Rawls's label
16th-century toleration between Catholics and ProtestantsNeither side could win. Each still thought rulers should suppress heresy.The stronger side drops toleration.Modus vivendi
Equal liberty of conscience todayA believer: faith cannot be forced. A liberal: people should choose their own beliefs.Nobody drops it, because each side thinks it right.Overlapping consensus
A ban on conduct most faiths call sinfulThe majority's faiths condemn it.Not the question: this is about private conduct, not political principles.Devlin's shared morality
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Legislating what the faiths share is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's overlapping consensus, which is a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice. Each doctrine affirms that conception on its own moral grounds, as believers and secular humanists both hold the Golden Rule. Because the agreement is moral rather than tactical, it survives shifts in political power, which a modus vivendi cannot. The overlapping consensus is therefore no modus vivendi in philosophical dress. Its weak point lies elsewhere, since the word "reasonable" decides who is allowed into the consensus at all.

66.4 Sorting reasons

🧩 Practise 6.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.4 Sorting reasons (word for word)
6.4 Sorting reasons whose morality is admissible; four MPs
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than [whose morality is admissible]: Rawls sorts reasons by kind, Chua by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones, but admits Catholic common-good views expressed in political values.
  3. So the lines blur: in TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade, a test more far-reaching than Rawls's.
  • CONCEDE Rawls: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises; TSH replies that process too rests on substance. I concede that merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).
  • A bad reason is not a non-public one, nor a motive the justification†; a Kantian's absolute ban on lying is barred too†. Public reason moves with the background culture.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Four MPs oppose a bill. One says "my faith forbids it". One says "it will hurt vulnerable people". One says "autonomy is the highest value". One says "life is a good no one may destroy". Which reasons count? Rawls sorts them by kind: is this a political value or a whole view of life? Chua sorted them by motive: is the speaker secretly religious? Finnis and TSH sort them by merit: is the argument any good?

What the statement claims

"Rawls and Finnis agree that law must be morally justified. They disagree only about whose morality is admissible." (Q49)
"During the second reading of a bill to legalise assisted dying, four MPs speak. … Which of these arguments are permissible under Rawls's ideal of public reason? How would Finnis assess Rawls's treatment of each? Are the lines Rawls draws between them as clear as he supposes?" (Q58)

The first statement is half right, which makes it tempting. Rawls and Finnis do agree that law needs moral justification. But "whose morality" makes it sound as if they share a method and only quarrel over the guest list. In fact they use different tests to decide which reasons count at all.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than whose morality counts. They sort reasons in different ways. Rawls sorts by kind: is this a political value, or part of a comprehensive doctrine? Chua, the Health Minister in Singapore's abortion debates, sorted by motive: is this speaker religious underneath? Finnis and TSH sort by merit: is the argument accessible to all, and is it sound?
  2. Rawls treats secular and religious doctrines alike. A secular philosophy is treated "the same way" as a religion. So a Kantian's absolute ban on lying is shut out just like a scriptural argument. And Rawls admits Catholic views of the common good when they are expressed in political values, so a religious speaker can use public reason.
  3. So the lines blur, and TSH shows how. She calls the result a Catch-22, a trap with no way out. Religious reasons would fail Rawls's test, while Chua dismissed opponents' medical reasons as a facade for religion. Chua's test of motive was more far-reaching than Rawls's test of kind, because it shut out religious citizens whatever they argued.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Sorting the four MPs
MPRawls (kind)A motive test (Chua)Finnis and TSH (merit)
A: faithComprehensive and religious. Allowed in debate only if public reasons follow in due course.Shut out.Not accessible as put. Can she argue from reasons all can examine?
B: pressure on the vulnerableA political value: protecting equal citizens. Admissible.Admitted, unless B is known to be devout. Then it is "a facade" (the Catch-22).Strong, if the evidence bears it out.
C: autonomy is the highest valueComprehensive and secular. Moral autonomy is not a political value (15.5), so it is barred like A.Admitted, since it is secular.Judged on merit. Finnis sees no objective ranking among basic goods, so he would reject "highest".
D: life is a basic good, evident on reflectionComprehensive, though offered as reason. Rawls calls rationalist believers "mistaken".Suspect, if D is religious.Accessible in principle, and sound for Finnis. But accessible is not accepted (5.7).

The three tests give three different guest lists. Rawls lets in B and nobody else without public reasons. A motive test lets in C, lets in B unless B is known to be devout, shuts out A, and treats D as suspect if D seems religious. Merit lets everyone speak and then asks who is right. That is the answer to Q58's last question: the lines are not as clear as Rawls supposes.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · merit-sorting rests on disputed premises. Rawls's best reply to Finnis and TSH is that judging arguments by merit assumes we can agree on what a good argument is, and in a pluralist society we cannot. TSH answers that Rawls's process rests on substantive values too, so he has no neutral ground either. Concede the core of Rawls's point: merit settles what is true, not what the state may coerce (5.7). Card 14.8 reaches the same verdict on Finnis. Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force, even where Finnis is right about the good.
  • What public reason is not. Liu adds two warnings. A bad reason is not thereby a non-public one, and a speaker's motive is not the justification offered†. MP B's argument might be weak, and B might be devout, yet B still argues from a political value. And a Kantian's absolute ban on lying is barred just like a religious argument†. Finally, public reason moves with the background culture. As views in wider society shift, so does the stock of reasons everyone can accept.
Card 14.11: TSH on religion and public reason
▤ Theorist bank
  1. 1Purpose. In a multi-religious democracy, may law-makers rely on religious arguments?
  2. 2Claim. Judge arguments by their accessibility and merit, not their religious motive. Bracketing a metaphysical question already answers it.
  3. 3Critique and reply. Rawls would call using state power against reasonable dissenters "unreasonable or worse". TSH replies that she asks only for accessible reasons, and that the line around a political sphere is artificial.
  4. 4Concession. Her pragmatic strategy, arguing from consequences, admits that principle alone may not move Parliament.
  5. 5Say it. This shatters the illusion of an accommodative solution.
  6. 6Verdict. TSH exposes the unfairness of sorting arguments by motive, but not how a divided Parliament should settle contested questions.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Rawls and Finnis differ on more than whose morality is admissible, because they sort reasons in different ways. Rawls sorts by kind, Chua sorted by motive, and Finnis and TSH sort by merit. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments the same way as religious ones, so a Kantian's ban on lying is barred, yet he admits Catholic views of the common good when they are expressed in political values. The lines therefore blur. In TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade, a test more far-reaching than Rawls's. I concede to Rawls that merit settles what is true, not what may be coerced.

76.5 Abortion

🧩 Practise 6.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.5 Abortion (word for word)
6.5 Abortion nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise
  1. [A permissive law is neutral] fails: Chua said learned men could not agree, then declared that an early conception is no human being.
  2. If [nobody can say when life begins], TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire.
  3. So [Parliament] cannot stand aside: permission settles the metaphysical question; I would argue for limits from accessible consequences.
  • Rawls called a doctrine denying the first-trimester "qualified right" unreasonable to that extent; later he accepted arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason, and said Catholics "need not exercise" it. For Finnis that is a slave-owner's reply, mere impudence or thoughtlessness.
  • AGAINST Macedo's "fairly close call" is no neutral midpoint: pro-choicers would reject a pro-life middle (TSH, reporting Wolfe and George).
  • AGAINST Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls: why draw the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity at birth?
  • CONCEDE TSH: consensus on human worth does not yet extend to who counts as human, so I argue for circumspection, not victory.
  • TRAP Finnis's article is no argument that abortion is wrong†: it tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, else it would be owed fair terms.
  • Is the unborn a clump of cells†? If not, must the woman "house" it (Thomson's violinist)? Either answer settles a moral question; for Finnis, Rawls cites another Thomson argument to lend pro-choice views a "reasonable" status they lack.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says: "Nobody knows when life begins, so the law should stay out and let each woman decide." TSH replies with a hunter. If you cannot tell whether the thing moving behind a bush is a deer or a person, you do not shoot. And a law that "lets everyone decide" has already decided something important, namely that the unborn may be ended.

What the statement claims

"On abortion, the state's only proper course is to stand aside. Since nobody can say when human life begins, a law leaving the decision to each pregnant woman imposes no view on anyone: those who believe abortion is wrong remain perfectly free not to have one. Every argument for restricting abortion ultimately rests on religious faith, which has no place in the reasons legislators owe one another. A permissive law is therefore the only neutral law a pluralist society can have." (Q43)

The statement makes the strongest neutrality claim in the archetype. It says that uncertainty about when life begins justifies leaving the choice to each woman, and that this imposes nothing on anyone. It is tempting because "you are free not to have one" sounds like perfect tolerance. The block shows that the permissive law has quietly answered the very question it says nobody can answer.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. A permissive law is not neutral, and Singapore's own debate proves it. Chua Sian Chin, the Health Minister, told Parliament that learned men had never been able to agree when human life begins. Then he declared that an early conception is not a human being. In other words, he settled the question while claiming it could not be settled.
  2. If nobody can say when life begins, uncertainty points to caution, not permission. TSH borrows an image from Brown. A hunter who is unsure whether the movement behind a bush is a deer or a person should not fire. On the statement's own premise, the state does not know whether abortion kills a human being, and that is a reason to hold back.
  3. So Parliament cannot stand aside. Permitting abortion settles what TSH calls the metaphysical question, meaning when life begins and what the unborn's life is worth. The better course is to argue for limits from consequences that everyone can assess, such as effects on women's health, rather than from faith alone.

The extra lines, explained

  • Rawls's retreat, and the slave-owner reply. In a footnote to Political Liberalism, Rawls weighed three political values: due respect for human life, the orderly reproduction of society, and the equality of women. He concluded that a doctrine denying a woman a "qualified right" to end a pregnancy in the first trimester is to that extent unreasonable. Later he softened. He accepted that arguments against the right, framed in political values, also count as public reason, and said that Catholics who oppose abortion "need not exercise" the right themselves. Finnis calls that a slave-owner's reply, like telling an abolitionist that nobody is forcing him to own slaves. The objection was never about one's own conduct, so Finnis dismisses the reply as mere impudence or thoughtlessness.
  • AGAINST · Macedo's middle ground is not neutral. Macedo treats abortion as a "fairly close call" and proposes a compromise that honours the woman's choice up to a point. TSH, reporting Wolfe and George, shows that pro-life writers have their own middle ground: ban abortion, but support women in difficult pregnancies and ease adoption. Pro-choicers would reject it. So where "the middle" lies depends on where you start.
  • AGAINST · Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls. Rawls says citizens enter society at birth. Finnis asks why the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity should be drawn there. A child a week before birth differs from a newborn mainly in location. If Rawls says the unborn falls outside the circle of fair terms, he has answered the hard question without arguing for it.
  • CONCEDE · TSH on who counts. TSH admits that our shared belief in human worth does not yet extend to agreement on who counts as human. So argue for circumspection, meaning care and caution, not for total victory.
  • TRAP · Finnis's article is not an anti-abortion argument. Liu stresses that the article tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions†. Its point is that Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, because if it were, it would be owed fair terms too. Never write "Finnis proves abortion is wrong".
  • The decision tree. Liu's slide asks whether the unborn is a clump of cells†. If not, must the woman "house" it? That is the question Thomson's violinist example raises: even if the unborn is a person, must she let it use her body? Either answer settles a moral question. Finnis adds that Rawls cites another of Thomson's arguments to lend pro-choice views a "reasonable" status they lack.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

A permissive law is not neutral, as Singapore's own debate shows. Chua told Parliament that learned men could not agree when life begins, then declared that an early conception is no human being. If nobody can say when life begins, TSH's hunter, unsure what moves behind the bush, should not fire, so uncertainty counsels caution rather than permission. Parliament therefore cannot stand aside, because permission itself settles the metaphysical question. Finnis presses the same point against Rawls, asking why the boundary of reciprocity falls at birth. I would argue for limits from accessible consequences, with circumspection, since agreement on human worth does not yet extend to who counts as human.

86.6 Finnis for law-makers, and 6.9 Close

🧩 Practise 6.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.6 Finnis for law-makers (word for word)
6.6 Finnis for law-makers never v should; rank the goods
  • See 5.
▤ On your sheet: 6.9 Close (word for word)
6.9 Close make people better
  1. Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but [the law's task is to make people better] overreaches.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two short blocks. 6.6 is a signpost: questions about Finnis's guidance for law-makers are taught in Lesson 5. 6.9 answers "the law should make people good". A referee keeps the game fair and safe. He does not coach each player to be a better person. Finnis thinks moral truth limits what law may do, but the state's job is the referee's, not the coach's.

What the statement claims

"Finnis tells legislators clearly what they must never do but offers them almost no guidance on what they should do." (Q47)
"The law's task is to make people better."

The first statement belongs to archetype 5, and block 6.6 simply sends you there (Lesson 5). The second runs the other way from most statements in this archetype. Instead of asking the state to take no side, it asks the state to take every side that matters and make its citizens good. It is tempting because it sounds like the natural lawyer's answer to neutrality. The block shows that even the natural lawyer refuses it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but "make people better" overreaches. The first half rejects the liberal claim that the state must stay neutral. Finnis's absolute limits are real: the law may never intend to destroy a basic good, and no law on a contested issue is neutral anyway (6.2). The second half rejects the opposite extreme. Finnis himself says the state's role is not to make people integrally good, meaning good through and through, but only to maintain peace and justice. That fuller task belongs to families, churches and individuals.

The extra line, explained

  • Liberal in means, not ends. Finnis and the liberals agree that the common good is a framework of conditions, and that the state's role is peace and justice alone (13.1). But Finnis is not neutral. Reason requires us to favour the basic goods and discourage their contraries. So he is liberal about the means the state may use, not about the ends it may favour. That is how he can reject both neutrality and moral perfectionism at once.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but the claim that the law's task is to make people better overreaches. Finnis's tradition gives the state a limited role. It is not to make people integrally good but only to maintain peace and justice, leaving the fuller work of virtue to families, churches and individuals. Finnis is therefore liberal in means, though not in ends, since reason still requires the state to favour the basic goods. The statement mistakes a floor of peace and justice for a ceiling of perfection.

96.7 Religion

🧩 Practise 6.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.7 Religion (word for word)
6.7 Religion religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious: the Good Samaritan may be cited if public reasons follow "in due course".
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to agnostic or negative answers, supports [religious freedom]; Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity.
  3. So [ban it because a faith condemns it] fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion little practical impact.
  • TSH: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical; whether it is political is itself contested (polygamy), so the classification arguably begs the question†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Can a religious MP argue for a law using her faith? Rawls says yes, as long as she also gives reasons others could accept. Finnis says that religion, the search for life's meaning, is itself one of the basic goods, so the state should protect it. Both protect religious freedom. Neither accepts "ban it because my faith condemns it".

What the statement claims

"In a parliamentary debate on legalising euthanasia, a Member who believes his faith can be defended by reason is entitled to press for a ban grounded in that faith, provided he argues courteously." (Q41)
"Every argument for restricting abortion ultimately rests on religious faith, which has no place in the reasons legislators owe one another." (Q43)
"Can a state that treats religion as a basic good remain fair to citizens who reject religion?" (Q50)

These statements sit at opposite poles. One says faith may ground a ban if argued politely. Another says faith has no place in law-making at all. The third asks whether Finnis's protection of religion is fair to unbelievers. The block's answer runs between them: faith may enter the debate, but it cannot carry a ban on its own.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious. An MP may cite the Good Samaritan in a debate on care for the dying. Under Rawls's proviso, that is fine so long as public reasons follow in due course. What public reason forbids is letting the faith do all the work.
  2. Rawls and Finnis both protect religious freedom, for different reasons. For Finnis, religion is one of the basic goods. It means asking about the ultimate source of meaning, and it is open to agnostic or negative answers, so it can be fair to unbelievers. For Rawls, denying basic liberties such as religious liberty normally breaks reciprocity. Neither justification is neutral. Finnis values the inquiry, whatever the answer. Rawls takes the truths of religion off the political agenda (13.1).
  3. So "ban it because a faith condemns it" fails, but TSH warns of the opposite danger. One faith's condemnation cannot alone justify coercing citizens who do not share it. Yet in 2009 Singapore's government said laws serve the national interest and collective good, not religious authority. TSH warns that a test like that may leave religion little practical impact.

The extra line, explained

  • TSH · is the political sphere begging the question? TSH argues that once an issue is classed as metaphysical rather than political, Rawls's political values make religious perspectives "nugatory", that is, of no effect. But whether an issue is political is itself contested. Her example is polygamy. Marriage law bans it, though some citizens see nothing wrong with it and call it a fundamental right. So drawing the line around "the political" arguably begs the question, assuming the answer to the very dispute it is meant to settle†.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three religious MPs in a euthanasia debate
What the MP saysRawlsFinnis and TSH
"The Good Samaritan teaches care for the dying. And the bill leaves vulnerable patients open to pressure."Allowed. The faith is followed by a public reason, so the proviso is met.Assess the public reason on its merits.
"My faith condemns it, so it must be banned."Fails. No public reason follows, so the faith alone grounds the ban.Fails too. Finnis requires reasons accessible to all, whatever their religion (15.4).
"My faith can be proved by reason, so the ban needs no other ground." (Q41)A rationalist believer. Rawls calls this "mistaken", because it denies reasonable pluralism.Finnis: calling it mistaken judges its merits, so Rawls is not neutral. TSH: examine the argument before dismissing it.

Politeness does not change the answer in rows two and three. Q41's "provided he argues courteously" confuses civility with justification (6.1).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Public reason bars no argument for being religious. A legislator may cite the Good Samaritan, provided public reasons follow in due course. Religious freedom is protected on both sides, by Finnis because religion is a basic good open to agnostic or negative answers, and by Rawls because denying basic liberties normally breaks reciprocity. The claim that conduct should be banned because a faith condemns it therefore fails. TSH warns of the opposite danger, since a national interest test may leave religion little practical impact, and the line between political and metaphysical questions is itself contested.

106.8 Whip

🧩 Practise 6.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.8 Whip (word for word)
6.8 Whip party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
  1. A whipped House may not represent majority opinion (TSH), so [one clear voice] need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip on occasion is "an option", with each member encouraged to see a role in deciphering higher law; another is judicial.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason; treating [s 377A] as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgment.
  • The abortion free votes of 1969 and 1974 arguably endorsed considering religious perspectives (TSH).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When a party "whips" its MPs, they must vote the party line. Does a whipped vote tell us what the country thinks is just? Not necessarily. It tells us what the party leadership decided. Lifting the whip lets MPs vote their conscience. But conscience is not the same as public reason either, because an MP voting freely may still give reasons only his own faith accepts.

What the statement claims

"Legislators who vote on moral questions according to party discipline rather than conscience cannot claim to be discerning what justice requires." (Q46)

The statement assumes there are two options, party discipline and conscience, and that only conscience can find justice. It is tempting in Singapore, where one party holds most seats and a whipped vote speaks with one clear voice. The block agrees with the first half and complicates the second.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. A whipped House may not represent majority opinion. TSH points out that when the whip is applied, the House speaks with one clear voice, but that voice is the party's. It may not reflect what most MPs, or most citizens, actually think. So a whipped vote need not show what justice requires.
  2. TSH's answer is to lift the whip on occasion. She calls this "an option". On certain moral questions, each member would be encouraged to see his role as working out higher law, the moral standard by which law itself is judged. Her other option is judicial: let the courts decide some questions.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason. An MP freed from the whip may still argue only from his own faith. And deciding that a question is not one for conscience is itself a moral judgement. When Shanmugam treated s 377A in 2022 as a matter of policy rather than conscience, he took a moral position.

The extra line, explained

  • The precedent. Singapore lifted the whip for its abortion votes in 1969 and 1974. In a House dominated by one party, that was unusual. TSH reads it as arguably an endorsement of considering religious perspectives in law-making. It is your best local evidence that a free vote is a real option on moral questions.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

A whipped House may not represent majority opinion, as TSH notes, so a vote with one clear voice need not show what justice requires. For TSH, lifting the whip on occasion is an option, with each member encouraged to see a role in deciphering higher law, and another option is judicial. Singapore took the first path on abortion in 1969 and 1974, arguably endorsing the consideration of religious views. But a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason, since a member voting freely may still argue only from his own faith. And treating s 377A as policy rather than conscience, as Shanmugam did in 2022, is itself a moral judgement.

116.10 Aim and mechanism

🧩 Practise 6.10 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.10 Aim and mechanism (word for word)
6.10 Aim and mechanism equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life
  1. The statement's aim, not imposing [a fixed conception of the good life], and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2), nor neutral: Rawls files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines.
  3. So [the statement] keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism: Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.
  • "Objectively" presupposes realism; "wrongdoer", a wrong; "others", who counts (6.5); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).
  • Read the sentences as a chain†: (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means. Finnis: a range of opinions is valid, not one, and protecting others is a ground, not the only one. Rawls: opinions are "equally valid" a priori, unreasonable doctrines excepted; critics: toleration is itself imposed.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Your aim is to get to the airport. Your method is "only ever take the number 7 bus". The aim is fine. The method is neither the only way there nor even a reliable one. Sample Question 1 is like that. Its aim, not forcing one way of life on everyone, is good. Its method, treating all opinions as equally valid and banning only harm to others, does not work.

What the statement claims

"Legislators governing a pluralist society should treat all moral opinions as equally valid. This can be achieved by refraining from passing any law restricting liberty unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct. Only then can legislators avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life." (Sample Question 1)

This is Liu's own sample question. It joins three ideas into one argument: a principle (equal validity), a method (the harm principle) and a goal (no fixed conception of the good life). It is tempting because each idea sounds liberal and generous. The block shows that the goal survives, but the method and the principle do not.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Split the aim from the mechanism. The statement's aim is not to impose a fixed conception of the good life. Its mechanism is to restrict liberty only to protect others from harm. The statement claims the second is the way, and the only way, to reach the first. That claim is where it breaks.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary nor neutral. It is not necessary, because Hart's paternalism shows another ground for coercion that imposes no way of life. Hart lets the law protect people whose consent is defective, through cravings or pressure, not because their conduct is immoral (7.2). And it is not neutral, because Rawls himself counts Mill's liberalism, the source of the harm principle, as one comprehensive doctrine among others.
  3. So the statement keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism. Each theorist supplies a piece of the repair. Finnis supplies substance, an account of which goods the law protects. Rawls supplies discipline, reasons every citizen can examine. Hart supplies a presumption against coercion.

The extra lines, explained

  • Word by word. Four words commit the statement to more than it can defend. "Objectively" presupposes moral realism, the view that there are moral facts. "Wrongdoer" presupposes that something is wrong. "Others" raises the question of who counts, including the unborn (6.5). And "equally valid" defeats itself, because the demand that everyone accept equal validity ranks that view above its rivals (4.7).
  • The chain†. Liu's model answer reads the three sentences as a chain. Sentence (2) is the means to sentence (1), and "only then" in sentence (3) makes it the only means. Then each theorist answers a link. For Finnis, a range of opinions is valid, not just one, but not all of them. Protecting others is a ground for law, not the only one. For Rawls, reasonable opinions are treated as equally entitled from the start, with unreasonable doctrines excepted. And Rawls's critics add that toleration, the very value the statement relies on, is itself imposed.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Word by word: what each loaded word assumes
Word in SQ1What it assumesWhere to go
"equally valid"That every moral opinion is as good as every other, which is itself a moral claim4.7: it defeats itself
"objectively necessary"That there are objective facts about what is necessaryMoral realism, which sits badly with the statement's own "equally valid" (4.7)
"wrongdoer"That some conduct is wrongThe harm test already needs a moral judgement (7.1)
"others"A view about who counts as another personThe unborn (6.5)
"only then"That the harm principle is the only route to the aimHart's paternalism (7.2)
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement's aim, not imposing a fixed conception of the good life, and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart. The mechanism is not necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent rather than immorality and imposes no way of life. Nor is it neutral, since Rawls himself files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines. Its premise fares worse, because treating all opinions as equally valid defeats itself. The statement therefore keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism, with Finnis supplying substance, Rawls discipline, and Hart a presumption against coercion.

126.11 Freestanding yet overriding

🧩 Practise 6.11 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 6.11 Freestanding yet overriding (word for word)
6.11 Freestanding yet overriding freestanding; overriding; contradictory
  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is political yet moral.
  2. On essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are "very great values", governing the basic framework of social life; reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital".
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it.
  • STEELMAN Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply secular, universal values, not individual religious beliefs (2022); even Finnis finds reciprocity broadly reasonable (14.10).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Rawls says his political values are "freestanding": they do not depend on any one religion or philosophy. Yet he says they "override" religious views on basic questions. Is that a contradiction? Not quite. Freestanding means "not built from one doctrine", not "value-free". And reasonable people can accept that fair terms come first. The trouble is who gets labelled "reasonable".

What the statement claims

"Rawls's political conception is both freestanding and overriding, which is contradictory."

The statement reasons like this. If Rawls's values stand apart from every doctrine, they have no authority over any doctrine. If they override doctrines, they must be a doctrine themselves. It is a clever objection, and it is half right. The block shows that the contradiction disappears for reasonable citizens, but returns for anyone Rawls calls unreasonable.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Freestanding" means built from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free. Rawls's political conception is political, but still moral. It is presented on its own terms, so that each citizen can fit it into his own religion or philosophy. It does not claim to have no values.
  2. On basic questions, political values normally win because they are very great values. They govern the basic framework of social life, which everyone lives inside. Reasonable doctrines can support them from within. And the habits of cooperation they build, such as tolerance and meeting others halfway, are "political capital": built up slowly and lost if not renewed.
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label does the work. A reasonable citizen accepts that fair terms come first, so being overridden is something he has agreed to. A citizen Rawls calls unreasonable has agreed to nothing. For him, the word "reasonable" is what does the overriding. TSH asks what standard grounds it. Unless it simply means the majority, it must be a standard outside the citizens, and then it looks like the objective standard of natural law that Rawls rejects.

The extra line, explained

  • STEELMAN · Rawls in Singapore. Masagos echoed Rawls in 2022 when he said the government's decisions apply secular, universal values, not individual religious beliefs. Even Finnis grants that Rawls's ideal of reciprocity seems broadly reasonable (14.10). So the overriding claim is not an odd philosopher's fancy. It describes how a pluralist government actually tries to work.
⚠ TRAP
Freestanding is not value-free

Do not write that Rawls's political conception is neutral or value-free. Rawls openly calls it a moral conception. The sharp objection is not "he smuggles in values", which he admits, but "who decides which citizens are reasonable?"

Card 14.10: Rawls on one card
▤ Theorist bank
  1. 1Purpose. When is coercion legitimate among citizens who reasonably disagree about the good?
  2. 2Test. Framework 15.5. Reciprocity requires reasons others might reasonably accept.
  3. 3Strength. Rawls explains how a law can bind people who reject its premises. He favours no doctrine in advance, and public reason is not secular reason.
  4. 4Critique. Finnis's dilemma, the need for a standard of "reasonable" outside the citizens (TSH), and Rawls's retreat on abortion.
  5. 5Reply. His standard is moral though political, not a head-count, and Finnis grants that reciprocity seems broadly reasonable. The dispute is who is reasonable.
  6. 6Verdict. Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, but deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side, and public reason may still end in a vote.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free, since Rawls's conception is political yet moral. On constitutional essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are very great values governing the basic framework of social life. Reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues they foster are political capital. There is therefore no contradiction for reasonable citizens. For dissenters, however, the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH rightly asks what standard grounds it.

13Putting it together: Sample Question 1 in full

You planned this question in Lesson 1. Here it is again with the whole archetype in place.

"Legislators governing a pluralist society should treat all moral opinions as equally valid. This can be achieved by refraining from passing any law restricting liberty unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct. Only then can legislators avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life."

Assume the usual instruction: discuss with reference to Rawls, Finnis, Hart and Devlin.

Sample Question 1 is a legislator question, so Core A (13.3) gives you ready verdicts. Its spine says that no law on a moral question is neutral, so pluralism must mean discipline on reasons, on coercion and on forum, not neutrality.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Core A on Sample Question 1
SQ1 says…Core A promptThe verdict, in short
"treat all moral opinions as equally valid"P2: moral opinions are equally validEqual validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, which counsels caution in coercion, not silence.
"refraining … unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct"P3: only harm to others justifies coercionHarm to others is the right presumption for punishment, but not the only ground, and not a neutral fact.
"avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life"P1: the state should be neutralNeutral outcomes are impossible. The kernel is narrower: no official comprehensive doctrine, and no coercion on reasons only its adherents can accept.

Two Core A tools finish the job. The pivot: "fixed" is a matter of degree, since no theorist imposes one complete life-plan and every theorist fixes some limits. The repaired line, for your close: legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

Everything turns on "equally valid", and that phrase commits the statement to more than it can defend. The statement's aim, that legislators should not impose a fixed conception of the good life, is sound, and Rawls and Finnis both share it. I make three claims. First, treating all opinions as equally valid is itself a moral position, so it defeats itself. Second, legislating only against harm to others is not the only route to the aim, since Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective. Third, that mechanism is not neutral either, since Rawls counts Mill's liberalism as one comprehensive doctrine among others.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Rawls (6.1, 6.2, 6.11). Claim: the aim echoes Rawls, but "equally valid" is not his view. Rawls asks for reasons every reasonable citizen could accept, and he excludes unreasonable doctrines, meaning those that refuse fair terms, not those that are false. His neutrality is of justification, not outcome, and he concedes that our actions imply a view. Objection: the label "reasonable" does the overriding (TSH). Reply: his standard is moral though political. Illustration: Masagos in 2022, applying secular, universal values. So Rawls supports the aim but not equal validity.
  2. Finnis (5.5, 6.2). Claim: a pluralist state can avoid a fixed conception of the good life without treating all opinions as equally valid. Finnis's common good is a set of conditions in which citizens pursue their own reasonable plans, not a ship bound for one port, and the state's job is peace and justice. Objection: Finnis is not neutral, since reason requires favouring the basic goods. Reply: concede it, because no law is neutral. Illustration: POFMA, where Finnis protects knowledge with prudence. So the aim survives on substantive grounds.
  3. Hart and Devlin, with self-critique (7.2, 7.3, 7.9). Claim: the mechanism is neither necessary nor sufficient. Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective, so harm to others is not the only ground. Devlin shows that every society takes a moral stand, though even he says a majority's dislike is not nearly enough. Self-critique (1.4): Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote. So replace "only harm to others" with a presumption against coercion that grows stronger as the coercion grows.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore partly right. Its aim, that a pluralist state should not impose one way of life, is shared by Rawls and Finnis alike. But its mechanism fails. Treating all opinions as equally valid defeats itself, and legislating only against harm to others is neither neutral nor the only route to the aim. A defensible version would say that legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine. Pluralism asks for equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions.

14Recap

Archetype 6 on one card
▤ Sections 6.1–6.11
  1. 1Rawls asks for more than a majority and less than unanimity, and civility is a duty to justify. Finnis's dilemma: a veto, or a judgement on the merits (6.1, 15.5).
  2. 2No law is neutral, and "unreasonable" does not mean "false" (6.2).
  3. 3An OC is moral, not a truce. Legislating what the faiths share is Devlin, not Rawls (6.3).
  4. 4Kind (Rawls), motive (Chua), merit (Finnis and TSH), and TSH's Catch-22 (6.4).
  5. 5Abortion: permitting is deciding. The hunter, the slave-owner reply, circumspection (6.5).
  6. 6Finnis's guidance for law-makers lives in Lesson 5 (6.6).
  7. 7No argument is barred for being religious, if public reasons follow (6.7).
  8. 8A whipped vote shows discipline, and a free vote serves conscience. Neither is automatically public reason (6.8).
  9. 9Moral truth limits law, but "make people better" overreaches (6.9).
  10. 10Sample Question 1: keep the aim, drop the mechanism (6.10).
  11. 11Freestanding is not value-free. The fight is over who counts as "reasonable" (6.11).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a town meeting with a translation booth. Rawls's rule is that you may speak in any language you like, your faith or your philosophy, but your argument only counts once it has been translated into the common language every citizen understands. Finnis and TSH add two things. A translated argument still has to be a good argument. And when the meeting ends, it decides something, so even "let everyone do as they please" is a decision that takes a side. Open, sound, fitted: and never neutral.
