LESSON 7 · ARCHETYPE 7 · ABOUT 66 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 2 ILLUSTRATIONS · 44 QUESTIONS

Enforcement of morals

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every answer to "should law enforce morality?", repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.

ARCHETYPE 7 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
7 Enforcement of morals
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Every answer to [whether law should enforce morality], repeal included, takes a moral stand; the question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.
Intro [The statement] treats [harm / autonomy / majority feeling] as a neutral test of when law may coerce. None is neutral: what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. I argue that [the statement] is [right / wrong / only partly right]: the issue is which reasons justify how much coercion.
Steelman: liberty The best case for [the statement] is what coercion costs: for Hart coercion is "prima facie objectionable" (7.9) and liberty may be valuable in itself; for Mill† the individual is sovereign over body and mind. This shows that the state needs a reason to punish [X]. It does not show [that harm to others is the only reason, or a neutral one].
Steelman: shared morality The best case for [the statement] is democratic. Majority rule treats citizens as equals; Indranee (2007) would usually follow the majority, and Lim Meng Suang left Hart v Devlin to Parliament. For Devlin, no society can do without intolerance, indignation and disgust. This shows that the legislature may decide moral questions. It does not show [that majority feeling makes its decision legitimate, let alone right].
7.1 Harm as plain fact Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham
  1. [Harm is a plain matter of fact] fails: what counts as harm, and who counts as an other, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns [X] is any reason to punish it.
  3. So [the quarrel is a sham] fails: both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.
  • AGAINST Arguably everything concerns others†. Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable, and for Devlin its bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality.
  • TRAP This is not positivism: Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law and argued what law should be; Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin†.
7.2 Paternalism, offence line protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency
  1. [Never protect adults from themselves] is Mill's anti-paternalism, taken to lengths Hart says may now seem fantastic.
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue: it supports [restricting sale], not obviously jailing the user it protects.
  3. So [the line is easy to draw] fails: paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.
  • FOR Hart explains punishing drug supply, even to adults without prescription, as protecting buyers: "transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent.
  • AGAINST TSH: morals pick targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports). Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts; teetotallers: 12.6.
7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man
  1. [Majority disgust is reason enough] borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads and wants slowness and, more tentatively, privacy: he licenses no majority to [act swiftly / ignore closed doors].
  3. So [majority feeling is the voice of the community] fails: disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands a deliberate judgement that the practice injures society.
  • Devlin's standard is what twelve at random might, after discussion, be expected to accept unanimously (Pollock's "practical morality"). Mere dislike is not enough: disgust counts only if deeply felt and not manufactured, and those swayed simply by it would be wrong.
  • AGAINST No expected unanimity exists on contested issues; Hart: critical morality must test that judgement (his racist society).
  • Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion: he gave no opinion either way and eventually backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022)†, though in 1959 repeal's difficulty weighed strongly against change.
7.4 Disintegration chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope
  1. [Repeal begins the end of society] is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society like treason, and much evidence points the other way.
  3. So [inevitably] overstates: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.
  • Four readings†: (1) society is its morality: for Hart "absurd", and moral change is more like a peaceful constitutional change; (2) empirical collapse: Hart finds seemingly no permissive drift in Europe; (3) interpersonal bonds (George): TSH replies that those rejecting a shared life may not regret the loss; (4) principled slope: Lawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†.
  • STEELMAN Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is by nature capable of threatening society's existence. Reply: that gives law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish [X].
  • QUALIFY Whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022; it dates only from 1938), but keeping it in 2007 was a choice.
  • QUALIFY Recast as mere change, the thesis can hardly justify harsh sanctions†; Devlin fears fragmentation and presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack or keep only by coercion†. Most jurists arguably side with Hart†.
7.5 Repeal neutral? takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
  1. [Repeal takes no side] fails: withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society takes a public stand on abortion; Shanmugam called repeal the right thing to do, itself a verdict.
  3. So [repeal is neutral] holds only weakly: withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.
  • FOR Shanmugam (2022): crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue (16.3), and private consensual adult acts raise no law-and-order concerns (also Faishal).
7.6 2007 majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
  1. In 2007 [majority feeling] prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met [no harm / religious only] with other grounds and spill-over, largely avoiding Devlin's treason analogy and disintegration thesis (perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So [majority feeling decides] describes the 2007 result, not its reasons: the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to rights, and retention's motive, deference to the majority or protecting what was right, was a "point of equivocation"; by 2022 tolerance had shifted.
  • AGAINST Spill-over to marriage and adoption was, in TSH's words, "tangible harm" by public consequences. Thio said harm can be physical or intangible and, per TSH, that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design.
7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes [s 377A] arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes there is no logic in this: each crime is weighed on its own, so legal adultery proves nothing.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence yet still sent "a symbolic message".
  • AGAINST Unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart) and hangs like a sword over gay men (Shanmugam).
  • QUALIFY TSH: policing varies with the offence; a 2007 MP: some laws, eg against nudity visible to the public, are hard to police.
7.8 Wrong before; order v good we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely
  1. [We were wrong before] defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery; that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. [Keep order, not make people good] fits Devlin's legal "minimum"; Stephen punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.
  • Hart: whether to punish and how severely are distinct questions, so a harsh penalty needs its own case.
7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
  1. [Enforcing morality] can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable": it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause misery of a special degree.
  3. So [legislators should not enforce morality] fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
  • CONCEDE I concede that promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption) and needs public reasons (6.1): for Rawls, appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines, though he leaves the question open. The 2022 package is arguably Rawlsian† (16.5).
7.10 Sin, crime and religion religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, sin and crime are separate.
  2. Even Devlin concedes law cannot rely on doctrines citizens may disbelieve, so [a faith-based ban] needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban [without exception] fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and it would catch sacramental or temple use.
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns.
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • CONCEDE I concede the 2007 debate's reply that majority opinion may indicate objective morality†. Yet consensus gauges but does not ground: majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch".
Conclusion The statement is therefore [right / wrong / only partly right]. No answer, repeal included, is neutral, and Hart v Devlin is a moral quarrel, not a positivist one. Harm, defective consent or public offence may justify punishment; majority feeling is evidence, never the reason; promotion needs public reasons. Devlin's disintegration thesis suits a society in deep agreement, not a pluralist one. Singapore's 2022 package fits: a Wolfenden-like presumption (public order or public interest) for crime, Art 156 for marriage.

1Start here: archetype 7 in plain English

Archetype 7 asks one question: may the law punish conduct just because most people think it is immoral? The famous example is s 377A, the Penal Code offence of sex between men. Singapore kept it in 2007 but promised not to enforce it proactively, then repealed it in 2022 and at the same time added Art 156 to the Constitution to protect marriage between a man and a woman.

Two camps fight over the question. Mill and Hart say the state may use force only for good reasons, and that harm to others is the main one, so private conduct between consenting adults should be left alone. Devlin says a society is held together by shared moral ideas, and it may protect them with law in the same way it protects itself against treason.

Exam statements in this family usually treat one test as obvious and neutral: "only harm counts", "personal autonomy decides", or "the majority's feeling decides". Your answer is the same every time. None of these tests is neutral, because deciding what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. Even repeal takes a moral stand. So the useful question is never "should law touch morality at all?" It is "is this reason strong enough to justify this much force?"

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Harm principleMill's rule: the state may force someone to do or stop something only to prevent harm to other people.
PaternalismUsing law to protect people from themselves, for example by restricting the sale of dangerous drugs.
Legal moralismUsing law to enforce morality for its own sake, even when nobody is harmed.
Positive v critical moralityPositive morality is what a society actually believes. Critical morality is the set of principles we use to judge those beliefs.
Wolfenden ReportA 1957 English report. It said private homosexual acts between consenting adults should not be crimes, because private morality is not the criminal law's business.
Devlin's jury boxDevlin's way of finding a society's shared morality. Imagine twelve ordinary people chosen at random. After discussing the practice, would they all condemn it? It is not a head count.
Disintegration thesisDevlin's claim that a society can fall apart if its shared morality is not protected.
Coercion gradientPunishing, regulating and promoting use different amounts of force. The more force the state uses, the stronger the reason it needs.
Art 156The constitutional article added in 2022. It shields laws on man–woman marriage from challenge under the fundamental liberties in Part 4.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral stand, and the question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.

Put simply, keeping a ban, repealing it and never having one are all moral choices. A government that repeals s 377A has decided that private consensual sex between men is not something the state should punish. That is a moral judgement, just as keeping the law was. So you should never let a statement pretend that one side is "neutral" and the other "moralising". The real work is matching each reason to the amount of force it can support.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement treats harm, autonomy or majority feeling as a neutral test of when law may coerce. None of them is neutral, since what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. You then say whether the statement is right, wrong or only partly right, and explain that the issue is which reasons justify how much coercion.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. No answer is neutral, repeal included, and Hart v Devlin is a quarrel about morality, not about positivism. Harm to others, defective consent and public offence can justify punishment. Majority feeling is evidence to weigh but never the reason on its own. Devlin's disintegration thesis fits a society in deep agreement, not a pluralist one like Singapore. Promoting a moral view, as Art 156 does, still needs public reasons, meaning reasons every citizen could reasonably be expected to accept, whatever their faith (6.1). Singapore's 2022 package fits this picture, with a Wolfenden-like presumption (crime needs a public order or public interest reason) and Art 156 for marriage.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before attacking it. Section 7 gives you two, one for each camp.

  • Steelman: liberty. Coercion is costly. Hart calls it prima facie objectionable, because it punishes the offender and also restricts everyone who would have liked to do the same thing. Hart also says liberty may be valuable in itself, not only for what it brings. Mill adds that over their own body and mind, individuals are sovereign†. This shows the state always needs a reason before it punishes. It does not show that harm to others is the only reason, or that the harm test is neutral.
  • Steelman: shared morality. Majority rule treats citizens as equals. Indranee Rajah said in 2007 that Parliament would usually follow the majority unless there was a reason to protect the minority, and the Court of Appeal in Lim Meng Suang (2014) left the Hart v Devlin debate to Parliament. Devlin adds that no society can do without some intolerance, indignation and disgust. This shows the legislature may decide moral questions. It does not show that majority feeling makes its decision legitimate, let alone right.

The eleven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
7.1"Harm is a plain fact, so Wolfenden needed no moral judgement."What counts as harm, and who counts as "others", are moral questions.
7.2"Never protect adults from themselves, but punish offence."Hart allows protecting people whose consent is weak. Both lines turn on whose choices and feelings count.
7.3"Majority disgust is reason enough."Devlin himself refused to count heads and called disgust only a sign. He wanted slowness and careful judgement.
7.4"Repeal will inevitably lead to the collapse of society."Unproven. Only the principled slope has bite, and Art 156 now guards against it.
7.5"Repeal takes no side."Repeal rests on a moral judgement too. Not endorsing is not the same as being neutral.
7.6"In 2007, majority opinion rightly won."That describes the result, not the reasons. The debate had moved to rights and harms.
7.7"Enforcing some morals but not others is arbitrary."Inconsistency alone does not make a law a sham, since each offence is weighed on its own.
7.8"We were wrong before, so don't enforce morality."Saying we were wrong assumes there is a right answer. Be slow, not silent.
7.9"Legislators should not enforce morality."All law promotes some morality. What matters is how much force. Punishing private conduct for immorality alone is the hard case.
7.10"A faith condemns it, so ban it."Sin and crime are different. A ban needs a reason that works for everyone.
7.11"85% support the ban, so let the people decide."A poll is evidence, not a mandate. If a right is at stake, following the majority could be oppression.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Every answer is a moral stand, so match the strength of the reason to the amount of force.

2The big picture: Hart v Devlin

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Should the law punish things that are "immoral" even if nobody else is hurt? One side (Mill, Hart) says the law should stop people harming others and leave private life alone. The other side (Devlin) says a society is held together by shared values, and it may protect them as it protects itself from treason. This lesson shows you that both sides are making moral arguments, and that the useful question is how much force each reason can justify.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
MillThe harm principle. The state may use force against someone only to prevent harm to others. Over their own body and mind, individuals are sovereign†.
Wolfenden Committee (1957)Private homosexual acts between consenting adults should not be crimes. The criminal law exists to keep public order and decency and to protect the vulnerable from exploitation, not to police private morality.
DevlinA society may use law to protect its shared morality against conduct that goes beyond the limits of tolerance. You find that morality by asking what the reasonable person in the jury box would condemn after discussion. For most of Devlin's essay, Hart calls his view the moderate thesis: shared morality is the cement that holds society together.
StephenHart calls this the extreme thesis: enforcing morality is valuable in itself, so the law may punish the grosser forms of vice simply because they are vice.
HartCoercion always needs justifying. Harm to others, defective consent (paternalism) and public indecency can justify it. Immorality on its own cannot.
TSH (Pragmatism)We cannot avoid the moral question. She maps six functions the criminal law might serve: preventing harm, paternalism, public decency, averting disintegration, enforcing morals as intrinsically good, and protecting the moral ecology (the moral climate in which people make their choices). She also analyses the 2007 s 377A debate.

Key distinctions

  • Positive morality v critical morality. Positive morality is what a society actually believes. Critical morality is the set of principles we use to judge it. Hart's question is a question of critical morality: is the bare fact that a society condemns something any reason to punish it?
  • Harm v paternalism v moralism. Preventing harm to others, protecting people from themselves, and enforcing morality for its own sake are three different reasons. Each needs its own justification.
  • Punish v regulate v promote (distinction 1.3(5)). These are three levels of force. Jailing someone is the strongest, licensing or restricting sits in the middle, and encouraging through schools or the Constitution is the mildest. This is the coercion gradient taught in 7.9.

The Singapore story

⚠ TRAP
Hart v Devlin is not positivism v natural law

Hart and Devlin agreed that the laws in question were valid law. They argued about what the law should be. Liu stresses that Hart's ideas are modular, so a legal positivist could side with Devlin on this question†. Never write "Hart was a positivist, so he opposed enforcing morals".

37.1 Harm as plain fact

🧩 Practise 7.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.1 Harm as plain fact (word for word)
7.1 Harm as plain fact Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham
  1. [Harm is a plain matter of fact] fails: what counts as harm, and who counts as an other, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns [X] is any reason to punish it.
  3. So [the quarrel is a sham] fails: both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.
  • AGAINST Arguably everything concerns others†. Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable, and for Devlin its bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality.
  • TRAP This is not positivism: Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law and argued what law should be; Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Only harm to others counts, and harm is just a fact." But is offence a harm? Is a broken family a harm? Is damage to "society" a harm? Before you can measure harm, you must decide what counts as harm and who counts as "another person", and those are moral choices.

What the statement claims

Two exam statements share this shape:

"The Wolfenden Committee got it exactly right … since harm is a plain matter of fact, it calls for no moral judgment at all." (Q61)
"The liberal–conservative quarrel is a sham: both sides point to harm." (Q66)

The first says the harm principle is a neutral, scientific test: just check the facts. The second says that because both sides talk about harm, their disagreement is fake. Both assume that "harm" is a word with an obvious, value-free meaning.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Deciding what harm is takes a moral judgement. Harm is not a plain matter of fact, because what counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions. Is damage to a society's way of life a harm? Is the distress of a neighbour who disapproves? You cannot answer by looking. You have to decide which interests deserve protection, and that is a moral decision.
  2. Hart's real question is narrower. He does not ask whether harm is a fact. He asks whether the bare fact that a society's actual morality condemns something is, on its own, any reason to punish it. That is a question about critical morality, the principles we use to judge a society's beliefs.
  3. So the quarrel is real, not a sham. Both sides moralise, and both may talk about harm. But they do not merely hold rival moral codes, one approving of the conduct and one condemning it. They disagree one level up, about which reasons can justify coercion at all. Hart calls these divergent critical principles. That is a genuine moral disagreement, not a dispute about the facts.

The extra lines, explained

  • AGAINST · Liu's question. Liu asks what conduct does not concern others. On a wide enough view, everything does†. A harm test is only as strong as the line it draws, and drawing the line is a moral choice.
  • AGAINST · Wolfenden's own reasons. The Wolfenden Report itself did not rely on harm alone. It also protected public decency and the vulnerable. And Devlin pointed out that its own bans on "corruption" assume a public morality, since you cannot say someone has been corrupted without a view of what an uncorrupted person is like.
  • TRAP · this is not positivism. Hart and Devlin agreed that the laws were valid law and argued only about what law should be. Because Hart's thought is modular, a positivist could even back Devlin†.
  • From card 14.12 · TSH: harm has no fixed edges. TSH argues that the words harm and self-regarding (conduct that affects only the person who does it) have no fixed edges. If only harm to interests the law already protects counts, the argument goes in a circle, because the law ends up deciding what counts as harm. The reply is that the harm line needs moral argument, made openly (14.12).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is it harm?

A bill would make it a crime to hold a private party where guests use a legal but strong sedative. Three people describe the "harm":

SpeakerClaimed harmWhat deciding it requires
A doctorGuests may overdoseWhether harm to a consenting adult counts. That is the paternalism question (7.2).
A neighbour"I can't sleep knowing it goes on next door"Whether distress at merely knowing counts. Hart says it does not.
A ministerIt weakens family life in the areaWhether harm to "society's way of life" counts. That is Devlin's question (7.4).

Each answer is a moral decision about which interests the law protects. None of them can be read off the facts. That is line 1 of the block in action.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement treats harm as a plain matter of fact, but it is not one. What counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions, so the harm principle cannot be applied without moral judgement. Hart's real question is narrower: is the bare fact that a society condemns conduct any reason to punish it? The two camps therefore do not merely dispute the facts. They hold divergent critical principles, which makes their quarrel a genuine moral one, not a sham.

47.2 Paternalism, offence line

🧩 Practise 7.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.2 Paternalism, offence line (word for word)
7.2 Paternalism, offence line protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency
  1. [Never protect adults from themselves] is Mill's anti-paternalism, taken to lengths Hart says may now seem fantastic.
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue: it supports [restricting sale], not obviously jailing the user it protects.
  3. So [the line is easy to draw] fails: paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.
  • FOR Hart explains punishing drug supply, even to adults without prescription, as protecting buyers: "transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent.
  • AGAINST TSH: morals pick targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports). Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts; teetotallers: 12.6.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Mill said never protect adults from themselves. Hart said that is too strong, because sometimes people's choices are not really free: they are addicted, under pressure, or acting on a passing craving. So the law may restrict selling dangerous drugs to protect buyers. That is very different from jailing the users for being immoral. And "offence" only counts for things done in public, not for being upset that something happens behind closed doors.

What the statement claims

"A liberal state must never use the criminal law to protect adults from themselves … The state may, however, punish conduct that offends public decency." (Q64)

The statement draws two lines and says both are easy. The first line bans all paternalism. The second allows punishment for offence. The block shows that both lines are harder to draw than the statement thinks, and for the same reason.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Never protect adults from themselves" is Mill's strict anti-paternalism. Hart thought Mill held it so firmly that, to modern readers, it may now seem fantastic. We already accept many laws that protect people from their own choices.
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue. When a choice is weakened by cravings, clouded judgement or subtle pressure, the law may step in. But the aim is to protect the person's real will, not to make them good. That supports restricting the sale of something harmful. It does not obviously support jailing the user, who is the very person the law claims to protect.
  3. So neither line is easy. Paternalism needs a judgement about whose choices are truly free, and offence needs a judgement about whose feelings deserve protection. Both turn on moral questions, so the statement cannot treat them as simple.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · Hart's drug example. Hart explains why the law can punish supplying drugs, even to adults without a prescription. Buyers' consent may be weakened by passing desires, clouded judgement and subtle pressure, so restricting supply protects them. This is your best authority for regulating sale.
  • AGAINST · TSH: morals pick the targets. TSH notes that the law targets apotemnophilia (wanting a healthy limb amputated) but allows dangerous sports. Both involve risky choices, so the choice of which to ban must come from moral views, not from paternalism alone.
  • AGAINST · offence means public offence. Hart's offence ground covers public indecency. It does not cover distress at the bare knowledge that others do something in private. If it did, a teetotaller could demand a ban on alcohol because the thought of others drinking upsets them (see 12.6).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Sale v consumption

A bill bans "the sale and consumption of alcohol". Split it into its two parts.

PartHart's viewWhy
SaleCan be justifiedLicensing or restricting supply protects buyers whose consent may be clouded by addiction or pressure.
ConsumptionHard to justifyJailing the drinker punishes the person paternalism claims to protect.

This split is the move students most often miss. It appears again in the two-hats problem (12.6).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement's first line is Mill's anti-paternalism, which Hart thought might now seem fantastic. Hart allows the criminal law to protect people whose consent is defective, through cravings, clouded judgement or pressure, but the aim is to protect consent, not to make people virtuous. That supports restricting sale, not obviously jailing the user it is meant to protect. The statement's second line is no easier: offence counts only when it is public, not when someone is distressed by the bare knowledge of private acts. Both lines therefore turn on whose choices and feelings count, which is a moral question.

57.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read

🧩 Practise 7.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read (word for word)
7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man
  1. [Majority disgust is reason enough] borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads and wants slowness and, more tentatively, privacy: he licenses no majority to [act swiftly / ignore closed doors].
  3. So [majority feeling is the voice of the community] fails: disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands a deliberate judgement that the practice injures society.
  • Devlin's standard is what twelve at random might, after discussion, be expected to accept unanimously (Pollock's "practical morality"). Mere dislike is not enough: disgust counts only if deeply felt and not manufactured, and those swayed simply by it would be wrong.
  • AGAINST No expected unanimity exists on contested issues; Hart: critical morality must test that judgement (his racist society).
  • Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion: he gave no opinion either way and eventually backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022)†, though in 1959 repeal's difficulty weighed strongly against change.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

People often think Devlin said "if most people find it disgusting, ban it". He did not. He said: imagine twelve ordinary people who discuss the practice calmly. Would they all agree it is intolerable? Even then, go slowly and respect privacy. Disgust is a clue, not a verdict.

What the statement claims

"Every society is entitled to defend its way of life. When ordinary citizens feel disgust at a practice, that feeling is the surest evidence that it threatens the shared values …" (Q62)

The statement sounds like Devlin, and that is the trick. It takes Devlin's starting point (a society may protect its shared morality) and drops everything he said to slow that power down. Your job is to read Devlin properly and show that he would not sign the statement.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The statement borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards. Devlin did say society may defend its shared morality. But he surrounded that claim with conditions, and the statement ignores all of them.
  2. Devlin refused to count heads. For the law-maker, he said, a majority is not enough. He also wanted the law to move slowly and, more tentatively, to respect privacy. Nothing in Devlin supports a majority acting swiftly or reaching behind closed doors.
  3. So majority feeling is not automatically the voice of the community. Devlin called disgust only a good indication, a sign worth noticing. He also demanded a deliberate judgement that the practice actually injures society before the law acts.

The extra lines, explained

  • Devlin's own standard. For the law-maker a majority is not enough. The test is what twelve people chosen at random might, after discussion, be expected to accept unanimously. Devlin borrowed the idea of a "practical morality" from Pollock: the morality ordinary reasonable people live by.
  • Disgust has limits. It is not nearly enough that a majority dislikes a practice. Disgust counts only when it is deeply felt and not manufactured, and Devlin said those swayed simply by disgust would be wrong.
  • AGAINST · no expected unanimity. On a contested issue such as s 377A, there is no realistic prospect that twelve random Singaporeans would agree, so Devlin's own test often gives no answer. Hart adds that critical morality must test the jury's judgement. A racist society's shared disgust would pass Devlin's test, yet it proves nothing about what is right.
  • Devlin and Wolfenden. Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion. He gave no opinion either way on decriminalising homosexuality and eventually supported it (as Shanmugam noted in 2022)†. In 1959, though, he said a morals law is hard to repeal without seeming to weaken moral judgement, and that this weighed strongly against changing the law on homosexuality.
⚠ TRAP
Devlin is a cultural relativist, not a moral realist

Liu reads Devlin as enforcing a society's actual morality, not objective truth†. Monogamy binds us, Devlin said, because it is built into the house in which we live. Honest belief, whether right or wrong, makes immorality a question of fact. Privacy is only one thing to be taken into account. So do not present Devlin as a natural lawyer defending moral truth.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards. Devlin refused to count heads: for the law-maker a majority is not enough, and the test is what twelve people at random would, after discussion, be expected to condemn unanimously. He wanted the law to move slowly and to respect privacy, and he called disgust only a good indication, adding that those swayed simply by disgust would be wrong. Even read generously, his test fails on contested questions, where no such unanimity exists, and Hart reminds us that a persecuting society's shared feeling must itself be tested by critical morality.

67.4 Disintegration

🧩 Practise 7.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.4 Disintegration (word for word)
7.4 Disintegration chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope
  1. [Repeal begins the end of society] is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society like treason, and much evidence points the other way.
  3. So [inevitably] overstates: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.
  • Four readings†: (1) society is its morality: for Hart "absurd", and moral change is more like a peaceful constitutional change; (2) empirical collapse: Hart finds seemingly no permissive drift in Europe; (3) interpersonal bonds (George): TSH replies that those rejecting a shared life may not regret the loss; (4) principled slope: Lawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†.
  • STEELMAN Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is by nature capable of threatening society's existence. Reply: that gives law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish [X].
  • QUALIFY Whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022; it dates only from 1938), but keeping it in 2007 was a choice.
  • QUALIFY Recast as mere change, the thesis can hardly justify harsh sanctions†; Devlin fears fragmentation and presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack or keep only by coercion†. Most jurists arguably side with Hart†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Devlin said shared morality holds society together, so losing it could make society fall apart. But what does "fall apart" mean? If it just means "society changes", that is not a disaster. If it means "chaos follows", where is the evidence? The strongest version is a slippery slope of principle: once a court accepts one argument, the next step follows by logic.

What the statement claims

"Decriminalising homosexual conduct inevitably sets off a chain reaction … same-sex marriage and discrimination claims against religious businesses must follow." (Q63)

The statement predicts that repeal is the first domino. The word that gives it away is inevitably. Your reply is to separate the different things "disintegration" can mean, and to show that only one of them has real force.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "The end of society" is either trivial or unproven. If a society simply is its present morality, then any moral change "ends" it, which is true but uninteresting. If the claim is a prediction that society will actually collapse, it needs evidence, and there is none.
  2. Hart found no evidence. Nothing shows that private conduct threatens society the way treason does, and much evidence points the other way. Hart says that, as a claim of fact, Devlin's thesis deserves no more respect than Justinian's statement that homosexuality caused earthquakes.
  3. So "inevitably" overstates. The only version with bite is the principled slope, where accepting one legal argument commits a court to the next. Singapore has blocked that route, because Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.

The extra lines, explained

  • Liu's four readings. These are the four meanings set out in the flowchart†. TSH answers Reading 3, and Reading 4, the principled slope, is also her point. In the United States, Lawrence (decriminalisation) was followed by Obergefell (same-sex marriage), and later cases such as Masterpiece Cakeshop and, in the UK, Bull v Hall tested claims against religious businesses. Contrast Singapore, where Art 156 stops that chain in the courts.
  • STEELMAN · Devlin's capacity claim. Devlin argued that immorality, like subversion, is by its nature capable of threatening society's existence. Reply: that shows only that the law may deal with morality (it has jurisdiction). It does not give a reason to punish this particular conduct now.
  • QUALIFY · whose morality? s 377A dates only from 1938, and Shanmugam said in 2022 that its origin looked like happenstance. So it is doubtful that it expressed a deep, ancient shared morality. But keeping it in 2007 was a deliberate choice.
  • QUALIFY · Liu's critique†. If disintegration only means change, it cannot justify harsh sanctions. Devlin fears a society splitting apart, but he assumes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may not have, or could keep only by coercion. Liu thinks most jurists side with Hart here.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The claim that repeal begins the end of society is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven if it predicts collapse. Hart found nothing to show that private deviation threatens society like treason, and much evidence against it. The only reading with force is the principled slope, where one legal argument commits a court to the next, as Lawrence led to Obergefell. Singapore has answered that risk directly: Art 156 shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge. "Inevitably" therefore overstates the case.

77.5 Repeal neutral?

🧩 Practise 7.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.5 Repeal neutral? (word for word)
7.5 Repeal neutral? takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
  1. [Repeal takes no side] fails: withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society takes a public stand on abortion; Shanmugam called repeal the right thing to do, itself a verdict.
  3. So [repeal is neutral] holds only weakly: withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.
  • FOR Shanmugam (2022): crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue (16.3), and private consensual adult acts raise no law-and-order concerns (also Faishal).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Repealing the law takes no side. It just leaves people free." But deciding that something should not be a crime is a decision about right and wrong in public life. Even the Minister who repealed s 377A called repeal the right thing to do, and that is a moral verdict.

What the statement claims

"Repeal takes no side; it leaves each citizen free." "The state simply stands aside."

The statement treats repeal as the absence of a decision. On this view the state that bans takes a moral stand, and the state that repeals simply steps back. The block shows that stepping back is a stand too.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Repeal is a moral decision. Withdrawing the criminal law rests on a judgement about what the state may punish. You cannot remove a crime from the statute book without deciding that the conduct does not deserve punishment.
  2. Finnis and Shanmugam both show it. Finnis argues that every society takes a public stand on questions like abortion, whatever it does. And Shanmugam told Parliament that repeal was the right thing to do, which is itself a moral verdict.
  3. So repeal is neutral only in a weak sense. Not punishing something is not the same as endorsing it, so repeal does not say the conduct is good. But the reasons for repeal are never neutral.

The extra line, explained

  • FOR · Shanmugam's test. In 2022 Shanmugam said crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue, and that private consensual acts between adults raise no law-and-order concerns. Faishal made the same law-and-order point in the 2022 debate. Shanmugam called Singapore's position broadly similar to Wolfenden's. This is a moral principle about the limits of the criminal law, which is exactly why repeal is not neutral.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Repeal does not take "no side". Withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish, and Shanmugam himself called repeal the right thing to do. Finnis makes the general point: whatever a society does on such a question, it takes a public stand. Repeal is neutral only in a weak sense. Withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.

87.6 2007

🧩 Practise 7.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.6 2007 (word for word)
7.6 2007 majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
  1. In 2007 [majority feeling] prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met [no harm / religious only] with other grounds and spill-over, largely avoiding Devlin's treason analogy and disintegration thesis (perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So [majority feeling decides] describes the 2007 result, not its reasons: the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to rights, and retention's motive, deference to the majority or protecting what was right, was a "point of equivocation"; by 2022 tolerance had shifted.
  • AGAINST Spill-over to marriage and adoption was, in TSH's words, "tangible harm" by public consequences. Thio said harm can be physical or intangible and, per TSH, that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In 2007 Singapore kept s 377A but promised not to actively enforce it. Was that just "the majority wins"? TSH shows it was more complicated. The people who wanted to keep the law gave other reasons, such as knock-on effects on marriage and adoption, and the whole debate had shifted towards rights.

What the statement claims

"In 2007 majority opinion prevailed, and rightly so: live and let live."

The statement reads the 2007 compromise as a simple victory for majority feeling. Your reply accepts the result but challenges the explanation.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Majority feeling did shape the 2007 result, with Devlin-style caution. s 377A was kept, which matched the majority's view, but it was not proactively enforced, which matched Devlin's preference for slowness and privacy.
  2. But the reasons given were not Devlin's. Those who wanted to keep the law met the objections "it harms no one" and "it is only religious" with other grounds, such as spill-over effects on marriage and adoption. They largely avoided Devlin's treason and disintegration theses (TSH thinks perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So "majority feeling decides" describes the 2007 result, not its reasons. TSH shows the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to arguments about rights. Whether the motive was deference to the majority or protecting what was right was, in her words, a point of equivocation. By 2022, tolerance had shifted again.

The extra line, explained

  • AGAINST · harm by spill-over. TSH summarises the retention case as a claim of tangible harm through public consequences: if s 377A went, changes to marriage and adoption might follow. Thio argued that harm can be physical or intangible. According to TSH, Thio also explained that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design. These are arguments about harm, not appeals to majority feeling.
⚠ TRAP
Whose words?

"Tangible harm" is TSH's summary of the retention case, not the words of the MPs who wanted to keep the law. Credit it to TSH.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

In 2007 majority feeling prevailed, but with Devlin's caution: s 377A was kept and not proactively enforced. That describes the result, not its reasons. Those who wanted to keep the law answered the "no harm" objection with other grounds, such as spill-over to marriage and adoption, and largely avoided Devlin's disintegration thesis. As TSH shows, the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to arguments about rights, and whether the motive was deference to the majority or protecting what was right remained a point of equivocation.

97.7 Consistency, non-enforcement

🧩 Practise 7.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement (word for word)
7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes [s 377A] arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes there is no logic in this: each crime is weighed on its own, so legal adultery proves nothing.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence yet still sent "a symbolic message".
  • AGAINST Unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart) and hangs like a sword over gay men (Shanmugam).
  • QUALIFY TSH: policing varies with the offence; a 2007 MP: some laws, eg against nudity visible to the public, are hard to police.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Adultery isn't a crime, so making gay sex a crime is inconsistent!" Devlin admits there is no neat logic: each kind of conduct is judged on its own. And a law that is not enforced is not automatically a sham. It can still send a message, though it gives officials worrying power.

What the statement claims

"A legislature that enforces some moral norms but not others is acting arbitrarily." (Q70)

A related statement says an unenforced law is a sham, so the state must either enforce it fully or repeal it. Both statements assume that a law is legitimate only if it is consistent and fully enforced.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement, on its own, makes a law arbitrary or a sham. Both are real concerns, but neither settles the question.
  2. Devlin concedes there is no logic in which immoralities are crimes. Each offence is weighed on its own merits. So the fact that adultery is legal proves nothing about whether s 377A was justified.
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark. Announcing that s 377A would not be enforced did break Fuller's requirement of congruence between the law on the books and official action (Lesson 3). Yet the law still sent what TSH calls a symbolic message.

The extra lines, explained

  • AGAINST · discretion is dangerous. Hart warned that an unenforced law gives police and prosecutors formidable discriminatory powers, since they can choose when to use it. Shanmugam said in 2022 that s 377A hung like a sword over gay men. This is the strongest argument for repeal, and you should concede it.
  • QUALIFY · enforcement always varies. TSH notes that policing naturally varies with the offence. A 2007 MP pointed out that some laws, such as the ban on nudity visible to the public, are hard to police. Imperfect enforcement is normal, so it cannot alone prove a law is a sham.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes s 377A arbitrary or a sham. Devlin concedes there is no logic in which immoralities are crimes: each offence is weighed on its own, so the legality of adultery proves nothing. "Enforce fully or repeal" is also too stark. Announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence and, as Hart warned, handed officials formidable discriminatory powers, yet the law still sent a symbolic message.

107.8 Wrong before; order v good

🧩 Practise 7.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.8 Wrong before; order v good (word for word)
7.8 Wrong before; order v good we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely
  1. [We were wrong before] defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery; that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. [Keep order, not make people good] fits Devlin's legal "minimum"; Stephen punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.
  • Hart: whether to punish and how severely are distinct questions, so a harsh penalty needs its own case.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"We were wrong about slavery, so don't use law to enforce morals." But to say we were wrong about slavery, there must be a right answer. That lesson teaches care and humility, not giving up. And "the law should just keep order" is a view some theorists hold (Devlin's minimum), while others go further.

What the statement claims

"We have been wrong about morality before, so we should not use law to enforce it now." (Q34)
"The law exists to keep order, not to make people good." (Q71)

The first statement argues from past mistakes to silence. The second sets a narrow goal for the law. They often appear together, so the block handles both.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "We were wrong before" defeats itself. To call a past law an error, such as the laws that upheld slavery, you must assume there is a right answer. So the statement relies on the very moral truth it tells us to stop acting on.
  2. The right lesson from past error is care, not silence. Siew Kum Hong argued in 2007 that disgust was once used to defend slavery. That supports Devlin's call for slowness and Hart's demand for reasons. It does not support abandoning moral judgement altogether.
  3. "Keep order, not make people good" matches Devlin's minimum. Devlin said the law sets a minimum standard, not the maximum. Stephen went further and would punish vice as such. Finnis goes further in a different way. For him the state aims at the common good, the conditions in which people can flourish, but he denies that its job is to make people integrally good, meaning good in every part of their lives (Lesson 5).

The extra line, explained

  • Hart on severity. Hart said that whether to punish and how severely to punish are separate questions. So even when some punishment is justified, a harsh penalty needs its own case. This is useful whenever a statement defends a severe sentence for a moral offence.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"We were wrong before" defeats itself, since calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery, but that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention. The claim that law should keep order rather than make people good fits Devlin's legal minimum. Stephen would punish vice as such, and Finnis aims at the common good, so the statement picks one side of a debate rather than stating a neutral truth.

117.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote

🧩 Practise 7.9 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote (word for word)
7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
  1. [Enforcing morality] can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable": it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause misery of a special degree.
  3. So [legislators should not enforce morality] fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
  • CONCEDE I concede that promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption) and needs public reasons (6.1): for Rawls, appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines, though he leaves the question open. The 2022 package is arguably Rawlsian† (16.5).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Enforcing morality" can mean three very different things: jailing people (punish), licensing or restricting (regulate), or encouraging through schools and the Constitution (promote). The more force involved, the stronger the reason you need. Almost all law promotes some morality, so the hard question is punishment.

What the statement claims

"Legislators should not enforce morality." "The state should let people regulate their own lives." "The state should defend marriage." (Q36, Q68)

These statements use "enforce morality" as if it meant one thing. It means at least three, and the block's whole move is to pull them apart.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Enforcing morality" can mean punishing, regulating or promoting. These use very different amounts of force, and the justification needed rises with the force used. A school curriculum and a prison sentence both express a moral view, but only one takes away someone's liberty. The gradient is your own rule, built on Hart: all law rests on force, and the criminal law most directly†. Hart's own question was only about punishment, and he says little about promotion.
  2. Hart explains why punishment needs the most justification. Coercion is prima facie objectionable. It punishes the offender, it restricts everyone else who would have done the same thing, and in sexual matters it may cause misery of a quite special degree.
  3. So the statement fails as stated but holds in one place. "Legislators should not enforce morality" is wrong as a general rule, because all law promotes some morality. But it is right about punishing private consensual conduct for its immorality alone.

The extra line, explained

  • CONCEDE · promotion coerces too. Curricula, media rules and adoption rules all put pressure on people, even without punishment. Rawls says appeals to monogamy as such come from comprehensive doctrines (whole religious or philosophical views of life that citizens do not all share), though he leaves the question open. So concede that promotion needs public reasons (6.1). Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian† (see 13.2).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The 2022 package on the gradient
LevelWhat Singapore did in 2022What it shows
PunishRepealed s 377A. Non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes.Hart's lines survive: harm, defective consent and public offence still justify punishment (Shanmugam, 2022).
RegulateNo new restriction on private consensual conduct.Nothing to justify.
PromoteArt 156 lets Parliament define, protect and promote man–woman marriage.Promotion is the mildest force, but it still needs public reasons.

The package is a deliberate split: punishment withdrawn, marriage promoted (13.2).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"Enforcing morality" can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used. Hart explains why punishment needs the most: coercion is prima facie objectionable, since it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else and, in sexual matters, may cause misery of a special degree. The statement therefore fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone. Singapore's 2022 package follows this gradient, withdrawing punishment while promoting man–woman marriage through Art 156.

127.10 Sin, crime and religion

🧩 Practise 7.10 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.10 Sin, crime and religion (word for word)
7.10 Sin, crime and religion religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, sin and crime are separate.
  2. Even Devlin concedes law cannot rely on doctrines citizens may disbelieve, so [a faith-based ban] needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban [without exception] fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and it would catch sacramental or temple use.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sin is wrong in the eyes of a faith. A crime is something the state punishes. In a country of many faiths, you cannot make something a crime just because one faith calls it a sin. You need a reason that works for everyone. Even Devlin agreed.

What the statement claims

"This conduct offends religious teaching, so it should be a crime." "Ban it without exception."

The statement moves straight from "a religion forbids it" to "the state should punish it". The block shows why that step needs another reason, and why "without exception" makes things worse.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Sin and crime are separate. As Pritam Singh told Parliament in 2022, in any secular society sin and crime are different categories. A faith may condemn conduct, but that alone does not make it the state's business.
  2. Even Devlin agreed. Devlin, the conservative in this debate, conceded that law cannot rely on doctrines that citizens are entitled to disbelieve. So a ban grounded in faith needs a secular reason that every citizen can assess.
  3. So a ban "without exception" fails twice. First, one faith cannot on its own justify coercing people who do not share it. Second, a blanket ban would also catch religious practice itself, such as sacramental wine or temple use, and so would burden other faiths.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, sin and crime are separate. Even Devlin concedes that the law cannot rely on doctrines citizens are entitled to disbelieve, so a faith-based ban needs a secular reason. A ban without exception fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and the ban would catch sacramental or temple use.

137.11 Polls are not a mandate

🧩 Practise 7.11 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 7.11 Polls are not a mandate (word for word)
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns.
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • CONCEDE I concede the 2007 debate's reply that majority opinion may indicate objective morality†. Yet consensus gauges but does not ground: majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A poll says 70% "frown on" something. That does not mean 70% want people jailed for it. And even if they did, if people have a right to do it, the majority overruling them is oppression. Polls are evidence of what people think, not proof of what is right.

What the statement claims

"85% of citizens at least somewhat support the ban; let the people decide."

The statement treats a poll as a mandate. Your reply is not that polls are irrelevant. It is that a poll answers a different question from the one the law-maker must answer.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Disapproval is not a mandate to criminalise. In 2007 Hri Kumar pointed out that the 70% in a survey who frowned on homosexuality were never asked whether it should be a crime. Disliking something and wanting it punished are different views.
  2. TSH's dilemma brings the moral question back. If people have a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression. If they have no such right, following the majority is democracy. Either way you must first decide whether there is a right, which is a moral question the poll cannot answer.
  3. So majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles the law. A poll tells the legislator what people think. It does not tell the legislator what is right.

The extra line, explained

  • CONCEDE · consensus as a sign. Among the replies made in the 2007 debate, Liu notes one you should concede: majority opinion may be a sign of objective morality†. Shared moral views are not worthless evidence. But majorities were wrong about slavery, and TSH admits a catch in her own test for when courts may strike down a law (a long-lasting consensus across many countries that it is manifestly unjust): consensus itself can go badly wrong (15.13). So a consensus can help you gauge what is right, but it cannot ground it.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise. In 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who frowned on the conduct were never asked about making it a crime. TSH's dilemma shows why the poll cannot settle the matter: if there is a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression, and if there is not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns. Majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.

14Putting it together: Practice Q61

"The Wolfenden Committee got it exactly right. The only legitimate purpose of the criminal law is to stop people harming others, and what consenting adults do in private is none of the state's business. This simple principle is all a legislator needs: since harm is a plain matter of fact, it calls for no moral judgment at all. Adopting it would finally end the quarrels over 'public morality' that have dogged the criminal law for centuries."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Mill, Hart and Devlin.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement's natural ally is Hart, yet Hart rejects it twice over. He allows the criminal law to protect people whose consent is defective, so harm to others is not its only legitimate purpose, and he insists that applying his principles takes moral judgement. I make three claims. First, harm is not a plain fact, since what counts as harm and who counts as an "other" are moral questions. Second, the harm principle is not all a legislator needs, since paternalism and public decency can justify regulation. Third, the statement is right where it matters most: punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone is unjustified.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Mill and Wolfenden, steelmanned and tested (7.1). Mill: individuals are sovereign over body and mind†. But Wolfenden itself protected decency and the vulnerable, Devlin showed its bans on corruption assume a public morality, and TSH shows "harm" is indeterminate.
  2. Hart's grounds (7.2, 7.9). Restricting drug supply protects defective consent. Offence counts only in public, not as distress at bare knowledge. The coercion gradient. Singapore 2022: Hart's lines survive repeal.
  3. Devlin rightly read, and the quarrel (7.3, 7.4). No head-counting, slowness, privacy. Disintegration fails except as a principled slope. Self-critique: TSH argues Hart's paternalism is itself based on morals in the end.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore right about its conclusion and wrong about its reasons. Wolfenden's line, that private consensual adult conduct is not the criminal law's business, survives, and Singapore's 2022 repeal adopted something broadly similar. But the line is drawn by moral argument, not read off the facts, and it will not end the quarrels, because those quarrels are about which reasons justify how much coercion.

15Recap

Archetype 7 on one card
▤ Sections 7.1–7.11
  1. 1Harm's boundaries are moral (7.1).
  2. 2Paternalism protects consent, so split sale from use. Offence means public, not bare knowledge (7.2).
  3. 3Devlin refused to count heads and wanted slowness and privacy. Disgust is a clue (7.3, 15.6).
  4. 4Disintegration: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 blocks it (7.4).
  5. 5Repeal is not neutral, though it is not endorsement (7.5).
  6. 62007: the result followed the majority, but the reasons were about harm and rights (7.6).
  7. 7There is no logic in which immoralities are crimes, and unenforced laws give officials discretion (7.7).
  8. 8Past error counsels slowness, not silence. Punishment and severity are separate questions (7.8).

🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a volume knob labelled promote → regulate → punish. Every time you turn it up, the reason you need gets heavier. Harm, defective consent and public offence are heavy enough to reach "punish". Majority feeling and a faith's teaching are not. And turning the knob down to zero (repeal) is still a choice about where to set it.

LESSON 8 · ARCHETYPE 8 · ABOUT 74 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 5 ILLUSTRATIONS · 48 QUESTIONS

Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity

⚡ BIG IDEA

An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and whether something is law never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it (Hart).

ARCHETYPE 8 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
8 Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [An unjust law] stays law unless intolerably unjust, but validity never settles whether [the judge or citizen] should obey.
Intro [The statement] runs two questions together: is [the statute] law, and must anyone obey it? I [agree only in part]: only intolerable injustice unmakes law (Radbruch, Alexy), and validity never settles obedience (Hart).
Steelman: for Hart The best case for [the statement] is honesty: denying evil law the name breeds romantic optimism that all values fit one system, and "insincerity" about a dilemma; Hart (1958) thought the formula useless during the regime and unneeded after†. This shows that candour is a virtue. It does not show [that the formula is dishonest].
Steelman: for Radbruch The best case for [the statement] is that constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on "equal moral worth", so Arts 9 and 12 may legitimately import a higher law, including Radbruch's formula (TSH), which he wrote (1946) to arm judges against the next tyranny†. This shows that extreme injustice can defeat validity. It does not show [that ordinary injustice does].
8.1 Grudge informer Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter
  1. Whether [the Nazi statute] was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish under a frankly retrospective law, which, Fuller replies, voids Nazi laws for informers, at least for that statute.
  3. So [she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute] can hold even if it was law: on Alexy's reading, Bamberg voided no statute.
