8.2 Hart's best case law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair
  1. Hart answers [judges taught that law is law will never resist]: validity leaves open the final moral question of obedience.
  2. Speaking plainly, [the decree] is law but too evil to obey, a condemnation everyone can understand.
  3. So [he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair] states the strong connection thesis, which no serious non-positivist defends (Alexy).
8.3 Alexy's replies how the word is used; any neutral standpoint; eye of the beholder; reaching back; determined tyranny
  1. Alexy grants [that is simply how the word is used] to observers, but a judge applying Ordinance 11†, which stripped citizenship on racist criteria, joins a procedure claiming correctness.
  2. The Federal Constitutional Court (1968) found its injustice "intolerable" and "evident", with nothing in common with law and justice.
  3. So [the decree is law] holds only for observers: a judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it law prima facie but in the end no law at all.
  • Alexy's replies (use two; language arguably weakest, effectiveness speculative both ways†). Clarity: adequacy precedes simplicity; at the extreme the ethical problem is also legal. Effectiveness: largely conceded; if lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds; risk effect (12.5). Certainty: the more extreme the injustice, the surer the knowledge; only an absolutist objects. Relativism: in rights-steeped states, rights consensus should thwart Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge; the minimum core is unargued here. Democracy, dispensability: core area only, else no judicial review; nulla poena may be unamendable (art 79(3)); Singapore: 11.7.
  • CONCEDE For Alexy, Hart's candour objection is the strongest argument against non-positivism but not its downfall: nulla poena can exempt past actors or, better, evident injustice leaves the legal position simply determined.
8.4 Does the label matter? a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; lawbreaker
  1. The label is a definitional quarrel, neither side less honest (Hart judges effect, Alexy concept†), but no mere [quarrel about words]: it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even if the wife's fate is the same either way, Hart ranks candour above a minor virtue.
  3. So [his conscience belongs to his private life] restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted.
8.5 A stable democracy unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate
  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not [an unelected veto]: legislation stands unless intolerably unjust (TSH).
  2. Judges must show such injustice by broad historical consensus, which generally checks idiosyncratic personal ideologies: racial genocide and slavery qualify; abortion limits did not in 1973, nor, for now, opposite-sex marriage laws.
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice] holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal, not for genocide.
  • CONCEDE TSH's "catch": decades on, the formula could impose a worldwide same-sex marriage trend (1.4); amid judicial oligarchies consensus may reflect only select groups of judges. I concede both and accept her reply: an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
  • QUALIFY Drawing on common morality (Alexy), the formula is arguably a transitional safeguard, primarily a tool of resistance, idle once morality has fully shifted†.
8.6 Retroactivity retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
  1. [Retrospective laws are always unjust] confuses a cost with a verdict: a curative statute may be essential to legality.
  2. The core is the new crime, commanding someone today to do something yesterday, which even Hart grants may be "odious".
  3. So [the statement] nearly holds for new crimes; a longer term is less objectionable, and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).
8.7 Obey or disobey? obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court
  1. [The statement] merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed faithful to him as king, not to his law, for he never made any.
  3. So [the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong] holds legally for Hart, for Radbruch only below the threshold; morally it stays open.
  • Hart: a legal duty; no moral duty to obey from validity alone; a moral duty to disobey past a certain degree of iniquity (Bentham, Austin).
  • Fuller: a legal duty by degree, none on total failure; a moral duty from reciprocity until its final and complete rupture; no simple principle for disobedience short of that, as under Hitler.
  • Radbruch, Alexy: no legal duty past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality†, where judges and lawyers should deny legal character; below that, law open to moral critique.
  • Finnis: unjust law is no nullity; no prima facie moral duty, though one can arise lest a largely just system weaken; applied, one may never choose directly against a basic value.
  • CITIZEN While the regime lasts, the disobedient face the usual consequences either way (Hoerster).
  • JUDGE What the highest court calls law is law for observers and LP; for participants its ruling claims correctness (Alexy), so at extreme injustice a later court or lawyer may call it legally wrong; below that, it is law. Lower courts: 15.10.
  • STEELMAN For the pigeon feeder†, deterrence is no moral reason to obey; fair play is: she gains from institutions others uphold. Every such reason is moral: legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons†.
8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice
  1. Radbruch's third tier asks not how unjust [the statute] is but whether it attempts justice: where equality is deliberately betrayed, it lacks the very nature of law†.
  2. On his first tier†, positive law prevails even when unjust; on the second, at an "intolerable level", it is "flawed law" that must yield to justice, arguably no nullity, though the outcome is the same†.
  3. So [the judge must apply it] fails for a statute aimed at one race; morally, too, no role excuses applying a facially racist law (Thunder).
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]: validity never settles what [the actor] should do. A law surviving the formula is not thereby just: that question stays with Parliament and conscience. Deviating can be unjust too: the judge's morality may be wrong (Hoerster), and Radbruch himself warned of "frightful dangers".

1Start here: archetype 8 in plain English

Archetype 8 asks two questions that sound like one: is a very unjust law still law, and must anyone obey it? The story behind it is Nazi Germany. After the war, German courts had to decide what to do with people who had acted under Nazi statutes. The most famous is the grudge informer, a wife who reported her husband's remarks against Hitler in 1944 to be rid of him, and who was prosecuted in 1949.

Two camps answer differently. Hart says a wicked statute is still law, but we should say plainly that it is too evil to obey. If we want to punish people who acted under it, we should pass a statute that openly admits it reaches back in time. Radbruch, and later Alexy, say that at the extreme a statute is not law at all. Once its injustice becomes intolerable, judges and lawyers should deny it legal character.

Exam statements in this family usually merge the two questions. Some say "it was valid, so it had to be obeyed". Others say "it was unjust, so it was never law". Your answer is the same every time. Keep the questions apart. An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust, and even a valid law never settles whether the judge or the citizen should obey it.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
ValidityWhether a rule counts as law in a legal system. It is a separate question from whether anyone should obey it.
Legal v moral obligationA legal obligation is what valid law requires. A moral obligation is what you ought to do, all things considered. The two can come apart.
Legal positivism (LP)The view that whether something is law depends on its sources (who made it, and how), not on its merits. Hart is its leading defender.
Radbruch formula (RF)Unjust law still counts as law, unless its injustice reaches an intolerable level, or it deliberately betrays equality. Then it must yield to justice, or is no law at all.
Strong v weak connection thesisStrong: every unjust law is not law. Weak (Radbruch, Alexy): only extremely unjust law is not law. No serious non-positivist defends the strong version.
Observer v participantAn observer describes a legal system from outside, like a historian. A participant must decide inside it, like a judge, a lawyer or the person the law addresses, and claims to decide correctly.
Grudge informerA wife who reported her husband's anti-Hitler remarks in 1944 to be rid of him. In 1949 she was prosecuted. Could the Nazi statute shield her?
Ordinance 11A Nazi decree under the Reich Citizenship Law that stripped people of citizenship on racist criteria. It is Alexy's example, not the informer's statute.
Retroactive (retrospective) lawA law that reaches back to change the legal position of acts already done.
Nulla poena sine legeLatin for "no punishment without a law". You cannot be punished for something that was not a crime when you did it.
Fidelity to lawBeing faithful to law as an enterprise of rules people can follow, which is not the same as obeying whoever is in charge.
Broad historical consensus (BHC)TSH's test for intolerable injustice: long-lasting agreement across many jurisdictions, for the same reason.
Risk effectAlexy's point that if non-positivism prevails, an official who applies evil law risks being prosecuted later, which may deter him.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: an unjust law stays law unless intolerably unjust, but validity never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey.

Put simply, most unjust laws are still laws. A harsh tax, a clumsy licensing rule or a law you would have voted against all remain law. Only the truly monstrous ones, such as a decree stripping people of citizenship on racist grounds, lose that status, and only on Radbruch's and Alexy's view. And whether something is law is a separate question from whether you should obey it. Hart, the leading positivist, insists on that, and your Position adopts it.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement runs two questions together: is the statute law, and must anyone obey it? You agree only in part. Only intolerable injustice unmakes law (Radbruch, Alexy), and validity never settles obedience (Hart).

The Conclusion gives your verdict. The statement is overstated, because validity never settles what the judge or the citizen should do. A law that survives Radbruch's formula is not thereby just. It has only been shown not to be intolerably unjust, and whether it is just stays a question for Parliament and for conscience. Finally, deviating from the law can be unjust too. The deviating judge's morality may be wrong, as Hoerster warned, and Radbruch himself saw frightful dangers in denying duly enacted statutes the name of law.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before answering it. Section 8 gives you two, one for each camp.

  • Steelman: for Hart. The best case is honesty. Hart argued that refusing to call evil law "law" breeds a romantic optimism that all our values fit into one system. It also breeds insincerity about a real dilemma, because punishing evil deeds after the fact may mean sacrificing the rule against retroactive punishment. Hart (1958) also thought the formula useless while the regime lasted and unneeded once it fell†. This shows that candour is a virtue. It does not show that the formula is dishonest, since Alexy can answer that where the injustice was evident at the time, nothing is being hidden (8.3).
  • Steelman: for Radbruch. The best case is constitutional. TSH argues that constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on equal moral worth. So Singapore's Art 9 (life and liberty only in accordance with law) and Art 12 (equality) may legitimately import a higher law, including Radbruch's formula. Radbruch wrote the formula in 1946 to arm judges against the next tyranny†. This shows that extreme injustice can defeat validity. It does not show that ordinary injustice does.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
8.1"The grudge informer could never shelter behind a Nazi statute."Whether the statute was law decides who bears the cost. Even if it was law, Hart's second honest option, a frankly retrospective statute, denies her the shield.
8.2"Judges raised on 'law is law' never resist, so a judge should refuse whatever he finds unfair."Validity leaves obedience open. Say the decree is law but too evil to obey. Refusing the merely unfair is a thesis nobody serious holds.
8.3"Calling the decree 'law' is simply how the word is used."True for observers. A judge who refuses it on legal grounds must call it law at first sight, but in the end no law at all.
8.4"It is only a quarrel about words."It is a quarrel about definitions, but it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
8.5"Judges must never strike down a law for injustice."Right for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal. Wrong for genocide or slavery, shown by broad historical consensus.
8.6"Retrospective laws are always unjust."Retroactivity is a cost, not a verdict. New crimes after the fact are odious, but cures and civil overruling differ.
8.7"The citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong, and fidelity means deference."There are three questions, not one. Rex's subjects stayed loyal to the king, not to his law.
8.8"The judge must apply even a racist statute."A statute that deliberately betrays equality does not even attempt justice, so it lacks the nature of law.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

"Is it law?" and "must I obey?" are two different questions, and only extreme injustice changes the answer to the first.

2The big picture: is a wicked law still law?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

During the Nazi era a woman reported her husband for criticising Hitler, hoping to get rid of him. Under the Nazi statutes, what she did seemed lawful. After the war, should a court punish her? If the statutes were law, she seems to have done nothing illegal. If they were so evil that they were not law, she has no legal shield. This lesson is about that choice: who makes it, how honestly, and whether calling something "law" tells anyone what to do.

Two questions, two standpoints

Two distinctions from the sheet's list in 1.3 do most of the work in this archetype, and a third split helps you place the arguments.

  • Validity v obligation (distinction 1.3(6)). Validity asks whether a rule counts as law. Obligation asks whether anyone should obey it. The statements in this archetype love to merge the two, either by saying "valid, so binding" or by saying "unjust, so not law". The distinction's home is 8.7.
  • Observer v participant (distinction 1.3(7)). An observer, such as a historian, reports what a society treated as law. A participant, such as a judge deciding a case, has to give an answer and claims that it is correct. Alexy's whole defence of Radbruch rests on this difference, so its home is 8.3.
  • During the regime v after it†. Two different problems are in play. While an evil regime lasts, should citizens obey and judges apply its laws? After it falls, how should the new legal order treat acts that were lawful under the old one? Hart's charge that the formula is useless during the regime and unneeded after it uses exactly this split.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
RadbruchA German legal philosopher who was a positivist before the war, at least in the results he reached. After the Nazi years he wrote his formula (1946). Unjust law usually still counts as law. At an intolerable level of injustice it must yield to justice, and where equality is deliberately betrayed it is not law at all.
Hart (1958)Law as it is must be kept apart from law as it ought to be. A wicked statute can be law, and the honest response is to say it is too evil to obey. Punishing those who acted under it needs an openly retrospective statute.
Fuller (1958)Replied to Hart. Nazi law so failed the requirements of legality, through secret and retroactive laws and uncontrolled discretion, that we must ask how much of a legal system survived. He defended the post-war courts but did not adopt Radbruch's formula.
AlexyDefends Radbruch's formula from the participant's point of view. Every judicial decision claims to be correct, and extreme injustice fails that claim. He answers the positivists' objections one by one, and concedes that the objection from candour is the strongest.
HoersterThe positivist critic Alexy answers. While the regime lasts, disobeying a wicked statute has the usual consequences either way. And a judge free to refuse unjust laws might apply a "Nazi morality" to just ones.
TSHApplies the formula to a stable democracy such as Singapore. Courts should presume a law constitutional unless Radbruch's threshold is met, proved by broad historical consensus.
Aquinas, FinnisNatural lawyers. For Aquinas an unjust law is a corruption of law. For Finnis it is no nullity, but it lacks prima facie power to bind in conscience (14.2).

The story behind the archetype

ℹ NOTE
Was there any law in Nazi Germany at all?

Three answers sit side by side on the sheet. For Hart, law is whatever the officials' rule of recognition picks out, so even Ordinance 11 may pass his test† (13.1). Dworkin presses him (14.4). Many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler only out of fear. If that counts as acceptance, Hart drifts back towards Austin's commands, and if it does not, there was no law in Nazi Germany. Hart's side replies that acceptance even from fear, self-interest or habit still treats the rules as standards. For Fuller, law is a matter of degree, so the question is how much of a legal system survived (14.6). For Radbruch and Alexy, the system may be law while particular statutes, past the threshold, are not.

⚠ TRAP
Three mix-ups to avoid
  • Fuller did not adopt Radbruch's formula. Fuller tests a law's form (is it general, public, prospective, clear?), while the formula tests its content. Fuller asks how much of a legal system survived, not whether a statute is intolerably unjust (14.6, 13.1).
  • Hart's minimum content of natural law is not a test of legality. Hart observed that people do not form suicide clubs, so every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit. That is a practical necessity, unlike Radbruch's moral override† (14.4).
  • The informer's statutes are not Ordinance 11. She relied on statutes of 1934 and 1938 against hostile remarks. Ordinance 11 is Alexy's separate example, a citizenship decree (8.3).

38.1 Grudge informer

🧩 Practise 8.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.1 Grudge informer (word for word)
8.1 Grudge informer Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter
  1. Whether [the Nazi statute] was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish under a frankly retrospective law, which, Fuller replies, voids Nazi laws for informers, at least for that statute.
  3. So [she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute] can hold even if it was law: on Alexy's reading, Bamberg voided no statute.
  • In 1944 she denounced her husband's anti-Hitler remarks; sentenced to death, he was sent to the front; in 1949 she was convicted under the 1871 Code.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A woman used a Nazi law to get rid of her husband. After the war, should she be punished? If the Nazi law really was law, she seems to have done nothing illegal. If it was so evil that it was never law, she has no legal shield. Hart says: don't pretend. Either let her go, or pass a new law that openly punishes her after the fact, and admit that it is a hard choice.

What the statement claims

"The Nazi experience proves that those who insist 'law is law' were simply wrong … the wife who denounced her husband could never shelter behind a Nazi statute." (Q16)

The statement treats the informer's case as proof that wicked statutes are not law. It assumes that the only way to deny her a defence is to deny that the Nazi statute was ever law. That is tempting, because the result (she is punished) feels right, and the reasoning seems to come free with it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Whether the Nazi statute counts as law decides who pays for past injustice. If the statute was law, she acted lawfully in 1944, and punishing her now makes her bear the regime's wickedness after the fact. If it was not law, she never had a legal shield, and she is simply an offender under the 1871 Code. So the label is not academic. It moves the cost of the past onto someone.
  2. Hart left two honest options, and Fuller says the second is no different from what the courts did. Hart said we could let her go, or punish her under a statute that frankly admits it reaches back in time. Either way, the choice between two evils is made in the open. Fuller replied that such a statute would itself treat the Nazi law as void for informers, at least for that statute. So the only real question, for Fuller, is who does the dirty work: the courts or the legislature.
  3. So "she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute" can be true even if the statute was law. You do not need Radbruch's formula to deny her the defence, since a frankly retrospective statute would do it too. And on Alexy's reading of the case, the Bamberg court did not void any statute at all. It convicted her by a contested reading of the ordinary criminal law.

The extra line, explained

  • The facts. In 1944 a soldier home on leave made private remarks against Hitler. His wife reported them because she wanted to be rid of him. He was sentenced to death but sent back to the front instead. In 1949 she was convicted under the Criminal Code of 1871, which had stayed in force throughout, for illegally depriving him of his liberty. These facts are the archetype's signature example (sheet 1.5), so use them whenever a statement is about punishing those who acted under an evil regime.

What the cards add

  • Fuller's reply (card 14.18). Fuller argues that positivism never gives fidelity to law a coherent meaning, and that Hart's statute leaves only the question of who should do the dirty work. Fuller also stressed that the post-war courts were dealing with an emergency and could not wait for Parliament. Hart's side can reply that only a statute sacrifices the principle against retroactivity openly, and that the bridge from validity to obedience is a moral one (8.7).
  • Alexy's reply (card 14.18). Where the injustice was evident at the time, the court is only finding the law then in force. So there is no hidden retroactivity, and Hart's charge of dishonesty misses. Even Alexy, though, grants that candour is the strongest objection to his view (8.3).
  • Radbruch's own view (card 14.19). Radbruch was not against denying legal quality to such statutes, but he warned of the frightful dangers of doing so. For the informers themselves, he too preferred a retroactive statute.
  • Liu: any open form will do†. Hart seems to have had in mind a statute that expressly makes the conduct a crime. Liu adds that any transparent form works, for example a statute saying that it is no defence to invoke the named Nazi laws†. What matters is admitting the retroactivity and choosing the lesser evil openly.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Four ways to treat the informer
RouteWho backs itWhat the court or Parliament saysThe cost
Let her goHart, option 1The statute was law, so her act was lawful when done.An evil deed goes unpunished.
A frankly retrospective statuteHart, option 2. Radbruch too preferred it.The statute was law, but Parliament now openly makes her act punishable.The rule against retroactive punishment is sacrificed, in the open.
Deny the statute legal characterRadbruch's formula, as the post-war courts were thought to apply itThe statute was intolerably unjust, so it never shielded her.Hart: this is retroactivity in disguise.
Evident injusticeAlexyThe injustice was so extreme that anyone could see it at the time, so the court only finds the law then in force.Works only where the injustice really was evident.

Notice that three of the four routes reach the same result. The disagreement is about how honestly you get there, which is the subject of 8.4.

⚠ TRAP
Hart got the facts wrong

Hart supposed that the Bamberg court declared the 1934 statute void. On Alexy's reading it voided no statute at all, and Hart later conceded the error (card 14.18). Use Hart's version as the debate's hypothetical, but if you discuss the real case, add Alexy's correction.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Whether the Nazi statute was law decides who bears the cost of past injustice. Hart left two honest options, to let her go or to punish her under a frankly retrospective law, and either way the choice between two evils is made in the open. Fuller replies that such a statute would itself void the Nazi law for informers, at least for that statute, so the real question is who does the dirty work. The statement's conclusion can therefore hold even if the statute was law. Indeed, on Alexy's reading the Bamberg court voided no statute at all.

48.2 Hart's best case

🧩 Practise 8.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.2 Hart's best case (word for word)
8.2 Hart's best case law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair
  1. Hart answers [judges taught that law is law will never resist]: validity leaves open the final moral question of obedience.
  2. Speaking plainly, [the decree] is law but too evil to obey, a condemnation everyone can understand.
  3. So [he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair] states the strong connection thesis, which no serious non-positivist defends (Alexy).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Hart's big point is honesty. Say "this is the law, but it is too evil to obey." Everyone understands that. Saying "it isn't really law" asks people to accept a philosophy first, and it can hide the hard choice. And being a positivist never meant you had to obey everything. Whether to obey was always a separate, moral question.

What the statement claims

"An unjust statute is no law at all, and a judge asked to apply an enactment he considers unfair should simply refuse." (Q77)
"Judges raised on 'law is law' will never resist."

The statement makes two claims. The first blames positivism for the Nazi judges: teach people that law is law, and they will obey anything. The second goes to the opposite extreme and lets any judge refuse any law he finds unfair. Both are tempting after the Nazi era. Hart answers the first, and Alexy the second.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Positivism never told judges to obey. The statement says judges taught that law is law will never resist. Hart answers that calling a rule valid leaves open the final moral question: should it be obeyed? A positivist judge can say "this is law" and still refuse to apply it, on moral grounds.
  2. Plain speech is the clearest condemnation. Hart's formula is that the decree is law but too evil to obey. Everyone can understand that sentence. Saying "it is not law" asks people to accept a disputed philosophy before they can even follow the criticism.
  3. Refusing whatever a judge finds unfair is a thesis nobody serious holds. The statement's second half, that a judge should simply refuse what he considers unfair, makes every unjust law void. Alexy calls this the strong connection thesis and says no serious non-positivist defends it. Radbruch and Alexy hold the weak thesis instead: only intolerable injustice unmakes law.

The steelman and the cards, explained

Block 8.2 has no tagged lines of its own, so here are the points from the section and the cards that you use with it.

  • Steelman: for Hart. This is Hart's best case, set out at the top of the lesson. Denying evil law the name of law hides a real dilemma behind a comforting philosophy. Use it to show you have taken Hart seriously before you answer him with Alexy (8.3).
  • Card 14.18 · the simplest criticism. Hart's formula is among the most powerful moral criticisms of a law precisely because it is the simplest. It needs no theory of law, only the words "too evil to obey".
  • Card 14.19 · Hart's charge against Radbruch, and Fuller's defence. Hart said Radbruch had only half digested the spiritual message of liberalism. Radbruch, he thought, overvalued the bare fact that a rule is valid law, as if that settled whether to obey it. Fuller defends Radbruch: he saw the dilemma clearly, as a conflict between order and good order.
  • Section 11.7 · law must not supplant morality. Hart's liberal answer to the slogan "law is law" is: very well, but that does not settle the question, because law is not morality and must not supplant it (11.7).
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Radbruch wrote his formula in 1946 to arm judges against the next tyranny. Hart replied in 1958 that it was useless while the regime lasted and unneeded once it fell†. Liu also notes that Hart and Fuller often talk across purposes: an evil regime that met all eight of Fuller's requirements would leave the formula question open†.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Four ways to describe the same wicked decree
SpeakerWhat they say about itThe thesis behind it
HartIt is law, but too evil to obey.Separation: validity is one question, obedience another.
Radbruch, AlexyBelow the threshold it is law, open to moral criticism. Past it, it is no law.The weak connection thesis.
The statement (Q77)Anything unfair is no law, and the judge should refuse it.The strong connection thesis, which nobody serious defends.
Pre-war RadbruchIt is law, and resisting it is a matter for private conscience.Positivist in result (8.4).

Only the third row lets the judge's personal sense of fairness decide. That is what makes the statement easy to attack.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Hart answers the charge that judges raised on "law is law" will never resist. Calling a rule valid leaves open the final moral question of whether to obey it, so positivism never told anyone to obey. Speaking plainly, a wicked decree is law but too evil to obey, a condemnation everyone can understand. The statement's other half, that a judge should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair, states the strong connection thesis, which no serious non-positivist defends. Radbruch and Alexy deny legal character only to intolerable injustice.

58.3 Alexy's replies

🧩 Practise 8.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.3 Alexy's replies (word for word)
8.3 Alexy's replies how the word is used; any neutral standpoint; eye of the beholder; reaching back; determined tyranny
  1. Alexy grants [that is simply how the word is used] to observers, but a judge applying Ordinance 11†, which stripped citizenship on racist criteria, joins a procedure claiming correctness.
  2. The Federal Constitutional Court (1968) found its injustice "intolerable" and "evident", with nothing in common with law and justice.
  3. So [the decree is law] holds only for observers: a judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it law prima facie but in the end no law at all.
  • Alexy's replies (use two; language arguably weakest, effectiveness speculative both ways†). Clarity: adequacy precedes simplicity; at the extreme the ethical problem is also legal. Effectiveness: largely conceded; if lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds; risk effect (12.5). Certainty: the more extreme the injustice, the surer the knowledge; only an absolutist objects. Relativism: in rights-steeped states, rights consensus should thwart Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge; the minimum core is unargued here. Democracy, dispensability: core area only, else no judicial review; nulla poena may be unamendable (art 79(3)); Singapore: 11.7.
  • CONCEDE For Alexy, Hart's candour objection is the strongest argument against non-positivism but not its downfall: nulla poena can exempt past actors or, better, evident injustice leaves the legal position simply determined.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Critics of Radbruch raise several objections. Calling evil law "not law" is confusing, it doesn't stop tyrants, it makes law uncertain, morality is relative, and it lets unelected judges overrule Parliament. Alexy answers each one. His key move is to ask who is speaking. A historian can call a Nazi decree "law". A judge who has to apply it cannot, without contradicting himself.

What the statement claims

"Seen from any neutral standpoint, a decree stripping a whole class of people of their citizenship, issued through the proper channels and enforced by the state's officials, is law; that is simply how the word is used." (Q79)

The statement assumes there is one neutral standpoint from which everyone, judges included, should describe the law. From there, a decree made through proper channels and enforced by officials is law, whatever it says. That is tempting because it matches ordinary usage, and because it seems to keep morality out of the description of law.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Alexy grants the statement, but only for observers. A historian describing Nazi Germany can call Ordinance 11 law, because that is how the word is used. But a judge applying Ordinance 11 is not describing it. Ordinance 11 stripped people of citizenship on racist criteria†, and a judge who applies it takes part in a procedure that claims to reach correct results.
  2. A German court has already found such a decree intolerable. In 1968 the Federal Constitutional Court held that Ordinance 11's injustice was intolerable and evident. An attempt to destroy parts of a population by racist criteria, it said, has nothing in common with law and justice.
  3. So "the decree is law" holds only from the outside. A judge who refuses the decree on legal grounds cannot coherently call it law and also refuse it. Alexy's answer is that the judge must call it law at first sight (prima facie), but in the end no law at all.

The extra lines, explained

  • Alexy's replies: use two. The block's note lists five objections to Radbruch's formula, each with Alexy's answer. They are set out in the table below. In an exam use two of them, not all five. Liu thinks the language argument is arguably the weakest, and the effectiveness argument speculative on both sides†, so pick two of the other replies (clarity, certainty, relativism, democracy) that fit the statement, and concede candour separately (the CONCEDE below).
  • CONCEDE · candour is the strongest objection. For Alexy, Hart's candour objection is the strongest argument against non-positivism, but not its downfall. He has two replies. First, the principle of nulla poena (no punishment without a prior law) can exempt those who acted under the old law. Second, and better, where the injustice was so extreme that it was evident at the time, the court is not changing the law after the fact. It is simply finding a legal position that was already settled. Concede the objection's force, then use the second reply (sheet 1.4).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The five objections and Alexy's replies
ObjectionThe positivist saysAlexy replies
Clarity (and language)Speak plainly. "Law" is simply how the word is used, and writing morality into it muddies the water.A concept must be adequate before it is simple. At the extreme, the ethical problem is also a legal one. Liu thinks the language point is arguably the weakest†.
EffectivenessRefusing to call a statute law will not stop a tyrant.Largely conceded. But if lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds, and the risk effect gives officials a reason to hold back (12.5). Speculative both ways†.
CertaintyJudges will disagree about what is unjust, so nobody will know the law.The more extreme the injustice, the surer our knowledge of it. Only someone who treats certainty as absolute could object.
RelativismNobody can prove what justice requires. A judge might even apply a "Nazi morality" (Hoerster).In a state steeped in rights, the shared consensus on rights should stop that judge. But the minimum moral core he relies on is not argued here.
Democracy, dispensabilityThe legislature, not judges, should deal with unjust laws, and it can pass a retroactive statute.The formula bites only in a narrow core of extreme cases. Constitutional review of rights already reaches much further, so an objection from democracy that defeated the formula would defeat all judicial review. And nulla poena may be beyond amendment (art 79(3) of Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, which puts some principles beyond amendment). For Singapore, see 11.7.

Pick the pair that fits the statement. Q79 talks about how the word is used and says morality muddies the water, so answer the language point with line 1 and use the clarity and certainty replies.

⚠ TRAP
Observer and participant are not two theories

Alexy does not say Hart is wrong about the observer. He accepts the positivist label from outside, and argues only that a judge deciding a case cannot use it at the extreme. So never write "Alexy proves that Ordinance 11 was never law". Write that, for a participant, it was law at first sight but in the end no law at all.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Alexy grants that a decree such as Ordinance 11 is law from an observer's standpoint, since that is how the word is used. But a judge applying a decree that stripped citizenship on racist criteria joins a procedure that claims correctness, and the Federal Constitutional Court found its injustice intolerable and evident. A judge who refuses it on legal grounds must therefore call it law at first sight but in the end no law at all. The objection from certainty fails, because the more extreme the injustice, the surer our knowledge of it. Alexy concedes that candour is the strongest objection, but not a fatal one, since where the injustice was evident the legal position was already settled.

68.4 Does the label matter?

🧩 Practise 8.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.4 Does the label matter? (word for word)
8.4 Does the label matter? a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; lawbreaker
  1. The label is a definitional quarrel, neither side less honest (Hart judges effect, Alexy concept†), but no mere [quarrel about words]: it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even if the wife's fate is the same either way, Hart ranks candour above a minor virtue.
  3. So [his conscience belongs to his private life] restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Who cares whether we call it 'law' or 'not law'? What matters is what people do." But the label changes things. It decides whether a judge can refuse on legal grounds, whether a citizen can hide behind the statute later, and whether a lawyer can call it lawless in court.

What the statement claims

"Whether a wicked statute deserves the name 'law' is a quarrel about words … A judge has sworn to apply whatever has been validly enacted, and his conscience belongs to his private life." (Q78)

The statement says the whole Hart–Radbruch debate is about vocabulary, and that the judge's conscience has no place in court. It assumes the label changes nothing in practice. That is tempting because, as the informer's case shows, both sides can reach the same result.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. It is a quarrel about definitions, but not an idle one. Neither side is less honest. Hart judges the label by its effects, and Alexy by what the concept of law should contain†. But the label decides who may lawfully refuse the statute, and who may shelter behind it afterwards.
  2. Hart himself ranks candour above a minor virtue. Even if the informer is punished either way, Hart insists that how we get there matters. Hiding a retroactive punishment inside a claim that the old law was never law is, for him, a real moral cost.
  3. "His conscience belongs to his private life" is the view Radbruch gave up. Before the war Radbruch held that resisting unjust law was a matter for personal conscience. After the Nazi years he recanted, and Hart notes how poignant that recantation was. So the statement revives a view that its best-known holder abandoned.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
What the label changes, actor by actor
ActorIf the decree is law (Hart)If it is not law (Radbruch, Alexy, past the threshold)
JudgeLegally bound to apply it. He may refuse, but only as a moral choice, at personal cost. After the regime falls, he can plead that he applied the law then in force.Has a legal reason to refuse, and must call the decree no law in the end. If he applies it, he risks later prosecution (the risk effect).
LawyerMay refuse to rely on it, but what he refuses is still the law.Should denounce it as having no legal character.
Citizen who refusesA lawbreaker, though perhaps morally justified, or even obliged, to refuse.Commits no legal wrong, though the regime may punish him anyway (Hoerster).
Citizen who obeysLegally protected at the time. A later statute may reach him, and Hart says it should do so openly.Has no legal defence based on the decree, if its injustice was evident. This is the informer's position.

Read down the columns. The label does not change what the regime does to people while it lasts. It changes who has a legal argument, and who is exposed once the regime has gone.

Behind the three lines

  • Effect v concept†. Liu's way of putting line 1 is that Hart judges the label by what it does, for the person convicted and for society, while Alexy judges it by what the concept of law should be. On Hart's view, convicting the informer is in effect retroactive. On Alexy's, if you accept his concept, nothing was hidden: the statute failed the formula, so it was never law†.
  • The practical case is a wash†. Card 14.19 adds that neither side argues about truth, only about which concept is more desirable, and that the practical arguments are, in Liu's words, a wash†. So on what basis should we decide? Alexy says his replies at least tie the score, and three things break the tie in his favour: the risk effect, the need for the formula after a regime collapses, and its fit with nulla poena.
  • Radbruch's recantation. Before 1933 Radbruch was a positivist in result, at least where judges were concerned. After 1945 he said positivism had left jurists and people alike defenceless against cruel statutes (card 14.19). The statement's "private conscience" judge is the judge Radbruch himself came to reject.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The label is a definitional quarrel, and neither side is less honest, since Hart judges its effect and Alexy the concept. But it is no mere quarrel about words, because it decides who may lawfully refuse the statute and who may shelter behind it afterwards. Even if the informer's fate is the same either way, Hart holds that candour is more than a minor virtue. The claim that a judge's conscience belongs to his private life restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted.

78.5 A stable democracy

🧩 Practise 8.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.5 A stable democracy (word for word)
8.5 A stable democracy unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate
  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not [an unelected veto]: legislation stands unless intolerably unjust (TSH).
  2. Judges must show such injustice by broad historical consensus, which generally checks idiosyncratic personal ideologies: racial genocide and slavery qualify; abortion limits did not in 1973, nor, for now, opposite-sex marriage laws.
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice] holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal, not for genocide.
  • CONCEDE TSH's "catch": decades on, the formula could impose a worldwide same-sex marriage trend (1.4); amid judicial oligarchies consensus may reflect only select groups of judges. I concede both and accept her reply: an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
  • QUALIFY Drawing on common morality (Alexy), the formula is arguably a transitional safeguard, primarily a tool of resistance, idle once morality has fully shifted†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In Nazi Germany the formula made sense. But in a normal democracy like Singapore, should judges ever strike down laws for being unjust? TSH says almost never. Only when the injustice is so extreme that people across many countries, for a long time, agree it is monstrous, as with genocide and slavery. Everything else is Parliament's job.

What the statement claims

"Justice lies in the eye of the beholder … A judge who strikes down a statute as unjust therefore merely substitutes his own morality for that of the elected legislature." (Q80)
"In a stable democracy, the Radbruch formula is an unelected veto."

The statement says that any judicial use of the formula lets an unelected judge put his private morality above Parliament's. It assumes that justice is purely personal, and that the formula is a general power to strike down laws the judge dislikes. Both assumptions make the democratic objection look stronger than it is.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not a veto. TSH argues that legislation stands unless it is intolerably unjust. That leaves almost every law, including many bad ones, to Parliament.
  2. Judges must prove intolerable injustice by broad historical consensus. The consensus must be long-lasting, cross many jurisdictions and rest on the same reason. This disciplines judges, because it generally screens out idiosyncratic personal ideologies. Racial genocide and slavery qualify. Limits on abortion did not in 1973 (the year of Roe), and opposite-sex marriage laws do not, for now.
  3. So "judges must never invalidate a law for injustice" is right for ordinary injustice and wrong for genocide. Ordinary injustice is Parliament's to repeal. A law ordering genocide must fall, even one passed by constitutional amendment.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · TSH's catch. TSH admits two weaknesses in her own test. First, decades from now a worldwide trend, such as the spread of same-sex marriage, could carry the formula into a country whose legislature is trying to do right. Where consensus has gone dreadfully wrong, for a moral realist the formula is a real problem, not merely ineffective (sheet 1.4). Second, amid judicial oligarchies, the "consensus" may reflect only select groups of judges. Concede both, then accept her reply: an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
  • QUALIFY · a transitional safeguard†. Because the formula draws on common morality (Alexy), Liu reads it as a transitional safeguard, primarily a tool of resistance. It matters while a regime is turning bad, and falls idle once morality has fully shifted†. In a stable democracy it is a backstop that is rarely, if ever, triggered.
  • Steelman: for Radbruch. The section's second steelman belongs here. Since constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on equal moral worth, TSH argues that Arts 9 and 12 may legitimately import a higher law, including Radbruch's formula. That answers the objection that the formula is not in the Constitution the nation accepted (card 14.26).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Does it cross the threshold?
LawBroad historical consensus that it is intolerably unjust?Result on TSH's test
A law ordering racial genocideYesStrike it down, even if passed by amendment.
A law permitting slaveryYesStrike it down.
Limits on abortion (voided in Roe, 1973)NoLegislatures decide.
Opposite-sex marriage laws (Women's Charter s 12)No, for nowParliament's to change, subject to TSH's catch (11.5).
Caning for third-time litteringArguably none (11.2)It stands, though open to criticism.
A ban on alcohol without exceptionNo consensus condemns prohibition (12.6)Harsh, but not intolerable.

The test is meant to be hard to meet. A judge who thinks a law unwise, or even unjust, has no power under it. Only the monstrous cases fall.

⚠ TRAP
Two attributions to get right
  • Presumed constitutional does not mean presumed just (card 14.26). A law that survives TSH's test has only been shown not to be intolerably unjust.
  • Broad historical consensus is TSH's test, not Alexy's (card 14.19). Alexy relies on a rational minimum of human rights. TSH supplies the consensus test for Singapore's courts, as evidence, not proof.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

In a stable democracy Radbruch's formula is a narrow check, not an unelected veto. On TSH's account, legislation stands unless intolerably unjust, and judges must show such injustice by broad historical consensus, which generally screens out idiosyncratic personal ideologies. Racial genocide and slavery meet that test, while abortion limits did not in 1973, and opposite-sex marriage laws do not, for now. The statement therefore holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal, but not for genocide. I concede TSH's catch, that a world trend could carry the formula decades on, and accept her reply that an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.

88.6 Retroactivity

🧩 Practise 8.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.6 Retroactivity (word for word)
8.6 Retroactivity retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
  1. [Retrospective laws are always unjust] confuses a cost with a verdict: a curative statute may be essential to legality.
  2. The core is the new crime, commanding someone today to do something yesterday, which even Hart grants may be "odious".
  3. So [the statement] nearly holds for new crimes; a longer term is less objectionable, and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Retroactive laws are always unjust." That is mostly true for making new crimes: you did something legal yesterday, and today you are punished for it. But a law that reaches back to fix a technical mistake, or to lower sentences, can actually help people.

What the statement claims

"Retrospective laws are always unjust." (Q25)
"A theory that wicked laws are 'not law' is a solution in search of a problem: a new parliament can simply pass statutes reaching back in time." (Q81)

The two statements pull in opposite directions. Q25 condemns every retroactive law. Q81 treats a retroactive statute as the easy, honest way to deal with a fallen regime, so that Radbruch's formula is unnecessary. Both assume that retroactivity is one thing, either always wrong or freely available.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Always unjust" confuses a cost with a verdict. Retroactivity always costs something, because people could not plan by a rule that did not yet exist. But Fuller shows that a curative statute, one that repairs an earlier failure of legality, may be essential to legality itself.
  2. The core wrong is the new crime. A law that punishes conduct which was lawful when done commands someone today to do something yesterday. Even Hart, who proposed a frankly retrospective statute for the grudge informer, grants that such a law may be odious.
  3. So the statement nearly holds for new crimes, and fails elsewhere. A longer term for an existing crime is less objectionable. In civil cases, a court's retrospective overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).

Keep these apart

Block 8.6 has no tagged lines, but three distinctions keep your answer precise.

  • Branding as criminals v constancy (3.8). When a court overrules a reading that said conduct was not criminal, people who relied on that reading are left branded as criminals. That is why retrospective overruling is acceptable in civil cases but not in crime. Abdul Nasir (CA 1997) is different. The court held that life imprisonment means natural life, but applied that only to the future. It engages Fuller's value of constancy through time, not branding.
  • Abuse, not all retroactivity†. Fuller's requirement of prospectivity bars only abuse (15.1). Liu's test is that retroactivity becomes abuse when it undermines the law's ability to guide: bad faith, frequent changes, or punishment after the fact†. Making a sentence more lenient is not abuse, though fairness to prisoners raises a separate moral question. And the common law is retroactive by default†.
  • Q81 and Alexy's reply. The positivist says the formula is dispensable because a new parliament can pass a retroactive statute. Alexy replies that nulla poena may be entrenched beyond even the constitution-amending power (Basic Law art 79(3)), so that route may be closed. And where the injustice was evident at the time, the formula involves no hidden retroactivity at all (8.3).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Six laws that reach back, sorted
LawWhat it doesVerdict
Hart's statute for the informerMakes past conduct punishableA new crime after the fact. Hart accepts it only as an open choice of the lesser evil.
A longer term for an existing crimeRaises the penaltyLess objectionable than a new crime.
A curative statuteRepairs an earlier failure of legalityMay be essential to legality. Used as a general practice, it robs every law of some of its significance (Fuller).
A civil precedent overruled by a courtChanges the rule for the parties before the courtA price worth paying (3.8).
Abdul Nasir (CA 1997)Life imprisonment means natural lifeApplied only to the future. It engages constancy, not branding as criminals.
Re-sentencing to a lower term†Makes the law more lenientNot abuse†, though fairness between prisoners is a separate question.

Only the first row is the clear wrong the statement has in mind. The others show why "always" fails.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement confuses a cost with a verdict. Retroactivity always costs something, yet a curative statute may be essential to legality itself. The core wrong is the new crime, which commands someone today to do something yesterday, and even Hart grants that such a law may be odious. The statement therefore nearly holds for new crimes. A longer term is less objectionable, and in civil cases retrospective overruling is a price worth paying.

98.7 Obey or disobey?

🧩 Practise 8.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.7 Obey or disobey? (word for word)
8.7 Obey or disobey? obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court
  1. [The statement] merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed faithful to him as king, not to his law, for he never made any.
  3. So [the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong] holds legally for Hart, for Radbruch only below the threshold; morally it stays open.
  • Hart: a legal duty; no moral duty to obey from validity alone; a moral duty to disobey past a certain degree of iniquity (Bentham, Austin).
  • Fuller: a legal duty by degree, none on total failure; a moral duty from reciprocity until its final and complete rupture; no simple principle for disobedience short of that, as under Hitler.
  • Radbruch, Alexy: no legal duty past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality†, where judges and lawyers should deny legal character; below that, law open to moral critique.
  • Finnis: unjust law is no nullity; no prima facie moral duty, though one can arise lest a largely just system weaken; applied, one may never choose directly against a basic value.
  • CITIZEN While the regime lasts, the disobedient face the usual consequences either way (Hoerster).
  • JUDGE What the highest court calls law is law for observers and LP; for participants its ruling claims correctness (Alexy), so at extreme injustice a later court or lawyer may call it legally wrong; below that, it is law. Lower courts: 15.10.
  • STEELMAN For the pigeon feeder†, deterrence is no moral reason to obey; fair play is: she gains from institutions others uphold. Every such reason is moral: legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three separate questions hide inside "must I obey?" Does the law legally require it? Do I have a moral duty to obey? Do I have a moral duty to disobey? Different theorists answer them differently. The statement in this block answers all three with one word: valid.

What the statement claims

"The citizen who defies an unjust statute may be admirable, but he is a lawbreaker; the citizen who obeys it has done nothing wrong … Fidelity to law means exactly this: deference to what the lawmaker has commanded." (Q78)

The statement moves from "it is valid" to "obeying it is never wrong" and "fidelity is deference". It is tempting because it sounds like respect for the rule of law. But it assumes that legal and moral duties always line up, and that being faithful to law means doing whatever the lawmaker says.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Must I obey?" hides three questions. Is there a legal duty to obey? Is there a moral duty to obey? Is there a moral duty to disobey? The statement answers all three at once by pointing to validity.
  2. Fidelity to law is not deference to the lawmaker. Fuller's King Rex failed in eight ways to make law. His subjects stayed faithful to him as king, but not to his law, because he never made any. Fidelity is owed to an enterprise of rules people can follow, not to whoever happens to be giving orders.
  3. So "the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong" is true only legally, and only up to a point. For Hart it holds legally. For Radbruch it holds legally only below the threshold of intolerable injustice. Morally, it stays an open question on every view. On Hart's account the grudge informer acted within the law of her day, yet she plainly did wrong.

The extra lines, explained

  • Hart. There is a legal duty to obey a valid law. Validity alone gives no moral duty to obey. And past a certain degree of iniquity there is a moral duty to disobey, a view Hart takes from Bentham and Austin. So for Hart, the obedient citizen is legally in the clear, but morally he may have done wrong.
  • Fuller. The legal duty comes in degrees, and disappears if legality fails completely. The moral duty to obey rests on reciprocity between government and citizen, and lasts until that reciprocity is finally and completely ruptured, as it was under Hitler. Short of that, Fuller offers no simple principle for when to disobey (3.7).
  • Radbruch, Alexy. There is no legal duty past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality†. There, judges and lawyers should deny the statute legal character. Below that line, the law stays law, open to moral criticism like any other.
  • Finnis. An unjust law is not a nullity, but it carries no prima facie moral duty to obey. A duty can still arise indirectly, so that a largely just legal system is not weakened by disobedience. And no law can require someone to choose directly against a basic value (Lesson 5). Aquinas, the older natural lawyer, calls an unjust law a corruption of law, though obeying it may sometimes be right to avoid scandal or danger (14.2).
  • CITIZEN · will they be punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way. Hoerster's point is that whoever disobeys must reckon with the usual consequences, whether the statute is called law or not. What differs is what happens after the regime falls.
  • JUDGE · the highest court says it is law. For observers and for legal positivists, what the highest court calls law is law. For participants, the court's ruling claims to be correct (Alexy). So at extreme injustice, a later court or a lawyer may call the ruling legally wrong, not merely immoral. Below that line, it is law. For what a lower court judge may do, see Kennedy's five courses (15.10): in a basically just system, go along while denouncing the law, or withdraw. Deciding openly on what the law should be is only for the Radbruch threshold, and the covert courses fail candour.
  • STEELMAN · the pigeon feeder†. Why obey a law at all, if you think it wrong? Liu's pigeon feeder shows that deterrence is no moral reason to obey, but fair play is. She gains from institutions that others uphold. Every such reason is a moral one. Legality only tells her that the by-law is law, so a positivist has exactly the same reasons to obey as anyone else†.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The obligation grid
TheoristLegal duty to obey?Moral duty to obey?Moral duty to disobey?
HartYes, if the law is valid.Not from validity alone.Yes, past a certain degree of iniquity.
FullerBy degree, and none on total failure of legality.Yes, from reciprocity, until it is finally and completely ruptured.No simple principle short of rupture.
Radbruch, AlexyYes, unless the injustice is intolerable or equality is betrayed.A default of obedience below the threshold, though the law stays open to moral criticism.The question turns legal: past the threshold there is no law to obey, and judges and lawyers deny it legal character.
FinnisAn unjust law is no nullity.No prima facie duty, but one can arise so that a largely just system is not weakened.Never choose directly against a basic value.
AquinasAn unjust law is a corruption of law.Perhaps, to avoid scandal or danger.Not settled on the sheet.

Use the grid to split any "must obey" statement. Q78's obedient citizen is protected in the first column, for Hart and below Radbruch's threshold, but the other two columns stay open.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement merges three questions. Is there a legal duty to obey, a moral duty to obey, or a moral duty to disobey? Fidelity is not deference, since Rex's subjects stayed faithful to him as king, not to his law, for he never made any. The claim that the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong therefore holds legally for Hart, and for Radbruch only below the threshold of intolerable injustice. Morally it stays open, because validity alone gives no moral reason to obey. The reasons that do exist, such as fair play, are moral reasons, which a positivist has too.

108.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb

🧩 Practise 8.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† (word for word)
8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice
  1. Radbruch's third tier asks not how unjust [the statute] is but whether it attempts justice: where equality is deliberately betrayed, it lacks the very nature of law†.
  2. On his first tier†, positive law prevails even when unjust; on the second, at an "intolerable level", it is "flawed law" that must yield to justice, arguably no nullity, though the outcome is the same†.
  3. So [the judge must apply it] fails for a statute aimed at one race; morally, too, no role excuses applying a facially racist law (Thunder).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Radbruch's last tier isn't about how much injustice there is. It asks whether the law is even trying to be just. A law aimed at one race, on purpose, isn't trying. It betrays equality, so it isn't law at all.

What the statement claims

"A statute that discriminates by race or faith must still be applied." "The judge must apply it."

The statement treats a racist statute like any other valid law. It assumes the only question is how unjust a law is, and that a judge must apply anything short of the worst. That overlooks a separate test in Radbruch's formula.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Radbruch's third tier asks about attempt, not degree. The second tier measures how unjust a statute is. The third asks whether it even tries to be just. Where equality is deliberately betrayed, the statute lacks the very nature of law†.
  2. The tiers run from law, to flawed law, to no law. On the first tier†, positive law prevails even when it is unjust. On the second, once injustice reaches an intolerable level, the statute is flawed law that must yield to justice. Liu reads this as arguably not a nullity, though the outcome is the same†.
  3. So "the judge must apply it" fails for a statute aimed at one race. Such a statute does not even attempt justice. And the moral answer is the same as the legal one: Thunder holds that no professional role excuses applying a facially racist law.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Degree or attempt? Placing statutes on Radbruch's tiers
StatuteWhich tier?Why
A by-law fining people who feed pigeonsTier 1Perhaps unwise or unfair, but it attempts a public good. Positive law prevails.
A statute making a private remark against the leader punishable by deathTier 2It attempts order, but its injustice is intolerable, so it is flawed law that must yield.
A statute barring one race from owning propertyTier 3It does not even attempt justice. Equality is betrayed on its face, so it lacks the nature of law.

The first two rows are about how much injustice. The third is about whether the law tries at all. That is why the betrayal limb can apply even where a statute's practical harm looks smaller than a tier 2 case.

Behind the three lines

  • Tier 2: whose reading? Calling a tier 2 statute "not law" is Alexy's reading of Radbruch (card 14.19 TRAP). Liu's reading is that flawed law can be disregarded where and to the extent it conflicts with justice. It is not a complete nullity like tier 3, but the result in court is the same†.
  • Thunder on roles. Thunder's point, from the lawyering topic, is that pointing to your role excuses nothing. No role, whether judge, official or lawyer, makes it acceptable to apply a facially racist law (14.24).
  • The statute, not the outcome. Keep the limb to statutes that betray equality deliberately and on their face. A just rule that produces an unjust result in one case is a different problem, the one distinction 1.3(10) separates (unjust system v rule v outcome†).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Radbruch's third tier asks not how unjust a statute is, but whether it attempts justice at all. Where equality is deliberately betrayed, the statute lacks the very nature of law. This differs from the second tier, where intolerably unjust law is flawed law that must yield to justice, arguably no nullity, though the outcome is the same. The claim that the judge must apply it therefore fails for a statute aimed at one race. Morally too, as Thunder argues, no role excuses applying a facially racist law.

11Putting it together: Practice Q78

"Whether a wicked statute deserves the name 'law' is a quarrel about words; what matters is how people ought to act. A judge has sworn to apply whatever has been validly enacted, and his conscience belongs to his private life, not to his courtroom. The citizen who defies an unjust statute may be admirable, but he is a lawbreaker; the citizen who obeys it has done nothing wrong, for he has simply kept faith with the law. Fidelity to law means exactly this: deference to what the lawmaker has commanded."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Fuller, Hart and Radbruch.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The grudge informer tests the statement at once. On Hart's account she acted within the law of her day when she reported her husband, yet no one thinks she did nothing wrong. The statement runs two questions together, whether a wicked statute is law and what anyone should do about it. I make three claims. First, the label is no mere quarrel about words, because it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute. Second, a judge's oath binds him to law, but at intolerable injustice there is, on Radbruch's formula, no law to apply. Third, fidelity to law is not deference, so the obedient citizen's legality settles nothing about his moral position.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. The label (8.4, 8.2, 8.3). Hart's honesty against Alexy's participant. Liu's point that Hart judges effect and Alexy concept†. The actor table shows what the label changes. Steelman for Hart: candour is a virtue, though it does not make the formula dishonest.
  2. The judge (8.2, 8.3, 8.5). Hart's answer, that the decree is law but too evil to obey, against Alexy's, that a judge refusing it must call it law at first sight but in the end no law at all. The private-conscience judge is pre-war Radbruch, who recanted. In a stable democracy, refusal is only for injustice shown by broad historical consensus, and Kennedy's five courses guide a lower court (15.10).
  3. The citizen and fidelity (8.7). The obligation grid. Rex's subjects. Hoerster: the disobedient face the usual consequences either way. The pigeon feeder shows that the reasons to obey are moral. Self-critique: Alexy grants that candour is the strongest objection to his own view.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Validity never settles what the judge or the citizen should do, and fidelity to law is owed to an enterprise that respects its subjects, not to whoever commands. A law that survives Radbruch's formula is not thereby just, and that question stays with Parliament and conscience. Deviating can be unjust too, since the judge's own morality may be wrong, as Hoerster warned, and Radbruch himself saw frightful dangers in denying enacted statutes the name of law.

12Recap

Archetype 8 on one card
▤ Sections 8.1–8.8
  1. 1Grudge informer: the label decides who bears the cost. Hart's two honest options. Bamberg voided no statute (8.1).
  2. 2Validity leaves obedience open. Law, but too evil to obey. Refusing the merely unfair is the strong thesis nobody defends (8.2).
  3. 3Observers may call it law. A participant, at the extreme, may not. Use two of Alexy's replies and concede candour (8.3).
  4. 4The label is definitional, but it decides who may refuse and who may shelter (8.4).
  5. 5In a stable democracy, a narrow check proved by broad historical consensus. Concede TSH's catch (8.5, 15.13).
  6. 6Retroactivity: new crimes are odious, while longer terms, cures and civil overruling differ (8.6).
  7. 7Three questions: legal duty, moral duty to obey, moral duty to disobey. Fidelity is not deference (8.7).
  8. 8Betrayal of equality: no attempt at justice, no law (8.8).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture two doors. The first is marked Is it law? It is almost always open. Only intolerable injustice, or a statute that betrays equality, slams it shut. The second is marked Must I obey? It has no automatic lock. You open it, or keep it shut, with moral reasons every time: fair play, reciprocity, or the iniquity of what the law demands. Every statement in this archetype pretends there is only one door.
