LESSON 9 · ARCHETYPE 9 · ABOUT 80 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 47 QUESTIONS

Adjudication: Dworkin, ALR, CLS

⚡ BIG IDEA

Judges justify by fit and political morality. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and in the open cases political morality, not personal preference, closes them.

ARCHETYPE 9 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
9 Adjudication: Dworkin, ALR, CLS
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] overstates: judges justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all.
Intro [The statement] treats adjudication as [politics in robes]. Realists rightly show that canons and ratios leave some cases open, and crits that principles meet counterprinciples. But a judge cannot predict his own ruling; he must justify it by the reading that best fits and justifies the law (Dworkin). So [the statement] is [overstated]: political morality, not preference, closes the open cases.
Steelman: restraint The best case for [the statement] is institutional. Rules have a core of meaning where morality sits idle, and being occupied with the penumbra is not being preoccupied with it (Hart). Deciding by personal morality would make each judge a law unto himself. This shows that judges must not decide by private conviction. It does not show [that law can be applied without theory or morality].
Steelman: indeterminacy The best case for [the statement] comes from the realists and the crits. Rules are construed different ways, or picked from the mass available, to fit results reached on other grounds; in Cheng San GRC† literal and purposive readings split; each principle meets a counterprinciple (Unger). This shows that law does not decide every case mechanically. It does not show [that law decides none, or that judges' fidelity is a pretence].
9.1 ALR decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely
  1. Realism rightly says [canons and ratios] leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. A judge's "alas" before finding for the defendant purports to justify; on its face it predicts nothing.
  3. So [law is prediction] holds at most for counsel; Llewellyn called realism a method, nothing more.
  • FOR Cheng San GRC (GE 1997)†: ruling-party candidates stood inside polling stations; Parliamentary Elections Act s 82(1)(d) bars waiting "outside", (e) loitering within 200 metres (pre-2023). Literally, only outside is caught; purposively, the mischief and the heading's "at or near" reach inside. The AG advised no offence. Precise canons left the outcome uncertain†.
  • QUALIFY ALR arguably oversimplifies†: a judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly. Kennedy's correction: law is a "medium" constraining like bricks, relative to one's project; moving it costs work and credibility.
  • QUALIFY ALR has weak and strong readings (Harris): minimally, rules are not all that matter; at the extreme, all reasoning is "mere surface talk".
9.2 Dworkin v ALR precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals
  1. Saying [the judge legislates once precedent runs out] mistakes a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds for a gap.
  2. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet split: Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable"; Edmund-Davies called that novel and startling.
  3. So leaving [floodgates] to Parliament is Scarman's contested view, which I defend as a choice, not as the case's lesson.
  • AGAINST Whether floodgates are policy or principle is open†: court congestion and insurance cost are policy, beyond the limits of the forensic process (Scarman); liability out of proportion to fault is principle.
9.3 CLS v Dworkin neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down
  1. Unger rightly denies [contract law is a neutral framework]: each principle meets a counterprinciple that the dominant view files as an anomaly.
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger).
  3. Yet [tear it down] overreaches: condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
  • FOR Doctrine legitimates hierarchy even when its user thinks he forwards progressive causes: hidden interests†. Crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism.
  • STEELMAN The crit's best point is that fit is conservative (9.7): the fairness fixes (duress, undue influence†) stay exceptions, "arbitrarily selective" (Unger).
  • AGAINST Harris: the liberal must show reformed legalism yields more "incremental justice" than deconstruction for its own sake.
  • QUALIFY ALR and CLS† agree that law is politics but split on what next: ALR keeps the system, given good judges; CLS would remake it, exposing class interests.
9.4 Precedent and theory like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory: [treating like cases alike] needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, says whether a mother reaching hospital two hours later is like one at the scene.
  3. So [precedent, not justice, makes law fair] fails: stare decisis itself is contested, strict or relaxed, and needs justification.
  • AGAINST Relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire), and interpretation must contain a doctrine of mistake.
9.5 Right answer single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute
  1. [A single right answer] is possible in principle: interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit will often yield no unique interpretation, and then substantive political theory decides.
  3. So [he need never refuse an unjust statute] fails: Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).
  • CONCEDE A judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share (Dworkin). I concede no answer is demonstrable, but the choice is political, not personal (9.8).
  • QUALIFY Arguably, where the practice includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice†; fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German nullity courts). TSH's catch: 8.5.
9.6 Judge-variance study outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
  1. A realist reads [the variance findings] as fact scepticism confirmed: the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies (Frank).
  2. Appeal arguably only moves that discretion up a level†.
  3. Yet the findings indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.
  • Rule v fact scepticism†: Llewellyn warned of "paper rules"; Frank charged rule-sceptics with "upper courtitis".
9.7 Synthesis answers the realists, victory to the crits
  1. Dworkin's judge answers [the realists]: he must justify by fit and value, not predict.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly; Harris reads Unger's jibe at a "pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective; arguably a third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs)†.
  • QUALIFY Dworkin is arguably text-first: the judge brings a political theory but owes a duty to the law, close to Fuller's fidelity; the crits are goal-first, moulding the text to the transformative aim. The work can overlap; the starting point differs†.
9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
  1. [Theories of law] are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words) but operative only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So [necessarily implicated] holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.
  • Morality enters, for Hart, at most where rules run out; for Fuller, in fidelity joined to the judge's responsibility for making law what it ought to be; for Dworkin, in every proposition of law (14.5).
  • FOR Riggs pitted Earl's legislative intention against Gray's fixed penalties: two morally grounded theories of a statute (2.8).
  • STEELMAN LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.
9.9 Why judges converge shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
  1. Judges converge less because of [shared backgrounds] than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer steeped in an appellate court's "folkways" could predict outcomes eight times out of ten.
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory; [the tenth case] is where that theory is argued, not predicted.
  • FOR ALR assumes "underlying ethical pluralism"†; for Kennedy, shared rule-application is not in fact objectivity, though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule.
  • AGAINST Dworkin: hard cases are perhaps just those where fit yields no unique reading.
9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
  1. The artist interprets while creating and the critic creates while interpreting, yet the two remain different.
  2. Each chain novelist after the first both interprets and creates; after the second, no single author's intentions decide.
  3. So the judge, a partner in a chain enterprise, must interpret the legal history found, not invent a better one.
  • QUALIFY Fit has "no algorithm"; value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis").
  • AGAINST Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (13.1).
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them. In open cases judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not the goal. Theory is always implicated and morality always presupposed, but morality decides only where fit runs out or injustice becomes intolerable.

1Start here: archetype 9 in plain English

Archetype 9 asks one question: when judges decide cases, are they applying law, or doing politics in robes? The question bites in hard cases. In Riggs v Palmer (1889) a grandson murdered his grandfather, and the statute of wills, read literally, still let him inherit. In McLoughlin v O'Brian (1983) a mother who saw her injured family in hospital two hours after a road accident sued for nervous shock, and no earlier case covered her facts. In both cases every judge knew the texts, yet the judges split over what the law required.

Three camps explain what the judges were doing. The American Legal Realists (ALR) say judges decide first and find legal reasons afterwards, so the honest definition of law is a prediction of what judges will do. Critical Legal Studies (CLS, or "the crits") go further. Legal doctrine is full of contradictions, because every principle meets a counterprinciple, and the way the law ranks them quietly protects some interests over others. Dworkin replies that a judge cannot simply predict or pick. She must justify her decision by the reading of the law that best fits the existing materials and best justifies them morally.

Exam statements in this family usually push one extreme. Some say judging is politics in robes, so rules decide nothing and judges please themselves. Others say judges just apply the law and need no theory or morality. Your answer is the same every time. The statement overstates. Rules leave some cases open, but not all. In the open cases judges must still justify their rulings, and political morality, not personal preference, closes them.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
American Legal Realism (ALR)A school of American judges and scholars, such as Llewellyn and Frank. They said law is what courts actually do, and that judges are moved by more than the rules.
Critical Legal Studies (CLS), "the crits"A later, left-leaning movement led by writers such as Unger and Kennedy. It says law is politics: each legal principle comes with an opposite one, and which wins reflects power, not logic.
Canons and ratiosCanons are rules for reading statutes, such as the literal rule and the purposive approach. A ratio is the reason a case was decided, which a later court can read narrowly or widely.
Rule v fact scepticismRule sceptics doubt that rules decide cases. Fact sceptics say the real uncertainty lies in how the trial court finds the facts, which decides whether a rule applies at all.
Core and penumbraHart's picture of a rule. The core is the settled meaning everyone agrees on. The penumbra is the fringe of doubtful cases, where judges must use discretion.
Fit and valueDworkin's two tests for a reading of the law. Does it fit the past decisions? Does it show them in their best moral and political light?
Chain novelDworkin's picture of the judge as one author in a chain, writing the next chapter of a story others began.
Principle v policyA principle is an argument about rights, about justice between the parties. A policy is an argument about society's collective goals, such as cost or court congestion. Dworkin says courts should decide on principle.
FloodgatesThe worry that allowing one claim will open the way to a flood of similar claims.
Stare decisisThe doctrine of precedent: courts follow earlier decisions so that like cases are decided alike.
Presupposed v operativeMorality is presupposed when it sits in the background of judging, for example in the value of legality. It is operative when it is the actual ground of a decision.
Theoretical disagreementDworkin's term for a dispute about what counts as law at all, as opposed to a dispute about whether agreed tests are met.
Radbruch formulaThe rule that an unjust statute stays law unless its injustice is intolerable. Professor Tan Seow Hon (TSH) says courts must show such injustice by broad historical consensus (BHC).

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the statement overstates, because judges justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all.

Put simply, the realists and the crits are right that rules do not settle every case. A statute can be read literally or purposively, a precedent can be read narrowly or widely, and contract law contains rival principles. But that does not make judging a matter of taste. A judge cannot treat the law as a forecast of her own ruling. She has to give the reading that best fits the legal materials and shows them in their best light. Where the materials run out, the choice is made by political morality, meaning principles about rights and justice that she must state and defend. It is not made by her personal or partisan preference.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement treats adjudication as politics in robes. Realists rightly show that canons and ratios leave some cases open, and the crits rightly show that principles meet counterprinciples. But a judge cannot predict his own ruling. He must justify it by the reading that best fits and justifies the law, as Dworkin argues. So the statement is overstated, because political morality, not preference, closes the open cases.

The Conclusion gives your verdict in four steps. First, rules leave some cases open, not all. Second, the cost of a flimsy ruling, in reputation, reversal on appeal and credibility, keeps most judges close to the rules. Third, in the open cases judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not from the outcome they want. Fourth, theory is always involved and morality is always in the background, but morality actually decides a case only where fit runs out or the injustice becomes intolerable.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before replying to it. Section 9 gives you two, and they pull in opposite directions. The first defends judges who keep out of morality. The second says the rules cannot keep them out.

  • Steelman: restraint. The best case for the statement is institutional. Hart argued that rules have a core of settled meaning where morality sits idle. Being occupied with the penumbra, he said, is not the same as being preoccupied with it. Hard cases exist at the fringe of a rule, but most cases are easy. And a judge who decided by personal morality would become a law unto himself. This shows that judges must not decide by private conviction. It does not show that law can be applied without any theory or morality, since even the choice to stay in the core reflects a view of what judges are for.
  • Steelman: indeterminacy. The best case for the statement comes from the realists and the crits. Rules can be construed different ways, or picked from the mass of available rules, to fit results reached on other grounds. In the Cheng San GRC episode† the literal and purposive readings of an election law pointed opposite ways. And Unger shows that each principle in contract law meets a counterprinciple. This shows that law does not decide every case mechanically. It does not show that law decides no cases, or that judges' fidelity to law is a pretence.

The ten blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
9.1"Judges decide first, so law is just prediction."Lawyers may predict, but judges must justify. A judge cannot predict her own ruling.
9.2"When precedent runs out, judges legislate."That mistakes a disagreement about what counts as law for a gap. In McLoughlin the Lords agreed on the result and split on the reasons.
9.3"Contract law is a neutral framework", or "tear it down".Unger rightly shows it is not neutral. But tearing it down needs a standard to judge by.
9.4"Precedent, not justice, makes law fair."Deciding which cases are "alike" needs a moral principle.
9.5"There is always one right answer, so never refuse an unjust statute."One best reading is possible in principle, but Dworkin gives no threshold for extreme injustice.
9.6"Results vary by judge, so law is just the judge."That shows some judges fail to justify, not that Dworkin's theory is wrong.
9.7"Dworkin beats the realists only by handing victory to the crits."Only if values are subjective. Natural law could say which principle should win.
9.8"Theory and morality are necessarily in every decision."Theory, yes. Morality is always in the background, but it decides only hard cases and extreme injustice.
9.9"Judges agree only because of shared backgrounds."They agree mainly because they share a practice of justification.
9.10"The judge writes the next chapter of one coherent story."Yes, but the judge must interpret the history she finds, not invent a better one.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Rules leave some cases open, not all, and in the open ones judges must justify by principle, not preference.

2The big picture: what do judges do?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three people watch a judge. The realist says: "She decides what she wants, then dresses it up with legal reasons. If you want to know the law, predict what she will do." The critical legal scholar says: "The legal reasons can always point both ways, and they quietly favour the powerful." Dworkin says: "She cannot just predict herself. She has to find the reading of the law that best fits what is already there and makes the most moral sense of it, like the next author in a novel written by many hands." This lesson shows you that each of them sees something real, and that the Dworkin picture best explains what a judge owes.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
HartRules have a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of doubtful cases. In the core, judges simply apply the rule. In the penumbra, they must use discretion. Hard cases are real, but they are the fringe of the law, not the whole of it.
Llewellyn (ALR)A rule sceptic. He warned against "paper rules", the rules in the books that do not really decide cases. Later he softened. A lawyer steeped in an appeal court's "folkways" could, he found, predict its decisions eight times out of ten, and he called realism only a method.
Frank (ALR)A fact sceptic. Even a clear rule decides little at trial, because the court that finds the facts decides whether the rule applies. He mocked the rule sceptics for "upper courtitis", their habit of studying only appeal courts.
DworkinLaw is interpretive. A judge reads the legal record by fit and political value, like a novelist adding a chapter to a chain novel. Law is therefore deeply political, but never personal or partisan. Judges should decide on principle (rights) and leave policy (collective goals) to the legislature.
Unger (CLS)Contract law is not one coherent scheme. Each principle, such as freedom of contract, meets a counterprinciple, such as fairness. The dominant view files the counterprinciples away as exceptions, which hides the choice being made.
Kennedy (CLS)Describes what it is like to be an activist judge. The judge starts from how he wants the case to come out, then works the legal materials toward that result, paying in time and in what he calls a legitimacy cost. Law is a medium that constrains, but what it rules out depends on what the judge is trying to build.
HarrisThe textbook writer who reports the realists and the crits and tests them. He asks whether reforming the law step by step yields more justice than tearing it down.

Key distinctions

  • Rule scepticism v fact scepticism. Both are realist views, but they place the uncertainty in different spots. Llewellyn, the rule sceptic, said general rules do not decide concrete cases. Frank, the fact sceptic, said that even when they do, the trial court that finds the facts decides whether a rule applies at all†. You use this distinction in 9.6.
  • Principle v policy (distinction 1.3(8)). A principle is an argument about rights and justice between the parties. A policy is an argument about the community's collective goals, such as avoiding a flood of claims or keeping insurance costs down. Dworkin says courts should decide on principle and leave policy to Parliament. It is the key to McLoughlin in 9.2.
  • Presupposed v operative (distinction 1.3(2)). Morality is always presupposed in judging, in the value of legality and in the reasons to defer to clear words. But it is an operative ground of decision only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. This is the home of 9.8.
  • Text-first v goal-first (distinction 1.3(17)). Dworkin's judge starts from the text and asks for its best reading. The crits' judge starts from the goal and moulds the text to reach it†. This separates Dworkin from Kennedy in 9.7 and 9.10.

The flow shows why Dworkin is neither a realist nor a mechanical rule-follower. The first test, fit, ties the judge to the past: a reading that ignores most of the decided cases is ruled out, however attractive it is. The second test, value, admits that the past often leaves more than one reading standing, and then asks which reading makes the law most just. That is why Dworkin calls law deeply political but never personal or partisan. The judge's politics enters, but only as a theory of justice she must state and defend, and only within the space fit leaves open.

Hart's famous example shows each camp's answer at a glance. For Hart, the car is an easy case in the rule's core, and the toy car is a penumbral case where the judge has discretion. Most cases, he insists, look like the car. That is the restraint steelman. For the realist, the toy car is the normal case, and the judge's hunch decides it, with reasons found afterwards. For Dworkin, there is still law in the penumbra: the purpose or principle that best explains the rule, which the judge must find and defend. For Kennedy, how much of a rule is open cannot be measured in itself, because it depends on what the judge is trying to do. Your Position takes something from each. The car shows that rules leave some cases closed. The toy car shows that they leave some open. And in the open case, the rule's purpose, not the judge's taste, should close it.

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

The realists v the crits. Liu's point is that the realists and the crits give the same description, that law is politics, but split on what to do next. The realists keep the system, provided the judges are good. The crits would remake it, exposing the class interests it hides†.

Dworkin v the crits. Dworkin is text-first. The judge brings a whole political theory to the case, but owes a duty to that law, which Liu compares to Fuller's fidelity to law. The crits are goal-first. They start from the transformative aim and mould the text to reach it. Their actual work can overlap, but the starting point differs†.
