39.1 ALR

🧩 Practise 9.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.1 ALR (word for word)
9.1 ALR decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely
  1. Realism rightly says [canons and ratios] leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. A judge's "alas" before finding for the defendant purports to justify; on its face it predicts nothing.
  3. So [law is prediction] holds at most for counsel; Llewellyn called realism a method, nothing more.
  • FOR Cheng San GRC (GE 1997)†: ruling-party candidates stood inside polling stations; Parliamentary Elections Act s 82(1)(d) bars waiting "outside", (e) loitering within 200 metres (pre-2023). Literally, only outside is caught; purposively, the mischief and the heading's "at or near" reach inside. The AG advised no offence. Precise canons left the outcome uncertain†.
  • QUALIFY ALR arguably oversimplifies†: a judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly. Kennedy's correction: law is a "medium" constraining like bricks, relative to one's project; moving it costs work and credibility.
  • QUALIFY ALR has weak and strong readings (Harris): minimally, rules are not all that matter; at the extreme, all reasoning is "mere surface talk".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A realist says, "Law is just a prediction of what the judge will do." That is useful for a lawyer advising a client, who wants to know the odds. But the judge cannot use it. She cannot sit on the bench predicting her own decision. She has to decide and give reasons. So realism describes the lawyer's view of the court, not the judge's view from the bench.

What the statement claims

"Anyone who watches the courts knows that judges decide first and find reasons afterwards … The only honest definition of law is therefore a prediction of what judges will actually do." (Q85)

The statement starts with an observation about judges and ends with a definition of law. It assumes that because judges have room to choose, the reasons they give are only decoration, and that the only thing worth calling law is the pattern of outcomes. It is tempting because the realists have real examples, and because every lawyer has read a judgment that seemed to start from its conclusion.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Realism is right that the tools of legal reasoning can leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict. The canons for reading statutes can point different ways, and a precedent's ratio can be read narrowly or widely. That leaves some cases open. But the realist's definition is written from outside the courtroom. The judge stands on the other side of the prediction, and her job is to give reasons showing that her ruling is correct.
  2. A judge's "alas" shows the point. Harris notes that a judge who says she must, alas, find for the defendant is not forecasting anything. She is saying that the law requires a result she dislikes. On its face that sentence predicts nothing. It purports to justify, which is exactly what the realist definition leaves out.
  3. So "law is prediction" holds at most for counsel. A lawyer advising a client can sensibly ask what this court is likely to do. A judge cannot ask that about herself. Even Llewellyn, a leading realist, later called realism a method, nothing more, rather than a full theory of what law is.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · Cheng San GRC†. This is the realist's best Singapore example, set out in the worked example below. At the 1997 general election ruling-party candidates stood inside polling stations, and although the canons for reading the election law could be stated precisely, the outcome stayed uncertain†. Use it as the kernel you concede.
  • QUALIFY · costs constrain the judge†. Realism arguably oversimplifies. A judge can write any decision. But judges work inside a system. A flimsy ruling damages the judge's reputation, invites reversal on appeal, uses up scarce time and spends credibility, as Lord Denning's reputation for pushing the limits showed. Kennedy makes the same correction from the crits' side. Law is a medium, like a pile of bricks. The bricks do not tell you whether to build a doghouse or a garden wall, but you cannot build anything you like from them, and moving them costs work and credibility.
  • QUALIFY · weak and strong readings. Harris shows that realism can be read two ways. On the minimal reading, rules are not all that matter in deciding cases, which is true. On the extreme reading, all legal reasoning is mere surface talk, which is false. Harris's speeding test makes the point: if rules had no effect, there would be no reason to expect drivers doing 60 to be convicted and drivers doing 20 to be acquitted. Concede the first reading and attack the second.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Cheng San GRC: precise canons, uncertain outcome

At the 1997 general election, ruling-party candidates stood inside polling stations in Cheng San GRC while people voted†. The Parliamentary Elections Act, s 82(1), as worded before 2023, said two things. Paragraph (d) barred anyone from waiting outside a polling station except to vote. Paragraph (e) barred loitering in any street or public place within a 200-metre radius of one. The section's heading spoke of undue influence at or near a polling station.

ReadingThe argumentResult
LiteralThe words catch people outside the station and in the area around it. Naming the outside implies that the inside is not caught.No offence. This is what the Attorney-General advised.
PurposiveThe mischief is undue influence on voters. If waiting outside is barred, standing inside is worse. The heading's at or near shows that being at the station counts.Offence.

Both canons can be stated precisely. Neither tells you for certain which one wins. That is the realist's point, and you should concede it. Your reply is that a judge deciding the case would still have to justify choosing one reading over the other, and that choice would be argued in public, with reasons, not simply predicted.

⚠ TRAP
No court ruled

Cheng San never reached a court. The Attorney-General advised that there was no offence. So never write that "the court held" anything. The example shows that precise canons can leave the outcome uncertain, not that judges ignore statutes.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Realism rightly says that canons and ratios can leave hard cases open, as Cheng San GRC shows, where literal and purposive readings of the election law pointed opposite ways. But a judge must justify, not predict. A judge who writes that she must, alas, find for the defendant purports to justify her ruling, and on its face predicts nothing. "Law is prediction" therefore holds at most for counsel advising a client, and even Llewellyn called realism a method, nothing more. Realism also oversimplifies, because a judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal and credibility make a flimsy one costly.

49.2 Dworkin v ALR

🧩 Practise 9.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.2 Dworkin v ALR (word for word)
9.2 Dworkin v ALR precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals
  1. Saying [the judge legislates once precedent runs out] mistakes a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds for a gap.
  2. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet split: Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable"; Edmund-Davies called that novel and startling.
  3. So leaving [floodgates] to Parliament is Scarman's contested view, which I defend as a choice, not as the case's lesson.
  • AGAINST Whether floodgates are policy or principle is open†: court congestion and insurance cost are policy, beyond the limits of the forensic process (Scarman); liability out of proportion to fault is principle.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"When the old cases run out, the judge just makes law up." Dworkin says no. Even when no precedent covers the facts, there is still law in the principles behind the precedents. In McLoughlin all five judges agreed that the mother should win, but they argued about whether courts may use policy, such as "too many lawsuits", to limit who can sue. That was an argument about what the law already was, not a gap.

What the statement claims

"When precedent runs out, a judge has no choice but to legislate … whether a mother who sees her injured family in hospital may sue for nervous shock is answered by no rule." (Q83)

The statement assumes that law is only what past decisions say in so many words. When they say nothing, there is a gap, and a judge who fills it is legislating. It is tempting because McLoughlin really was new. Every earlier claimant who recovered had been at the scene or had arrived within minutes.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Saying the judge legislates once precedent runs out mistakes a disagreement about law's grounds for a gap. Dworkin calls this a theoretical disagreement. The judges disagree about what counts as law, for example whether principles embedded in past cases are part of it. The statement assumes the plain-fact view, that law is only what past decisions explicitly say. But whether that view is right is the very point in dispute (2.5).
  2. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet they split on the reasons. Lord Scarman held that where to draw a policy line was not justiciable, meaning it was not a question a court can properly decide. Lord Edmund-Davies called Scarman's view novel and startling. So the case shows judges arguing about the grounds of law, not about whether to obey it.
  3. So leaving floodgates to Parliament is Scarman's contested view. The sheet defends it, but as a choice you argue for, not as the lesson the case teaches. Three of the Lords thought policy could limit liability in a proper case, and Lord Bridge thought stopping at the decided cases would be an unwarranted abdication.

Look at the last two boxes. The Court of Appeal accepted that Mrs McLoughlin's shock was foreseeable but refused her on policy grounds: a flood of claims, fraud, insurance costs and harder proof. The Lords reversed it unanimously. Yet their reasons divide along the line between principle and policy. That division is what Dworkin means by a theoretical disagreement, and it is why "answered by no rule" overstates. The judges did not think they were legislating into a void. They disagreed about which kinds of argument the law already allowed.

The extra line, explained

  • AGAINST · floodgates: policy or principle?† Whether a floodgates argument is policy or principle is an open question. Framed as court congestion, fraudulent claims or insurance costs, it is policy, a matter of collective goals that Scarman thought lay beyond the limits of the forensic process. Framed as liability out of all proportion to the defendant's fault, it is principle, because it concerns what is fair between these parties. So the same worry can be argued either way, and a careful lawyer runs both.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Saying that the judge legislates once precedent runs out mistakes a theoretical disagreement about the grounds of law for a gap in it. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the mother's appeal, yet they split on whether policy may limit liability. Lord Scarman held that line-drawing on policy grounds was not justiciable, while Lord Edmund-Davies found that view novel and startling. The judges were therefore arguing about what the law already was, not filling a void. Leaving floodgates to Parliament is Scarman's contested view, which I defend as a choice, not as the lesson of the case.

59.3 CLS v Dworkin

🧩 Practise 9.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.3 CLS v Dworkin (word for word)
9.3 CLS v Dworkin neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down
  1. Unger rightly denies [contract law is a neutral framework]: each principle meets a counterprinciple that the dominant view files as an anomaly.
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger).
  3. Yet [tear it down] overreaches: condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
  • FOR Doctrine legitimates hierarchy even when its user thinks he forwards progressive causes: hidden interests†. Crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism.
  • STEELMAN The crit's best point is that fit is conservative (9.7): the fairness fixes (duress, undue influence†) stay exceptions, "arbitrarily selective" (Unger).
  • AGAINST Harris: the liberal must show reformed legalism yields more "incremental justice" than deconstruction for its own sake.
  • QUALIFY ALR and CLS† agree that law is politics but split on what next: ALR keeps the system, given good judges; CLS would remake it, exposing class interests.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Contract law says people are free to make any deal they like. But it also has rules that protect people from unfair deals, such as duress and undue influence. The crits say these are not small exceptions. They are a whole rival principle, fairness, that the law pretends is minor. That is a fair point. But if you want to tear the system down, you need some standard for saying what would be better.

What the statement claims

"Contract law is a neutral framework that simply gives effect to the free choices of equal parties." (Q86)
"Private law is ad hoc truces drawn up by an elite; tear it down." (Q87)

The two statements sit at opposite ends. The first says contract law takes no side. It only carries out what free and equal parties choose. The second accepts the crits' diagnosis and jumps straight to demolition. The block agrees with the crits against the first statement and disagrees with them about the second.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Unger rightly denies that contract law is a neutral framework. Each principle in contract law meets a counterprinciple. Freedom of contract, the right to choose your terms, meets fairness, the idea that unfair bargains should not be enforced. The dominant view treats the counterprinciple as an anomaly, a set of exceptions, and so hides the choice it has made about which idea comes first.
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant theory rules far less than it claims. Unger points out that classical contract theory leaves out whole fields, such as family, labour and company law. It treats fiduciary relationships as a special case, and it handles long-term dealings by ad hoc departures. It is an empire whose claimed authority far outruns its real power.
  3. Yet "tear it down" overreaches. To condemn the law for serving hidden interests, you need a standard for what would serve people better, and that standard cannot be mere opinion. Finnis's basic goods (5.1) can supply one. Without such a standard, the crits can expose the law but cannot show that anything else would be better.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Unger's two pairs
PrincipleCounterprincipleWhere the counterprinciple shows up
Freedom to contract. You choose whether, and with whom, to deal.Community. That freedom may not undermine the communal side of social life.Promissory estoppel, which protects justified reliance, and the rule that family and social arrangements carry no presumed intention to be bound.
Freedom of contract. You choose the terms.Fairness. Unfair bargains should not be enforced.Duress, undue influence†, unconscionability and frustration.

Nothing in the rules says which column holds the principle and which the counterprinciple. Unger argues that the ranking reflects existing institutions and power, which the dominant view simply takes as given. His deviationist doctrine aims to turn the exceptions into the starting points. If the counterprinciples came first, the law would begin from fairness and treat freedom of contract as the special case.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · hidden interests†. Doctrine can legitimate hierarchy even when the lawyer using it thinks he is advancing a progressive cause. Harris gives an example: arguing for broad employee rights still assumes employer control as the starting point. The crits generally distance themselves from crude Marxist instrumentalism, the idea that law is simply a tool of the ruling class. Their claim is subtler. The law's categories make existing power look natural.
  • STEELMAN · fit is conservative. The crits' best point against Dworkin is that fit favours the past. If the judge must fit the existing record, the dominant principle, freedom of contract, wins by default, and the fairness fixes such as duress and undue influence† stay exceptions. Unger adds that because correction stays sporadic, it is arbitrarily selective: for every unfair situation corrected, a similar one is left untouched. This point returns in 9.7.
  • AGAINST · Harris's challenge. Harris sets the test that decides between the crits and their opponents. The liberal must show that reformed legalism, improving the law step by step, yields more incremental justice than deconstruction for its own sake. It is a fair test, because it asks both sides for results, not slogans.
  • QUALIFY · realists v crits†. The realists and the crits agree that law is politics but split on what to do next. The realists keep the system, provided the judges are good. The crits would remake it and expose the class interests it serves. So do not lump them together.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Unger rightly denies that contract law is a neutral framework. Each principle, such as freedom of contract, meets a counterprinciple, such as fairness, which the dominant view files away as an anomaly, and with its exclusions, exceptions and repressions the dominant theory rules far less than it claims. The crits' best point against Dworkin is that fit is conservative, leaving duress and undue influence as mere exceptions. Yet "tear it down" overreaches, because condemning hidden interests needs a standard that is not merely subjective, which Finnis's basic goods can supply. As Harris insists, the real question is whether reformed legalism yields more incremental justice than deconstruction for its own sake.

69.4 Precedent and theory

🧩 Practise 9.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.4 Precedent and theory (word for word)
9.4 Precedent and theory like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory: [treating like cases alike] needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, says whether a mother reaching hospital two hours later is like one at the scene.
  3. So [precedent, not justice, makes law fair] fails: stare decisis itself is contested, strict or relaxed, and needs justification.
  • AGAINST Relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire), and interpretation must contain a doctrine of mistake.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Treat like cases alike" sounds simple. But is a mother arriving at the hospital two hours later "like" a mother at the crash scene? You cannot answer without a principle that says which differences matter. That principle is a moral one.

What the statement claims

"Precedent guarantees that like cases are treated alike. That, and not any theory of justice, is what makes the common law fair." (Q92)
"Stare decisis treats authority as a substitute for argument." (Q89)

The first statement praises precedent as a substitute for theory. The second attacks it for the same reason. Both assume that following precedent is a mechanical matter of matching cases, which needs no argument about justice. That is the assumption the block breaks.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory. "Treat like cases alike" is a sound rule of justice, but it is empty until you know which likenesses matter. No two cases are identical, so a court must decide which differences count. That test is a moral one.
  2. Only a principle can say whether two cases are alike. Was a mother who reached hospital two hours after the accident like a mother who saw it happen at the roadside? A principle of physical risk says no, because she was never in danger. A principle of foreseeability says yes, because her shock was foreseeable. The precedent alone cannot choose between them.
  3. So "precedent, not justice, makes law fair" fails. Even the doctrine of precedent is contested. On the strict view, a court must follow some earlier decisions even if they were wrong. On the relaxed view, it only gives them weight. Choosing between these views needs a justification too.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is the new claimant "like" the precedent?

Dworkin builds a version of McLoughlin to show the problem. Suppose a precedent lets a mother at the roadside recover for shock. Two principles fit that precedent equally well.

New claimantPrinciple of physical riskPrinciple of foreseeability
Mother at the roadside (the precedent)Alike: she was in the zone of dangerAlike: her shock was foreseeable
Mother at the hospital two hours later (McLoughlin)Unlike: she was never in dangerAlike: even the Court of Appeal accepted her shock was foreseeable
Aunt told of the accident by telephone (Dworkin's example)UnlikeArguable: it turns on what is reasonably foreseeable

Because both principles fit the precedent, fit cannot choose. Dworkin says the foreseeability principle is probably the better reading, and only because it states a sounder principle of justice. So deciding what counts as "alike" was a moral judgement all along.

The extra line, explained

  • AGAINST · precedent can be a mistake. Dworkin argues in Law's Empire that relaxed precedent gives way when an earlier decision is sufficiently wrong. Any useful theory of interpretation must also contain a doctrine of mistake, a way of saying that some past decisions were wrongly decided or should be confined to their own facts. Deciding which precedents are mistakes is, again, a judgement of principle, so precedent cannot stand in for justice.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Precedent cannot replace theory. Treating like cases alike needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral. Whether a mother who reached hospital two hours after an accident is like one who saw it at the scene depends on a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, which the precedent itself cannot supply. Stare decisis is also contested between strict and relaxed versions, and Dworkin argues that precedent yields when sufficiently wrong, so any account of it needs a doctrine of mistake. Precedent therefore does not make the common law fair without a theory of justice. It needs one to work at all.

79.5 Right answer

🧩 Practise 9.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.5 Right answer (word for word)
9.5 Right answer single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute
  1. [A single right answer] is possible in principle: interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit will often yield no unique interpretation, and then substantive political theory decides.
  3. So [he need never refuse an unjust statute] fails: Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).
  • CONCEDE A judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share (Dworkin). I concede no answer is demonstrable, but the choice is political, not personal (9.8).
  • QUALIFY Arguably, where the practice includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice†; fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German nullity courts). TSH's catch: 8.5.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Dworkin thinks hard cases have one best answer, the way a good critic thinks one reading of a poem is best. But even he admits that the "fit" test often leaves several readings standing, and then the judge's political morality decides. And his theory does not say when a law is so evil that a judge should refuse to apply it.

What the statement claims

"The ideal judge reads the whole of the law as one coherent story … Because the law always holds a single right answer, he need never refuse an unjust statute." (Q84)

The statement makes two claims and links them. First, there is always a single right answer. Second, because of that, the judge never faces a choice between law and justice. It is tempting because Dworkin really does defend a right answer. But the first claim is weaker than it sounds, and the second does not follow from it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. A single right answer is possible in principle. Dworkin says interpretation neither finds the law ready-made, like a fact in the books, nor invents it from nothing. It is a reading, and one reading can be better than another, so one can be best of all. Disagreement among judges does not show there is no best answer.
  2. But fit will often give no unique interpretation, and then substantive political theory decides. Dworkin admits that several readings may fit the legal record. At that point the judge's political theory, her view of what makes the law just, chooses between them. So the right answer is reached through contestable political argument, not discovered like the answer to a sum.
  3. So "he need never refuse an unjust statute" fails. Dworkin's judge must interpret the history he finds, even a wicked one, and Dworkin gives no threshold at which injustice becomes too great to apply. The Radbruch formula does, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus (15.13). Only intolerable injustice, shown by long-lasting agreement across many legal systems, justifies refusal. Genocide and slavery meet that test.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · no answer is demonstrable. Dworkin himself accepts that a judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share. So concede that no right answer can be proved to everyone's satisfaction. But insist that the choice is political, about principles of justice the judge must state and defend, not a matter of personal taste (9.8). This is also the Dworkin self-critique in 1.4.
  • QUALIFY · a Dworkinian judge can refuse, if the practice allows it†. Arguably, where a legal practice already includes Radbruch's formula, a Dworkinian judge can tell a coherent story that both fits and refuses extreme injustice. The story runs: our law gives effect to Parliament's choices, but subject to an overriding value, so a statute may be departed from where its injustice is intolerable, and this is such a case. Fit is also a matter of degree. Lord Denning pushed the law forward by appealing to deeper principles already in it, and the post-war German courts that treated a Nazi statute as void claimed to apply a basic justice that had been there all along. TSH's own catch applies as well (8.5). Broad consensus can itself go dreadfully wrong. If a worldwide trend, such as on same-sex marriage, lasted for decades, it might come to count as broad historical consensus, and the formula would then stop a local legislature from doing what it thinks right. Concede this, as TSH does, and adopt her reply that an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

A single right answer is possible in principle, because interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best. But Dworkin concedes that fit will often yield no unique interpretation, and then substantive political theory decides. I concede that no answer is demonstrable, since a judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share, but the choice is political, not personal. The claim that the ideal judge need never refuse an unjust statute fails, because Dworkin gives no threshold for intolerable injustice. The Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, supplies one, and it is met for genocide and slavery, not for ordinary injustice.

89.6 Judge-variance study

🧩 Practise 9.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.6 Judge-variance study (word for word)
9.6 Judge-variance study outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
  1. A realist reads [the variance findings] as fact scepticism confirmed: the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies (Frank).
  2. Appeal arguably only moves that discretion up a level†.
  3. Yet the findings indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.
  • Rule v fact scepticism†: Llewellyn warned of "paper rules"; Frank charged rule-sceptics with "upper courtitis".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A study finds that the result depends on which judge you get. The realist says, "Told you so: law is just the judge." But it might only show that some judges are not doing their job well. Dworkin's theory says how judges should decide. It does not claim that they all do.

What the statement claims

"Suppose a study found that outcomes of materially similar cases varied significantly by judge. What would a realist conclude?" (Q90)

This is a question rather than a statement, and it invites you to set out the realist reading and then test it. The realist conclusion is tempting because the data seem to speak for themselves: same kind of case, same rules, different results. Your job is to say what the data do and do not prove.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. A realist reads the variance findings as fact scepticism confirmed. Frank argued that the court finding the facts decides whether a rule applies. If outcomes vary by judge, that seems to prove him right: the same rule, different judges, different results.
  2. Appeal arguably only moves that discretion up a level†. The obvious fix is an appeal. But appeal courts are slow to disturb findings of fact, and even when they do, the appeal judges exercise the same kind of discretion. The discretion has been moved, not removed.
  3. Yet the findings indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory. Dworkin's theory says how judges should decide: by fit and value, giving reasons. A study showing that some judges decide inconsistently is evidence that those judges fall short of the standard. It is not evidence that the standard is wrong.

The scene is the realist's picture of judging in miniature. Each judge reaches a view first and writes reasons afterwards, and the outcome turns on the facts each judge finds. Frank would say this proves his point, and he is partly right: the rule was clear, yet it did not decide the case. Now look at what the scene does not show. Both judges applied the same rule. Both had to give reasons that an appeal court can test. And if one judge reasoned badly, for example by ignoring the expert without saying why, that is a failure to justify. It is a criticism of that judge, measured against exactly the standard Dworkin sets.

The extra line, explained

  • Rule v fact scepticism†. Keep the two realist doubts apart. Llewellyn, the rule sceptic, warned of "paper rules", the rules in the books that do not decide real cases. Frank, the fact sceptic, charged the rule sceptics with "upper courtitis", meaning that they studied only appeal courts and missed the trial, where the facts are found. A variance study is evidence for Frank's doubt more than Llewellyn's.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

A realist would read the variance findings as fact scepticism confirmed. As Frank argued, the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies, so different judges produce different outcomes under the same rule. Appeal is no full answer, since it arguably only moves that discretion up a level. Yet the findings indict judges who fail to justify their rulings, not Dworkin's normative theory, which says how judges should decide rather than how every judge does. The study therefore supports the weak realist claim that rules are not all that matter, not the strong claim that law is only the judge.

99.7 Synthesis

🧩 Practise 9.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.7 Synthesis (word for word)
9.7 Synthesis answers the realists, victory to the crits
  1. Dworkin's judge answers [the realists]: he must justify by fit and value, not predict.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly; Harris reads Unger's jibe at a "pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective; arguably a third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs)†.
  • QUALIFY Dworkin is arguably text-first: the judge brings a political theory but owes a duty to the law, close to Fuller's fidelity; the crits are goal-first, moulding the text to the transformative aim. The work can overlap; the starting point differs†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Dworkin beats the realists by saying judges must justify, not predict. But to justify, he uses "fit", which might just crown whatever the law already says, and his "value" step might just be the judge's politics. If moral values are only opinions, the crits win. If some answers really are better than others, they do not.

What the statement claims

"Dworkin's judge can answer the American Legal Realists, but only by handing victory to the Critical Legal Scholars." (Q88)

The statement grants Dworkin a win against the realists and then says the price is too high. Dworkin's answer relies on fit and value, and the crits say both are politics in disguise. It is tempting because the crits' attack on fit is strong. The block shows that the crits win only on one condition.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Dworkin's judge does answer the realists. He must justify his ruling by fit and value, so he cannot treat the law as a forecast of what he will do. Whatever he decides, he owes reasons showing that it is the best reading of the law.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly. If the judge must fit the existing record, the dominant principle of the past will usually win, and the counterprinciples stay exceptions. Harris reads Unger's jibe at a pre-established harmony, the comfortable assumption that the legal materials already add up to a coherent scheme, as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective. If the value step is just the judge's personal politics, the crits are right that law is politics. But if some principles really are sounder than others, value is not mere preference. Arguably a third option, natural law, would say which principle should win, as the appeal to universal principles in Riggs suggests†.

The extra line, explained

  • QUALIFY · text-first v goal-first†. Dworkin is arguably text-first. The judge brings a political theory to the case but owes a duty to the law he finds, which is close to Fuller's fidelity to law. The crits are goal-first. They start from the transformative aim and mould the text to reach it. Their actual work of argument can overlap, but the starting point differs. This is distinction 1.3(17), and it is the cleanest way to stop the statement from merging Dworkin into the crits.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Dworkin's judge answers the realists, since he must justify by fit and value rather than predict his own ruling. The crits have a real point, because fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly, and Harris reads Unger's jibe at a pre-established harmony as aimed at Dworkin. But victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective. If some principles are sounder than others, value disciplines the judge, and arguably natural law could say which principle should win, as Riggs suggests. Dworkin's judge also starts from the text, not from the goal, which is exactly what separates him from the crits.

109.8 "Necessarily" implicated?

🧩 Practise 9.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? (word for word)
9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
  1. [Theories of law] are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words) but operative only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So [necessarily implicated] holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.
  • Morality enters, for Hart, at most where rules run out; for Fuller, in fidelity joined to the judge's responsibility for making law what it ought to be; for Dworkin, in every proposition of law (14.5).
  • FOR Riggs pitted Earl's legislative intention against Gray's fixed penalties: two morally grounded theories of a statute (2.8).
  • STEELMAN LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Theory and morality are necessarily involved in every judicial decision." Half true. Every judge relies on some theory of what law is, since even "I just apply the statute" is a theory. And morality is always in the background, for example in why we should follow clear words at all. But morality is not the reason for deciding most everyday cases. It steps in only for hard cases and monstrous laws.

What the statement claims

"Theories of law and morality are necessarily implicated in every judicial decision, whether on the common law or statutes, in a constitutional democracy."

Everything turns on the word necessarily, which commits the statement to more than it can defend. The statement is right about theory, and partly right about morality. Your job is to split it, using distinction 1.3(2): presupposed v operative.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Theories of law are always implicated. A judge who says "I simply apply the statute" has already taken a side on what counts as law, for example that the words, read literally, are the law. That is a theory, even if it is an unexamined one.
  2. Morality is always presupposed, but operative only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. Morality sits in the background of every decision, in the value of legality and in the reasons a judge has to defer to clear words at all. But in most cases it is not the ground of decision. It becomes operative, the actual reason for the result, only in hard cases where fit runs out, and at the extreme of intolerable injustice.
  3. So "necessarily implicated" holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision. Split the statement into three parts. Agree with it about theory. Agree with it about morality in the background. Deny it about morality deciding every case.

Riggs is the hard case that makes the flowchart's middle branch real. Everyone agreed on the words of the statute and on the facts. They split over what law those words made. Dworkin reads the two judgments as two morally grounded theories of how to read a statute (2.8). Earl's reading guards the coherence of the law, so that a statute is read in harmony with the principle that no one profits from his own wrong. Gray's reading looks like plain textualism, but it too guards a principle of justice: penalties are fixed in advance by the legislature, and courts may not add to them. So even the judge who sticks to the text is relying on morality. Liu adds that Riggs bears two readings, and you need not choose between them†. On one, both sides argued about law, and the majority simply included common-law principle in it. On the other, the real dispute was whether law is always subject to universal moral principles, as Earl's appeal to universal law suggests.

The extra lines, explained

  • Where morality enters, for each theorist. For Hart, morality enters at most where the rules run out, in the penumbra. For Fuller, it enters through fidelity to law, joined to the judge's responsibility for making the law what it ought to be. For Dworkin, it enters in every proposition of law, because every statement of what the law is rests on an interpretation shaped by political morality (14.5). Use this to show that "necessarily" means something different on each theory.
  • FOR · Riggs. Riggs pitted Earl's appeal to legislative intention against Gray's insistence on fixed penalties. These were two morally grounded theories of one statute (2.8), which is strong evidence that theory, and in hard cases morality, is implicated in judging.
  • STEELMAN · Lim Meng Suang. In Lim Meng Suang (2014) the Court of Appeal upheld s 377A of the Penal Code, which then made gross indecency between men an offence, against a challenge under the equality clause, Art 12. It refused to judge whether the law's object, its purpose, was legitimate without legal standards to judge it by, as TSH notes. That is judicial restraint, and a strong local example of it. Card 14.5 adds that the Court invoked what it called a central motif of Dworkin's theory to put aside extra-legal considerations that belonged to the legislature, and TSH surmises that the motif was principle v policy. The reply is that restraint is itself a theory of judging: a view about what courts are for and when they should defer.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is right about theory and only partly right about morality. Theories of law are always implicated, since a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law. Morality is always presupposed, in the value of legality and in the reasons to defer to clear words, but it is the operative ground of decision only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. Riggs shows the hard case, where Earl's legislative intention and Gray's fixed penalties were two morally grounded theories of one statute. "Necessarily implicated" therefore holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.

119.9 Why judges converge

🧩 Practise 9.9 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.9 Why judges converge (word for word)
9.9 Why judges converge shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
  1. Judges converge less because of [shared backgrounds] than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer steeped in an appellate court's "folkways" could predict outcomes eight times out of ten.
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory; [the tenth case] is where that theory is argued, not predicted.
  • FOR ALR assumes "underlying ethical pluralism"†; for Kennedy, shared rule-application is not in fact objectivity, though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule.
  • AGAINST Dworkin: hard cases are perhaps just those where fit yields no unique reading.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Most of the time, judges agree. Why? Not just because they went to the same schools. It is because they have learned the same way of giving legal reasons. Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory without noticing it. Hard cases are where that shared theory runs out and has to be argued.

What the statement claims

"Judges converge only because of shared backgrounds; what apart from rules explains agreement?"

The statement offers a sociological explanation of agreement: judges come from similar schools and social circles, so they think alike. It is tempting because backgrounds plainly matter, and the realists and crits have stressed them. The block accepts that background matters but says it is not the main reason judges agree.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Judges converge less because of shared backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification. Judges agree in most cases because they have learned the same way of giving legal reasons: which arguments count, how precedents are read, what a sound judgment looks like. Shared schooling helps, but what is shared is mainly a craft of justification, not a set of private sympathies.
  2. Llewellyn showed how far that shared craft goes. Harris reports Llewellyn's later view. A lawyer steeped in an appeal court's folkways, its habits and style of reasoning, could predict its decisions eight times out of ten. That is high, but not perfect.
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory, and the tenth case is where that theory is argued, not predicted. In the eight cases the shared theory gives one answer, so nobody notices it. In the tenth, the shared theory runs out or splits, and the judges must argue about it openly. This is the memorable line in 1.2.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three explanations of why judges agree
ExplanationWhat it gets rightWhere it falls short
Rules alone decideClear rules do guide most conduct. Harris's speeding test: if rules did nothing, we could not expect drivers doing 60 to be convicted and drivers doing 20 to be acquitted.It cannot explain the tenth case, where judges who know the same rules split.
Shared backgrounds (the realists and crits)Background does shape judges. Kennedy admits that his gut sense of a case is itself conditioned by legal training.The shared background includes training in the rules and in giving reasons, so it is not really a rival to them.
A shared practice of justification (your answer)It explains both the eight easy cases and why the tenth is argued rather than guessed.Concede that it does not settle every case. Dworkin says hard cases may just be those where fit gives no unique answer.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · underlying ethical pluralism†. The realists assume that beneath the surface judges hold a variety of ethical views, so agreement cannot come from shared morals alone. Kennedy adds that shared application of a rule is not in fact objectivity: judges agreeing does not prove that the rule decided the case. Yet Kennedy also admits that sometimes he meets a rule he can't budge, which concedes that rules do sometimes bind.
  • AGAINST · Dworkin on hard cases. Dworkin suggests that hard cases are perhaps just those where fit yields no unique reading. On that view, the line between easy and hard cases is not drawn by the judges' backgrounds. It is drawn by how much the legal record settles.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Judges converge less because of shared backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification. Harris reports Llewellyn's finding that a lawyer steeped in an appellate court's folkways could predict its decisions eight times out of ten. Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory, which is why nobody notices it. The tenth case is where that theory is argued, not predicted, and Dworkin suggests that hard cases are perhaps just those where fit yields no unique reading. Shared background matters, but what judges share is above all a craft of giving reasons.

129.10 Chain novelist, author and critic

🧩 Practise 9.10 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic (word for word)
9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
  1. The artist interprets while creating and the critic creates while interpreting, yet the two remain different.
  2. Each chain novelist after the first both interprets and creates; after the second, no single author's intentions decide.
  3. So the judge, a partner in a chain enterprise, must interpret the legal history found, not invent a better one.
  • QUALIFY Fit has "no algorithm"; value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis").
  • AGAINST Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (13.1).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a novel written chapter by chapter by different authors. You are writing chapter 10. You cannot ignore chapters 1 to 9, which is fit, but you also want the story to be as good as possible, which is value. That is Dworkin's judge: interpret what is there, then write the next chapter well, without rewriting the earlier ones.

What the statement claims

"The ideal judge reads the whole of the law as one coherent story, written by many hands, and writes the next chapter …" (Q84)

This is the same practice question as 9.5, read for its picture of the judge. The statement adopts Dworkin's chain novel. It is right in outline. Your job is to explain exactly what the chain novelist does, and why that both frees and binds the judge.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The artist interprets while creating, and the critic creates while interpreting, yet the two remain different. An author writing a novel must have at least a rough theory of what makes the work good, so she interprets as she goes. A critic explaining a finished novel adds something of her own. But the author controls the whole work, while the critic is bound by one that is already finished.
  2. Each chain novelist after the first both interprets and creates. In a chain novel, each writer receives the chapters so far and must add the next. She must form a view of what the story is about and continue it well. After the second chapter, no single author's intentions decide what the story means, because it is the joint work of many hands.
  3. So the judge, a partner in a chain enterprise, must interpret the legal history found, not invent a better one. The common-law judge is in the chain novelist's position. She must read what earlier judges have collectively done and continue it in its best light. She may not tear up the earlier chapters to write the story she would have preferred.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Author, critic, chain novelist, judge
RoleInterprets?Creates?Bound by
AuthorYes, while creatingYes, the whole workOnly her own sense of what makes it good
CriticYesYes, while interpretingA finished work someone else wrote
Chain novelistYes, the chapters so farYes, the next chapterEarlier chapters she did not write, with no single author's intention to defer to
JudgeYes, the legal recordYes, the ruling in this caseWhat earlier judges collectively did (fit), and the law's point as a scheme of justice (value)

The extra lines, explained

  • QUALIFY · no algorithm. Dworkin admits there is no algorithm for deciding when a reading fits well enough. And the value side is political, not aesthetic. Dworkin's political hypothesis replaces the literary critic's aesthetic one, so the judge asks which reading shows the law at its best as a scheme of justice, not as a story.
  • AGAINST · Kennedy. Kennedy's judge works the field toward how-I-want-to-come-out (13.1). He starts from the result, not the text, and treats the legal materials as a medium to be worked. That is the strongest challenge to the chain-novel picture, because it describes what judging can feel like from the inside.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Kennedy's strikers' lie-in

Kennedy imagines himself as a federal trial judge in Boston. Union bus drivers are on strike, and on the first day members lie down in the street to stop the company's buses, driven by replacement drivers, from leaving. His first impression of the law is that workers may not interfere with the owner's use of the means of production, so the company should get an injunction. That rule at first seems to apply itself. But his how-I-want-to-come-out is for the workers. So he works the materials, recasting the lie-in as non-violent political expression rather than obstruction, and he pays for each step in time and in legitimacy cost. That is goal-first judging, described honestly.

Kennedy v the chain novel
▤ Comparison 13.1
  1. 1Shared. Both put the judge inside inherited materials. Fit and value constrain Dworkin's judge. Work and the risk to credibility constrain Kennedy's.
  2. 2Split. Kennedy starts from how-I-want-to-come-out, Dworkin from the text†. Kennedy answers Dworkin's right-answer thesis with his experience of indeterminacy and of free ethical or political choice, and he disclaims a verdict.

When Kennedy's judge has done all the work he can and the law still points against how he wants to come out, framework 15.10 lists his five courses. He can (1) go along with the law and write an opinion denouncing it, (2) withdraw from the case and leave the dirty work to another judge, (3) decide openly on what the law should be, (4) use a legal argument he thinks implausible, or (5) find facts he knows are false, which Kennedy calls an extreme measure. Kennedy endorses or excludes none of them a priori. The sheet adds its own rule, built on candour.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Dworkin's chain novel shows why judging is neither mechanical nor free. The artist interprets while creating and the critic creates while interpreting, yet the two remain different. Each chain novelist after the first both interprets and creates, and after the second no single author's intentions decide. So the judge, a partner in a chain enterprise, must interpret the legal history found, not invent a better one. There is no algorithm for fit, and Kennedy's judge works the field toward how he wants to come out, but even Kennedy concedes that the materials constrain him, at a cost in work and credibility.

13Putting it together: Practice Q85

"Anyone who watches the courts knows that judges decide first and find reasons afterwards. Whether a Prime Minister found inside a polling station has broken the rule against loitering within 200 metres of it turns not on the statute but on which canon of interpretation the judge happens to prefer, and the statutory instruction to favour the Act's purpose merely adds one more option. Precedents fare no better: they can be read narrowly, read widely or dismissed as archaic at will. The only honest definition of law is therefore a prediction of what judges will actually do."

Instruction: ALR, Dworkin, Hart; plus implications for how lawyers argue and judges justify.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

Cheng San GRC is the realist's best case. Precise canons, literal and purposive, pointed different ways, and the Attorney-General advised that there was no offence. But it shows less than the statement claims. I make three claims. First, canons and ratios leave some cases open, as the weak realist reading holds, but not all. Second, prediction is a lawyer's stance, while a judge cannot predict his own ruling and must justify it by fit and political morality. Third, "at will" ignores the costs of a flimsy ruling, so judges are constrained even where the rules run out.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. The realist kernel (9.1, 9.6). Cheng San and the competing canons. Rule v fact scepticism. Concede the weak reading, that rules are not all that matter.
  2. Justify, not predict (9.1, 9.2, 14.5). The judge's "alas". Dworkin's fit and value. Hart's core of settled meaning explains the easy cases, which is the restraint steelman. McLoughlin shows judges arguing about the grounds of law, not guessing.
  3. Constraint, and the crits (9.1 QUALIFY, 9.3, 9.10). Reputation, reversal and credibility†. Kennedy's medium. Self-critique from 1.4: fit is often not unique, so whose political morality decides? Then the implications the instruction asks for. Lawyers should argue fit and value, not just the odds, and judges should state openly the political morality that closes an open case.

Core card B (13.4) gives you two ready verdicts for this family. Against "judges only apply the law", morality is always presupposed in judging and sometimes operative, and a judge concerned only with what the law is already holds a theory of what law is. Against "adjudication is politics", judging is political in Dworkin's sense, because where fit runs out judges choose between principles of political morality. It is not politics in the partisan sense that a word like "pretence" needs, because rules leave some cases open, not all, and judges must justify, not predict.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them. Where the rules run out, judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not the goal. That is neither prediction nor preference.

ℹ NOTE
A defensible version (one per script)

If one sentence would repair the statement, use the Core B line: adjudication is political in the sense of political morality, not partisanship, and where the rules leave a case open, judges must justify, not pretend (13.4).

14Recap

Archetype 9 on one card
▤ Sections 9.1–9.10
  1. 1Realism is true for counsel, not for judges, and costs constrain the judge (9.1).
  2. 2Precedent running out is a theoretical disagreement, not a gap. Floodgates can be policy or principle (9.2).
  3. 3The crits are right that counterprinciples are real, but critique needs a standard (9.3).
  4. 4"Like cases alike" needs a moral test (9.4).
  5. 5A right answer exists in principle, but fit is often not unique and Dworkin gives no threshold (9.5).
  6. 6Variance indicts judges, not the theory (9.6).
  7. 7The crits win only if value is subjective (9.7).
  8. 8Theory is always implicated. Morality is always presupposed, but operative only at the margins (9.8).
  9. 9Convergence comes from a shared practice of justification (9.9).
  10. 10Chain novel: interpret, don't invent. Kennedy's five courses meet your candour rule (9.10, 15.10).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a novel written by many hands, open at chapter ten, with the judge holding the pen. Most of the page is already printed: those are the easy cases, where the earlier chapters leave only one way to go on. A few lines are blank: those are the open cases. The judge must fill them so the story fits what came before and becomes the best story it can be. She may not tear out earlier chapters, which would be inventing, and she may not write whatever she fancies, which would be preference. Only if the story has become monstrous may she refuse to go on with it.

LESSON 10 · ARCHETYPE 10 · ABOUT 74 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 50 QUESTIONS

Lawyering: Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy

⚡ BIG IDEA

The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, moral dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it. Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.

ARCHETYPE 10 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
10 Lawyering: Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.

  1. [Lawyers are like soldiers] is the "dramatic bifurcation" Thunder rejects: merely pointing to the role does not explain it.

  3. So [no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do] overstates: roles are not wholly idiosyncratic, and prudence applies the virtues (4.7).

  3. So [the junior] shares responsibility: raise it in dialogue first, and refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others.
  • Mei (Q100, Q103 only): pleading the time bar is lawful, yet the win may be unjust, so dialogue comes first. The concealed defect endangers the public, so she may object (10.1).
  • JUDGE Kennedy's five courses are a judge's (12.4; 15.10), not a junior's.

  1. [Leave your conscience at the door] describes an outlook lawyers are trained into; it does not justify it.
  2. Pepper reports "all realists now" as a comment often heard from contemporary law professors.
  3. So [theory isn't relevant] is itself an unexamined theory: the realist lawyer already advises "breach as cost".
  • Kennedy: progressive-minded people, fearing conversion without choice, ask whether law school will warp their minds.

  1. In litigation, especially criminal defence, the law may allow more: implying a truthful witness lied brings no liability; similar half-truths selling [a termite-ridden house] may be misrepresentation.
  2. So [the statement] holds in part: realism is likelier from a lawyer advising a large corporate enterprise, where no judge or opposing counsel checks the client.
10.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view why we hold such views, purpose of law, hired gun, just do your job
  1. Thunder traces the amoral view's appeal largely to the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality.
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make role-based reasons morally suspect, prudence, the profession's bread and butter, amoral, and right conduct separate from the good life.
  3. Realism gives the view a congenial philosophical home; against both, law is intended, ultimately if not always immediately, for ends naturally good for man.
  • CONCEDE I concede that a diagnosis is no refutation; arguably the likelier source is an intuition Thunder shares, that a lawyer should not substitute personal judgment for the client's†, which 10.1 must answer.
  • QUALIFY Same act, different reasons†: a Thunder lawyer may disclose a live victim as part of the role, or because duties as a human being trump it; a Pepper lawyer may too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is mindset, not necessarily outcome; positive law sets its width.

  1. Ask in order†: is the system by and large just; if so, is this rule intolerably unjust; if not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question†: is the institution justified by truth-finding, dignity or replacement costs?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than excused; Pepper names both as adversary-system defences.
  • Law is Pepper's limit: if the RF denies a racist statute legal character, even his lawyer may refuse.
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels: Pepper keeps objection, and Thunder accepts role morality and that no legal system is perfect. They differ in mindset more than outcome, and the more robust the conduct rules, the narrower the gap†. The live question is how often conscience may override [the role]: rarely and openly, after dialogue, where serving the client would subvert the law's point.

1Start here: archetype 10 in plain English

Archetype 10 asks one question: may a lawyer's own morals affect what the lawyer does for a client? The test case is always a client who wants help with something lawful that the lawyer thinks is wrong, such as defeating an admitted debt with a time bar.

Two writers frame the debate. Stephen Pepper says the lawyer should help with anything lawful. The law already marks the limits, and a lawyer who screens clients by personal morals becomes a gatekeeper over everyone else's access to law. David Thunder says the lawyer stays a moral person at work. The legal role exists to serve justice and the common good, so a good lawyer brings judgement into the job instead of leaving it at the door.

Most exam statements in this family try to seal the lawyer's role off from morality: "just do your job", "if no rule forbids it, you may do it". A few go the other way and say the lawyer must refuse whenever the result looks unjust. Your answer is the same in both directions. The lawyer's role is itself moral. The law sets the floor. Above it, prudence, conversation with the client and, rarely, open refusal decide the hard cases. Pepper and Thunder differ more in how they reason than in what they do. The same verdict answers Core card B's question on lawyers (13.4).

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Amoral role (the standard conception)The lawyer helps the client with anything lawful and does not screen the client's aims through the lawyer's own morals. The client, not the lawyer, is morally accountable. Pepper defends this role on moral grounds.
First-class citizenshipPepper's idea that everyone has the same legal rights on paper, but most people need a lawyer to use them. A lawyer who filters that access through personal morals turns the client into a second-class citizen.
Moral dialogueThe lawyer raising moral concerns with the client and even trying to persuade, while leaving the decision to the client.
Conscientious objectionThe lawyer refusing, on grounds of conscience, to do what the role would otherwise require. Pepper says it should be rarely exercised.
Legal realismThe view that law is a prediction of what officials will actually do. On this view a breach of contract is just a cost.
Natural-teleological viewThunder's view that law exists for purposes naturally good for people, such as justice and public order. "Teleological" means "to do with purposes".
Neo-Kantian moralityThunder's label for moral thinking that treats morality as universal rules. He blames it, with legal realism, for making the amoral role seem natural.
PrudencePractical wisdom: applying good values to a real situation. Thunder calls it the bread and butter of legal practice.
Conduct rulesThe professional rules that bind Singapore lawyers, for example not to mislead the court (16.4).

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the statement fails, because the lawyer's role is moral; law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases above it. Put simply, you cannot take morality out of lawyering, because even the case for "just help the client" is a moral argument.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement seals the lawyer's role off from morality, the view Thunder caricatures as simply focusing on the law. Yet even Pepper, the role's best defender, justifies it morally, by appeal to client autonomy and equal access to law. So you reject or qualify the statement. The role is moral, it is bounded by law, and dialogue comes before refusal.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. The statement is overstated. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels. Pepper keeps a right to object, and Thunder accepts that roles carry their own duties and that no legal system is perfect. They differ in mindset more than in outcome, and the more robust the professional conduct rules, the narrower the gap between them†. The live question is how often conscience may override the role. Your answer is rarely and openly, after dialogue, and only where serving the client would defeat the law's own point.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before replying. Section 10 gives you two steelmen, one for each direction a statement can take.

  • Steelman: for Pepper. Use it when the statement defends the amoral role. Pepper argues that giving people access to the law makes the lawyer "a good person", and that the law, not the lawyer's private morality, should limit what clients may do. This shows that lawful help is morally defensible. It does not show that the role is amoral. Pepper's own lawyer keeps four zones of moral choice: whether to practise law at all, which clients to take, moral dialogue with the client, and conscientious objection, which is always available. Pepper says that together these leave the lawyer "a meaningful field".
  • Steelman: for Thunder. Use it when the statement says the lawyer must refuse. Thunder argues that Pepper's role leaves the lawyer morally powerless for the sake of a moral principle, client autonomy. The amoral lawyer loses both the right and the duty to take some responsibility for what the work serves. This shows that the amoral role has a moral cost. It does not show that the lawyer must refuse, because dialogue comes before refusal.

The eleven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
10.1"Turning a client away on moral grounds abuses the lawyer's position."That overstates Pepper. And to spot his extreme cases, the lawyer must weigh morality all the time.
10.2"Tell clients how the law is really enforced, since law is what officials do."Accurate advice is fine. But if law is only what officials do, Pepper's limit empties out.
10.3"Is moral dialogue a real answer?"Only in part. It is costly and needs a willing client. For Thunder it is ordinary practice.
10.4"Lawyers are like soldiers, and private virtue makes them judges, policemen or deceivers."Pointing to the role does not explain it. The lawyer stays accountable as a person.
10.5"If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it."The rules are a floor with a purpose. Exploiting them against justice subverts them.
10.6"Defending a client you believe guilty is wrong."A fair trial is the role working. Refusal fits only an unjust system or an intolerable rule.
10.7"Juniors following lawful orders bear no responsibility."Lawful is not blameless. Raise it first, and refuse only where others would be seriously harmed.
10.8"Leave your conscience at the door; theory isn't relevant."That describes how lawyers are trained, not why it is right. It is itself an unexamined theory.
10.9"With no judge in transactional work, the lawyer must supply the moral scrutiny."Partly right. Realism tempts most where nobody checks the client.
10.10"Just do your job: you're a hired gun."Thunder traces that view to realism plus rule-based morality. But a diagnosis is not a refutation.
10.11"No lawyer can hide behind the system when the result is unjust."Ask in order: is the system just, is this rule intolerable, or is only this outcome unjust?†
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

The lawyer's role is moral: law is the floor, and above it come prudence, dialogue and rare, open objection.

2The big picture: can a good person be a lawyer?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A client asks a lawyer for help with something legal but nasty, such as defeating a debt the client admits it owes because the claim was filed too late. Pepper says the lawyer should help. The law already says what is forbidden, and it is not the lawyer's place to judge clients. Thunder says the lawyer is still a person with a conscience. The job exists to serve justice, so a good lawyer stays a good person at work. This lesson shows that the two are closer than they look, and that their real disagreement is about mindset.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
PepperPepper defends the lawyer's amoral ethical role on moral grounds. Law is a public good open to all, and autonomy is a moral good. Most people can use the law only through a lawyer, so a lawyer who screened clients by personal morals would subject everyone to rule by an oligarchy of lawyers.
ThunderThunder argues that a lawyer's role is justified only by what it adds to justice and human flourishing. Splitting professional from personal ethics fragments the lawyer's moral life, and amoral lawyers become slaves of their clients' consciences, however warped.
KennedyDuncan Kennedy, a critical legal scholar, appears for the way law school shapes students' outlook (10.8). His five courses describe a judge, not a junior lawyer (12.4, 15.10).
FishFish argues that legal practice always serves a purpose, a vision of how the state may use its monopoly of legalised violence. So a lawyer who never cites theory still works inside one (2.6, 14.1).

Pepper and Thunder side by side

QuestionPepperThunder
What is law?A public good everyone may use, and the limit on what a lawyer may doAn institution aimed at ends naturally good for people, such as justice and public order
What is the lawyer for?Giving clients full access to the law, so that they are first-class citizensFurthering justice, public order and the rule of law
When does the lawyer's own morality come in?Through dialogue, choice of client and, rarely, objectionAll the time, because the lawyer interprets the role in the light of a good life
Is the role a separate compartment?In part: the lawyer sets personal morals aside while actingNo: a role is no pocket universe†
A client reveals a victim still aliveDisclose only as extreme-case objection, stepping outside the roleDisclose as part of the role, or because duties as a human being trump it

Key distinctions

  • Amoral v immoral. Pepper's lawyer sets personal morality aside while acting for the client, without approving of the client's aims. Pepper thinks that is the morally right thing to do, so his case is a moral argument for amorality†.
  • Floor v ceiling (distinction 1.3(3)). The law, including the conduct rules, is the minimum, not the whole of what a good lawyer considers (10.5, 11.7).
  • Personal v institutional wrong. Pepper says a bad result of the lawyer's proper work is the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's. Liu asks why that should be any more acceptable (10.11)†.
  • Unjust system v rule v outcome (distinction 1.3(10))†. A lawyer troubled by injustice must first locate it, because each location calls for a different response (10.6, 10.11).
  • Mindset v outcome (distinction 1.3(18)). Pepper's and Thunder's lawyers often do the same thing for different reasons (10.10).

Pepper's framework: the limit and the remedies

Framework 15.11 asks: the client's plan is lawful but wrong, so what may the lawyer do? First, the law is the limit. Conduct bad enough should, it seems, be made explicitly unlawful. Second, Pepper admits that legal realism threatens his model (10.2). Society could respond with more enforcement, a daunting prospect, or by rebuilding moral authority beyond law. The lawyer's response is not to act as the client's policeman, judge or deceiver, but to engage in moral dialogue. Third, the lawyer may object on grounds of conscience, but only rarely.

⚠ TRAP
Pepper is not legal positivism

Legal positivism only identifies law. As Hart argued against Radbruch, a moral decision about what to do still remains, so a positivist may side with Pepper or Thunder. Pepper is hard to square with natural law theory, for which finding the law already involves morality†.
