310.1 Floor

🧩 Practise 10.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.1 Floor (word for word)
10.1 Floor turn away a client, distaste, abuses his position, hidden bodies
  1. [Turning a client away abuses his position] overstates Pepper: choice of client is troubling if it forecloses access to the law.
  2. Pepper poses a dilemma: conduct bad enough should, it seems, be made explicitly unlawful; if not, why impose "the happenstance" of one lawyer's conscience?
  3. So [the client's conscience must govern] is itself a moral claim, and spotting Pepper's "extreme cases" means weighing morality throughout (like Radbruch's judge, though a refused client can find another lawyer†): the role is less amoral than it looks.
  • AGAINST The statement's verbs, [abuses] and [denies], are moral premises.
  • Hidden bodies (Q95 only): objection should be rarely exercised but may reveal "the live victim".
  • TRAP LP does not entail Pepper: it only identifies law, leaving a moral decision (Hart v Radbruch), so an LP may side with Pepper or Thunder; Pepper is hard to square with NLT, for which finding the law already involves morality†.
  • AGAINST Inequality: the rich buy more law, so a filter could level it. Replies: access to justice; distribution is not content; filters may hurt the poor more (Pepper)†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Pepper's best argument goes like this. If something is bad enough, make it illegal. If it is not that bad, why should a client's access to the law depend on the luck of which lawyer they hired? But Pepper also lets lawyers object in extreme cases. To spot an extreme case, the lawyer has to be thinking morally all the time. So his "amoral" lawyer is not so amoral after all.

What the statement claims

"A lawyer who turns away a client, or refuses to help him do something lawful, because he finds it distasteful abuses his position … A lawyer who imposes his own morals denies his client equal access to justice." (Q95)

The statement says the law already marks out what society will not tolerate, so above that floor only the client's conscience counts. It is tempting because it is very nearly Pepper's own argument. Your task is to show that it goes further than Pepper does, and that its own wording gives the game away.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The statement overstates Pepper himself. Pepper does not say that turning a client away is always an abuse. He says that choosing clients is troubling only if it shuts a person out of the law altogether. A lawyer who declines one client, when others will act, is using one of the zones of choice Pepper deliberately leaves open.
  2. Pepper's real argument is a dilemma. If the client's conduct is bad enough, it seems it should be made explicitly unlawful, and then the law itself stops the lawyer. If it is not that bad, why should the client's access to the law depend on the happenstance of one lawyer's conscience? Either way, Pepper says, the lawyer's private morality is the wrong filter.
  3. So "the client's conscience must govern" is itself a moral claim, and the role is less amoral than it looks. Pepper still lets the lawyer object in extreme cases, and he never defines "extreme". To spot an extreme case, the lawyer must keep weighing morality all the time. Liu compares this to Radbruch's judge, who always assesses the law but overrides it only at intolerable injustice†. The comparison is not exact, because a refused client can find another lawyer, while a judge's ruling binds everyone†.

The extra lines, explained

  • AGAINST · the statement's verbs. The statement says the refusing lawyer abuses his position and denies the client equal access. Those are moral words. A statement that keeps morality out by using morally loaded verbs is making a moral argument. This is your hook.
  • Hidden bodies (Q95 only). Pepper's own extreme case. Objection should be rarely exercised, but the writers he relies on separate keeping quiet about a dead body from revealing the live victim. For other 10.1 statements, use the ledger's alternative, Freedman v Wasserstrom (see the scene below).
  • TRAP · Pepper is not positivism. See the trap box above. A positivist may side with Pepper or Thunder†.
  • AGAINST · inequality. The rich buy more law, so a moral filter on rich clients might level the field. There are three replies†. Better access to justice, such as legal aid, shrinks the problem. Pepper says the distribution of legal services is a separate issue from their content. And a filter may hurt the poor more, since a wealthy client can fire a scrupulous lawyer while a poorer client may be stuck with the one lawyer they can afford.

The will shows Pepper's point at its strongest: a lawyer who refuses to draft it replaces the client's paternalism with the lawyer's own. The hidden bodies show where his point runs out, since few would let a client's interest prevail while a victim dies.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is nearly Pepper's own case, but it overstates him. Pepper calls choice of client troubling only when it forecloses a person's access to the law, and he keeps conscientious objection for extreme cases. His strongest point is a dilemma: conduct bad enough should be made explicitly unlawful, and otherwise subjecting the client to one lawyer's conscience is mere happenstance. Yet the statement's own verbs, "abuses" and "denies", are moral premises, so the claim that the client's conscience must govern is itself a moral claim. And because Pepper never defines "extreme", his lawyer must weigh morality throughout, which makes the role less amoral than it looks.

410.2 Effluent

🧩 Practise 10.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.2 Effluent (word for word)
10.2 Effluent enforcement risk, what officials will actually do, full access
  1. Advising on [enforcement risk] is accurate and useful to the client (Pepper); the trouble is what realism does to his limit, "the law".
  2. In Pepper's effluent case (limit .050 g/l; up to .075 ignored), a client without strong moral guidance faces no pressure to obey the law as written.
  3. So if [law is only what officials will actually do], the promise of not encouraging lawbreaking holds only by emptying the word.
  • AGAINST Thunder: autonomy may yield to our shared environment's beauty and others' health.
  • QUALIFY The example is arguably "lopsided"†: the moral duty not to lie by omission, and probably the standard of care, require telling both figures; weighing morality to reach "tell" is Thunderian, while Pepper tells without asking†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A factory's legal limit for pollution is 0.050 grams per litre, but the regulator never acts below 0.075. Should the lawyer tell the client? Pepper says yes, because it is accurate advice. But now the "law" the client hears about is "what officials will do", and the client may pollute up to 0.075. Pepper's own limit, which was "don't help break the law", quietly disappears.

What the statement claims

"A good lawyer tells clients the whole truth about the law, including how it is enforced in practice … Law, after all, is in the end only what officials will actually do. Advising on enforcement risk is not encouraging lawbreaking; it is giving the client full access to the law and leaving the choice with him." (Q96)

The statement relies on legal realism: law is a prediction of what officials will do. On that view, telling the client about the regulator's real practice is simply telling him the law. The block shows that the advice itself is fine, but the realist premise eats away at Pepper's model from the inside.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Telling the client about enforcement risk is fine in itself; the problem is what it does to Pepper's limit. Pepper accepts that advice about enforcement is accurate and useful to the client. But his whole model says the lawyer's limit is "the law". If the law is understood the realist way, as a prediction of what officials will do, the limit moves.
  2. Pepper's effluent case shows the slide. The written limit is .050 g of ammonia per litre, but readings up to .075 are ignored. A client who does not bring strong moral guidance of his own now faces no pressure to obey the law as written. Pepper himself says that morality comes through the door as part of the client, and many clients bring little.
  3. So if law is only what officials will actually do, Pepper's promise not to encourage lawbreaking holds only by emptying the word. On the realist view, a reading of .070 is not lawbreaking at all, so the promise is kept, but only because "the law" no longer means the rule as written.

The extra lines, explained

  • AGAINST · Thunder on autonomy. Thunder denies that client autonomy trumps everything. It may give way to the beauty of our shared environment and to other people's health. An effluent limit serves real human goods, so a lawyer who sees law as aimed at those goods will not treat .050 as a mere price.
  • QUALIFY · the example is lopsided†. Liu doubts that Pepper set the example up fairly†. Ordinary morality already says the lawyer should tell the client both figures. There is a moral duty not to lie by omission, and mentioning only .050 implies that penalties start at .050, which misleads. The standard of care probably requires it too, since the .075 practice falls within the advice sought. A lawyer who weighs morality and concludes "tell" is reasoning like Thunder. Pepper's lawyer tells without asking the moral question at all†.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three lawyers, one effluent question
LawyerWhat the client hearsHow the route works
The lawyer as policeman or deceiverOnly the .050 limit, presented as if strictly enforcedPepper rejects this. Withholding the truth to steer the client is deception and overrides the client's autonomy.
Pepper's lawyerBoth figures, with no moral question asked firstThis is his model. But if "the law" now means .075, his limit has moved.
Thunder's lawyerBoth figures, with a warning that .050 is still the lawThe same advice, reached by weighing honesty and harm to others. That route is Thunderian†.

The advice is nearly the same for two of the three lawyers. What differs is how they got there, which is the mindset point of 10.10.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Advising on enforcement risk is, as Pepper accepts, accurate and useful to the client. The trouble is what realism does to his limit, "the law". In his own effluent case, where the limit is .050 but readings up to .075 are ignored, a client without strong moral guidance faces no pressure to obey the law as written. If law is only what officials will actually do, the promise not to encourage lawbreaking holds only by emptying the word. Thunder adds that client autonomy may yield to our shared environment and to others' health, and the example is arguably lopsided, since the duty not to mislead already requires telling the client both figures.

510.3 Dialogue

🧩 Practise 10.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.3 Dialogue (word for word)
10.3 Dialogue moral dialogue, cost, criminal defendant, corporate officer
  1. [Moral dialogue] is a real answer only in part: it makes the lawyer a "moral educator" without judging or policing the client (Pepper).
  2. Pepper admits its limits: it is expensive, and a criminal defendant will be less open to it than a corporate officer.
  3. So dialogue works where it matches Thunder's prudence and tact; for his lawyer it is ordinary practice, not a repair.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Pepper says that if you think your client is doing something wrong, you can talk to them about it, as a kind of moral teacher, without refusing to help. That is a good idea, but it costs money, because lawyers charge for their time. And some clients, such as a criminal defendant under pressure, will not be in the mood to listen.

What the statement claims

"Pepper proposes moral dialogue between lawyer and client as a way to temper the dangers of amoral lawyering. Is this a real answer?" (Q102)

This is a question, not a statement, but it has an assumption built in: that the amoral role needs a repair, and that dialogue might be it. Your answer is that dialogue helps only in part, and that Thunder would not see it as a repair at all.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Moral dialogue is a real answer, but only in part. Pepper lets the lawyer raise moral concerns and even try to persuade the client. Since the client still decides, this does not impair the client's autonomy. Pepper calls the lawyer in this mode a moral educator: someone who neither judges nor polices the client.
  2. Pepper admits its limits himself. Dialogue is expensive, because the lawyer's time is what the client pays for. And it needs a receptive client. Pepper says a criminal defendant will be less open to it than a corporate officer.
  3. So dialogue works where it looks like Thunder's prudence and tact. For Thunder's lawyer, raising the moral side of a matter is simply part of being a good lawyer. It is ordinary practice, not a repair to a faulty role.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pepper's own limits on dialogue
LimitWhat it means
CostThe lawyer's time is what the client pays for, so every moral conversation is billed.
ReceptivenessA criminal defendant will be less open to dialogue than a corporate officer.
DistancePepper adds that the wider the cultural and economic gap between lawyer and client, the less likely dialogue becomes.
Client expectationsLiu doubts that many clients would welcome it, since moral talk is not what they think they are paying for†.

None of these makes dialogue worthless. Together they show why it cannot carry the whole weight of Pepper's model.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Moral dialogue is a real answer only in part. It lets the lawyer act as a moral educator, raising concerns and even persuading, without judging or policing the client, who still decides. But its limits are Pepper's own: it is expensive, and a criminal defendant will be less open to it than a corporate officer. So dialogue works where it matches Thunder's prudence and tact. For Thunder's lawyer it is ordinary practice, not a repair to a role that has lost its moral input.

610.4 Compartments

🧩 Practise 10.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.4 Compartments (word for word)
10.4 Compartments soldiers, separate compartments, chaos, no one can say objectively
  1. [Lawyers are like soldiers] is the "dramatic bifurcation" Thunder rejects: merely pointing to the role does not explain it.
  2. Pepper fears the moralising lawyer turns policeman, judge or deceiver; for Thunder the lawyer stays accountable as a human being.
  3. So [no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do] overstates: roles are not wholly idiosyncratic, and prudence applies the virtues (4.7).
  • QUALIFY Thunder accepts role morality: the police officer owes courtesy and compassion, not cold mechanical precision. But a role is no "pocket universe"†: the lawyer interprets it constantly by the good life, where Pepper steps outside only in extremes†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Lawyers are like soldiers: they serve the system and don't pick which orders to follow." Thunder says that view splits a person in two, with one moral person at home and a different "professional" at work. That split cannot be right. Saying "I was just doing my job" explains nothing, because the job itself has to be justified.

What the statement claims

"Lawyers are like soldiers: they serve a system larger than themselves and have no business picking which lawful instructions to obey. A lawyer who brings his private virtues into the office soon becomes a judge, a policeman or a deceiver, and the system descends into chaos. Professional and private morality are therefore rightly kept in separate compartments. The lawyer still has room enough outside his cases to be a good person, if not always a comfortable one; and in any event, no one can say objectively what a 'virtuous' lawyer would do." (Q97)

The statement says personal and professional morality belong in separate compartments, and that mixing them leads to chaos. It ends with a sceptical flourish: no one can say objectively what a "virtuous" lawyer would do. Each step sounds modest, but together they amount to a theory of roles that Thunder rejects.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Lawyers are like soldiers" is the sharp split Thunder rejects. Thunder calls it a dramatic bifurcation: one moral self at home, another at work. Merely pointing to the role does not explain it. A role has to be justified by what it is for, and asking that is already a moral question.
  2. Pepper fears one danger, and Thunder answers it. Pepper worries that a lawyer who moralises will turn into the client's policeman, judge or deceiver. Thunder replies that the lawyer simply stays accountable as a human being. That does not make the lawyer a busybody. It changes how the lawyer understands the role, not how often the lawyer interferes.
  3. So "no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do" overstates. Roles are not wholly idiosyncratic. They come with shared purposes and standards of excellence, and prudence applies the virtues to the case in hand. The sceptical claim also defeats itself, since demanding that the lawyer stay in the compartment is a moral demand (4.7).

The extra line, explained

  • QUALIFY · Thunder accepts role morality. Thunder does not say one set of rules applies regardless of role. His example is a police officer who is insulted in the street. Because the officer represents the law, the officer owes courtesy and compassion, not cold mechanical precision, and is more restrained than in private life. But a role is no pocket universe†. Thunder's lawyer interprets the role constantly in the light of a good life, as a parent does, while Pepper's lawyer steps outside the role only in extreme cases†.

Thunder accepts role morality: a police officer owes courtesy and compassion, not cold mechanical precision. Yet a role is no pocket universe, and the lawyer interprets it constantly in the light of a good life. The claim that no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do therefore overstates, since roles are not wholly idiosyncratic and prudence applies the virtues.

710.5 Rules only

🧩 Practise 10.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.5 Rules only (word for word)
10.5 Rules only conduct rules, nothing more nothing less, as written, too vague
  1. [If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it] mistakes a floor for the whole: conduct rules presuppose a purpose (16).
  2. Thunder calls codes "legalistic": mostly general rules, not aspirations; the lawyer's function is not slavish observance of the letter.
  3. So [serving justice is too vague] overstates: Thunder admits disagreement on particular cases, but norms "exploited" against justice are "subverted".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"A lawyer's ethics are the conduct rules. If no rule forbids it, do it." But rules are written to serve a purpose, such as a fair process and a court that is not misled. Using the rules to defeat their own purpose is not following them. It is subverting them. The rules are the floor of a lawyer's ethics, not the whole building.

What the statement claims

"A Singapore lawyer's ethical duties are found in the Professional Conduct Rules, the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code: nothing more, nothing less. If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it." (Q98)

The statement treats the written rules as a complete code. It adds that the rules should be read as written, not by their spirit, and that talk of "serving justice" is too vague to guide anyone. It is tempting because rules look certain and justice looks contested.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it" mistakes the floor for the whole. The conduct rules set the minimum. They also presuppose a purpose: rules on not misleading the court and on fairness to unrepresented persons exist because fair process matters (16.4). This is distinction 1.3(3), floor v ceiling.
  2. Thunder calls codes legalistic. Codes are mostly general rules, not aspirations. The lawyer's function is not slavish observance of the letter of the law, nor slavish obedience to the client. It is to further justice, public order and the rule of law.
  3. So "serving justice is too vague" overstates. Thunder admits that lawyers will disagree about particular cases. But when the rules are exploited to defeat justice, they are subverted, and a good lawyer can recognise that without a formula.

The linked lines, explained

The block has no tagged lines of its own, but three lines elsewhere on the sheet belong here.

  • Singapore bank 16.4 · the conduct rules†. Pepper's limit is the law binding the lawyer, and that includes the enforced conduct rules, such as fairness to unrepresented persons, not misleading the court and disclosing adverse authority. Breaching them is unlawful, not merely immoral. So the more robust those rules are, the less the Pepper v Thunder debate changes what a lawyer actually does†.
  • Card 14.1 · Fish. Practice marshals doctrine inside a purposive enterprise, shaped by a vision of how the state may use its monopoly of legalised violence. Rules recited without that sense of purpose are, in Fish's phrase, an empty gesture (2.6).
  • CONCEDE · virtue under-determines cases. Thunder admits there will be disagreement on particular cases, and that integrity is rarely if ever fully achieved. Concede that he guides character more than cases, then add your answer: hard cases go to dialogue first, with refusal only at the extremes (14.24).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Floor v ceiling with the conduct rules
SituationPepper's lawyerThunder's lawyer
A rule requires fairness to an unrepresented personBound. The rule is part of the law, his limit.Bound, and sees the rule as part of what the role is for.
A rule forbids misleading the courtBound, for the same reason.Bound, for the same reason.
A rule requires disclosing adverse authorityBound.Bound.
No rule covers it, such as pleading a time bar against a debt the client admitsFree to proceed. Dialogue is optional.Weighs whether the win would be just. Dialogue comes first.

The first three rows show why robust rules narrow the gap. The last row shows why the rules can never be the whole story: the floor runs out exactly where the hard cases begin.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it" mistakes a floor for the whole: the conduct rules presuppose a purpose, such as a fair process and a court that is not misled. Thunder calls codes legalistic, mostly general rules rather than aspirations, and denies that the lawyer's function is slavish observance of the letter. The charge that serving justice is too vague overstates. Thunder admits disagreement on particular cases, but norms exploited against justice are subverted. Even Pepper's limit includes the enforced conduct rules, so the more robust they are, the less the debate changes what a lawyer does.

810.6 Guilty client

🧩 Practise 10.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.6 Guilty client (word for word)
10.6 Guilty client acquittal, believed guilty, technicality, refuse any part
  1. [Winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty is wrong] fails: defending the accused is the role working.
  2. Thunder's lawyer serves by ensuring the accused a fair trial; for Pepper, full access is clearer and more dramatic in criminal cases.
  3. So [he must refuse any part] fits an unjust system, or invoking an intolerably unjust rule such as a racist statute, but not a just rule's unjust outcome† (10.11).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Defending someone you think is guilty is not wrong. The system works by making the prosecution prove its case, so the defence lawyer is the system doing its job. Refusing to take part fits only if the whole system is unjust, or the law being used is monstrous, like a racist statute. It does not fit just because one particular result seems unfair.

What the statement claims

"A defence lawyer who wins an acquittal for a client he believes guilty commits a moral wrong, whatever the conduct rules say. Nor can any lawyer hide behind 'the system' when the outcome or the law itself is unjust: whether the only evidence was obtained by police coercion or the statute discriminates by race, he must refuse to take any part in the case." (Q99)

The statement runs three different situations together: a client believed guilty, evidence obtained by police coercion, and a statute that discriminates by race. It says the lawyer must refuse any part in all of them. The block pulls them apart.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty is not a wrong. Defending the accused is the role working, not failing. The lawyer is not the judge of guilt, and the prosecution must prove its case.
  2. Both theorists agree here, for different reasons. Thunder's lawyer serves justice by ensuring the accused a fair trial. For Pepper, the case for full access to the law is clearer and more dramatic in criminal cases than anywhere else.
  3. So "he must refuse any part" fits only two situations. It fits an unjust legal system, or a case that would require invoking an intolerably unjust rule, such as a racist statute. It does not fit a just rule that produces an unjust outcome in one case†. That is Liu's order of questions, taught in 10.11.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Q99's three examples, sorted
Example in the statementWhere is the injustice?Response
Winning an acquittal for a client believed guiltyNowhere yet. The trial decides guilt, not the lawyer.Defend fully. The fair trial is the role working.
The only evidence was obtained by police coercionIn one outcome of a just rule, the rule excluding coerced evidenceDefend fully. A just rule's unjust outcome is no reason to refuse†.
The statute discriminates by raceIn the rule itselfRefusal fits. Radbruch's formula may deny the statute legal character (8.8).
⚠ TRAP
Do not lump the three together

Q99 treats coerced evidence and a racist statute as the same kind of problem. They are not. One is an unjust outcome of a just rule, the other an unjust rule (distinction 1.3(10)†). Blanket refusal would also abandon the accused, which ignores Thunder's own point that serving justice includes a fair trial.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty is not a moral wrong, because defending the accused is the role working. Thunder's lawyer serves justice by ensuring the accused a fair trial, and for Pepper the case for full access to law is clearest in criminal cases. The demand that the lawyer refuse any part fits only an unjust system, or a case that would invoke an intolerably unjust rule such as a racist statute. It does not fit a just rule's unjust outcome, such as the exclusion of a coerced confession. The statement's error is to treat an unjust outcome, an unjust rule and an unjust system as one problem.

910.7 Juniors

🧩 Practise 10.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.7 Juniors (word for word)
10.7 Juniors junior lawyers, lawful instructions, superiors, public officials
  1. [Juniors following lawful instructions bear no moral responsibility] fails: legality settles what may be done, not who answers for it.
  2. Thunder's "lazy lawyer" tends to take for granted the standards of peers and superiors; courage resists the pressure to conform.
  3. So [the junior] shares responsibility: raise it in dialogue first, and refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others.
  • Mei (Q100, Q103 only): pleading the time bar is lawful, yet the win may be unjust, so dialogue comes first. The concealed defect endangers the public, so she may object (10.1).
  • JUDGE Kennedy's five courses are a judge's (12.4; 15.10), not a junior's.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A junior lawyer is told by a partner to do something legal but unfair. "I was only following instructions" does not fully let her off. Being legal tells you what you may do, not who is responsible for doing it. The junior should raise her concern first, and refuse only if the instruction would seriously harm other people.

What the statement claims

"Junior lawyers and public officials who carry out lawful instructions they believe to be unethical bear no moral responsibility; that lies with those who give the instructions." (Q100)

The statement moves responsibility up the chain of command, so that only the person giving the order answers for it. It is tempting because juniors have little power and the instruction is lawful. The block separates two questions the statement merges: what may be done, and who answers for doing it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Legality settles what may be done, not who answers for it. An instruction can be lawful and still wrong to carry out. The junior who carries it out is acting, and so shares the responsibility.
  2. Thunder's lazy lawyer conforms. Thunder describes a lawyer who tends to take for granted the standards and expectations of peers and superiors. The virtue that resists this is courage, the strength to withstand the pressure to conform.
  3. So the junior shares responsibility, and should act in order. First raise the concern in dialogue, with the partner and, through the partner, with the client. Refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others.

The extra lines, explained

  • Mei (Q100, Q103 only). The practice problem gives a junior two issues. Pleading the time bar is lawful, yet winning that way may be unjust, so dialogue comes first. The concealed product defect endangers the public, so she may object, which is the extreme case of 10.1. Use Mei only for those two questions.
  • JUDGE · Kennedy's five courses. Kennedy describes what a judge can do when the law conflicts with how the judge wants the case to come out: go along while denouncing the law, withdraw and leave the work to another, decide openly on what the law should be, use an implausible legal argument, or find facts known to be false (12.4, 15.10). These are a judge's options, not a junior lawyer's. Citing them for Mei confuses the roles.

For public officials, the same reasoning sits in 12.5: officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank, and merely pointing to the role explains nothing.

Mei's two problems, side by side
The time-barred debtThe concealed defect
Lawful?Yes. A limitation defence is a lawful plea.Concealing a public danger is a different matter from pleading a defence.
Who is harmed?A small family business loses a debt it is owed.Members of the public could be injured.
Pepper's lawyerPleads it. Dialogue is optional, and the client decides.An extreme case: objection is available.
Thunder's lawyerWeighs whether the win would be just, and raises it in dialogue first.Acts as a human being, not merely an employee.
The sheet's answerDialogue first.She may object (10.1).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The claim that juniors following lawful instructions bear no moral responsibility fails, because legality settles what may be done, not who answers for it. Thunder warns against the lazy lawyer who takes for granted the standards of peers and superiors, and he names courage as the virtue that resists the pressure to conform. The junior therefore shares responsibility. She should raise her concern in dialogue first and refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others. So Mei may plead the time bar after raising it, but the concealed defect, which endangers the public, is the kind of extreme case in which she may object.

1010.8 Lawyers' training and outlook

🧩 Practise 10.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.8 Lawyers' training and outlook (word for word)
10.8 Lawyers' training and outlook conscience at the door, law school, argue any side, theory isn't relevant
  1. [Leave your conscience at the door] describes an outlook lawyers are trained into; it does not justify it.
  2. Pepper reports "all realists now" as a comment often heard from contemporary law professors.
  3. So [theory isn't relevant] is itself an unexamined theory: the realist lawyer already advises "breach as cost".
  • Kennedy: progressive-minded people, fearing conversion without choice, ask whether law school will warp their minds.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Leave your conscience at the door" is not a theory lawyers chose. It is an attitude law school trains into them. Pepper reports that law professors often say they are all realists now. So the claim that theory is irrelevant to lawyers is itself a theory, just one that nobody has examined.

What the statement claims

"Lawyers must leave their conscience at the door; law school teaches you to argue any side; theory isn't relevant to practice."

The statement moves from how lawyers are trained to how they ought to work. It is tempting because it matches experience: students really are taught to argue either side. The block shows that the training explains the outlook without justifying it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Leave your conscience at the door" describes an outlook; it does not justify it. Lawyers are trained into this attitude, which explains why so many hold it. It does not show that the attitude is right.
  2. Pepper reports the training at work. He notes that "all realists now" is a comment often heard from contemporary law professors. Law school teaches law as a prediction of what officials will do, which is the realist view of 10.2.
  3. So "theory isn't relevant" is itself an unexamined theory. The realist lawyer who tells a client that a breach of contract is simply a cost, the damages a court may award, is already acting on a theory of what law is.

The extra line, explained

  • Kennedy · will law school warp my mind? Kennedy reports that progressive-minded students fear being converted without choice, and so ask whether law school will warp their minds. Use it to show that the outlook in the statement is a product of training, which is exactly why it needs examining.

The Core card makes the same point for every lawyer. Lawyers rarely cite theory, and most cases are easy, but every lawyer acts on a theory of what law is and what the role permits. The only choice is between an examined and an unexamined theory (13.4, Q3).

Find the hidden theory
The lawyer says…The theory hiding insideWhere it is tested
"Breach of contract is just a cost."Law is a prediction of what officials will do: legal realism.10.2, 10.8
"If no rule forbids it, I may do it."The written rules are the whole of a lawyer's ethics.10.5
"I'm just doing my job."The role explains itself and needs no justification.10.4, 10.10
"The client decides; I don't judge."Client autonomy outweighs the lawyer's moral judgement, which is Pepper's moral argument.10.1
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

"Leave your conscience at the door" describes an outlook lawyers are trained into; it does not justify it. Pepper reports that "all realists now" is a comment often heard from contemporary law professors, and Kennedy notes that progressive students, fearing conversion without choice, ask whether law school will warp their minds. The claim that theory is irrelevant is therefore itself an unexamined theory. The realist lawyer who advises that breach is merely a cost is already acting on a view of what law is. The choice is never between theory and no theory, but between an examined theory and an unexamined one.

1110.9 Transactional

🧩 Practise 10.9 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.9 Transactional (word for word)
10.9 Transactional transactional work, no opposing counsel, no judge
  1. In litigation, especially criminal defence, the law may allow more: implying a truthful witness lied brings no liability; similar half-truths selling [a termite-ridden house] may be misrepresentation.
  2. So [the statement] holds in part: realism is likelier from a lawyer advising a large corporate enterprise, where no judge or opposing counsel checks the client.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In court, the other side's lawyer and the judge check what you do. In a deal, such as selling a house or drafting a contract, there is often nobody checking. So some people say the lawyer must supply the moral check. That is partly true, because realism is most tempting exactly where nobody is watching.

What the statement claims

"In transactional work, there is no opposing counsel and no judge to check the client. The lawyer must therefore supply the moral scrutiny that the adversarial system would otherwise provide." (Q101)

The statement assumes that the adversarial system does the moral work in court, so the lawyer must take it over outside court. Pepper himself accepts the premise that most lawyering happens where courts never enter, with no judge and often no second advocate. That is why he grounds the lawyer's role in first-class citizenship, not in the adversary system.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The law asks different things in different settings. In litigation, especially criminal defence, the law may allow more. A lawyer who implies that a truthful witness lied faces no liability. Yet similar half-truths used to sell a termite-ridden house may be misrepresentation.
  2. So the statement holds in part. The realist approach, which treats law as costs and predictions, is likelier from a lawyer advising a large corporate enterprise, where no judge or opposing counsel checks the client. With fewer outside checks, more rests on the lawyer's own judgement.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Same half-truth, two settings
SettingThe half-truthLegal resultWho checks it?
Criminal trialImplying that a truthful witness liedNo liabilityThe judge and opposing counsel
Selling a houseSimilar half-truths about termite damageMay be misrepresentationNobody at the time of the sale

The same conduct is treated differently because the setting differs. Outside court, the law itself draws a tighter line, but nobody is there to enforce it in the moment. That is where the lawyer's own judgement, and Thunder's prudence, matter most.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement holds in part. In litigation, especially criminal defence, the law may allow more: implying that a truthful witness lied brings no liability, while similar half-truths used to sell a termite-ridden house may be misrepresentation. Realism is likelier from a lawyer advising a large corporate enterprise, where no judge or opposing counsel checks the client. But the lawyer need not become the client's judge. Above the legal floor, the right response is Thunder's prudence and Pepper's own moral dialogue, with objection only in extreme cases.

1210.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view

🧩 Practise 10.10 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view (word for word)
10.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view why we hold such views, purpose of law, hired gun, just do your job
  1. Thunder traces the amoral view's appeal largely to the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality.
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make role-based reasons morally suspect, prudence, the profession's bread and butter, amoral, and right conduct separate from the good life.
  3. Realism gives the view a congenial philosophical home; against both, law is intended, ultimately if not always immediately, for ends naturally good for man.
  • CONCEDE I concede that a diagnosis is no refutation; arguably the likelier source is an intuition Thunder shares, that a lawyer should not substitute personal judgment for the client's†, which 10.1 must answer.
  • QUALIFY Same act, different reasons†: a Thunder lawyer may disclose a live victim as part of the role, or because duties as a human being trump it; a Pepper lawyer may too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is mindset, not necessarily outcome; positive law sets its width.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Thunder asks why so many people believe lawyers should be hired guns. He blames two hidden influences. One is a philosophy that treats morality as following universal rules, so the craft of good judgement starts to look amoral. The other is legal realism, which says law is just what officials do. Against both, Thunder says law exists for real human goods like justice, and a good lawyer serves them.

What the statement claims

"Just focus on doing your job: the lawyer is a hired gun, and the purpose of law is the client's."

The statement assumes that the lawyer's role needs no deeper justification and that law has no purpose of its own. Thunder's answer is unusual: before arguing back, he explains why so many people find this view attractive.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Thunder explains why the amoral view appeals. He traces its appeal largely to two unwitting collaborators: legal realism and neo-Kantian morality. Neither set out to defend the hired gun, but together they make it seem natural.
  2. Neo-Kantianism makes the lawyer's working morality invisible. It treats morality as universal rules. That makes reasons arising from a role, such as duties to this particular client, look morally suspect. It makes prudence, the bread and butter of the profession, look like mere technique. And it separates right conduct from living a good life.
  3. Realism gives the amoral view a congenial home, and Thunder answers both with law's purpose. If law is only a prediction of what officials will do, there is nothing for the lawyer to serve except the client. Against both influences, Thunder holds that law is intended, ultimately if not always immediately, for ends naturally good for man, such as justice and public order. That is the natural-teleological view.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · a diagnosis is no refutation. Explaining why people hold a view does not show that the view is false. Liu also doubts the neo-Kantian half of the diagnosis and suggests a likelier source: the common-sense intuition that a lawyer should not substitute personal judgement for the client's†. Thunder shares that intuition, since he is not defending a moral busybody. Concede the point, and answer the intuition with 10.1.
  • QUALIFY · same act, different reasons†. A lawyer who learns of a live victim may disclose under either theory. Thunder's lawyer may disclose as part of the role, because a good lawyer serves law's purposes, or because duties as a human being trump the role. Pepper's lawyer may disclose too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is one of mindset, not necessarily of outcome (distinction 1.3(18)), and the positive law sets its width.
⚠ TRAP
"Just focus on the law" is the target, not Thunder's view

Thunder's line about simply focusing on the law voices the amoral view he rejects, as does the practice question's call to just do your job (card 14.24, TRAP). Quote it in your hook as Thunder's caricature of the opposing view, never as his own position.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Thunder traces the appeal of "just do your job" largely to the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality. Neo-Kantianism makes role-based reasons morally suspect, treats prudence, the profession's bread and butter, as amoral, and separates right conduct from the good life. Realism then gives the amoral view a congenial home, since law becomes a prediction with no purpose of its own. Against both, Thunder holds that law is intended, ultimately if not always immediately, for ends naturally good for man. I concede that a diagnosis is no refutation, and that the likelier source is an intuition Thunder shares, that a lawyer should not substitute personal judgement for the client's.

1310.11 Liu's three scenarios

🧩 Practise 10.11 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 10.11 Three scenarios† (word for word)
10.11 Three scenarios† racist statute, coerced evidence, hide behind the system, institutional wrong
  1. Ask in order†: is the system by and large just; if so, is this rule intolerably unjust; if not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question†: is the institution justified by truth-finding, dignity or replacement costs?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than excused; Pepper names both as adversary-system defences.
  • Law is Pepper's limit: if the RF denies a racist statute legal character, even his lawyer may refuse.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When something feels unjust, ask where the injustice lies. Is the whole legal system rotten? Is this particular law monstrous? Or is the law fine, and only this one result unfair, like a guilty person going free because a confession was forced out of him and so excluded? The right response is different for each.

What the statement claims

"Nor can any lawyer hide behind 'the system' when the outcome or the law itself is unjust." (Q99)

The statement denies that a lawyer can ever plead "the system made me do it". Pepper's model relies on exactly that plea, since he calls a bad result of the lawyer's proper work an institutional wrong, not a personal one. The block gives you an order of questions for testing the plea.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Ask in order: system, rule, outcome†. Is the legal system by and large just? If so, is this particular rule intolerably unjust? If not, is it only this outcome that is unjust?
  2. Blaming the institution only moves the question†. Pepper says a bad result of the lawyer's proper work is the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's. But an institutional wrong is more acceptable only if the institution is justified. Liu offers three candidate justifications: the system is best at finding the truth, it respects human dignity, or replacing it would cost too much.
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good, rather than merely excused. Replacement costs show only that we are stuck with the system. Pepper himself names truth-finding and dignity as defences of the adversary system, so he has the materials for the stronger answer.

The extra line, explained

  • Law is Pepper's limit. Pepper says client autonomy is limited by the law, not by the lawyer's morality. So if Radbruch's formula denies a racist statute legal character, there is no law left for the lawyer to give access to, and even Pepper's lawyer may refuse (8.8). Core card B adds that the three scenarios are a test, not a side: they belong to neither Pepper nor Thunder, and either can run them (13.4).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Whether a lawyer may hide behind the system depends on where the injustice lies, so I ask in order: is the system by and large just, is this rule intolerably unjust, or is only this outcome unjust? Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question to whether the institution is justified, by truth-finding, by dignity or merely by the cost of replacing it. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than merely excused, and Pepper himself names both as defences of the adversary system. And since law is Pepper's limit, if Radbruch's formula denies a racist statute legal character, even his lawyer may refuse.

14Putting it together: Practice Q95

"A lawyer who turns away a client, or refuses to help him do something lawful, because he finds it distasteful abuses his position. The law already marks out what society will not tolerate; above that floor the client's conscience, not the lawyer's, must govern, for the client can neither work the legal machinery alone nor check the advice he is given. Even when a murder suspect reveals where he hid the bodies of his two victims and one turns out to be still alive, the lawyer must keep that confidence. A lawyer who imposes his own morals denies his client equal access to justice."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Pepper and Thunder.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

This statement is almost Pepper's own case for the lawyer's amoral role, and the question is whether it survives Pepper's own exception. It does not survive the hidden bodies. I make three claims. First, Pepper is right that screening clients by a lawyer's taste threatens equal access to the law. Second, the law is a floor, not a ceiling, and Pepper himself keeps conscientious objection open for extreme cases such as a living victim. Third, spotting those cases requires a lawyer who weighs morality throughout, so Thunder's good person as lawyer differs from Pepper's more in mindset than in outcome.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Pepper steelmanned (10.1, 15.11). Law is a public good, autonomy is a moral good, and the client cannot work the legal machinery alone, so screening means rule by an oligarchy of lawyers. Then Pepper's dilemma: conduct bad enough should be made unlawful, and otherwise one lawyer's conscience is happenstance.
  2. The floor and the live victim (10.1, 10.5). "Abuses" and "denies" are moral premises. Objection is rarely exercised but may reveal the live victim. Pepper never defines "extreme", so his lawyer weighs morality throughout. Then inequality and its three replies.
  3. Thunder and the gap (10.4, 10.10). A role is no pocket universe, and merely pointing to it explains nothing. Same act, different reasons: both lawyers may disclose. Self-critique: Thunder's virtue under-determines hard cases (1.4), so dialogue comes first.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels. Pepper defends the role on moral grounds and keeps objection, which needs a lawyer who weighs morality throughout, while Thunder accepts role morality and that no legal system is perfect. The live question is how often conscience may override the role. The answer is rarely and openly, after dialogue, and certainly where keeping a confidence would leave a living victim to die.

ℹ NOTE
One-sentence repair

If you want to show the examiner what a defensible version would look like, use the Core card's repaired line (13.4): a lawyer serves the client within the law, but the law is a floor, with dialogue above it and refusal only at the extremes.

15Recap

Archetype 10 on one card
▤ Sections 10.1–10.11
  1. 1Pepper's floor and dilemma: choice of client is troubling only if it forecloses access, and spotting extreme cases needs moral attention (10.1, 15.11).
  2. 2Effluent: realism empties Pepper's limit, and the example is lopsided (10.2).
  3. 3Dialogue is real but partial: costly, and it needs a receptive client (10.3).
  4. 4No compartments: pointing to the role does not explain it (10.4).
  5. 5The rules are a floor with a purpose, and exploiting them subverts them (10.5).
  6. 6Defending the guilty is the role working. Refusal fits only an unjust system or an intolerable rule (10.6).
  7. 7Juniors share responsibility: dialogue first, refusal for serious harm to others (10.7).
  8. 8"Conscience at the door" is trained, not justified, and is an unexamined theory (10.8).
  9. 9Transactional work: realism tempts most where nobody checks the client (10.9).

🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a building. The ground floor is the law, including the conduct rules, and no lawyer may go below it. Above it are the rooms where lawyers actually work: prudence and dialogue with the client. There is also a fire exit, conscientious objection, clearly marked, rarely used, and opened only in an emergency such as a living victim. Pepper and Thunder work in the same building and often walk out of the same door. Pepper thinks the fire exit leads outside the building. Thunder thinks it was always part of the building's design.

LESSON 11 · ARCHETYPE 11 · ABOUT 83 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 51 QUESTIONS

Constitution and judicial role

⚡ BIG IDEA

A supreme written Constitution relocates the natural law v positivism debate rather than settling it. Courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.

ARCHETYPE 11 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
11 Constitution and judicial role
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] is [overstated]: the Constitution relocates, not settles, the NLT v LP debate; courts should presume validity save at intolerable injustice.
Intro [The statement] assumes a supreme, written Constitution settles what law is. It does not: Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted, and Part 4's "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal" are contested moral terms. I [qualify] it: courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.
Steelman: Parliament decides The best case for [the statement] is that Singapore has already decided. Art 4 makes the Constitution supreme; on Rajeevan (HC 1998; TSH), the legislature rightfully determines individual rights absent specific guarantees; and in 2022 change came through Parliament (Art 156). This shows that judges should presume validity. It does not show [that Part 4's open terms need no theory, or that intolerable injustice must stand].
Steelman: Part 4 speaks morally The best case for [the statement] is that Part 4's terms are moral: equality is empty without a higher moral law, and a natural-law judge refusing manifest injustice is faithful to law (TSH). This shows that reading Part 4 takes moral judgment. It does not show [that NLT wins]: an LP may follow moral terms outward†.
11.1 Supremacy Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text
  1. Art 4 makes [the written Constitution] supreme, but a master rule exists only because it is accepted; it cannot be inferred from the text alone (TSH).
  2. TSH holds that LP sheds no light on Part 4's morally loaded concepts, and doubts that a state which does not give life should define person, life and liberty.
  3. So [the Constitution sets the criteria of validity] only formally: Part 4's moral terms force a choice of school (11.2, 11.3).
  • QUALIFY Teo Soh Lung (HC) rejected basic features, which YVK (2015) left open; TSH relies on equal moral worth: even a genocide amendment falls to the RF.
  • TRAP That the Constitution includes morality does not mean NLT wins: one may be an LP happy that morality is now positive law†. TSH's own thesis is that constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  • CONCEDE I concede that in practice the master-rule point may not lead to much; what matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law†.
11.2 Art 9(1) "law" validly passed; fair trial only; invent rights; caning; international norms
  1. Reading "law" as [whatever is validly passed] begs the question: what breaches Art 9 would not be in force (TSH).
  2. On my application of TSH's test, [caning for third-time littering] survives the other readings and falls under the RF only if broad historical consensus condemns it; arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at [fair-trial rules] is a choice of theory, not text; the RF adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.
  • FOR YVK (2015): courts cannot make from natural law a right absent from the Constitution, so none against caning (no ruling on natural law's view of it; George: 12.1).
  • AGAINST TSH: the CA targeted US substantive due process, the antithesis of natural law theory. LMS: no privacy right; Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and detention; YVK (2015)† adds unlawful use of force.
  • STEELMAN Richer readings risk making each judge a law unto himself. Reply: for TSH, letting manifest injustice stand defeats certainty's very purpose.
  • "Law" has four readings. Validly passed: Jabar dictum; YVK (2010)†: not about constitutionality; Nguyen read it to include constitutional validity. Natural justice: Ong Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open; YVK (2015)†: procedural; TEH (HC): Art 12 imports none. Not absurd or arbitrary: YVK (2010)† suggested it; TSH: TEH's plea failed on evidence, not principle. International law: Nguyen: statute beats custom; YVK (2010)†: read consistently where possible; no inhuman-punishment bar adopted.
11.3 Art 12 intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers
  1. For LMS (CA), [an intelligible line rationally related to the object] usually suffices, since courts are not "mini-legislatures".
  2. On [a double fee for left-handed drivers], the CA asks if the line rationally serves its aim; the HC would also void an "inherently bad" aim.
  3. So [judges who probe the object become legislators] overstates: the RF voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness.
  • FOR LMS (CA): a threshold test with no free-standing legitimacy review; Wednesbury rejected; use Art 12(2).
  • QUALIFY This is not cleanly LP v NLT: a limited element of illegitimacy remains, since extreme illogicality or incoherence fails a limb, and a women-driving ban might fail limb two; TSH calls the test natural law at work.
  • AGAINST For TSH the question is which differences are morally significant, so moral arguments cannot be dismissed as "extra-legal" under Art 12(1); without a higher moral law, laws treating everyone "equally badly" pass†.
11.4 Four walls within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality
  1. [Reading the Constitution primarily within its own four walls], Colin Chan's LP approach† (TSH), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau charitably, TSH finds fairness universal, though its manifestation varies with local conditions.
  3. So [universal morality] need not mean foreign values, if confined to manifest injustice (11.5).
  • CONCEDE I concede that higher law cuts both ways: a "true-blue Thomist" may get judges with a very different view of dignity (Lawrence; TSH), so I defend only a narrow trigger.
  • QUALIFY Arguably TSH's LP is too narrow†: LP mandates little but is compatible with more. Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, as commercial reasonableness imports trade practice; a purposive LP may read the Constitution as guarding individuals. TSH: reference to natural law is then "mandatory"; can such a judge stop at popular morality?
11.5 Who decides (courts) for Parliament, not the courts; ballot box; unelected judges; activism
  1. I accept that [contested rights are for Parliament], but only until Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met (TSH).
  2. That threshold (BHC: 15.13) is met for genocide and slavery, not for the laws voided in Roe and Obergefell, nor for Women's Charter s 12 (catch: 8.5).
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law for injustice] goes too far: rubber-stamping is a vice too (12.2), and intolerable injustice must fall.
  • QUALIFY LMS left Hart v Devlin to the Legislature (16); TSH: only if no constitutional right was at stake.
  • LEGISLATOR Where objective morality is unclear, a deliberative democracy can take a stand through its legislature (12.3).
  • Asking who decides returns us to where we started, but wiser†.
11.6 Art 156 repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
  1. In 2022 [change through Parliament] came: s 377A went, and Art 156, a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism (TSH), shielded man-woman marriage laws from Part 4.
  2. So [leaving it to Parliament] moved the question rather than removed it: a two-thirds majority (Art 5(2)) put those laws beyond Part 4 (11.7).
  • FOR Shanmugam: courts can only make binary decisions (Hansard, 29 Nov 2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: repeal was for risk, not unconstitutionality, so differentiating laws are not incoherent in principle. After UKM, s 377A failed to do its work, which might explain the change of tactic.
11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception
  1. [The statement] is itself a legal philosophy, too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion: law is not morality and must not supplant it.
  3. So [compliance always gives sufficient moral guidance] fails: law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.
  • Either way theory is needed: Hart's penumbral judge may have to reach beyond the law; Dworkin's finds the answer in community morality that is also law.
  • LAWYER Law sets the minimum, not the maximum (Devlin); Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): a "special two-thirds majority" amends most provisions (TSH), with no express core like Basic Law art 79(3) (implied limits: 11.1); so treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgment to whoever holds two-thirds.
  • STEELMAN Personal morality is subjective, so keep it out; and most cases are routine (9, Steelman: restraint). Reply: refusing manifest injustice is fidelity to law, not mere conscience (TSH), and subjectivism defeats itself (4.7).
  • Without exception: try an as-applied Art 15 challenge, though Art 15(4), read literally, lacks ICCPR art 18(3)'s "necessary" test (TSH; 12.6).
11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper
  1. [The people's acceptance] cannot alone found legitimacy: the framers' will begs the question why it still binds us, and treating non-revolt as acquiescence is artificial (TSH).
  2. Only co-equal dignity under natural law makes consent meaningful; NLT answers from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory†.
  3. The charge that [NLT defeats the separation of powers] fails: on the weak thesis morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and for TSH the legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms.
  • QUALIFY Two further answers: reason converges, so properly applied all three branches reach one result; and NLT v LP asks what law is, separation of powers how power is organised, so a democrat or a dictator could hold either†.
  • AGAINST An LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper; an NLT judge tests law against higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch). German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws†; whether Singapore judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis; against a sitting legislature it is untested†.
  • Basic features: Kesavananda (India) held some unamendable, those suggested including separation of powers and secular character (TSH); rejected here (11.1). Arguably NLT justifies them more easily†, as a good constitution has a telos some amendments destroy; TSH argues from natural law, not by second-guessing the framers' intention.
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]: Art 4 and Part 4 relocate, not settle, the NLT v LP debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution narrows the practical gap between NLT and LP judges and makes Radbruch's formula rarely needed, but leaves open the extreme case, our attitude to law, and who decides by what standard†. Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice; no clause relieves anyone of conscience.

1Start here: archetype 11 in plain English

Archetype 11 asks one question: now that Singapore has a supreme, written Constitution, is the old quarrel between legal positivism (LP) and natural law theory (NLT) over? Positivists say law is whatever a society's accepted sources make law. Natural lawyers say law must also answer to a higher moral law, so that a manifestly unjust "law" is not law. Art 4 makes the Constitution the supreme law and voids any law inconsistent with it, so it is tempting to think the text has settled the matter in favour of the positivists.

Exam statements in this family say yes, in several different ways. Judges need only check the text. "Law" in Art 9 means whatever Parliament validly passed. Equality asks only for a rational line. The Constitution must be read within its own four walls. Rights questions belong to Parliament. Your answer is the same every time. The Constitution relocates the debate. It does not settle it. Art 4 is supreme only because officials accept it, and Part 4's key words, "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal", are moral words that no judge can read without a theory.

The second half of your answer says what judges should do while the debate goes on. Courts should presume that laws are valid, and refuse only intolerable injustice. Tan Seow Hon (TSH), whose two articles anchor this archetype, supplies the test: Radbruch's threshold of injustice, proved by broad historical consensus.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
LP and NLTLegal positivism and natural law theory. LP identifies law by social facts, such as what officials accept. NLT says law must also conform to a higher law of morality.
Art 4 (with Art 162)Art 4 makes the Constitution the supreme law: a later law inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency. Art 162 says earlier laws are read so as to conform.
Master ruleHart's rule of recognition: the top rule that tells officials what counts as law. It exists because officials accept and use it, not because a text says so.
Part 4The fundamental liberties part of the Constitution. It includes Art 9 (life and liberty), Art 12 (equality) and Art 15 (religion).
Art 9(1)No one may be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law. The fight is over what "law" means there.
Art 12Everyone is equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection.
Reasonable classification testThe Art 12 test. Is the law's line between groups intelligible, and is it rationally connected to the law's object? Lim Meng Suang (LMS) used it to uphold s 377A.
Art 5(2)Two-thirds of elected MPs can amend most of the Constitution. Unlike Germany's Basic Law, it has no express core that no amendment may touch.
Art 156Added in 2022. Parliament may define and promote marriage, and laws based on the man–woman definition cannot be struck down under Part 4.
Radbruch formula (RF)A statute stops being law only when its injustice reaches an intolerable degree. Ordinary injustice leaves it valid.
Broad historical consensus (BHC)TSH's proof that Radbruch's threshold is met: long-lasting agreement across many jurisdictions, for the same reason, as with genocide and slavery.
Presumption of constitutionalityThe court's starting point that a statute is valid. The challenger must displace it.
Four wallsReading the Constitution from within itself and its local context, without importing outside values (Colin Chan).
Basic features doctrineIndia's idea that some parts of a constitution cannot be amended at all. Singapore's High Court rejected it.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the statement is overstated, because the Constitution relocates, not settles, the NLT v LP debate, and courts should presume validity save at intolerable injustice.

Put simply, the argument has moved house. Before a written Constitution, positivists and natural lawyers argued about what makes a rule law. Under the Constitution they argue about what "law" in Art 9 and "equal" in Art 12 mean, and about why Art 4 is supreme at all. Judges still need a theory to answer those questions. The second half of the Position tells judges how to behave while the argument continues: respect Parliament's laws in the ordinary case, and refuse only the intolerable.

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement assumes that a supreme, written Constitution settles what law is. It does not, for two reasons. Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted, and Part 4's words "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal" are contested moral terms. You then qualify the statement: courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.

The Conclusion gives your verdict. Art 4 and Part 4 relocate the debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution still does real work. Its moral content narrows the practical gap between natural-law and positivist judges, and its express grounds for striking laws down mean that Radbruch's formula is rarely needed. But it leaves three things open†. It does not say what a judge should do in an extreme case where the text gives no answer. It does not settle our basic attitude to law. And it does not say who should decide contested moral questions, Parliament or the judges, or by what standard, whether the majority's view, an overlapping consensus, or a universal morality open to all. Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice, and no clause relieves anyone of conscience.

The two steelmen

A strong answer states the best case for the other side before attacking it. Section 11 gives you two, because statements in this family can lean either way.

  • Steelman: Parliament decides. The best case for the statement is that Singapore has already decided. Art 4 makes the Constitution supreme. In Rajeevan (HC 1998), as TSH reports it, the court said the legislature rightfully determines individual rights where the Constitution gives no specific guarantee. And in 2022 change came through Parliament, with Art 156. This shows that judges should presume laws valid. It does not show that Part 4's open words need no theory, or that intolerable injustice must stand.
  • Steelman: Part 4 speaks morally. Use this one when the statement leans the other way, for example "the Constitution is full of moral words, so natural law has won". Its best case is TSH's. Equality is empty without a higher moral law, and a natural-law judge who refuses manifest injustice is being faithful to law, not just following private conscience. This shows that reading Part 4 takes moral judgement. It does not show that NLT wins, because a positivist judge may also follow moral words outward when the text points there†.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
11.1"Art 4 settled the debate. Judges just check the text."A master rule exists because it is accepted, not because it is written. And Part 4's moral words force a choice of theory.
11.2"'Law' in Art 9 means whatever Parliament validly passes."That reading goes in a circle. Stopping at fair-trial rules is a theory choice, and the Radbruch formula adds only a floor.
11.3"Equality asks only for an intelligible, rational line."Usually, for the Court of Appeal. But probing a law's aim does not make judges legislators, and equality needs a moral standard.
11.4"Read it within its four walls. No foreign values."Universal is not the same as foreign, if it is confined to manifest injustice.
11.5"Rights are for Parliament, not unelected judges."Yes, until Radbruch's threshold, proved by broad historical consensus. Rubber-stamping is a vice too.
11.6"Leave marriage to Parliament. Courts are blunt."That happened in 2022 with Art 156, but it moved the question rather than removed it.
11.7"With a Constitution, judges need no philosophy or personal morality."That claim is itself a philosophy. Law is a floor, not a ceiling.
11.8"Consent makes it legitimate. Natural law ruins the separation of powers."Consent means something only given equal dignity. Weak natural law overrides only at the extreme.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

The Constitution moves the debate without ending it, because its key words need a theory, so courts should presume validity and refuse only intolerable injustice.

2The big picture: does a written Constitution end the debate?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says: "Singapore has a written Constitution, and it is the supreme law. So we don't need philosophy. Just check the text." But the text uses words like "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal". To decide what they mean, a judge has to pick a theory. And why is the Constitution supreme in the first place? Because judges and officials treat it as supreme. A sentence in a book cannot make itself the top rule. So the Constitution moves the old argument into new rooms. It does not end it.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
TSH, Constitutional Jurisprudence (2009)No declaration of supremacy can settle the natural law v positivism debate. The Constitution's contested words force judges to choose a school, and constitutionalism itself affirms a higher law. This is the course reading (card 14.25).
TSH, Between Judicial Oligarchy and Parliamentary Supremacy (2016)How a natural lawyer would use Radbruch's formula under a written Constitution. Courts should presume laws constitutional unless the injustice reaches Radbruch's threshold, shown by broad historical consensus (card 14.26, framework 15.13).
HartThe master rule exists because officials accept it from the inside, as a standard (card 14.4). He also warns that law is not morality and must not replace it (11.7).
Radbruch and AlexyThe weak connection thesis. Positive law yields to morality only at intolerable injustice. Below that line, an unjust law is still law.
Robert GeorgeNatural law does not itself settle who should review laws. In a basically just regime, judges should respect the limits of their authority (12.1). The Court of Appeal cited him in YVK (2015).
LiuTSH's picture of positivism is too narrow. A positivist judge may follow the text outward to moral ideas when the text points there†.
Singapore's courtsMostly cautious. They presume laws constitutional, read natural justice in Art 9 as procedural, and treat Art 12 as a threshold test.

The Articles and cases you need

The Articles you need
▤ 16.1
  1. 1Art 4 (with Art 162): the Constitution is supreme. A later law inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency, and an earlier law is read so as to conform†. This does not mean Singapore chose LP (11.1).
  2. 2Art 5(2): two-thirds of elected MPs can amend most provisions. Singapore's High Court rejected the basic features doctrine in Teo Soh Lung, and the Court of Appeal left it open in YVK (2015).
  3. 3Art 9(1): no one may be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law. "Law" has four possible readings† (11.2).
  4. 4Art 12: all persons are equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection. Courts apply the reasonable classification test (11.3).
  5. 5Art 156 (2022): the law may define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote marriage, and Part 4 cannot void laws or executive acts based on the man–woman definition. That definition itself stays in statute (Interpretation Act s 2(1); Women's Charter s 12(1)), where a simple majority may change it†. TSH calls Art 156 a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism (11.6).
The cases you need
▤ 16.2
  1. 1Ong Ah Chuan (Privy Council): "law" in Art 9 includes the fundamental rules of natural justice. Whether it also demands substantive fairness was left open, and has since been narrowed (YVK 2015†).
  2. 2Jabar (CA 1995), in a dictum: a law validly passed binds, whether fair or not. This is the positivist reading, which YVK (2010) confined: it was not a statement about a statute's constitutionality†.
  3. 3Colin Chan (HC 1994): the Constitution is read within its own four walls, with national unity the paramount mandate. Liu calls this a positivist approach†.
  4. 4Lim Meng Suang (LMS, CA 2014): s 377A passes Art 12. Art 9 protects against unlawful deprivation of life and unlawful detention, not privacy. The Hart v Devlin debate is quintessentially for Parliament.
  5. 5Yong Vui Kong (YVK, CA 2010)†: Art 9 may exclude laws so absurd or arbitrary that the framers could not have meant them as law. This is a natural-law hook that stops short of the Radbruch formula.
  6. 6YVK (CA 2015), the caning case: courts cannot make a right out of whole cloth as natural law, so there is no right against caning. The court did not rule on what natural law says about caning, and it treated natural justice as procedural†.
  7. 7Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022): the challengers lacked standing. In obiter, Arts 9 and 14 were likely not breached, but the court was less definite about Art 12, where, on the reasonable classification approach taken in Syed Suhail, s 377A might fail. s 377A was unenforceable until the AG gave notice†.
  8. 8Taw Cheng Kong (CA 1998): a corruption law reaching citizens' acts abroad did not breach Art 12, since all were caught as a class. It states the presumption of constitutionality.
  9. 9Rajeevan (HC 1998), as TSH reports it: the legislature rightfully determines individual rights where there is no specific guarantee. Teo Soh Lung (HC): the basic features doctrine is rejected.

Key distinctions

  • The two approaches. TSH contrasts what each school implies under a Constitution. For the LP, law is identified by the master rule, a social fact, and the judge's job is to ensure compliance with it. The LP legislator is not bound by universal principles unless the master rule includes them. For the NLT, posited law must conform to higher law, a manifestly unjust law is not law, and the legislator makes law by reference to natural law. Liu stresses that these are two approaches, not two buckets of judges†. Most judges have never asked which camp they belong to.
  • Mandated v compatible (distinction 1.3(16)). What LP requires a judge to do is small. What LP allows is much larger. A positivist judge may follow the text outward to a moral idea, without ceasing to be a positivist. This is home at 11.4.
  • Floor v ceiling (distinction 1.3(3)). Law sets the minimum, not the maximum. Compliance with the Constitution tells you what you must not do, not everything you should do. This is home at 11.7.
  • Who decides v what is right (distinction 1.3(1)). A rule that gives a question to Parliament settles who decides. It does not make Parliament's answer right (11.5, 11.6).
  • Presumed constitutional v presumed just. When a court applies TSH's test and lets a law stand, it has not found the law just. It has only left the law's justice to Parliament (card 14.26).

The Singapore story

⚠ TRAP
Two approaches, not two buckets

Do not write "Singapore's judges are positivists" or "TSH says judges are natural lawyers". TSH explores what each set of beliefs implies for the judge and the legislator. She is not sorting individuals into camps†. Write "on a positivist approach, the judge would …".
