311.1 Supremacy

🧩 Practise 11.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.1 Supremacy (word for word)
11.1 Supremacy Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text
  1. Art 4 makes [the written Constitution] supreme, but a master rule exists only because it is accepted; it cannot be inferred from the text alone (TSH).
  2. TSH holds that LP sheds no light on Part 4's morally loaded concepts, and doubts that a state which does not give life should define person, life and liberty.
  3. So [the Constitution sets the criteria of validity] only formally: Part 4's moral terms force a choice of school (11.2, 11.3).
  • QUALIFY Teo Soh Lung (HC) rejected basic features, which YVK (2015) left open; TSH relies on equal moral worth: even a genocide amendment falls to the RF.
  • TRAP That the Constitution includes morality does not mean NLT wins: one may be an LP happy that morality is now positive law†. TSH's own thesis is that constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  • CONCEDE I concede that in practice the master-rule point may not lead to much; what matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A rulebook can say on its cover "I am the top rulebook". That sentence works only if people actually treat the book as the top rulebook. Hart called that shared acceptance the rule of recognition. So Art 4 is supreme because Singapore's judges and officials accept it, not just because it says so. And once you open the book, its big moral words still need interpreting.

What the statement claims

"The old quarrel over whether a law must be morally sound to count as law is over in Singapore: our written Constitution settled it. Article 4 voids any law inconsistent with the supreme law … judges need no higher law; they need only check the text." (Q104)

The statement treats Art 4 as the final answer to legal philosophy. Because the Constitution declares itself supreme and voids inconsistent laws, it says, the test of valid law is now written down, so positivism has won and judges need no theory. It is tempting because Art 4 really does look like Hart's master rule in written form.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. A master rule exists because it is accepted, not because it is written. Art 4 makes the written Constitution supreme. But on Hart's own view the master rule is a social practice: it is the rule officials actually use to identify law. TSH points out that you cannot infer it from the text alone. Singapore is a constitutional supremacy because its judges and officials accept the Articles as the master rule, not because the Articles read like one.
  2. Positivism cannot give content to Part 4's moral words. TSH argues that LP sheds no light on Part 4's morally loaded concepts. Does "person" include a foetus? Is "life" more than bare survival, perhaps including dignity and a livelihood? Is "personal liberty" only freedom from detention, or also a right to travel? TSH doubts that the state, which does not give life, should be the one to define person, life and liberty.
  3. So the Constitution sets the test of valid law only formally. Art 4 tells you that a valid law must fit the Constitution. It does not tell you what the Constitution's moral words mean. Reading them forces a choice of school, which is the work of 11.2 and 11.3.

The extra lines, explained

  • QUALIFY · basic features. Some legal systems hold that certain features of a constitution cannot be amended at all, a view India adopted in Kesavananda. Singapore's High Court rejected the doctrine in Teo Soh Lung, which upheld amendments to Art 149, and the Court of Appeal left the question open in YVK (2015). TSH does not need the doctrine. She relies on equal moral worth instead, so that even a constitutional amendment authorising genocide would fall to the Radbruch formula. The Constitution's own amendment rule does not have the last word either.
  • TRAP · morality in the text is not a win for NLT. Do not argue "the Constitution includes moral words, so natural law has won". A positivist can welcome moral words in the text. He is simply a positivist who is happy that morality is now part of the positive law†. NLT claims more, namely that a higher law binds whether or not the text mentions it. TSH's own thesis is that stronger one: constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  • CONCEDE · the master-rule point changes little in practice. Nobody doubts that Singapore's judges take Art 4 at face value. So concede that the first point may not lead to much in practice†. What matters is the second: theory still shapes how judges see their duty to the law, whether they may give effect to morality, and how citizens see their duty to obey.
  • A related point (card 14.3). Against anyone who says the sovereign is simply Parliament, Art 4 voids statutes to the extent they are inconsistent with the Constitution. Parliament is not Austin's sovereign who obeys no one.
TSH's Constitutional Jurisprudence on one card
▤ Card 14.25
  1. 1Question: does a written, supreme Constitution make Singapore positivist?
  2. 2Claim: no declaration of supremacy can settle the natural law v positivism debate. Contested words force a choice of school, and constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  3. 3Test: the choice arises at two levels. First, how to read a contested word, such as "law", "life" or "personal liberty" in Art 9(1). Second, what Art 4's supremacy clause itself means.
  4. 4Concede: who rightfully decides? George says that in a basically just regime judges respect the limits of their authority, and TSH admits there is no available formula. Concede the impasse: consensus may be the best gauge of morality, but it is not its ground.
  5. 5Verdict: the Constitution relocates the debate rather than ending it, and leaves the authority question open.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement assumes that Art 4 settled what law is, but it settled less than it seems. Art 4 makes the written Constitution supreme, yet on Hart's own account a master rule exists only because it is accepted, so it cannot be inferred from the text alone. Nor can positivism give content to Part 4's morally loaded words: TSH doubts that a state which does not give life should be the one to define person, life and liberty. The Constitution therefore sets the criteria of validity only formally, and its moral terms force a choice of school. That does not mean natural law has won, since a positivist can welcome moral words in the text. It means the debate has moved, not ended.

411.2 Art 9(1) "law"

🧩 Practise 11.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.2 Art 9(1) "law" (word for word)
11.2 Art 9(1) "law" validly passed; fair trial only; invent rights; caning; international norms
  1. Reading "law" as [whatever is validly passed] begs the question: what breaches Art 9 would not be in force (TSH).
  2. On my application of TSH's test, [caning for third-time littering] survives the other readings and falls under the RF only if broad historical consensus condemns it; arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at [fair-trial rules] is a choice of theory, not text; the RF adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.
  • FOR YVK (2015): courts cannot make from natural law a right absent from the Constitution, so none against caning (no ruling on natural law's view of it; George: 12.1).
  • AGAINST TSH: the CA targeted US substantive due process, the antithesis of natural law theory. LMS: no privacy right; Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and detention; YVK (2015)† adds unlawful use of force.
  • STEELMAN Richer readings risk making each judge a law unto himself. Reply: for TSH, letting manifest injustice stand defeats certainty's very purpose.
  • "Law" has four readings. Validly passed: Jabar dictum; YVK (2010)†: not about constitutionality; Nguyen read it to include constitutional validity. Natural justice: Ong Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open; YVK (2015)†: procedural; TEH (HC): Art 12 imports none. Not absurd or arbitrary: YVK (2010)† suggested it; TSH: TEH's plea failed on evidence, not principle. International law: Nguyen: statute beats custom; YVK (2010)†: read consistently where possible; no inhuman-punishment bar adopted.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Art 9(1) says nobody loses life or liberty except in accordance with law. If "law" just means "whatever Parliament validly passed", the promise is empty, because every statute would satisfy it. So courts and writers have tried richer readings: fair procedure, no absurd or arbitrary laws, respect for international law. Choosing among them means choosing a theory. Even the narrowest reading is a choice.

What the statement claims

"Article 9(1) promises that no one will be deprived of life or personal liberty 'save in accordance with law', and 'law' can only mean an enactment validly passed by Parliament. Any richer reading invites judges to invent rights." (Q106)

The statement says the text fixes the meaning of "law" as "enacted law", and that anything more lets judges make up rights. Its fuller version accepts fair-trial rules as part of "law" but nothing further. It is tempting because the Constitution's own definitions seem to point that way: Art 2 says law includes written law, and the Interpretation Act defines written law as the Constitution and enactments in force.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. "Whatever is validly passed" goes in a circle. The definitions point to laws in force. But a statute that breaches Art 9 is void under Art 4, so it is not in force. To know whether a statute counts as "law" for Art 9, you must first know whether it complies with Art 9. The reading assumes its own answer, which is what TSH means when she says it begs the question. It would also empty Art 9, since the state could then take life or liberty by any duly passed statute.
  2. Run the readings on a hard case: mandatory caning for third-time littering. TSH supplies the test, but the caning example is not hers, so in an essay present the result as your own application of her test. On that application, the penalty survives the other readings. It was validly passed, a fair trial can be held, and harsh is not the same as absurd. It falls under the Radbruch formula only if broad historical consensus condemns it as intolerably unjust, and arguably no such consensus exists.
  3. So stopping at fair-trial rules is a choice of theory, not something the text forces. The courts' middle path, natural justice read as procedure plus a residual bar on absurd or arbitrary laws, is a defensible choice, but it is a choice. The Radbruch formula adds only a floor against intolerable injustice. It does not license judges to invent rights.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · YVK (2015). In the caning case the Court of Appeal held that courts cannot use natural law to make a right the Constitution does not contain, so there is no right against caning. The court did not rule on what natural law itself says about caning, and it cited Robert George on the limits of judicial authority (12.1). This is the statement's best Singapore authority.
  • AGAINST · TSH: the court aimed at the wrong target. TSH argues that what the Court of Appeal really rejected was US substantive due process, the American doctrine under which judges read rights of privacy and autonomy into the guarantee of due process. She calls it the antithesis of natural law theory, because natural lawyers such as George subject autonomy to an objective moral law. The courts have read Art 9 narrowly in other ways too. In LMS the Court of Appeal found no right to privacy and held that Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and unlawful detention. YVK (2015) adds unlawful use of force†.
  • STEELMAN · each judge a law unto himself. Richer readings risk letting every judge apply a private morality, which would wreck legal certainty. TSH replies that certainty serves the rule of law, and the rule of law serves justice. So letting manifest injustice stand defeats the very purpose that certainty serves.
  • The four readings, case by case. The sheet's last line lists the cases behind each reading. The table below sets them out and runs the caning example through each.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The four readings of "law" in Art 9(1)
ReadingThe casesCaning for third-time littering
1. Validly passedJabar (dictum). YVK (2010) said Jabar was not about a statute's constitutionality†. Nguyen read "validly passed" to include constitutional validity.Passes, but this reading cannot test Art 9 itself.
2. Natural justiceOng Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open. YVK (2015) read natural justice as procedural†. In Tan Eng Hong (TEH) the High Court found that Art 12 imports no substantive standard either.Passes, if the trial is fair.
3. Not absurd or arbitraryYVK (2010) suggested it†. TSH notes that the plea in TEH failed on the evidence, not in principle.Harsh, but arguably not absurd or arbitrary.
4. International lawNguyen: a statute beats customary international law. YVK (2010): read domestic law consistently with it where possible†. No bar on inhuman punishment was adopted.The statute prevails.
Radbruch's floor (TSH)Her 2016 proposal, tested by broad historical consensus.Arguably no consensus condemns it, so it stands.

The point of the exercise is the last column. Every reading lets the penalty stand, yet each reading rests on a different theory of what "law" means. The text did not choose among them. The courts did.

⚠ TRAP
Natural law is neither international law nor substantive due process

Statements often lump "universal morality", "international human rights norms" and American judicial activism together. Keep them apart. International law is a separate body of rules, and in Singapore a statute beats customary international law (Nguyen). Substantive due process is a liberal doctrine of privacy and autonomy, which TSH calls the antithesis of natural law. Natural law, in TSH's sense, is a higher moral law known by reason. It may agree with either one on a given point, but it is neither.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Reading "law" in Art 9(1) as whatever Parliament validly passes begs the question, because a statute that breaches Art 9 would not be in force, and it would leave the guarantee empty. The courts have not stopped there. Ong Ah Chuan read "law" to include the fundamental rules of natural justice, and YVK (2010) suggested that laws too absurd or arbitrary to be meant as law are excluded. Yet YVK (2015) refused to make from natural law a right the Constitution lacks, and TSH replies that the court's real target was US substantive due process, the antithesis of natural law theory. Stopping at fair-trial rules is therefore a choice of theory, not text. On my application of TSH's test, even mandatory caning for third-time littering survives, since arguably no broad historical consensus condemns it: the Radbruch formula adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.

511.3 Art 12

🧩 Practise 11.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.3 Art 12 (word for word)
11.3 Art 12 intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers
  1. For LMS (CA), [an intelligible line rationally related to the object] usually suffices, since courts are not "mini-legislatures".
  2. On [a double fee for left-handed drivers], the CA asks if the line rationally serves its aim; the HC would also void an "inherently bad" aim.
  3. So [judges who probe the object become legislators] overstates: the RF voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness.
  • FOR LMS (CA): a threshold test with no free-standing legitimacy review; Wednesbury rejected; use Art 12(2).
  • QUALIFY This is not cleanly LP v NLT: a limited element of illegitimacy remains, since extreme illogicality or incoherence fails a limb, and a women-driving ban might fail limb two; TSH calls the test natural law at work.
  • AGAINST For TSH the question is which differences are morally significant, so moral arguments cannot be dismissed as "extra-legal" under Art 12(1); without a higher moral law, laws treating everyone "equally badly" pass†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Equality doesn't mean treating everyone the same. Laws sort people all the time: adults and children, drivers and pedestrians, careless killers and deliberate ones. Courts ask whether the line a law draws makes sense and links to the law's purpose. The harder question is what happens if the purpose itself is bad. The Court of Appeal mostly won't ask that. TSH says equality is empty unless you have a moral standard for deciding which differences matter.

What the statement claims

"The courts were right to leave s 377A to Parliament. The guarantee of equal protection asks only whether a law draws an intelligible line that is rationally connected to its purpose." (Q65)
"A statute sets the licence fee for left-handed taxi drivers at double the fee charged to other drivers." (Q109)

Q65 claims that Art 12 is a thin, technical test, and that asking whether a law's purpose is morally sound would turn judges into unelected legislators. Q109 is a problem question. It asks you to apply the test as the High Court and the Court of Appeal stated it in LMS, and to say whether the difference between them is really positivism against natural law. Both rest on the idea that equality can be tested without moral judgement.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. For the Court of Appeal, a rational line usually suffices. In LMS the Court of Appeal asked two things. Is there an intelligible line between the groups, and is it rationally related to the law's object? If so, the law usually passes. The court went no further because courts are not mini-legislatures. Whether a law's aim is wise is for Parliament.
  2. The two courts would treat the left-handed drivers differently. Suppose a statute doubles the licence fee for left-handed taxi drivers, for road safety. The Court of Appeal would ask whether the line between left- and right-handed drivers rationally serves road safety, which needs some evidence that handedness affects safety. The High Court in LMS went one step further: it would also strike down an aim that is inherently bad.
  3. So probing a law's aim does not make judges legislators. The statement says judges who look at the object become legislators. That overstates it. The Radbruch formula voids only intolerable injustice, which is a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness, the administrative-law test for decisions no reasonable authority could make. A court using the formula leaves almost every policy choice to Parliament.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · LMS (CA). The Court of Appeal treated reasonable classification as a threshold test. It refused any free-standing review of whether a law's purpose is legitimate, rejected Wednesbury review, and said challenges on particular grounds should go through Art 12(2), which lists forbidden grounds such as race. This is the statement's best authority: Art 12(1) is kept thin on purpose.
  • QUALIFY · not cleanly positivism v natural law. Even the Court of Appeal kept a limited element of moral review. A line so illogical or incoherent that it offends any idea of equality fails a limb, and the court accepted that a ban on women driving might fail limb two. TSH calls the test natural law at work. So the two courts differ in degree, not in kind, which answers Q109's last question.
  • AGAINST · equality needs a moral standard. For TSH the real question under Art 12 is which differences between people are morally significant. That is why moral arguments cannot be dismissed as extra-legal under Art 12(1). Every law differentiates: the law punishes a negligent killing less than an intentional one because blameworthiness differs. Without a higher moral law, Art 12 would let through a law that treats everyone equally badly†.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Left-handed taxi drivers (Q109)

The minister says the double fee improves road safety. Run each approach.

ApproachThe question it asksResult on the double fee
Court of Appeal (LMS)Is there an intelligible line? Is it rationally connected to road safety?The line is clear. Without evidence that left-handers drive less safely, the connection fails.
High Court (LMS)The same, plus: is the aim itself illegitimate or inherently bad?Road safety is a legitimate aim, so the extra question adds nothing here.
TSHIs handedness a morally significant difference?Not without evidence that it affects safety.
Radbruch formulaIs this intolerable injustice?No. A fee is nothing like genocide or slavery.

Notice that the two courts reach the same result on these facts. Their split matters only where the aim itself is bad, such as a law whose purpose is to humiliate a group. That is why the QUALIFY line says the difference is one of degree.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

For the Court of Appeal in LMS, an intelligible line rationally related to the law's object usually satisfies Art 12, since courts are not mini-legislatures, and there is no free-standing review of the law's purpose. On a double licence fee for left-handed drivers, the Court of Appeal would ask whether the line rationally serves road safety, while the High Court would also strike down an inherently bad aim. The split is not cleanly positivism against natural law: even the Court of Appeal fails extreme illogicality, and it accepted that a ban on women driving might fail. TSH goes further, arguing that the real question is always which differences are morally significant, so equality is empty without a higher moral law. Yet judges who probe a law's aim do not become legislators, because the Radbruch formula voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness.

611.4 Four walls

🧩 Practise 11.4 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.4 Four walls (word for word)
11.4 Four walls within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality
  1. [Reading the Constitution primarily within its own four walls], Colin Chan's LP approach† (TSH), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau charitably, TSH finds fairness universal, though its manifestation varies with local conditions.
  3. So [universal morality] need not mean foreign values, if confined to manifest injustice (11.5).
  • CONCEDE I concede that higher law cuts both ways: a "true-blue Thomist" may get judges with a very different view of dignity (Lawrence; TSH), so I defend only a narrow trigger.
  • QUALIFY Arguably TSH's LP is too narrow†: LP mandates little but is compatible with more. Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, as commercial reasonableness imports trade practice; a purposive LP may read the Constitution as guarding individuals. TSH: reference to natural law is then "mandatory"; can such a judge stop at popular morality?
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Read the Constitution only from inside its own pages and its local setting. Don't import foreign values." That's fair up to a point, since Singapore is not America. But some standards, like basic fairness, are universal even when they look different from place to place. And even a positivist judge may follow the text when it points outward to a moral idea, just as commercial law follows the text outward to trade practice.

What the statement claims

"That is why our courts rightly read the Constitution within its own four walls instead of importing universal moral ideals." (Q104)
"Foreign values have no place here."

The statement treats "universal" and "foreign" as the same thing. It assumes that any standard not found in Singapore's text or context must come from somewhere else, usually the West. It is tempting because Singapore's courts have often warned against importing foreign cases and values.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Reading within the four walls need not shut out universal standards. In Colin Chan the High Court read the Constitution primarily within its own four walls, with national unity as the paramount mandate. TSH notes the court meant local context, not the bare text, and Liu calls this a positivist approach†. But reading in local context is compatible with recognising standards that hold everywhere.
  2. TSH reads Haw Tua Tau charitably. In Haw Tua Tau the Privy Council declined to list the rules of natural justice and suggested they change with the times. TSH reads that to mean fairness is universal, though what it requires in practice varies with local conditions. A universal standard can wear a local face.
  3. So universal morality need not mean foreign values, if it is confined to manifest injustice. The objection to "foreign values" is an objection to importing another society's contested choices. A narrow floor against manifest injustice, of the kind 11.5 defends, imports nothing of the sort.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · higher law cuts both ways. A natural lawyer who wants judges to protect rights may be disappointed by the judges he gets. TSH warns that a true-blue Thomist may end up with judges who hold a very different view of dignity, as in Lawrence, the American decriminalisation case decided on privacy and autonomy. So concede the risk and defend only a narrow trigger, not wide review.
  • QUALIFY · TSH's picture of positivism is arguably too narrow†. Liu argues that LP mandates little but is compatible with much more. Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, just as the doctrine of commercial reasonableness sends a judge to trade practice, which is not itself a source of law. A purposive LP may also read the Constitution as guarding individuals against the state, rather than putting unity first as Colin Chan did. TSH's likely reply is that once the positive law admits arguments from critical morality, reference to natural law becomes mandatory. The live question for an essay is whether such a judge can stop at popular morality.
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

The difference is the reason, not the result†. Liu's LP judge and TSH's NLT judge may both read "equal" in Art 12 by moral standards. The NLT judge says morality is always part of the law. The LP judge says it is part of the law here, because the positive law sends him there, and not where those provisions are not engaged. So do not score the debate by outcomes. Ask why each judge looks to morality, and whether the positivist can then stop at popular morality (distinction 1.3(16), mandated v compatible).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three judges read a fair-trial guarantee
JudgeWhere the content of "fair" comes fromWhy
A Colin Chan-style positivistLocal context, with national unity firstThe Constitution is read within its own four walls.
Liu's purposive positivistWherever the text points, including moral ideasThe positive law requires it here, and only here†.
TSH's natural lawyerNatural law, known by reason, applied to local conditionsA fair trial means one that is objectively fair.

The second and third judges may well agree on the result. They disagree on why, and on whether the inquiry can stop at what most people currently think is fair.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Reading the Constitution primarily within its own four walls, as Colin Chan did, need not exclude universal standards. Read charitably, Haw Tua Tau treats fairness as universal, though its manifestation varies with local conditions, so universal morality need not mean foreign values, provided it is confined to manifest injustice. I concede that higher law cuts both ways, since a natural lawyer may get judges with a very different view of dignity, and so I defend only a narrow trigger. Nor does positivism forbid looking outward. It mandates little but is compatible with more, so where the text points to a moral concept a positivist judge may follow it, though TSH would ask whether he can then stop at popular morality.

711.5 Who decides (courts)

🧩 Practise 11.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.5 Who decides (courts) (word for word)
11.5 Who decides (courts) for Parliament, not the courts; ballot box; unelected judges; activism
  1. I accept that [contested rights are for Parliament], but only until Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met (TSH).
  2. That threshold (BHC: 15.13) is met for genocide and slavery, not for the laws voided in Roe and Obergefell, nor for Women's Charter s 12 (catch: 8.5).
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law for injustice] goes too far: rubber-stamping is a vice too (12.2), and intolerable injustice must fall.
  • QUALIFY LMS left Hart v Devlin to the Legislature (16); TSH: only if no constitutional right was at stake.
  • LEGISLATOR Where objective morality is unclear, a deliberative democracy can take a stand through its legislature (12.3).
  • Asking who decides returns us to where we started, but wiser†.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Contested questions about rights belong to elected MPs, not unelected judges." Mostly yes. But if judges never step in, even against something monstrous, that is a failure too: they become a rubber stamp. TSH's line is simple. Leave contested questions to Parliament, unless a law is so unjust that history and the world broadly agree it is intolerable, as with genocide and slavery.

What the statement claims

"In a democracy, the scope of fundamental rights is for elected representatives to settle … proposals to widen the rights of accused persons belong in Parliament, not the courts." (Q105)

The statement gives every rights question to Parliament. Its fuller version adds that anyone who believes in a higher law must want judges to override Parliament whenever they think it wrong. It is tempting because Singapore's courts have often said something similar, and because a court that strikes down laws freely would be a judicial oligarchy.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Accept the presumption: contested rights are for Parliament. TSH agrees that in a constitutional democracy contested rights questions belong to the legislature. But only up to a point. When a law's injustice reaches Radbruch's threshold, the court may refuse it.
  2. The threshold is high, and broad historical consensus proves it. TSH's test (15.13) asks for long-lasting agreement across many jurisdictions, for the same reason. It is met for genocide and slavery. It is not met for the laws voided in Roe (abortion limits) and Obergefell (marriage laws), nor for s 12 of the Women's Charter, which voids a marriage that is not between a man and a woman. TSH admits a catch in her own test, which you should concede (8.5).
  3. So "judges must never invalidate a law for injustice" goes too far. A court that rubber-stamps whatever Parliament passes fails in its own role, just as one that legislates fails by taking Parliament's (12.2). Ordinary injustice is for Parliament to repeal. Intolerable injustice must fall.

The extra lines, explained

  • QUALIFY · Hart v Devlin is for Parliament, unless a right is at stake. In LMS the Court of Appeal left the Hart v Devlin debate to the legislature (16.2). TSH accepts that only if no constitutional right was at stake. She imagines a legislature that removed race from Art 12(2) and enforced racial extermination. Taking a side in Hart v Devlin cannot be open to Parliament where fundamental rights are engaged.
  • LEGISLATOR · Parliament can take a stand. Where objective morality is unclear, TSH says a deliberative democracy can take a stand through its legislature. This is the other half of her position. The presumption is not a grudging concession but a positive role for Parliament (12.3).
  • Back where we started, but wiser. Liu ended the course on this question. The Constitution does not tell us who should decide contested moral questions, or by what standard, so asking who decides returns us to where we started, but wiser†. Use it as a closing line, once.
TSH's Judicial Oligarchy on one card
▤ Card 14.26
  1. 1Question: how far may courts strike down laws on moral grounds?
  2. 2Claim: courts should presume legislation constitutional unless Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met, shown by broad historical consensus.
  3. 3Strength: the alternatives are worse. A lower threshold invites judicial temerity, and positivism leaves a brute majority unchecked.
  4. 4Critique and reply: the formula is not in the Constitution the nation accepted. Reply: constitutionalism rests on equal moral worth, so no majority may sanction its violation, even by amendment.
  5. 5Concede: her own catch (8.5). Concede the risk and adopt her reply that an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
  6. 6Singapore: LMS rightly avoided rule by judges, but was overly sanguine about future Parliaments.
  7. 7Verdict: TSH's threshold is the most defensible test for Singapore judges, once her own catch is conceded.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is the threshold met?
The lawBroad historical consensus against it?Result on TSH's test
A law, even a constitutional amendment, authorising racial genocideYes, across history and nationsStruck down
A law permitting slaveryYesStruck down
The abortion limits voided in RoeNo, not in 1973The legislature decides
The marriage laws voided in Obergefell; Women's Charter s 12No, not for nowThe legislature decides
Mandatory caning for third-time littering (11.2)Arguably noneIt stands
A double licence fee for left-handed drivers (11.3)NoneIt stands, and Art 12 does the real work
⚠ TRAP
Presumed constitutional is not presumed just

A law that survives TSH's test has not been declared just. It has only been left to Parliament. Write "the law stands, and its justice is a question for Parliament", never "the court found the law just" (card 14.26).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

I accept that contested rights are for Parliament, but only until Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met. On TSH's test, courts should presume legislation constitutional unless broad historical consensus, long-lasting and across many jurisdictions, shows the law to be intolerably unjust. That threshold is met for genocide and slavery, but not for the laws voided in Roe and Obergefell, nor for s 12 of the Women's Charter. I concede TSH's own catch: a world trend could one day become consensus, and consensus can go dreadfully wrong. Even so, "judges must never invalidate a law for injustice" goes too far, because rubber-stamping is as much a vice as judicial legislation, and intolerable injustice must fall.

811.6 Art 156

🧩 Practise 11.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.6 Art 156 (word for word)
11.6 Art 156 repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
  1. In 2022 [change through Parliament] came: s 377A went, and Art 156, a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism (TSH), shielded man-woman marriage laws from Part 4.
  2. So [leaving it to Parliament] moved the question rather than removed it: a two-thirds majority (Art 5(2)) put those laws beyond Part 4 (11.7).
  • FOR Shanmugam: courts can only make binary decisions (Hansard, 29 Nov 2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: repeal was for risk, not unconstitutionality, so differentiating laws are not incoherent in principle. After UKM, s 377A failed to do its work, which might explain the change of tactic.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In 2022 Parliament repealed s 377A and, at the same time, added Art 156 to the Constitution. Art 156 stops the courts from using fundamental-rights arguments against laws based on marriage between a man and a woman. So "leave it to Parliament" really happened. But the moral question did not disappear. Parliament decided where it would be answered from now on: in Parliament.

What the statement claims

"Moral questions like marriage should be left to Parliament; courts are binary and blunt."

The statement says courts are the wrong place for questions like marriage, because a court can only say yes or no. It is tempting because Singapore did exactly this in 2022, and the government gave the same reason.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. In 2022 change came through Parliament. Parliament repealed s 377A and added Art 156, which shields laws based on the man–woman definition of marriage from challenge under Part 4. TSH describes Art 156 as a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism: it stops a court from doing what Obergefell did in the United States. Both changes took effect on 3 January 2023.
  2. So leaving it to Parliament moved the question rather than removed it. A two-thirds majority, as Art 5(2) requires, put those marriage laws beyond Part 4 (11.7). The moral question about marriage is still open. What changed is who answers it. This is the memorable line: a constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions, but cannot remove them.

The extra lines, explained

  • FOR · Shanmugam: courts can only make binary decisions. Speaking in Parliament on 29 November 2022, the Law Minister said a court can only decide yes or no. It cannot weigh the knock-on effects on housing, education and other marriage-based policies, or craft a calibrated compromise. Parliament can. Masagos added that MPs have a duty to decide even, and perhaps especially, polarising social questions (16.3).
  • QUALIFY · repeal was for risk, not because s 377A was unconstitutional. TSH stresses why Parliament repealed. If it had repealed because s 377A breached Art 12, that would imply the two kinds of relationship are on a par, and every law that distinguishes them would be in doubt. But the government's stated reason was the risk that a court would strike s 377A down after Tan Seng Kee. On that reason, repealing s 377A while shielding marriage is not incoherent in principle. TSH adds that after UKM (2018), where a gay man was allowed to adopt his surrogate-born son despite s 377A, the section had failed to do the work its defenders expected. That might explain the change of tactic, from the criminal law to the Constitution.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The 2022 package, part by part
PartWhat it didWhere to use it
Repeal of s 377AWithdrew punishment of private consensual conduct between men. Non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes.7.9, the coercion gradient
Art 156(1)–(2)Lets Parliament, by law, and the executive define, protect and promote marriage.11.6
Art 156(3)–(4)Part 4 cannot void laws or executive acts based on the man–woman definition.11.6
The definitionStays in statute: Interpretation Act s 2(1) and Women's Charter s 12(1). A simple majority may change it†.16.1

Read together, the package withdrew punishment and moved the marriage question out of the courts. It did not answer the marriage question. It decided who would.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

In 2022 change through Parliament came: s 377A was repealed, and Art 156, which TSH calls a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism, shielded man–woman marriage laws from Part 4. The government's reason was that courts can only make binary decisions, while Parliament can weigh consequences and craft a compromise. But leaving the question to Parliament moved it rather than removed it, since a two-thirds majority under Art 5(2) put those laws beyond Part 4 without answering the moral question. As TSH notes, repeal was for legal risk, not unconstitutionality, so laws that differentiate between relationships are not incoherent in principle. A constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions, but cannot remove them.

911.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary?

🧩 Practise 11.7 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? (word for word)
11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception
  1. [The statement] is itself a legal philosophy, too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion: law is not morality and must not supplant it.
  3. So [compliance always gives sufficient moral guidance] fails: law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.
  • Either way theory is needed: Hart's penumbral judge may have to reach beyond the law; Dworkin's finds the answer in community morality that is also law.
  • LAWYER Law sets the minimum, not the maximum (Devlin); Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): a "special two-thirds majority" amends most provisions (TSH), with no express core like Basic Law art 79(3) (implied limits: 11.1); so treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgment to whoever holds two-thirds.
  • STEELMAN Personal morality is subjective, so keep it out; and most cases are routine (9, Steelman: restraint). Reply: refusing manifest injustice is fidelity to law, not mere conscience (TSH), and subjectivism defeats itself (4.7).
  • Without exception: try an as-applied Art 15 challenge, though Art 15(4), read literally, lacks ICCPR art 18(3)'s "necessary" test (TSH; 12.6).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Judges and lawyers need neither philosophy nor personal morality. Just follow the Constitution and the laws." But that sentence is itself a philosophy: a view about what law is and what it asks of us. Even Hart, the great positivist, said law is not morality and must not replace it. Law is a floor, not a ceiling. It tells you the least you must do, not everything you should do.

What the statement claims

"In a constitutional democracy, judges and lawyers need neither philosophy nor personal morality: compliance with the Constitution and the laws always gives sufficient moral guidance."

Statements in this family use trigger words such as neither philosophy nor personal morality, always sufficient, I just apply the law, my morals are private and without exception. They make two claims at once: legal actors need no theory, and they need no personal morality. They are tempting because most legal work really is routine.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The statement is itself a legal philosophy. It says what law is (a complete guide) and what it asks of us (nothing beyond compliance). That is a theory, and an unstable one. It is too moralised for a positivist, who says validity and morality are separate questions, and too amoral for a natural lawyer, who says law answers to a higher law.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion. Hart warned that law is not morality and must not be allowed to supplant it. A positivist separates law from morality so that we can criticise the law, not so that we can stop thinking morally.
  3. So compliance cannot always give sufficient moral guidance. Law is a floor, not a ceiling (distinction 1.3(3)). It sets the minimum and leaves the rest to judgement. And its open words, such as "law" and "equal", need a theory before they can guide anyone.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where compliance runs out
SituationWhat the law givesWhat is still needed
A routine case under a clear statuteThe answerLittle. This is the statement's kernel: most cases are like this.
A penumbral case, where the rule's words are unclearNo settled answerHart: the judge uses discretion beyond the law. Dworkin: the answer lies in community morality that is also law. Either way, a theory.
An open constitutional word, "law" in Art 9 or "equal" in Art 12A word, not a meaningA theory of what law is, or which differences matter (11.2, 11.3).
A two-thirds majority amends the ConstitutionWhatever the new text saysCompliance alone would hand moral judgement to whoever holds two-thirds.
A lawful course of action that will hurt othersPermissionLaw sets the minimum. The lawyer must still decide whether to do more (10.1).
A ban on alcohol without exception catches sacramental wineA clear ruleAn as-applied Art 15 challenge, which is weak, or the legislator's own judgement (12.6).

The extra lines, explained

  • Either way, theory is needed. In unclear cases Hart's judge, working in the penumbra of a rule, may have to reach beyond the law and use discretion. Dworkin's judge finds the answer in the community's political morality, which on his view is also law. These are opposite theories, but both need moral judgement, and neither lets the judge do without theory.
  • LAWYER · law sets the minimum. Devlin said the law is concerned with the minimum, not the maximum. Pepper's own premise implies the same: the law is the limit of what a lawyer may help a client do, not a guide to everything a good lawyer should do (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): two-thirds can change most of it. TSH notes that a special two-thirds majority can amend most provisions. Unlike Germany's Basic Law, whose art 79(3) puts a core beyond amendment, Singapore's Constitution has no express core of that kind (implied limits are discussed at 11.1). So treating compliance as moral guidance hands moral judgement to whoever holds two-thirds of Parliament.
  • STEELMAN · keep personal morality out. Personal morality is subjective, so judges should keep it out of their work, and most cases are routine anyway (section 9's restraint steelman). The reply has two parts. Refusing manifest injustice is fidelity to law, not mere conscience, as TSH argues. And the subjectivist premise defeats itself (4.7).
  • Without exception. If a statute bans something without exception, such as all alcohol, try an as-applied challenge under Art 15 (religious freedom) for sacramental use. Be candid that it is weak. Art 15(4), read literally, lacks the necessary test in art 18(3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), as TSH notes (12.6).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is itself a legal philosophy, and an unstable one: too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion, since for him law is not morality and must not supplant it. Either way theory is needed: Hart's judge in the penumbra may have to reach beyond the law, while Dworkin's finds the answer in community morality that is also law. And because a special two-thirds majority can amend most of the Constitution, with no express core like art 79(3) of Germany's Basic Law, treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgement to whoever holds two-thirds. Law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.

1011.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers

🧩 Practise 11.8 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers (word for word)
11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper
  1. [The people's acceptance] cannot alone found legitimacy: the framers' will begs the question why it still binds us, and treating non-revolt as acquiescence is artificial (TSH).
  2. Only co-equal dignity under natural law makes consent meaningful; NLT answers from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory†.
  3. The charge that [NLT defeats the separation of powers] fails: on the weak thesis morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and for TSH the legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms.
  • QUALIFY Two further answers: reason converges, so properly applied all three branches reach one result; and NLT v LP asks what law is, separation of powers how power is organised, so a democrat or a dictator could hold either†.
  • AGAINST An LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper; an NLT judge tests law against higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch). German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws†; whether Singapore judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis; against a sitting legislature it is untested†.
  • Basic features: Kesavananda (India) held some unamendable, those suggested including separation of powers and secular character (TSH); rejected here (11.1). Arguably NLT justifies them more easily†, as a good constitution has a telos some amendments destroy; TSH argues from natural law, not by second-guessing the framers' intention.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Why should a Constitution written decades ago bind us today? "Because the people accept it" sounds right, but not rebelling is not the same as agreeing. TSH says consent only means something because people already have equal dignity, which is a natural-law idea. And does natural law let judges overrule Parliament whenever they disagree? No. On the weak version, judges step in only at the extreme, so the separation of powers survives.

What the statement claims

"The Constitution is legitimate because the people consent to it." "Some features must be unamendable." "Natural law theory destroys the separation of powers by making judges moral gatekeepers."

These statements raise three questions. What makes the Constitution morally binding? Is any of it beyond amendment? And does natural law hand power from Parliament to judges? They are tempting because consent and the separation of powers are democratic ideals that seem to need no further argument.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Acceptance alone cannot make the Constitution legitimate. The usual answers stay within positivism. The framers' will cannot explain why the Constitution still binds us, decades later. Treating the fact that people have not revolted as consent is artificial: one can emigrate only with the means to do so, and even then one lives under some social contract†. Even for a positivist, being the master rule as a social fact does not make the Constitution morally legitimate.
  2. TSH: only equal dignity makes consent meaningful. TSH argues that our consent counts for something only because we are co-equal in dignity under natural law. That gives NLT an advantage here. It is all of one piece and answers the legitimacy question from within. LP only tells us what the law is, so it must borrow some other moral or political theory to answer it†.
  3. So natural law does not destroy the separation of powers. On the weak thesis of Radbruch and Alexy, morality overrides positive law only at the Radbruch threshold. Below it, the natural-law judge applies unjust or unwise laws like anyone else. TSH herself says the legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three answers to "why is the Constitution legitimate?"
CandidateThe problem with itVerdict
The framers' willIt begs the question why their will still binds us (TSH).Not enough on its own.
Our acquiescenceTreating non-revolt as consent is artificial. Leaving takes means, and even emigrants live under some social contract†.Not enough on its own.
Our co-equal dignityIt is a natural-law answer, so LP cannot give it from within†.TSH's answer: it makes consent meaningful.

A further point from card 14.4: on Hart's view only officials need accept the master rule, so LP is not necessarily democratic (TSH). Describing a system is not praising it.

The extra lines, explained

  • QUALIFY · two further answers on separation of powers†. First, reason converges. On NLT the judge is not imposing a private view but using reason that everyone shares, so properly applied all three branches should reach the same result. Second, the two debates ask different questions. NLT v LP asks what law is, and separation of powers asks how power is organised. A democrat or a dictator could hold either theory. Together with line 3, these are Liu's three answers to the charge.
  • AGAINST · the gatekeeper conflict is real. An LP judge defers to Parliament's view of morality, which leaves the legislature as moral gatekeeper. An NLT judge tests law against higher law, which makes the judge a gatekeeper too. That can be a real conflict, not just a gap. Radbruch's formula is the example: there the judge's morality differs from the legislature's, and the clash is genuine, since legislators who pass wicked laws rarely think them wicked. German courts applied the formula to the laws of a fallen regime†. Whether Singapore's judges hold the power is debatable, since they prefer a constitutional basis for striking a law down, and its use against a sitting legislature is untested†.
  • Basic features. In India, Kesavananda held some features of the constitution unamendable, and those suggested include the separation of powers and the constitution's secular character (TSH). Singapore's High Court rejected the doctrine (11.1). Arguably NLT justifies such limits more easily, because a good constitution has a purpose, a telos, that some amendments would destroy†: take the legs off a chair and you have a cushion. TSH would argue from natural law directly, not by second-guessing what the framers intended.
⚠ TRAP
Do not say Radbruch's formula has never been used

German courts did apply it, to the laws of a past regime†. What is untested is a court using it against a sitting legislature in a working constitutional system†. Frame it that way: "untested against a sitting Parliament", not "never applied".

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The people's acceptance cannot alone found the Constitution's legitimacy: the framers' will begs the question why it still binds us, and treating non-revolt as acquiescence is artificial. As TSH argues, only our co-equal dignity under natural law makes consent meaningful, and NLT can say so from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory. Nor does natural law defeat the separation of powers. On the weak thesis, morality overrides positive law only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees that the legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms. The conflict between a deferring judge and a testing judge is real, but it arises only at the extreme, and the formula's use against a sitting legislature remains untested.

11Putting it together: Practice Q104

"The old quarrel over whether a law must be morally sound to count as law is over in Singapore: our written Constitution settled it. Article 4 voids any law inconsistent with the supreme law, and Article 162 requires existing laws to be read so as to conform to it, so judges need no higher law; they need only check the text to know which laws are valid. Even the fundamental liberties are simply rights the text confers, carrying whatever meaning the state gives them. That is why our courts rightly read the Constitution within its own four walls instead of importing universal moral ideals."

Instruction: discuss with reference to Hart, Radbruch and TSH, using local cases on Arts 9 and 12.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement treats Art 4 as the end of jurisprudence, but everything turns on the word "simply": if the fundamental liberties are simply rights the text confers, someone must still decide what they mean. A supreme Constitution relocates the old quarrel rather than settling it. I make three claims. First, Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted, which no text can supply. Second, Part 4's words, "law" in Art 9 and "equal" in Art 12, force judges to choose a theory, as Ong Ah Chuan, YVK and LMS show. Third, reading within the four walls need not exclude universal standards, if they are confined, as TSH proposes, to intolerable injustice shown by broad historical consensus.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Supremacy and Hart (11.1). Hart's master rule rests on acceptance, so Art 4's supremacy cannot be read off the text. Should a state that does not give life define person, life and liberty? Trap: morality in the text does not mean NLT wins. Concede that the master-rule point changes little in practice†.
  2. Arts 9 and 12 (11.2, 11.3). The four readings of "law": Jabar, Ong Ah Chuan, YVK (2010) and YVK (2015). TSH: YVK (2015) targeted substantive due process, not natural law. LMS: courts are not mini-legislatures, yet extreme incoherence still fails. TSH: equality is empty without a higher moral law.
  3. Four walls and Radbruch (11.4, 11.5). Haw Tua Tau read charitably. Liu: TSH's positivism is too narrow, since LP is compatible with more than it mandates†. Radbruch's threshold, proved by broad historical consensus. Self-critique: TSH's catch (8.5).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Art 4 and Part 4 relocate, not settle, the debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution narrows the practical gap between natural-law and positivist judges and makes Radbruch's formula rarely needed, but it leaves open the extreme case, our attitude to law, and who decides by what standard. Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice, and no clause relieves anyone of conscience.

12Recap

Archetype 11 on one card
▤ Sections 11.1–11.8
  1. 1Supremacy rests on acceptance, and Part 4's words need a theory. Morality in the text does not mean NLT wins (11.1).
  2. 2"Law" in Art 9 has four readings, and each is a theory choice. "Validly passed" begs the question (11.2).
  3. 3Art 12 asks for a rational line, but deciding which differences matter is a moral question (11.3).
  4. 4Four walls need not exclude universal standards. LP mandates little but is compatible with more (11.4).
  5. 5Parliament decides contested rights, until Radbruch's threshold, proved by broad historical consensus (11.5, 15.13).
  6. 6Art 156 moved the marriage question to Parliament. It did not remove it (11.6).
  7. 7"No philosophy needed" is itself a philosophy. Law is a floor, not a ceiling (11.7).
  8. 8Legitimacy needs equal dignity, and weak natural law leaves the separation of powers standing (11.8).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a removal van with "Art 4" painted on its side. It has not demolished the old argument between natural law and positivism. It has carried it into new rooms labelled law, life, liberty, equal, where it still needs unpacking with a theory. At the front door stands a guard (the court) who lets Parliament rearrange the furniture as it likes, and bars the door only against fire: genocide and slavery.

LESSON 12 · ARCHETYPE 12 · ABOUT 59 MIN · 9 FLOWCHARTS · 4 ILLUSTRATIONS · 38 QUESTIONS

Roles: who decides

⚡ BIG IDEA

Roles have limits, so "stay in your lane" is right as a presumption. But where a role ends is contested, drawing the line is a moral judgment, and refusing your own role's work (abdication) is as much a vice as taking another's (usurpation).

ARCHETYPE 12 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
12 Roles: who decides
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] is right as a presumption: roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.
Intro [The statement] treats each role's limits as settled. Roles do have limits, but drawing them is a moral judgment; refusing one's own work is as much a vice as taking another's; refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation.
Frame (Roles question) The statement is almost verbatim George as TSH reports him: at least in a basically just regime, natural law requires judges and officials to respect the limits of their authority. It drops the proviso and adds lawyers.
Steelman: role limits The best case for [the statement] is that a constitutional democracy divides power: Rajeevan (11, Steelman: Parliament decides) and YVK (2015; 12.1) support it. This shows that restraint is the presumption. It does not show [that each role's limits are settled].
12.1 Source and frame limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts
  1. [The statement] assumes we know where roles end; for George allocating authority is a determinatio, a prudent choice among morally acceptable options.
  2. TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: who rightfully decides whether it is prudentially made?
  3. So [what is rightfully others'] assumes its answer: a role's limits come from a theory of the role.
  • STEELMAN YVK (2015), citing George: some contend natural law requires judges to respect the boundaries of authority.
  • CONCEDE I concede TSH's impasse: natural law condemns vesting authority in a random group of bandits but cannot say who decides; still, the proviso must be right in principle.
12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law
  1. Every role can fail twice, by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication); [the statement] names only the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: in bad faith they would legislate judicially or rubber-stamp whatever Parliament passes.
  3. So [respecting the limits of one's role] is half the duty; the other half is doing the role's own moral work.
  • OFFICIAL s 377A (2007), kept but not proactively enforced: arguably Parliament abdicated and the executive quasi-legislated (7.7).
  • JUDGE Bridge called stopping at decided cases an "unwarranted abdication" (McLoughlin; 2.8).
  • LAWYER Screening clients usurps (Pepper); simply focusing on the law abdicates (Thunder).
12.3 Legislator's hat majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what the law is or should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that a majority is not enough: his standard does not count heads.
  3. So the legislator does what [the sole concern] forbids: he judges, as a trustee, not a stenographer.
  • STEELMAN Equal respect amid disagreement and fear of juristocracy (TSH) support it. Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being a matter of social norm.
  • LEGISLATOR Masagos to Poa: MPs must decide even, perhaps especially, difficult and polarising social issues (2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: non-NLT legislators may not regard themselves as bound by higher standards. Arguably they will still weigh morality†: one who wants good, not merely valid, laws must (14.4's minimum content; Hart v Devlin). LP uses morality in one dimension (good law), NLT in two (good law, and law at all).
12.4 Judge's hat if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law
  1. The judge asks not whether [the law] is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. I climb a ladder: validity, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then discretion within the statute; refusal comes only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So [I would enforce it] is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.
  • Kennedy's five courses (15.10): he endorses or excludes none "a priori". The public's "devil's compact" (defend as plausibly legal, change, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy insiders know is false; he is unconvinced that the rule of law means obeying it.
  • Candour, my standard, bars his covert last two. The refusal line is genocide and slavery, not the laws voided in Roe.
  • CONCEDE I concede TSH's own catch and adopt her reply (8.5).
12.5 Official's and junior's hat officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
  1. Officials, like Fuller's citizens, owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: respect for constituted authority must not be confused with it.
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches a judge or other office-holder, neither saint nor hero: if non-positivism prevails, that official risks later prosecution.
  3. So [obeying lawful instructions] is not blameless: merely pointing to the role explains nothing (Thunder).
  • CONCEDE Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5). My answer: dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under official library policies, cannot plead the role.
12.6 Two-hats problem frame a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
  1. As an MP I would [vote against the bill and propose narrower measures]; as a judge I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and [without exception] catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.
  • Faith: addiction subverts practical reasonableness; but denying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity, so faith is a voice, not a ground.
  • Harm: Hart accepts paternalism; but it protects buyers, which supports licensing, not jail.
  • Poll: 85% at least "somewhat" support it; but that is not Devlin's real feeling of reprobation, so it is evidence, not mandate.
  • Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned. Critics' teetotallers: offence is selected morally.
  • JUDGE Read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH), so an as-applied claim is weak. The law is harsh, not intolerable: no BHC condemns prohibition.
Conclusion [The statement] is right only as a presumption: roles divide moral work, but no role ends moral duty.

1Start here: archetype 12 in plain English

Archetype 12 asks who gets to decide what, and how each person should stay within their role. It is the last archetype on the sheet, and it pulls the others together. It covers judges, legislators (MPs), officials and junior lawyers. It also covers one special exam format, the two-hats problem. A question describes a bill, then asks two things: as an MP, would you vote for it? And if it passed, would you, as a judge, enforce it?

The statements in this family sound like sober common sense. "Officials must respect the limits of their authority." "The legislator's sole concern is to express the majority's will." "A judge just applies whatever is validly passed." Each one treats the limits of a role as already settled, so that the only way to go wrong is to overstep them.

Your answer is the same every time. The statement is right as a presumption. A constitutional democracy divides power, so each role does have limits. But where a role ends is contested, and drawing that line is itself a moral judgement. A role can also fail in the opposite direction: refusing to do your own work (abdication) is as much a vice as taking over someone else's (usurpation). And a judge or official who refuses to enforce an intolerably unjust law is being faithful to law, not usurping anyone.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
UsurpationDoing another role's work. A judge who rewrites a statute because they prefer a different policy usurps Parliament's job.
AbdicationRefusing your own role's work. A judge who rubber-stamps every law, or an MP who just follows the latest poll, abdicates.
DeterminatioA natural-law idea used by Robert George. Where morality allows several acceptable options, someone must make a sensible choice among them. How a constitution shares power between courts and Parliament is one such choice.
Basically just regimeGeorge's condition. Natural law requires officials to respect the limits of their authority at least where the system as a whole is basically just.
Trustee v stenographerDistinction 1.3(15). A trustee MP uses their own judgement on the people's behalf. A stenographer just writes down what the majority wants.
Fidelity to lawFuller's idea. Being faithful to the law itself is different from obeying whoever ranks above you.
Radbruch thresholdThe point at which a statute's injustice becomes intolerable. Below it, unjust law is still law. Above it, for the judges and others who apply it, the statute is no longer law (8.3, 8.5).
Broad historical consensus (BHC)Tan Seow Hon's (TSH's) test for showing that a law has crossed the Radbruch threshold: long-lasting agreement across many jurisdictions, for the same reason. Genocide and slavery meet it. The abortion limits struck down in Roe did not (15.13).
Risk effectAlexy's point about officials in a rogue state. If the view that extreme injustice is not law wins out after the regime falls, an official who enforced its worst laws risks being prosecuted later.
Two-hats problemA question that asks you to answer as an MP and as a judge. The two roles ask different questions, so a "no" and a "yes" can both be right.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line reads: the statement is right as a presumption, since roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.

Put simply, start by respecting role limits. Judges should not make policy, officials should not make law, and lawyers should not police their clients' private morals. But do not treat those limits as obvious, and remember that hiding behind your role is a failure as well. A judge who says "not my place" to everything has not respected the judicial role. That judge has refused to perform it.

The Frame tells you where the statement usually comes from. It is almost word for word Robert George, as TSH reports him: at least in a basically just regime, natural law requires judges and other officials to respect the limits of their own authority. The exam version changes George in two ways. It drops his condition about a basically just regime, and it adds lawyers, whom George did not mention. Naming George in your first two sentences, and then asking whether his own condition survives, is the natural Hook: source from the menus (1.2).

The Intro turns this into your opening. The statement treats each role's limits as settled. Roles do have limits, but drawing them is a moral judgement. Refusing your own work is as much a vice as taking someone else's. And refusing extreme injustice is fidelity to law, not usurpation.

The Conclusion gives the verdict. The statement is right only as a presumption. Roles divide moral work between different people, but no role ends anyone's moral duty.

The steelman

A strong answer states the best case for the statement before testing it. Section 12 gives you one.

  • Steelman: role limits. The best case for the statement is that a constitutional democracy divides power. Two Singapore authorities support it. In Rajeevan (HC 1998), the court held that the legislature rightfully decides individual rights where the Constitution gives no specific guarantee (archetype 11 uses the same case in its steelman, Parliament decides). And in Yong Vui Kong (YVK, 2015), the Court of Appeal cited George for the view that natural law requires judges to respect the boundaries of their authority. This shows that restraint is the right presumption. It does not show that each role's limits are settled, or who gets to settle them.

The six blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
12.1"Respect the limits of your authority, and leave others what is rightfully theirs."That assumes we know where roles end. Deciding that is itself a judgement, and George leaves open who makes it.
12.2"Refusing instructions usurps. Leave it to Parliament."Every role can fail twice: by taking over others' work, or by refusing its own.
12.3"The legislator just expresses the majority's will."The majority decides who makes law, not what it should say. Even Devlin says counting heads is not enough.
12.4"Would you, as a judge, enforce it?"Climb a ladder: validity, interpretation, discretion. Refuse only at the Radbruch threshold. "I would enforce it" is a moral conclusion.
12.5"Officials just follow lawful instructions."Fidelity is owed to law, not to rank. Pointing to your role explains nothing.
12.6The two-hats problem (an alcohol ban).As an MP, vote against and propose narrower measures. As a judge, apply it if validly passed, unless it is intolerable.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Respect role limits as a presumption, but drawing them is a moral judgement, and abdication is a vice too.

2The big picture: who decides?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A football match has a referee, players, and a league that writes the rules. The referee should not rewrite the rules halfway through the game, because that is the league's job. But a referee who never blows the whistle, because "it's not my place", is failing too. Every role can fail in two directions. This last archetype asks how judges, MPs, officials and lawyers should each stay within their role without hiding behind it.

Earlier archetypes ask what the law should say, whether an unjust law is still law, and how judges and lawyers should work. Archetype 12 asks who should make each of these decisions, and what each person must do when the decision belongs to someone else. So it often appears alongside another archetype: a judge refusing an unjust law is archetype 8 and archetype 12 at once.

The players

WhoTheir position, in plain words
Robert George (as TSH reports him)A natural lawyer. In a basically just regime, natural law itself requires judges and officials to respect the limits of their authority. How authority is shared out is a determinatio, a sensible choice among morally acceptable options. So a judge who oversteps acts unjustly, even for what the judge believes is a good cause.
Tan Seow Hon (TSH)Accepts George's condition as right in principle, but asks the question he leaves open: who rightfully decides whether the allocation was prudently made? She also names both ways a judge can fail. Acting in bad faith, judges would either legislate from the bench or rubber-stamp whatever Parliament passes.
DevlinThe conservative in the Hart–Devlin debate (Lesson 7). Even he tells law-makers that a majority is not enough. His jury-box test asks what twelve people would unanimously condemn after discussion, and it does not count heads.
FullerFidelity to law is not deference to whoever holds power. Respect for constituted authority must not be confused with it.
AlexyThe risk effect. Under a rogue regime, even an ordinary official, neither saint nor hero, has a self-interested reason not to enforce extreme injustice, because a later court may treat that law as never having been law.
KennedyA critical legal scholar. When the law points one way and the judge's sense of justice points the other, the judge has five possible courses. Kennedy endorses or rules out none of them in advance.
ThunderA lawyer's role is justified only by what it contributes to justice and human flourishing. So merely pointing to your role explains nothing.

Key distinctions

  • Who decides v what is right (1.3(1)). This is the archetype's home distinction. Settling who may make a decision (Parliament, the courts, the people) is one question. Settling what the right decision is, is another. A democratic mandate answers the first question and leaves the second open.
  • Usurpation v abdication (1.3(11)). A role can fail by doing too much (taking over another role's work) or by doing too little (refusing its own). Most statements in this family warn only against the first failing.
  • Trustee v stenographer (1.3(15)). A trustee legislator judges on the people's behalf. A stenographer only records what the majority wants.
  • What the law should be v what fidelity to it requires. This is the two-hats distinction. The MP asks the first question. The judge asks the second. The same person can therefore vote against a bill and later enforce it without contradiction.

The Singapore picture

Singapore has answered "who decides?" again and again, and each answer was itself a choice: Rajeevan chose deference, Art 156 moved a question away from the courts, and the 2007 compromise left a law unused. Each choice can be defended, but none was obvious, and none was morally neutral.

⚠ TRAP
Credit the summary to TSH, and keep George's condition

The typical exam statement is George as TSH reports him, so say "as TSH reports George". And never present George as saying "always defer". His claim holds at least in a basically just regime. A statement that drops that condition is not George's claim, and pointing that out is your first move.

Words in a question that send you here

sale v consumption; supplysplit them: paternalism targets supply12.6, 7.2
