312.1 Source and frame

🧩 Practise 12.1 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 12.1 Source and frame (word for word)
12.1 Source and frame limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts
  1. [The statement] assumes we know where roles end; for George allocating authority is a determinatio, a prudent choice among morally acceptable options.
  2. TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: who rightfully decides whether it is prudentially made?
  3. So [what is rightfully others'] assumes its answer: a role's limits come from a theory of the role.
  • STEELMAN YVK (2015), citing George: some contend natural law requires judges to respect the boundaries of authority.
  • CONCEDE I concede TSH's impasse: natural law condemns vesting authority in a random group of bandits but cannot say who decides; still, the proviso must be right in principle.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Everyone should respect the limits of their authority." Sure, but where are the limits? The statement assumes we already know. George says the limits are set by a sensible choice built into the legal system. TSH asks: who decides whether that choice was sensible? That question has no easy answer, and the statement quietly assumes one.

What the statement claims

"Natural law requires that judges, lawyers and other officials respect the limits of their own authority, leaving to others what is rightfully theirs."
"That question is for Parliament, not the courts."

The statement presents itself as modesty. It assumes two things: that we know where each role ends, and that the speaker is entitled to say what is "rightfully" someone else's. It is tempting because a respected natural lawyer, Robert George, said something very close to it, and because in a working democracy it is usually good advice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The statement assumes we already know where each role ends. For George, the way authority is shared out between courts, Parliament and officials is a determinatio: a prudent choice among several morally acceptable options. Natural law does not dictate one arrangement. It requires that, once a basically just system has made its choice, its officials respect it.
  2. TSH asks the question George leaves open. If the allocation is a prudent choice, who rightfully decides whether it was prudently made? A court that reads its own powers widely and a Parliament that reads them narrowly are both making that judgement. Nothing in George's principle says which of them has the last word.
  3. So "what is rightfully others'" assumes its own answer. To say that a question belongs to Parliament, you need a view of what courts are for and what Parliament is for. The limits of a role come from a theory of the role, and a theory of the role is a moral argument.

The extra lines, explained

  • STEELMAN · YVK (2015) citing George. In Yong Vui Kong (2015), the Court of Appeal noted that some have argued natural law requires judges to respect the boundaries of their authority, and cited George. The same case held that a court cannot create a right, such as a right not to be caned, out of natural law when the Constitution does not contain it (11.2). This is the statement's best Singapore support. Use it to show you take restraint seriously, then ask whether YVK settles where the boundary lies. It does not: it tells judges to respect the boundary, not how to find it.
  • CONCEDE · TSH's impasse. Concede that TSH's question binds your side too. Natural law can rule out absurd allocations. It condemns handing authority to a random group of bandits. But it cannot say exactly who should decide hard questions. TSH admits there is no available formula (14.25). Still, she holds that George's condition, despite the impasse, must be right in principle. So your concession is honest but limited: the impasse shows the line is hard to draw, not that there is no line.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where is the boundary? Three readings of one sentence

The government tells a court: "Whether to allow assisted dying is rightfully for Parliament, not the courts."

ReadingWhat it assumes about the court's roleWhat it decides
Courts guard individual rightsThe court exists to protect individuals against majorities on fundamental rightsThe court must hear the claim on its merits
Courts defer on contested moralsThe court should leave contested moral questions to the elected body, as Rajeevan suggestsThe court presumes the ban valid
Courts act only at the extremeThe court defers, except where injustice is intolerable by broad historical consensus (11.5)The court presumes validity unless the ban is intolerably unjust by that test

Each reading is a theory of what courts are for. The words "rightfully for Parliament" choose one of them without saying so. That is line 3 of the block in action.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement is almost verbatim George, as TSH reports him, but it drops his condition that the regime be basically just, and it adds lawyers. For George, sharing out authority is a determinatio, a prudent choice among morally acceptable options, and in a basically just regime officials should respect it. That makes restraint the right presumption, as Rajeevan and YVK (2015) confirm. But TSH asks the question George leaves open: who rightfully decides whether the allocation was prudently made? To say what is "rightfully" another's, the statement must already hold a theory of each role, and that theory is a moral judgement, not a given.

412.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication

🧩 Practise 12.2 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication (word for word)
12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law
  1. Every role can fail twice, by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication); [the statement] names only the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: in bad faith they would legislate judicially or rubber-stamp whatever Parliament passes.
  3. So [respecting the limits of one's role] is half the duty; the other half is doing the role's own moral work.
  • OFFICIAL s 377A (2007), kept but not proactively enforced: arguably Parliament abdicated and the executive quasi-legislated (7.7).
  • JUDGE Bridge called stopping at decided cases an "unwarranted abdication" (McLoughlin; 2.8).
  • LAWYER Screening clients usurps (Pepper); simply focusing on the law abdicates (Thunder).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A judge can go wrong by acting like a legislator and inventing new law, or by rubber-stamping anything Parliament passes. An MP can go wrong by passing the buck. A lawyer can go wrong by refusing every client whose views she dislikes (taking over the law's job of deciding who gets its help), or by saying "I just do the law" (switching off her own conscience). Taking over and checking out are both failures.

What the statement claims

"Officials who refuse lawful instructions usurp others' authority."
"Leave it to Parliament." "Just focus on the law."

These statements name one danger only: overstepping. They assume that the safe course is always to do less, so that a role-holder who holds back can never be at fault. The block shows that holding back can be a failure too.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Every role can fail in two ways. It can do others' work (usurpation) or refuse its own (abdication). The statement mentions only the first, so it treats doing less as always safe.
  2. TSH names both failings for judges. Judges acting in bad faith, she says, would either legislate from the bench or rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes. The second is just as much a betrayal of the judicial role as the first.
  3. So respecting your role's limits is only half the duty. The other half is doing your role's own moral work. A judge must still judge, an MP must still decide, and a lawyer must still think about what the work is for.

The extra lines, explained

Section 12.2 gives one example for each kind of actor. Each shows that a single decision can involve both vices, or that the vice people forget is the one that matters.

  • OFFICIAL · the 2007 compromise. In 2007 Parliament kept s 377A, but the government announced that the police would not proactively enforce it. Arguably this was both vices at once. Parliament abdicated: it avoided deciding whether the conduct should really be a crime. And the executive quasi-legislated: by announcing non-enforcement, it changed the law in practice without changing the law on the books. Archetype 7 adds the costs. Fuller's requirement of congruence between law and official action was breached, and Hart warned that unenforced laws hand officials discriminatory power (7.7). Perera said in 2022 that an unenforced law resting on the government's word is unsatisfactory and dangerous.
  • JUDGE · Bridge in McLoughlin. In McLoughlin v O'Brian, a mother who was not at the scene of an accident saw her injured family in hospital hours later. The House of Lords held her shock recoverable. Lord Bridge said that refusing to go beyond the facts of the decided cases would be an unwarranted abdication (2.8). For a judge, standing still when principle requires the law to develop is not modesty. It is refusing the court's own job.
  • LAWYER · Pepper and Thunder. For a lawyer, the two vices map onto the two great theories of lawyering (Lesson 10). Screening clients by your own moral views usurps: Pepper argues that lawmakers, not lawyers, should decide what the law forbids, and that screening would create rule by an oligarchy of lawyers. Simply focusing on the law abdicates: Thunder uses that phrase to sum up the amoral view he rejects, because such a lawyer hands every moral question to the client.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Both vices, actor by actor
ActorUsurpation looks like…Abdication looks like…
JudgeStriking down a tax law because the judge thinks a flat tax is fairerUpholding every law because "it's not my place", or refusing to develop the law beyond decided cases (Bridge)
MPNot the usual risk, since deciding is Parliament's jobKeeping a law Parliament will not stand behind (2007), or handing every hard question to a poll (12.3)
OfficialAnnouncing that a law will not be enforced, which changes the law in practice (2007)Enforcing any instruction without asking what the law is for (12.5)
LawyerScreening clients by personal morals (Pepper's oligarchy of lawyers)"Just focus on the law" (Thunder's summary of the amoral view)

Read across each row. The statement's warning covers only the left-hand column. Your answer adds the right-hand column.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement names only one way a role can fail. Every role can fail twice: by doing others' work, which is usurpation, or by refusing its own, which is abdication. TSH names both for judges: acting in bad faith, they would either legislate from the bench or rubber-stamp whatever Parliament passes. Lord Bridge made the same point in McLoughlin, calling a refusal to go beyond the decided cases an unwarranted abdication. Respecting the limits of one's role is therefore only half the duty. The other half is doing the role's own moral work, and a judge who refuses intolerable injustice is doing exactly that, not usurping anyone.

512.3 Legislator's hat

🧩 Practise 12.3 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 12.3 Legislator's hat (word for word)
12.3 Legislator's hat majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what the law is or should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that a majority is not enough: his standard does not count heads.
  3. So the legislator does what [the sole concern] forbids: he judges, as a trustee, not a stenographer.
  • STEELMAN Equal respect amid disagreement and fear of juristocracy (TSH) support it. Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being a matter of social norm.
  • LEGISLATOR Masagos to Poa: MPs must decide even, perhaps especially, difficult and polarising social issues (2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: non-NLT legislators may not regard themselves as bound by higher standards. Arguably they will still weigh morality†: one who wants good, not merely valid, laws must (14.4's minimum content; Hart v Devlin). LP uses morality in one dimension (good law), NLT in two (good law, and law at all).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An MP is not a stenographer who just writes down what the majority wants. An MP is more like a trustee: elected to use their own judgement for the people. Even Devlin, the conservative who thought society may enforce its shared morality, said that a majority's opinion is not enough for a law-maker.

What the statement claims

"The legislator's sole concern is to express majoritarian will as accurately as possible: poll the people and, if needed, hold a referendum."

The statement turns the legislator into a measuring device. Its tempting point is democratic: in a democracy the people rule, so who is an MP to substitute their own views? Its words "sole concern" and "as accurately as possible" are what overreach.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Majority will decides who may make law in a democracy, not what the law should say. Elections tell you why this Parliament, and not some other body, gets to legislate. They do not tell you what a good law on legal aid, alcohol or marriage looks like. That is distinction 1.3(1), who decides v what is right.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, rejects it. Devlin is the theorist most willing to let law enforce a society's shared morality, so the statement would expect his support. Yet Devlin tells law-makers that a majority is not enough. His standard asks what twelve people chosen at random would unanimously condemn after discussion, and it deliberately does not count heads (15.6).
  3. So the legislator does exactly what "sole concern" forbids. An MP has to judge. The MP is a trustee, using judgement on the people's behalf, not a stenographer who transcribes their wishes (distinction 1.3(15)).

The extra lines, explained

  • STEELMAN · equal respect and fear of judges. The best case for following the majority has two parts. When citizens disagree deeply, counting each person's view equally shows them equal respect. And the alternative to the people deciding may be judges deciding, which TSH calls the risk of juristocracy (rule by judges). In Parliament in 2022, Poa of the Progress Singapore Party proposed a referendum on marriage, because marriage is a matter of social norm. Concede that this is serious. It shows the legislature must listen, and that courts should be slow to take questions away from it. It does not show that an MP's sole concern is to measure opinion.
  • LEGISLATOR · Masagos to Poa. Masagos answered Poa in the same debate. MPs, he said, must come to a decision even, and perhaps especially, on difficult and polarising social issues. This is the legislator's own voice for the trustee model: elected representatives have a duty to decide, not to pass the hardest questions back.
  • QUALIFY · need not, but will. TSH notes that legislators who do not hold natural-law views may not regard themselves as bound by any higher standard. That is true as far as it goes. A legal positivist need not consider morality to make a valid law. But such a legislator arguably will still weigh morality†, because anyone who wants good laws, and not merely valid ones, must. Hart shows this. He was a positivist, yet he held that every legal system needs a minimum content of natural law (rules against violence, theft and deceit, 14.4), and he spent a whole debate with Devlin arguing about what the law should be. The neat summary: legal positivism uses morality in one dimension (is this a good law?), while natural law uses it in two (is it a good law, and is it law at all?).
  • Fuller's warning about accuracy. A legislator who tracks a shifting majority "as accurately as possible" would change the law every time opinion moved. Fuller would say this breaks constancy, one of his eight requirements, like King Rex's daily amendments (3.7).
⚠ TRAP
Devlin is the ally who turns

Do not cite Devlin for majority will. He is the theorist the statement would expect to back it, and he refuses: for the law-maker, a majority is not enough. That reversal is the Hook: ally turns (1.2) in its purest form.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

The statement confuses who decides with what is right. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what that law should say. Even Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that a majority is not enough, since his standard asks what twelve people would condemn after discussion rather than counting heads. The strongest case for the statement is equal respect amid disagreement, and Poa's 2022 call for a referendum on marriage voiced it. But as Masagos replied, MPs have a duty to decide even, perhaps especially, polarising issues. The legislator therefore does what "sole concern" forbids: the MP judges, as a trustee, not a stenographer.

612.4 Judge's hat

12.4 Judge's hat if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law
  1. The judge asks not whether [the law] is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. I climb a ladder: validity, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then discretion within the statute; refusal comes only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So [I would enforce it] is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.
  • Kennedy's five courses (15.10): he endorses or excludes none "a priori". The public's "devil's compact" (defend as plausibly legal, change, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy insiders know is false; he is unconvinced that the rule of law means obeying it.
  • Candour, my standard, bars his covert last two. The refusal line is genocide and slavery, not the laws voided in Roe.
  • CONCEDE I concede TSH's own catch and adopt her reply (8.5).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A judge does not ask "is this law wise?" A judge asks "what is the law, and what does being faithful to it require?" Think of a ladder. First, check the law is valid. Then read it by its principles and purpose. Then use any discretion it leaves you. Only at the very top, where the law is monstrously unjust, may the judge refuse.

What the statement claims

"If the bill were passed, would you, as a judge, enforce it?"
"Judges must apply whatever is validly passed."

The question invites one of two lazy answers. One is "yes, because judges just apply the law", as if enforcing were morally empty. The other is "no, because the law is unwise", as if a judge could refuse any law the judge dislikes. The block steers between them.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. The judge does not ask whether the law is wise. That was the MP's question, and the MP has answered it. The judge asks what the law is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. The judge climbs a ladder. First, validity: was the law properly made and is it consistent with the Constitution? Second, interpretation: read it by its principles and purpose, not only its bare words. Third, discretion: use whatever room the statute leaves, for example in sentencing. Refusal comes only at the top, at the Radbruch threshold of intolerable injustice.
  3. So "I would enforce it" is a moral conclusion. It is reached through a theory of the judicial role: that a judge in a basically just system owes fidelity to valid law, read by its purpose, until injustice becomes intolerable. It is not a way of escaping morality.

The extra lines, explained

  • Kennedy's five courses. Duncan Kennedy imagines a judge whose sense of how the case should come out conflicts with the law. If the conflict survives the judge's best legal work, there are five courses, set out in the table below (15.10). The second, withdrawing, leaves the dirty work to another judge. Kennedy endorses or excludes none of them a priori, that is, in advance.
  • The devil's compact. Kennedy describes what the public assumes a judge has promised: either to show that the ruling is plausibly what the law requires, or to change the ruling, or to withdraw. He calls this the devil's compact, and argues that it presupposes a law far more determinate than insiders know it to be. He is also unconvinced that the rule of law simply means obeying the law (14.22).
  • Candour, the sheet's standard. Kennedy refuses to choose, but your answer must. Your standard is candour, and it rules out his last two courses, because both are covert: an argument you do not believe, and findings you know are false. So in a basically just system, take course (1) or (2). Course (3), deciding openly against the law, is open only at the Radbruch threshold.
  • The refusal line. Where is the threshold? TSH's test of broad historical consensus answers: genocide and slavery cross it. The abortion limits struck down in Roe did not (15.13).
  • CONCEDE · TSH's own catch. TSH admits a weakness in her test (8.5). Decades from now, the formula could be used to impose a worldwide trend, such as same-sex marriage, and where courts form judicial oligarchies, the consensus may reflect only a select group of judges. Concede the risk, then adopt her reply: an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority would do no better.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Kennedy's five courses, sorted by candour
CourseWhat the judge doesCandid?The sheet's verdict
(1) Go along, denouncingApplies the law, and says openly it is wrongYesAllowed in a basically just system
(2) WithdrawLeaves the case to another judgeYesAllowed in a basically just system
(3) Decide openly on what the law should beRefuses the law and says soYesOnly at the Radbruch threshold
(4) Implausible legal argumentReaches the result through reasoning the judge does not believeNoFails candour
(5) Find facts known to be falseRewrites the facts to escape the lawNoFails candour
⚠ TRAP
Five courses, never three

Kennedy's list has five courses, not three. The devil's compact (defend as legal, change, or withdraw) is the public's three-way bargain, which Kennedy criticises. Do not confuse the two. And remember that the five courses are a judge's options. They are not a junior lawyer's (10.7).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

As a judge, I would not ask whether the law is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires. I would climb a ladder: validity first, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then any discretion the statute leaves, with refusal only at the Radbruch threshold. Kennedy endorses or excludes none of his five courses in advance, but candour excludes his covert last two, an implausible argument and false findings of fact. The refusal line, shown by broad historical consensus, is genocide and slavery, not Roe. So "I would enforce it" is not an escape from morality but a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role.

712.5 Official's and junior's hat

🧩 Practise 12.5 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 12.5 Official's and junior's hat (word for word)
12.5 Official's and junior's hat officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
  1. Officials, like Fuller's citizens, owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: respect for constituted authority must not be confused with it.
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches a judge or other office-holder, neither saint nor hero: if non-positivism prevails, that official risks later prosecution.
  3. So [obeying lawful instructions] is not blameless: merely pointing to the role explains nothing (Thunder).
  • CONCEDE Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5). My answer: dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under official library policies, cannot plead the role.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A civil servant or a junior lawyer is told to do something lawful but wrong. "I was just following orders" is not a full answer, because loyalty to the law is not the same as obedience to your boss. Under a wicked regime, officials who go along may later be prosecuted, and they do not need to be heroes to see that coming.

What the statement claims

"Junior lawyers and public officials who carry out lawful instructions they believe to be unethical bear no moral responsibility; that lies with those who give the instructions." (Q100)
"Officials tasked with enforcing the law must follow lawful instructions."

The statement moves responsibility upwards. The person who acts is blameless because someone above them chose. It is tempting because organisations need discipline, and because juniors usually know less than their superiors.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank. Fuller made the point about citizens, and it applies to officials too: respect for those in authority must not be confused with fidelity to law. The instruction is lawful, but the official still owes something to the law and its purpose, not just to the person giving orders.
  2. Alexy's risk effect reaches ordinary officials. In a rogue state, a judge or other office-holder who is neither saint nor hero still has a reason not to enforce extreme injustice. If the view that such laws are not law (non-positivism) prevails after the regime falls, that official risks prosecution later. Alexy's point is that this works even on officials who care more about their own fate than about anyone else's.
  3. So obeying lawful instructions is not automatically blameless. As Thunder puts it, merely pointing to the role explains nothing. A role has to be justified by what it is for, and following an instruction is right only if the role, so understood, requires it.

The extra lines, explained

  • CONCEDE · virtue does not decide every case. Thunder admits that virtue under-determines cases: good people will disagree about particular hard cases (10.5). Concede it. Your answer is procedural: dialogue first, and refusal only at the extreme. That keeps the official from becoming a law unto themselves, which is the usurpation the statement fears.
  • Thunder's librarian. Thunder imagines a librarian who mistreats customers and says she is only following official library policies. She cannot plead the role. The example is deliberately mundane. Roles shape how you act, but they never make acting badly someone else's responsibility.
  • Juniors, specifically. Block 10.7 answers Q100 for junior lawyers. Legality settles what may be done, not who answers for it. So the junior shares responsibility, raises the issue first, and refuses only where the instruction would seriously harm others.

On the sheet's reasoning, the answer is no. The decree targets one group, which archetype 8 treats under Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† (8.8). Fidelity is owed to law, not to the superior, and Alexy's risk effect gives even a self-interested clerk a reason to refuse.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

Officials, like Fuller's citizens, owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: respect for constituted authority must not be confused with fidelity to law. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches even an ordinary office-holder, neither saint nor hero, who risks later prosecution if non-positivism prevails. Obeying lawful instructions is therefore not blameless, and as Thunder says, merely pointing to the role explains nothing, as his librarian shows. I concede, with Thunder, that virtue does not settle every case. So the official should raise concerns in dialogue first, and refuse only at the extreme.

812.6 Two-hats problem frame

🧩 Practise 12.6 on hypos →
▤ On your sheet: 12.6 Two-hats problem frame (word for word)
12.6 Two-hats problem frame a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
  1. As an MP I would [vote against the bill and propose narrower measures]; as a judge I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and [without exception] catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.
  • Faith: addiction subverts practical reasonableness; but denying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity, so faith is a voice, not a ground.
  • Harm: Hart accepts paternalism; but it protects buyers, which supports licensing, not jail.
  • Poll: 85% at least "somewhat" support it; but that is not Devlin's real feeling of reprobation, so it is evidence, not mandate.
  • Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned. Critics' teetotallers: offence is selected morally.
  • JUDGE Read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH), so an as-applied claim is weak. The law is harsh, not intolerable: no BHC condemns prohibition.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some questions describe a bill and ask you two things. Part A: as an MP, would you vote for it? Part B: if it passes, would you, as a judge, enforce it? You can answer "no" to A and "yes" to B without contradicting yourself. The MP asks what the law should be. The judge asks what being faithful to the law requires. Different jobs, different questions.

What the problem asks

Liu sets problems in this two-hats format†, and the sheet's trigger words include Ruritania, the imaginary country such problems may be set in. The sheet prepares you with an alcohol ban:

A bill proposes to ban the sale and consumption of alcohol, without exception, to protect families and public health. A poll finds 85% of citizens at least "somewhat" support it. (a) As a Member of Parliament, would you vote for it? (b) If it is passed, would you, as a judge, enforce it?

Supporters may also defend it on religious grounds, so the sheet tests three grounds: faith, harm and the poll.

The trap is to give one answer to both parts, either "it's a bad law, so I'd vote against it and refuse to apply it", or "Parliament passed it, so it must be fine". Both merge the two hats.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. Two hats, two answers. As an MP, vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. As a judge, apply it if it was validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage. It bans drinking as well as selling, and its words "without exception" would catch communion wine and temple wine. A narrower bill might be defensible. This one is not.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions. The MP asks what the law should be. The judge asks what fidelity to the law requires. Both are moral questions, and they can have different answers.

Part A: the MP's hat

The MP tests each ground for the bill in the same three steps: put the ground at its strongest (the steelman), test it, then give a verdict.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The three grounds, tested
GroundAt its strongestThe testVerdict
FaithAddiction undermines practical reasonableness, one of Finnis's basic goodsOne faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and even Devlin concedes that law cannot rest on doctrines citizens may disbelieve (7.10). Denying worship normally breaks Rawls's reciprocity, and this bill would stop communion and temple wine (15.5)A voice, not a ground
HarmHart accepts paternalism, as with restricting drug supplyHart's paternalism protects buyers whose consent may be clouded. That supports licensing sale, not jailing drinkers (7.2)Regulate sale, not consumption
Poll85% at least "somewhat" support the ban"Somewhat" is not Devlin's real feeling of reprobation (15.6). Disapproval is not a mandate to criminalise (7.11)Evidence, not a mandate

Part B: the judge's hat

Now the bill has passed. The judge does not reopen Part A. The judge climbs the ladder from 12.4.

The extra lines, explained

  • Faith, harm and poll. These three lines are the table above. Each one puts a ground at its strongest, then tests it. Reciprocity, in the faith line, is Rawls's test of whether others could accept a law as free and equal citizens.
  • Singapore texture · Yaacob and the teetotallers. Yaacob Ibrahim said in 2005 that drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned in Singapore. It is a Singapore reminder that the law does not ban everything one faith counts as a vice. Critics of the offence ground add the teetotallers: public drinking may offend them, yet the law ignores that offence. So which offences count is selected morally (TSH, citing Harris). Use one of these in Part A, under faith or harm.
  • JUDGE · Art 15 and the threshold. Art 15 protects religious freedom, and Art 15(4) lets general laws on public order, public health or morality limit it. ICCPR art 18(3) allows such limits only where they are necessary, but TSH notes that Art 15(4), read literally, has no such test (11.7). So a church's as-applied claim for communion wine is worth making, but weak. The law is harsh, not intolerable, because no broad historical consensus condemns prohibition, so the judge applies it.
The two-hats word budget
▤ Prep page 0.3 and 0.5
  1. 1Part A (MP), about 750 words: bill anatomy 100; the three grounds at about 180 each (steelman, test, verdict); vote and alternatives 100.
  2. 2Part B (judge), about 600 words: validity 100; the threshold 120; how to enforce 250; the obligation 80.
  3. 3Close, about 80 words: why the two answers differ.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready paragraph

As an MP I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. Its aims are legitimate, but its scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and "without exception" catches communion and temple wine. Its grounds fail the test. Faith is a voice, not a ground, harm supports licensing sale rather than jailing drinkers, and an 85% poll of "somewhat" support is evidence, not a mandate. As a judge, I would apply the Act if validly enacted, because it is harsh but not intolerable. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.

9Putting it together: a two-hats problem

The exact wording of Liu's own two-hats sample is not in your folder, so here is the problem from 12.6 again, now worked as a full answer:

A bill proposes to ban the sale and consumption of alcohol, without exception, to protect families and public health. A poll finds 85% of citizens at least "somewhat" support it. (a) As a Member of Parliament, would you vote for it? (b) If it is passed, would you, as a judge, enforce it?
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Part A opening (MP)

As an MP I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. Its aims, protecting families and public health, are legitimate, but its scope does the damage: it criminalises consumption as well as sale, and its "without exception" catches communion and temple wine. I test its three grounds in turn: faith, harm and the poll.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Part A body (three grounds, about 180 words each)
  1. Faith. Steelman: addiction undermines practical reasonableness (Finnis). Test: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others. Even Devlin concedes that law cannot rest on doctrines citizens may disbelieve, so the ban needs a secular reason. And denying worship normally breaks Rawls's reciprocity. Verdict: a voice, not a ground.
  2. Harm. Steelman: Hart accepts paternalism where consent is clouded. Test: paternalism protects buyers, so it supports licensing supply, not jailing drinkers, and Hart's offence ground does not reach private drinking (the teetotallers). Verdict: regulate sale.
  3. Poll. Steelman: majority rule treats citizens as equals. Test: "somewhat" support is not Devlin's real feeling of reprobation, and disapproval is not a mandate to criminalise (Hri Kumar, 2007). Verdict: evidence, not a mandate.

Vote and alternatives. Against. Propose licensing, age and hours limits, treatment, and an express exemption for worship.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Part B opening (judge)

As a judge I would enforce the Act if validly enacted. My question is no longer whether it is wise but what fidelity to it requires: validity first, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then any discretion the statute leaves, with refusal only at the Radbruch threshold, which a harsh prohibition does not reach.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Part B body
  • Validity (about 100 words). Passed by Parliament, and consistent with the Constitution, which Art 4 makes supreme.
  • Threshold (about 120 words). No broad historical consensus condemns prohibition, so it is harsh, not intolerable (15.13).
  • How to enforce (about 250 words). Consider an as-applied Art 15 claim for sacramental use, though Art 15(4) lacks a "necessary" test. Use sentencing discretion and read the penal provisions strictly. Candour bars Kennedy's covert courses.
  • Obligation (about 80 words). A legal duty to apply the Act. My moral disagreement goes into a judgment that applies the law while denouncing it (Kennedy's first course), not into refusal.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions. The MP asks what the law should be, and finds the bill's reasons too weak for the coercion it uses. The judge asks what fidelity to a validly enacted law requires, and finds the Act harsh but not intolerable. No role ends moral duty. Each assigns a different one.

10Recap

Archetype 12 on one card
▤ Sections 12.1–12.6
  1. 1The roles statement is George via TSH, minus his condition and plus lawyers. Who decides whether the allocation was prudent? (12.1).
  2. 2Twin vices: usurpation and abdication, for every actor (12.2).
  3. 3Legislator: who decides is not what is right. A trustee, not a stenographer. Need not consider morality, but will (12.3).
  4. 4Judge: the ladder, with refusal only at the threshold. Candour bars Kennedy's covert courses (12.4, 15.10).
  5. 5Officials and juniors: fidelity is not deference. The risk effect. The role is no excuse (12.5).
  6. 6Two hats: different questions, consistent answers (12.6).
🧠 MEMORY HOOK
One picture for the whole archetype

Picture a coat stand with two hats on it: an MP's rosette and a judge's wig. Under the stand is a line painted on the floor, marking where each role ends. Two warnings hang on the stand. One says don't step over the line (usurpation). The other says don't sit down on your side (abdication). And someone has scribbled beside the line: who painted this?
