13 Across topics

13.1 Comparisons
  • LP v Rawls on pluralism: both bracket contested morals, LP finding law in sources, Rawls legitimacy in shared political values. Neither is neutral: acceptance is LP's test, "reasonable" Rawls's filter; Finnis: some basic rights have one right answer.
  • Autonomy: Mill, Hart, Finnis and Pepper all value and bound it: Mill by harm to others; Hart allowing some paternalism; Finnis by practical reasonableness; Pepper, whose first-class citizenship serves it, by law alone, not the lawyer's morality, save "extreme cases".
  • Kennedy v chain novel: both put the judge inside inherited materials: fit and value constrain Dworkin's; work and credibility risk, Kennedy's. Kennedy starts from "how-I-want-to-come-out", Dworkin from the text†; Kennedy answers the right-answer thesis with felt indeterminacy and free ethical or political choice, disclaiming a verdict.
  • Fuller v RF: both deny enactment alone settles legality: Fuller tests form, the RF content. Fuller grades by degree, an unclear statute being "less a law"; the RF voids only "intolerable" injustice.
  • Religious freedom: Finnis and Rawls both protect it, neither neutrally: Finnis as a basic good, Rawls as equal liberty of conscience. Rawls takes religion's truths off the political agenda; Finnis values inquiry, whatever the answer.
  • Whose morality (obscenity, immoral contracts): beyond the judge's preference lie Devlin's right-minded man, Hart's critical morality (Devlin too invokes a "critical principle") and NLT's objective morality. Devlin: honest belief, "right or wrong"; TSH's judicial "option", not favoured in Rajeevan, lets judges filter incoherent opinions.
  • Finnis v liberalism: like liberalism, Finnis makes the common good a framework of conditions and limits the state to peace and justice; but he is not neutral: reason requires us to favour the basic goods, so he is liberal in means, not ends.
  • Finnis v Fuller: complementary: Fuller procedure, Finnis substance†. For Finnis, law treats citizens as partners in public reason by promulgation, clarity, generality and stability; he can condemn punitive retroactivity by its effects†.
  • Fuller v Hart on validity: compatible: Fuller tests form; Hart takes what officials accept, so Ordinance 11 may pass†.
  • Hart v Devlin: both usually spare private acts (7.3) but are not fully reconciled: Devlin can punish what meets none of Hart's grounds (his example: cruelty to animals; Hart: their suffering)†.
  • Devlin v Rawls, Finnis: all seek shared ground and "reasonable" judgement; but Rawls needs only enough overlap, Devlin deep agreement; Devlin's reasonable man feels, Finnis's reasons†.
13.2 Current controversies
  • s 377A repeal and Art 156 (2022)† Both took effect on 3 Jan 2023 (11.6, 16.4). This is the coercion gradient at work: punishment withdrawn, marriage promoted (15.7, 7.9).
  • QUALIFY Hart's lines survive: non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes; only private consensual adult conduct is freed (Shanmugam, 2022). Exercises: 16.5.
13.3 Core A: law-making and morality legislator questions
Spine No law on a moral question is neutral: permitting, punishing and promoting all take a stand. So pluralism cannot mean neutrality. It means discipline on three things: reasons (accessible to every citizen and sound on the merits), coercion (graded to the strength of those reasons) and forum (the legislature decides, as a trustee, not a stenographer).

P1 The state should be neutral · not endorse moral values; take no side; fixed conception; moral truth

  • Flaws F1 gap (therefore, however, only then, lest): hook word, thesis distinction · F2 absolute (only, all, simply, must): word, conditional · F3 self-refutation: self-application once, numbered · F4 equivocation: concession, conditional.

P2 Moral opinions are equally valid · equally valid; denial of moral truth; suspension of judgment; skeptical

  • VERDICT Neutrality of outcome is impossible, and even Rawls's neutrality of justification rests on moral values. The defensible kernel is narrower: the state should not make one comprehensive doctrine official, or coerce on reasons only its adherents can accept.
  • Hart partly agrees; Devlin rejects it; Rawls, the natural ally, accepts only the weak form; Finnis rejects the strong form but accepts a limit (6.2, 7.5, 6.10).

P3 Only harm to others justifies coercion · only; protect others; wrongdoer; objectively necessary

  • VERDICT Equal validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, which counsels deliberation, provisional judgment and caution in coercion, not silence.
  • Hart rejects it; Devlin partly accepts it, a dangerous ally; Rawls partly does†; Finnis rejects it, but not always for one right answer (4.2, 4.7, 6.10).

P4 A right to decide intimate matters · fundamental decisions; own destinies; intimate relationships; child rearing; private behaviour

  • VERDICT Harm to others is the right presumption for punishment, but it is not the only ground, and it is not a neutral fact: what counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions.
  • Hart partly agrees; Devlin rejects it; for Rawls it is the wrong test; Finnis partly agrees: a ground, not the only one, and he requires no ban on all that fails to pursue a good (7.1, 7.2, 6.10).

P5 Majority or societal morality · majority; majoritarian will; certain groups; minority rights; poll

  • VERDICT The right is real, but it is itself a moral claim with moral limits. It rules out punishing private consensual conduct for its immorality alone. It does not rule out regulation or promotion, and it cannot settle cases where a third party, the child or the unborn, is at stake.
  • Hart largely agrees; Devlin rejects it in principle but often agrees in practice; Rawls and Finnis partly agree (4.5, 7.9).

P6 Enforcing morality is (il)legitimate · legislating morals; unjust; illegitimate; intractable moral conflicts

  • VERDICT The majority settles who decides, not what is right. Majority feeling is evidence to weigh, never the reason that settles the law; and protecting minorities is itself a moral judgment, not an escape from one.
  • Hart rejects it as a reason; Devlin, the natural ally, refuses to count heads; Rawls rejects it; Finnis rejects it from the other side (7.3, 7.11, 12.3).
  • VERDICT Enforcing morality is not illegitimate as such, since every law enforces some morality. What can make it unjust is the reasons used, the coercion chosen and who bears it. So the limits are moral and prudential, not sceptical.
  • Devlin and Finnis hold enforcement legitimate; Hart and Rawls only in part (7.5, 7.9).
  • Pivots Neutrality is impossible (6.5, 7.5). · The coercion gradient applies (7.9). · Majority is not legitimacy (7.11, 12.3). · Scepticism is answered (4.7). · "Fixed" is a matter of degree: no theorist here imposes one complete life-plan, and each fixes some limits.
  • Repaired (one per script) Neutrality: Legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine. · Harm: Legislators should presume against punishing conduct that harms no one else, and need stronger reasons the more coercive the law. · Autonomy: Choices about one's intimate life deserve strong protection from punishment, but not immunity from all regulation, or from the state's promotion of other goods. · Majority: The majority decides, but must decide on reasons it can defend to the minority. · Enforcement: Enforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate; scepticism is no objection, but fallibility is a reason for restraint.
13.4 Core B: judges, lawyers and morality judge and lawyer questions
Spine No judge or lawyer works without theory or morality: identifying the law is already an evaluation, hard cases turn on rival theories of law's grounds, and every role is justified by what it is for. But that makes legal work neither preference nor private conscience. Morality is presupposed always, operative at the margins (hard cases, intolerable injustice), and disciplined by role: fit and candour for judges, the law as a floor for lawyers.

Q1 Judges only apply the law · no substantive moral judgments; only what the law is; I just apply the law

Q2 Adjudication is politics · politics; pretence; rules don't decide; essentially

  • VERDICT Morality is always presupposed in judging and sometimes operative: presupposed in legality and in every claim that a ruling is correct; operative in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. A judge concerned only with what the law is already holds a theory of what law is.
  • Hart partly agrees; Dworkin rejects it; the realists reject it for a different reason; TSH rejects it for constitutional cases (9.8, 11.2, 11.3).

Q3 Theory is irrelevant to practice · theory isn't relevant; just do your job; no practical need

  • VERDICT Adjudication is political in Dworkin's sense, because where fit runs out judges choose between principles of political morality. It is not politics in the partisan sense that "pretence" needs: rules leave some cases open, not all, and judges must justify, not predict.
  • The realists partly agree; Unger and the crits agree in part; Kennedy, the most honest witness, partly agrees; Dworkin rejects the partisan reading (9.1, 9.3, 9.7).

Q4 Lawyers serve clients within the law · client; lawful; adversarial system; hired gun

  • VERDICT True in a weak sense: lawyers rarely cite theory, and most cases are easy. False in the strong sense: every lawyer acts on a theory of what law is and what the role permits, and the only choice is between examined and unexamined theory.
  • Fish partly agrees; Dworkin rejects it; Thunder rejects it and names the source; positivism rejects it even on its own terms (2.6, 10.8, 10.10).

Q5 Stay within your role · limits of their own authority; usurp; officials; for Parliament, not the courts

  • VERDICT The lawyer's role is itself moral, and law sets its floor, not its ceiling. Above the floor, prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases; Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.
  • Pepper agrees, on moral grounds, but his own limits undercut him; Thunder rejects it; the three scenarios† are a test, not a side (10.1, 10.2, 10.11).

Q6 Law and justice · rule of law; essence; certainty, procedure; necessarily connected

  • VERDICT Right as a presumption: a constitutional democracy divides power, so roles have limits. But where a role ends is contested, abdication is as much a vice as usurpation, and refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation.
  • George and TSH agree, then TSH asks who decides; TSH's twin vices add the missing half; for Fuller fidelity is not deference; Alexy and Kennedy address the outer limit (12.1, 12.2, 12.4, 12.5).
  • VERDICT Justice is the rule of law's point and its outer limit; certainty and procedure are its everyday content. Validity never settles obedience, and only intolerable injustice defeats legal character.
  • Fuller partly agrees; Hart separates them, for candour; Radbruch and Alexy allow a narrow link; TSH disciplines that link for courts (3.3, 8.2, 8.5).
  • Pivots Morality is presupposed, not always operative (9.8). · Easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9). · Law is a floor, not a ceiling (11.7). · Roles have twin vices (12.2). · The judge's hat (12.4). · On practical need, concede that extremes are rare; the law still leaves several lawful paths, above all for lawyers, and cannot choose between them (11.1, 10.7).
  • Repaired (one per script) Judges: Judges should not decide by personal conviction; they bring political morality to bear through fit and candour, and override the law only at intolerable injustice. · Politics: Adjudication is political in the sense of political morality, not partisanship; where the rules leave a case open, judges must justify, not pretend. · Theory: Lawyers need not cite theory, but they cannot practise without one; the choice is between examined and unexamined theory. · Lawyers: A lawyer serves the client within the law, but the law is a floor: dialogue above it, and refusal only at the extremes. · Roles: Legal actors should respect the limits of their roles and do their roles' own moral work, refusing only intolerable injustice. · Rule of law: use the Q6 verdict.
13.5 Core C: what law is, and what we owe it nature of law; citizens
Spine People make law, so its sources can be found by looking. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation, and finding the law never settles what it should be or what anyone should do. Keep three questions apart: what counts as law (sources, plus for non-positivists a narrow moral limit), what the law should be (reasons, not facts about opinion) and what I owe it (a moral question on every theory, with a strong default of obedience).

L1 Law is a social fact · made by human beings; social fact; what people accept; whatever is enacted

L2 No necessary link between law and morality · absurd; necessarily connected; law is law

  • VERDICT Law's sources are facts, and usually a lawyer needs no more. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation. Law is a social fact only on a theory of what law is.
  • Hart agrees, more narrowly; natural law accepts the premise but denies the conclusion; Dworkin rejects it; for TSH naming law is an evaluation† (2.1, 2.5).

L3 Facts about opinion settle the debate · positions and views; solely concerned; as a matter of fact; naturally follows

  • VERDICT "Absurd" fails: a narrow necessary link is a serious position. But the link that survives is weak. Only extreme injustice defeats legal character, and ordinary unjust laws stay law.
  • Hart agrees, with care; Fuller rejects it, thinly; Radbruch and Alexy reject it, narrowly; Finnis and weak natural law reject "absurd" but keep the distinction (2.3, 8.2, 8.3).

L4 Law is simply will or power · simply an expression; majoritarian will; command; whatever Parliament enacts

  • VERDICT Facts about what people think are evidence to weigh, and they fix the stakes. They cannot settle what the law should be, because no ought follows from an is alone.
  • Hart rejects it; Devlin, the nearest ally, stops short; Rawls starts from a fact and ends with a norm; Finnis rejects it outright (4.4, 6.3, 7.1).

L5 Valid law must be obeyed · validly-enacted; obligation to obey; recipe for disaster; chaos

  • VERDICT Will makes law only through rules that officials accept and that also bind the will. Law is more than what the strongest or the most want, which is why we can criticise them by it.
  • Austin agrees, crudely; Hart and Fuller reject it; TSH rejects it for Singapore (3.7, 12.3, 14.3).

L6 A moral link licenses private disobedience · own moral reasoning; justifiably disobey; conscience; who decides

  • VERDICT There is a strong default of obedience, but it is a moral default: validity only tells us the rule is law. It can be defeated, though only by grave injustice, not by disagreement.
  • Hart separates the questions; Fuller grounds obedience in reciprocity; Radbruch and Alexy set a default, then a threshold; Aquinas and Finnis deny that unjust law binds in conscience, with a brake (8.7, 3.7).
  • VERDICT The licence, if it is one, is not peculiar to those who link law and morality. Every theory leaves room for moral refusal and every serious one confines it. The real problem is who decides.
  • Hart gives the same licence, stated honestly; Alexy rejects the target; TSH accepts the question of who decides; for Fuller the risk runs both ways (8.2, 8.7, 12.1).
  • Pivots What people made is not what they should make (4.4). · A social fact is not public opinion: sources v positive morality (12.3, 7.1). · Obedience raises three questions (8.7). · The formula is a threshold, not a licence (8.2, 8.5).
  • Repaired (one per script) Social fact: Law's sources are matters of social fact, but what law should be is not, and facts about opinion are evidence to weigh, never the answer. · Necessary link: Law and morality may be separable in identifying most law, but validity never settles obedience; extreme injustice is the narrow case where the two questions meet. · Disobedience: Citizens owe a strong moral duty to obey, which grave injustice can defeat and mere disagreement cannot. · Will: Majority will settles who may make law, within rules that bind it; it does not settle what the law should say.
13.6 Core D: testing a theory on a new issue soundness; "[X]'s theory"; bear on this debate; the best way
Spine A theory is not refuted by needing moral judgment, or by failing to dictate an answer. Each of these four supplies a question, not a verdict: Rawls asks which reasons, Finnis asks what the act does to a basic good, Hart asks what justifies this coercion, and Devlin asks what society can tolerate. So test a theory three ways: does it hold together, does it give a defensible answer on the hard case, and does it beat its rivals?
  • Tasks Assess a theory: cards 14.8, 14.10, 14.13, 14.15. Apply it: say what it rules out, what it requires and what it leaves open (16.5). Compare: "best" needs a rival, a job and a cost.
  • Pivots Needing moral judgment is fatal only if the theory promised to avoid it (14.13). · A framework needs inputs, so "demands" is usually wrong. · Sound means it holds together, answers the hard case and beats its rivals. · Of the four, Hart limits punishment most tightly but says little on promotion (7.9).
  • Repaired (one per script) Autonomy: Autonomy deserves great weight in the common good, but it demands no particular law; Parliament must decide on reasons those who disagree can examine, and protect those whose consent is least free. · Hart: Hart's theory needs moral judgment, which is no objection to it, and it limits punishment more tightly than Devlin, Finnis or Rawls; it is not a complete account of what law may do. · Named theory: [Theory] sets a sound discipline on [reasons / coercion], but its contested premise means it cannot settle [the issue] alone.

14 Theorist bank I

14.1 Fish use: 2.6, 10.5, 10.8
  • PURPOSE Is theory useless to a lawyer, beyond doctrine and tactics?
  • CLAIM Practice marshals doctrine inside a purposive enterprise informed by a vision of how the state may and may not use its monopoly of legalised violence.
  • STRENGTH Searle's football: brute description misses the game; an expert's field is already configured by understanding what is at stake.
  • CRITIQUE The complaint Segal reports: law school, jurisprudence included, never taught the tricks of the trade. Reply: those tricks amount to little without knowing what the trade is.
  • SAY Law is a practice but also a subject.
  • VERDICT Fish is right that practice presupposes a view of the state's force, but he never says which view is true.
14.2 NLT and Aquinas use: 2.1, 2.3, 2.8, 8.7, 11.2
  • PURPOSE Must law meet a higher standard, knowable by reason, to bind?
  • CLAIM Human law binds so far as it derives from natural law, by deduction or determination; law contrary to it is defective as law.
  • TEST Aquinas: unjust law is a corruption of law, though obedience is owed perhaps in special cases, to avoid scandal or danger; Finnis: it merely lacks prima facie power to bind in conscience; TSH: manifestly unjust law is no law.
  • CRITIQUE TSH asks who may pronounce on higher law's content. Reply: discernment, unlike fiat, must cohere and stay revisable.
  • VERDICT Natural law explains why some enactments fail as law, but must first settle who decides.
14.3 Austin use: 2.2, 8.7, 11.1, 12.3
  • PURPOSE What is law, as a fact, without moral premises?
  • CLAIM Law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed and obeying no one, backed by a sanction.
  • STRENGTH Candour: law's existence is one thing, its merit another.
  • CRITIQUE Hart: habits miss the internal "ought", and power-conferring rules enable rather than require. Reply: Dworkin grants that Austin's main idea, restated by Hart, has never wholly lost its grip.
  • SG Against [the sovereign is simply Parliament]: Art 4 voids statutes to the extent they are inconsistent with the Constitution (TSH; 11.1).
  • VERDICT Austin is honest that wicked law gets enforced, but commands and habitual obedience cannot explain why officials treat law as binding.
14.4 Hart: concept of law use: 2.1, 2.2, 11.1, 11.7, 12.3
  • PURPOSE Why do lawyers say "ought" if law is neither command nor morality?
  • CLAIM Law is the union of primary duty rules and secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication, which officials accept from an internal point of view.
  • TEST A system exists when primary rules are generally obeyed and officials accept secondary rules, which cure uncertainty, rigidity and diffuse pressure; soft positivism lets the rule of recognition contingently adopt moral tests.
  • CRITIQUE Dworkin: many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler only from fear: if that is acceptance, Hart nears Austin; if not, there was no law in Nazi Germany. Reply: acceptance even from fear, self-interest or habit still treats rules as standards.
  • CRITIQUE TSH: only officials need accept, so Hart may be little different from the power view, and LP is not necessarily democratic. Reply: describing law is not praising it.
  • SAY Hart's "critical reflective attitude"; where only officials accept, the sheep may end in the slaughter-house.
  • TRAP Hart's minimum content of natural law is no legality test: people do not belong to suicide clubs, so every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit, a practical necessity, unlike Radbruch's override†. Harris: a "sociological" conception, consistent with institutionalised slavery or racial oppression.
  • VERDICT Hart maps a working legal system most accurately, yet deciding what the map shows is already an evaluation.
14.5 Dworkin use: 2.4, 2.5, 9.2, 9.5, 9.10
  • PURPOSE Why do judges disagree about the law, and what constrains them in hard cases?
  • CLAIM Law is interpretive: judges read the legal record by fit and political value, so law is political but never personal or partisan.
  • TEST A reading must fit the practice and show its point or value; where several fit, political morality decides.
  • STRENGTH It explains theoretical disagreement, which the plain-fact view cannot, though Dworkin is arguably unfair to LP† (2.5).
  • CRITIQUE Realists and crits: fit leaves readings open, so value is the judge's politics. Reply: Dworkin concedes fit often yields no unique interpretation, not that law is "personal or partisan".
  • CONCEDE A judge's best reading rests on contestable beliefs (9.5), and integrity gives no exit from a wicked legal history (2.4). I concede both; Radbruch guards the outer limit (14.19).
  • SG LMS (CA) invoked "a central motif" of Dworkin's theory to disregard extra-legal considerations within the Legislature's purview; the principle v policy reading is TSH's surmise.
  • SAY Law is deeply and thoroughly political.
  • VERDICT Dworkin best explains how principle constrains hard cases, granted that fit often cannot settle them alone.
14.6 Fuller use: 3, 8.7, 2.4, 13.1
  • PURPOSE What separates law from naked power, and why do failures of form wrong citizens?
  • CLAIM Law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight desiderata.
  • TEST → 15.1.
  • STRENGTH It binds lawmakers first: being at the top of the chain of command "intensifies" their duty of legality.
  • CRITIQUE Is it about morality at all, or efficacy†? Reply: legality respects responsible agents† and grounds the duty by reciprocity (3.3).
  • CONCEDE Legality is thin: a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. I concede it and let the Radbruch formula test content (13.1).
  • SAY A secret statute is the greatest legal monstrosity; balancing the eight requirements takes a lawgiver's skill.
  • TRAP Fuller's remark that not all cases are hard concerns legality, not adjudication. Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula; he asks how much of a legal system survived.
  • VERDICT Fuller shows legality is a genuine but modest morality binding rulers, not that it makes their laws just.
14.7 TSH: moral subjectivism use: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, 4.7
  • PURPOSE Is morality a matter of personal or cultural opinion, and can subjectivists argue with anyone?
  • CLAIM Subjectivists cannot hold others to any standard independent of their belief without ceasing to be subjectivists, so their moral dialogue is gravely limited.
  • TEST Does a sceptic's premise bind someone who rejects it? A relativist who binds outsiders invokes a "meta-cultural standard"; if it honours equal moral worth, that relativist is a moral realist.
  • STRENGTH Genocide hypothetical: moral dialogue breaks down. If all may do as they please, everyone becomes "equally worthless"; concede limits and the subjectivist is just another moral realist.
  • CRITIQUE Epistemic sceptics (TSH's second kind) ask who knows the moral facts. Reply: a legitimate variant, but a dead end for law-making; Finnis's goods offer a way forward† (14.8); realism commits one to deliberation, with judgements held more provisionally.
  • CONCEDE She shows that subjectivists' moral dialogue is "gravely limited", not which realist content is right (4.2).
  • VERDICT TSH shows that a subjectivist who holds others to a standard must give up subjectivism and that subjectivism's case is inconclusive, not that moral facts exist; how we know what is right is left to deliberation.
14.8 Finnis use: 5, 6.2, 6.5, 2.3, 4.4
  • PURPOSE What makes choices and laws reasonable, without deriving "ought" from nature?
  • TEST → 15.3, 15.4.
  • STRENGTH Finnis guides legislators without a state life-plan, and can condemn a law most people approve (5, Steelman: for Finnis).
  • CRITIQUE Method and the seventh requirement are his weak points (5, Steelman: against Finnis; 5.7); since consent cannot cure intended harm, the means/side-effect line is a heavy limit on autonomy†. Reply: there is no magic in the number seven, dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", and Harris calls the method reasoning, not logical necessity.
  • VERDICT Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
14.10 Rawls use: 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.11, 13.1
  • PURPOSE When is coercion legitimate among citizens who reasonably disagree about the good?
  • TEST See 15.5. Reciprocity requires reasons others might reasonably accept.
  • STRENGTH Rawls explains how a law can bind people who reject its premises. He favours no doctrine a priori, and public reason is not "secular reason": secular comprehensive doctrines are limited in the same way.
  • CRITIQUE Finnis poses a dilemma (6.1) and calls the legitimacy principle illegitimate, unreasonable and uncivil, leaving the gravest questions to sheer numbers or influence. "Reasonable" needs a standard external to the citizens (TSH). On abortion Rawls retreated (6.5). Reply: his standard is moral though political, not a head-count, and Finnis grants that reciprocity seems broadly reasonable. The dispute is who is reasonable.
  • VERDICT Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, but deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side, and public reason may still end in a vote.
14.11 TSH: religion and public reason use: 6.4, 6.5, 6.7
  • PURPOSE In a multi-religious democracy, may law-makers rely on religious arguments?
  • CLAIM Judge arguments by their accessibility and merit, not their religious motive; bracketing a metaphysical question already answers it.
  • CRITIQUE Rawls: using state power against reasonable dissenters is "unreasonable or worse". Reply: she asks only for accessible reasons; the line around a political sphere is artificial.
  • CONCEDE Her close (6.5) suggests a "pragmatic strategy" of arguing from consequences. I concede that principle alone may not move Parliament.
  • SAY This shatters the illusion of an accommodative solution.
  • VERDICT TSH exposes the unfairness of sorting arguments by motive, but not how a divided Parliament should settle contested questions.
14.12 Mill and Wolfenden use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.5
  • PURPOSE What may the criminal law prohibit: only harm to others, or private immorality too?
  • CLAIM Coercion is justified only to prevent harm to others; private immorality that neither harms nor offends in public is not the criminal law's concern.
  • TEST Wolfenden: preserve public order and decency, protect citizens from the offensive or injurious, and safeguard the vulnerable against exploitation or corruption.
  • STRENGTH Free choice may be valuable in itself, or because it lets individuals "experiment" in living (Hart).
  • CRITIQUE Devlin: consent is no defence to murder or assault, so the law already enforces moral principle. Reply: for Hart such rules can be paternalist, not moralist.
  • CRITIQUE TSH: "harm" and "self-regarding" are indeterminate, and if only legal interests count, the argument looks circular. Reply: the harm line needs moral argument, openly made.
  • SG Shanmugam (2022): Singapore's position is "broadly similar" to Wolfenden's (7.5).
  • SAY A realm of private immorality is not the law's business (Wolfenden).
  • VERDICT Mill and Wolfenden rightly make liberty the default, but cannot draw the harm line without moral argument.
14.13 Hart: Law, Liberty and Morality use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.9
  • PURPOSE May the criminal law enforce morality as such, beyond preventing harm to others?
  • TEST → 15.7.
  • STRENGTH Hart asks the right question (7.1). He finds no evidence for disintegration, which merits no more respect than Justinian's statement on earthquakes. Bigamy may be punished as a nuisance, not as irreligious or immoral.
  • CRITIQUE TSH: paternalism is ultimately "based on morals", since morals pick its targets (7.2). "Harm" is indeterminate (14.12), and teetotallers can be offended too. Reply: Hart can grant that applying his grounds takes moral judgment; he denies only that immorality as such is a reason to punish†.
  • VERDICT Hart wins against punishing private immorality as such, but moral judgment still decides where his paternalism and decency bite.
14.15 Devlin use: 7.3, 7.4, 15.6
  • PURPOSE May society enforce its shared morality by law, and how is it found?
  • TEST → 15.6.
  • STRENGTH Devlin rightly denies that law is morally neutral: consent is no defence to murder because the offence is against society.
  • CRITIQUE Hart: no evidence that private deviation threatens society. Devlin argues as a cultural relativist†: monogamy binds because it is built into the house we live in, so a persecuting society has the same claim. Pluralist Singapore may lack the consensus he presupposes†. Reply: he says only that immorality can threaten society, and that if morality changes the law can change. But if it only can, why harsh sanctions now†?
  • SAY The "invisible bonds" of common thought hold society together.
  • TRAP Honest belief, "right or wrong", makes immorality a question of fact; privacy is only to be taken into account.
  • VERDICT Devlin leaves much to individual morality in practice, but he lets common feeling, not reason, fix what the law enforces.
14.16 TSH: Pragmatism use: 7.6, 7.7
  • PURPOSE What is criminal law for, and what did the 2007 compromise settle?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that we "simply cannot shun" the moral question: by 2007 the camps arguably clashed over what is right.
  • TEST Six functions: harm; paternalism; public decency; averting disintegration; morals as intrinsically good; moral ecology.
  • CONCEDE The map ranks no function, and her principled slope may read as advocacy; I concede both and rank functions with Hart or Finnis.
  • TRAP "Tangible harm" is TSH's summary of the retention case, not retentionists' words.
  • VERDICT TSH's map is the best diagnostic: it shows the moral question unavoidable without answering it.
14.18 Hart: separation (1958) use: 8.1, 8.2, 8.7
  • PURPOSE Should an iniquitous rule be denied the name of law, or called law and condemned?
  • CLAIM Hart separates law as it is from law as it ought to be: validity never settles whether to obey.
  • TEST If punishment needs retroactivity, choose openly "between two evils" by statute.
  • STRENGTH Calling it law but too evil to obey is among the most powerful moral criticisms because the simplest.
  • CRITIQUE Fuller: positivism never gives fidelity to law a coherent meaning; the question then seems to be who should do the dirty work. Reply: only a statute sacrifices a principle openly; the bridge to obedience is moral (8.7).
  • CRITIQUE Alexy: where the injustice was evident at the time, the court ascertains the law then in force, so there is no covert retroactivity. Reply: even Alexy grants that candour is the strongest objection (8.3).
  • SAY Candour is no minor virtue.
  • TRAP Hart wrongly supposed Bamberg voided a 1934 statute, as he later conceded (Alexy).
  • VERDICT Hart wins on labels for observers and historians; a judge deciding today needs more than candour.
14.19 Radbruch and Alexy use: 8.3, 8.4
  • PURPOSE Does extreme injustice strip a norm of legal character, and for whom?
  • CLAIM Positive law prevails even when unjust, unless its injustice reaches an "intolerable degree" (Alexy); then, for the participant, it is not law.
  • TEST See 8.3. A participant is eg the court, the lawyer or the law's addressee†; Alexy's example is the judge.
  • STRENGTH Every judicial decision necessarily claims correctness, which extreme injustice cannot meet.
  • STRENGTH Neither side argues truth, only desirability, and the practical case is "a wash": on what basis should we decide†? Alexy: the objections were answered well enough to tie the score; the risk effect, necessity after a regime collapses and fit with nulla poena break the tie.
  • CRITIQUE Hart: Radbruch only half digested liberalism's spiritual message. Reply: Fuller credits him with seeing the dilemma as order against "good order".
  • CONCEDE Answering relativism needs a rational justification for some minimum moral requirements. I concede the formula is only as sound as that core; TSH's BHC (14.26) disciplines judges but is evidence, not proof.
  • SAY Positivism left jurist and people alike defenceless (Radbruch, in Alexy).
  • TRAP Radbruch did not oppose denying legal quality; he warned of its "frightful dangers", and for the informers he too preferred a retroactive statute. "Not law" at tier 2 (8.8) is Alexy's reading; BHC is TSH's test, not Alexy's.
  • VERDICT The formula earns its place as a narrow backstop, if its minimum core can be defended without counting votes.
14.22 Kennedy use: 12.4, 15.10, 13.1
  • PURPOSE What is judging like when law and the judge's sense of justice conflict?
  • CLAIM Kennedy's judge is neither simply bound nor free: law is a medium that constrains, but what it rules out depends on the judge's project.
  • TEST Strikers' lie-in: the rule at first seems to apply itself; the judge then works it toward "how-I-want-to-come-out", paying in time and "legitimacy cost".
  • STRENGTH Legality requires building the best case for the other side; what would betray it is the wrong attitude at the end. Sometimes the rule is "a felt objectivity" he "can't budge".
  • CRITIQUE Hart, against rule sceptics: rules have a core of central meaning. Reply: how much of a field is open, in itself, is simply unanswerable.
  • SAY Work may be deployed in any direction, but the field is oneself, resisting oneself.
  • TRAP Five courses, never three: 15.10, 12.4. Against the right-answer thesis he sets experience of free ethical or political choice, not a thesis.
  • VERDICT Kennedy describes judging more honestly than he justifies it: he shows the choice is moral, then leaves it "for another time".
14.23 Pepper use: 10.1, 10.3, 15.11
  • PURPOSE May a lawyer help a client do lawful things the lawyer thinks immoral?
  • CLAIM Pepper argues that lawful help is morally justified because access to law serves autonomy and equality; the client, not the lawyer, is accountable.
  • TEST See 15.11. Law is a public good available to all; autonomy is "a moral good"; access needs lawyers, so screening means rule by an oligarchy of lawyers.
  • STRENGTH Equality: screening would compound inequality; conduct bad enough should, it seems, be made explicitly unlawful.
  • CRITIQUE Pepper's own problem: realism plus the amoral role leaves no moral input or constraint. Reply: he keeps dialogue, choice of client, and conscientious objection "rarely exercised".
  • CRITIQUE Why is an institutional wrong more acceptable than a personal one, and is the institution justified†? Reply: first-class citizenship justifies it.
  • SAY Morality comes through the door as part of the client; the lawyer can be good, though uncomfortable.
  • VERDICT Pepper justifies access to law, not every service: his own exceptions leave the lawyer a conscience the role cannot silence.
14.24 Thunder use: 10.4, 10.10, 12.5
  • PURPOSE Can a good person be a lawyer without splitting professional from personal ethics?
  • CLAIM Thunder holds that a lawyer's role is justified only by its contribution to justice and flourishing, so the good lawyer stays a good person.
  • TEST Natural-teleological view: law aims ultimately, if not always immediately, at natural goods such as justice; the lawyer's function is to further justice, public order and the rule of law.
  • STRENGTH Diagnosis: the amoral view draws its appeal primarily from two "unwitting collaborators", neo-Kantian rule-morality and legal realism.
  • CRITIQUE Pepper: screening means rule by an oligarchy of lawyers. Reply: access to law is not access unchecked by others' judgment; projects are properly "hampered".
  • CONCEDE Thunder admits disagreement on particular cases and that integrity is rarely if ever fully achieved. I concede he guides character more than cases; I send hard cases to dialogue, refusing only at the extremes (10).
  • SAY Amoral lawyers become slaves of their clients' consciences, however warped.
  • TRAP Thunder's line about simply focusing on the law voices the amoral view he rejects, as does the practice question's call to just do your job.
  • VERDICT Thunder says better than Pepper what lawyers are for, but virtue names the goal without deciding the hard case.
14.25 TSH: Constitutional Jurisprudence use: 11.1, 11.7, 12.1
  • PURPOSE Does a written, supreme Constitution make Singapore positivist?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that no declaration of supremacy can settle the natural law–positivism debate: contested terms force a choice of school, and constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  • TEST Two levels: a contested term's conception ("law", "life", "personal liberty" in Art 9(1)); and the import of Art 4's supremacy clause.
  • CONCEDE Who rightfully decides? George: in a basically just regime judges must respect their limits; TSH admits "no available formula". I concede the impasse: consensus may be the best gauge of morality, not its ground.
  • VERDICT TSH shows the Constitution relocates the natural law–positivism debate rather than ending it, leaving the authority question open.
14.26 TSH: Judicial Oligarchy use: 11.3, 11.5, 15.13
  • PURPOSE How far may courts strike down laws on moral grounds?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that courts should presume legislation constitutional unless Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met, shown by broad historical consensus.
  • TEST See 15.13 and 8.5; peremptory norms are evidence only.
  • STRENGTH The alternatives are worse: a lower threshold invites judicial "temerity", and positivism leaves "a brute majority" unchecked.
  • CRITIQUE TSH's own objection: the RF is not in the Constitution the nation accepted. Reply: constitutionalism rests on equal moral worth, so no majority may sanction its violation, even by amendment.
  • CONCEDE Her "catch" (8.5): I concede the risk and adopt her reply.
  • SG LMS (CA) rightly avoided a juristocracy but was "overly sanguine" about future Parliaments.
  • TRAP Presumed constitutional does not mean presumed just.
  • VERDICT TSH's threshold is the most defensible test for Singapore judges, once her own catch is conceded.
14.27 Same-question grid
  • Aquinas (14.2): unjust law is a corruption of law, so law is necessarily moral; rulers decide, for the common good; unjust law does not bind, save perhaps to avoid scandal.
  • Hart (14.13, 14.18): law need not be moral and may be too evil to obey; only harm, paternalism and decency justify punishment; the legislature decides, by critical morality; unjust law is valid, obedience being a moral question.
  • Fuller (14.6): law is necessarily moral through legality's internal morality; facing unjust law, ask how much of a legal system survived.
  • Finnis (14.8): unjust law lacks prima facie moral binding force; law may secure peace and justice and ban acts intending harm to a good; reason decides, not the "power of numbers"; one may owe obedience lest a just system weaken.
  • Dworkin (14.5): law is necessarily moral, seen in its best light; judges decide, by fit and value.
  • Rawls (14.10): law may not rest on comprehensive doctrines alone; citizens decide, as ideal legislators.
  • Devlin (14.15): whether law is necessarily moral is not his question, existing law being "a good starting-point"; law may enforce morality against conduct beyond the limits of tolerance; the law-maker decides, via the jury box.
  • Radbruch, Alexy (14.19): law is necessarily moral only weakly, since extreme injustice is not law; judges decide at extreme injustice only, and deny it legal character.
  • Kennedy (14.22): legal argument is a branch of ethical argument; judges decide, within work and credibility; of the five courses none is endorsed or excluded a priori.
  • TSH (14.16, 14.25–14.26): law is necessarily moral, though not all morals need legislating; the moral question cannot be shunned; the legislature decides, save at the BHC threshold; courts strike only manifest injustice, by BHC.
  • Pepper (14.23): lawmakers, not lawyers, decide what law may enforce; the client decides, within the law.
  • Thunder (14.24): law aims at justice and the common good; each lawyer decides by prudence; the role is no excuse for racist law.

15 Frameworks

15.1 Fuller: legality checklist key question: can people follow this rule as made and applied? · use: 3.1
  • Is the rule (1) general, (2) promulgated, (3) prospective, (4) clear, (5) consistent, (6) possible, (7) constant and (8) congruent with official action?
  • Total failure of one leaves no legal system at all; short of that, legality is a matter of degree, not substantive justice (15.13).
  • Rex: (1) case-by-case rulings; (2) a secret code; (3) rulings with hindsight; (4) an obscure code; (5) contradictions; (6) impossible demands; (7) constant amendment; (8) rulings unrelated to the code: no law at all.
  • TRAP (1) means rules at all, not breadth: palm-tree justice, attainder and unfettered discretion fail it; (2) needs access, not universal knowledge; (3) bars only abuse†.
15.3 Finnis: is this act permissible? key question: does it choose directly against a basic good? · use: 5.3
  • (1) Which basic good is pursued? (2) Is a basic good damaged as end or means? If so, the act is wrong: never choose directly against a basic value.
  • (3) Side effects must pass the golden rule: would I have thought the act reasonable had I been the person harmed? Intended damage, never; side effects, only if fair.
  • Rulings†: barred: the hostage (even a volunteer), probably the footbridge push, self-injury for insurance, the death penalty (even for Hitler), euthanasia, suicide; permitted or arguable: the trolley switch, triage, a lung-damaging mining job, shooting to disarm with death foreseen. (6) weighs; (7) vetoes.
15.4 Finnis: may the state legislate this? key question: does it serve the common good, intending no harm? · use: 5.5
  • (0) Two uses†: judge laws directly (authorising an act against a good is wrong: for Finnis, the death penalty and abortion) and judge facilitation; coordination counts (one side of the road); requirement (3) bars arbitrary distinctions between citizens. (1) Aim: "peace and justice", not making people integrally good. (2) Means: never intend damage to a good; may prohibit acts that intend it†.
  • (3) Reasons accessible to all, whatever their religion. (4) Prudence: non-enforcement can be reasonable, to avoid an unwinnable war. So prohibit intended harm on accessible reasons, where prudent.
15.5 Rawls: is this law legitimate? key question: could every reasonable citizen endorse the reasons? · use: 6.1
  • (1) Constitutional essential or basic justice? (2) Public-forum actor, including citizens voting as if legislators? (3) Political values, or comprehensive reasons backed by public ones "in due course" (proviso)?
  • (4) Reciprocity: acceptable to others as free and equal, not as dominated or manipulated? Denying basic liberties "normally" fails. The law is legitimate if (3) and (4) hold.
  • Completeness: no arguing directly from doctrine to policy, which is too immediate and fragmentary; not political values: moral autonomy, moral desert, monogamy "as such".
15.6 Devlin: the interrogatories key question: is it beyond the limits of tolerance? · use: 7.3
  • (1) May society judge morals? (2) May law enforce that judgment? (3) Always, or on what principles? (4) Without counting heads, what might twelve at random, after discussion, be expected to accept unanimously?
  • (5) Elastic principles: the maximum freedom consistent with society's integrity; a real feeling of reprobation. A majority's dislike is not nearly enough.
  • (6) A vice so abominable that its mere presence offends may be eradicated; one tolerable if confined calls for a balance. Law sets the minimum, not the maximum.
15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? · use: 7.9
  • Coercion is "prima facie objectionable". (1) Harm to others? Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count. (2) Paternalism, if consent is defective: punishing drug supply save on prescription.
  • (3) Public decency: offence serious and likely, weighed against the freedom lost. (4) Moralism alone: never. My rule (all law rests on force, criminal law most directly†): the more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed; Hart's own question is punishment only.
15.10 Kennedy: the five courses key question: law and how-I-want-to-come-out conflict: what may the judge do? · use: 12.4, 8.7
  • (1) Go along, denouncing the law; (2) withdraw, leaving "the dirty work" to another; (3) decide openly on what the law should be; (4) use an implausible legal argument; (5) find facts known to be false, an extreme measure.
  • Kennedy endorses or excludes none "a priori". My rule: in a basically just system, (1) or (2); (3) only at the Radbruch threshold; (4) and (5) fail candour (12.4).
15.11 Pepper: the limit and the remedies key question: lawful but wrong: what may the lawyer do? · use: 10.1
  • (1) Law is the limit: conduct bad enough should, it seems, be made explicitly unlawful (Pepper). (2) Responses to legal realism: more enforcement ("daunting") or rebuilt moral authority beyond law; for lawyers, not policeman, judge or deceiver, but moral dialogue, costly and needing a receptive client.
  • (3) Conscientious objection, "rarely exercised". So advise on the law, add moral dialogue, and object only in extreme cases.
  • Leaving practice is a weak answer†; choice of client is "more respectable", but assumes someone else will act, which fails if a view is widespread or only the lowest-scruple lawyers remain†; Pepper concedes that foreclosing access means "second-class citizenship".
15.13 TSH: should a court strike it down? (RF plus BHC) key question: is it manifestly unjust by broad historical consensus? · use: 11.5, 12.4
  • (1) Presume constitutionality unless Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met (TSH). (2) Proof: long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions, extending to the reason for repeal.
  • (3) Met (genocide, slavery): strike down, even an amendment; not met (the laws voided in Roe): legislatures decide.
  • Her "catch": decades on, the formula could impose a worldwide trend; consensus can go "dreadfully wrong". The rule is for courts only; legislators need no such consensus.

16 Singapore bank

16.1 Articles
  • Arts 4, 162: the Constitution is supreme; later inconsistent law is void; earlier law is read to conform†. LP is not thereby chosen (11.1).
  • Art 5(2): two-thirds of MPs, nominated MPs excluded, amend most provisions; basic features rejected (Teo Soh Lung), left open in YVK 2015.
  • Art 9(1): no deprivation of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law; four readings of "law"†.
  • Art 12: all persons are equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection; reasonable classification (11.3).
  • Art 156: (1) law may define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote marriage; (3)–(4) Part 4 cannot void laws or executive acts based on the man-woman definition, which stays in statute (Interpretation Act s 2(1); Women's Charter s 12(1)). TSH: a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism; yet the definition is unentrenched, so a simple majority may change it†.
16.2 Cases
  • Ong Ah Chuan (PC): Art 9 "law" includes fundamental rules of natural justice; substantive fairness left open, since narrowed (YVK 2015†).
  • Jabar (CA 1995), dictum: law validly passed binds, fair or not; LP; confined by YVK (2010)†: not about a statute's constitutionality.
  • Colin Chan (HC 1994): the Constitution is read primarily within its own four walls, unity the "paramount mandate"; an LP approach†.
  • Abdul Nasir (CA 1997)†: life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only; constancy (3.8).
  • LMS (CA 2014): s 377A passes Art 12; Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and detention, not privacy; Hart v Devlin is "quintessentially" for Parliament.
  • YVK (CA 2010)†: Art 9 may exclude laws so absurd or arbitrary the framers could not mean them as law†, a natural-law hook short of the RF.
  • YVK (CA 2015): courts cannot make a natural-law right from "whole cloth", so no anti-caning right; no ruling on what natural law says of caning; natural justice is procedural†.
  • Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022): no standing; obiter, Arts 9 and 14 likely not breached, Art 12 less definite; s 377A might fail the Syed Suhail test; unenforceable until AG notice†.
  • UKM (HC 2018): a gay man adopted his surrogate-born son despite s 377A; the moral signpost failed.
  • Taw Cheng Kong (CA 1998): Prevention of Corruption Act s 37(1) reaches citizens' acts abroad, even without effects here; no Art 12 breach, all being caught as a class; presumption of constitutionality.
  • Ong Ming Johnson (HC 2020): s 377A upheld against Arts 9 and 12; the last ruling before Tan Seng Kee's Art 12 doubt.
16.3 Hansard: who said what
  • Ho Peng Kee, 22 Oct 2007: feedback was "emotional, divided", a majority calling for retention; police would not proactively enforce.
  • de Souza, 22 Oct 2007: what is private will not remain private.
  • Siew Kum Hong, 22 Oct 2007: s 377A breaches Art 12(1); citing Hor, harm must be recognisable and tangible.
  • Indranee Rajah, 22 Oct 2007: in most cases we follow the majority unless there is reason to protect the minority.
  • Thio Li-ann, 22 Oct 2007: harm can be physical or intangible.
  • Hri Kumar Nair, 22 Oct 2007: toothless laws hurt credibility.
  • PM Lee, 23 Oct 2007: keep the status quo; stay a step behind on moral change.
  • Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022: crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue, "broadly similar" to Wolfenden.
  • Perera, 28 Nov 2022: unenforced law resting on the government's word is unsatisfactory and dangerous.
  • Pritam Singh, 28 Nov 2022: in a secular society, sin and crime are separate.
  • Masagos, 29 Nov 2022: Art 156 aims to prevent a change in social norms following repeal; MPs have a "duty" to decide.
  • Poa, 29 Nov 2022: the PSP proposed a referendum, as marriage is a matter of social norm.
  • He Ting Ru, 29 Nov 2022: a plainly discriminatory law signals that an identity should be criminal, even if only on paper.
16.4 Statutes and PCR
  • Penal Code s 377A criminalised acts of "gross indecency" between males, public or private; repeal (2022) in force 3 Jan 2023.
  • Penal Code s 121A (before 2019)†: imagining the President's death, hurt or restraint carried death or life imprisonment; a congruence and discretion example† (3.2, 3.4).
  • Termination of Pregnancy Act (as TSH described it, 2010–11): up to 24 weeks for any reason, from 16 weeks only by a qualified practitioner; later only to save life or prevent grave permanent injury; counselling, then 48 hours. The 1969 Act passed 32–10 on a free vote; 1974 left the choice to the woman, among the world's most liberal laws.
  • Professional conduct†: Pepper's limit includes the enforced conduct rules (fairness to unrepresented persons, not misleading the court, disclosing adverse authority), so the more robust they are, the less Pepper v Thunder changes what a lawyer does.
16.5 Applying the theorists: the 2022 package, lecture prompts
  • Exercise†: Mill: arguably not enough, a safeguard added because the majority was not ready. Finnis: likely approves (common good; life, including procreation; Art 156 promotes marriage); whether s 377A's distinction was "arbitrary" depends on one's premises.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves: consultation was the background culture; consensus reached "not criminal", not full equality; Art 156 stops courts outrunning it, and sending a divisive question to Parliament, not unelected judges, is a public reason. Against: Rawls's exemplar of public reason is the Supreme Court†.
  • Prompts†: apply Rawls and Finnis to surrogacy, casino gambling, POFMA and euthanasia†, using 15.4 (POFMA: 5.5), 15.5, 6.4, 5.7 (casinos); surrogacy: UKM (16.2); euthanasia: Hart's "clouded" judgement (7.2); for Finnis, intending death chooses against life.

Glossary: people, terms and abbreviations

NameWho, in one lineMain lesson

Thomas AquinasMedieval natural lawyer: an unjust law is "a corruption of law". Four kinds of law: eternal, divine, natural, human.2, 8
John AustinClassical positivist: law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed, backed by a sanction.2
HLA HartLeading 20th-century positivist. Law is a union of primary and secondary rules accepted by officials. Also the liberal side of the Hart–Devlin debate.2, 7, 8
Lon FullerLaw's "inner morality": eight requirements of legality (generality, promulgation, prospectivity, clarity, consistency, possibility, constancy, congruence). Debated Hart in 1958.3, 8
Ronald DworkinLaw as interpretation: judges read the legal record by fit and value. Theoretical v empirical disagreement; the chain novel.2, 9
David HumeSceptic: morality rests on sentiment; no "ought" from an "is".4
John FinnisNew natural lawyer: seven basic goods, nine requirements of practical reasonableness, the common good as a framework.5, 6
John RawlsPolitical liberalism: legitimacy, public reason, overlapping consensus, reciprocity.6
John Stuart MillThe harm principle: power may be used against someone only to prevent harm to others.7
Wolfenden Committee1957 English report: private consensual homosexual acts between adults should not be crimes.7
Patrick DevlinSociety may protect its shared morality by law; the "man in the jury box".7
James Fitzjames StephenVictorian judge: law may punish "the grosser forms of vice" as such.7
Gustav RadbruchGerman jurist: the Radbruch formula (intolerably unjust law is not law).8
Robert AlexyModern defender of the Radbruch formula; the participant's perspective.8
American Legal Realists (ALR)Llewellyn, Frank and others: law is what courts will do; rules leave leeways.9
Critical Legal Studies (CLS)Unger, Kennedy: doctrine is contradictory and legitimates hierarchy.9
Roberto UngerCLS: every principle meets a counterprinciple.9
Duncan KennedyCLS: law is a "medium" that constrains relative to the judge's project; five courses when law and justice conflict.9, 12
Stephen PepperThe lawyer's "amoral ethical role": access to law serves autonomy and equality.10
David ThunderA good lawyer stays a good person: the role serves justice and human flourishing.10
Stanley FishPractice marshals rules inside a purposive enterprise; theory is not a luxury.2
Robert GeorgeNatural lawyer whom TSH reports: in a basically just regime officials respect the limits of their authority.12

2The key terms

TermPlain meaning
Legal positivism (LP)Law is a matter of social fact (what is enacted and recognised). There is no necessary connection between law and morality.
Natural law theory (NLT)Law is answerable to a higher, reason-known standard; a sufficiently unjust "law" is defective as law.
Strong v weak NLTStrong: every rule must embody morality to be law. Weak: legal status is lost only at extreme injustice.
Rule of recognitionHart's master rule that officials accept, telling them what counts as law.
Internal point of viewTreating a rule as a standard you ought to follow, not merely a habit or a threat.
Theoretical v empirical disagreementDworkin: disagreement about what the grounds of law are, as against whether agreed grounds are met.
Inner morality of lawFuller's eight requirements of legality.
Moral realismThere are moral truths independent of what anyone believes.
Subjectivism / relativism / non-cognitivismMorality is personal opinion / varies by culture / is mere feeling, neither true nor false.
Is–ought gapHume: no moral conclusion follows from facts alone.
Basic goodsFinnis's seven: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, "religion".
Practical reasonablenessFinnis's nine requirements for pursuing the goods well.
Double effectIntending harm as a means differs from causing it as a foreseen side effect.
Common goodFinnis: "a set of conditions" letting members pursue their own reasonable objectives.
Public reasonRawls: on basic questions, justify coercion by reasons all reasonable citizens could accept.
Overlapping consensus (OC)Reasonable doctrines each endorsing the same political conception, for their own reasons.
Modus vivendiA truce based on the balance of power, which collapses if power shifts.
Harm principleMill: coercion only to prevent harm to others.
Legal paternalismCoercion to protect people from themselves (Hart: where consent is defective).
Legal moralismCoercion to enforce morality as such.
Positive v critical moralityThe morality a society actually holds v the principles used to criticise it.
Disintegration thesisDevlin: loss of shared morality threatens society, so society may protect it.
Radbruch formula (RF)Positive law prevails even when unjust, unless its injustice is intolerable; then it must yield.
Observer v participantAlexy: an observer reports what is treated as law; a participant (a judge) asks what the right legal answer is.
Broad historical consensus (BHC)TSH's test for when injustice is "intolerable": long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions.
Fit and valueDworkin: the best reading fits the legal record and shows it in its best moral light.
Principle v policyRights-based arguments (for courts) v collective-goal arguments (for legislatures).
Chain novelDworkin's image: each judge writes the next chapter of a novel others began.
Amoral ethical rolePepper: the lawyer is morally justified in helping with any lawful end.
Conscientious objectionPepper's rare exception: a lawyer may refuse in extreme cases.
DeterminatioA prudent choice among morally acceptable options (George's term for allocating authority).
Usurpation v abdicationDoing another role's work v refusing your own role's work.
Art 4, 9, 12, 156Singapore Constitution: supremacy; life and liberty "in accordance with law"; equality; marriage (added 2022).
s 377APenal Code offence for gross indecency between men; kept but not enforced from 2007; repealed from 3 Jan 2023.
